   Statements about rationals can obviously be translated into statements about whole numbers. Statements about whole numbers can be translated into statements that donâ€™t contain any number-expressions. (See Sections 2.5.1â€“2.5.2.) Thus, statements about irrational numbers can always be translated into statements that donâ€™t contain any number-expressions.
2.6 A problem with Fregeâ€™s analysis
Though basically identical with the analysis given by Frege, the one given in Section 2.3 differs from Fregeâ€™s in one important respect. Frege identified numbers, not with properties of sets, with sets of sets. Frege identified the number two with the set containing all and only those sets S such that, for some x and some y, x is a member of S and y is a member of S and x â‰  y and such that, for any z, if z is a member of S, then z = x or z = y. So, for Frege, the number two is the set of all sets of the sort just described. The number one is the set containing all and only those sets S such that something x belongs to S and such that anything y that belongs to S is identical with x. The number zero is the set containing all and only those sets to which nothing belongs.
   The problem is that, if numbers are identified with sets rather than properties, it follows that the number two could have been something other than what it actually is. Consider some pair of objects (e.g., your two favorite socks) and let it be the set containing just those two things. Given a universe where those two socks donâ€™t exist, if K2 is the class of all pairs in that universe, then K2 wonâ€™t be identical with the class of all pairs in our universe. Since two sets cannot be identical unless they have the same members, it follows that the number two could have something other than what it is, which is absurd. The same thing mutatis mutandis holds of any other whole number: if a whole number N is identified with a set of sets, that whole number will be different things in different universes.
   (The only exception to this is the number zero. If defined in the way that Frege proposesâ€”that is, as the set of all sets S such that nothing belongs to Sâ€”it doesnâ€™t change from universe to universe. This is because, in order for two sets to differ, one of them must have a member not had by the other. This is known as the axiom of extensionality. Since no empty set has any members not had any other empty set, there cannot be two distinct empty sets. Thus, there is only one empty set; and this is true in every universe, not just ours).
   But what it is to be a two-membered doesnâ€™t vary from universe to universe. In any given universe, for S to be a two-membered set is for it to be such that, for some x and some y, x is a member of S and y is a member of S and x â‰  y and such that, for any z, if z is a member of S, then z = x or z = y. Thus, the property of 

being a two-membered set doesnâ€™t vary from universe to universe. To that extent, itâ€™s better to identity the number two with the property of being a two-membered set than it is to identity with the set of all such sets.
   But numbers can still be identified with sets of similar sets. The number two can be identified with sets of all pairs, actual and possible. This variant of Fregeâ€™s analysis isnâ€™t open to the objection just made.
3.0 Incompleteness
Logicism was a failure. There is nothing wrong with the (set-theoretic) analyses of number, and of number statements, put forth by Frege and Russell and other logicists. What turned out to be false was Fregeâ€™s claim that there is some one algorithm such that, given any statement of arithmetic, that algorithm can correctly say whether or not that statement is true or false.
   This must be understood aright. Given any finite set of arithmetical statements, there is an algorithm that, given any statement falling into that set, correctly says whether or not that statement is true. But there is no one algorithm that, given any arithmetical statement, correctly says whether or not that statement is true.
   One must master some exceedingly intricate mathematics to understand precisely why this claim is false. But some of the philosophical conceits underlying this mathematics are pretty straightforward.
   First of all, the word â€œlogicâ€ is ambiguous. Sometimes it refers to formal truths, e.g., â€œeither Smith is tall or it is not the case that Smith is tallâ€; and sometimes the word â€œlogicâ€ refers to analytic truths, e.g., â€œany case of knowledge is a case of justified belief, but not vice versaâ€.
   When logicists proclaimed that arithmetical truths are â€œlogicalâ€ truths, they meant that they are formal truths. Formal truth, it must be emphasized, is a property of sentences and, therefore, of expressions; it is not a property of sentence-meanings.
   For argumentâ€™s sake, letâ€™s make the following three concessions to the logicist. First, â€œ1 + 1 = 2â€ is a formal truth in disguise. Second, the logicist paraphrase of â€œ1 + 1 = 2â€ is a formal truth. Weâ€™ll refer to that paraphrase as TPT.(For the reasons given in section 2.5.1, TPT is some statement along the lines of â€œtwo non-overlapping unit classes form a dual class.â€) Third, what we just said about 
â€œ1 + 1 = 2â€ is true mutatis mutandis of any given arithmetical truth.
   Bearing these assumptions in mind, consider the statement that:

(EQ) â€œThe logicist translation of â€˜1 + 1 = 2â€™ is TPT.â€

EQ is not a formal truth. After all, it has the same form as:

(EQ2) â€œThe Spanish translation of â€˜there will be justiceâ€™ is TPT,â€

which is obviously false.
   It may be that EQ is analytically true. But that fact hurts logicism as much as it helps it. To describe a sentence as â€œanalytically trueâ€ is to make an elliptical statement about a proposition. It isnâ€™t analytic that â€œtriangles have three sidesâ€ is true. That sentence could have meant anything; itâ€™s an empirical fact that it means what it does and, therefore, that itâ€™s true. What is analytic is the proposition that, the semantic rules of English being what they are, â€œtriangles have three sidesâ€ must be true. The same thing mutatis mutandis is true of any other â€œanalyticâ€ sentence, including EQ.
   As previously stated, all formal truths are analytic truths (but not vice versa). Thus, to describe a sentence as â€œformallyâ€ true is to make a statement about the proposition describing the relationship between the semantic rules of the language to which that sentence belongs, on the one hand, and that sentence, on the other: it is to describe that proposition as analytic.
   There is thus no way to formalize every sentence describing such a proposition. If S1 is any one such sentence, formalizing S1 involves using some other sentence S2 that describes the relationship between the semantic rules of the language to which S1 belongs, on the one hand, and S1, on the other. S2 will invariably fail to be a formal truth. This is because S2 will have the form: â€¹given such and such semantic rules, it follows

that S1 is formally trueâ€º, which isnâ€™t formally true. The reason it isnâ€™t formally true is that it has the same form as the false sentence: â€¹given such and such semantic rules, it follows that â€œgrass is greenâ€ is formally true. â€º
   Thus no matter how many truths one formalizes, the justifications for those formalizations will always be given by informal truths. This means that, given any viable method M of formalizing some body of informal analytic truths, there is no complete formalization of the truths that establish the viability of M.
3.1 The concept of a formal procedure
In the last section, we often used words like â€œformalâ€ and â€œformalize.â€ And in what follows, weâ€™ll often use the term â€œformal procedure.â€ Weâ€™ll also use the related term â€œdecision-procedure.â€ So let us make it clear what these terms mean.
   Consider the statement: â€œ2 + 2 = 4.â€ You know that itâ€™s true. But how do you know this? You know what it means; and you know that, given what it means, it must be true. Your judgment was based, not on the form, but on the content, of that sentence. Your decision-procedure (your way of determining whether â€œ2 + 2 = 4â€ is true or not) wasnâ€™t formal.
   Your decision would have been a formal one if it had been based entirely on rules that had nothing to do with the meanings of symbols. A story will clarify this statement. Although you are intelligent and literate (in your native language), you donâ€™t speak English and you donâ€™t know what â€œ1â€, â€œ2â€, â€œ+â€, etc. mean. (You are a good mathematician; but in your native country, different symbolic conventions are used to express mathematical statements.) You are on a military mission. This mission involves your being able, within certain very narrow limits, to distinguish between false arithmetical statements and true ones. Your commanding officer tells you that an inscription whose initial segment is â€œ2 + 2 =â€ is true if it ends with a â€œ4â€ and flase if it ends with a â€œ5.â€ You have no idea what â€œ2 + 2 = 4â€ means. (Youâ€™re not supposed to know.) You come across inscriptions of 
â€œ2 + 2 = 4â€ and â€œ2 + 2 = 5â€; and, on the basis only of your commanding officerâ€™s instructions, you judge that the first is true and the second is false. In this context, your decision-procedure was a formal one.
   This decision-procedure had minimal scope. Obviously mathematicians want to find decision-procedures that deal with large classes of statements. In order for there to be any decision-procedure for a sizeable class of arithmetical truths, those truths cannot be expressed in the customary way. Supposing the standard symbolic conventions to be in place, the truths of arithmetic cannot be expressed using symbols like â€œ2â€, â€œ+â€, etc. The reason is that, when arithmetical propositions are expressed in that way, there is no non-semantic method whereby true arithmetical sentences can be distinguished from false ones. Thus, in order for there to be a decision-procedure for arithmetic, sentences such as â€œ2+2=4â€ must be rephrased (or â€œparaphrased,â€ as weâ€™ll say). Logicists attempted to provide the requisite paraphrases. And, thanks to their paraphrases, it was possible to identify formal-decision procedures for huge classes of arithmetical truths.
   Kurt GÃ¶del (1906â€“1978) showed that there is no way of paraphrasing or otherwise representing arithmetical truths that permits the construction of some one formal decision-procedure that decides the truth of any given arithmetical truth. He showed that logicism was doomed and also that any other attempt to formalize arithmetic was doomed. Let us now discuss his achievement in a little (operative word â€œlittleâ€) more detail.
3.2 Incompleteness (continued)
GÃ¶del mathematically proved that there is no one formal decision-procedure such that, given any arithmetical statement, that procedure correctly says whether or not that statement is correct. His proof is extremely complex. But here is a way of stating the main idea that, although both inaccurate and incomplete, will at least initiate an interest on the part of the reader in the fascinating discipline of mathematical logic.
   First a definition: An â€œarithmeticalâ€ predicate is one that expresses a property of whole numbers, or a relation holding among whole numbers, that can be understood entirely in terms of (i) the concepts of addition and multiplication; (ii) the concepts expressed by the connectives â€œorâ€, â€œnotâ€, â€œandâ€, â€œfor anyâ€ (â€œallâ€), and â€œfor someâ€ (â€œthere existsâ€); and (iii) the numbers zero, one, two, etc. (i.e., the members of the least inclusive set that contains zero and the successor of anything that it contains). Examples of arithmetical

predicates are â€œis evenâ€, â€œis less than fiveâ€, and â€œwhen added to seven yields twelve.â€ (To say that 3 is less than 5 is to say that there is some whole number n such that, when n is added to 3, the result is 5.)
   Given any arithmetical predicate P, there is a class of numbers C such that a whole number n belongs to C iff P(n) (read: â€œn has Pâ€). Consider, for example, the predicate â€œis even.â€ There is obviously a class containing every number n such that â€¹n is evenâ€º is true and containing no number m such that â€¹m is evenâ€º is false.
   For argumentâ€™s sake, suppose there to be formal procedure FM such that, for any whole number n and any arithmetical predicate P, FM assigns a TRUE to the sentence P(n) if that sentence is true, and assigns a FALSE to if itâ€™s false. (In this context, TRUE and FALSE may be thought of as physical stamps. When given an ink-deposit (or whatnot) that expresses an arithmetical proposition, FM stamps TRUE on that ink-deposit if itâ€™s true and a FALSE on it if itâ€™s false.) This is the same as assuming that:

(1) There exists a formal procedure that correctly says of any given arithmetical statement whether it is true or false.
   
   Any given arithmetical predicate contains a finite number of letters. There are only finitely many different letters. This means that itâ€™s possible to produce a list such that, given any finitely long combination of letters Z, there is some whole number n such that Z is the nth member of that list. A fortiori itâ€™s possible to produce a list such that, given any arithmetical predicate P, there is some whole number n such that P is the nth member of that list. Let L be such a list; and assume that the items composing L are arranged alphabetically. Further, let L* be a list whose first entry is 1, whose second entry is 2, and so on.
   Given either list, the nth item on it can be thought of as being â€œcoordinatedâ€ with the number n, i.e., as having n for its coordinate. Thus, the first item on L* (namely 1) has coordinate 1; the second (namely 2) has coordinate 2; and so on. To simplify exposition, letâ€™s suppose that â€œis bigger than ten,â€ â€œis even,â€ and â€œis less than twentyâ€ are, respectively, the tenth, twentieth, and thirtieth items on L.
   Let G be a graph whose x-axis consists of L* and whose y-axis consists of L. Thus, the coordinates on G of the statements â€œ1 is bigger than 10,â€ â€œ2 is even,â€ and â€œ3 is less than 20â€ are, respectively, (1,10), (2,20), and (3,30).

   Thus, given either axis, an item mâ€™s having position n on that axis is a strictly arithmetical fact. Thus, Q(q) is an arithmetical statement. Since, as we saw, Q(q) is true iff itâ€™s false, itâ€™s false. (No true statement entails its own negation.) But FM stamps a TRUE on it, even though, by supposition, FM stamps a TRUE only true statements.
   
We started with the assumption that there exists a procedure that correctly says of any given arithmetical statement whether it is true or false. This was the only substantive (as opposed to purely procedural) assumption that we made. This assumption entails a false statement and is therefore itself false. There is thus no formal decision-procedure for arithmetic. There is no correct and complete formal characterization of arithmetical truth. Logicism, the doctrine that arithmetical truth is formal truth, is therefore false.
4.0 Analysis by abstraction
In the process of generating his insightful analysis of number, Frege used, for the first time in history, a powerful technique known as definition by abstraction.
   The term â€œdefinition by abstractionâ€ refers to a way of analyzing properties. This term is thus a misnomer. Expressions are defined; properties arenâ€™t expressions. Iâ€™ll therefore drop the term â€œdefinition by abstractionâ€ and use the term â€œanalysis by abstractionâ€ in its stead.
   Analysis by abstraction is a technique for analyzing comparative properties. (A comparative property is one that can be had to varying degrees. Thus, weight and speed are comparative properties, whereas four-sidedness is not.) Given a comparative property phi, an analysis by abstraction of phi is given by a statement that explains what phi is in terms of what it is for one thing to have phi to a degree equal to, or exceeding, the degree to which some other thing has phi.
   It can be said what it is for two sets to have the same number of members, or for one set to have more members than another, without knowing how many members either set has. If the members of the one set can be paired off with the members of the other, they have the same number of members. If not, the set whose members donâ€™t all have partners is the better populated one. Thus, for two sets to be similar (capable of being paired off in the way just described) is for them to be equally populated. We may therefore identify the degree to which a given set is populated with the class of (possible) sets that are similar to it, and we may also identify a setâ€™s being populated to that degree with its being a member of that class.
   This technique can be used to analyze any comparative property. (In fact, there is no other way to analyze such a property.) To say that one event preceded some other is to say that the second exceeds the first in respect of the lateness of the time at which it occurred. One can know that one event preceded some other without knowing when either occurred. If there is some possible causal process (e.g., a light ray), beginning with the one and ending with the other, the event on the receiving end of that process is the later one; if there is no such process, the two events are simultaneous. Let us say that one event is â€œindifferentâ€ to another if there is no possible causal process beginning with either and ending with the other. (If x is indifferent to y, y is indifferent to x.) Two events are simultaneous just in case they occur at the same time, and they are simultaneous if either is indifferent to the other. We may therefore identify the time at which an event occurs with the class of events that are indifferent to it.
   We defined â€¹x precedes yâ€º as â€¹some causal process begins with x and ends with y.â€º Since the italicized terms are obviously temporal in nature, our analysis might be thought to be viciously circular.
   This isnâ€™t so. Our analysis appears circular only to the extent that it is question-beggingly assumed to be false. If that analysis is right, the concept of causal-influence (i.e., of oneâ€™s event being the initiator of a causal process of which the other is the recipient) is more primitive than that of order in space-time. So the concept expressed by â€¹x causally influences yâ€º (in other words, â€¹x is the initiator of a causal process of which y is the recipientâ€º) is the primitive concept, and the concept expressed by â€¹x precedes yâ€º is the derivative one.
   Itâ€™s true that we defined â€¹x influences yâ€º as â€¹some causal process begins with x and ends with yâ€º. But that was merely a way of identifying the meaning of that expression. That act of identification, being one that preceded the analysis in question, had to be given in terms that would be meaningful to those who still held onto the idea that causal influence was to be understood in terms of order in time, and not vice versa.
   The concept of weight is to be understood along similar lines. One neednâ€™t know how heavy two objects are to know that they have the same weight or that the one is heavier than the other. That means that, given any two objects, there is some relation such that their having the same mass can be non-circularly identified with the oneâ€™s bearing that relationship to the other. An objectâ€™s weight (the degree to which it has weight)

may therefore be identified with the class of all things to which it bears that relationship. The same thing mutatis mutandis holds of speed, length, conductivity, and of any other given comparative property.
   A moment ago we said that one can know that x is heavier than y without knowing the weights of either. This must be qualified. When you say that you know only the comparative weights of x and y, but donâ€™t know the actual weight of either, what you are really saying is that, although you know how x and y compare to each other in respect of weight, you donâ€™t know how either compares in that respect to objects in general. And when you say that you know the weights of x and y, and not merely their relative weights, you are saying that you know how each compares in respect of weight, not only with the other, but with objects in general.
   Thus, all knowledge of weight is comparative knowledge. The difference between knowing how xâ€™s weight compares with yâ€™s, on the one hand, and knowing how many pounds x weighs, on the other, is simply one of degree. â€¹x weighs 27 lbsâ€º is a condensed way of reporting a great many relative judgments concerning xâ€™s weightâ€”of reporting a great many judgments concerning xâ€™s weight relative to some other objectâ€™s weight. What we think of as non-comparative knowledge is a condensed mass of comparative knowledge. It followsâ€”though I leave it to the reader as an exercise to say exactly how it followsâ€”that no viable analysis of a weight, or indeed of any other comparative property, is ever not an analysis by abstraction.
5.0 Putting Fregeâ€™s successes into perspective
Even though logicism turned out to be a failure, Fregeâ€™s formalization of logic was a success. (This is subject to heavy qualifications that lie outside the scope of the present work.) Many have thought that, to the extent that he was able to formalize logic, Frege succeeded in â€œmechanizingâ€ the making of inferencesâ€”in showing that no thought need be involved in the making of inferences and, therefore, that inferences could be made by beings (e.g., punch-card automata) that are otherwise incapable of thought. The idea is that, given a sentence like:

(1) â€œfor any object x, if x is a mammal, then, if x is intelligent, x doesnâ€™t have pointy ears; and Smith is a mammal and Smith has pointy ears,â€

   Itâ€™s granted, of course, that Frege formalized only a miniscule class of inferences.    This is deeply absurd. First of all, itâ€™s tantamount to saying that thinking can be done without thinking. To make an inference is to think. So an unthinking being  ipso facto canâ€™t make inferences.
   This argument is likely to be seen as nothing more than a joke. And it is a joke. But itâ€™s a joke only because, like any good joke, it states the obvious.
   In any case, hereâ€™s a joke-free argument. Suppose that device M is given tokens of (i) and (ii) as inputs and that, in response, it outputs a token of (iii).    Imagine the following. You say to me: â€œThe one copy of your manuscript has just been destroyed.â€ As a result of your saying this I faint. But I faint not because of what your utterance meant.    Letâ€™s change the story. Because of experiments that I underwent as a child, I say â€œfourâ€ whenever I hear very loud sounds.    For exactly similar reasons, given only that M is outputting T3 in response to its being fed inputs T1 and T2, it doesnâ€™t follow that Mâ€™s outputting T3 embodies an inference.    Thus, so far as itâ€™s correct to say that Frege â€œmechanizedâ€ thought, what it means is not that, thanks to his efforts, no thought is needed to execute inferences that were previously thought-dependent. 6.1 Putting Fregeâ€™s successes into perspective (continued)
The inferences one must make in order to algorithmize a given task are often harder to make than the inferences that the algorithm, once applicable, will enable one to make. The same is true of the inferences one must make in order to superintend the application of an already identified algorithm.
   Once again consider Arguments #1 and #2. Theyâ€™re obviously valid and invalid, respectively.    Imagine the following. You run a company that makes cars. You recently hired a new worker, who goes by the name of â€œBucky.â€ Unlike your current employees, Bucky isnâ€™t intelligent or skilled. Algorithms are a lot like Bucky. A lot of time and effort is needed to put them to work; and once put to work, they can only do very specific things. Chapter 8
The Relationship between Thought and Language: Literal Meaning vs. Cognitive Content
1.0 The objects of thought are always truths or falsehoods, and never objects, except in a derivative sense
We obviously think about rocks, trees, people, and other things. But things are the objects of thought only in a derivative sense. The real object of thought is always some truth or falsehood concerning a thing.
   Some fiction will help. At time t, you are looking at a rock. You recognize the rock. Itâ€™s the rock that Joey, your arch nemesis, threw at your car. That incident was an emotionally charged one for you, and you decided to write a book about it. In order to have a concise way of referring to it, you gave it a name: you decided to call it â€œR.â€ Itâ€™s been a while since youâ€™ve seen R. But when, at time t, you see it, you instantly recognize it. You recognize it as Râ€”as the rock that Joey threw at your car.
   Your eyes are obviously telling you something. But what exactly? Here we must be careful to distinguish what your visual perception itself is telling from what, given the backlog of knowledge at your disposal, you can read into that perception. No sooner do you see R than you recognize it. But do your eyes tell you that it is R you are seeing? No. Given only what they are telling you, you could be looking at some other rock that happened to look just like that rock. Maybe you know that this is unlikely. Maybe you know that thereâ€™s basically no real chance of this. And maybe you know all of this instantaneously. You donâ€™t have go through a conscious, drawn out process of inference. Itâ€™s obviousâ€”just as obvious as it is that the person in front of you at your wedding is your beloved fiancÃ©e.
   But your eyes arenâ€™t telling you any of this. Given only the information encoded in your visual perception, you could be seeing some duplicate of R. Given only what your eyes are telling you, itâ€™s possible that R no longer exists and that what you are seeing is a perfect duplicate of it.
   What your eyes tell you isnâ€™t: â€œthatâ€™s R over there.â€ What they tell you is:

(RO) â€œthere is a rock having such and such characteristics over there.â€

R satisfies that existence-claim; and you know that. On the basis of that knowledge along with the information bequeathed to you by your visual perception, you know that R has such and such characteristics. But that perception itself doesnâ€™t bear any R-specific message. What your eyes are telling you, taken by itself, is consistent with Râ€™s not even existing. Obvious extensions of these points show that, given any message given to you through vision or any other sensory modality, and given any object in the external world, that message is consistent with that objectâ€™s not existing.
1.1 The exact way in which sense-perception is descriptive
Our sense-perceptions obviously represent objects to us and can thus be said to describe them. But what isnâ€™t obvious is that there is nothing to perceiving anything other than being perceptually apprised of some existence-claim satisfied by that object.
   
Letâ€™s suppose you are looking at your good friend Pat. Your seeing Pat obviously involves your seeing instances of various properties of various different kinds. Some of these property-instances are morphological (shape-related); others are chromatic (color-related); others are kinematic (motion-related). And so on.
   But you donâ€™t just see various property-instances. You see an organized structure consisting of them. Your visual perception of Pat represents these property-instances as bearing various relations to one another. Being thus interrelated, they collectively form a coherent structure. Your seeing a coherent structure of property-instances, as opposed to a disorganized jumble of them, consists in your seeing various instances of various relations. It consists in your seeing that certain property-instances are to the right of certain others, that other property-instances are behind certain others, etc. Thus, your seeing Pat involves your seeing various instances of various properties and relations.
   It follows that your seeing him involves your being (visually, not verbally) apprised of an existence-claim: â€œthere are, at the present moment, instances of such and such properties, in such and such places, bearing such and such relations to one another.â€ From now on, when I mention â€œproperty instances,â€ I am referring to instances of properties and of relations.
   We must now confront a delicate but deeply important question. You see Pat. Thatâ€™s a given. This involves your seeing various instances of various properties and relations. That too is a given. But do you see anything other than property-instances instances? Is there something to your seeing Pat above and beyond your beholding these various instances? Do you see these instances, on the one hand, and Pat, on the other?
   No. Clearly you just see the instances. Your perception doesnâ€™t represent Pat in addition to the various property-instances that are associated with him. Were your perception to have such a structure, it would involve Patâ€™s being represented to you as a featureless lump, a blank undifferentiated entity, with various property-instances piled on top of it, so to speak.
   But that clearly isnâ€™t how that perception works. Itâ€™s absurd to suppose that a thing possibly be perceptually represented independently of the property-instances that it is being represented as having. That would involve its being represented as a featureless blank. The very idea of a thingâ€™s being perceptually represented as a featureless blank is a non-starter. Thus, there is nothing to seeing (or otherwise sense-perceiving) an object other than seeing (same qualification) the property-instances associated with it.
   These properties are time- and place-indexed. Supposing what you are seeing is round, what you see isnâ€™t just an instance of roundness, but an instance of roundness in a certain place, at the present time. So if O is what you are seeing, your seeing O consists in your being visually told that there are instances of various (time- and place-indexed) properties, these being properties had by O.
   Your seeing a given object consists in your being apprised of the truth of an existence-claim that it uniquely satisfies. And your seeing that a given object has property P consists in your being apprised of the truth of some existence-claim of the form: there exists exactly one object having such and such properties; moreover, any such object has P.
   Let me clarify these statements. Look at the last word of this very sentence. Your eyes donâ€™t only tell you that certain (time- and place-indexed) properties are instantiated. They donâ€™t only tell you that, at the present time, in a certain place, there is an instance of a certain morphology (i.e., that had by the following inscription: â€œsentenceâ€) and of certain chromatic properties, and so on. They tell you that, in that place, at that time, there is exactly one such instance.
   Thus, you see objects by being visually apprised of existence-claims that they uniquely satisfy. And, of course, what we just said about vision is true of all sensory modalities. Perception is purely descriptive. For you to perceive an object is for you to be apprised (in a certain way) of an existence-claim that it uniquely satisfies. (Perceiving an object involves being causally connected to it. Some think this is inconsistent with the idea that perception is fundamentally descriptive in nature. Reasons to think otherwise are given later in the present Chapter.)

1.2 The pre-semantic basis of communicated meaning
The idea that anything should be perceptually represented as a featureless blank is not a complete non-starter, and so is the idea that anything should be cognitively represented in that way. Conception, like perception, is and must be fundamentally descriptive. To think of an object is to think some existence-claim that it uniquely satisfies. Russell (1917) saw this.
   But itâ€™s easy to confuse issues relating to conception with issues relating to language. What people think isnâ€™t always in complete lock-step with what is literally meant by the expressions that they use. Cognitive content doesnâ€™t always coincide with literal meaning.    Another example will make it clear what I mean by this and will help us avoid confusing facts about thought with facts about language. (And this, in its turn, will help us develop a correct semantics along with a correct understanding of thought.)

   Your visual perception tells you that, standing in front of you, at the present moment, there is a person (or, in any case, person-like entity) having such and such features (e.g., it has a certain general shape and height; it has certain facial and bodily characteristics; it has certain kinematic (movement-related) characteristics; itâ€™s wearing clothes of a certain kind; and so on). 1.3 Interlude: Mill on reference
A moment ago we said that, for some object x (namely Fred), SF merely slaps the label â€œFredâ€ on x. 1.6 No non-descriptive knowledge
Butâ€”and this must be emphasizedâ€”there is no way that you can non-descriptively think about Larry (or anything else). Larry canâ€™t just be represented to you. But this all seems very wrong. IHP is non-trivial. H1 and P1 convey very different propositions (namely, O*1 and P*1); the same is true, for any property psi of IHP and IHH. Given these facts, it seems de rigueur to accept the Russell-Frege position that â€œHesperusâ€ and â€œPhosphorousâ€ are synonymous with different definite descriptions (â€œthe morning starâ€ and â€œthe evening star,â€ or whatnot).
   But this reasoning is no good. Weâ€™ve already seen why. But letâ€™s adapt what we said earlier to deal with the Hesperus-Phosphorous case. Letâ€™s go back to the time when your friend was first telling you what â€œHesperusâ€ refers to. (HSR) â€œHesperusâ€ refers to x.

And HSR2 would convey this even though its literal meaning would be the descriptively more impoverished proposition that:

for some object O.

In general, for any psi, an utterance of (H*1) would convey the information that:

(HSRG3) something is a last celestial body to disappear from the morning sky and any such thing has psi.

And, echoing what we just said, an utterance of H*1 would convey that even though its literal meaning was simply:

(O*1) O has psi.

And for the same reasons mutatis mutandis, an utterance of P*1 would convey:

(PSRG3) something is a last celestial body to disappear from the morning sky and any such thing has psi

   Russell and Frege overlooked the fact that semantics isnâ€™t learned in a vacuum and that, as a result, the non-semantic information through which semantic rules are learned is sometimes smuggled into the messages borne by utterances.
Reason #3: Replacing co-referring sometimes proper names changes truth-value
A person can know that:

(H1) â€œHesperus is less massive than the Earthâ€

   This data is naturally accounted for by supposing that â€œHesperusâ€ is synonymous with â€œthe morning starâ€ and â€œPhosphorousâ€ is synonymous with the evening star. The supposition that H1 (IHH) and P1 (IHP) coincide in literal meaning does model that data provided that the points concerning pre-semantic information made earlier are taken into account.
2.0 Kripkeâ€™s revival of Mill
In 1969, Saul Kripke gave three very clever lectures in which he definitively showed that the Russell-Frege analysis of proper names is wrong. Those lectures are now published under the title Naming and Necessity. He said many insightful things in the course of those lectures, many of which went far beyond the scope of semantics. He also said some things that are quite clearly false, but that, oddly, were nevertheless accepted and, indeed, turned into orthodoxies. Letâ€™s start with the insightful, correct things that Kripke said.
2.1 The modal differences between names and definite descriptions
For argumentâ€™s sake, suppose that:

(SOC) â€œSocratesâ€ is synonymous with some definite descriptionâ€”with, let us suppose, â€œthe great philosopher who died of hemlock poisoning.â€

If SOC is right, then:

(1) â€œSocrates did not die of hemlock poisoningâ€

(2) â€œthe great philosopher who died of hemlock poisoning did not die of hemlock poisoning.â€

But (1) isnâ€™t self-contradictory at all. We could imagine its being true. Suppose that historical research reveals that it wasnâ€™t hemlock poisoning that killed Socratesâ€”that the poison he drank was some other sort of poisoning. In that case, (1) would be false. This may not be likely, but thereâ€™s nothing incoherent in the idea of its happening; supposing this about Socrates isnâ€™t like supposing that squares were really circles.
2.1.1 The modal differences between names and definite descriptions (continued)
A related point is that:

(3) â€œSocrates died of hemlock poisoningâ€

is not analytic. (An analytic statement is one that, given only what it means, must be true. So â€œsquares have four sidesâ€ is analytic, but â€œSocrates was a wrestlerâ€ is not.) But it would be analytic if SOC were right, since it would then be synonymous with:

(4) â€œthe great philosopher who died of hemlock poisoning died of hemlock poisoning.â€

Why isnâ€™t (3) a tautology? Because lots of people who know who â€œSocratesâ€ refers toâ€”who know that heâ€™s the lead character in the Republic, or whatnotâ€”may not know that he died of hemlock poisoning. Those people are not, for that reason, guilty of some semantic deficiency; they may know as well as anyone what the semantic rule governing â€œSocratesâ€ is. There is some x (namely, Socrates) such that â€œSocratesâ€ refers to x, and they know that. (4) is thus an empirical point.
2.1.2 The modal differences between names and definite descriptions (continued)
A consequence of these points is that:

(5) â€œitâ€™s necessarily the case that the great philosopher who died of hemlock poisoning died of hemlock poisoningâ€

is true, whereas

(6) â€œitâ€™s necessarily the case Socrates died of hemlock poisoningâ€

is false. Even if Socrates did die of hemlock poisoning, he might not have; he might fallen off a bridge on his way to the hemlock-drinking ritual.
   For exactly similar reasons, â€œBenjamin Franklinâ€ isnâ€™t synonymous with â€œthe inventor of bifocals.â€ For:

(7) itâ€™s necessarily the case that the inventor of bifocals invented bifocalsâ€

is true, but

(8) â€œitâ€™s necessarily the case that Benjamin Franklin invented bifocals.â€

   Kripkeâ€™s basic point is that proper names donâ€™t have the same modal properties as co-referring definite descriptions. The â€œmodal statusâ€ of a sentence lies, not in whether it is true, but in whether it, or its negation, can be true. The proposition that squares have four sides is necessarily true. That is its modal status. To say that it is necessarily true is to say that it cannot be false. (1) and (2) express propositions that have different modal statuses and are therefore distinct. Thus, replacing the occurrence in (1) of â€œSocratesâ€ with â€œthe great philosopher who died of hemlock poisoningâ€ results in a sentence that expresses a proposition different from that expressed by (1). Thus, â€œSocratesâ€ isnâ€™t synonymous with â€œthe great philosopher who died of hemlock poisoningâ€ or, by the same logic, with any other definite description. Given obvious extensions of this reasoning, no proper name is synonymous with any definite descriptions.
2.2 Kripke on identity and necessary a posteriori truth
To understand Kripkeâ€™s influential non-semantic claims, we must define four terms and also assimilate an important principle that Kripke discovered.

2.2.1 A priori vs. a posteriori knowledge
The first two terms are â€œa prioriâ€ and â€œa posteriori.â€ These expressions are adjectives, and they modify expressions denoting knowledge. A priori knowledge is knowledge that one either has, or can acquire, merely by virtue of how oneâ€™s mind is structured; it can be thought of as knowledge that is coded into oneâ€™s cognitive structure or that follows from such knowledge. When you a buy a new computer, it typically comes â€œbundledâ€ with new software. A priori knowledge can be compared to such software. A posteriori knowledge is knowledge that is not a priori.
2.2.2 Rigid vs. non-rigid designators
The remaining two terms are â€œrigid designatorâ€ and â€œnon-rigid designator.â€ For reasons that will emerge in due course, the distinction between rigid and non-rigid designators is meaningless unless definite descriptions are taken to be referring terms. So in this context, weâ€™ll suppose, just as Kripke does in Naming and Necessity, that definite descriptions are referring terms.
   Consider a world W that is semantically just like ours except that, in it, Al Gore, not Barack Obama, is the U.S. President in 2009. In W, â€œthe U.S. President in 2009â€ would refer to Al Gore. So even though that expression would have the semantics that it has in our world, it wouldnâ€™t pick out the same thing that it picks out in our world. In fact, given that, in W, Barack Obama isnâ€™t the president in 2009, if â€œthe U.S. President in 2009â€ did pick out â€œBarack Obamaâ€ in W, it couldnâ€™t possibly have the same semantics that it has in our world.
   But suppose that, in world W* that is distinct from both W and our world, â€œBarack Obamaâ€ referred to Joseph Biden. In that case, W* would ipso facto not be semantically identical with our world. In our world, there is some individual x such that x is Barack Obama and, as a matter of semantics, â€œBarack Obamaâ€ refers to x. And any language in which â€œBarack Obamaâ€ picked somebody else would to that extent semantically diverge from the specific version English actually spoken (even if it was otherwise just like it). Given that â€œBarack Obamaâ€ refers to Barack Obama, it couldnâ€™t possibly fail to refer to him in a world that is semantically like ours. It could fail to refer to him only in a world where expressions were not in all cases governed by the semantic rules that govern them in our world.
   â€œBarack Obamaâ€ is a rigid designator. E â€œrigidly designatesâ€ x if there is no possible world that is semantically just like ours where E fails to designate x. Proper names are rigid designators. Definite descriptions are not. â€œThe inventor of bifocalsâ€ refers to Bob Denver in some possible worlds, to Walt Disney in others, and so on.
   Sometimes demonstrative expressions (e.g., â€œthat personâ€) are described as â€œrigid designators.â€ The reasons for this are explained in Chapters 6 and 9. Suffice it to say that they are not rigid designators. In fact, they are about as non-rigid as designators can be. â€œThe inventor of bifocalsâ€ is non-rigid in the sense that there are possible universes in which it refers to people other than Benjamin Franklin. But â€œthat personâ€ refers to many different people in our world.
2.3 Identity and necessity
Suppose that x and y are contingently identicalâ€”that, in other words, theyâ€™re identical but they donâ€™t have to be. By Leibnizâ€™s law, x and y have the very same properties. Obviously x is necessarily identical with x. Therefore, y has that property as well and, contrary to what we assumed, is necessarily identical with x.
   In general, identities hold necessarily if they hold at all. It isnâ€™t a contingent fact that you are identical with you. If you exist, you canâ€™t fail to be you.
   Some sentences seem to be counterexamples to this; for example, â€œthe person standing over there is the person who owns the ice-cream store down the street.â€ But that isnâ€™t really an identity claim. We know from Russell that its real meaning is: â€œsomething is both a person standing in that corner, unaccompanied by other people, and is also a sole proprietor of the ice-cream store down the street.â€ Given any apparent exception to

the principle that, when it holds, identity holds necessarily, reparsing that sentence shows it not to be an identity claim.
   A sentence of the form â€œA is identical with Bâ€ expresses an identity claim only if â€œAâ€ and â€œBâ€ are rigid designators. Thus:

(IHP) â€œHesperus is identical with Phosphorousâ€

is an identity claim. And so is

(WH) â€œwater is H2Oâ€

and so is

(MT) â€œMark Twain is Samuel Clemens.â€
2.4 Why Kripke believes that there are necessary a posteriori truths
Kripke made it clear that â€œHesperusâ€ isnâ€™t synonymous with â€œthe morning starâ€ or with any other non-rigid designator, and he showed the same thing mutatis mutandis to be true of â€œPhosphorous.â€ Given that Hesperus is Phosphorous, Hesperus can no more fail to be Phosphorous than it can fail to be Hesperus. So given that it holds, IHP holds necessarily.
   Kripke says that â€œIHPâ€ encodes an a posteriori truth. The idea is that it canâ€™t be known a priori that IHP (or any other synonymous sentence) is true. It can be known only through astronomical observation. Given that IHP is necessarily true, it follows that IHP is both necessary and a posteriori.
2.5 Evaluating Kripkeâ€™s attempt to show that there are necessary a posteriori truths
This is not a good argument. We made it clear earlier in this chapter that, although it doesnâ€™t have such a claim for its literal meaning, IHP communicates a proposition of the form the phi is identical with the psi. In other words, it (non-literally) communicates a proposition of the form: something uniquely has phi, and anything that has phi also uniquely has psi.
   So IHP communicates a contingent truth. It communicates, as we saw, the proposition that is expressed by the sentence:

(MS) â€œthe last celestial body to disappear from the morning sky is identical with the first to appear in the evening skyâ€ (which weâ€™ve abbreviated as: â€œthe morning star is identical with the evening starâ€).

The proposition meant by MS is:

(MSP) something is uniquely a last body to disappear from the morning sky, and anything having that property also uniquely has the property of being a first thing to appear in the evening sky.

MSP is a posteriori. But itâ€™s also contingent. It wouldnâ€™t be true if matter were differently distributed.
   Kripke is quite right that IHP has a necessarily true proposition for its meaning. But that proposition is also analytic and knowable a priori.
   Hereâ€™s why. Weâ€™ve agreed with Kripke that, for any property phi, â€œHesperusâ€ isnâ€™t synonymous with â€¹the phi.â€º And weâ€™ve also agreed with Kripke, and with commonsense, that â€œHesperusâ€ is a referring expressionâ€”

that, in other words, there is some object x such that â€œHesperusâ€ picks x out. Trivially, either â€œHesperusâ€ picks out this object through the mediation of a description or it doesnâ€™t. In other words, supposing that O is what â€œHesperusâ€ picks out, it either is, or is not, by virtue of Oâ€™s fitting some description that â€œHesperusâ€ picks out it. If it is, then â€œHesperusâ€ is ipso facto a non-rigid designatorâ€”a definite description. So â€œHesperusâ€ does not refer to O through the mediation of a description. It picks O outâ€”but not because it has this or that property. It picks it out because the semantic rule for â€œHesperusâ€ is to the effect that, no matter what properties O has, â€œHesperusâ€ is to pick it outâ€”because, in other words, â€œHesperusâ€ picks out O, this not being contingent on Oâ€™s satisfying any condition (other than its being O). Thus, there is some object x (namely, O) such that the semantic rule for â€œHesperusâ€ is to the effect that, no matter how O is, â€œHesperusâ€ picks it out.    A consequence is, for some object x (such that x is Hesperus) such that, in virtue of having the form, â€¹Hesperus has psiâ€º, a sentence is true if and only if x has phi. For exactly similar reasons, â€œPhosphorousâ€ is directly referential. It co-refers with â€œHesperus.â€ Thus, there is some object x (such that x is Hesperus and Phosphorous) such that, in virtue of having the form, â€¹Hesperus has psiâ€º, a sentence is true if and only if x has phi and such that, in virtue of having the form, â€¹Phosphorous has psiâ€º, a sentence is true if and only if x has phi. Thus, â€¹Hesperus has psiâ€ºand â€¹Phosphorous has psiâ€º have the very same literal meaning. In general, inter-substituting â€œHesperusâ€ and â€œPhosphorousâ€ doesnâ€™t change literal meaning. (This is entirely consistent with the fact such inter-substitutions may dramatically change suggested meaning, the reason being that one may learn what those two words refer to under very different circumstances and thus in connection with very different bodies of descriptive data. The way the â€œreferent is fixedâ€ will obviously affect the connotation of sentences containing the word in question, even though it wonâ€™t affect the literal meanings of such sentences.) Given that such inter-substitutions preserve meaning, it follows that:

(IHP) â€œHesperus is identical with Phosphorousâ€

has the same literal meaning as

(IHH) â€œHesperus is identical with Hesperusâ€

(even though, given how it is typically made known what these words refer to, they have very different non-literal connotations). Weâ€™ve agreed that, for some x, each of â€¹Hesperus has psiâ€º and â€¹Phosphorous has psiâ€º is true just in case x has phi. (XSI) x is x.

And XSI is an analytic, a priori knowable proposition if ever there was one.
   There is no a posteriori necessary truth. It appears otherwise only if one fails to distinguish sentences from the propositions that are their meanings. The gulf between the two can be large. This is but another example of the fact that metaphysics canâ€™t be read off of sentential structure. Kripkeâ€™s disregard for this shibboleth of analytic philosophy comes as a shock. But that shock is nothing compared to the one weâ€™re in for.
3.0 A cure for Salmonella
Kripke (1979) wrote an article in which he put forth a new argument (one not stated in Naming and Necessity) as to why the Russell-Frege analysis of the non-triviality of IHP fails. Pierre is a monolingual speaker of French. He reads many books about London (which he knows as â€œLondresâ€). On the basis of the information

contained in those books, he draws the rational inference that London is a beautiful city. Expressing this belief, he says:

(1) â€œLondres est jolie.â€

It is to be emphasized that, given the data at his disposal, it is rational of Pierre to accept (1).
   Our story continues. Pierre is kidnapped and forced to live in a terrible part of London. He doesnâ€™t know that heâ€™s living in the city known to him as â€œLondres.â€ He learns English, but he learns it as one learns a first language. In other words, he doesnâ€™t learn what English words mean by learning what their French translations areâ€”he learns them the way that a native speaker of English learns them. He learns what â€œsnowâ€ means, not by learning that it co-refers with â€œneige,â€ but by learning a certain crystalline substance that falls on rooftops in the winter is called â€œsnow.â€ And he learns what â€œLondonâ€ refers to in the same way. Given the data at his disposal, it is rational of Pierre to believe that the sentence:

(2) â€œLondon is not prettyâ€

expresses a truthâ€”a truth to the effect that the city he is living in is not pretty. And Pierre does assent to it, and he utters that very sentence, knowing what it means.
   Of course, (2) is the (English translation of the) negation of (1).
   â€œLondonâ€ is the translation of â€œLondres.â€ So if â€œLondonâ€ is synonymous with some definite descriptionâ€”with, let us suppose, â€œthe most populous city on the Thamesâ€â€”then â€œLondresâ€ is synonymous with the French translation of that definite description. But if that were the case, then (1) would mean the same thing as:

(1R) â€œthe most populous city on the Thames is prettyâ€

and (2) would be mean the same thing as:

(2R) â€œthe most populous city on the Thames is not pretty.â€

Pierre clearly isnâ€™t in the same category as somebody who accepts both (1R) and (2R). So even if, as Russell and Frege thought, â€œLondonâ€ was synonymous with some definite description, that wouldnâ€™t explain the fact that (1) and (2) communicate such different propositions. In other words, it would fail to account for the cognitive values of those sentences. (The â€œcognitive valueâ€ of a sentence is what it communicates.) Since the whole point of the Frege-Russell theory that proper names are (abbreviated) definite descriptions is to account for the cognitive values of sentences containing proper names, that theory fails to do what itâ€™s supposed to do.
3.1 A cure for Salmonella (continued)
But Kripkeâ€™s parable exposes a problem much more profound than anything having to do with the semantics of a proper name. Itâ€™s a datum that Pierre understands each of (1) and (2), that he assents to each, and sincerely utters each. So itâ€™s a datum, or follows from data, that Pierre is rationally accepting some sentence and its negation.
   This seems like a problem. A paradox. Whatâ€™s the solution? Pierre is rational. No denying it. And Pierre understands each of (1) and (2). No denying that either. (To be sure, he doesnâ€™t know as much about the thing that is referred to as â€œLondonâ€/â€Londresâ€ as some other people. But so what? If I know who it is that â€œLarryâ€ refers to, then I know the semantics of â€œLarry.â€ Obviously I donâ€™t know who Larry is as a person as well as his therapist. Kripke says that he doesnâ€™t know how to solve the problem. He says only that heâ€™s inclined to suspect that â€œthe apparatus of propositions breaks down here.â€ He doesnâ€™t say what he means by this. Nor does it matter, since, whatever it means, itâ€™s false, as weâ€™ll see.
   Nathan Salmon says that, given Kripkeâ€™s parable, it follows that, at a given time, one can rationally accept a proposition and its negation. Pierre would be rational, given what weâ€™ve said so far, to believe that â€œLondres â‰  Londonâ€ is a true sentence. Thus, there is some x (namely, London) such that, according to Salmon, Pierre can rationally believe that: x â‰  xâ€”that is, that x is not self-identical. Thus, Salmonâ€™s position is that one can rationally believe that London is not self-identicalâ€”that, in fact, any given object is not identical with itself.
3.2 Why, contrary to what Nathan Salmon ways, it is not rational to believe both P and not-P
Salmonâ€™s solution is not only desperate, but utterly incoherent. What is rationality? Itâ€™s the ability to draw the consequences of the information at oneâ€™s disposal. No truth is a consequence of its own negation, and every truth is incompatible with its own negation. Given that P and not-P is always false, it can never be rational to accept it or, therefore, to infer it. Salmonâ€™s position is inconsistent with the very meaning of the word â€œrational.â€
   Salmon sometimes defends his position by saying that one can rationally accept P and not-P only if one doesnâ€™t know that what one is accepting is a proposition and its negation. But this makes no sense. You are irrational if you believe P and not-P or if you grasp both P and not-P and yet fail to generate the additional belief that theyâ€™re inconsistent with each other. For acceptance of P and not-P to be rational, it would be necessary that the data at your disposal not make it clear that you were accepting some proposition and its negation, which would be possible only if you didnâ€™t know what it was you were accepting. And this seems to be what Salmon holds.
   But, contrary to what Salmon evidently thinks, you canâ€™t accept a proposition without knowing what it is. The counterexamples to this are spurious. Suppose that Smith believes anything that he believes Jones to believe. If Jones believes that Lima is the capital of Peru, does it follow that Smith also believes it? No. What follows it is if Smith were to know that Jones believed it, then Jones would believe it. In order to accept a proposition, it is not enough that it be described to you. You must actually grasp it. Another story will make this clear.
   Person X is never convinced of anything unless it actually is true. This has been verified, and I know this. Smith and I have a mutual friend, Green, who has been missing for the last three weeks. One day Smith tells me that he knows where our friend Green has been for the last three weeks. I have no idea where Green has been. I couldnâ€™t even guess. But Smith doesnâ€™t tell me where Green has beenâ€”only that he knows where heâ€™s been. So there is some proposition P such that, if correct, P says where Green has been and such that Smith accepts P. I know that whatever it is that Smith believes about Greenâ€™s whereabouts is correct. But do I, under these circumstances, accept the proposition that identifies his whereabouts? No. If I were told what that proposition was, I would accept it. But I do not now do so. I donâ€™t know what the right value of P is.
   Suppose that, as Smith knows, Green has been in Spain for the last three weeks but that Iâ€™m not told this. Under these circumstances I donâ€™t accept the proposition: Green has been in Spain for the last three weeks. I would accept it if I knew that Green accepted it. But I donâ€™t yet know this, and I donâ€™t yet accept it. The proposition that I do accept is this: I know that, whatever Smith believes to be the proposition describing Greenâ€™s whereabouts over the last three weeks, that proposition must be correct. But that proposition is very different from Green has been in Spain for the last three weeks. And I donâ€™t yet accept the latter.
   What this shows is that one cannot accept a proposition without knowing that one is doing so. When it seems as though one does this, one accepts some distinct proposition that describes some unknown proposition. If you accept a proposition, you know it. So if, for some P, you accept both P and not-P, you know it. But if you know it, youâ€™re not rational, since anyone who makes a faulty inference is ipso facto irrational (to that extent), and any inference whose conclusion is P and not-P is ipso facto faulty. 

3.2.1 Why, contrary to what Nathan Salmon says, it is not rational to believe both P and not-P (continued)
Salmon was driven to accept this preposterous view by his failure to take into account even the most basic points concerning the relationship between thought and language. Pierre doesnâ€™t learn what â€œLondonâ€ refers to in a vacuum. He is air-dropped into a horrible part of a certain city. There is garbage all around.    What Pierre is being told, in being told this, is something along the lines of:

(L1) there is some vile, squalid, garbage-infested city x such that I am now in x and such that I was dragged here against my will and such that, because of xâ€™s obvious horridness, I am now depressed; moreover, â€œLondonâ€ refers to x.

An inevitable consequence of the fact that these are the circumstances under which Pierre learns what â€œLondonâ€ refers to is that what an utterance of

(2) â€œLondon is not prettyâ€

would impart (not semantically encode) is something along the lines of:

(L2) there is some vile, squalid, garbage-infested city x such that I am now in x [etc.] and such that â€œLondonâ€ refers to x; moreover, x is not pretty

(Ln) â€¹London has psiâ€º

would impart (not semantically encode) something along the lines of:

(L*P2) there is some vile, squalid, garbage-infested city x such that I am now in x [etc.] and such that â€œLondonâ€ refers to x; moreover, x has psi.

   Weâ€™ve already made it clear why, even though Ln would convey L*P2, Pierre wouldnâ€™t be under any illusions as to what the former literally means. Itâ€™s also obvious that, since itâ€™s through L1 that Pierre knows what â€œLondonâ€ refers to, it is rational of him to accept (2).

   There is no proposition that Pierre both accepts and rejects. Salmon is just plain wrong to think otherwise. And his contention that one can rationally accept propositions and their negations involves a number of rather obvious fallacies. First, sentences are not propositions. Suppose that sentence S1 encodes proposition P1 and that sentence S2 encodes the negation of P1. But he thinks this is because one can rationally accept propositions that are inconsistent with each other; Salmon thinks that one accept the propositions P and not-P without being irrational. This is a deeply irrational belief. Irrationality is acceptance of incoherencies, such as P and not-P.
   Salmon holds, correctly, that Pierre is rational in accepting both (1) and (2). According to Salmon, it follows from this that Pierre is rationally accepting some proposition and its negation. But that would follow only if what (1) and (2) conveyed to Pierre were confined to what they literally mean. But what sentences convey isnâ€™t always confined to what they literally mean. Itâ€™s seldom confined to it. (See Chapters 9 and 18.) Every semanticist knows this. Itâ€™s unclear why Salmon doesnâ€™t know it or why, if he does, he didnâ€™t see its bearing on this issue.

3.3 Some final remarks on Fregeâ€™s conception of reference: Fregeâ€™s distinction between sense and reference are a distortion of the distinction between pre-semantics and semantics
Weâ€™ve seen that if a proper name N refers to some object x, then, in virtue of having the form â€¹N has psiâ€º, a sentence S is true just in case:

(i) x has psi.

It immediately follows, as weâ€™ve noted, that Fregeâ€™s analysis of proper names is false. According to Frege, proper names, and indeed all referring expressions, have â€œsenses.â€ If a referring term M refers to y, Mâ€™s sense is some property phi that y uniquely instantiates. And, if Frege is right, in virtue of having the form â€¹M has psiâ€º a sentence S* is true just in case:

(ii) phi is uniquely instantiated; moreover, any such instance has psi.

   No sooner is Fregeâ€™s analysis made clear than its incoherence is plain to see. (ii) is an existential generalization, and the reason for this is that it contains what Frege regards as a referring term. Thus, if Fregeâ€™s analysis of proper names is right, they are semantically indistinguishable from existential quantifiers and, therefore, are such quantifiers. But Frege says theyâ€™re referring terms. Since, therefore, Fregeâ€™s position is, in effect, that proper names both are and are not quantifiers, it is incoherent.
3.3.1 Indirect reference = quantification = non-reference, direct reference = only true form of reference
Fregeâ€™s position is that names refer indirectly. In other words, they refer through the mediation of a sense, and that sense is what makes it into the propositions meant by sentences containing those names. The referents of those names donâ€™t make it into those propositions. By virtue of containing proper names of those objects, sentences containing those names merely describe their referents. But weâ€™ve just seen that â€œindirect referenceâ€ is really just quantification.
   Fregeâ€™s distinction between â€œsenseâ€ and â€œreferenceâ€ is an incoherent way of describing the distinction between semantics and pre-semantics. There is some entity O, namely London, such that the proposition literally meant by 2 is true just in case:

(ONP) O is not pretty,

but such that, because of how Pierre learned what â€œLondonâ€ refers to, what 2 conveys to him is (L*P2).
   Frege would have said that the sense of â€œLondonâ€ is some property uniquely had by London (e.g., the property of being a city that is vile, squalid, etc.). But that isnâ€™t true. Oneâ€™s knowing what â€œLondonâ€ refers to consists in there being a property phiâ€”it doesnâ€™t matter which oneâ€”such that one knows that phi is uniquely instantiated and that â€œLondonâ€ refers to any instance of it.    And yet Frege constantly speaks of the sense of â€œSocrates,â€ â€œLondon,â€ etc. Although this view is patently false, Frege has a good reason for holding it. But weâ€™ve already seen why this is spurious. And there is some x such that you know that x is where your grandmother lives and such that â€œLondonâ€ refers to x and, finally, such that, when you say â€œLondon is pretty,â€ what you are affirming, and what other English-speaking auditors (who know that you speak English) know you to be affirming is

(LP) x is pretty.

   So while itâ€™s a fact that â€œLondonâ€ has one sense for me and a different sense for you, that doesnâ€™t prevent us from using it to make ourselves understood to each other.    Bearing these points in mind, letâ€™s wrap up our discussion of Pierre. Pierre has a thorough grasp of the semantics of â€œLondon.â€ For him, the sense of â€œLondonâ€ is a squalid and horrible city where my kidnappers have forced me to live, or some such. This is because what the sense of â€œLondonâ€ is for a given person depends, not on its literal meaning, but on the information through which that person grasps that literal meaning. Sense, therefore, is pre-semantics, not semantics.
3.4 Salmon on non-existence and mythical objects
Nathan Salmon holds that one can say of a given thing x that x exists or that it does not exist. Indeed, Salmon says that one can correctly say of a given thing x that x does not exist. Of course, for one to correctly say of a given thing x that it doesnâ€™t exist there must exist some thing such that one is correctly saying of it that it doesnâ€™t exist. So there must exist something that doesnâ€™t exist. Since this isnâ€™t possible, Salmon is wrong.
   But arguments like the one just given have been around since Russell first produced them over a hundred years ago; and Salmon, being a devotee of Russellâ€™s works, is well aware of these arguments. So why does he hold that one can correctly attribute non-existence and existence to objects?
   Salmon has a couple of reasons. The sentence:

(1) â€œSocrates is Socratesâ€

doesnâ€™t mean the same thing as

(2) â€œSocrates is the main character in most of Platoâ€™s dialogues.â€

Thus, â€œSocratesâ€ isnâ€™t synonymous with â€œthe main character in most of Platoâ€™s dialoguesâ€ or, by obvious generalizations of this argument, with any other definite description.    Definite descriptions describe their referents. To be referred to by â€œthe tallest person in the room,â€ you have to have certain characteristics. You must uniquely be a tallest person in the room. If a taller person walks in the room, that expression wonâ€™t pick you out. But, whatever your name is, there isnâ€™t any way you have to be

for that expression to pick you. It doesnâ€™t matter how tall or short you are; what your job is; etc. Thus, names are mere labels.
   It follows that, if you say â€œBill Jeffries is tall,â€ there is some individual x such that â€œBill Jeffriesâ€ refers to x and such that for your statement to be true, it is necessary and sufficient that x be tallâ€”it being entirely irrelevant what other properties x has.    Thus, if N is a proper name (that isnâ€™t a make-believe name or is otherwise one that doesnâ€™t pick anything out) and psi is any property, there exists some object x such that â€¹N has psiâ€º is true iff x has psiâ€”it being irrelevant what other properties x has or lacks.
   But now we have a problem. â€œWinston Churchillâ€ isnâ€™t an â€œemptyâ€ (non-referring) name.    Some people deal with this by trying to revive the idea that proper names are definite descriptions. But this isnâ€™t a good idea, since the arguments just given are clearly probative.    Unfortunately, the way Salmon deals with the problem is no more plausible than the two views that he rightly rejects.    If Salmon were right to say that one could say of specific non-existent things that they were non-existent, it would follow that one could say of specific non-existent things that they were existent.    Of course, in saying that â€œWinston Churchillâ€ has a non-existent referent, Salmon is saying that there exists something x such that â€œWinston Churchillâ€ refers to x and such that x doesnâ€™t exist.    Salmon is quite right to hold that proper names are mere labels. But, contrary to what he thinks, that fact doesnâ€™t license his desperate and incoherent views about existence. Consider the sentence:

(S1) â€œJMK plays tennis.â€

This sentence is meaningful. In other words, there is some proposition that it expresses. Let P1 be this proposition.    In any case, it isnâ€™t the right view. Under what circumstances is P1 true? First of all, the property of being a tennis player must be instantiated. (If nobody plays tennis, P1 is false.)    Supposing that P# is the set containing PTP, PJMK, and PJMT, and not containing anything else, the members of P# are collectively instantiated if and only if P1 is true. There is thus no reason not to say that P1 is P# and that for P1 to be true is for all of P#â€™s members to be instantiated.
   The property of being identical with JMK will exist even after I no longer do, and it existed before I was born.    (TCS1) x likes tennis
   
After I die, there wonâ€™t exist an object of the kind just described. But thatâ€™s irrelevant.    It will be true at that point that JMK did play tennis. But our analysis is consistent with that fact as well.
The sentence:

(S2) â€œJMK used to play tennisâ€

According to our analysis, S3 is true iff PTP, PJMK, and PJMT used to be collectively instantiated.    This is disastrousâ€”and unnecessary. Unlike Salmonâ€™s analysis, ours doesnâ€™t require that there exist anything that doesnâ€™t exist.    I happen to be a Platonist, and I happen to think that each of those three things is a non-spatiotemporal object. But thatâ€™s irrelevant. This analysis goes through as long as those three things exist. It doesnâ€™t matter how theyâ€™re thought of.
   Salmon doesnâ€™t even consider anything like this analysis. Instead, he holds that, since proper names are labels, it follows more or less directly that there exist things that donâ€™t exist.    Note: ZA is a sentence of English. But it will help if, whenever necessary, you let ZA represent its Ancient Greek translation.

   Salmon published an article, titled â€œMythical Objects,â€ in which he attempts to corroborate these views of his. Here is the argument presented therein:

4.1 Evaluating KA

5.0 The causal vs. the descriptive theories of conception
According to Russell, â€œSocratesâ€ is synonymous with a definite description; this might be â€œthe great philosopher of antiquity who died of hemlock poisoning.â€ To understand the word â€œSocrates,â€ and thus to understand sentences of the form â€¹...Socrates...â€º, one must obviously know the semantics of â€œSocrates.â€ So one must know that â€œSocratesâ€ is synonymous with that definite description. 5.1 The causal theory of reference
Rightly rejecting Russellâ€™s view, according to which â€œSocratesâ€ is a definite description that picks out Socrates, Kripke an alternativeâ€”to wit, â€œSocratesâ€ refers to Socrates because a certain kind of causal relation holds between tokens of â€œSocratesâ€ and Socrates himself (or, more exactly, states of affairs involving Socrates).

   In general, if an expression E refers to an object O, that is because tokens of E stand in a certain causal relation to states of affairs involving O.

5.2 The anti-descriptivist theory of conception
Weâ€™ve see that, for any property phi uniquely had by Socrates, one can refer to Socrates using the word â€œSocratesâ€ without knowing that â€œSocratesâ€ refers to a unique instance of phi. This position is, of course, antithetical to the descriptivist conception of conception advocated by Russell.
5.3 The causal theory of conception
Because of Kripkeâ€™s work, many philosophers accept both a causal theory of reference and an anti-descriptivist theory of conception. Many such philosophers believe that, since these two views of theirs are true, it is de rigueur to accept a causal theory of conception. According to such a theory, x has a concept of y if and only if y has certain sorts of effects on x.
   David Kaplan (1968), himself an advocate of this view, made a point that helps bring out the raison dâ€™Ãªtre for it. Let X be a low-resolution, distorted photograph of Smith. X can be thought of as a distorted, low-resolution, inaccurate, description of Smith, and Y can be thought of as a very good and accurate description of some Smith look-alike. The reason that, despite its shortcomings, X is a picture of Smith is that X is an effect of Smith (or, more accurately, of some situation involving Smithâ€”light bounced off Smith and headed in the direction of a certain camera, etc.). And the reason that, despite its encoding a description that Smith satisfies to a tee, Y is not a photograph of Smith is that it lacks just this sort of causal connection to him.
   Advocates of the causal theory of reference hold that concepts of Smith are to Smith what photographs of Smith are to him and that, for any x, concepts of x are to x what photographs of x are to x.
   I reject this view. I accept Kripkeâ€™s point that names arenâ€™t definite descriptions. And, with some qualifications to be stated forthwith, I accept Kripkeâ€™s theory of reference. There is, we will see, an ineliminable causal component to it. But that component is internal to a description that singles out Socrates. And I agree with Russell that oneâ€™s concept of Socrates is descriptive and is expressed by a definite description. But, contrary to what Russell says, those definite descriptions arenâ€™t at all like the ones that Russell had in mind.
   How can all of this be true? Simple: pre-semantics isnâ€™t semantics. For elucidation, read on.
5.4 The causal-descriptivist theory of conception
Imagine the following. There are 30 numerically different, but qualitatively identical men in a certain place. Your friend Bob goes up to one of them, put his hand on his shoulder, and says:

Your knowing who â€œFredâ€ refers to also depends on your having a causal connection to Fred. 5.4.1 The causal-descriptivist theory of conception (continued)

5.5 The problem of forgotten start-up descriptions
One typically forgets the existence-claim through which one added a name to oneâ€™s lexicon. One typically forgets the first time one heard â€œShakespeareâ€ or â€œAristotleâ€; one often forgets oneâ€™s first meeting of a person. Given this, one is tempted to say:

Now that you have E3, you can drop E2 and E1. You can completely forget them; and that will not jeopardize your ability to think about Fred. Supposing that a moment has passed and that you have stopped talking with Fred, the mere passage of time replaces E3 with a slightly different claim:

Given that you now know E4, you can forget each of E1â€“E3 without ceasing to be able to think about Fred. And, so long as you are able to think about Fred, this will continue to be the case.

   Oneâ€™s ability to think about, and refer to, something can only be started up by oneâ€™s acquiring knowledge of the right kind of existence-claim. Typically, that specific claim is forgotten.    None of this belittles the role that causal connections play in conception and reference. What enables me to think about Fred is my knowledge of some existence-claim that describes him: there is some guy whom I am now seeing and attending to, who is wearing a bowler hat, and â€œFredâ€ names that guy. The causal connection is involved in my seeing Fred; and my seeing Fred, in its turn, is involved in my having a uniquely individuating description of him.    Here we need to very clear about a certain distinction: the distinction between literal meaning and cognitive content. â€œFredâ€ is just a label. The following statement is true:

(*) â€œFred looked puffy and paleâ€

   But remember that one knows what â€œFredâ€ refers to only insofar as one knows some claim of the form: somebody x uniquely has phi and â€œFredâ€ refers to x.
   
Tyler Burge (1941â€“) overlooked these points.
