1.6      Rationality vs. autonomy, practical vs. theoretical reason
 
Immanuel Kant was a great epistemologist and also a great ethicist. Unfortunately, his insights are often embedded in confusion, and it isnâ€™t always easy to separate what is of value in his work from what isnâ€™t. This is especially so where his views on ethics are concerned, as weâ€™re about to see.
Kant held that it is categorically in oneâ€™s interest to act ethically and, therefore, that morality and self-interest coincide. To understand Kantâ€™s theory as to why this is so, we must know what Kant believes morality to be. Kant puts forth two theories of morality. According to the first, an act is moral just in case, were everyone else to act similarly, that act would not be self-defeating. According to the second, an act is moral to the extent that it embodies a respect for peopleâ€™s autonomy. Autonomy is self-determination, and for a person to be autonomous is for him, not someone else, to decide how heâ€™ll live. The opposite of autonomy is â€œheteronomy.â€ Somebody is heteronomous to the extent that others decide how he lives. Thus, according to Kantâ€™s second ethical theory, autonomy-conducive acts are good and heteronomy-conducive acts are bad.
Kant believes these two positions to be equivalent. Heâ€™s wrong. One can respect other peopleâ€™s autonomy without acting in such a way that, were everyone else to act similarly, oneâ€™s act would be self-defeating. Because it wrongly assumes otherwise, Kantâ€™s attempt to link morality with self-interest fails.
 
1.1 Kantâ€™s two categorical imperatives
 
A categorical imperative is a rule that one should follow no matter what. (â€œImperativeâ€ means â€œcommandâ€ or â€œrule,â€ and â€œcategoricalâ€ means â€œunconditional.â€) Kant asked:
 
(ACI[1]) Are there any categorical imperatives?
 
He said â€œyes.â€ Before we can say whether he was right, we must point out that there are three distinct questions that ACI can reasonably be seen as asking:
 
(1) Are there any moral rules that one simply should follow?
(2) Are there any rules of any kind at all that one simply should follow?
3) Are there any moral rules that hold without exception? In other words, supposing that oneâ€™s intention is to be moral, are there any moral rules that one must follow under any circumstances?
 
The answer to (1) seems to be â€œno.â€ The statement:
 
(a) â€œOne should refrain from committing immoral actsâ€
 
is ambiguous between:
 
(b) â€œOne should act morally if oneâ€™s objective is to act morally,â€
 
and
 
(c) â€œOne should act morally, even if it itâ€™s in oneâ€™s interest not to do so.â€
 
(a) expresses a hypothetical imperative. (Itâ€™s also utterly vacant.) And (b) is clearly false.
In general, what one should do depends on what oneâ€™s intentions are. Therefore (1) is false. Similar reasoning shows that (2) is false.
Is (3) correct? Yes. One has a categorical moral obligation, I should think, to refrain from obliterating all life. And, of course, one has a categorical moral obligation to act morally.
But are there any categorical moral imperatives that, unlike the two just mentioned, arenâ€™t utterly trivial? Kant said â€œyes.â€ And he identified what he believed to be two non-trivial categorical imperatives:
 
(CI1) An act is moral if it wouldnâ€™t be self-defeating were everyone else to act similarly
 
and
 
(CI2) An act is wrong if itâ€™s a case of treating a person as an object, not a subject, and an act is right if itâ€™s a case of treating a person as a subject not an object.
 
CI2 doesnâ€™t need much of an explanation. Itâ€™s obviously wrong to undermine another personâ€™s autonomy. And, although it may well be right to undermine one personâ€™s autonomy to preserve the autonomy of a million others, that doesnâ€™t really redound to the discredit of CI2.
The idea behind CI1 is that, given any bad act x, if everybody did x, nobody could successfully pull x off. It be pointless to lie in a world where everybody lied, since nobody would believe anybody. It would be pointless to try to steal in a world where everyone was a thief, since everyone would go out of their way to make their possessions utterly theft-proof.
Kant thinks that CI1 and CI2 are equivalent. An act is one of using somebody else, Kant believes, if it would be self-defeating in a world where everybody acted that way, and an act is one of not using somebody else if it wouldnâ€™t be self-defeating in such a world.
One can see why one would think this. In a world where everyone was constantly trying to con (or otherwise use) everyone, everyone would be on their guard, making it impossible, so one might infer, for anyone to con (or otherwise use) anyone.
But CI1 and CI2 are not equivalent. First of all, people could use people in a world where everybody was a user. In a world of con-men, the smart con-men could con the not so smart con-men.
In addition to showing that CI1 and CI2 are not equivalent, this shows that CI1 is wrong. Though obviously morally bad, acts of con-artistry wouldnâ€™t necessarily be self-defeating in a world of con-artists. By the same token, there are morally good forms of conduct that, if engaged in universally, couldnâ€™t be successfully carried out. Physicians heal people; healing people is good. But nobody could successfully practice medicine in a world of physicians. Who would grow crops, build roads, enforce the law, and so on?
 
1.2 The fallacy embodied in Kantâ€™s search for a categorical imperative
 
A story will expose a confusion that vitiates Kantâ€™s ethical system. You are friends with Smith. Smith has money. You donâ€™t.
Your children need medication. If they donâ€™t get it right away, theyâ€™ll die. Smith is a genuinely well meaning person who doesnâ€™t want your children to die. But (for some reason or other) itâ€™s impossible for him to lend you the money.  The only way for you to get it is to steal it from him.  There truly are no other alternatives. You have exactly two choices: (1) Steal from Smith. (2) Let your children die. You choose to steal from Smith. The result: your children live, and Smith is bankrupt. You obviously did the right thing. Lost money can be regained. Lost life cannot. You donâ€™t regret making this choice. But you do regret having to make it. Smith is a good guy, and you really wish you hadnâ€™t had to steal from him.
Does this scenario show that there are exceptions to the principles that stealing is wrong? No.[2] Stealing from Smith is the lesser of two evils. Itâ€™s obvious that, under the circumstances, the right thing to do was to steal the money. But in some cases the â€œrightâ€ thing to do is merely the least wrong thing to do; and this is one of those cases.
Thus, the principle that stealing is wrong does hold categorically. But this doesnâ€™t mean that you should never steal. What it means is that, although you have an obligationâ€”a categorical obligationâ€”not to steal, you have an even stronger obligation not to let your children die. A moral principle outweighed is not a moral principle extinguished. There are many categorical moral obligations. Lying, cheating, stealing, manipulating, woundingâ€”these are all bad things. They are things that are categorically bad. But oftentimes these bad things are the lesser of two evils. Torture is wrong. But itâ€™s more wrong to allow a nuclear device to be detonated in the middle of a city. The circumstances being what they are, torturing one person may be far less wrong than the alternative (namely, letting many innocents die).
Suppose that, by virtue of the fact that you had to steal from Smith to save your children, you ceased to have any obligation not to steal from Smith. In that case, any remorse you felt as a result of stealing from him would have no objective basis. It would be the emotional counterpart of a hallucination. But, under the circumstances, it would be monstrous of you to feel no remorse at stealing from Smith. Of course, your choosing not to steal from him would have been far more monstrous, that being why, under the circumstances, the right thing to do was to steal. That said, itâ€™s appropriate that you feel some remorse at having depleted Smithâ€™s lifesavings. The reason for this is that, even though your obligation to save your children was far stronger than your obligation not to steal from Smith, the latter obligation did not cease to exist. It was merely outweighed. This suggests that the obligation not to steal does hold categorically. In contexts where it appears not to hold, it does hold, but is outweighed by some other, stronger obligation. Presumably, the obligation not to kill innocent people is one that holds categorically, even though there are circumstances (e.g., ones where, in order to save a hundred innocent people, one must kill two innocent people) where it can be overridden.
Bearing these points in mind, letâ€™s reconsider Kantâ€™s two categorical imperatives:
 
(CI1) Never commit an act that would be self-defeating if performed generally.
(CI2) Always treat people as subjects, never as objects; in other words, respect other peopleâ€™s autonomy, without fail.
 
CI1 entails that one should never lieâ€”even if one must do so to save a hundred people.
CI2 entails that one must never manipulate anyoneâ€”even if one must do so to prevent a nuclear bomb from going off in a crowded city.
The fact that Kantâ€™s ethical system has these consequences definitively shows that it is false. The nearest thing to Kantâ€™s ethical system that isnâ€™t obviously false is this:
 
(CI2*) Although itâ€™s categorically wrong to treat people as objects, there are circumstances where oneâ€™s obligation not to treat one person as an object is outweighed by some other obligation (e.g., by oneâ€™s obligation not to allow ten million people to die).
 
1.3    Another Kantian blunder: his failure to distinguish the good from the praiseworthy
 
Kant held that nothing other than a â€œgood willâ€ has any moral value. By a â€œgood willâ€ he meant an intention to follow â€œthe moral law.â€ By â€œthe moral lawâ€ Kant meant CI2. Here is Kantâ€™s reasoning:
 
(KR) An intention to do good cannot possibly be bad. Of course, an intention to do good can have bad effects. Sincerely intending to save the children, you feed them X, which is lethal, genuinely believing that itâ€™s Y, which is nutritious. But in and of itself your intention to do good is utterly beyond reproach.
But anything other than an intention to do good can be bad. A cool-headed, intelligent villain is that much more diabolical than a hysterical, unintelligent one. A wealthy, healthy villain is that much worse than a poor, sickly one. It is only if good people have them that intelligence, self-control, wealth, and health are good things. This means that those things are not inherently good.
There is ultimately but one moral law, namely: respect other peopleâ€™s autonomy. It follows that anything other than an intention to treat people as subjects, as opposed to objects, lacks any inherent moral worth.
 
It might be that, unless lobotomized, a certain villain will use his formidable cognitive powers to do harm. But surely lobotomizing someone is, at best, the lesser of two evils. This shows that, although a villainâ€™s intelligence is inherently good, the existence of that inherent good may be incompatible with the some other, far greater inherent good. If, supposing that he isnâ€™t lobotomized, that criminal will kill millions of people, many of them intelligent, then one inherent good (saving the lives, and a fortiori the intellects, of millions of people) outweighs some other inherent good (preserving the intellect of some one person).
Imagine the following. Brown is a happy two year old infant. Brown didnâ€™t have to work for his happiness. He just happens to be happy. Question: Does Brownâ€™s happiness have moral value? Yes. Obviously. Thatâ€™s why it would be wrong to make Brown unhappy. Second question: Does Brown deserve praise for being happy? No. His happiness, though morally good, isnâ€™t commendable. Many things that are morally good are not commendable. This point is clarified and defended in my book Sections 3.0â€“4.0 of my book Ethics.
In addition to being false, Kantâ€™s position is self-undermining. It would make no sense at all to say (a) that autonomy isnâ€™t inherently good, while also saying (b) that an intention to respect autonomy is inherently good. So if Kant is right to think it inherently good to intend to respect autonomy, then autonomy must itself be inherently good. But in that case, Kant is ipso facto wrong to think that there is nothing inherently good other than an intention to respect autonomy. Which is not to mention that the intelligence of a villain is indistinguishable from his autonomy: take his intellect away, and you take away a good part of his autonomy, if not the entirety of it.
 
1.3.1   Another Kantian blunder: his failure to distinguish the good from the praiseworthy (continued)
 
A brief detour through the philosophy of law will help us identify the blunders in Kantâ€™s reasoning that underlie his ghastly view that nothing other than a good will has any inherent worth.
In his (1977) article â€œIs law a system of rules?â€ Ronald Dworkin (1931â€“) made the profound point that moral principles1 have a â€œdimension of weight,â€ whereas legal statutes do not. There arenâ€™t degrees of legality. An act is either legal or it isnâ€™t. Laws either hold or they donâ€™t. Of course, some laws are hedged with exception clauses. (â€œKilling is illegalâ€”unless done in self-defense.â€) But given a duly hedged law, one is either in violation of it or one is not in violation of it. Legality is binary.
By contrast, morality is not binary. I have a professional and ethical responsibility to teach class on Tuesday. But I also promised a friend that Iâ€™d meet him for lunch. (When making that promise, I forgot that I had to teach.) I canâ€™t cancel the lunch-date. (I have no way of reaching my friend.) Presumably, my obligation to teach outweighs my obligation to keep my lunch-date with my friend. Each obligation has some weight; but one of them has more weight than the other. I still have an obligation to meet my friend. But I canâ€™t fulfill that obligation without shirking some greater obligation. But I still have that obligation. Thatâ€™s why, in standing my friend up, Iâ€™m behaving in a decidedly substandard way.
Kant evidently thought that, just like legal statutes, moral laws are binary: a given law either holds or it doesnâ€™t. Kant was wrong. Moral laws, unlike legal statutes, can have varying degrees of relevance.
 
1.4 Kantâ€™s argument as to why morality and self-interest coalesce (KA)
 
(KA)We have value to the extent that we are rational. Weâ€™re better than chipmunks and jellyfish to the extent that we are rational and they are not. (If chipmunks were to become rational and we were to become irrational, theyâ€™d have more value than we would.) Thus, so far as we subvert our own rationality, we undermine ourselves. Given an immoral act, the very idea of a world in which everyone committed that act is an incoherent one. It follows that immoral acts themselves are incoherent and, therefore, irrational. Since irrationality is self-undermining, and so is immorality; and itâ€™s thus inherently in oneâ€™s interest to be moral.
 
This argument involves a massive non-sequitur. Kant says that the very idea of a world in which everybody lies and in which people still benefit from lying is an incoherent one. He concludes from this that in our world one is acting incoherently in lying. But this doesnâ€™t follow. Whether an act is rational in a given situation depends on how that situation is. Other situations are irrelevant. Whether an act is rational in our world depends on how our world is. In our world, a personâ€™s lying doesnâ€™t entail that everyone else lies; nor is a personâ€™s lying necessarily self-defeating for some other reason.
Kant was an exceptionally brilliant man. So why did he commit this ghastly logical faux pas? A story will help us answer this question. Smith is an auto mechanic who, being self-taught, relies entirely on rules of thumb. He doesnâ€™t know general principles of engineering and must deal with each car on a case by case basis. Given a car problem, Smith canâ€™t bring general principles to bear on it, and it is only by becoming intimately familiar with the idiosyncrasies of the car in question that he can figure out what is wrong with it.
Letâ€™s contrast Smith with that paragon of rationality, Isaac Newton. Newton could understand a certain phenomenon (e.g., a certain planetâ€™s orbiting in a certain manner around a certain star) in terms of general principles. This was why Newton, unlike his predecessors, was able to see that the tides were to be explained in terms of the same physical principles as the trajectory of a cannonball and that both were to be explained in terms of the same principles as the orbiting of the Earth around the Sun. So far as he was able to see such inner similarities between apparently different situations, Newton was able to discern the real structure of the world and was, to that extent, genuinely rational. By the same token, in failing to understand particulars in terms of universals, Smith is failing to see the real structure of the world and is thus failing to be rational. This suggests that thought is rational to the extent that it is driven by a knowledge of principles that can be universalizedâ€”that is, that hold generally and arenâ€™t context-specific.
Given these very reasonable points, all of which the present author accepts, Kant infers that an act is rational to the extent that it is driven by principles that can be universalized. The principle that underlies a lieâ€”viz. I can tell a lie and benefit from itâ€”isnâ€™t one that can be universalized and for that  reason, Kant believes, isnâ€™t rational. So by lying, thinks Kant, one is making oneself less like Newton and more like Smith, and one is therefore diminishing oneself.
So far as this argument appears probative, it is because the term â€œuniversalizableâ€ is being used in an equivocal manner. Let us suppose that, from every standpoint other than a purely ethical one, my lying to Larry is the right move. Iâ€™ve figured out the relative weights of the various pros and cons, and factored them into an accurate and honest appraisal of my own objectives. Letâ€™s go even further and suppose that the reasoning that goes into my decision to tell this lie is driven by a thorough understanding of general principles. In this context, we are in effect supposing, I am a Newton, not a Smith.
Under these circumstances, the principle governing my act is universalizable in one sense and non-universalizable in another. Itâ€™s non-universalizable in the sense that it shouldnâ€™t be universalized. But it is universalizable in the sense that, like Newtonâ€™s reasoning and unlike Smithâ€™s, itâ€™s guided by an understanding of principles that hold generally. Given only what weâ€™ve said, we have no choice but to see Kant as having utterly failed in his attempt to link morality and self-interest.
 
1.5 Why Kantâ€™s attempt to connect morality and self-interest is not a complete failure
 
But that attempt was by no means a failure. The principles driving that attempt are accurate and profound ones. He just wasnâ€™t putting those worthy principles to good use in this particular context. But Kant has real insight into the nature of rationality and autonomy and into their relationship to morality; and so far as there is a connection between rationality and autonomy, on the one hand, and morality, on the other, it is, I believe, to be understood in Kantian terms.
The essence of Kantâ€™s ethics is generally seen as lying in his contention that:
 
(CI1) An act is moral if it wouldnâ€™t be self-defeating were everyone else to act similarly.
 
CI1 is false, and Kantâ€™s ethics is a failure if CI1 is the core of it. But the real essence of Kantâ€™s ethics lies, not in CI1, but in his contention that:
 
(CI2*[3]) An act is good to the extent that itâ€™s autonomy-conducive and bad to the extent that itâ€™s heteronomy-conducive.
 
If it isnâ€™t outright correct, CI2 is a very good approximation to the truth. It is morally acceptable to undermine a given personâ€™s autonomy only to the extent that doing so is necessary to prevent some greater violation of autonomy. Thus, we consider it morally appropriate to attack or kill somebody only to the extent that, by doing so, weâ€™re protecting somebody elseâ€™s autonomyâ€”for example, our own or that of our loved ones. And although we consider it morally acceptable to micromanage the lives of children and thus to encroach on their autonomy, we hold this only because we feel that, were we not to do this, our children would fail to develop their autonomy. Theyâ€™d become undisciplined slobs who, having no self-control, lacked autonomy.
By the same token, protecting a given personâ€™s autonomy is wrong only to the extent that doing so leads to some greater violation of autonomy. We put people in jail and thus violate their autonomy. But so far as this is justified, itâ€™s because, were we not to do so, those criminals, and those who followed in their footsteps, would be responsible for even greater violations of autonomy.
Thus, just as CI2* says, an act is moral to the extent that it is autonomy-conductive and immoral to the extent that it is heteronomy-conducive. Given how intuitive CI2* is, itâ€™s easy to see how an acceptance of it could be an ethicistâ€™s starting point; and given how well it fits the data, itâ€™s easy to see how it could be an ethicistâ€™s finishing point. But given how contrived CI1 is, thereâ€™s no real chance that it could be an ethicistâ€™s starting point; and given how wrong it is, itâ€™s unlikely to be an ethicistâ€™s finishing point.
Taken collectively, these points suggests that CI2* was Kantâ€™s starting point and that, so far as he accepted CI1, it wasnâ€™t really because he believed it, but because, for some reason internal to the mechanics of his theory, he felt he had to accept it. This analysis is substantiated by the fact that, despite his gargantuan intellect, saw CI1 and CI2* as being equivalent, even though they very clearly are not.
All of these facts fall into place when we remember that, in Kantâ€™s view, what gives us value is our rationality. Our rationality is what makes us better than animals. It is what makes us human. It is what makes us what we are. This suggests that, in Kantâ€™s view, rationality is the greatest good. How is this to be reconciled with Kantâ€™s belief that goodness is identical with autonomy-conduciveness and badness is identical with heteronomy-conduciveness?
 
1.6 Rationality vs. autonomy, practical vs. theoretical reason
 
The answer lies in the fact that Kant believes that rationality is autonomy. There is much to be said for this position, as weâ€™ll now see.
First of all, what do the terms â€œrationalityâ€ and â€œautonomyâ€ mean? To be autonomous is to decide for oneself what to do and how to live. A creature that canâ€™t make decisions canâ€™t be autonomous. To be rational is to regulate oneâ€™s own thought processes in accordance with logical norms. Thus, to be autonomous is to decide for oneself how to live, and to be rational is to decide for oneself how to think.
â€œBut couldnâ€™t one be irrational,â€ one might ask, â€œand still decide for oneself how to think? Couldnâ€™t one learn all the relevant logical norms, and make a decision not to comply with them in oneâ€™s thinking? To be sure, it isnâ€™t likely that one would do this. But isnâ€™t it at least a theoretical possibility? And given that it is, doesnâ€™t it follow that your definition of â€œrationalityâ€ is wrong?â€
In order to carry out such a program, oneâ€™s thinking would have to be rational. In any given situation, one would, by the objectorâ€™s own terms, (a) have to figure out what the rational thing to think was, and (b) decide not to think it. And the first part, at least, would involve being rational. The second part, admittedly, wouldnâ€™t be rationalâ€”if one knows that the right conclusion to draw is Q, but one infers not-Q instead, one isnâ€™t being rational. But in the case of the person just described, that irrationality would be parasitic on an existing rationality.
Also, if somebody knowingly draws the wrong inference, one is â€œirrationalâ€ in a different way from somebody who fails to see what the right inference is to begin with. The second sort of irrationality is purely cognitive. The first has to do with the relationship between cognition and action. The one has to do with what philosophers sometimes refer to as theoretical reason; the other has to do with what philosophers call practical reason. Theoretical reason has to do only with the drawing of inferences; it has nothing to do with the choices that one makes on the basis of oneâ€™s inferences. The degree to which one is â€œtheoretically reasonableâ€ is a function only of the degree to which one draws the right inferences, it being irrelevant what one decides to do on the basis of those inferences. Practical reason has to do with the relationship between the inferences one draws, on the one hand, and the intentions in which they eventuate, on the other.[4]
Given this, suppose that Smith decides to live the sort of life described by the objector. In other words, Smith has resolved that heâ€™ll always conclude the opposite of what the norms of good reasoning require him to conclude. This means that, in any given context, heâ€™ll (a) figure out what, given the relevant data, the right conclusion to draw is, and (b) having figured that out, heâ€™ll take it upon himself to draw the opposite inference.
Smith is a paragon of a theoretically reasonable person: by hypothesis, Smithâ€™s reasoning is impeccable, at least to the extent that heâ€™s successful in his efforts to carry out his agenda. So far as Smith is irrational, itâ€™s because of what he decides to do with the correct inferences that heâ€™s irrational. To be sure, what he decides to do with those inferences is have a beliefâ€”it isnâ€™t to do anything overt, like go for a bike ride or have a beer. But itâ€™s still, in the relevant sense, an action. So Smith is rational, at least insofar as rationality has to do with reasoning. So far as heâ€™s irrational, it is in the practical, not the theoretical, sense. Thus, we donâ€™t have in Smith a counterexample to the principle that to be rational is to decide for oneself how to think.
â€œVery well,â€ one might retort. â€œContrast Smithâ€™s case with Brownâ€™s. Brown skips the first part of Smithâ€™s two-step approach. Brown resolves one day that, in any given context, he wonâ€™t figure out what the right inference to draw is. Smith first figures out what he, given the available data along with the relevant logical norms, ought to believe. Having done that, he resolves to believe the opposite. But Brown skips the first part. He has resolved just to let his beliefs arise spontaneously and, therefore, not to be responsive, even in a negative way, to the demands of canons of logic. Itâ€™s a datum that, so far as he carries out this plan, Brownâ€™s thoughts arenâ€™t rational. (They may be correct. But, being entirely reflexive, they arenâ€™t rational.) But itâ€™s also a datum that Brown has decided for himself how to think. This straightforwardly shows that you are wrong to say that to be rational is to decide for oneself how to think.
But Brown has decided for himself what to think in the sense that heâ€™s decided not to decide for himself what to think. He has decided that, henceforth, he wonâ€™t decide for himself what to think. Once he gives himself over to that life-course, he is ex hypothesi no longer rational. Therefore, we donâ€™t have in Brown a real counterexample to our analysis.
Basically, deciding for oneself how to think always involves regulating oneâ€™s thoughts in accordance with norms. Even if one picks the wrong normsâ€”even if one decides not to go with modus ponens, modus tollens, etc. and to go with other, spurious forms of inferenceâ€”oneâ€™s correctly applying these spurious forms of inference itself involves oneâ€™s having non-spurious beliefs as to how they apply to the data at oneâ€™s disposal. So given somebody who decides to think in accordance with the wrong principles, he can carry out his agenda only to the extent that he correctly sees how those principles bear on the data and, therefore, only to the extent that he is rational.
No matter how you slice it, rationality is intellectual autonomy. In other words, to be rational is to decide for oneself how to think.
Letâ€™s compare rationality with autonomy. To be autonomous, I have said, is to live as one chooses. Oneâ€™s being autonomous, I propose, is the same thing as oneâ€™s deciding what to do on the basis of norms that one has adopted. A good way to see why this is (I believe) the right approach is to consider an obvious objection to it:
 
(NSG[5]) Your analysis is definitely wrong. Consider the case of Williams. Williams has decided that heâ€™ll do whatever he wants to do. He wonâ€™t examine his actions, or the intentions behind them, in light of norms. Heâ€™ll just act. But heâ€™s autonomous. Thatâ€™s a datum. After all, heâ€™s deciding for himself how to live.
 
Hereâ€™s why this is off the mark. To the extent that Smith carries out his agenda, he isnâ€™t deciding anything at all. Trueâ€”it is indeed a decision on his part that initiates his entry into a life of the sort described (viz. one in which he just does what he wants, never bothering to assess the consistency of his desires with norms of any sort). But once heâ€™s in that life, he isnâ€™t choosing anything at all. A creature that doesnâ€™t deliberate doesnâ€™t decide anything. It just acts. And a creature that deliberates is ipso facto one that is trying to act on intentions that are in compliance with some set of norms.
Do dogs make choices?[6] Obviously dogs have intentions. (The dog intends to get to the ball before the other dog. Thatâ€™s why itâ€™s running so frantically.) But it seems wrong to say that dogs â€œchooseâ€ (or â€œdecideâ€). Dogs donâ€™t deliberate. They just react. The dog sees red meat: he pounces on it. He sees his brutal master: he cringes. The dogâ€™s life is a series of programmed and therefore compulsive reactions to immediate stimuli. The dog doesnâ€™t call the shots; these hardwired reaction protocols call the shots for him, and it therefore doesnâ€™t make choices. Only creatures that deliberate make choices. Sub-rational[7] creatures donâ€™t make choices. Non-rational creatures donâ€™t act; they react.
Rational creatures donâ€™t just react. Their responses to situations are considered. That doesnâ€™t mean that they deliberate before every act. (Nor should they, since a life spent deliberating would be one of â€œanalysis paralysisâ€â€”of over-thinking what one should do and therefore never doing anything. Itâ€™s therefore irrational to deliberate too much. Itâ€™s irrational to be too rational![8]) But their responses to situations are guided by choices that theyâ€™ve made, and those choices result from prior deliberations on their part. I see an ice-cold beer in the fridge. Were I to react instinctively, Iâ€™d drink it. But long ago I made a choice to live a certain way (to be an author and, therefore, to avoid things, such as getting drunk in the morning, that would make it hard for me to ply my trade), and my instantaneous decision not to drink it reflects that choice. So even though I donâ€™t deliberate, my act (of refraining from drinking the beer) is the embodiment of prior deliberation on its part. The dogâ€™s reactions, by contrast, do not reflect previously made life choices.
One last point before we close the argument: given a set of norms that one has decided to comply with, itâ€™s not always obvious how to comply with them. In such cases, thought is needed to know how it is that, given those norms, one ought to act in a given situation if one is to comply with those norms. And even in cases where it is obvious how to comply with those norms, itâ€™s obviously only to the extent that the right judgments come naturally to one. Thus, a prerequisite for practical rationalityâ€”that is, for autonomyâ€”is theoretical rationality.
We can now say how rationality and autonomy are related. To be rational is to regulate oneâ€™s thinking in accordance with norms. To be autonomous is to regulate oneâ€™s actions in accordance with norms. The latter is a special case of the former, since, as we just saw, oneâ€™s thinking must be appropriately norm-driven if one is to know how which actions on oneâ€™s part will be incompliance with the norms of conduct one has adopted. Thus, rationality and autonomy are the same thingâ€”or, rather, autonomy is a special case of rationality. Rationality is intellectual autonomy, and autonomy is practical rationality. So rationality is autonomy. A creature can make decisions only to the extent that it is autonomous and, therefore, rational. (Non-rational/nonautonomous creatures have intentions. But they donâ€™t make choices. They donâ€™t deliberate. They just react.)
A creature that doesnâ€™t make decisions isnâ€™t an agent, at least not in the sense in which you and I are. It doesnâ€™t form its own intentions. Its intentions result from a convergence of factors (its innate and acquired psychological and physiological structure, its past experiences, the present context). But it doesnâ€™t form them. Its intentions are formed in an impersonal way. An autonomous being forms its own intentions. So an autonomous being is responsible for its intentions and, therefore, for the acts to which they lead. By contrast, a sub-rational, non-autonomous creature is responsible only for its actions. The intentions of a non-autonomous creatures are not the results of agency. Agency, for the non-autonomous, begins with intentions, but doesnâ€™t itself generate them. For the autonomous, on the other hand, agency is itself responsible for intentions. Words like â€œagent,â€ â€œagency,â€ etc. are ambiguous; and words like â€œsubjectâ€ (as in, â€œhe is a human subjectâ€) are correspondingly ambiguous. In one sense, dogs and infants are agents. In another, they are not. Which is why we donâ€™t hold 3-year olds criminally responsible for their acts. Two-year olds are agents in a sense of the word, but not in the same, robust sense in which you and I are agents. Words like â€œsubjectâ€ (as in, â€œhe is a human subjectâ€) are correspondingly ambiguous. For the reasons just given, agency in this more robust sense is identical with rationality and, therefore, with autonomy; and agency in this sense is identical with moral responsibility. Respect for a personâ€™s autonomy is therefore nothing other than respect for his agency and thus for his very existence, to the extent as he is, in the robust sense of the word, a subject.
Contrary to what Kant tries to show, none of this entails that oneâ€™s own welfare necessarily involves oneâ€™s respecting other peopleâ€™s autonomy (rationality/agency/subjecthood). But it shows that oneâ€™s welfare depends on, if it isnâ€™t identical with, oneâ€™s being moral to oneselfâ€”on oneâ€™s not encroaching on oneâ€™s own autonomy. It also shows that ethical responsibility and agency are coeval with rationality and autonomy. In any case, Kantâ€™s attempt to identify morality with self-interest, though not itself a success, is driven by a cogent analysis of the nature of agency and its connection to rationality and morality.

The empirical sciences make assumptions that they are not themselves capable of justifying. Philosophy justifies those assumptions; that is its job.

What it is and why philosophy-departments don't want you to have it
