Induction by enumeration vs. inference to the best explanation 
Given only that every single one of the 5,000 first editions you ve ever come across smelled like pipe tobacco, you cannot reasonably infer that all first editions smell like pipe tobacco. What if all of those first editions were the property of your pipe-smoking friend Larry? In that case, you d have good to reason to suspect that their smelling like pipe tobacco had to do, not with their being first editions, but with their being things that had been around Larry. By the same token, so far as you are entitled to infer that all first editions smell like pipe tobacco, it s only to the extent that you have reason to believe that a thing s smelling like pipe tobacco is rooted in its being a first edition. But that means that, if the data entitles you to infer that all first editions smell like pipe tobacco, it s only because it also entitles you to accept some inference to the best explanation (one to the effect that a thing s being a first edition is, for some reason or other, responsible for its smelling like pipe tobacco). In general, induction by enumeration is parasitic on inference to the best explanation. 
Another example: You are playing a game of roulette. You know that nothing about the game is in any way rigged and that that there is nothing about you---your body, mind, or dice-throwing practices---that disposes a die that you ve thrown to roll one way as opposed to anotherYou ve rolled the dice seven times. Each time, at least one of the die has landed in slot #27. Under these circumstances, it would be natural to predict that you ll roll a 27 next time. But that prediction would be irrational: you have no more reason to believe that you ll roll a 27 than you will any other number. By the same token, no matter how many consecutive 27s you roll, you are never any more entitled to bet that, next time, you won t roll a 27 than you are to bet that you won t roll any one of the other available numbers. Since, by hypothesis, the conditions that obtain on any two occasions are identical, it would be irrational on any given occasion to think any one outcome any more or any less likely than any other. 
When would it become rational to believe that, next time, you re more likely than not to roll this as opposed to that number that, for example, you re especially likely to roll a 27? This belief becomes rational when, and only when, you have reason to believe that a 27-roll is favored by the structures involved in the game. It would be rational were to you learn that the dice are magnetically attracted to the 27-slot, or that the 27-slot is much bigger than any of the other slots. So a long-run of 27 s is evidence of another 27 to the extent that it s evidence of a mechanism that programs for a 
27. In and of itself, a long of 27 s is, as Hume made clear, evidence of nothing. Supposing that (i) no roll affects any later and (ii) that there s nothing underlying the various rolls that directs them towards a common outcome, the fact that you ve rolled consecutive 27 s is ipso facto irrelevant to what you ll roll next. 
The best, and the only, explanation of the fact that all known phi s are psi s is that, thanks to some mechanism, a thing s being a phi disposes it to be a psi; and as soon as such a mechanism has been posited, and not one second sooner, your knowing of a given thing that it s a phi is a reason for you to hold that it s a psi. So any non-fallacious  induction by enumeration  is parasitic on a case of inference to the best explanation. 
A consequence According to the frequency interpretation of probability, for it to be probable that x has psi, given that x has phi, is for phi s that are psi s to outnumber phi s that are non-psi s. Given what we ve just said, this must be qualified. Supposing the number of phi s that are psi s to be high (relative to the number of phi s that are non-psi s), that is evidence that the next phi will be a psi only to the extent that it s evidence of something that disposes phi s to be psi s. 
A small but heterogeneous class of phi s that are psi s may definitively establish that that all phi s are psi s and a large but homogenous class of phi s 
[497] 

that are psi s may provide no support for it. Why does a heterogeneous reference class matter? If two otherwise dissimilar phi s are psi s, we know that, if anything about either is responsible for its having psi, it is its having phi. But if two otherwise similar phi s are psi s, we don t (for that reason alone) have any reason to conclude that either one s being a psi has anything to do with its being a phi. 
Thus, the more resilient the connection is between a thing s being a phi and its being a psi---the more varied are the contexts within which a thing s being a phi is accompanied by its being a psi---the better the chance that the next known phi will be a psi. Presumably this is because causal relations do, whereas mere correlations do not, tend to be context-independent. 
Also, there are many perfect concomitances that, for reasons having nothing to do with their degree of context-invariance, we instinctively know to have no predictive or explanatory importance. We know that every green emerald is grue (green if examined before t (today s date) or blue and examined thereafter); but we don t think that tomorrow emeralds will be blue. Be it noted that the property of being an emerald no less resiliently, context-invariantly associated with the property of being grue than with the property of being green. So there is no reason to suppose that the next phi will be given only the fact that, in each of many qualitatively different contexts, they are frequently (always) conjoined. Given that fact with some other fact, which we have to identify, it is likely that the next phi will be a psi. But this suggests that concomitances have no predictive value, save what they leach off of something underlying them. 
Why is so little predictive stock to be put in the fact that all known emeralds are grue? xxx 
This is made clear by the following paradox, commonly referred to as the  lottery paradox  ( LP,  for short): 
(LP) There s a lottery. One million tickets are sold. There s one winner. So, given any one ticket, the probability of its losing are 999,999 in 1,000,000. You buy a ticket. Let x be this ticket. You know that ( LT  is short for  losing ticket ): 
(LT) the probability of ticket x s losing is 999,999 in 1,000,000. 
But do you know that it ll lose? No. It may even have been rational for you to buy the ticket. Given what you stand to lose by buying the ticket and given what you stand to gain in the remote chance that you win, it may have been in your interest to buy it, even after you take into account that the chances of your losing is 999,999 in 1,000,000. But this decision couldn t possibly have been rational if you knew that your ticket would lose. 
In general, there s no knowledge where there isn t certainty. If, given the information at your disposal, there is any chance, no matter how small, that P isn t the case, then you don t know P. We all know (or so let us suppose) that: 
(UB) the probability that future unsupported objects will fall is extremely high, given that such objects have fallen so far. 
Is there any chance that, all of a sudden, unsupported objects will no longer fall? Yes. (The statement  all of a sudden, unsupported objects will no longer fall  isn t ruled out by the laws of logic. So it could, theoretically, be true.) Therefore, you don t know that they won t fall; and, by obvious extensions of this arguments, you don t know anything about the future (apart from sterile trivialities; e.g.,  whatever happens, happens ). The very concept of  probable  knowledge is incoherent. The merely probable is ipso facto not known. To know it to be 99.9999% likely that unsupported objects will continue to fall is to not know that they ll fall. 
The problem with LP 
LP uses word  probability  in an equivocal manner. Once this is seen, LP loses any appearance of cogency that it might otherwise have had. Let s take another look at: 
(LT) the probability of ticket x s losing is 999,999 in 1,000,000. 
LT says that there are one million tickets but only one winner. That s all it says. But UB doesn t say anything of the sort. UB doesn t make a statistical point. It doesn t say:  nine times out of ten, unsupported objects fall.  UB makes a point about the relative merits of two competing hypotheses, these being: 
(H1) unsupported objects will continue to fall, 
And: 
(H2) unsupported objects will not continue to fall. 
UB is true if, given the data that we have, H1  s being true would undermine the integrity of our belief system to a lesser degree than H2  s being true. Given the information that we have right now: 
[498]
(SB) there is only an extremely low probability that walking on stilts for an hour while wearing a beanie with a propeller on it is a foolproof cure for cancer. 
Does SB say that better than nine cases of cancer out of 10 aren t cured in this way? No. It doesn t make any sort of statistical claim. SB is a claim, not about statistics, but about explanatory integrity. It says that more damage will be done to our belief system if it turns out that cancer can be cured in that way than if it turns out that it cannot. If, by some remote chance, cancer can be cured in that way, everything we  know  about medicine and pathology is false. But the damage wouldn t end there. Our medical beliefs are rooted in general assumptions about the causal structure of the world. (For example, given the information that Smith has gone into anaphylactic shock whenever he s eaten peanuts or anything with peanuts in it, even cutting-edge medical researchers will assume that Smith will go into anaphylactic shock if he eats peanuts that have been painted green. This assumption is rooted in generally held causal beliefs. No inside information is involved.) Were it found out that SB was false, many of the commonsense-based underpinnings of our medical beliefs would have to be reconsidered. But all of those beliefs remain intact if cancer cannot be cured in that way. It is improbable that walking on stilts (etc.) cures cancer to the extent that our current beliefs depend on its not being a cure. And it s probable that walking on stilts (etc.) isn t a cancer cure to the extent our beliefs depend on it. 
In general, P is probable to the extent that our beliefs depend on it, and improbable to the extent that they depend on its negation. 
Counterstatistical vs. counterexplanatory 
Counterstatistical events are innocuous, but counter-explanatory events are not. Smith rolls double-sixes five times in a row. Statistically unlikely  yes. Important no. Must we change our belief system because of it? No. Need we reconsider our assumptions about the basic structure of the world? No. And it makes no difference whether it s five double-sixes in a row or a billion. The improbable sometimes happens, and that s the end of it. When it happens, we have a nice anecdote for cocktail parties; we don t have a situation worthy of scientific scrutiny. But we do have such a situation if it turns out that Smith is using telekinetic powers to make the dice come up sixes. For, in that case, some deeply held convictions of ours have to be revised. 
In describing Smith s rolling double-sixes five times in a row as  improbable,  what one is saying is very different from what one would be saying in describing Smith s having telekinetic powers as  improbable.  In the first case, one is affirming a mere statistical improbability. One is saying only that such things don t often happen. In the second case, one isn t saying anything of the sort. One is saying Smith s having such powers is inconsistent with some fundamental beliefs of ours with beliefs that, if jettisoned, would take a lot of other obviously (or at least presumably) correct beliefs with them. 
Given any event, there is a way of describing it that makes it improbable in the statistical sense. In fact, any given event, described at all precisely, has a statistical probability of vanishingly close to zero. I flip a coin. Nothing improbable about this. But it s a safe bet that no coin has ever moved in exactly the way this one did after I flipped it. Described as a case of my flipping a coin, the event isn t improbable at all. 
But that same event is extremely improbable if described as a case of an object s moving in manner M, where M is the exact way that it did move. But even though nothing apart from that coin has ever moved in manner M, that coin s doing so isn t a matter that deserves the slightest scientific scrutiny. Its moving in that way is consistent with everything we know about the world, and there is therefore nothing to be explained. But there is something to be explained if Smith turns out to have telekinetic powers, since his having such powers is improbable in the explanatory sense. It s irrelevant that it is also improbable in the statistical sense. Every event is improbable in the statistical sense. 
My winning the lottery is improbable in the statistical sense, but not in the explanatory sense. And that s why, before the winner is announced, we can t say that we know it won t win: my winning is consistent with everything we know about the world. My sprouting wings in the next five minutes is improbable in the explanatory sense. And that s why we can say that we know it won t happen. It s inconsistent with everything (or much, at any rate) that we know about the world. 
Grue: the problem of counterinduction 
[499] 
A puzzle devised by Nelson Goodman will clarify, as well as support, what we ve said: 
[500]
(GA) : Let s invent a new word:  grue,  to be defined as follows. Something is grue if it is green before Jan. 1, 2010, or blue thereafter. So a shirt that s green on Oct. 12, 2007, is grue, as is a shirt that s blue on Nov. 11, 2012. Let s assume that, before Jan. 1. 2010, all emeralds have been green. (From now on, we ll abbreviate  Jan. 1, 2010,  as  2010. ) In that case, all emeralds have been grue prior to 2010. Anything that is green-and examined-before-2010 is also grue. So the fact that all emeralds examined before 2010 are green means that all emeralds examined before 2010 are grue. We are assuming for argument s sake that, given the fact that all emeralds examined before 2010 were green, we are inductively warranted in believing that all emeralds examined after 2010 are green. By that logic, it follows that, given the fact that all emeralds examined before 2010 were grue, we are inductively warranted in believing that all emeralds examined after 2010 are grue. But anything examined after 2010 that is grue is blue, not green. So, given that all emeralds before 2010 were green, our inductive grounds for believing they ll be blue after 2010 are as strong as our grounds that they ll be green. 
The degree to which a given fact is statistically improbable depends on how it is described. Given some emerald x that was examined before 2010 and found to be green,  x is grue after 2010  is, from a strictly statistical viewpoint, equiprobable with  x is green after 2010  and also with  x is blue after 2010.  But that s no cause for alarm. Statistical improbability is innocuous. It s explanatory improbability that you have to worry about. But the explanatory probability of  x is green after 2010  dwarfs that of  x is grue after 2010  and, therefore,  x is blue after 2010.  The supposition that objects don t change color (except under conditions that emeralds don t satisfy, at least not in virtue of making it to 2010) is deeply embedded in scientific theory and also in the commonsense underpinning of scientific theory. If it s wrong, then science is in serious trouble, and so is human knowledge in general. 
In response to this, it will be said that: 
[501]
(OA) If GA is right, emeralds that  turn blue  at the beginning of 2010 don t change color. They stay the same color grue. And emeralds that  stay green  do change color, since they go from being grue to having some other color. (Or, to be more precise, emeralds do change color at the beginning of 2010 but only relative to one set of color-terms [ red,   green,  etc.]. But emeralds stay the same color relative to different color terms [ grue,   bleen,  etc.].) 
OA simply isn t true. Pictures of green emeralds (taken before 2010) show them not to have the same color as blue things after 2010. Grueness and greenness are different properties. But they re not different colors. Grueness isn t a color at all it s a color-related property. Let s say that x is a  squiangle  (rhymes with  triangle ) if it s square-shaped before 2010 and triangle-shaped thereafter. If, for some reason, some object that was square before 2010 suddenly becomes a triangle, it s obviously changed shape. It used to have four sides. Now it has three. And a  squiangular  object that is square-shaped after 2010 has started in other words, an object that had four straight sides, etc., before 2010, and continued to have that shape hasn t changed shape; it hasn t gone from being a  squiangle  to being a square. It s stayed the same shape. The same goes for  grue.

Inevitably, some will quibble over whether, when they are interpreted in this (Russellian) fashion, definite descriptions are quantifiers. First of all, it doesn t matter. If, when read attributively, the meaning of  the inventor of bifocals is smart  is identical, or equivalent, with the proposition something or other uniquely invented bifocals and any such thing is smart, then, thus read, that sentence is an existence-claim; in which case, the occurrence of the  inventor of bifocals  therein isn t a singular term and, at the very least, quantifier-like. Second, when read attributively, definite descriptions are functioning as quantifiers. 
But, for what it's worth, definite descriptions are quantifiers if Russell is right about them. A quantifier is an expression that, when coupled with a predicate yields a sentence saying how many things of a given kind have that property.  All people  is a quantifier, since, when coupled with  snore,  which denotes the property of snoring, yields  all people snore,  which says how many things of a certain kind have the property of snoring.  No fish  is a quantifier since, given the expression snore, yields the sentence  no fish read Shakespeare,  which says how many things of a given kind have the property of reading Shakespeare. 
Thus  no fish  is to be defined thus: in virtue of having the form   no fish ,  a sentence says that the class of fish doesn t overlap with the class of things x such that x ( No fish snore  says that the class of fish doesn t overlap with the class of things x such that x snores.  Jim hates no fish  says that the class of fish doesn t overlap with the class of things x such that x snores.)  All people  is defined thus: in virtue of having the form   all people ,  a sentence says that the class of people is a subset of the class of things x such that x ( All people snore  says that the class of people is a subset of the class of things x such that x snores.  Jim hates all people  says that that the class of people is a subset of the class of things x such that Jim hates x.) 
Assuming for argument s sake that the CBR is the proposition meant by CB, the semantic rule for  the inventor of bifocals  is given by the proposition that, in virtue of having the form   the inventor of bifocals . , a sentence says that the class of things that uniquely invented bifocals has exactly one member in common with the class of things x such that x A consequence is that, given the aforementioned assumption,  the inventor of bifocals  is a quantifier. Given any other definite description, the same argument mutatis mutandis shows that, when read attributively, it is 
functioning as a quantifier.

To clarify the parenthetical qualification: given what is meant by  bald ,  is  and all of the material occurring in that sentence besides  Benjamin Franklin , if you couldn t attribute baldness to BF by saying  Benjamin Franklin is bald , then, in that context at least,  Benjamin Franklin  wouldn t refer to BF. Strictly speaking, there is no such thing as the sentence "snow is white." There is the sentence-type; and there are tokens of that sentence. And, for reasons that I've identified elsewhere (note to editor: I've omitted the references since the present paper is still being reviewed I'll supply them upon your request) that sentence-type is not semantically comparable, at least not in any respects that are relevant here, to its tokens. 
Also, it seems to me that, in this context, it's important to distinguish between embedded occurrences of "snow is white" (an utterance of that sentence that is constitutive of an utterance of some other sentence, e.g. the occurrence of it in a given utterance of "if snow is white, then at least one substance is white") and non-embedded occurrences of that sentence. There is a difference between saying "snow is white", on the one hand, and "the proposition that snow is white." A non-embedded utterance of the latter is neither true nor false. A non-embedded utterance of the former is true or false (since it's true). And if, having been ordered to identify a proposition that attributes a color to some substance, I say "the proposition that snow is white", I've clearly done what I've been told. But if, having been given that same order, I say "snow is white", I haven't clearly done what I've been told. This suggests that, if it isn't outright false, the thesis that "snow is white" refers to the corresponding proposition must be heavily qualified. 
And even when it occurs as a proper part of another sentence, "snow is white" isn't interchangeable with "the proposition that snow is white." Whereas " grass is green and snow is white" is true, "grass is green and the proposition that snow is white" is ill-formed and is therefore neither true nor false. 
That said, the semantic gulf between "grass is green and snow is white" and "grass is green and the proposition that snow is white" is miniscule compared to the semantic gulf between "grass is green and snow is white" and "grass is green and the property of being true." And 
My feeling is thus that both embedded and non-embedded occurrences of "snow is white" do refer to the proposition that snow is white---but that this isn't all that they do. I suspect that such occurrences contained phonetically unrealized material not contained by "the proposition that snow is white"; and it is because of these (alleged) differences, I suspect, that "snow is white" isn't, at least not categorically, interchangeable with "the proposition that snow is white."

Given a vague expression E, a  precisification  of E is an assignment of meaning to E that, although non-vague, is otherwise like E s existing meaning. See Section 1.2. The term  bald  is vague. But we d be precisifying the word  bald  were to say exactly how many hairs (of a certain 
thickness) a person x (whose cranium was of a certain size) had to have for +x is bald+, x is bald to be true. (It seems to me that this sort of precisification may not be in quite the same category as the precisifications put forth by science (e.g.  temperature=mean kinetic energy ). There are (at least) two reasons for this. First, scientific precisifications are less stipulative, and more descriptive, in nature than precisifications of the sort just discussed. Second, whereas non-trivial, non-linguistic discoveries must be made to successfully precisify terms such as  temperature  and  acid , such discoveries are irrelevant when it comes to precisifying terms like  bald  and  nice : the requisite knowledge is of a highly generic and, for the most part, strictly linguistic nature.

Why do I say "seems"? CB is a sentence. Given only that CB is equivalent with CBR, it doesn't follow that the proposition meant by the one is equivalent with the proposition meant by the other. Strawson (1950) made this clear. (Strawson's insight was popularized by Kaplan (1989.) Suppose for argument's sake that the semantic rule for "that person over there is" is: if, in a context C, somebody O 
is uniquely a salient person, then an utterance in C of +that person over there is has phi+ has for its meaning some proposition equivalent (if not identical) with O has phi; and if, in C, there is no uniquely salient person, then such an utterance is neither true nor false (the reason being that the demonstrative 
doesn't have a referent). But, given that same supposition, the sentence +that person over there is has phi+ would be true exactly if, in the relevant context, somebody x were uniquely a contextually salient person and, moreover, any such person had phi. Thus, given only that Russell's theory correctly models the logic of CB and other sentences containing definite descriptions, it doesn't follow that it correctly identifies the propositions meant by such sentences. My own view is that, indeed, TD is false. But I also believe, partly for the reasons given here, that Frege's view is false. My alternative to their analysis is put forth else where (note to editor: I'll supply the references upon request).

In his paper "Theories of meaning and learnable languages", Davidson masterfully shows why, if Frege's semantics is correct, no human language would be learnable. That paper is published in Inquiries into Meaning and Truth. Also published in that volume is Davidson's paper "True to the facts", in which he argues that there is only one fact. This argument of his is discussed in Section 1.3 of the present paper. That argument, it will be recalled, is a variant of SS. And, as Frege himself realized, a corollary of Frege's semantics is that SS is cogent. Thus, Davidson himself showed that Frege s semantics is fallacious; and he does this in the very same book where, on the basis of SS, he tries to show that there is, at most, one fact. SS assumes the truth of Frege s semantics and, therefore, of the very semantics on which Davidson s one-fact (or no-fact) argument is based. In that same book, Davidson puts forth an entire philosophical system that is, in part, based on the assumption that there is, at most, only one fact. It follows that, in one and the same book, puts forth a philosophical system and refutes that same system.

I say that almost all of the solutions involve an abandonment of some law of classical logic; for there is the so-called epistemicist view, according to which there is a sharp cut-off between being bald and not-bald, rich and not rich. Also, it is hard to believe that rich has such a precise meaning, given that absolutely no one knows what that meaning is: but surely since it is people who give meaning to terms like  rich  and  bald  through their use of such terms, it makes no sense to suppose that people should be so radically ignorant of the conditions of their application. [25] 
It is true that we are unlikely to characterize someone who is only marginally more intelligent than average as  smart compared to the average person.  But that has to do with pragmatics, not with semantics. The margin of difference would be negligible and would thus be of no pragmatic significance (except in rare contexts, like the present one, where delicate points about meaning are just what is at issue). A comparison might help. For something to be  massive  is, technically, just for it to have mass. But no one would ever describe a mouse as  massive  (except in comparison to, say, a proton); for it would be very misleading to do so, even though such a characterization would technically be correct. Similarly, it would be misleading   though technically correct   to say that George was smart  compared to average person  so long as George s IQ is so much as one point higher than average. In this paper, we are concerned with the finer aspects of meaning, not with the course-grained analogues of them constitute the bulk of everyday discourse. So we will use the expression  compared to  in its strict and literal meaning; we will say that George is  smart compared to the average person  iff George is smarter than the average person, no matter by how little. I further discuss this point at the end of the present paper.

Of course, Carl. Hempel (1945a, 1945b) discovered the paradox. The paradox has been re-articulated many times, sometimes with interesting twists. (See Maher 1999). Hempel bit the bullet, saying that one does confirm (R1) by encountering non-black non-ravens. An intuitively more plausible view is proposed by Quine (1969). (My solution here has some vague affinities with Quine s view.) Some sharp --in fact, devastating --criticisms of the views prevailing during his time, including Quine s, is given by Ayer (1971). Scheffler (1981) admirably reviews all the major solutions prevailing at the time of his writing. Most solutions propose that (R1) and (R2) are, indeed, equivalent. See Schlesinger (1974), Trusted (1979), Cohen (1989), Leavitt (1996), Sainsbury (1997), Maher (1999). 
There are views that try to destroy the alleged equivalence between (R1) and (R2). But these views always resort to non-classical logics. (See Sylvan and Nola (1991)).So in effect these views do concede that, within a classical framework, (R1) and (R2) are indeed, equivalent. So these views presuppose that (R1) and (R2) are equivalent, if only within a classical framework: otherwise non standard logics wouldn t be invoked to block the equivalence. 
These are all worthy views. For reasons of space I cannot review them all here. But what I can say is that, since they all presuppose a certain equivalence between (R1) and (R2), they are hobbled at the outset. Again, I grant that on a legitimate reading, (R1) and (R2) are, within the framework of classical logic, logically equivalent. But  all  statements are not always so transparent in terms of their content. And this is a case where the nuances of the word  all  are relevant. I submit that once we make these nuances explicit, we will find that even within a classical framework, what is said (or at least meant or insinuated) by (R1) and (R2) is not equivalent.

When I use the term  cause , I mean to include partial causes. Obviously total causes are very hard to identify, and definitely are not to be found in the paradigms we are considering. When I say  x causes y , I mean  x is causative of y , not  x is causally sufficient for y  or even  x is causally necessary for y . If you eat rotten fish, that is causative of your becoming ill. But it is not sufficient; if you had different digestive processes you wouldn t have become ill. And it isn t even necessary: you could have eaten rotten pork. But, in some legitimate sense of the word  cause , your eating the fish is still a cause of your becoming ill. That is the sense in which  cause  is used in this paper. (It probably corresponds to Mackie s (1977) INUS analysis. But we can leave that aside.)

Again, not all the solutions take for granted the equivalence of R1 and R2. But those that do not invoke deviant or non-standard logics to block the equivalence. The essence of my discussion is that, read the appropriate way, (R1) and (R2) are not equivalent: if we give the  all  the appropriate valence, there is no equivalence   even within the strictures of classical logic. So no non-classical logics are resorted to. 
And this, surely, is a good thing. All other things being equal, it is usually best to try to solve a paradox within the framework of classical logic. Otherwise we run the risk of a global conceptual upheaval in our effort to deal with a relatively local one. We don t want to induce systemic alterations of our conceptual system unless no alternative is possible. The solution here doesn t involve systemic changes   it doesn t involve any non-conservative logical moves.

Examples of definite descriptions are  the king of France ,  the table , and  my neighbor . A definite description might be defined as one that is either (i) of the form  the phi  (where this expression is in the singular, not the plural, case) or (ii) as one that is synonymous with such an expression. So  the king of France  is a definite description by (i). And  my neighbor  is a definite description by (ii); for  my neighbor  is surely synonymous with  the person who is my neighbor.  The expression  the people over there  is not a definite description, since it is in the plural case.

[68] 
In this paper, by  proposition  I mean simply  sentence meaning.  I am not using the term to denote some specific conception of what a proposition. Everybody agrees that a proposition is the meaning of a sentence. Where people disagree is as to what sort of a thing a sentence-meaning is. Russell thought that such things are complexes of objects and properties. Others think that they are sets of possible worlds or functions from worlds to truth-values. My use of the word  proposition  is neutral with respect to these different theories as to what a proposition is; I am, to repeat, using the term to mean  sentence meaning , not to denote this or that particular theory as to what sort of a thing a sentence-meaning is.

In 1990 Stephen Neale published a brilliant defense of Russell s theory (Neale [1], chapters 5 and 6.) But the topic of D-questions and D-imperatives and D-optatives   of D-sentences that are not assertoric --is not mentioned even once, let alone discussed. And in 1984 Simon Blackburn wrote a brilliant exposition and defense of Russell s theory, which masterfully showed how a Russellian could deal with the fact that e.g.  the man in the corner is bald  might be de re about a certain man (which prima facie favors the view that  the man in the corner  is functioning as a referring expression and not pace Russell as a kind of quantifier) and with the fact that, if we heard  the king of France is bald  we would be unlikely to reply  that s false  (which prima facie suggests that  the King of France is bald  does not, pace Russell, assert that there is a king of France.) But Blackburn completely ignores the question whether the theory of descriptions applies to definite descriptions occurring in non-assertoric contexts. Kent Bach published an extended defense of the Theory of Descriptions, in which he ably challenged a number of traditional attacks on it. But he does not even a single time discuss D-questions or D-imperatives. In the anthologies on definite descriptions that I have read through, the only D-sentences discussed are D-assertions. (See e.g. Ostertag [1]. ) There is not a single mention of   let alone discussion of   the question whether Russell s theory is viable so far as definite descriptions occurring in non-assertoric contexts are concerned. For some reason, contemporary discussions of the viability of Russell s theory tend to concern anaphora (See e.g. Neale [1]) and the apparently referential function performed by (some uses of) definite descriptions, e.g.  the man in the corner is an economist ,  the table is covered with books. Notice that, if you disambiguate a sentence uncharitably, there is a feeling of strangeness or discomfort. Consider the following sequence:  Bob has no self-control. He can t strop drinking. He can t stop smoking. He can t stop gambling.  Now force yourself to disambiguate the boldfaced sentence uncharitably (i.e. read it to mean he can t prevent people in general from gambling). As long as you force yourself to read it that way, there is a feeling of discomfort. But once you disambiguate charitably   once you read it to mean he cannot resist his own compulsion to gamble   the sentence falls into place, and your feeling of discomfort vanishes. But now consider the following sequence:  Bob has no self-control. He can t strop drinking. He can t stop smoking. He can t prevent gambling.  The last sentence is not ambiguous between a meaning that is appropriate and one that is inappropriate. It is incorrigibly or irremediably out of place; and this is manifested by an ineradicable feeling of oddness (as opposed to the eradicable oddness borne by  He can t stop gambling  in (b).

One might object:  Suppose A said  Does your one neighbor drink?  Wouldn t that normalize his response?   I have two points to make in response. We ve already seen (section II) several reasons not to think that this tactic is available to the Russellian. For example, A s question seems to be a strict use of a definite description, if there ever was one (it is  proper ). But even if we leave that aside, the objector s point is doubtful. To my ear the following dialogue still sounds markedly strange even if we replace A s response with  does your one neighbor drink?  And the most obvious diagnosis of why it sounds strange is the one we ve given all along: that B is required, not to presuppose, but to assert the uniqueness and existence of A s neighbor, and that by using a definite description   even one with  one  added   he has really only presupposed this.

[81] 
It will be noticed that here I am talking as though force operators are applied not to bits of verbiage but to the meanings (propositions or fragments thereof) borne by bits of verbiage. This is indeed how I wish to be understood. Force-operators do not apply to sentences; they apply to propositions. Any (well-formed) sentence, by virtue of its grammatical properties, necessarily embodies a force.  Bob went to the store  already embodies a force; and so do  did Bob go to the store  and  make Bob go to the store.  So force-operators cannot significantly be applied to sentences   doing so would be redundant. However propositions are initially force-less. The sentences  did Bob go the store  and Bob went to the store  and  would that Bob went to the store  all encode the same proposition (Bob went to the store). But by virtue of their grammatical properties, these sentence embody the application of different force-operators to that same proposition. Basically the application of a force operator is expressed in natural language by such things as word order (in English the order of subject and verb is inverted in questions) and inflection (the tone of a question tends to be a rising one, whereas that of an assertion tends not to do this); in short, the application of a force operator is, in natural language,  written into  the grammar of a sentence (and is not usually indicated by the application of a single character). To sum up, it is propositions that are assigned forces, not sentences. Sentences come into existence already having force: a well-formed sentence is ipso facto something that has a force. Not so of a proposition.

[84] 
Notice I am not saying that the proposition in question would be Bob went to the store and did Bob buy some cheese. I am taking it for granted that  Bob bought some cheese  and  did Bob buy some cheese  are associated with the same proposition (Bob bought some cheese) but have different forces. I think it s a good idea not to try to assimilate force to propositional content: we want to be able to say that one can assert, ask, command one and the same proposition (at different times). If we reduce forces to components of propositions, then a given proposition will be capable only of being (say) asserted, not of being asked or commanded; and this is probably not the case.

Of course, oftentimes in writing, we encounter sentences that begin with  And : e.g.  people are mean. And they are greedy too.  But we shouldn t be misled by orthography here.  And they are greedy  cannot by itself be assigned a force. Obviously what is assigned a force is that sentence in conjunction with the preceding one. To make this clear, suppose someone came up to you out of the blue and said:  And people are greedy . You could obviously make sense of  people are greedy , but not of the  and . You would assume, I think, that either you were hearing the second conjunct of some conjunction or that you were hearing something that wasn t quite well-formed.

Technically, there is the option of saying that some sentences are, as wholes, to be assigned  mixed forces   are e.g. both questions and assertions   but (ii) that those sentences contain no well-formed assertoric part and/or no well-formed interrogative part. So  Bob went to the store and did Bob buy some cheese  is irreducibly a question-assertion: as a whole, it is a question-assertion, but it cannot be neatly divided into a part that is a question and a part that is an assertion. It would take us too far afield to argued against this. But surely I am not alone in feeling that such a proposal stretches the limits of the intelligible. In any case, it is ad hoc.

Suppose I say:  I wish to know whether the king of France went to the store; therefore there is something I wish to know.  At the level of literal meaning, those words express a valid argument. It is hard to see how replacing a synonymous sentence with a synonymous sentence could turn good sense into nonsense. So surely  I wish to know whether the king of France went to the store  is not synonymous with  did the king of France go the store?

Clarence Lewis (1929) argued compellingly that every statement about the physical world   even those that seem to have no counter-factual component   are in fact implicitly counterfactual. When you say that something is steel, you are saying something about how it would behave if it were subjected to certain conditions. I am inclined to agree with Lewis. There is no way to purge our discourse of counter-factual elements. So we have to find a way to make counterfactuals work. 
[96] Lewis 1973 (1). 
[97] When they are true. 
[98] 
Though perhaps not in all his views, e.g. his modal realism. But the truth is that Lewis  modal realism is, I think, common sense through to its logical conclusion. It is usually thought that Lewis  modal realism   his belief that possible worlds are real worlds that are not identical with this one   is a monstrosity created by a logician with his head in the clouds. The truth is, in my view, that the ordinary person thinks of counterfactuals in factualist terms: as expressing relations among concrete things   states of affairs   with the qualification that these concrete things don t exist here. But unless one is willing to take a completely non-factualist view   is willing to see counterfactuals as something like disguised probability statements   then it is (I think) impossible to avoid modal realism. For any state of affairs is per force a concrete state of affairs: something that exists in space and time. A  non-concrete  state of affairs must be an obscure way of saying  proposition  or  concept . And , of course, a concrete thing can exist only in a concrete world, not a merely possible one. For a  merely possible concrete world  is an oxymoron. 
Lewis  modal realism is, in this respect, like Wittgenstein s picture theory. The picture theory has always been reviled. But if one takes seriously the idea that a proposition s being true consists in its  corresponding  with the facts   and how could one not take such a view?   then, of course, one must say what this  correspondence  consists in. And   although the picture theory is probably false 
  the picture theory is the only non-trivial conception, thus far produced, of what that correspondence consists in. I think the picture theory delineates a conceit that is operative in virtually everyone s thinking about propositions: only, before Wittgenstein came along, it was never stated clearly, so the falsity of it was never seen. Inevitably, Wittgenstein was attacked. But really we should be attacked for endorsing the picture-theory (if, in fact, it is wrong). Similarly, although Lewis is attacked for his modal realism, he is, I think, simply saying in a logically developed way what everybody thinks in an inchoate, confused way. So if modal realism is wrong (which, I argue, it is: at least in connection with counter-factuals), it is not Lewis who should be attacked, but us.

[114] The obvious response is this: 
Suppose that Bob and Bob* have the exact same beliefs concerning what has happened, but Bob knows about laws that Bob* doesn t know about. For example, Bob knows that metal expands when heated, Bob* doesn t know this, but their respective knowledge of what has happened   of what states of affairs have obtained   is the same. In that case, Bob and Bob* can rationally assign different probabilities to, say, the possibility of some metal s expanding upon being heated. 
Fine. But remember that whatever probability can reasonably be attached to a putative law of nature, the sole basis for that evaluation must lie in what has happened: ultimately all probability-assessments flow from what has happened and, indeed, from what is known. Of course, Bob may believe in some law L not because he has personally witnessed states of affairs that confirm it, but because some scientist told him about it or because he read about it in a book written by an authority. But in this case, Bob s  knowledge  is obviously parasitic on other people s knowledge of singular states of affairs. In the end, what gives probability to a position is the totality of known singular states of affairs. So the way to respond to the objector is to say: if we leave aside parasitic knowledge (like Bob s knowledge of the laws of physics) or, alternatively, if we take into account the singular knowledge had by the communities to which Bob and Bob* belong, and from which their knowledge of laws is derivative, then there cannot be a divergence in the probability-assessments of these two people unless one of them is being irrational or, in any case, unless one of them is evaluating the data less competently than the other.

[120] 
Just as, in my view,  probably  would be ambiguous if it had both epistemic and non-epistemic meanings. That is why I think, even in statements like  the probability the electron will jump is .8  the  probably  is really epistemic. The electron will either jump or it won t. It could be that there s no law, and no hidden variable, that  makes  it jump now as opposed to later. It could be that it just jumps. Let us suppose that to be the case. Where, in that picture, is there room for non-epistemic probability? I see room for epistemic probability: in the past, 80% of cases like this one have involved the electron jumping, and the other s have not. So the current situation gives an 80% probability to the proposition the electron jumps. But what about  objective  probability? What is it for something other than a proposition to probabilify something other than a proposition? Do the circumstances involving electrons make the electron jump 80% of the time but not the other 20% of the time. That would be incoherent. By assumption there is no hidden variable; nothing is making anything happen in the one set of cases that isn t also operative in the other. So does the  objective  probability in this case mean that the state of the universe prior to the electron jumping is 80% responsible for its jumping? That is even more blatantly incoherent. When we have an irreducibly indeterministic law   a law that doles out probabilities (of less than 100%) that we can t exchange for deterministic laws, no matter how much we come to know   we are still dealing with purely epistemic probabilities: the only difference is that, in this sort of case, an increase in knowledge won t change the probabilities, whereas when we are dealing with reducibly probabilistic laws (e.g. 75% of people shot in the chest die), we can, with increases in knowledge, exchange that law for ones that dole out probabilities closer to (and sometimes coincident with) 100%.

Let me explain the  very roughly  qualification. A token of  that I am tired  is not true or false. If I 
say, simply,  that I am tired , I have not said anything true or false, even though the proposition 
denoted by my words is true or false. On the other hand, a token of  I am tired  is true or false. So there 
is a semantic difference between a token of  I am tired  and a token of  that I am tired , even though, 
plainly, those expressions are closely related in meaning. So the semantic content that a token of  I am 
tired  is assigned by the corresponding type is different from the semantic content had by  that I am 
tired . After all, a token of  I am tired  is true or false, whereas a token of  that I am tired  is neither. 
Thus the type  I am tired  does more than assign propositions to its tokens; it seems to assign 
propositions plus assertoric force-operators. So it is not entirely accurate to say that the semantic 
content of  I am tired  is a function that assigns propositions to its tokens: the function in question assigns propositions and it also assigns a force to the propositions. But in this context, it will help discussion if we speak approximately, and say that the semantic content of the type  I am tired  is a function that assigns propositions to its tokens. This slight inaccuracy won t vitiate any of the points argued for here. And it can be corrected by mentally replaced the term  proposition  with  proposition plus assertoric force .

See Barwise and Perry 1999, and also McCawley 1981. This point pervades linguistic literature. 
[126] 
Keep in mind the caveat stated in the first footnote. The meaning of the type  I am tired  is a 
function that assigns propositions plus forces to its tokens; that function doesn t merely assign 
propositions to its tokens   though, of course, it does do that. [127] 
Given the right circumstances, one could use any term, no matter what its literal meaning, to refer 
to anything. I could sarcastically use the term  Genghis Kahn  to refer to Bob. Such a usage is non-
literal. I can use  Plato  in a literal way to refer to Plato. Obviously this fact is fact is essentially 
connected to the fact that  Plato  refers to Plato. [128] 
Give or take some subtleties relating to force. Strictly speaking, the semantic content of a token 
of  I am tired  is in part a proposition. But that semantic content also has assertoric force. That is 
why a token of  am I tired  won t have the same exact semantic content as a token of  I am tired , 
even though both may encode the very same proposition [129] 

The special cases I have in mind are analytic propositions like  Socrates is identical with Socrates . It isn t even clear that a grasp of the semantic content of these sentences necessarily involves a grasp of their truth. Even if it does, that has nothing to do with semantics; it has to do with epistemology. 
[130] 
There is an obvious   and erroneous --way to deal with this. One can say: 
 You say that  presumably, the referent of a referring term is at least part of its semantic content . But your presumption is wrong. The referent of a referring term is not a part of its semantic content.  The inventor of bifocals  has the same semantic in both w and w*, even though it refers to different things in those worlds. This is perfectly acceptable. What an expression refers to simply doesn t have anything to do with what its semantic content is.  
The position is a non-starter.  Plato  refers to Plato. Its having that referent is, to say the least, an integral part of its semantics. If  Plato  referred to Aristotle it would have a very different semantics. So it really isn t feasible to deny that what a term refers to is an integral part of its semantic content. 
Frege actually did hold that, even if  Plato  referred to Aristotle, it wouldn t necessarily have a different semantic content from what it actually has. For the semantic content of  Plato , in Frege s view, is a sense; and so long as it  Plato  keeps the same sense, it keeps the same semantic content: it doesn t matter whether its referent changes. So a Fregean might deny our claim that reference is essential to semantic content. 
Later on, we ll see that, if Frege were right about  Plato , then  Plato  would actually be a quantifier, and not an expression that referred to some individual. But our defense of this will have to wait. 
But right now we can make a couple of points that render Frege s position innocuous, at least in this context. First of all, given what Kripke said, it is pretty clear that Frege is wrong about  Plato . Kripke s work also makes it clear that, if  Plato  had a different referent, it would have a different 
semantic content. Putnam s work also makes this clear. If  water  referred to xyz, as opposed to H2O, it would have a very different semantic content. So, to say the least, it is unnatural to deny that, if a term refers, its reference is integral to its semantic content. Conceivably, one could counter by saying: 
 Granted, the referent of a proper name, like  Plato , is part of its semantic content. But this is not the case with other referring terms (e.g.  you ,  the inventor of bifocals ). In some cases, reference is essential to semantic content; in others, it is not.  
But this is an extremely tortured and arbitrary view. It is clear that where some referring terms 
(e.g. proper names) are concerned, reference and semantic contribution are inextricably linked. If we say that this is not the case where other referring terms are concerned, we are in a position like that of someone who says  atomic structure is essential to some elements, but quite inessential to others . So it is surely best not to say  the referent of a referring term is no part of its semantic content . To put it in positive terms, if an expression refers to something, its referring to that thing is an integral part of its semantics. A corollary is that if two expressions refer to different things, then they have different semantics. 
So we still have a conundrum. If two expressions refer to different things, then they have different semantic contents. At the same time, it seems that if  the inventor of bifocals  is a singular term, then it can refer to different things in different worlds, while keeping the same semantics.

Where definite descriptions are concerned, the context of utterance is defined by much more than just the world in which the tokening occurred. But the niceties are not important here. What is important here is that if  the inventor of bifocals  is taken as a non-quantifier, then what a token of it refers to is semantically dependent on the context of utterance, in some sense of the word  context . 
[133] 

It should be made clear that the foregoing discussion has nothing to do with the actual semantics of definite descriptions. Some hold that  the inventor of bifocals  is not a singular term; it is a 
[133] quantifier, and   the inventor of bifocals   means (roughly ): something x uniquely invented bifocals and x So  the inventor of bifocals snored  means: something x uniquely invented bifocals and x snored. 
Even if this view is right, it in no way confutes our principle that, if a term refers, one must know what it refers to know its semantic content. Quite the contrary. Let us define  ze phi  as follows. If there some x such that x is a unique phi, then  ze phi  refers to x. If there is no such x, then  ze phi  is abortive. Everything we just said about  the phi  applies to  ze phi . Suppose that, in w and w*,  ze inventor of bifocals  has the same semantics. But in w*, it refers to Franklin, whereas in w* it refers to Jefferson. Here we seem to have a case where a single expression has a semantics but variable reference. But, for reasons we ve seen, we don t want to say this; and there is an easy way to avoid saying this. The type  ze inventor of bifocals  has the same semantics in both w and w*. But the semantic content of the type is a function that assigns referents to its tokens. The type itself doesn t refer to anything. So our principle continues to be upheld. (For our principle is: if an expression refers to something, one must know to what it refers if one is to know its semantics.) Tokens of  ze inventor of bifocals  are what refer. The semantic content of such a token is what the function described a moment ago assigns to it; so the semantic content of such a token is its referent. Thus, to know the semantic content of a token of  ze inventor of bifocals , one must know what that referent is. 
[134] This is how Richard Montague, along with many other contemporary semanticists, think of 
 and ,  not , and other connectives. [135] 

This line of thought is obviously not an innocuous one, and perhaps requires development. I would like to outline how that development would go. The sentence: 
(sn)  snow is not white  
is equivalent to: 
(sn*) not* <snow is white>, 
where  not*  ascribes falsity to the proposition encoded in the sentence-token falling in its scope. So the  not  in (sn) can be seen as a second-level property   on that ascribes falsity to the proposition encoded in the sentence-token falling in its scope. (Equivalently, it can be seen as encoding a function that assigns truth to a sentence-token exactly if the proposition encoded in that token is false.) The reason that  snow is white  occurs truth-functionally in (sn) and (sn*) is not that it contributes a truth-value; it is that a truth-value (falsity) is ascribed to the proposition it encodes. So we see, once again, that for a sentence-token to occur truth-functionally is not for it to contribute a truth-value; it is for a truth-value to be ascribed to the proposition that it encodes. 
The case is not significantly different when we re dealing with atomic sentences. But here we have to proceed very cautiously. Obviously the truth of 
(sw)  snow is white  
depends on whether the proposition encoded in that sentence (namely that snow is white) has the property of truth. We ve seen that, when it occurs in the scope of  and  or  not ,  snow is white  doesn t contribute a truth-value. It would be highly unnatural to suppose that  snow is white  makes one semantic contribution in (sg) and a different one in (sw). It very much seems to make the same contribution in both. We ve seen that, in (sg),  snow is white  does not contribute a truth-value. 
Given all of this, here is what I would propose. In (sw),  snow is white  isn t flanked by any verbiage. So it is occurring in what is sometimes called a  null  context. Null contexts, as linguists know, are often semantically pregnant. (They are null in a phonetic, not necessarily a semantic sense.) In English, when a sentence-token occurs in a null-context, truth is to be ascribed to the proposition encoded in that sentence-token. The null context is thus a phonetically invisible way of ascribing truth to the proposition encoded in the sentence. But here the relevant point is that what ascribes truth   what contributes the truth-value true   is, strictly speaking, the null context, not the token  snow is white  per se. 
Here is another way of looking at it. Whether the sentence-token: 
(st)  that snow is white is true . 
is true is a function of whether that snow is white is true. As we saw, this is equivalent to saying that (st) attributes truth to that proposition. Obviously (sw) is a function of whether that snow is white is true. So (sw) attributes truth to that proposition. Thus, (st) attributes truth to that snow is white and so does (sw); and neither does anything besides that. (st) is true exactly if that snow is white is true, and the same holds of (sw). So the differences between (st) and (sw) do not lie in what they say. Those differences appear to have nothing to do with content and to be entirely phonetic. In the case of (st), the ascription of truth is phonetically realized. In the case of (sw), it is not phonetically realized. Given this, it seems reasonable to say that, in the case of (sw), the absence of phonetically realized neighboring material performs the very function that, in the case of (st), is performed by phonetically realized material.

Frege actually gives two quite distinct arguments for the thesis that sentences refer to truth-values. For reasons of space, I will consider only the second (the slingshot). If cogent, the first argument   the one I don t give   shows that sentences do refer to truth-values. If cogent, the second one   the famous one (the  slingshot )   only shows that if sentences refer to anything, it is to truth-values.

Where definite descriptions are concerned, the context of utterance is defined by much more than just the world in which the tokening occurred. But the niceties are not important here. With some qualifications, I believe this point can be extended to the distinction between intension and extension. The word  whale , we are told, has both intension and extension. The intension is a property or function (from objects to the truth-values). The extension is the class of whales (Shamu, Willy, Moby Dick ) 
But there is no one expression that has both intension and extension. Tokens of  whale  have extension; the expression-type  whale  have intension. Nothing has both. We don t want to say that the expression-type  whales  denotes different classes in different worlds, while having the same semantics. That is perilously close to absurdity. 
What we say is: tokens of  whales  denote different classes in different worlds; the type has an 
invariant meaning: it pairs off a token of  whale  in a world W with a class C iff C is the class 
containing al and only whales in W. So intensions are the semantics of expression-types. Extensions are the semantic content of 
expression-tokens. So what has  intension  is entirely different entity from what has  extension . Having said this, the parallel between  the inventor of bifocals  and  whales  is not perfect. Consider the sentence  whales are mammals . This is capable of very different readings. (Whether we are dealing with a semantic distinction, or merely a pragmatic one, is a question I leave open.) It is capable of both  referential  and  attributive  readings. The attributive reading is this: 
(A) 
if a thing is a whale, then it is a mammal. 

The referential reading is: 

(R) 
Shamu and Willy and Moby Dick are mammals. 


The referential reading says of those things that are whales that they are mammals. The referential reading is to the effect that the things that are actually whales are mammals; so the referential reading makes the proposition in question turn on the mammal-hood of Willy, Shamu, and so on. It is object-involving with respect to those creatures. 
The same is true (mutatis mutandis) if all plural nouns. They can be read attributively, as quantifiers, or they can be read referentially, as terms that pick out the things that in fact have the relevant property. 
If  whales  is a quantifier, then one can understand a token of  whales are mammals  without knowing exactly which things are whales. (This is the reading that Frege (1884) favored.) If  whales  is what it appears to   a term that refers to the actual whales that exist   then one could not understand a token of  whales are mammals  without knowing exactly which things are whales. 
This would seem to favor the attributive analysis of  whales . But such a conclusion would be premature. (Similar conclusions favor the view that Kaplan s  Newman 1  is not a referring term. But it is a referring term.) 
But, in this context, the relevant point is that, if anything has for its extension the class of those things that are whales in this world, that thing is not the expression-type  whale : rather tokens of that type have that extension. If  whales  is a quantifier, then nothing   not the type  whale  and not tokens of it   has that class for its extension. Either way, there is never any one thing that has both intension and extension. If anything has that extension, it is tokens of  whales  (or  men  or  swans ), and not the type  whale . And if anything has that intension, it is the type  whale  (or  men  or  swans ), not tokens thereof. 
Granted, matters are more complicated than I ve made them out to be. For there different attributive readings of, for example,  whales are mammals , and different referential readings of that sentence. Sometimes when a person says  x s are y s , he means that some x s are y s ( people kill other people ); sometimes he means that all x s are in fact y s ( all antelopes are in Brazil ); sometimes he means that not all x s are y s, but there is some kind of tendency for x s to be y s ( people are mean ); sometimes he means that, as a matter of necessity, nothing can be an x without being a y ( all pieces of metal conduct electricity ,  all triangles are planar figures . I myself do not think that plural nouns have different meanings corresponding to all these different readings. The significant semantic question is: is  whales  ambiguous between referential and attributive readings? It is, I think, safe to assume that the various sub-readings within those two categories are generated by pragmatics. In any case, the principle we ve been arguing for holds up no matter how the actual semantics turns out; there is never any one entity that has both intension and extension. 
A historical point might be made here. Frege said that  whales are mammals  doesn t say anything about whales. People balk at this. But this reasoning is good. According to him, that sentence means: if a thing is a whale, it is a mammal. It doesn t say that this or that particular thing is a mammal. So if we consider the whales that exist   Shamu, Willy -- whales are mammals  does not say of any one of them that it is a mammal. Therefore  whales are mammals  doesn t say anything about any whale. 
So Frege s view is plausible. But it has the counter-intuitive consequence that  whales are mammals  doesn t say anything about any actual whale. It should be pointed out that there is a reading of  whales are mammals  on which it does make a statement about whales. That is the referential reading. In my view, the referential reading is probably the one that is closest to its literal meaning. On the referential reading,  whales are mammals  says of those things that are actually whales that they are mammals. 
But the referential reading has the counter-intuitive consequence that one doesn t know what (a token of)  whales are mammals  means unless one knows exactly which things are whales and which aren t. And no human being does know that.

See Barwise and Perry (1990: 398-400): 
 Church gives a form of the slingshot .Church considers these sentences: 
(5) 
Sir Walter Scott is the author of Waverly. 

(6) 
Sir Walter Scott is the man who wrote the twenty-nine Waverly novels altogether. 

(7) 
The number, such that Sir Walter Scott is the man that wrote that many Waverly novels altogether, is twenty-nine. 

(8) 
The number of counties in Utah is twenty-nine. 


Church argues that we as go from each sentence to the next, what the sentences denote is the same. But the first and last seem to have nothing in common except their truth-value; he says,  elaboration of examples of this kind leads us quickly to the conclusion, at least plausible, that all sentences have the same denotation.  
Sentence (6) results from (5) by replacement of one description by another, where both descriptions describe the same person, Scott. Sentence (*) results from (&) by a similar move, with the descriptions describing th same number, twenty-nine. The step form (6) to (7), however, is of a different sort. Church says that (6), though perhaps, not synonymous with (&),  is t least so nearly so as to ensure having the same denotation.  
The argument is like an ambiguous figure or an Escher drawing. If you are aware of situations, you have to keep shifting perspective to let the argument trick you. From one perspective the first and last steps re fine but the middle step is all wrong. From a second perspective the middle step is reasonably good but he fist and last steps are completely unfounded. 
Intuitively, situations are complexes of objects and relations (under which we shall from now on subsume properties). Given this conception, the role of the parts of the sentence to identify objects and relations out of which the complex is constructed, Let us hold this in mind, and go through the steps of the ar4gument from both perspectives. 
To get from (5) to (6), we need to suppose that the great difference between  the author of Waverly  and  th mean who wrote twenty-nine Waverly novels altogether  makes absolutely no difference to the situations described by the two sentences, that is, that the contribution these two descriptions make to the situation is just to identify Scott. Thus, the first perspective is the one where all four definite descriptions are interpreted by the objects they happen to describe, Scott in two cases, the number twenty-nine in the other two. 
But from this perspective, the step from (6) to (7) does not work at all. Recall we are attempting to show that all four sentences must designate the same situations. But from our current perspective [that according to which sentences designate situations], (6) designates a situation whose only constituent object is Scott, whereas, (7) designates one whose only constituent object is the number twenty-nine. 
Now let us focus on the step from (6) to (7). If we attempt to see these sentences as designating the same situation, then it must be that of Scott s having written exactly twenty-nine Waverly novels altogether. To see them as designating this situation, however, we must pay close attention to the properties involved in the definite descriptions. This is not unreasonable. If you take situations seriously, it quite natural to distinguish two ways in which descriptions might contribute to the sentences. The need is for the material to build t a situation, a complex of objects and properties, and why should the description not contribute the individual described or the properties involved in the description of the situation? 
Thus, the second perspective, which is suggested anyway if we take situations seriously, is the one where  the author of Waverly  is not interpreted simply as Scott, but contributes the complex of objects and properties it mentions to the situation the sentence describes. But this perspective is absolutely fatal to the step from (5) to (6) or from (7) to (8). The descriptions of Scott, and those of twenty-nine even more so, contribute radically different objects and properties to the overall situation. Sentence (7) designates twenty-nine s being the number of Waverly novels Scott wrote, but sentence (8) designates twenty-nine s being the number of counties in Utah: distinct situations if ever there were distinct situations. 
So we see that from the first perspective, the one Frege would have us take, wherein the reference of the description all that is specific is obliterated, the first and last steps of the argument are fine but eh middle is all wrong. From the second perspective, more in line with Russell s theory of descriptions, the middles step comes of better but the first and last steps are wrong. Under neither reading are we compelled to accept the argument.  
For right now, let us focus only the very last sentence of this passage:  Under neither reading are we compelled to accept the [slingshot].  
The readings in question are, basically, the one where the definite description contributes only its referent and the one where it contributes a complex of properties: the referential and the attributive. 
Read referentially, the argument fails. Read attributively the argument fails. 
This is the real point that Barwise and Perry are making. And it is correct. 
But in their exposition of this point, they keep on adverting to their situation-semantics; they make it seem as though the argument they are presenting requires us to sign off on the idea that sentences contribute situations. 
Their argument does not really require this. But their exposition makes us think otherwise. And this, presumably, accounts for criticisms like the following (Olson 1998: 96-97): 
 Thus, according to Barwise and Perry, we are free to interpret our descriptions any way we like, so long as we choose one interpretation and stick to it, instead of changing in the middle of an argument. 
This is a persuasive diagnosis, and the accompanying prescription certainly removes the symptoms. But it relies quite explicitly upon the structuralist criterion, taking for granted that where there are different constituents there must be different facts.  
Olson then goes on to say how, according to some viewpoints, one and the same fact can be analyzed into different constituents. Therefore, the  structuralist criterion  is questionable. Therefore, Olson concludes, what Barwise and Perry say against the slingshot is questionable. 
Olson is wrong. What Barwise and Perry say about the slingshot doesn t require that one adopt a  structuralist  or any other conception of facts or propositions or situations or meanings. Their attack on the slingshot is totally neutral on these matters. 
Their thesis that sentences stand for situations is another matter. But that is a different thing from their attack on the slingshot. 
Barwise and Perry (1999: 23-26) give a shorter version of their argument against the Slingshot. The problem is that the argument they give there is far worse than the argument just quoted. In Barwise and Perry (1999) they simply assume that logically equivalent sentences may differ in reference. This obviously makes their argument less than compelling. 
Neale (2001, 1995) devoted an entire book, and a very long article, to the Slingshot. (The article was absorbed into the book practically verbatim.) Astonishingly, he says essentially nothing about Barwise and Perry (1990) or Barwise and Perry (1999). He mentions Barwise and Perry (1990), but somehow doesn t register its importance or even its relevance, except to some minor technical problems. Perry (2000: 290-294) restates the view just quoted from Barwise and Perry (1990/1983). But Perry s (2000) restatement is even more opaque than the 1990 version.

It is, I believe, a completely dispensable part. Consider the following semantic rule. If there some person x who uniquely was a protagonist in most of Plato s dialogues, then let  SOC  refer to x. If there is no such person, then let  SOC  refer to nothing. 
Obviously  SOC  refers to Socrates every bit as much  Socrates  does. But it seems that one s being able to use  SOC  to refer to Socrates doesn t involve having any particular causal connection to Socrates. 
The causal theorist is guilty of the same fallacy as the descriptivist. Both confuse reference-fixing with meaning-giving. The descriptivist says:  Socrates  means  the unique hemlock drinking philosopher . He says that to refer is to describe. Descriptions are certainly exploited by semantic rules, as we just saw. We can invent rules that assign G del to  G del  by way of descriptions. (An example is: if there is some x such that x uniquely proved the incompleteness of arithmetic, then let  G del  refer to x. Here a description is being exploited to assign a referent to a word. But the reference relation   not here, not anyway   is identical with the describing relation. Similarly, causal relations can be exploited by semantic rules. We can say  if there is some entity x such that uniquely stands in R [some causal relation] to tokens of  Igaguk , then let any such token refer to x.  Here a causal relation is being exploited by a semantic rule assigning a referent to a word   just as a description can be. But no causal relation   not here, not anywhere   is ever identical with the reference relation. It were absurd to think otherwise.

I myself have no doubt that quantifiers are referring terms and that they refer to second-order properties. But, strictly speaking, the properties in question are properties, not of propositions or of open-propositions, but of sequences of such things. The quantifier  for all x  refers to a property had by certain sequences of open-propositions.  For all x, x is mortal, if x is a man  says: The sequence <x is a man, x is mortal> is such that anything instantiating the first member instantiates the second. 
So, in that case,  for all x  denotes the property is such that anything instantiating the first member

On the Fregean view,  1+1=2  and  triangles have three sides  do indeed co-refer. Indeed, on the Fregean view, they co-refer, as a matter of logical necessity. At first this seems to be an advantage over my view. It is not. 
When two sentences are said to be  logically equivalent , S-equivalence is not what is meant. If you ask a competent person,  what is it for two sentences to be logically equivalent? , he absolutely will not say:  it is for the open proposition that a thing must satisfy to be picked out by the one expression to entail, and be entailed by, the open proposition that a thing must satisfy to be picked out by the other.  What he will say is: it is for the proposition meant by the one to entail, and be entailed by, the proposition meant by the other. So the kind of  logical equivalence  that people have in mind when they talk of logically equivalent sentences is not the kind of  logical equivalence  that people have in mind when they talk about expressions like  Plato  and  the unique x such that 1+1=2 and x=Plato . When it said that two sentences are  logically equivalent , S-equivalence is not meant; so the kind of  logical equivalence  that guarantees co-reference is not what is meant. Some completely different kind of logical equivalence is meant. And this other kind of logical equivalence has very little to do with co-reference. So to think that  1+1=2  and  triangles have three sides  must co-refer because they are  logically equivalent  is to make the false and confused assumption that those two sentences are logically equivalent in the sense in which  Plato  and  the unique x such that 1+1=2 and x=Plato  are logically equivalent. We have two very different notions of logical equivalence here, not one. The one kind of logical equivalence involves co-reference. But that leaves it totally open whether the other kind involves co-reference. 
Let us close the argument. It is often thought that 1+1=2  and  triangles have three sides  must co-refer. Frege thought this; so do all proponents of slingshot arguments. The reasoning behind this view is: 
Those two sentences  logically equivalent ; and  logically equivalent expressions    e.g.  Plato  and  the unique x such that 1+1=2 and x=Plato    must co-refer. 
But that view involves a complete failure to distinguish to kinds of  logical equivalence . And the view that a correct semantic theory must make logically equivalent sentences co-refer is based on that very confusion. So, therefore, is the view that Frege s analysis has an advantage over mine, in that his view makes  logically equivalent  sentences co-refer while mine does not. The idea that that is an advantage involves a confusion of two very different meanings of the term  logically equivalent .
