Strawson believed the same thing mutatis mutandis to hold of any other ascription of moral responsibility. So held that, if they are true, the statements 
(b) Â“X should be blamed for doing YÂ“ and 
(c) Â“X is responsible for doing Y, but does not on that account deserve either praise or blameÂ” 
hold in virtue of, respectively, the fact that (b*) Y is counterstatistical in a way that we donÂ’t like and the fact that (c*) Y is not counterstatistical. 
If Strawson is right, X doesnÂ’t even have to have intentions for any of these statements to be true. Strawson's position thus entails that intentions either donÂ’t exist or donÂ’t do anything and therefore might as well not exist. 
Strawson's analysis of ascriptions of moral responsibility is obviously false. Inanimate objects donÂ’t have intentions; so we canÂ’t be held responsible for anything. And it's only a person's behavior is the result of an intention of his that we hold him responsible for it. We donÂ’t hold somebody with ParkinsonÂ’s responsible for his tremors. 
If Strawson were right, a corpse that fell on Smith could appropriately be blamed for Smith's subsequent death. But we don't blame the corpse; we blame the prankster who threw the corpse off a nearby rooftop. 
Strawson is saying that whether a given person has a given intention depends on whether we ascribe an intention to him. So he's advocating the antithesis of the traditional view, which I regard as self-evidently correct, that whether that ascription is correct depends on whether that person has that intention. Strawson's view turns the living into the dead and the dead into the living. Sad about grandma's death? No problem! Just ascribe an intention to her---that'll bring her back. Don't like your boss? No need to worry! Just stop ascribing intentions to him---that'll zombify him. 
Strawson was a brilliant man. So why did he advocate this grotesquely mistaken view? Because Wittgenstein advocated it. But whereas Wittgenstein said obscurely and he provided no argument for it, Strawson said it clearly and provided a semblance of an argument for it. So Strawson's article wasn't redundant. 

4.2.3.2 StrawsonÂ’s expressivism 
According to Strawson, the expression Â“trueÂ” means nothing. Â“It is true that snow is whiteÂ” has the same meaning as Â“snow is white.Â” In prefacing the words Â“snow is whiteÂ“ with the words Â“it is true thatÂ”, one is doing in a polite way what one would be doing in an impolite way by shouting Â“snow is whiteÂ” while banging oneÂ’s fist on a table: one is showing oneÂ’s collocutor how convinced one is that snow is white. So the term Â“trueÂ” helps one express oneÂ’s feelings about a claim: they give one a civil way of express oneÂ’s certainty as to its truth. But thatÂ’s all that word does. 
Strawson's expressivism is no less misguided than his acriptivism. First of all, the word Â“trueÂ” is not redundant. There is no sentence that means that same thing as Â“everything Plato said was trueÂ” that doesnÂ’t contain the word Â“trueÂ” or some synonym thereof. Suppose that S1.Â…Sn is a complete list of 
everything every said by Plato. The sentence Â“everything Plato said was trueÂ” would not have the same meaning as Â“S1 is true and S2 is true andÂ…Sn is 
true.Â” Supposing that S37 is the proposition that there are infinitely many prime numbers, the statement Â“everything Plato said is true, but Plato never said that there are infinitely many prime numbersÂ”, though false, would be coherent. (That's why one would have to know about PlatoÂ’s life to know whether that statement was true or not.) But statement Â“Plato said that there are infinitely many prime numbers and Plato never said that there are infinitely many prime numbersÂ” would contradict itself. (That's why one wouldn't have to know anything about PlatoÂ’s life to know whether that 
statement was true or not.)[17] 

"What about StrawsonÂ’s claim that Â“snow is whiteÂ” and Â“it is true that snow is whiteÂ” are synonymous? Surely that's got to be right." 
It is not. The first attributes a color to a substance. The second attributes a truth-value to a proposition; so the second, unlike the first, is only indirectly about snow. Consider the sentence: Â“it is probable that snow is white.Â” That sentence clearly concerns a proposition. Snow is either white or it isnÂ’t. When you say that snow is probably white, youÂ’re not saying that itÂ’s vaguely white or that its whiteness is only semi-existent. You are saying that, in saying that snow is white one, what one is saying is more likely than not to be correct. 
The meaning had by the expression Â“that snow is whiteÂ” in Â“it is probable that snow is whiteÂ” coincides with counterpart in Â“it is true that snow is white.Â” So the latter, though equivalent with "snow is white", is about a proposition about snow, and therefore isnÂ‘t in any direct sense about snow. Â“Snow is whiteÂ“, on the other hand, clearly does directly concern snow. Two statements are equivalent if neither can possibly be true if the other is false. 
Strawson had precisely the sort of intelligence one needs to see that, for these reasons, Â“trueÂ” is meaningful. So why did Strawson say otherwise? Because Wittgenstein said otherwise. 
Why did Wittgenstein say otherwise? An integral part of WittgensteinÂ’s philosophical system is that meanings donÂ’t exist. Wittgenstein granted that some noises were meaningful and that others werenÂ’t; but he denied that there are such things as meanings. 
Why did Wittgenstein hold this? It's a corollary of his rejection of the presumption that a least part of what distinguishes my saying Â“itÂ’s raining,Â” which is a genuinely linguistic act, from a coffee machine's accidentally making those the same noises, which is not a linguistic act, is that, in the first case but not the second, those noises resulted from intentions embodying certain beliefs (e.g. my belief that it's raining). A belief is necessarily a belief that such and such is the case: the object of a belief is always a proposition. A proposition is what one affirms when one makes a statement (e.g. when one sincerely says "it's raining"). Since Wittgenstein didnÂ’t believe in beliefs, he didnÂ’t believe in meanings; and since he didnÂ’t believe in meanings, he didnÂ’t think that Â“trueÂ”, which denotes a property of meanings, can possibly have a meaning. 
Of course, it isn't just propositions that can be described as "true." Occurrences of sentences can also be so described. But, in saying Â“JimmyÂ’s words are the truth," one is saying in an abbreviated that the thing Jimmy affirmed is true. And propositions are, by definition, things that are affirmed (and denied and questioned, etc.). 



4.3 WittgensteinÂ’s expressivism and the erroneousness thereof 
Wittgenstein dedicated the second half of his professional career to establishing the non-existence of beliefs and everything else that exist only if meanings do as well. This led him to make a number of demonstrably false claims. 
One of such claim is that, if a person says Â“I am in painÂ”, he is no more stating anything about his mind than he would be by writhing in agony. Saying "I am in pain," according to Wittgenstein, is merely a way of showing that one is in pain. So it's meaningless, except in the same non-linguistic sense as a baby's sobbing. 
HereÂ’s one way of showing that this position is false. Suppose that, in response to your saying that I am in pain but am trying to conceal it, I say: 
(A) If I am in pain, then certain neurons in my brain are firing that wouldnÂ’t otherwise be firing; since, with the help of modern technology, I can demonstrate to you that those neurons are not firing, it is not the case that I am in pain. 
If Wittgenstein were right to say that Â“I am in painÂ” was as devoid of meaning (in the linguistic sense) as the pain-driven howling of an injured animal, then (A) would have the same meaning, or lack thereof, as: 
(B) If aaargh!, then certain neurons in my brain are firing that wouldnÂ’t otherwise be firing; since, with the help of 
modern technology, it is not the case that ouch![18] 

But B is meaningless and A is meaningful. So they don't have the same meaning, and Wittgenstein is wrong. 

4.4 John Austin: WittgensteinÂ’s final victim 
This blunder of WittgensteinÂ’s led John Austin (1911-1960), a faithful follower of his to make a similar, albeit subtler, mistake. Here is Austin's reasoning[19]: 
(AA)[20] 
Let S be a case of my saying to a friend: "I promise to give you a ride to the airport" S is not affirmation of some pre-existing fact. The promised referred to in S is S itself. But S doesn't describe itself. No utterance describes itself (with a few contrived exceptions, e.g. "this statement is false"). But, supposing for argument's sake that S does describe itself, S's function isn't to describe itself, but rather to oblige the person who uttered it to perform a certain act. 
For exactly similar reasons, if a preacher says: "I now pronounce you man and wife," he's not describing some preÂ­existing fact. In uttering those words, the preacher was performing a social function. His wasn't a descriptive, but performative utterance, as was S. 
Performative utterances are meaningful. S isn't like "glarbojibjibjabber." Therefore, it isn't in virtue of affirming propositions that performative utterances are meaningful. To this extent, Wittgenstein was right to deny that meanings must exist in order for statements to be meaningful. 
Austin's contention is false. If I say, "grass is green," what I am saying is either true or false. There is some truth or falsehood that I'm affirming---some proposition, in other words. And if I say "if grass is green, then grass isn't colorless," I am saying of that proposition that some other proposition follows from it. If, when occurring on its own, "grass is green" didn't affirm anything, then "if grass is green, then grass isn't colorless" would be as meaningless as: (i) "If glarbojibjibjabber, then grass isn't colorless." 
Also, if embedding "grass is green" in a larger sentence changed what it meant, then "if grass is green, grass isn't colorless" wouldn't say that grass's not being colorless was a consequence of its being green. 
By parity of reasoning, if x is an utterance of the obviously meaningful sentence: 
(ii) Â“If I promise to give you a ride to the airport next Tuesday, youÂ’ll kill me if I break my word,Â” 
and y is an utterance of: 
(iii) Â“I promise to give you a ride to the airport next Tuesday,Â” 
then y must affirm some truth or falsehood. If it didn't, x would be as meaningless as an utterance of (i). But clearly does affirm some truth or falsehood. And the same is therefore true of utterances of (i) 
Thus, the spuriousness of Austin's position is a consequence of the fact, about to be demonstrated, that embedding a sentence P in Â‹if P, then QÂ› does not typically change P's meaning. The fact that 
(I) there is an even prime larger than two 
is false can be deduced from that: 
(II) If there is an even prime larger than two, there is a prime number that is divisible by one, itself, and two, which is not possible 
is true. 
But (II) wouldn't necessarily be true if the occurrence in it of (I) had a meaning different from its usual one. For example, (II) would be true if that occurrence meant that 4 is an even prime larger than two. More importantly, if that occurrence had a meaning different from its usual one, (II) wouldn't mean what it currently does, and it wouldn't necessarily say anything relevant to whether there was an even prime greater than two. 
In general, if P meant one thing on its own and a different thing in Â‹if P, then QÂ›, it would become impossible state indirect arguments.[21] 
(An indirect argument is one of the form: if P, then Q; not-Q; therefore not-P.) But, to Austin's discredit, such arguments obviously can be stated. 
In conclusion, so far as the philosophers just discussed are representative of philosophers in general, first-class philosophical thinkers are more likely to use their intelligence to defend orthodoxies, even wretchedly misguided ones, than to look for the truth. Ryle, Strawson, and Austin were at the world's first or second highest ranking philosophy department. And yet that they not only advocated views that any ten year old knows to be false. But they didn't just advocate them: they spent years of their lives urging acceptance of them. So these high-ranking members of high-ranking departments advocated views that were 100% false. So no one, even at a bottom-tier institution, could possibly say anything that's more false than what these high-rollers said. Hence my view students and professors of philosophy at first-tier institutions aren't as likely as one would think to produce better work than their counterparts at bottom-tier universities. 
Part 1 The Analysis of Analysis 
Chapter 1 Analytic Philosophy as Logical Analysis 
1.0 Philosophy as the analysis of the categories in terms of which we understand the world 
The world isnÂ’t homogeneous. It is articulated into events bearing various causal and, more generally, spatiotemporal relations to one another. Many of these events involve more or less persistent things (rocks, trees, etc.). Some of these things have minds. Most animate (mind-having) beings have sense-perceptions; i.e., they see things, hear things, etc. Most percipient (perception-having) creatures have beliefs. Some of these beliefs are true; others are false. Some of the true ones are cases of knowledge. Some percipient creatures communicate with one another through the use of language. Mastery of a language makes it easier for one to communicate oneÂ’s beliefs to others, and it also enhances oneÂ’s ability to reason. Rational (reason-capable) creatures tend to make value-judgments. They judge one anotherÂ’s actions, and sometimes their own, to be good or bad. Creatures that make such judgments tend to regulate their behavior towards one another by means of systems of law, the supposed purpose of which is to ensure that such behavior satisfies the requirements of justice. 
Event, space, time, cause, persistence, thing, mind, perception, belief, knowledge, language, truth, value-judgment, law, justice. Whatever we know, we know it through these categories (and others like themÂ—the list is not complete). Philosophy studies these categories. It delineates their structures. This is its sole function. Thus, philosophy is the discipline that delineates the structures of the categories in terms of which we think about the world. For reasons soon to be disclosed, this is the same as saying that philosophy is the science of science. 
1.1 Knowledge vs. meta-knowledge 
Although it is only through the aforementioned categories that we can think about the world, they are seldom the objects of thought. The result is that, although weÂ’re adept at using them, we know little about them. But for them, we are blind. And yet we are all blind to them. We know much, but have little idea what it is that we know. It is the philosopherÂ’s job to supply us with this missing knowledge. 
For example, we are excellent at distinguishing linguistic from nonÂ­linguistic behavior, which suggests that, at some level, we know what conditions a creatureÂ’s behavior must meet if it is to embody knowledge of a language. But when asked to make these conditions explicit, we find we can do so only with great difficulty and only with partial success. So even though we are good at knowing who knows a language and who does not, we donÂ’t know what it is that we know by virtue of knowing this. 
The same thing mutatis mutandis[22] 
is true of each one of these categories. WeÂ’re excellent at distinguishing between moral and immoral behavior. We know that rape is immoral and that donating money to charity (for selfless reasons) is moral. But when asked to identify the principles embodied in these pedestrian and uncontroversial judgments, we have trouble producing theories that donÂ’t distort them. 
In general, itÂ’s hard to identify the principles that guide our thoughts. Self-understanding isnÂ’t the mindÂ’s primary function. Nor could it be. The idea of a mind that thinks about nothing other than itself is an incoherent one. Thus, any case of self-awareness, and therefore of self-understanding, is necessarily derivative of, and for that reason of lesser quality than, some other more fundamental sort of understanding. 
Being the discipline whose purpose is to delineate the structures of these categories, philosophy has the very non-trivial job of identifying, in as clear and explicit a manner as possible, the conditions that a given thing must satisfy if it is to fall into any given one of these categories. So far as philosophy succeeds in this endeavor, it clarifies what we are doing by virtue of doing anything cognitive, be it making an observation or engaging in an extended piece of abstract reasoning. Philosophy is the analysis of the preconditions of all knowledge. 
Just as the scientistÂ’s job is to make us aware of the structure of the physical universe, so the philosopherÂ’s job is to make us aware of our knowledge of the knowledge of the universe. Philosophy is thus the Â“science of science," as John Stuart Mill put it. 
1.2 The relationship of philosophy to other disciplines 
The philosopher is interested in the laws governing the laws. He doesnÂ’t want to know what in fact holds. He wants to know what it would even make sense to claim to hold. He wants to know the laws that the laws canÂ’t break. 
Philosophical knowledge is meta-knowledgeÂ—knowledge about knowledge. The non-philosopher wants to know specifics. What happened? When did it happen? What did it cause? How did it cause it? The philosopher is interested in these questions only to the extent that knowing the answers to them helps him understand the categories (cause, place, time, etc.) underlying such knowledge. 
The stranded motorist wants his car to work. He doesnÂ’t care what will get it to do so. The engineer is interested in this. But the engineer is not entirely innocent of the motoristÂ’s epistemic parochialism. 
The engineer has no interest in what the laws of physics are except in so far as he must know them to create the right mechanisms. But the physicist wants knowledge of these mechanisms only to the extent it will give him knowledge of the laws embodied therein.[23] 

The philosopher is to the physicist what the physicist is to the engineer, and what the engineer is to the stranded motorist. It isnÂ’t for its own sake that the philosopher wants to know what causes what and what mechanisms were involved. He is interested in this knowledge only to the extent that knowing this helps him understand what it is for one thing to cause anotherÂ— only, that is to say, in so far as it helps him know what it is that one knows in knowing that one thing made another thing happen. 
1.3 How is analytic philosophy different from non-analytic philosophy? 
John Stuart Mill (1806Â–1873), the great philosopher and economist, said that he was an expert in but one science, that being the science of science. What he meant was obviously similar to what weÂ’ve been saying, and it was similar to what the great philosopher and mathematical logician Gottlob Frege (1848Â–1925) meant when he said that logic studies not the laws of nature but the Â“laws of the laws of nature.Â” Whether Frege was right depends on what exactly one means by Â“logic.Â” But if by Â“logicÂ” he meant Â“philosophy,Â” then FregeÂ’s dictum was spot-on. 
Frege is often described as the first analytic philosopher. Michael Dummett (1925Â–), an exceptionally capable contemporary philosopher of language, said that Â“analytic philosophy is post-Fregean philosophy.Â” What does Dummett mean? 
With some exceptions, pre-Fregean philosophers thought they were studying the most general features of the actual world. They thought that, like the botanist, they were in the business of saying how the world is, the only difference between their work and the botanistÂ’s being that theirs is concerned with more general features of reality than the botanistÂ’s. 
Frege showed that this is wrong. Any interest that botanists have in plants that might exist, but donÂ’t, is subordinate to their interest in what plants actually exist. Like all scientists, they are interested in what there could be only to the extent that it helps them figure out what there is. But with philosophers, itÂ’s the other way around. Any interest they have in the actual is subordinate to their interest in the possible. Unlike non-analytic philosophers, analytic philosophers do figure out what there could be by analyzing statements. Statements that make sense are those that can be true, and statements that donÂ’t are those that canÂ’t. Therefore, statements that make sense describe possible realities and those that donÂ’t, donÂ’t. 
But what exactly did Frege do? 
2.0 FregeÂ’s key insight: Logical form . grammatical form 
FregeÂ’s legacy to philosophy can be summed up thus: 
(FL) When people have an obviously correct belief that seems to have an absurd consequence, they should ask themselves whether that absurdity really is a consequence of that belief. But they frequently donÂ’t. Instead they accept the absurdity and, in order to make this mistake of theirs work, they develop ad hoc hypotheses as to the nature of reality that undermine the integrity of their own belief system. 
2.0.1 FL explained 
Consider the statement: 
(SC) nothing is a square circle. 
SC is true. Everybody knows this. But what does SC say? Judging by its grammatical similarity to Â“Smith is a very capable lawyer,Â” which attributes a certain property (that of being a capable lawyer) to a certain individual (Smith), SC would seem to say that a certain entity has the property of being a square circle. Presumably, the entity in question is some non-entity. If this presumption is correct, SC says that: 
(SC*) some non-entity, some featureless un-thing, is a square circle. 
But SC* is doubly incoherent. If anything is a square circle, then SC is falseÂ—it being irrelevant how much of a cipher the entity in question is. Second, the very idea of a non-entity is an absurd one. (It makes no sense to say that there exists a non-entity, since anything that exists is, for that very reason, an entity.) But it is hard to find a layperson or scholar who, when asked what SC means, comes up with anything substantively different from SC*. 
Given what a rank absurdity SC* is, we canÂ’t accept it, even though it seems to be an obvious consequence of SC. But we canÂ’t reject SC, since itÂ’s an obvious truth. 
To get out of this jam, we need only reflect a bit on what our words mean. If you say that nobody likes Larry, youÂ’re not saying that some un-person likes Larry. YouÂ’re saying that if you gathered together all the people who liked Larry and put them in an otherwise empty room, that room would remain empty. Which is the same as saying that if you put all the people in existence in an otherwise empty room, there would be no things that liked Larry in that room. 
Thus, what Â“nobody likes LarryÂ” means is not that some un-person likes Larry, but instead that the set of people who like Larry is empty or, alternatively, that the set of people doesnÂ’t overlap with the set of things that like Larry. 
SC is to be understood along similar lines. If you put all the square circles in existence in an otherwise empty room, that room would remain empty. This is another way of saying that, if you put all the square things in an otherwise empty room, there would be no circles in that room. So SC says, not some un-thing is a circle, but that: 
(i) the set of things that are both circular and square is an empty one 
or, alternatively, that: 
(ii) the set of circles doesnÂ’t overlap with the set of squares. 
(i) 
is a way of saying that any given thing lacks the property of being both a circle and a square. Alternatively, itÂ’s a way of saying this property doesnÂ’t have any instancesÂ—that itÂ’s uninstantiated. 

(ii) is a way of saying that anything having the property of being a square lacks the property of being a circle. Alternatively, itÂ’s a way of saying that these two properties donÂ’t have any instances in commonÂ—that they are not coinstantiated. 

(i) 
and (ii) thus attribute properties to properties. They say, respectively, that the property of being both a square and a circle is uninstantiated and that the properties of being a square and of being a circle are not coinstantiated. 


Since (i) and (ii) are just different ways of saying what SC says, the latter doesnÂ’t make the absurd statement that some non-entity is a circle, and it instead makes the innocuous statement that the set of squares doesnÂ’t overlap with the set of circles or, alternatively, that the property of being a square circle is uninstantiated. 
What this shows is that, in at least some cases, philosophical insight is acquired not by doing para-science, but by analyzing meaningsÂ—not by positing entities, but by clarifying statements.[27] 

Analytic philosophy is philosophy that is driven by acceptance of FL. Let us now expand on FL and make it clear why it is true. 
2.1 The wrong way to react to grammatical surface-structure 
In respect of its grammatical form: 
(JS) Â“John smokesÂ” 
is comparable to: 
(MS) Â“Mary smokes.Â” 
JS attributes the property of being a smoker to John; MS attributes that property to Mary. 
In respect of its grammatical form, each of JS and MS is comparable to: 
(LJ) Â“Larry jugglesÂ” 
and also to: 
(JJ) Â“Jane jogs.Â” 
Each of these sentences says of some individual that he or she has a certain property. The obvious inference to make is that any sentence grammatically comparable to any one of these four sentences says of some individual that he or she (or it) has some property. 
In light of these points, consider the sentence: 
(SS) Someone smokes. 
Given what we just said, the obvious thing to say about it is that it attributes the property of smoking to some individual. But which individual could that be? Which individual does Â“someoneÂ” pick out? 
Â“It picks out an ambiguous person,Â” said one logician.[28] 
But this answer is no good. Words are ambiguous, not people. Â“BankÂ” is ambiguous, since it has two meanings. But IÂ’m not ambiguous, and neither are you. And if per impossibile there did exist some ambiguous personÂ—some blank, featureless shell of a person who was picked out by Â“someoneÂ”Â—SS would unambiguously say of that person that he or she smoked. But there clearly isnÂ’t any one person to whom SS attributes the property of smoking. This is easily shown.[29] 
If Smith smokes, the sentence: Â“someone smokes but Smith does notÂ” will be false. But it wonÂ’t be self-contradictory; it wonÂ’t be like Â“Smith smokes but Smith does not smoke.Â” (For a statement to be self-contradictory is for it to bear two mutually opposed meanings.) Of course, there isnÂ’t anything special about the name Â“Smith,Â” what we just said could have been said in connection with Jones or Brown or any other expression that refers to some individual. Thus, there is no individual N such that it is self-contradictory to say that someone smokes but N does not. Therefore Â“someoneÂ” doesnÂ’t refer to anyone. 
Â“But youÂ’ve misunderstood my thesisÂ” it will be said. Â“The word Â“someoneÂ” doesnÂ’t unambiguously pick out an ambiguous person. It is itself ambiguous. It refers to Fred and Ethel and Mary. It refers to all people indifferently.Â” 
ThatÂ’s false. Â“SomeoneÂ” isnÂ’t ambiguous; it isnÂ’t like the word Â“dumb.Â” SS has one meaning, unlike Â“John is dumb,Â” which could mean either Â“John is unintelligentÂ” or Â“John is mute.Â” Also, if Â“someoneÂ” were ambiguous between Â“JohnÂ” and Â“EthelÂ” and so on, then, depending on the circumstances, it would be synonymous with Â“John smokesÂ” or Â“Ethel smokes.Â” And in that case, Â“someone smokes, but John does notÂ” would sometimes have the same meaning as Â“John smokes, but John does not smoke,Â” in which case it would be self-contradictory. But, as we just saw, Â“someone smokes, but John does notÂ” is not self-contradictory under any circumstances. If John does smoke, it will be false, but it wonÂ’t be self-contradictory. 
Also, it isnÂ’t clear what it means to say that Â“someoneÂ” picks out everyone Â“indifferently.Â” But if, as is surely the case, picking out everyone indifferently involves picking out everyone, then itÂ’s just wrong to say that Â“someoneÂ” picks out everyone Â“indifferentlyÂ” (or in any other way). For if it did, Â“someoneÂ” would have the same meaning as Â“everyone,Â” which it doesnÂ’t. 
2.2 The right way to react to grammatical surface-structure 
What all this shows is that Â“someoneÂ” isnÂ’t in the same category as Â“JohnÂ” and Â“Ethel.Â” It doesnÂ’t function in the same way, even though, given its grammatical function, one would expect it to. SS is obviously true. The wrong way to react to that fact is to twist reality to make it conform to our assumption that Â“someone,Â” being grammatically comparable to Â“John,Â” must refer to something. If we take that path, we must say that it refers to an Â“ambiguousÂ” or Â“non-specificÂ” person, given that it obviously doesnÂ’t refer to anyone specific. But then weÂ’re stuck with the absurd thesis that there is some non-specific entity in the worldÂ— that there exists something that isnÂ’t identical with any particular thing and therefore isnÂ’t identical with anything. 
The right way to react to it is to think more deeply about what SS is really saying. Frege did this, and he solved the puzzle. SSÂ’s logical form diverges from its grammatical form. In terms of what its grammar suggests that it is saying, SS is indistinguishable from sentences that attribute the property of smoking to specific objects. In terms of what it really is saying, it is evidently very different from such sentences. 
What SS is saying, as Frege made clear, is that the characteristicÂ—or as analytic philosophers put it, the propertyÂ—of being a smoker is instantiated. SS is making a statement, not about some non-specific individual, but about a very specific property, and itÂ’s saying of this property that itÂ’s instantiated. (For a property to be instantiated is for there to be an instance of it. An instance of a property is something that has it. You are an instance of, and therefore instantiate, the property of being human since, being human, you have that property.) 
There are properties that nothing has. Nobody has run a three-minute mile. Given any individual, x, it is false to attribute the property of being a person who has run a three-minute mile. Thus, there are no instances of that property. It is uninstantiated. The grammatical form of[30]: 
(TM) Â“nobody has run a three-minute mileÂ” 
is just like that of: 
(JTM) Â“John has run a three-minute mile.Â” 
JTM clearly attributes that property to an individual. That isnÂ’t what TM does. TM says of that property that it canÂ’t be attributed to anyone. So TM says that: 
(UP) [31] 
the property of being a person who has run a three-minute mile is uninstantiated. 
Notice that UPÂ’s grammatical form is the opposite of TMÂ’s. The grammatical subject of TM is Â“nobodyÂ”; the grammatical predicate is Â“has run a three-minute mile.Â” By contrast, the grammatical subject of UP is Â“the property of being a person who has run a three-minute mile,Â” which corresponds to Â“has run a three-minute mile,Â” and the grammatical predicate of UP is "is uninstantiated," which corresponds to Â“nobody.Â” 
If one were to take TM at face value, and were thus to assume that its meaning paralleled that of JTM, one would have to say that it attributed the property of being a person who has run a three-minute mile to some unÂ­person. But if this is what it said, then in order to be true, somebodyÂ— namely, this unpersonÂ— would have had to have run a three-minute mile, in which case TM would be false. When we align TMÂ’s real meaning with its grammar, we donÂ’t have to swallow this rank absurdity. For UP says of some very much existent property (that of being a person who has run a three-minute mile) that it has a certain very much existent property (that of being uninstantiated). So we get the right result if we do linguistic analysis. We get the wrong result if we para-scientifically posit new entities in order to account for the datum that TM is true. 
The same thing is true of: 
(NS) Â“Nothing smokes.Â” 
Pre-Fregeans said that NS says of some non-thingÂ—some blank entityÂ— that it smokes. So, supposing that in 500 years nobody smokes, and that NS is therefore true, it will be in virtue of the fact that some blank entity is around that is smoking. 
But if there is such a thing, and itÂ’s smoking, then NS is false. As long as one thing smokes, NS is false. It doesnÂ’t matter how blank or otherwise deficient that thing is. 
Frege straightened this all out. By obvious extensions of what we just said, NSÂ’s real meaning is: 
(NS2) The property of being a smoker is uninstantiated. 
NS2Â‘s grammatical subject (the italicized expression) corresponds to NSÂ’s grammatical predicate; and NS2Â’s grammatical predicate (the bold-faced expression) corresponds to NSÂ’s grammatical subject. So when we align NSÂ’s logical form (what it actually says) with its grammatical form (what, given its grammar, it appears to say), we no longer have to say, completely absurdly, that NS attributes to some non-specific individual. 
Similar remarks hold with respect to SC. That statement says of two properties that they arenÂ’t coinstantiated. It doesnÂ’t say of some non-entity that it is both a square and a circle. 
Philosophical puzzles are solved by making it clear what statements mean. This is the basic tenet of analytic philosophy. Philosophy explains by clarifying statements. Science explains by positing entities. Science posits entities that are not themselves directly encountered but that, if assumed to exist, would account for phenomena that are directly encountered. 
It used to be thought that philosophical explanation was to be understood in the same wayÂ—that philosophical progress was to be made by positing entities that are not themselves directly known but that, if assumed to exist, explain what is directly known. This is not the case. Philosophy isnÂ’t paraÂ­science. Philosophy is conceptual analysis. To make a philosophical discovery is not to discover a new entity; it is to make explicit a previously unrecognized implication of an existing belief. Philosophy is explication; it is the clarification of the statements that we accept but whose depths we havenÂ’t yet fully fathomed.[32] 

3.0 Analysis vs. ontogenesis 
In the works of analytic philosophers, one sometimes comes across the word Â“ontology,Â” which, etymologically, means Â“the study of beingÂ” (Â“ontosÂ”= Â“being,Â” Â“logosÂ”= Â“studyÂ”). These days the word Â“ontologyÂ” is usually used to refer to a given philosopherÂ’s beliefs as to what exists. Some philosophers donÂ’t believe in non-spatiotemporal entities. So such entities donÂ’t belong to their Â“ontology.Â” Since I do believe in them, they do belong to my Â“ontology.Â” 
Analytic philosophers are, almost by definition, ontologically very conservative. In other words, they donÂ’t want to grant existence to anything whose existence hasnÂ’t been demonstrated beyond a shadow of a doubt. 
Pre-analytic, pre-Fregean philosophers were ontologically very liberal. Consider the statement: 
(TP) No person is over 20-feet tall. 
Pre-Fregean philosophers took TP to say that there existed some nonÂ­person who was over 20-feet tall; and, attempting to validate this analysis, they engaged in a great deal of spurious ontologizing. (To ontologize is to posit an entity, or class of entities, not previously believed to exist.) Frege showed that this ontologizing, in addition to being futile, is unnecessary. TP says that a certain property (that of being a person who is over 20-feet tall) has another property (that of not being instantiated). No 20-foot tall (un)person need be postulated. No ontologizing need be done. By contrast, non-analytic (pre-Fregean) philosophers often countenanced bizarre and even logically impossible entities to cover up deficits in their analyses. 
3.1 When is it appropriate to ontologize? 
As a general rule, analytic philosophers do not try to solve philosophical problems by ontologizing. They try to solve them by clarifying statements. In some cases, the results of a successfully clarified statement do demand that we grant existence to something to which weÂ’d otherwise deny existence. But, whenever this happens, the Â“entityÂ” being posited is never a denizen of the spatiotemporal world; the thing thatÂ’s posited is never a person or a table or a mountain or a monster. ItÂ’s always an abstract object of some kind, and itÂ’s posited only because, were it not to exist, it would be impossible to account for the truth of obviously true statements. 
For example, given the premise that Bob and Sally are both humans who are intelligent, it follows that there exist characteristicsÂ—or, to use the word preferred by analytic philosophers, properties[34]Â—that Bob and Sally have in common, and from this it follows that properties exist. 
Given that properties exist, are they identical with spatiotemporal entities (i.e., with things that have locations in space and time)? Obviously, instances of properties at least sometimes exist in space-time. Bob and Sally, both instances of many properties, exist in space and time. But although you may encounter many instances of intelligence, youÂ’ll never encounter intelligence per se and it would make no sense to assign any spatiotemporal location to it. Attempts to rebut this argument are doomed to fail, as weÂ’ll see in Chapter 2. Thus, unless there exists a property that Bob and Sally have in common, the inference from Â“Bob and Sally are both intelligent and kindÂ” to Â“there is a property that they have in commonÂ” is illegitimate. Since that inference clearly is legitimate, such a property must exist. 
Both every day and scientific thought are replete with inferences of this kind. Indeed, there would be no thought, let alone scientific thought, were it not for such inferences. Consider the inference from: 
(*) There is no actual or possible situation in which object xÂ’s behavior differs from object yÂ’s. 
to: 
(**) x and y have similar microstructures; i.e., there is some 
microstructural property that they have in common. 
Were it denied that properties exist that inference would be invalid, and so would every other inference, the result being that Â“thought would grind to a halt,Â” to use Laurence BonjourÂ’s expression. So not only do property-instances exist: properties themselves do as well. 
So far as they give any thought to the matter, most people hold that properties donÂ’t exist, being nothing more than fictions created by philosophical chicanery. (When I applied to graduate school, my application-essay was an attempt to prove that, although property-instances obviously exist, properties per se do not.) But weÂ’ve already seen one reason why such a view cannot possibly be correct, and weÂ’re now about to see another. 
There would be no truths unless there existed properties.[35] 
(Not property-instances, mind you, but properties per se.) Every truth is to the effect that some object has some property. There are apparent counter-examples to this. (For example, Â“nothing is a square circleÂ” seems not to attribute any property to anything. But this is not the case, as weÂ’ve already seen. In Section 4.9 of the present chapter, it will be shown that there cannot possibly be any actual counterexamples to this contention.) There would not be thoughts---or at least no correct ones----unless there existed truths. Thus, there would be no correct thoughts if there were no properties. Thus, lest we take the self-undermining position that all thoughts are false, we must posit the existence of properties whose existence weÂ’d otherwise be inclined to deny. We must ontologize, in other words. 
In Chapter 2, weÂ’ll consider each of the many attempts to prove that properties do not exist; and weÂ’ll also consider many attempts to prove that, although properties do exist, they have no existence apart from their own instances. WeÂ’ll see that all of these attempts fail. WeÂ’ll also see that, given a correct understanding of what properties are, any instinctual misgivings we have about positing their existence melt away. 
3.1.1 When is it appropriate to ontologize? (Continued) 
Even though both scientists and philosophers ontologize, they donÂ’t do so for the same reason. When scientists ontologize, it is in order to Â“model empirical data.Â” It is in order to explain phenomena that, so they feel, they are not otherwise able to explain. Individuals x1Â….xn come down with various 
symptoms s1Â…sm. These symptoms must be explained. The causes of these symptoms must be identified. What we know about medicine and biology puts limits on what these causes might be, and so does what we know about the specific circumstances under which the relevant individuals fell ill. Given these two bodies of data, along with some principles of a generally logical nature, the most reasonable conjecture is that the source of the problem is a virus having such and such characteristics. 
When analytic philosophers ontologize, they do it only when there is no other way of demonstrating the legitimacy of some indisputably correct form of inference, and they never posit anything non-spatiotemporal in the process. When scientists ontologize---that is, when they posit previously unknown entities---it is in order to identify the causes of states of affairs whose causes 
are still known. When scientists ontologize, it is in order to reconcile our knowledge of raw data (e.g., that Individuals x1Â….xn come down with various symptoms s1Â…sm) with our presumptions as to the causal structure of the universe---with, that is to say, our presumptions as to what states of affairs 
other states of affairs are likely to bring about. In Chapter 2, we'll see (i) that it is necessary to posit the existence of non-spatiotemporal entities and (ii) that, in positing such entities, one is no way deviating from either common sense or empirical science: one is simply make explicit what they both implicitly assume. 
Whereas scientists ontologize in order to reconcile raw data with what we believe to be the principles governing redistributions of mass-energy, philosophers ontologize in order to show the legitimacy of the forms of inference underlying the specific inferences made by scientists. 
It will be easier to see how the jobs of the scientist and the philosopher differ if we revisit the case of the medical researcher who identifies the Ebola virus as the cause of so and soÂ’s symptoms. That medical researcher is making a number of assumptions, all of them incapable of being questioned outside of a purely theoretical context by a sane human being, but not a single one of them admitting of any obvious, strictly logical justification. Those assumptions include, but not are limited to, the following: 
(i) The testimony of his senses can generally be trusted. 
(ii) No knowledge concerning the external world or, therefore, concerning the causes of illness can be learned except through sense-perception. 
(iii) Nothing happens for no reason. Everything has a cause. Nothing comes from nothing. 
(iv) 
Even though things change, the structures within which they change tend to stay the same. People lose their health and then regain it; diseases come, go, and then sometimes come back in new, more virulent forms. But these changes happen within stable frameworks. Supposing that they change at all, the laws of biology change slowly, and they certainly donÂ’t change with every new case of illness or recovery. And even if, over a long period, the laws of biology do change, the laws of chemistry in terms of which those laws are to be understood do not change, and neither a fortiori do the laws of physics in terms of which the laws of chemistry are to be understood. 

(v) 
Good explanations try to reconcile our presumptions as to how the world works---as to what the laws are that govern it---with the testimony of our senses. Sometimes those reconciliations are not possible: Either we must throw out the raw data or we must throw out one or more theories of ours as to how the world works. (We may throw out raw data if we discover that the microscopes we were using were defective. We may throw out a theory if, having exercised due diligence, we simply cannot find reason to question the raw data.) 


Most reasonable people would accept most of these principles, if not all of them. But there can be no observation-based or, therefore, experimentation-based way of determining whether or not any given one of these given principles is false. 
Consider the principle that the testimony of the senses can generally be trusted.[36] 
Though integral to scientific and everyday practice, observations couldnÂ’t possibly verify it. After all, no observation is to be trusted until the truth of (i) has been established. 
What about by asking others what their sense-perceptions were? That would be to no avail. First of all, it is only through your own sense-perceptions that you have any knowledge of what sense-perceptions others are having. So unless your own senses can be trusted, you canÂ’t trust other peopleÂ’s testimony as to what their senses are. 
In fact, to continue further in this same vein, unless you assume the truth of (i), you cannot coherently assume that there exist other people. Nor, therefore, can you assume that, if there are other people, those people, when speaking to you, are being either honest or truthful. 
3.1.2 A historical aside: Wittgenstein's blunder 
Incidentally, the preceding remarks make it clear why one of the most famous philosophical arguments of all time is a failure. Ludwig Wittgenstein argued that one must know what others say and do in order to know what one is oneself thinking. He argued, for reasons that we will examine in Chapter 5, that one is to trust oneÂ’s own views as to what one is thinking, feeling, etc., only if those views have been seconded by other members of the community of which one is a part. 
The flaw in this argument is obvious. If I canÂ’t trust my senses, I have no way of knowing what you believe to be going on in my mind. If my senses canÂ’t be trusted, I donÂ’t even know that you exist, let alone that you have these or those views concerning my mental contents. So WittgensteinÂ’s position is rank absurdity. 
Let us now examine (iv). This contention is notoriously hard to justify. We know nothing about the future unless we know the laws that connect the present to the future. (If I know that the vase will shatter, itÂ’s because I know 
(i) that the vase is about to collide with a hard surface and (ii) that, the laws of nature being what they are, objects relevantly like that vase break when they collide with objects relevantly like that surface. If I know (i) but not (ii), I couldnÂ’t possibly know that the vase was about to break.) Thus, a precondition for knowledge of what will be the case at some future time is knowledge of the laws governing events between now and that time. Therefore, I have no way of knowing what those laws will be. Since I must know those laws to know the future, I cannot know what they will be. I cannot predict what they will be without knowing the future. Therefore, I canÂ’t know the laws linking the present to the future and I therefore canÂ’t know the future. 
Of course, weÂ’re obviously disposed to believe that the natural laws that will govern the world coincide with those that have governed it. But the past is evidence of the future only to the extent that the mechanisms that have governed past events can be predicted to govern the future. Since this cannot be predicted, as weÂ’ve just seen, nothing follows as to what the laws of nature will be from what they have been. 
Are we to conclude that we canÂ’t know the future? No! WeÂ’re to conclude that thereÂ’s a problem with the argument just given. What is that problem? 
See Chapter 7. 
3.2 Brentano and Meinong: the non-analytic method epitomized 
According to Franz Brentano (1838Â–1917), the essence of the mental is intentionality. In this context, the word Â“intentionalityÂ” refers not to the property of being done deliberately, but to the property of being representational. So, in BrentanoÂ’s view, for something to be a mental entity is for it to be representational and for something to fail to be a mental entity is for it to be non-representational. To be sure, there are non-mental things (e.g., deposits of ink or paint) that are representational. Utterances and ink deposits are representational, even though they arenÂ’t mental. But this isnÂ’t a threat to BrentanoÂ’s position. Utterances (etc.) are representational only in a derivative sense. ItÂ’s because we endow it with meaning that an utterance of Â“snow is whiteÂ” is meaningful; in a world devoid of sentient beings, it would just be another noise. So BrentanoÂ’s thesis is that for something to be mental is for it to be non-derivatively representational. 
There is an apparent problem with BrentanoÂ’s thesis. To be representational is presumably to represent something. Hallucinations are mental entities. But what does a hallucination of a pink elephant represent? A pink elephant? NoÂ—pink elephants donÂ’t exist. More formally, there is nothing x such that x is a pink elephant. A fortiori there is nothing x such that x is a pink elephant that is represented by some hallucination. Still, there is clearly a sense in which hallucinations of pink elephants and other nonÂ­entities are representational. How is this to be explained? 
The solution to this problem lies in the fact that perception is description. If youÂ’re looking at an actual elephant, which weÂ’ll call Â“Larry,Â” the information encoded in your visual perception isnÂ’t the effect that: 
(LP) Larry is standing over there, next to that tree, looking ill (etc.). 
When you look at an elephant, or a person, or a rock, you donÂ’t just see that object. Seeing Larry involves seeing a thing having various propertiesÂ— having a certain color, shape, size, position (relative to you), etc. So seeing Larry involves seeing that various properties are instantiatedÂ—that there is an instance, in a certain place, of a certain morphology, color, etc. 
Perceptions of things arenÂ’t like sentences about them. In the sentence: 
(LS) Â“Larry is standing over there, next to that tree, looking ill (etc.)Â” 
Larry is represented by a single, semantically simple symbol (namely, Â“LarryÂ”).[ But in no sense-perception of Larry is he represented by some simple, homogenous, non-composite cipher. So far as he is perceived, Larry is represented as having these or those properties. This means that seeing him involves seeing that these or those properties are instantiated. 
ItÂ’s not as though in addition to seeing an instance of a certain morphology, color, etc., you also, separately from that, see Larry. No, for you to see Larry at a given time is for you to see that, at that time, certain properties are instantiated in a certain place. Thus, the content of your perception of Larry is given by some existence-claim similar to the following: 
(LC) there exists, over in that place at the present time, instances of such and such properties. 
An existence-claim is any claim to the effect that some property is instantiated. Thus, Â“there are prime numbersÂ” is an existence-claim, and sufficient since it says that the property of being a prime number has at least one instance. 
Given any existence claim, anything having the requisite properties is said to satisfy it. So the number seven satisfies the just-mentioned existence-claim. The number two uniquely satisfies Â“there is an even prime,Â” since (a) it satisfies it and (b) nothing else does. 
When you look at Larry, your eyes are giving you an existence-claim. Given that Larry, and Larry alone, satisfies that existence-claim, he is the object of your perception. So given that Larry uniquely instantiates the property of being a thing in such and such a place that has such and such a morphology (etc.), Larry is the object (or, more likely, one of the objects) of your current perception. So, yes, your perception does represent Larry. But it represents him by way of encoding an existence-claim that he satisfies. 
Given this, suppose that, the next day you have a hallucination that is experientially just like the veridical perception weÂ’ve been talking about. (A Â“veridicalÂ” perception is an accurate one. Â“VeridicalÂ” is to perceptions what Â“trueÂ” is to sentences. For some reason, perceptions are described as Â“veridical,Â” not as Â“true.Â”) So even though neither Larry nor anything that looks like him is in front of you, your visual experience is telling you otherwise. That hallucination thus gives you a false message. The message encoded in it will be similar to LC. That message is to the effect that in a certain place there is a thing having such and such morphological, chromatic, and kinematic properties. On this occasion, the messageÂ—the existence-claim Â—in question is false, the reason being that nothing satisfies it. (Yesterday, the message represented by your visual experience was correct, the reason being that the existence-claim in question was satisfied.) The important point is that, although it was hallucinatory, your visual experience encoded an existence-claim and was therefore representational. It wasnÂ’t representational in the sense that there was something that it picked out. It was representational in the sense that it gave you a message, albeit a false one, and thus represented the world as being a certain way. 
Your visual perception of yesterday, unlike your visual perception of today, encoded a true existence-claim. But your visual experience of today no more represents some non-existent entity than your sense perception yesterday. Your visual experience today has for its content a false proposition to the effect that there is a thing having thus and such properties. But just as the sentence Â“there does not exist a ten-foot tall manÂ” does not, in order to be true, require the existence of a ten-foot tall man, so your perception doesnÂ’t require the existence of an elephant before you. 
The same thing is true of thoughts about the non-existent. When you think about some non-existent numberÂ—for example, an even prime greater than twoÂ—there isnÂ’t some mathematically impossible entity that youÂ’re cognitively locking onto. WhatÂ’s going on is that youÂ’re thinking some false existence-claim along the lines of: there is some number n such that n is larger than two, even, and prime. 
Mental entities have propositions for their contents. When correct, those propositions describe existing things. When false, they donÂ’t. But nothing non-existent or quasi-existent can be the object of a thought or perception. When we describe a thought or perception as having a Â“non-existent object,Â” what we mean, so far as what we mean is coherent, is that it has for its content an existence-claim that nothing satisfies. 
But Brentano dropped the ball. He realized that hallucinations are, in some significant sense, representational. Wishing to reconcile this with the fact that there are no pink elephants (etc.), he said that a hallucination of a pink elephant has a non-existent pink elephant for its object. 
But thatÂ’s absurd, since itÂ’s the same as saying: Â“there exists some elephant x such that x doesnÂ’t exist and such that what you are hallucinating is x.Â” 
In a failed to attempt to deal with this, Brentano distinguished different kinds of non-existence, and he used different terms to mark them (Â“inexistent,Â” Â“non-existent,Â” Â“un-existent,Â” etc.) His pupil, Alexius Meinong (1853Â–1920), added another bogus category to this listÂ—the category of Â“subsistentÂ” entities. An entity Â“subsistsÂ” if it doesnÂ’t quite fail to exist, but doesnÂ’t quite succeed in existing either. 
This entire approach is misguided. Brentano and Meinong were ontologizing when they should have been analyzing. Properly analyzed, hallucinations no more require the existence of non-existent existents than veridical perceptions. The same is true of thoughts about Bart Simpson, the Fountain of Youth, etc. (This is further discussed in Chapters 6, 8, 9, and 25.) 
4.0 Empirical puzzles vs. philosophical puzzles 
Some puzzles result from ignorance of spatiotemporal facts. My valuables start disappearing. IÂ’m puzzled. I learn the relevant facts: Larry has been sneaking into my house and stealing my valuables. IÂ’m no longer puzzled. 
The puzzles that science deals with typically involve a failure to know all the facts. Typically, the problem is not, at least not in its entirety, that anyone is making erroneous inferences. At least part of the problem is that not all the facts are in. It isnÂ’t yet known that disease X results from an over-production of antibody Y. The reason it isnÂ’t yet known is that given the available data there isnÂ’t yet good reason to believe it. But once the data is in, it will be believed, and a cure will be forthcoming. 
Of course, scientific puzzles seldom result entirely from a failure to have the relevant data. In most cases, scientific breakthroughs involve somebodyÂ’s figuring out a new and better way to model already available data. 
The pre-history of relativity theory vividly illustrates this principle. If a train rushes past you at a rate of 100 mph, and I rush past you at a rate of 70 mph, the train is traveling at a rate of 30 mph with respect to me. But if a light beam rushes past you at a rate of 186,000 miles/second, and I rush past you at a rate of 180,000 miles/second, the light beam rushes past me at a rate of 186,000 miles/second. For this reason, there is no optical test for determining oneÂ’s own state of motion.[42] 
In other words, no matter how quickly you travel, you will not be able to detect any change in your velocity relative to that of a light beam. People and instruments not traveling with you will be able to detect changes in your velocity relative to that of a light beam, and you will be able to detect changes in their velocities relative to that of a light beam. But nobody can detect any changes in his own velocity relative to that of a light beam. 
This deeply puzzling fact was established in 1879. But nobody had any idea how to explain it until, in 1905, Einstein put forth the Special Theory of Relativity. Einstein didnÂ’t cite any data that hadnÂ’t been available to the physics community for decades. EinsteinÂ’s great innovation was of a conceptual nature. The facts were in, but he was the first to make sense of them. 
Be all of this as it may, Relativity Theory is an empirical theory. ItÂ’s based on observational and experimental data, much of which would be impossible to acquire except through carefully executed experiments. This data wasnÂ’t in until 1879. So even though nobody came up with Relativity Theory before 1879, that fact canÂ’t be chalked up to the fact that nobody drew the right inferences. It is due, at least in part, to the fact that the necessary data simply wasnÂ’t available. (What can be chalked up to a failure to draw the right inferences is that nobody came up with Relativity Theory during the period from 1879 to 1905.) 
In general, scientific breakthroughs have two components: (i) a strictly fact-based component (new raw data is acquired), and (ii) a purely conceptual component (already known data is modeled in a new and better way). 

4.1 Empirical puzzles vs. philosophical puzzles (continued) 
Unlike scientific puzzles, philosophical puzzles are not solved by generating new raw data. Philosophical puzzles are purely conceptual in nature and have no strictly factual component. Philosophical puzzles result, not from a failure to know the facts, but from a failure to draw the right inferences. They result, not from ignorance, but from confusion. In figuring out that: 
(NS2) the property of being a smoker is uninstantiated 
is what is meant by: 
(NS) Â“nothing smokes,Â” 
Frege solved a number of outstanding philosophical problems. But Frege didnÂ’t make any new empirical discoveries. In fact, his work didnÂ’t involve him having access to any empirical information that wasnÂ’t available to anyone who knows what (NS) (or its German equivalent) means.[44] 
EinsteinÂ’s work, by contrast, had a heavy empirical component: He was modeling facts that a layperson would know nothing about, and the same thing mutatis mutandis is true of any scientific discovery. 
4.2. Philosophical analysis .linguistic analysis 
Impressed by FregeÂ’s philosophical successes, many came to the conclusion that all philosophical puzzles are of a purely linguistic nature. The most famous, and also the most vehement, advocate of this view was Ludwig Wittgenstein (1889Â–1951). This thesis was the cornerstone of his work. He urged acceptance of it in practically everything he wrote during his long career. He said it before others said it, and he held onto it long after most of its erstwhile supporters rejected it, for reasons to be described forthwith. Â“Philosophical confusion begins when language goes on holiday,Â” he said. Elsewhere[45] 
he said that all philosophical confusion Â“lies in a failure to understand the workings of our own language.Â”[46] 

4.2.1 The Spuriousness of WittgensteinÂ’s position 
There are many philosophical puzzles that donÂ’t have anything to do with language, and the solutions to these puzzles cannot be modeled on FregeÂ’s solutions to the puzzles discussed a moment ago. 
HereÂ’s an example from epistemology.[ Nothing can sense-perceive anything that doesnÂ’t affect it. You couldn't see the book in front of you unless light-rays bouncing off it struck your eyes. You couldn't hear the chirping of a bird unless that bird's chirping caused air-disturbances that led to ear-disturbances. All knowledge of what is in space-time is rooted in sense-perception. (If itÂ’s in space-time, it isnÂ’t known unless itÂ’s directly perceived or evidence of it is perceived.) Taking it for granted that nothing that isnÂ’t in space-time can possibly be known, many contemporary epistemologists; e.g., Jerry Fodor[48], hold that one canÂ’t know of anything without being affected by it. Thus, such philosophers hold that: 
(JK) JohnÂ’s being aware of the fact that 1 + 1 = 2 involves his being on the receiving end of some causal process initiated by that fact. 
I personally regard JK as being absurd in the extreme.[49] 
The fact that 1 + 1 = 2 isnÂ’t comparable to the fact that there is a book in front of you. Were mass-energy distributed differently, there wouldnÂ’t be a book in front of you. But 1 + 1 would equal 2 no matter how mass-energy were distributed. Thus, Â“1 + 1 = 2Â” says nothing about how mass-energy is distributed, and it therefore says nothing about the spatiotemporal world. The fact it describes must therefore be non-spatiotemporal. Nothing outside of space-time can bear any causal relation to anything. Therefore, JK is wrong.[50] 

In any case, the dispute between those who accept JK and those who reject it has nothing to do with language. ItÂ’s agreed what JK means. What isnÂ’t agreed is whether the thing that itÂ’s agreed to mean is true. 
But the controversies surrounding NS do concern language; they concern the semantics of the word Â“nothing.Â” Those who see Â“nothingÂ” as being a referring term, like Â“Socrates,Â” see NS as saying that some featureless entity smokes. Those who deny that Â“nothingÂ” and Â“SocratesÂ” belong to the same semantic category donÂ’t see NS as saying this. Therein lies the controversy. Nothing comparable to this holds in connection with JK. 
Analytic philosophers do agree that the right way to figure out whether or not JK is correct is by carefully analyzing its meaning. But they also hold that it isnÂ’t to be solved through linguistic analysis. They're right on both counts. 
It must be emphasized that, according to analytic epistemologists, this puzzle is of a logical, not an empirical, nature. It is to be resolved through statement-analysis alone, not through statement-analysis combined with empirical research. TheyÂ’re clearly right about this. JK says that JohnÂ’s knowing that 1 + 1 = 2 is inconsistent with his not being on the receiving end of a causal process initiated by that fact. For P to be inconsistent with Q is for it to be impossible for both P and Q to be true. What doesnÂ’t exist cannot be observed. A fortiori what cannot exist cannot be observed. Thus, observation cannot tell you that anything is inconsistent with anything. So there is no way for it to tell you whether JK is correct.[51] 

No philosophical assertions are empirical. Philosophy analyzes the categories in terms of which we think about the world. It does this by saying exactly what it is that is ruled out by a given thingÂ’s falling into a given categoryÂ—by, for example, a given thingÂ’s being an instance of knowledge. Since observation canÂ’t tell one whether one statement is inconsistent with another, philosophical assertions are non-empirical. 
W.V.O. Quine is the only philosopher I know to hold that epistemological disputes are not to be settled by analyzing concepts. In his paper Â“Epistemology Naturalized,Â” Quine said that epistemological questions are not to be answered in this way, and are to be answered in the same way as scientific questions; e.g., Â“what is the MoonÂ’s chemical composition?Â” 
There are two points to make here. First of all, even though Quine was an analytic philosopher by trade, it doesnÂ’t follow that all of his views were those of an analytic philosopher; and in this context, I would suggest, he was not being an analytic philosopher. He was being an opponent of analytic philosophy. Second, QuineÂ’s view is incoherent. Natural science is based on empirical observation. Empirical observation cannot tell you that it itself is a source of knowledge. Therefore, it cannot be known through natural science that observation is a source of knowledge, and it must therefore be known in some non-empirical, and therefore non-scientific, manner. Jaegwon Kim (1993) makes a similar point. 

4.2.2 Not all philosophical analysis is identical with linguistic analysis (continued) 
Thus, not all philosophical puzzles are linguistic puzzles; and Wittgenstein was wrong to say otherwise. But didnÂ’t we ourselves say that philosophical analysis is the analysis of statements? Yes we did, and we were right to do so. To see why Wittgenstein is nonetheless wrong, we must distinguish sentences from propositions. Propositions are the things meant by sentences. Â“Snow is white,Â” Â“schnee is weiss,Â” and Â“la neige est blancheÂ” all mean the same thing. There is some one proposition that is the meaning of each of them.[52] 

A sentence is true or false depending on whether it has a true or false proposition for its meaning. Thus, when a sentence is described as Â“true,Â” the property being attributed to it isnÂ’t the same as the property that is attributed to a proposition that is so described. For a sentence to be Â“trueÂ” is for it to encode a true proposition. But this isnÂ’t what it is for a proposition to be true, since propositions donÂ’t encode anything. In Chapter 3, weÂ’ll say what exactly it is for a proposition to be true. But the obvious answer, though imprecise, is the right one; namely, for a proposition to be true is for it to fit the facts. 
The term Â“statementÂ” is ambiguous; it has three distinct meanings. Sometimes it refers to propositions, sometimes it refers to the sentences used to affirm them, and sometimes it refers to the act of using a sentence to affirm a proposition. Wittgenstein didnÂ’t countenance the existence of propositions, and this obviously had a hand in his erroneously believing that philosophy is the analysis of sentences, when the truth is that philosophy is the analysis of propositions. Even FregeÂ’s analyses of sentences such as Â“someone snoresÂ” and Â“nothing is a square circleÂ” fail to conform to WittgensteinÂ’s conception of what philosophy is supposed to do, since, as weÂ’ll see in a moment, theyÂ’re analyses of propositions that involve analyses of sentences and therefore are not themselves analyses of sentences. 
One must know at least some English to understand the sentence: 
(1) Â“John knows that 1 + 1 = 2.Â” 
But the proposition meant by that sentence can be grasped without speaking English; and one neednÂ’t know English, or any other given 
language, to be able to analyze that proposition correctly. 
But analyzing (1)Â—the sentence, not the corresponding propositionÂ—does involve such knowledge. A sentence is an expression; it consists of nouns, verbs, etc. Analyzing (1) involves knowing the various grammatical nuances involved in its structure. Analyzing the corresponding proposition has nothing to do with anything relating to grammar or any other aspect of language. No such knowledge is needed to analyze the corresponding proposition. 
Even though FregeÂ’s work inspired many to identify philosophy with sentence-analysis, Frege himself always made it very clear that propositions are not sentences and that although sentences are human creations, their meanings are not.[53] 

The sentence Â“the moon is less massive than EarthÂ” is a human artifact; it didnÂ’t exist until a few centuries ago. But the truth it expresses is in a different category. That truth exists independently of us. After all, the moon was less massive than the Earth before we came along, and itÂ’ll be that way after we sign out. For the same reason mutatis mutandis, the truth expressed by Â“the Earth is more massive than the moonÂ” exists independently of our thoughts and deeds, even though that sentence itself is a human artifact. 

4.2.3 Not all philosophical analysis is identical with linguistic analysis (continued): the nature of sentence-meanings (as opposed to sentences) 
What are propositions? TheyÂ’re properties. For a proposition to be true is for the world to be a certain way. The proposition that Smith is in Richmond is true if the world is a certain way and itÂ’s false if it isnÂ’t. (If mass-energy is distributed one way, Smith is in Richmond; if itÂ’s distributed some other way, he isnÂ’t.) For a thing to be a certain way is for it to have a certain property. To be round is to be one way; to be square is to be some other way. To be round is to have one property; to be square is to have some other property.[54] 
Thus, the worldÂ’s being a certain way is identical with its having a certain property. Since, therefore, the worldÂ’s being a certain way is identical with some propositionÂ’s being true, propositions must be identified with properties and a propositionÂ’s being true must be identified with its being instantiated. Propositions are properties and truth is instantiatedness.[55] 

ItÂ’s widely thought that propositions are human creations. This is false. The world was a certain way before we were around; it will be a certain way after weÂ’re gone; and the way it is while weÂ’re around is up to us only to a limited extent.[56] 
It follows that, independently of our having any beliefs or, indeed, our doing or thinking anything, certain propositions are true; and it follows from this that propositions are not human creations. Sentences, on the other hand, are human creations. They wouldnÂ’t be around if it werenÂ’t for us. So sentential analysis is a very different thing from propositional analysis. 

4.2.4 Not all philosophical analysis is identical with linguistic analysis (continued): FregeÂ’s accomplishments reassessed 
But didnÂ’t we say that FregeÂ’s great accomplishment lay in his insights concerning sentencesÂ—in his seeing that a sentenceÂ’s surface structure sometimes pulled part from its deep structure? And didnÂ’t we say that, for this very reason, Frege was the first analytic philosopherÂ—that, as Michael Dummett put it, analytic philosophy is post-Fregean philosophy, the reason being that analytic philosophy is statement-analysis? Yes, we did say all this. And yet we just spent a lot of time saying how analytic philosophy is Â“statement-analysisÂ” only in the sense of being statement-meaning-analysis; that is, proposition-analysis, as opposed to sentence-analysis. How are we to reconcile those various statements with one another? 
The term Â“analytic philosophyÂ” can be construed narrowly or broadly. Construed narrowly, analytic philosophy is post-Fregean philosophy in the sense that it directly flows out of FregeÂ’s work. Frege was interested in reference, quantification, the nature of logical truth, the extent to which itÂ’s possible to formalize intuitively valid inferences, etc. (These terms will be defined soon enough, if they havenÂ’t been already.) The term Â“analytic philosophyÂ” sometimes refers to what is done by those people who write about those very questions and who, in so doing, are taking what Frege had to say about them into account. In other words, Â“analytic philosophyÂ” sometimes refers to the philosophy of language, along with a related branch of philosophy, known as philosophical logic.[57] 

But FregeÂ’s work had a profound influence on philosophers who were working in areas that have no direct connection to language or logic. Frege showed that, by thinking clearly, systematically, and self-critically, one could make real headway on philosophical problems in which others had yet to make so much as a dent, despite hundreds of years of trying. Â“The devil is in the details,Â” as they say. Pre-Fregean philosophers tended to disregard the details. Frege did not. He was a stickler for them. And it was partly, though obviously not entirely, for this reason that he was able to solve problems that his predecessors could not. The word Â“analytic philosopherÂ” sometimes refers to the sort of philosophy done by people who aspire to approach philosophical problems in the same careful and clear-headed way as Frege. 
Thus, there are analytic philosophers of law, analytic ethicists, analytic philosophers of religion, etc. What makes them analytic philosophers isnÂ’t that theyÂ’re talking about language or logic or any of the things that Frege talked about. ItÂ’s that they believe the problems theyÂ’re concerned with can be solved in the same coolheaded, logical way that Frege solved problems relating to language and logic. 
But even when taken in the narrow sense, Â“analytic philosophyÂ” (i.e., philosophical logic/the philosophy of language) is only misleadingly described as the analysis of sentences. Philosophers of language are interested in the sentence: 
(NS) Â“Nothing is a square circle,Â” 
only to the extent that by understanding it they will deepen their insight into concepts of a general kind (e.g., meaning, analytic truth, modality). Linguists, on the other hand, are interested in those concepts only to the extent that an understanding of them will help them understand specific sentences, such as NS. Frege did indeed painstakingly analyze specific sentences. But he did so only because he knew that, by so doing, he could identify general logical principles. Thus, for Frege, his insight that logical and grammatical form pull apart was ultimately just a means to an end, the end being the identification of the actual nature of the bearing-relations that propositions have with respect to one another. So, yes, analytic philosophy is statement-analysis; and, yes, it was FregeÂ’s brilliant analyses of sentences that availed philosophers of the principles needed to analyze statements properly. But analytic philosophy, even the narrow sense of the term, is not itself sentential analysis. 

4.2.5 Not all philosophical analysis is identical with linguistic analysis (continued): WittgensteinÂ—an introduction 
WittgensteinÂ’s two best-known works are the Tractatus LogicoÂ­philosophicus (TLP), which he completed in 1921, and the Philosophical Investigations, which he completed in 1949. In many ways, these works are antithetical to each other. But in both of them, Wittgenstein insists that philosophical problems arise when, and only when, sentences are misused and are solved when, and only when, it is made clear how they are being misused. 
In the TLP, Wittgenstein contends that all philosophical problems result from a failure to understand the syntactic rules of the languages we use. Sentences that would, if meaningful, express philosophical propositions are in all cases ungrammatical nonsense and thus fail to say anything. All such sentences violate the syntactic rules of the languages to which they belong. (For the time being, Â“syntacticÂ” may be taken to be synonymous with Â“grammatical.Â” See Chapter 4, Section 3.3 for a definition of Â“syntax.Â”) Because they violate these rules in subtle, easily overlooked ways, they arenÂ’t always seen for the abject nonsense that they are. But we mustnÂ’t let appearances deceive us. All such sentences are syntactically ill-formed and therefore devoid of meaning, and there would be no philosophical problems if people fully understood the syntactic rules of the languages they spoke. So far as philosophy has any legitimate function, it is to identify these rules, thereby heading off the syntactic blunders that lead to philosophical puzzlement. 
In the Philosophical Investigations Wittgenstein says, just as he does in the TLP, that philosophical problems arise when language is misused. But in the Investigations he denies that such misuses involve violations of hidden syntactic rules, and instead says that such misuses consist exclusively in oneÂ’s using words in ways in which they are not ordinarily used. Thus, WittgensteinÂ’s position in the Investigations is that all philosophical problems can be quickly and definitively solved by looking at how words are actually used and, on the basis of the knowledge thereby obtained, ceasing to use words in deviant ways. What we think of as philosophical puzzles concerning knowledge, logic, and morality are puzzles about the words Â“knowledge,Â” Â“logic,Â” and Â“morality.Â” Those puzzles are created by our using those words in non-standard ways, and theyÂ’re solved by our ceasing to do so. 


4.2.6 Is meaning identical with use? 
In a moment, weÂ’ll evaluate WittgensteinÂ’s (1922) contention that all philosophical statements are ungrammatical nonsense. Right now, let us consider WittgensteinÂ’s (1958) contention that philosophical puzzles are dissolved by looking at how words are used. 
This contention is incoherent on many levels. Given only the acoustical and morphological properties of its spoken and written occurrences, the word Â“knowledgeÂ” could mean anything.[58] 
So, supposing that itÂ’s the concept of knowledge that we wish to learn about, we canÂ’t possibly know that the word Â“knowledgeÂ” is the right word to study unless we know that it expresses the right concept. But we canÂ’t possibly know that unless we have some way of grasping that concept that doesn't involve our operating with that word.
