So we canÂ’t even act on WittgensteinÂ’s exhortation that we study knowledge by studying how people use the word Â“knowledgeÂ” unless we have some way of grasping the concept of knowledge that doesnÂ’t involve that word. But if we donÂ’t need that word to grasp that concept, we donÂ’t need it to study it; and if we donÂ’t need it to study it, then Wittgenstein is simply wrong to say that one must study how it is used to understand the concept it expresses. Given any expression E and any concept C, an obvious extension of this argument shows that one canÂ’t learn about C by studying E unless one can grasp C, and can therefore examine it, without EÂ’s help. Thus, Wittgenstein is simply wrong to contend that one learns about concepts by learning about how the corresponding words are used. 
Â“But youÂ’ve overstated what Wittgenstein is claiming,Â” it will be said. Â“Contrary to what you allege, he wasnÂ’t saying that concepts are to be learned about solely by looking at how the corresponding words are typically used. He was saying only that knowledge of expression-usage would be a useful adjunct to some other, more important way of knowing about concepts.Â” 
If thatÂ’s what Wittgenstein is saying, then heÂ’s conceding everything said in the paragraph preceding the last one.[59] 
To grant that there is any expression-independent way of grasping concepts is to grant that expression-usage is to be evaluated in light of the very conceptual knowledge that, according to WittgensteinÂ’s thesis, one is supposed to acquire through the study of expression-usage. 
But thereÂ’s a problem with our argument. It assumes that, given a meaningful expression (e.g., Â“knowledgeÂ”), there is some object that is its meaning. Wittgenstein rejects this assumption. He holds that there is no entity that is the meaning of Â“knowledge.Â” WittgensteinÂ’s position is, I quote, that Â“meaning is use.Â”[60] 
In other words, for an expression to have a given meaning is for it to be used in a certain way. An expressionÂ’s having a given meaning does not, in WittgensteinÂ’s view, involve there being some entity that is its meaning. 
Before we evaluate this contention, we must make a few facts about it clear. Wittgenstein isnÂ’t making the uncontroversial point that how expressions are used is a function, in part, of what they mean. Nor is he making the equally innocuous point that how an expression is used may have effects on what it means. (Â“ProbableÂ” used to mean Â“capable of being definitively established.Â” Enough people used it to mean Â“likely, but not certainÂ”; and, for that reason, thatÂ’s what it now means.) He is saying that what it is for an expression to have a given meaning is for it to be used in a certain way. Here, in my words, not Wittgenstein's, is his argument: 
(WA)[61] 
According to some philosophers, there is some entity that is the meaning of Â“snow is whiteÂ” and some other entity that is the meaning of Â“grass is green.Â” These entities are known as propositions. Propositions (if existent) are nonÂ­spatiotemporal entities. 
The very idea of such an entity is of doubtful coherence. And even if such entities do exist, theyÂ’re nothing to us. We canÂ’t see them or touch them or otherwise have anything to do with them. So, even if they do exist, they have no role in human affairs. At the same time, Â“snow is whiteÂ” and Â“grass is greenÂ” differ in meaning. 
So we must find a way of saying what it is for two expressions to Â‘differ in meaningÂ’ that doesnÂ’t involve our positing meanings. 
This can be done. Â“Snow is whiteÂ” isnÂ’t used in the same way as Â“grass is green.Â” There are situations that prompt utterances of the one that donÂ’t prompt utterances of the other. 
By the same token, if they were used in the same wayÂ—i.e., if there were no situation that prompted utterances of the one that didnÂ’t prompt utterances of the otherÂ—then they wouldnÂ’t differ in meaning. If the sensory stimulations that induced people to say Â“grass is greenÂ” coincided with those that prompted people to say Â“snow is white,Â” there would be no significant sense in which they Â“differed in meaning.Â”[62] 
Thus, two sentences S1 and S2 coincide 
in meaning exactly if they are used in the same way. So instead of identifying the meaning of Â“grass is greenÂ” with some nonÂ­spatiotemporal entityÂ—with some entity whose existence is in doubt and whose role in human affairs, supposing it to exist, is also in doubtÂ—we can just say that two expressions Â“have the same meaningÂ” if theyÂ’re used in the same way. An obvious corollary is that for an expression to have this as opposed to that Â“meaningÂ” is for it to be used in this as opposed to that way. 
Were WA cogent, Wittgenstein would be doing to meanings what Frege did to square circles. Frege got rid of square circles by showing that sentences appearing to require their existence (e.g., Â“square circles simultaneously have, and lack, uniform curvaturesÂ”) are equivalent to sentences that donÂ’t (e.g., Â“the statement x is a circle entails x has a uniform curvature and the statement x is a square entails x does not have a uniform curvatureÂ”). Wittgenstein wishes to get rid of meanings by showing that statements appearing to require the existence of expression-meanings are equivalent to statements (about expression-usage) that donÂ’t. 
This wish of WittgensteinÂ’s embodies some very wrong views as to what linguistic expressions are. A burst of noise that doesnÂ’t have a meaning is just a burst of noise. A burst of noise is an expression only if it has a meaning. But if it already has a meaning, then how it is being used isnÂ’t what gives it its meaning. 
Our knowledge of what words mean is what guides our linguistic behavior. Expressions have meanings. We know this. And thatÂ’s why we use expressions in the way we do. I know what Â“hugÂ” means; I also know what Â“discussÂ” means. ThatÂ’s why, when talking to my students, I say Â“I want to discuss the exam,Â” and not Â“I want to hug the exam.Â” If meaning were use, meaning couldnÂ’t guide use. But it obviously does. 
To the extent that meaning doesnÂ’t guide use, people are misspeaking. Wanting to tell you that youÂ’re an absolute genius, I say Â“youÂ’re an absolute moron,Â” since, despite my generally good command of the English language, I wrongly think that Â“moronÂ” means genius. To the extent that my uttering those words embodied a failure to know the actual meaning of what I was sayingÂ—to the extent that meaning failed to guide use, in other wordsÂ—I misspoke. And to the extent that my uttering those words embodied a knowledge of what they meantÂ—to the extent that meaning did guide use, in other wordsÂ—I spoke properly. This shows that, to the extent that utterances arenÂ’t simply defective, meaning guides use and consequently that use is not constitutive of meaning. 
Bearing these points in mind, let us revisit WittgensteinÂ’s (1958) contention that itÂ’s a philosopherÂ’s job, not to analyze concepts or meanings or other such alleged phantasms, but merely to take note of when words like Â“justice,Â” Â“knowledge,Â” and Â“truthÂ” are used. What would it be to do this? The situations in which the word Â“justiceÂ” is used donÂ’t necessarily have any observable characteristics in common with one another. ItÂ’s not as though people utter the word Â“justiceÂ” when, and only when, theyÂ’ve just been bitten by a cat. This isnÂ’t to say that uses of the word Â“justiceÂ” cannot be correlated in any way with facts about the situations in which those uses occur. Such correlations clearly can be made. People are likely to use that word when theyÂ’re in classes concerning ethics or the philosophy of law; theyÂ’re likely to use it when they believe that theyÂ’ve been wronged; theyÂ’re likely to be used by politicians who want people to believe them to be worthy of holding office. 
The italicized terms express extremely abstract concepts; and utterances of those words are no more capable than utterances of the word Â“justiceÂ” being correlated with observable facts about the contexts in which they occur. So, while a personÂ’s decision to use the word Â“justiceÂ” (or Â“knowledgeÂ” or Â“law,Â” etc.) may obviously have a situational basis, there is no way to identify that basis except in terms of the very concepts that, according to Wittgenstein, are to be studied by figuring when those terms are used. In other words, any correct generalization as to when words like Â“justice,Â” Â“logic,Â” Â“knowledgeÂ” and Â“moralityÂ” are used will itself employ the very concepts that, according to Wittgenstein, knowledge of such generalizations is supposed to yield. 
These reflections bring us face to face with an incoherence inherent in all of the different variants of the contention that philosophy is sentence-analysis. To speak isnÂ’t just to make noises; itÂ’s to make noises for the reason that one believes those noises to have certain meanings. IÂ’m with my friend Larry. All of a sudden he starts convulsing and foaming at the mouth. I call 9-1-1 and say: 
(i) Â“My friend is foaming at the mouth and convulsing; please send help.Â” 
I did not say: 
(ii) Â“I like pizza,Â” 
or: 
(iii) Â“Giraffes are friendly creatures.Â” 
Why did I utter (i)? Why didnÂ’t I utter (ii) or (iii)? Because I know that (i) has the right meaning and that (ii) and (iii) donÂ’t. In general, speaking consists of making noises for the reason that one believes that, given existing semantic rules, those noises have certain meanings. If somebody makes a noise that he does not believe to be assigned a meaning by any semantic rule, he isnÂ’t speaking. If, not believing that the noises IÂ’m about to make are assigned any meaning by any semantic rules, I say Â“blurga dunga blurbo,Â” I am not speaking. IÂ’m just making noise. Maybe the semantic rules of some language do assign them a meaning. That doesnÂ’t matter. My making that noise wasnÂ’t guided by my knowledge of such rules. So I wasnÂ’t saying anything.[63] 
And as we saw earlier, I am misspeaking if I misidentify the meaning assigned by existing semantic rules to the noises I am making. So there is no bona fide speech where there isnÂ’t awareness of semantic rules. 
Thus, the analysis of sentences isnÂ’t the analysis of noises. (In this context, take references to Â“noisesÂ” to be short for references to anything that can constitute the occurrence of an expressionÂ—e.g., hand-movements, patterns of light on a monitor, etc.) In and of themselves, noises arenÂ’t speech, as we just saw. It is only when a noise embodies an attempt to follow a semantic rule that it constitutes speech. So the analysis of speechÂ—that is, of spoken sentencesÂ—concerns noises only to the extent that they embody attempts to follow such rules; and for the same reason mutatis mutandis, the analysis of sentences per se, as opposed to their spoken (or written) occurrences, necessarily involves, if it doesnÂ’t coincide with, the analysis of those rules. 
Those rules are not themselves sentences. The semantic rule that assigns meaning to Â“snow is whiteÂ” is not itself a sentence.[64] 
Given these points, 
what might it mean to say that philosophy is sentential analysis? It could mean that philosophy is the empirical study of different languages; i.e., that philosophy is linguistics. But that clearly isnÂ’t what philosophy is. So it must mean that philosophy is the study of semantic rules qua semantic rulesÂ—that, in other words, it is the study of the concept of a semantic rule. 
In that case, philosophy is also the study of those concepts that must be understood to understand the concept of a semantic rule. And there are many such concepts. Among them are narrowly semantic concepts such as compositionality, reference, quantification, force, and negation.[65] 

But many of these concepts arenÂ’t only of relevance to semantics. As weÂ’ve seen, no noise constitutes a sentence-utterance unless it embodies an intention of a certain kind; and there is no linguistic behavior of any kind where people arenÂ’t intentionally following what they believe to be existing semantic rules. Some believe that semantic rules are conventions. Others believe that they are functions (in the mathematical sense)Â— assignments of meanings or truth-conditions to noises or to properties that are instantiated by noises (or ink marks, etc.). There is no way to figure out what semantic rules are without examining these concepts. 
And even if these questions are side-stepped, and philosophers focus only on narrowly semantic concepts (e.g., reference, compositionality, etc.), philosophy ends up being the analysis, not of sentences, but of concepts. Thus, the thesis that philosophy is the study of sentences either collapses into the obviously false thesis that philosophy is the empirical study of language or into the thesis that philosophy is conceptual analysis (i.e., the analysis of the concepts in terms of which the world is understood). Thus, WittgensteinÂ’s contention that philosophy is the study of sentences collapses into the very view to which it is meant to be an alternative (viz., that philosophy is the analysis of concepts, as opposed to expressions), and is therefore false. 
Let us now turn to WittgensteinÂ’s (1922) Tractarian contention that philosophical statements are ungrammatical nonsense. 

4.2.7 The Tractarian contention that philosophical statements are syntactically ill-formed nonsense 
The sentence: 
(a) Â“One can be aware of the fact that 1 + 1 = 2 without being causally affected by that fact,Â” 
appears meaningful. So does the sentence: 
(b) Â“There could in principle be a legal system that failed to embody any morality at all.Â” 
But in the TLP Wittgenstein says that this is an illusion. Here is the viewpoint underlying this bold contention: 
(TA)[67] 
All philosophical statements are ungrammatical nonsense, and all philosophical problems would vanish if we spoke grammatically. Â“All philosophical problems belong to the same class as the question whether the good is more or less identical than the beautiful.Â”[68] 
Thus, all philosophical statements belong to the same class as: 
(BG) Â“the good is more or less identical than the beautiful.Â” 
BG is obviously meaningless. The reason for this is that itÂ’s syntactically ill-formed. If we produced only syntactically well-formed sentences, we wouldnÂ’t produce nonsense like BG. Since all philosophical statements are in the same class as BG, weÂ’d never produce any sentences whose merits it was the job of philosophy to determine. 
Were the logical forms of (a) and (b) brought into alignment with their grammatical formsÂ—in other words, were their actual meanings reflected in their grammarÂ—theyÂ’d be ungrammatical since they have no meanings. 
Although TA is a paraphrase, not a quotation, the part in quotes is an exact quotation from the TLP.[69] 

What Wittgenstein is saying isnÂ’t confined to the defensible claim that philosophical problems are to be solved by clarifying statements. Wittgenstein is making two additional claims. First, no sentence that appears to make a philosophical statement means anything. Second, itÂ’s only because theyÂ’re syntactically ill-formed that such sentences are meaninglessÂ—there is no other reason. 
Let us evaluate these claims. Though ungrammatical, the sentence: 
(MH) Â“Me and Herby play tennis every day, and me always win because Herby not in good shape,Â” 
is perfectly meaningful. Ungrammatical statements are often meaningful. Thus, BGÂ’s failure to mean anything cannot be entirely blamed on its being ungrammatical. 
WhatÂ’s the real problem with BG? The expression Â“more identical thanÂ” is obviously supposed to function in the same way as relational expressions, like Â“more important thanÂ” or Â“identical with.Â” But there is no relation that it picks out. Though it consists of English expressions, the expression Â“more identical thanÂ” is itself no more a part of the English lexicon than Â“blurga derba gurb.Â” For that reason, the meaninglessness of BG is to be accounted for in the same way as the meaninglessness of: 
(BG#) Â“The beautiful is blurga derba gurb the good.Â” 
The problem with BG# is that Â“blurga derba gurbÂ” doesnÂ’t mean anything. It may be that its meaninglessness is reflected in its syntax. It may be that because Â“blurga derba gurbÂ” doesnÂ’t mean anything, BG#Â’s syntax is off. But, if so, its syntactic shortcomings are to be explained in terms of its lack of meaning, not vice versa. 
The same holds of BG. The reason that BG doesnÂ’t mean anything is that Â“more identical thanÂ” doesnÂ’t mean anything. BGÂ’s syntactic shortcomings are to be explained in terms of its lack of meaning, and not vice versa. 
This is easily verified. Given any relation R, if Â“more identical thanÂ” denoted R, BG would be meaningful. If, for example, it denoted the relation that is in fact picked out by the expression Â“a better dancer than,Â” BG would say that the good is a better dancer than the beautiful; and it would thus have the same meaning as: 
(BG*) Â“The property of goodness is a better dancer than the property of being beautiful.Â” 
BG* isnÂ’t meaningless; itÂ’s false. The property of goodness canÂ’t dance; neither can any other property, including the property of being beautiful. Therefore, the former property isnÂ’t a better dancer than the latter. Nothing false is meaningless, since to be false is to bear a false meaning. So BG* is meaningful. 
Incidentally, according to Gilbert Ryle (1900Â–1976), a career-long Wittgenstein-hardliner, it cannot meaningfully be said of properties that they can, or cannot, dance.[70] 
It can be said of a human being that he can, or cannot, dance. But nothing that can meaningfully be said of non-properties, such as human beings, can be meaningfully said of properties themselves. 
RyleÂ’s position is false. There are many differences between people and properties. One of them is that people can dance, whereas properties cannot. RyleÂ’s position is also self-refuting. In saying that it cannot be said that properties cannot dance, Ryle is saying exactly what it is that, according to his theory, cannot be said. 
Ryle is confusing absurdity with meaninglessness. The sentence Â“triangles have four sidesÂ” makes an absurd, but meaningful, statement. Given that triangles have three sides, not four, itÂ’s false. Given that itÂ’s false, itÂ’s meaningful. Â“Properties can danceÂ” is absurd, and therefore false, and therefore meaningful. 
There are two kinds of Â“nonsense.Â” A sentence can be nonsense by failing to have any meaning. (BG# is nonsense in this sense.) And a sentence can be nonsense by virtue of having of an absurd meaning. (Â“Properties can danceÂ” is nonsense in this sense.) Ryle doesnÂ’t distinguish between these two kinds of nonsense. Neither does Wittgenstein. And WittgensteinÂ’s position, like RyleÂ’s, is self-refutingÂ—and for much the same reason. If Wittgenstein is right to say that all philosophical assertions are ungrammatical nonsense, that very assertion is ungrammatical nonsense and therefore isnÂ’t true.[71] 

Given how implausible and illogical it is, why on Earth did Wittgenstein hold that philosophical statements are always ungrammatical nonsense? The answer, I believe, is that Wittgenstein thought this view to be the distillation of FregeÂ’s groundbreaking philosophical successes. Frege showed that reparsing sentences sometimes solves philosophical problems. By reparsing: 
(NS) Â“Nothing is a square circle,Â” 
we show that it doesnÂ’t attribute the property of being a square circle to some non-entity, thereby dissolving an age-old riddle. Wittgenstein seems to have inferred from these successes of FregeÂ’s that all philosophical problems are to be solved by reparsing sentences. 
This inference is fallacious. Given only that some philosophical problems are to be solved by reparsing sentences, it doesnÂ’t follow that they are all to be solved in that way. And weÂ’ve seen that, indeed, many of them are not to be solved in that way. 
Also, there were no cases where FregeÂ’s reparsing of a problematic sentence showed it to be ill-formed. For example, in reparsing NS, Frege showed that its logical syntax differed from its apparent syntax. He didnÂ’t show that there was anything wrong with its logical syntax. 
To be sure, philosophers often produce deeply absurd statements. For example, according to pre-Fregean philosophers, NS entails that: 
(NS1) There exists some non-entity that is a square circle. 
If NS1 is right: 
(NS2) There exists some entity that does not exist that is a square and a circle. 
NS2 is self-contradictory and therefore absurd. But itÂ’s obviously 
meaningful. If it werenÂ’t, it wouldnÂ’t contradict itself. (For a sentence to contradict itself is for it to bear two opposed meanings. Â“Smith is a lawyer and Smith is not a lawyerÂ” because the one conjunct[72] 
contradicts the 
other.) But whereas this sentence is explicitly self-contradictory, the self-contradictory sentences that people actually utter are usually only implicitly so. 
But supposing for argumentÂ’s sake that philosophical statements are meaningless, it isnÂ’t because theyÂ’re ungrammatical that theyÂ’re meaningless. 
Second, theyÂ’re not meaningless. The statement that theyÂ’re meaningless is itself a philosophical statement. That statement is therefore false if itÂ’s true. Therefore it is false. (Any statement that entails its own negation is false.) 



4.3 The Tractarian roots of Logical Positivism 
Although one of the TLPÂ’s contentions is that all philosophical statements are ungrammatical nonsense, this is not its main contention. The main contention of the TLP is that: 
(CT) A sentence is meaningful if, and only if, it is either a tautology or an observation report. 
A Â“tautologyÂ” is a definitional truth (e.g., Â“fathers are male,Â” Â“there are three feet in a yardÂ”). 
An Â“observation reportÂ” is a statement that reports what oneÂ’s senses have told one (e.g., Â“I am now seeing a dog,Â” Â“there is chocolate syrup (or, in any case, a brown discoloration of some kind or other) on SmithÂ’s ice-cream,Â” Â“I can see your house from hereÂ”). 
CT can be broken down into two claims: 
(1) All meaningful non-empirical statements are tautologies, 
and: 
(2) All meaningful non-tautologous statements are 
observation-reports. 
(1) entails that non-empirical disciplines (e.g., philosophy, mathematics) consist of statements that say nothing about anything. (2) entails that anything non-tautologous that cannot be known strictly on the basis of what oneÂ’s senses tell one is meaningless. 
WittgensteinÂ’s claim that all philosophical statements are ungrammatical nonsense is a corollary of CT. If theyÂ’re meaningful, philosophical statements, unlike tautologies, are non-trivial. Consider the statement that: 
(KC) Â“Knowing a truth doesnÂ’t necessarily involve oneÂ’s being affected by the state of affairs described by that truth.Â” 
KC isn't empirical and neither is its negation. KC isn't a tautology and neither is its negation. But KC is a philosophical statement and so is its 
negation. If CT is correct, it immediately follows that both KC and its negation are ungrammatical nonsense. Since philosophical assertions are never tautologous, CT entails, as Wittgenstein knew, that philosophical assertions are categorically meaningless. 
The position that (1) and (2) are both correct is known as logical positivism (LP). During the decade or so following the publication of the TLP, and largely because of it, LP was very popular.[75] 
But (1) and (2) are false. Let us now say why. 


4.4 Verificationism and falsificationism 
(2) is identical with a doctrine known as verificationism. According to verificationism a non-tautologous statement is meaningful iff itÂ’s capable of being verified strictly on the basis of sensory observation.[76] 

Verificationism is false. The statement Â“all metal expands when heatedÂ” is meaningful. But it cannot be conclusively verified (i.e., shown to be true) strictly on the basis of observation. No matter how many metal objects you find to expand when heated, itÂ’s a possibility that some metal object that you havenÂ’t yet considered will fail to do so.[77] 

Even though it cannot be verified, Â“all metal expands when heatedÂ” can be falsified (i.e., shown to be false) strictly on the basis of observation. Advocates of LP saw this and, having for this reason rejected verificationism, they accepted a doctrine known as falsificationism. According to falsificationism, a non-tautologous statement is meaningful if and only if itÂ’s capable of being falsified strictly on the basis of observation.[78] 

Falsificationism is false. Though obviously meaningful, the statement Â“there exists a gold ball that weighs exactly 27.13654 lbs.Â” cannot be conclusively falsified, since no matter how many gold balls you consider it is possible that some gold ball that you havenÂ’t considered has that weight. 
Falsificationism is really a version of verificationism. According to verificationism, S is meaningful if verifiable. According to falsificationism, S is meaningful if SÂ’s negation is verifiable. So given that verificationism fails, itÂ’s no surprise that falsificationism does as well. 
In light of the failure of falsificationism, advocates of LP decided to soften their views about meaningfulness one more time. This time, they said that a non-tautologous statement is meaningful if possible observations can confirm it. (P confirms Q if, other things being equal, Q is more likely to be true if P is true than if not-P is true. Other things being equal, Smith is more likely to be wealthy if he wears fancy clothes than if he doesnÂ’t wear fancy clothes. Thus, Â“Smith wears fancy clothesÂ” confirms Â“Smith is wealthy.Â”) WeÂ’ll refer to this view as Â“confirmationalism.Â” 
Confirmationalism is equivalent with the position that all meaningful non-tautologous statements are empirical. An empirical statement is one that, if true, expresses a truth that must be known through observation and that, if false, is the negation of a true empirical statement. Â“There are trees in Santa Barbara, CAÂ” is a true empirical statement, and Â“there are no trees in Santa Barbara, CAÂ” is a false one. The negation of an empirical statement is an empirical statement. This is because, if itÂ’s an empirical question whether or not S is true, then itÂ’s an empirical question whether or not S is false, and therefore whether or not not-S is true. (As we will see, there are very few truths, if any, that can be known strictly through observation. A statement is empirical if the truth or falsity of it is to be decided on grounds that are at least partly observational.) 
Henceforth when we refer to Â“logical positivismÂ” (LP), we will refer to the position that a statement S is meaningful if and only if (i) S is a tautology (e.g., Â“sisters are female siblingsÂ”) or (ii) S is an empirical statement (e.g., Â“there are trees in Santa BarbaraÂ”).[79] 


4.5 Logical Positivism Evaluated 
Consider the statement: 
(1) Â“Triangles are three sided figures.Â” 
(1) is plausibly seen as being true by convention. The same is true of: 
(2) Â“Pentagons have five sides.Â” 
For argumentÂ’s sake, weÂ’ll grant that, indeed, (1) and (2) are true by conventionÂ—that theyÂ’re definitional truths.[80] 

Given (1) and (2), it follows that: 
(3) If x is the number of sides of an arbitrary triangle and y is the number of sides of an arbitrary pentagon, then w is an even prime iff w is one less than x and three less than y. 
But (3) clearly isnÂ’t a conventional truth. Though it follows from conventions, (3) is not itself a convention. (3) is thus a non-tautologous, non-empirical truth. It follows that LP is false. 
ItÂ’s possible to have conventions that are inconsistent with one another. (Two statements are inconsistent with each other if it is logically impossible for them both to be true. Thus, Â“Smith has three carsÂ” is inconsistent with Â“Smith has no cars.Â”) If I stipulate that Â“xÂ” unambiguously refers to the number two, and I also stipulate that Â“xÂ” refers to the number of sides of a triangle, my definitions are inconsistent with one another. The internal consistency of conventions is not itself a matter of convention. It isnÂ’t an empirical fact that the conventions just described are inconsistent with each other. To say that P is inconsistent with Q is to say that P must be false if Q is true. Observation cannot tell you what must be the case; it can tell you, at most, what is the case. So it cannot tell you that two linguistic conventions are inconsistent with each other. 
Since observation cannot tell you whether or not two statements are inconsistent with each other, it cannot tell you whether or not one statement is a necessary consequence of some other. This is because for Q to be a necessary consequence of P is for P to be inconsistent with the negation of Q. (The negation of "John has an even, positive number of cars" is "it is not the case that John has an even, positive number of cars" or, more simply, "John does not have an even, positive numbers" In general, the negation of a Q is not-Q. "John has an even, positive number of cars" entails "John has at least one car" because the second sentence cannot be false if the first is true, 
i.e. the negation of the second sentence (namely, "it is not the case that John has at least one car" or, more simply, "John has no cars") cannot possibly be true if John has an even, positive numbers.) 
When evaluating LP, one must be careful to distinguish sentences from their meanings. Two different sentences can have the same meaning (e.g., Â“snow is whiteÂ” and Â“schnee ist weissÂ”). The meaning of a sentence is a proposition. A proposition is what is affirmed by an utterance or a sentence in the indicative mood. (So an example of a proposition is the thing that is affirmed by an utterance of Â“snow is white.Â”) Propositions are not sentences. The thing meant by Â“snow is whiteÂ” is not itself a sentence. (Â“Schnee is weissÂ” is not the same sentence as Â“snow is white," but they both affirm the same proposition.) Some sentences express propositions that are logically true. A proposition is logically true if the laws of logic prohibit its negation from being true. The proposition meant by: 
(4) Â“If a given thing is round, then that thing is not a square,Â” 
is logically true, since the laws of logic donÂ’t allow round things to be square. For this reason, some authors would describe (4) itself, the sentence, as logically true. But what they mean is that given what it is that it means, (4) must be true. So what they are in fact describing as logically true is the proposition that (4) couldnÂ’t be false, given what it is that it means. 
Thus, it is always propositions, and never sentences, that are logically true. But no proposition is true by convention. ItÂ’s up to us what our symbols mean. But itÂ’s not up to us whether those meanings are correct. ItÂ’s up to us what it is that Â“the moon is not made of cheeseÂ” means. But it isnÂ’t up to us whether that meaning is correct. LP identifies logical truth with conventional truth: truths of logic are sentences that are true by convention. But thatÂ’s false. Logical truths are never sentences; theyÂ’re always propositions, and propositions are never conventionally true. 
Incidentally, (ii) collapses into (i). Linguistic conventions are known empirically. It can be known only through observation that Â“triangles have three sidesÂ” is true. That sentence could mean anything.[81] 
It could mean that penguins are smarter than humans; and itÂ’s only because youÂ’ve had the requisite sense-perceptions that you know it not to mean this. 
It should be pointed out that logical positivists were unanimous in denying the existence of propositions and of meanings generally. Logical positivists didnÂ’t accept the view that for a lecture to concern triangles is for the meaning of that lecture to concern triangles. This is why Rudolph Carnap[82] 
(1890Â–1970), an LP-hardliner for many years, said that for a lecture to concern triangles is for the word Â“triangleÂ” to occur in the lecture. 
CarnapÂ’s view is false. Many a lecture that doesnÂ’t contain the word Â“triangleÂ” concerns triangles. (Think of all the mathematics lectures given in Japanese, Swedish, and Arabic. How often does the word Â“triangleÂ” occur in them?) And a lecture that contains the word Â“triangleÂ” isnÂ’t necessarily about triangles. Somebody giving a lecture on linguistics may use the word "triangle" to illustrate some point about phonetics; but in so doing, that person isnÂ’t talking about triangles. TheyÂ’re talking, not about triangles, but about the word Â“triangle.Â” 
The distinction between the word Â“triangleÂ” and the corresponding meaning is one that Carnap couldnÂ’t countenance without ceasing to be a logical positivist. The very essence of logical positivism is the denial of meaning. For argumentÂ’s sake, suppose there were to exist objects that are the meanings of sentences. (Following convention, weÂ’ll refer to these things as Â“propositions.Â”) Given the existence of propositions, whether a given sentence is meaningful is not to be explained in terms of its being either tautologous or confirmable. Rather, a sentenceÂ’s being tautologous or confirmable is to be explained in terms of its bearing a proposition of a certain kind. A tautologous sentence would be one that had a logically correct proposition for its meaning, and a confirmable sentence would be one that had a confirmable proposition for its meaning. But if there are logically true propositions, then some truths are ipso facto not empirical. 
We can use words in any way that we like. We can use the words Â“if Smith has three boats, then Smith has more than one boatÂ” to mean that 1 + 1 = 3. But whatever meaning we end up assigning to those words, itÂ’s not up to us whether that meaning is correct. And if that meaning is of a logical nature, as is actually the case, there is ipso facto non-empirical truth, an immediate consequence being that LP is wrong. 
CarnapÂ’s attempt to do away with meanings consisted his saying (though he did not himself put it this starkly) that the meaning of the word Â“snowÂ” was that very word and, in general, that words are their own meanings.[83] 
Given how brazenly wrong this view is, CarnapÂ’s attempt to do away with meanings never had many takers. 
A much better received attempt to do away with meanings is to be found in a doctrine known as conceptual role semantics (CRS). According to CRS, two sentences have the same meaning if, and only if, they are used in the same way. So Â“hace mucho calorÂ” is the Spanish translation of Â“itÂ’s hotÂ” not because those sentences share a meaningÂ—meanings donÂ’t exist, according to CRSÂ—but because the one sentence is used in the same way as the other. 
[84] 

CRS seems to coincide with the Wittgenstein thesis that Â“meaning is use.Â” It is thus no surprise that, when scrutinized, CRS proves unfeasible. So far as she isnÂ’t misspeaking or randomly barking out noises, anyone who says Â“itÂ’s hot outÂ” or Â“hace mucho calor,Â” or any other sentence, does so because she knows that existing semantic rules assign a certain proposition to those words and she wishes to put that proposition into words. 
One immediate consequence of this is that CarnapÂ’s position is false. Another immediate consequence is that what it is for those two sentences to have the same meaning is not for them to be Â“used in the same way.Â” 
Also, given any natural language, there are infinitely many sentences belonging to it that have never been used. The thesis that sentences have the same meaning iff theyÂ’re used in the same way has the absurd consequence that any two sentences that havenÂ’t been used before have the same meaning. (If two sentences arenÂ’t used at all, they arenÂ’t used differently, and are therefore used in the same way Â– if only in a vacuous sense.) 

4.6 Logical Positivism Evaluated (continued) 
LetÂ’s resume our discussion of Logical Positivism (LP). WeÂ’ve seen that, contrary to what LP says, there are non-empirical truths that have nothing to do with anyoneÂ’s linguistic practices. WeÂ’ll now see that, contrary to what LP says, there are facts about the spatiotemporal world that cannot possibly be known strictly on the basis of sense-perception. 
Let NT be the body of assertions jointly constituting NewtonÂ’s physics.[85] 
There is no denying that NT is meaningful. But by itself NT doesnÂ’t make any predictions or otherwise have observable consequences. Physical laws are expressed by conditional assertionsÂ—that is, by statements of the form Â‹if P, then Q.Â›[86] 
NT doesnÂ’t say anything about how this or that physical object will behave. It says how a given object will behave if certain conditions are met. For example, NT says an object will behave if it has a certain mass and is within a certain distance of another body having a certain mass.[87] 
But NT itself obviously doesnÂ’t say that this or that object has this or that mass or is within this or that distance of this or that other specific body. Thus, taken by itself, NT isnÂ’t confirmable. What is confirmable isnÂ’t NT, but NT plus statements describing specific matters of fact. In other words, what is confirmable isnÂ’t NT, but rather some statement of the form Â‹given such and such, NT makes it likely that thus and such.Â› 
But NT is obviously meaningful. This is a problem for LP. To deal with it, advocates of that doctrine proposed that (ii) be replaced with the position that (ii*) a statement S1 is meaningful if there is some statement S2, such that 
given S2, S1 is confirmable (i.e., capable of being supported by observation). 
By this standard, Â“the nothing nothingsÂ” qualifies as meaningful and so does every other nonsense sentence one can think of. Given the statement Â“if grass is green, then the nothing nothings,Â” anything that confirms Â“grass is greenÂ” confirms Â“the nothing nothings,Â” and Â“the nothing nothingsÂ” thus qualifies as meaningful. 
LP replaced (ii*) with other, similar proposals. But they all failed for reasons similar to the one just discussed.[88] 

4.6.1 An incoherence internal to verificationism and falsificationism 
In this section, weÂ’ll identify an incoherence that lies at the heart of both verificationism and falsificationism. But before we can identify that incoherence, we must make a preliminary point concerning what it is that verificationism and falsificationism allege. (For the sake of brevity, weÂ’ll focus on verificationism, leaving unstated the obvious corollaries concerning falsificationism.) 
Verificationism is not the doctrine that in order for a statement to be meaningful it must in fact have been verified. There are several reasons why such a doctrine would be too absurd to have so much as a veneer of plausibility. First of all, it would have the false consequence that false statements couldnÂ’t be meaningful. (Since meaningless statements are neither true nor false, false statements are always meaningful.) Secondly, such a doctrine would have the consequence that statements that havenÂ’t been verified are categorically meaningless---even if they could be verified. So, supposing that no one has looked inside the cupboard, it would have the consequence that, since it hasnÂ’t been verified, the sentence Â“there is bread in the cupboardÂ” is meaningless. Thus, such a doctrine would have the consequence that statements are meaningless if we cannot yet verify them, even though we could verify them were circumstances to change. So such a doctrine would entail that, if we didnÂ’t have the technological wherewithal to open the cupboard, the statement Â“there is bread in the cupboardÂ” would be meaningless even though (a) it obviously does have a meaning and (b) we might soon have the requisite technology. Finally, such a doctrine would entail that hitherto meaningless statement would become meaningful upon being verified. So Â“there is bread in the cupboardÂ” would be meaningless until it was verified; and, upon being verified, it would be meaningful. 
But statements cannot become meaningful by being verified. Statements arenÂ’t in a position to be verified unless they are already meaningful. Because it has no meaning, Â“yarblek truflo blurgoÂ” cannot be verified. And itÂ’s only because Â“there is bread in the cupboardÂ” does have a meaning that it can be verified. 
For these reasons, verificationism, if it is to have any plausibility at all, cannot possibly be the doctrine that a statement is meaningful iff it has been verified, and it must instead be the doctrine that a statement is meaningful iff it could be verified, at least in principle. So verificationism must be the doctrine that a statement S is meaningful iff there are possible observations that definitively establish its truth. In other words, S is meaningful iff, setting aside the limitations on our powers of observation set by our current circumstances, there are possible observations O1Â…On such that, if those observation were had, S would ipso facto have been proven correct. 
Bearing these points in mind, consider the following passage: 
(*) There are possible observations that, were they actual, would verify statement S. To put this in a way that doesnÂ’t suggest, absurdly, that there exist non-existent objects: there are observation-types that are not instantiated but whose instances, supposing that the aforementioned types were instantiated, would verify S. 
WeÂ’ve seen, unless (*) is meaningful, verificationism collapses into the brazenly absurd doctrine that a statement is meaningful only if it has been verified---only if, in other words, actual observations have proven it correct. 
But, supposing that verificationism is correct, how is (*) to be verified? Not through observation. For ex hypothesi the relevant observation-types have not, as of yet, been instantiated. So there is no direct, experiential evidence that those types could be instantiated. Thus, (*) is false unless there exist entities for which there can be no direct experiential or observational evidence. Therefore, according to verificationism, (*) is meaningless. No meaningless statement is true. Verificationism is false unless (*) is true. Therefore, verificationism is false. 
Also, if verificationism is right, claims about what is possible but non-actual are meaningless. What is non-actual cannot be observed and claims about it thus cannot be verified. So (*) is meaningless if verificationism is correct, and verificationism is therefore false. 
Falsificationism (Â“S is meaningful iff not-S is verifiableÂ”) is false for the same reasons mutatis mutandis as verificationism. 


4.7 Logical Positivism self-defeating 
For the reasons just given, it soon became clear that LP was unsalvageable, and soon everybody jumped ship. In fact, it was some of LPÂ’s most staunch proponents who first made it clear what LPÂ’s shortcomings were. 
WeÂ’ll see this in this chapter when we discuss the brilliant criticisms of LP put forth by Carl Hempel (1905Â–1997), who was one of LPÂ’s first and most ardent advocates. But erstwhile advocates of LP tended not to see the incoherence that lies at the center of that doctrine. When saying why they rejected LP, they usually cited narrow, technical problems of the sort just discussed. What they didnÂ’t do, but what weÂ’re about to do, is to say why LP is at its very core a broken and illogical doctrine.[89] 

Anything that is true or false is meaningful. Truth implies meaningfulness and so does falsity. Thus, LP is meaningful if itÂ’s correct. LP says that any meaningful statement is either a tautology or is empirical. So if LP is correct, it is itself either a tautology or it is empirical. 
It isnÂ’t a matter of convention that the expression Â“meaningful sentenceÂ” is interchangeable with the expression Â“sentence that is either a tautology or is empirical.Â” Therefore, LP isnÂ’t a tautology. 
Since it isnÂ’t a tautology, LP is an empirical truth if it isnÂ’t false. (A similar argument: LP is a theory. It is a theory concerning the conditions sentences must satisfy to be meaningful. Tautologies arenÂ’t theories. Tautologies are conventions. Conventions arenÂ’t theories. Therefore, LP isnÂ’t a tautology.) 
But LP isnÂ’t an empirical truth. Any attempt to provide an observational basis for any statement presupposes the meaningfulness of that statement and thus presupposes an answer to the question Â“what conditions must a statement fulfill to be meaningful?Â” For this reason, the question Â“what conditions must a statement satisfy if it is to be meaningful?Â” isnÂ’t empirical in nature. It follows that one cannot coherently attempt to find empirical grounds for accepting LP, since any attempt to do so itself presupposes the meaningfulness of LP. Thus, LP isnÂ’t an empirical theory. 
Thus, LP is neither an empirical truth nor a tautology. It is thus a counterexample to itself and is therefore false. 
Interestingly, in the TLP, Wittgenstein seems to be aware that one cannot coherently say that there can be non-tautologous meaningful statements. Not a single one of the assertions in the TLP is empirical; and not a single one of them is a tautology. This means that, if the TLP's main thesis is correct, the TLP is nonsense. 
Wittgenstein acknowledges this. For he ends his book by saying that every point that he has made is meaningless and, consequently, that not a single one of them is true. But, Wittgenstein says, those enable one to see the truth, even though they are not themselves true. These non-truths, Wittgenstein says, are like ladders that help one get to the truth. (I would have used a different metaphor, e.g. "much as telescopes help us see the stars even though they themselves obviously aren't stars, so the points Wittgenstein makes help us see certain truths, even though they are not themselves truths.") Here are the very last words of the TLP: 
My propositions serve as elucidations in the following way: anyone who understands me eventually recognizes them as nonsensical, when he has used themÂ—as stepsÂ—to climb up beyond them. (He must, so to speak, throw away the ladder after he has climbed up it.) He must transcend these propositions, and then he will see the world aright. What we cannot speak about we must pass over in silence.[90] 

So far as they arenÂ’t trivial, these magisterial words are false. To understand something is to see its meaning. Therefore, anything that is understood has a meaning. So WittgensteinÂ’s words, if understood, have a meaning, and Wittgenstein is therefore contradicting himself in saying that those who understand his words will see that theyÂ’re meaningless. WittgensteinÂ’s awe-inspiring injunction that we pass over in silence what we canÂ’t speak about involves a similar solecism. To remain silent about something is to pass over it in silence. So Wittgenstein is asking, emptily, that we not say anything about what we canÂ’t possibly say anything about. 
4.7.1 Empiricism self-refuting 
These points are easily extended to show that empiricism is false if itÂ’s true and, therefore, that itÂ’s false. 
Empiricism isnÂ’t the claim that: 
(1) Whatever we know now, we learned it through senseÂ­perceptionÂ—but itÂ’s possible that at some time in the future weÂ’ll acquire knowledge in some other way. 
Empiricism is the doctrine that everything that 
2) ItÂ’s inherent in the nature of knowledge that all knowledge be strictly observation-based. 
But it cannot be known through observation that (2) is correct. According to (2), Â‹x is knowledgeÂ› is inconsistent with Â‹x isnÂ’t known through observation.Â› But, as we noted on page 24, observation cannot tell you whether one statement is consistent with some other statement. Thus, any body of observational data is consistent with the assumption that empiricism is false. 
This means that there cannot be strictly observational grounds for believing empiricism correct. Thus, so far as empiricism is correct, there are no grounds for believing it correct; and so far as there are such grounds, empiricism is false. Thus, the likelihood that empiricism is correct is inversely proportional to the degree of probability that the information at our disposal confers on it. And this means that if itÂ’s a certainty that empiricism is correct, itÂ’s a certainty that itÂ’s false. Therefore, empiricism, if true, is false; therefore itÂ’s false. 

4.7.2 A Famous Argument of RussellÂ’s 
A famous argument given by Bertrand Russell (1872-1970) ends with a sentence very similar to the last one. (This was deliberate.) Since the argument in question is to the effect that Â“naÃ¯ve realismÂ” is false, naÃ¯ve realism being a doctrine that falls within the scope of the present chapter (though the reasons for this are not easily stated, and therefore wonÂ’t be), and we will therefore critique it, after first quoting it verbatim: 
We all start from naÃ¯ve realism, i.e., the doctrine that things are what they seem. We think that grass is green, that stones are hard, and that snow is cold. But physics assures us that the greenness of grass, the hardness of stones, and coldness of snow are not the greenness, hardness, and coldness that we know in our experience, but something very different. The observer, when he seems to himself to be observing a stone, is really, if physics is to be believed, observing the effects of the stone upon himself. Thus, science seems to be at war upon itself. When it most means to be objective, it finds itself plunged into subjectivity against its will. NaÃ¯ve realism leads to physics; and physics, if true, shows that naÃ¯ve realism is false. Therefore, naÃ¯ve realism, if true, is false; therefore itÂ’s false.[91] 

Though eloquently stated, this argument consists of spurious reasoning for a false conclusion. In observing the paper-weight on my desk, IÂ’m not observing some effect of the stone upon myself: IÂ’m observing the stone itself.[92] 
To be sure, my observing the stone is itself an effect of some event involving the stone. (Light bounces off the stone and, in due course, strikes my retinas, precipitating various physiological and psychological responses, among them the aforementioned sense-perception.) But that doesnÂ’t mean that what IÂ’m seeing, in having that sense-perception, is some effect that the stone had on me; and unless weÂ’re perpetually hallucinating, in which case weÂ’re never observing anything external, we very obviously do observe external objects. 
This brings us to the second problem with RussellÂ’s argument. Russell says that the greenness, hardness, and coldness of daily observation are not identical with their counterparts in physics. This is false. Physics has a lot to say about greenness, hardness, and coldness that commonsense does not. But thatÂ’s very different from saying that the coldness we feel, the greenness we see, etc., arenÂ’t the greenness, coldness, and hardness of physics. Physics tells us what it is for something to have the properties we know them to have through sight, touch, etc. When you grab an object and feel that itÂ’s cold, you donÂ’t feel or otherwise sense-perceive the micro-events in virtue of which it is cold. (More precisely, when you grab an object and feel that itÂ’s cold, its coldness is not thereby presented to you as consisting of the micro-events of which it does, in fact, consist.) It is the job of the theoretical physicist to tell you about these micro-events. This means that the coldness studied by the physicist is identical with the coldness that you feel. Physics tells us that many of our pre-theoretic beliefs as to what that coldness is are wrong; and in order to do that, it has to study the coldness that those pre-theoretic beliefs concern. So RussellÂ’s argument, despite EinsteinÂ’s high regard for it, is a failure.[93] 


4.7.3 The objects of perception distinct from their causes 
A moment ago I said that Â“[W]hen you grab an object and feel that itÂ’s cold, you donÂ’t feel or otherwise sense-perceive the micro-events in virtue of which it is cold.Â” Many are likely to object to this: All of our sensations are the results of micro-events, it will be said, and there is thus is a sense in which we perceive such events. 
This line of thought involves the spurious belief that the cause of a perception is identical with its object. When I see your face, the immediate causes of my perception are various disturbances of retinas. But I donÂ’t perceive those disturbances. In order for an experience x to be a perception, as opposed to a mere effect, of some event y, it is necessary that, by virtue of having x, one have some knowledge of what y is. By virtue of seeing your face, I am aware of the structure of your face. By virtue of feeling a surface, I am aware of the texture of that surface. Visual and tactile perceptions resemble their objects. My visual perception of your face has the same structure as your face, that being why, by virtue of having that perception, I am aware, within limits, of the structure of your face. 
To be sure, the object of a given perception is among the causes of that perception. I cannot see your face unless I am in some way affected by it. (Light rays must bounce off of your face, then strike certain surfaces of mine, and so on.) But the object of a perception is always a distal, never a proximal, cause of that perception. 
Not all perceptions bear any (obvious) structural resemblance to their objects. For example, if I hear a loud noise, I am not, by virtue of that fact, aware of the structure of the object of my perception. Nonetheless, I am, by virtue of having that experience, dimly aware of facts about the external world. I am aware that there has been an abrupt change of some kind. I am dimly aware of the location and distance, relative to myself, of that noise. Similar points hold with respect to olfactory and gustatory experiences. The unpleasant experience of smelling rotten food doesnÂ’t bear any resemblance to its object. But, by virtue of having that experience, I am aware of some irregularity in the world that I wouldnÂ’t otherwise be aware of, and I am aware of at least some basic facts about it. 
But, supposing that I am having some sensation caused by various micro-events, I am not, by virtue of having that sensation, aware of those micro-events at all. I couldnÂ’t possibly hear a loud noise or smell a foul odor without thereby knowing of the existence of some object in the external world of which IÂ’d otherwise be ignorant. But people can obviously have sensations that are caused by micro-events without knowing of the existence of those events. In fact, most people, when having sensations, havenÂ’t the faintest idea that their experiences are by-products of sub-atomic activity. So merely having a sensation that is caused by such and such micro-events isnÂ’t enough for perceiving those events. 
Russell says that the greenness and the hardness studied by the physicist are distinct from the greenness and the hardness known to the non-physicist. That is absurd. The leaf that the botanist looks at through a microscope is obviously identical with the leaf looked at with the naked eye by the non-botanist. The leaf is a complex entity. The botanist knows more about it than the non-botanist. But that doesnÂ’t mean that the leaf studied by the botanist is distinct from the leaf observed by the non-botanist. A given leafÂ’s color is a complex entity; and the physicist knows more about that entity than the non-physicist. But it obviously doesnÂ’t follow that the green studied by the physicist is distinct from the green known to the non-physicist. The same is true of the leafÂ’s temperature and mass and, indeed, of any feature of anything that is both known to the layperson and scrutinized by the scientist. 

4.7.4 The empiricism-unfriendliness of the concept of confirmation 
Confirmationalism, the doctrine that a non-tautology is meaningful iff 
confirmable, is a form of empiricism. But weÂ’ll now see that the concept of 
confirmation is an incoherent one unless itÂ’s granted that there is non-
empirical knowledge and, therefore, that confirmationalism is incoherent. An argument put forth by Nelson Goodman (1954) makes this clear: 
(GA)[94] 
LetÂ’s say that an object is Â“grueÂ” if itÂ’s green and examined before Jan. 1, 2010, or itÂ’s blue and examined anytime thereafter. All green objects examined before Jan. 1, 2010, are grue. So, supposing that weÂ’ve examined ten million emeralds before Jan. 1, 2010, and found them all to be green, weÂ’ve also found them to be grue. Presumably, the fact that theyÂ’ve all been green warrants the inference that theyÂ’ll be green after Jan. 1, 2010. But, so far as that data entitles us to infer that theyÂ’ll be green, it also entitles us to infer that theyÂ’ll be grue and, therefore, blue after Jan.1, 2010. 
This line of thought is easily extended to show that anything can confirm anything.[95] 
Let phi, psi, and chi be three properties such that (i) a thing is phi if itÂ’s examined by a human being who knows and therefore truly believes that, at that time, no human being can fly; (ii) a thing is psi if examined by a human who knows that, at that time, all human beings can fly; and (iii) a thing is chi if itÂ’s examined before Jan. 1, 2010, and known to have phi or itÂ’s examined after that time and is known to have psi. Since everything ever examined as of the present time (May 24, 2009) has had phi, itÂ’s also had chi. So given that, thus far, no human has been able to fly, weÂ’re no less entitled to infer that in 2015 theyÂ’ll all be able to fly than we are entitled to infer that, at that same time, none of them will. 
GA can be taken to show either that no inductive inference is better than 
any other or that, since some inductive inferences clearly are better than 
others, GA must involve an error of some kind. Supposing that the second 
interpretation is the right one, itÂ’s easy to identify the problem with GA. 
Contrary to what that argument tacitly assumes, induction does not have strictly observational basis. From a strictly observational standpoint, itÂ’s no less correct to describe an emerald examined in 2009 as Â“grueÂ” than it is to describe it as Â“green.Â” 
Given any body of data, there are different, but equally observationally legitimate ways of describing it. This means that, if any inductions are better than any others, we must have legitimate but at least partly nonobservational grounds for believing that, when making inductive inferences, certain properties (e.g., green) are relevant and others (e.g., grue) are not. (These grounds are identified in Chapters 17.) 


4.8 The brokenness of the concept of tautological truth 
In this section we'll see that it is utterances of sentences, not sentences per se, that are tautologies. For reasons that will become clear, this entails that, contrary to what LP alleges, non-empirical truth cannot be identified with conventional truth. 
Whether a given utterance is tautologous very much depends on the manner in which the person hearing that utterance learned the meanings of the expressions composing it. A story may help make this clear. You donÂ’t know to what length the word Â“yardÂ” refers, and you ask your friend Smith to give you this information. In response, he points to some object L and says: Â“the length of that object is one yard.Â” L is in fact three-feet long. But you canÂ’t tell this just from looking at it. You can tell roughly, but not exactly, how long L is. You donÂ’t bother to measure L. This all happens on Monday. 
The next day, you see some object M. You measure it and find that its length is three feet. You tell your (still present) friend Smith that M is exactly three-feet long. You know, of course, that MÂ’s length is more or less comparable to LÂ’sÂ— that neither length is, for example, ten times as great as the other. But you donÂ’t have precise knowledge of their comparative lengths; you donÂ’t know, for example, whether LÂ’s length is within six inches of MÂ’s. Because you have a passion for knowing the comparative lengths of objects, you find this upsetting, and you tell Smith that you wish you knew how LÂ’s length compared to MÂ’s. Smith says: Â“I donÂ’t know why youÂ’re upset. YouÂ’ve measured M and found that it is three-feet long. Since, as you know, L is a yard long, itÂ’s patently obvious what MÂ’s length is.Â” You donÂ’t quite know what he means, and you tell him this. Somewhat irritated, he says: 
(i) Â“There are three feet in a yard.Â” 
Under these circumstances, (i) is not trivial and, therefore, is not a tautology. It would be tautologous if you had learned the meaning of the word Â“yardÂ” by being told that Â“yards are lengths of three feet.Â” But this isnÂ’t how you learned that word's meaning. You were shown a yard-long object and told that the word Â“yardÂ” refers to its length. Obviously that visual perception did apprise you of that objectÂ’s length. But the way it described that length to you was different from the way that this same information would be conveyed to you by an utterance of: Â“the length of that object is one yard.Â” 
And given the information embodied in your visual perceptions of L and M, it wouldnÂ’t be a trivial matter to know that the length described by the contents of your L-perceptions coincided with that described by your M-perceptions. Therefore, (i) would not, under those circumstances, express a tautology, at least not from your perspective. But it would express a tautology from the perspective of somebody to whom Â“yardÂ” had initially been defined as Â“distance of three feet.Â” 
So even though itÂ’s standard practice among philosophers to describe sentences as Â“tautologies,Â” this practice embodies a serious confusion. A given sentence may or may not be tautology, depending on the manner in which the auditor learned the meanings of its constituent expressions and depending, therefore, on the information on the basis of which the auditor knows those meanings. 
It might be thought that, so far as (i) is non-trivial to you, itÂ’s only because you donÂ’t really understand it. This isnÂ’t true. To somebody who doesnÂ’t speak Albanian, a sentence of Albanian isnÂ’t trivial or non-trivial. It doesnÂ’t mean anything to such a person and is, from his perspective, just so much noise and is no more Â“trivialÂ” or Â“non-trivialÂ” than the sound of wind chimes. But, in our story, you do know what is meant by (i). ItÂ’s not as though youÂ’re hearing a sentence of Albanian (or, if you happen to speak Albanian, a sentence of some language that you donÂ’t know). Therefore, it is only because you understand SmithÂ’s utterance of (i) that it is nontrivial for you. Therefore, tautologousness and non-tautologousness are properties, not of sentences, but of the information on the basis of which auditors figure out the meanings of sentences. And itÂ’s wrong to say that sentences per se are, or are not, tautologies.[96] 

This story illustrates some deeply important facts that are in the philosophy of language. First, one knows the meanings of expressions descriptively. It is through sight and hearing (and other sensory modalities; e.g., touch) that you learn what words mean. Your perceptions apprise you of facts about the world by describing them to youÂ—by apprising you of their colors, shapes, etc. Two very different descriptions can pick out some one thing (cf. Â“the third U.S. PresidentÂ” and Â“the President responsible for the Louisiana PurchaseÂ”). Therefore, the perceptually encoded descriptions through which one learns what two expressions mean may differ enormously, even if those expressions mean the same thing. A consequence is that what utterances tell you is as much a function of the information through which you learn their meanings as it is of those meanings themselves. Thus, a given sentence may convey very different propositions to different people, all of whom know what it means, the reason being that those people access that meaning through different descriptions. 

4.9 An alternative to the logical positivist conception of meaningfulness 
The logical positivistÂ’s analysis of meaningfulness was a complete failure. IÂ’d like to propose an alternative to it. 
First of all, when asked to give examples of meaningless statements, the logical positivists tended to cite sentences that nobody ever uses; for example, Â“the nothing nothings,Â”[97] 
Â“the all is one,Â” Â“the absolute is perfect.Â” This is deeply suspicious: a theory that only takes on straw men canÂ’t be much of a theory. 
And LP canÂ’t even prevail against these straw men. For, contrary to what its advocates said, the problem with these so-called statements is not that theyÂ’re incapable of empirical corroboration. Consider the sentence: 
(i) Â“The universe is a perfect unity.Â” 
Much loved by many a freshman narco-intellectual, this is a meaningless sentence if ever there was one; and it is just the sort of sentence that logical positivists had in mind. 
But if it were said what exactly it means to describe something as a Â“perfect unity,Â” (i) would be meaningful, as it would then be true or false. If, by a Â“perfect unity,Â” one means an object that consists of events bearing a specified causal or logical relationship to one another, then (i) is either true or false, depending on the identity of that relationship. For example, if a Â“perfect unityÂ” is an object such that, given any two non-simultaneous events composing it, there is a possible causal process connecting the first of those two events with the second, then (i) is true. (In contemporary physics, Â‹x precedes yÂ› is defined as: Â‹there is a possible causal process, e.g., a light-signal, beginning with x and ending with y.Â›) On the other hand, if by a Â“perfect unityÂ” one means an object such that if x and y are any two of its parts, the very idea of x existing in the absence of y is an incoherent one, then 
(i) is meaningfulÂ—and false. (One can coherently imagine a universe in which Cheney exists but Biden does not.) 
In any case, the term Â“perfect unityÂ” is clearly intended to refer to some sort of causal or logical integratedness, and once that mode of integration is pinpointed, (i) speedily becomes a true or false claim. 
Â“StatementsÂ” such as Â“the universe is a perfect unity,Â” Â“the nothing nothings,Â” and so on, arenÂ’t really statements at all. TheyÂ’re statement-forms. (A statement-form is what results when one of the constants in a bona fidesentence is replaced with a variable. So "x is an even numberÂ” is a statement-form, since it is what results when the occurrence of "4" in "4 is an even numberÂ” is replaced with a variable. "4 is an even number" is an instance of the statement-form "x is an even number,Â” and so is "8 is an even number." Unlike their instances, statement-forms are neither true nor false.) But (i) is obviously supposed to attribute some property to the universe. Since this property isnÂ’t identified, (i) contains an undefined term and therefore says nothing. Once that term is defined, a meaningful statement results. 
ItÂ’s true that (i) is neither tautologous nor confirmable. But thatÂ’s a consequence of the real problem, viz., that Â“perfect unityÂ” is undefined. (i) is comparable to Â“x is tall.Â” The reason Â“x is tallÂ” says nothing is that Â“xÂ” is undefinedÂ—it hasnÂ’t been assigned a referent. And no sooner is a referent assigned to Â“xÂ” than Â“x is tallÂ” becomes meaningful. (Â“x is tallÂ” comes to have the same meaning as Â“Bob Dole is tallÂ” the moment Bob Dole is assigned to Â“x.Â”) 
Before Â“xÂ” is assigned a referent, Â“x is tallÂ” is neither confirmable nor tautologous. But thatÂ’s only a symptom of the real problem, viz., that Â“xÂ” doesnÂ’t have a referent. The same thing mutatis mutandis is true of (i). 
LetÂ’s move onto the next phase of our argument. If S is a meaningful sentence, there is some object x and some property phi such that S says that x has phi. In other words, any given sentence is equivalent to one that has the form: Â‹x has phi.Â› Let us now say why this is so. 
Any non-compound sentence (i.e., any sentence that doesnÂ’t consist of other sentences) either says of some individual or item that it has some property, or it says that two or more individuals or items are interrelated in a certain way. Thus, Â“Smith is tallÂ” says of some individual (Smith) that he has a certain property (tallness), and Â“Bob loves SallyÂ” says that one individual (Bob) bears a certain relation (that of loving) with respect to some other individual (Sally). 
Â“Smith is tall,Â” Â“Jerry snores,Â” and all other non-relational, non-compound sentences obviously have the form Â‹x has phi.Â› The same is true of Â“Bob loves Sally,Â” Â“Wilma detests Linda,Â” and all other non-compound sentences that affirm the existence of relations between two or more objects. Let Â“RÂ” be defined as follows: for any objects x and y,Â‹<x,y> has RÂ› is true iff x loves y. (So for any objects x and y, the ordered pair <x,y> has R exactly if x loves y.) 
Thus, Â“Bob loves SallyÂ” is equivalent with Â“<Bob, Sally> has R,Â” which has the form Â‹x has phi.Â› 
A similar procedure can be performed on sentences (such as Â“Bob is standing in between Sally and LarryÂ”) that affirm the existence of relations involving three or more objects. Let Â“R*Â” be defined as follows: for any objects x, y, and z, Â‹<x,y,z> has R*Â› is true iff x is standing in between y and z. Thus, Â“Bob is standing in between Sally and LarryÂ” is equivalent with Â“<Bob, Sally, Larry> has R*,Â” which has the form Â‹x has phi.Â› Other non-compound relational sentences are to be dealt with similarly. 
What about compound sentences? Not a problem. Let Â“KÂ” be defined as follows: for any sentences S1 and S2, Â‹ <S1, S2> has KÂ› is true iff the state of affairs described by S1 is a consequence (of some kind or other) of the state 
of affairs described by S2. Thus, Â“Smith broke his leg because he fell out of a treeÂ” is equivalent with Â“<Smith broke his leg, Smith fell out of a tree.> has K,Â” which has the form Â‹x has phiÂ›. Other compound sentences are to be dealt with similarly. 
Negative sentences are particularly easy to deal with. Â“Smith doesnÂ’t smokeÂ” is equivalent with Â“the proposition that Smith smokes is false,Â” which clearly has the form: Â‹x has phi.Â› Other negative sentences are to be dealt with similarly. 
There is only one kind of sentence that we havenÂ’t yet considered, namely, quantified generalizations. A Â“quantified generalizationÂ” is any statement that says how many members one class of objects has in common with some other class of objects. Examples are: (a) Â“some person smokes,Â” (b) Â“no giraffes fly,Â” and (c) Â“all mice read Tolstoy.Â” (a) says that the class of people has at least one member in common with the class of smokers. (b) says that the class of giraffes has no members in common with the class of things that fly. And (c) says that the class of mice has no members in common with the class of things that donÂ’t read Tolstoy. 
Bearing this in mind, let Â“EÂ” be defined as follows: for any properties P and Q,Â‹<P, Q> has EÂ› is true iff the class of things having P has a least one member with the class of things having Q. Thus, (a) is equivalent with: Â“<the property of being a person, the property of being a smoker>, has EÂ” which obviously has the form Â‹x has phi.Â› Other quantified generalizations are to be dealt with similarly. 
We have thus established that any given sentence S is equivalent to some sentence having the form Â‹x has phi.Â› Given this fact, there is an obvious answer to the question Â“what is it for a sentence to be meaningful?Â” A sentence is meaningful if it attributes some property to some object. A sentence S is meaningful if, for some object x and some property phi, S says that x has phi. ItÂ’s irrelevant whether it can be perceptually confirmed, let alone verified, that x has phi. 
How could this theory be wrong? If a sentence attributes any property to any thing, it says something about something and is therefore meaningful. And if a sentence doesnÂ’t attribute any property to anything, it doesnÂ’t say anything about anything and is therefore meaningless. 
5.0 The picture theory of meaning 
One of the most interesting contentions put forth in the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (TLP) is the so-called Â“picture theory of meaning.Â” In the TLP, Wittgenstein says that sentences are Â“picturesÂ” of the facts they describe. 
What does he mean? Maybe he means that sentences are picture-like in that they, like pictures, represent facts. But in that case what Wittgenstein is saying is completely and utterly trivial. 
Thus, so far as what Wittgenstein is saying has substance, it isnÂ’t that sentences are like pictures of the facts they describe; and it must therefore be that they are such pictures. 
But in that case, what Wittgenstein is saying is false. It is only relative to arbitrary conventions that Â“Smith punched JonesÂ” describes the fact that Smith punched Jones. But it isnÂ’t relative to such conventions that a film or painting of Smith punching Jones describes that fact. 
To be sure, there is a non-conventional component to sentential representation. Let P be the proposition meant by the sentence: 
(1) Â“Given that Socrates was a philosopher, it follows from the fact that Socrates was bald that there has been at least one bald philosopher.Â” 
The fact that (1) means P is not itself a convention. It is a logical consequence of our semantic conventions (e.g., that Â“SocratesÂ” refers to Socrates, etc.). But for that very reason, there is a conventional component to that fact. And since graphic resemblance is a non-conventional method of representation, it follows that, so far as (1)Â’s relation to the fact it describes is conventional, that relation is fundamentally not like the relation borne by a picture of an event to the event itself. Thus, the picture-theory is false if taken literally and it is empty if taken non-literally. 
But maybe thereÂ’s some way of interpreting that theory that weÂ’ve overlooked. To see whether this is so, letÂ’s consider WittgensteinÂ’s own way of wording his own argument for it: 
At first sight a sentenceÂ—one set out on the printed page, for exampleÂ—does not seem to be a picture of the reality with which it is concerned. But neither do written notes seem at first sight to be a picture of a piece of music, nor our phonetic notation (the alphabet) to be a picture of our speech. And yet these sign-languages prove to be pictures, even in the ordinary sense, of what they represent[98] 
. . . There is a general rule by means of which the musician can obtain the symphony from the score, and which makes it possible to derive the symphony from the groove on the gramophone record, and, using the first rule, to derive the score again. That is what constitutes the inner similarity between these things which seem to be constructed in such entirely different ways. And that rule is the law of projection which projects the symphony into the language of musical notation. It is the rule for translating this language into the language of gramophone records. 
The idea seems to be that just as laws of projection coordinate the painting of the bowl of fruit with the bowl of fruit itself, so the semantic rules of a language coordinate its sentences with the realities they describe. (A semantic rule is what is expressed by any sentence saying what is meant by an expression of a language. So if, while pointing to individual xÂ—who, we will stipulate, is Mick JaggerÂ—I say Â“that guyÂ’s name is Mick Jagger,Â” IÂ’m stating a semantic rule, since what IÂ’m saying is that Â“Mick JaggerÂ” refers to x.) 
But this analogy is a shallow one; and when itÂ’s scrutinized, it becomes even apparent than before how unlike pictures sentences are. If, because of some change in the environment, snow turned black, the English language would, without having to change, give us the resources to describe this change. We could describe it by saying Â“snow is black.Â” Thus, as far as the English language is concerned, snow can be any color. The semantic rules of English donÂ’t say that snow is white. They say that, if snow is white, one can express that fact by saying Â“snow is white.Â” Thus, the semantic rules of English do not associate the sentence "snow is white" with the fact that snow is white; for those rules leave it open whether or not snow is white. Rather, they associate "snow is white" with a proposition such that, if it's true, it is a fact that snow is white.[99] 
Thus, sentences depict facts by way of having propositions for their meanings. 
But this isnÂ’t how photographs work. A photograph doesnÂ’t go through the corresponding proposition. It goes straight to the fact (when there is one). No picture goes through a proposition. Pictures, unlike sentences, go straight to the facts, if any there be, that they represent. This shows how fundamentally unlike pictures sentences are. 
A related point is that pictures have structures that are radically different from those of any sentences. Sentences are digital structures.[100] 
They have a unique decomposition into a finite number of discrete parts. (Â“The cat is on the matÂ” decomposes into Â“cat,Â” Â“mat,Â” etc.) Pictures arenÂ’t like this. A picture of a cat on the mat doesnÂ’t have one, minimal unit of significance corresponding to the cat, another to the mat, etc. The part of the picture corresponding to the cat may also contain a part corresponding to the catÂ’s ear and to the catÂ’s leg, etc. 
The fact that sentences, unlike graphic representations, are digital structures is a consequence of the fact that the former, unlike the latter, have a conventional component. The reason for this is a subtle one. But itÂ’s worth stating since it shows how deeply wrong the picture-theory is and since, in so doing, it reveals a lot about language. 
Let D1 be some random photograph of a person smiling. D1 isnÂ’t a symbol of a language. But that could easily change. For this to happen, some convention would have to arise whereby it had a fixed a meaningÂ—whereby it meant, for example, that people are sometimes happy, and the same thing mutatis mutandis happens in connection with each of several other photographs. So for example, there is some photograph D2 of a person who is crying, and some convention is created whereby D2 means that people are sometimes unhappy; and so on. Let L be the language defined by the totality of these conventions. 
Even though D1 is an image, it isnÂ’t functioning as an image so far itÂ’s functioning as an expression of L. The fact that D1 is a picture of a smiling person may obviously make it easier for people to remember that, in L, D1 
means that people are sometimes happy. But it wonÂ’t be what it is for D1 to bear that meaning, or any other, in L. The character Â“0Â” is an unfilled hole and can thus be taken as graphic representation of emptiness. But so far as Â“0Â” is functioning in that way, it isn't functioning as a numeral that picks out zero. The same point mutatis mutandis holds of D1.
