Also, D1 doesnÂ’t graphically represent the fact that people are sometimes happy; it graphically represents the tenuously related fact that, on some one 
occasion, some one individual was happy, along with various other specific facts about that personÂ’s appearance that have nothing to do with anyoneÂ’s being happy. So it isnÂ’t by virtue of graphically representing the fact that people are sometimes happy that, when functioning as a sentence of L, D1 
describes that fact.[101] 

So far as D1 is a sentence of a language, what it actually picks out is irrelevant; the various nuances of the smiling gentlemanÂ’s face are irrelevant. In general, its internal structure is irrelevant. Considered as an expression of L, it has no internal structure. (It is what philosophers of language call a semantic primitive. A Â“semantic primitive,Â” or Â“primitive symbol,Â” is one that doesnÂ’t consist of other symbols and that, so far as it is an expression of a language, thus has no internal structure.) For exactly similar reasons, each of the other photographs composing L is, when considered as an expression of L, devoid of internal structure and thus, in the most extreme way possible, not like a graphic representation. 
We must make one more point before we can close the argument. Let N be a photograph of a bolt of lightning, and suppose that N is the L-translation of the English expression Â“it is not the case that.Â” So if S is the L-translation of Â“grass is green,Â” NS is the L-translation of Â“grass is not green.Â” (NS is formed by putting N to the left of S.) Even though NS consists of pictures, it is not itself a picture. Putting two pictures together isnÂ’t one picture; itÂ’s just two pictures that are next to each other. For exactly similar reasons, if conventions were created whereby the sentences of L could be conjoined, disjoined,[102] 
or otherwise combined, the resulting compound sentences would not be pictures. 
Let us take stock. Not a single one of the simple symbols belonging to L is a graphic representation of the fact that it depicts, and not a single one of the complex symbols belonging to L is a graphic representation of the fact depicted by any one of its components. In general, to the extent that a given thing is functioning as a linguistic expression, it is not functioning as a picture. Things that happen to be pictures cannot function as pictures so far as they are functioning as linguistic expressions or, therefore, as sentences. Thus, Wittgenstein's contention that sentences are pictures of the facts they describe is the antithesis of the truth. In addition to showing that WittgensteinÂ’s picture-theory is false, this shows that any conventional assignment of meaning to any collection of symbolsÂ—any language, in other wordsÂ—necessarily yields symbols that have a unique decomposition into 
discrete parts. This is obviously, almost tautologically, true of compound symbols; and itÂ’s vacuously true[103] 
of non-compound symbols, since no such symbol has any internal structure at all. 

5.1 The picture theory of meaning (continued) 
ItÂ’s not entirely clear why Wittgenstein said that sentences are pictures. But it is clear that this contention of his is consistent with his empiricism. 
According to empiricism, all knowledge is known strictly on the basis of sense-perception. If know it, either 
(a) You directly observed it 
or 
(b) Without using any inferences rules of whose legitimacy your senses didn't apprise you, you inferred it from what you did observe, 
Our sense-perceptions give us pictures. Not all sensory modalities give us visual pictures, of course. Hearing gives us auditory pictures, touch gives us tactile pictures, etc. But perceptual representation is pictorial representation. (In what follows, when I say Â“see,Â” I mean Â“see or hear or touch [etc.].Â”) 
But much of what we know canÂ’t be embodied in images of any kind. (In this context, IÂ’ll use the word "image" to refer to represent moving pictures as well as still-images.) I know that: 
(1) The moon is not made of cheese. 
What would an image of this fact be? An image of a cheesy moon with a big X on it? No. The big X wouldnÂ’t be an image at all. Like the word Â“not,Â” it would be a conventional sign of negation. Whereas a picture of a cheesy moon would indeed resemble a cheesy moon, a big X doesnÂ’t resemble the operation of negation. Nothing could physically resemble that operation, since it isnÂ’t something that could possibly be seen or otherwise sense-perceived. 
Also, a picture of a cheesy moon corresponds to a lot of different propositions.[104] 
Any such picture will also depict an object having a certain color, shape, etc. Since (1) doesnÂ’t say anything about the moonÂ’s shape or color, it isnÂ’t identical with such an image. No proposition is identical with any image, since any image will contain information not contained in the proposition. 
Thus, there are at least some cases where oneÂ’s knowing of some fact doesnÂ’t consist in there being an image in oneÂ’s mind of that fact. How is the strict empiricist to deal with this? First of all, itÂ’s hard to see how sense-perception, which gives us nothing but one image after another, could apprise us of truths that are incapable of being expressed in a strictly imagistic form. For argumentÂ’s sake, letÂ’s concede to the empiricist that itÂ’s strictly through perception that I know that the Moon is made of XYZ. How are we to deal with my subsequent knowledge that the Moon is not made of cheese? Obviously that knowledge is largely based on my knowledge that itÂ’s made of XYZ. But it canÂ’t be entirely based on it. What doesn't exist can't be seen. It may be that on the basis of what I see, I know that the moon isn't made of cheese. But I don't see its non-cheesiness. So some kind of non-perceptual knowledge is involved in my making the leap from the moon is made of XYZ to the moon is not made of cheese. 
Here is a similar argument. Even if image-resistant facts (e.g., those expressed by negative statements) are learned in a strictly perceptual manner, the mental states that mediate our knowledge of them are not themselves images. The information borne by those mental states must be encoded in some non-iconic form. This means that, at some point, pictorial information was converted into non-pictorial information. But if our post-perceptual mental states are to be knowledge, that conversion process must be a legitimate one. In other words, it canÂ’t, when given pictorial input x, yield some output y that is inconsistent with x. Moreover, we must know that the conversions being made are legitimate. For argumentÂ’s sake, suppose that I donÂ’t know, given my (let us assume) strictly perception-based knowledge that the moon is made of XYZ, that it is correct to hold that the moon is not made of cheese. In that case, to the extent that my belief that it isnÂ’t made of cheese is based on my knowledge that itÂ’s made of XYZ, that belief isnÂ’t knowledge. I donÂ’t know P if I believe it on the basis of testimony given by a source of whose reliability I have no knowledge. Uncorroborated testimony is not itself enough for knowledge. For much the same reason, if I donÂ’t know the rules that permit the derivation of non-perceptual beliefs from strictly perceptual ones, then, even if my post-perceptual beliefs are correct, they arenÂ’t knowledge. 
But there couldnÂ’t possibly be any strictly perceptual way of knowing that those conversions were accurate. Those conversions, by supposition, turn pictures into non-pictures. So our knowledge of their existence, or (a fortiori) of their legitimacy, cannot itself be strictly pictorial. This is the real problem with empiricism. The rules that we use to make inferences from perceptual experience cannot themselves be learned strictly on the basis of sense-perception. This will be discussed at length in Chapters 6 and 9. 

5.2 The picture theory of meaning (continued) 
Interestingly, Wittgenstein made points at least vaguely like these in the 
TLP. I quote[105]: 
In order to be able to represent logical form, we should have to be able to station ourselves outside of logic, that is to say outside the world. Sentences cannot represent logical form: it is mirrored in them. What finds its reflection in language, language cannot represent. What expresses itself in language, we cannot express by means of language. Sentences show the logical form of reality. They display it. 
Thus, supposing that "F(x)" shows that x occurs in its sense, "F(x)" and "G(x)" show that the same object is mentioned in both of them. Given any two sentences, if they contradict each another, their structure shows it; the same is true if one of them follows from the other. And so on. What can be shown, cannot be said. 
Wittgenstein seems to be saying that we cannot correctly describe the relationship holding between our words and the facts they describe. But, if correct, that point itself describes that relationship, calling into question its own coherence.[106] 

In any case, contrary to what Wittgenstein says, we can identify the logical forms of our own utterances. To identify the logical form of a statement is simply to make it clear what it means. We can do this. We do it all the time. We do it whenever we put the meanings of words into words. There are some qualifications to this, as weÂ’ll see in a moment, but none that redound to the credit of WittgensteinÂ’s point. 
WittgensteinÂ’s assertion that Â“what can be shown, cannot be saidÂ” is obviously false. I tell you that I can do fifty push-ups. (I say Â“I can do fifty push-ups.Â”) You donÂ’t believe me. So I show you that I can do fifty push-ups. (I do fifty push-ups in front of you.) And, as we just saw, that principle holds no less in connection with logical forms than in connection with a personÂ’s ability to do push-ups. 
Echoing what we said earlier, although it isnÂ’t clear why Wittgenstein made these claims or what he meant by them, it is clear that they are consistent with his view that sentences are pictures of reality. A picture cannot picture itself. If P is a picture of a seagull, P canÂ’t contain a picture of itself, for the simple reason that nothing can be a proper part of itself. Of course, P might be a picture of a big seagull and also of some other, much littler, but otherwise identical seagull. But the big-seagull part of the picture isnÂ’t identical with the little-seagull part. The big part contains two seagull-images; the little part only contains one. 
So if sentences were pictures, then a given sentence S1 couldnÂ’t be a picture of itself. But it doesnÂ’t follow that some other picture S2 couldnÂ’t be a picture of S1. Nor, therefore, does WittgensteinÂ’s much stronger claim that nothingÂ—no picture, no set of pictures, no sentenceÂ—could depict or otherwise represent the rules by which true statements are paired off with the facts they described. 
WittgensteinÂ’s claim that we cannot state the logical forms of sentences, which collapses into the brazenly false claim that we can never say what our words mean, has two roots. One of them is his just-discussed belief that sentences are pictures of the facts they describe. The other is his not yet discussed belief that if itÂ’s assumed that we can say what our words mean, we have no way of dealing with paradoxes like the following. Consider the sentence: 
(i) Â“what IÂ’m saying is false.Â” 
It would seem that an utterance of that sentence is true just in case it's false, and therefore that it's both true and false---which is impossible, since whatever is true is, for that very reason, not false. (In Chapter 7, we'll find that (i) is ambiguous and that neither of its disambiguations is paradoxical in any way.) Wittgenstein was keenly interested in this paradox during his pre-Tractarian years.[107] 
His reaction to it, it appears, was to hold that any attempt to articulate semantic rules would self-refer in the same paradox-engendering way as (i) and, therefore, that such rules cannot possibly be put into words. 
WittgensteinÂ’s reasoning is not good. When I say, while pointing at the person exiting the limo, Â“thatÂ’s Mick Jagger,Â” IÂ’m stating a semantic rule. 
There is some individual x such that I am saying (correctly, we may suppose) that itÂ’s a semantic rule that Â“Mick JaggerÂ” refers to x. The semantic rule IÂ’m expressing doesnÂ’t self-refer and isnÂ’t otherwise defective. 
As weÂ’ll see in a moment, there are reasons to think that some semantic rules cannot be put into words, and Wittgenstein seems to have had at least a vague knowledge of some of them. But given only that some semantic rules can't be put into words, it obviously doesnÂ’t follow that none of them can. 

5.3 "Truth" defined 
Having spent pages dwelling on the shortcomings of the Tractatus, letÂ’s end this section on a sunnier and more constructive note. 
It is often said that truth is indefinable. Many people say this without meaning anything by it. Setting such people aside, those who say this seem to mean either: 
(a) that it cannot be said what it is for a proposition to be true, 
or: 
(b) that no language can state all of the semantic rules that belong to it. 
(a) is false (for reasons given at the end of Chapter 3). (b) is true. 
(b) isnÂ’t the absurd claim that no language can state any of its own semantic rules. Every time one uses an English sentence to define an English expression, one is expressing a semantic rule of English in English. But neither the English language, nor any other, can state all of its own semantic rules. 
HereÂ’s why. Given any meaningful expressions, there is a semantic rule r saying what sÂ’s meaning is. (This is trivially true. A meaningful expression is one that has a meaning and is therefore one such that some true proposition identifies that meaning; and any proposition that, like r, says what an expression means is ipso facto a semantic rule.) So, for example, supposing that x is Dick Cheney, there is a semantic rule of English to the effect that Â“Dick CheneyÂ” refers to x. That rule is not itself a sentence, but it can be expressed by a sentence. In general, semantic rules, though often capable of being expressed by sentences, are not themselves sentences. In light of this fact, suppose for argumentÂ’s sake that for each semantic rule of English there is a sentence of English that expresses that rule. Let K be the least inclusive class containing every sentence of English that correctly expresses a semantic rule of English. Let SRE be the conjunction of all of KÂ’s members. SRE is a true and therefore meaningful sentence of English. SRE is also a member of 
K. After all, K contains every sentence that correctly says what is meant by at least one expression of English, and SRE obviously satisfies that requirement. But given that SRE is also a conjunction consisting of all of KÂ’s members, it follows that SRE is one of its own conjuncts. No conjunction can be one of its conjuncts. (The conjunction Â“snow is white and snow is whiteÂ” is not one of its own conjuncts, since that sentence is a conjunction, whereas Â“snow is whiteÂ” is not.) WeÂ’re forced to reject this obvious truth if we grant the supposition that the English language can express each of its own semantic rules. Therefore, the English language cannot state all of its own semantic rules. Given any language L, what we just said about English is true of L. Thus, no language can express all of its own semantic rules.[108] 

6.0 (ii) revisited: formal truth . analytic truth 
One of the main contentions of the TLP is that all entailment is formal entailment. One statement entails another if, supposing the first is true, the second couldnÂ’t possibly be false. So Â“Smith is a triangleÂ” entails Â“Smith has more than one side.Â” One statement, S1, formally entails another sentence, S2, if the statement Â“if S1, then S2Â” is a formal truth. A statement is a formal truth if every statement having the same form as it is true. Thus: 
(1) Â“If Smith is in the barn, then it is not the case that it is not the case Smith is in the barn,Â” 
is a formal truth, since every statement of the form: 
(2) Â“If P, then it is not the case that it is not the case that P,Â” 
is true. 
(1) is also an example of a formal entailment. ItÂ’s a formal entailment since itÂ’s a formal truth that is also an entailment. (ItÂ’s an entailment since itÂ’s 
to the effect that that one statement (Smith is in the barn) entails another (it is not the case that it is not the case that Smith is in the barn). 
In the TLP, Wittgenstein asserted that all entailments are formal entailments. He was aware that there are apparent counterexamples to this. For: 
(3) Â“Brown is a bachelor,Â” 
entails that: 
(4) Â“Brown is unmarried.Â” 
But: 
(5) Â“if Brown is a bachelor, then Brown is unmarried,Â” 
isnÂ’t formally true, since it has the same form as: 
(6) Â“if Brown is a bachelor, then Brown is a cupcake,Â” 
which isnÂ’t true at all, let alone formally so. 
Wittgenstein deals with this by saying, very reasonably, that (4) is synonymous with: 
(3F) Â“Brown is unmarried, and Brown is an adult and is male.Â” 
Unlike (3), (3F) does formally entail (4). According to Wittgenstein, all apparent counterexamples to his thesis that all entailment is formal entailment can be dealt with similarly. 
But the method used in connection with this particular counterexample fails in connection with others. The sentence: 
(7) 
Â“Brown is a circle,Â” 

(8) 
Â“Brown is a two-dimensional figure.Â” 


entails: 
Since (7) obviously doesnÂ’t formally entail (8), Wittgenstein must say that 
(7) 
is synonymous with some other expression that does. If there is any sentence that is synonymous with (7) that formally entails (8), itÂ’s: 

(9) Â“Brown is a closed, planar, two-dimensional figure of uniform curvature.Â” 

(9) 
does indeed formally entail (8). But (9) isnÂ’t synonymous with (7). ThatÂ’s why: 


(10) Â“Brown is a circle iff Brown is a circle,Â” 
is trivial, and says nothing, whereas: 
(11) Â“Brown is a circle iff Brown is a closed, planar, two-dimensional figure of uniform curvature,Â” 
is non-trivial. 
(11) doesnÂ’t say anything about the spatiotemporal world. (11) is logically true; its truth is guaranteed by the structures of the concepts composing it. But (11) isnÂ’t a tautology. Therefore, itÂ’s a non-tautologous, non-empirical truth. Thus, there are non-formal entailments. 

7.0 Why the concept of a logically perfect language is an incoherent one 
LetÂ’s say that a sentence is perspicuous iff its logical and grammatical forms coincide; and letÂ’s say that a language is logically perfect iff every sentence belonging to it is perspicuous. 
Many non-perspicuous sentences belong to any given natural language (e.g., English, Swedish). One of WittgensteinÂ’s objectives in the TLP is to identify the conditions that a language must meet if it is to be logically 
perfect. Wittgenstein takes it for granted that the concept of such a language is a coherent one. Influenced by the TLP, many early analytic philosophers longed for the day when logically perfect languages would replace natural languages.[109] 

In any case, the concept of a logically perfect language is not a coherent one. It isnÂ’t possible for everything about a sentenceÂ’s meaning to be reflected in its grammar. And if per impossibile there did exist a logically perfect language, it would be expressively inferior to English, Arabic, and every other natural language. In other words, there would be much that couldnÂ’t be said in it that could be said in any natural language. 
More precisely, for each analytic truth capable of being expressed by a logically perfect language, there would be infinitely many more that it could not express and that English or Spanish or any other natural language could express. At the same time, there would be no truth that could be expressed in a logically perfectly language that couldnÂ’t also be expressed in a logically imperfect language, such as English. Let us now discuss why this is so. 
A sentence belonging to a logically perfect language is analytically true iff it is formally true. Why is this? A sentence is perspicuous only to the extent that its grammatical form makes it clear what it says and, therefore, makes it clear what it entails and what entails it. Bearing this in mind, let S be some arbitrary sentence. To the extent that there are false sentences, or true but non-analytic sentences, that have the same surface-structure as S, SÂ’s grammatical and logical forms donÂ’t coalesce and, consequently, S isnÂ’t perspicuous. So an analytically true sentence is perspicuous only if all other sentences having the same form are true. A sentence is formally true if, and only if, any sentence having the same form is true. Thus, a sentence is perspicuous only if formally true. Therefore, a sentence belonging to a logically perfect language is analytic only if it is formally true.[110] 

A consequence is that, for each analytic truth that a logically perfect language can express, there are infinitely many that it cannot express. Given any object x and any property phi, the sentence 
(S1) "Â‹if x has phi, then it is not the case that x does not have phiÂ›," 
is perspicuous, the reason being that nothing having the same surface structure is false. But the superficially similar sentence: 
(S2) Â“Â‹given any object x and any property phi, if x has phi, then x does not have phiÂ›,Â” 
is not perspicuous, since it has the same surface structure as: 
(S3) Â“Â‹given no object x and no property phi, if x has phi, then x does not have phiÂ›,Â” 
which is false. Formally true sentences are instances of informally true universal generalizations. So no sentence capable of expressing such generalizations is logically perfect. 
This point has important and often overlooked consequences. Making a valid deductive inference involves recognizing an entailment. Your deductively inferring Q from P involves your recognizing that P entails Q. The only way to know that some formal entailment is valid is to know that some informal entailment is valid. You know that: 
(S4) Â“Jerry is in Richmond,Â” 
entails that: 
(S5) Â“itÂ’s not the case Jerry is not in Richmond.Â” 
And thatÂ’s why, if you accept S4, you also accept S5. 
But how do you know that S4 entails S5? Is it on the basis of your knowledge that all instances of S1 are true? No. How could you possibly know that all of S1Â’ s instances were true unless you could recognize the validity of specific inferences that it licenses (such as the inference from S4 to S5)? If you couldnÂ’t recognize that S4 entailed S5, then you obviously wouldnÂ’t have any idea why all of S1Â’s instances were correct. 
This point is a psychological corollary of an epistemological point, which, in its turn, is a corollary of a logical point. The reason why every instance of S1 is trueÂ—in other words, the reasonwhy S2 is trueÂ—is that each of 
infinitely many specific inferences, of which the inference from S4 entails S5 is but a single instance, is valid. There are, quite literally, infinitely many informally valid inferences for each formally valid one. So WittgensteinÂ’s allegation that all entailments are formal entailment is not feasible. 
7.1 Hempel on the limits of strict empiricism 
Carl Hempel (1905Â–1997) provided the following rigorous proof of the falsity of strict empiricism (what follows is not a quotation_[111]: 
(HA)[112] 
If xÂ’s[H1] 
length is one unit, and yÂ’s length is Ã–2 units, then there is no length L such that L goes an integral number of times into both xÂ’s length and yÂ’s length. Measurement is comparison with respect to some standard. To compare xÂ’s length with yÂ’sÂ—in other words, to establish their comparative lengthsÂ—it is necessary to find some third body z that is taken as a standard[113]; and the relative lengths of x and y are determined by finding out how many z-length segments each of x and y can be divided into. (If one object can be divided into exactly twice as many z-length segments as some other, then the first is twice as long as the second.) Supposingthat xÂ’s length is one unit and yÂ’s length is Ã–2 units, it follows that there is no body z such that both x and y can be divided, without remainder, into z-length segments.[114] 
It follows that, if an objectÂ’s length is given by an irrational number, that fact cannot be known directly on the basis of measurement. It therefore follows that there is no strictly observation-basedway to know that yÂ’s length equals xÂ’s multiplied by Ã–2. In general, for any two objects x and y, there is no strictly observation-based way of establishing that xÂ’s length (or mass, etc.) is incommensurable with yÂ’s. (Two magnitudes M1 and 
M2 are incommensurable if there is no magnitude M3 that goes an integral number of times into both M1 and M2.) The branch of mathematics known as Â“calculusÂ” is integral to modern physics. Calculus is the study of continuously changing quantities. In order to describe physical phenomena in a way that makes it possible to use the powerful techniques 
of the calculus to describe them, it must be assumed that they change continuously and, therefore, that the degree to which a given phenomenon has a given property may sometimes be given by an irrational number.[115] 
Thus, it must be assumed that, at certain junctures, the velocities, lengths, masses, etc., of objects are sometimes given by irrational numbers. But there cannot, as weÂ’ve seen, be strictly observational grounds forbelieving that a given objectÂ‘s length is Ã–2 meters (or that its mass is Ã–2 lbs, etc.).[116] 
Since the calculus canÂ’t be applied to observable phenomena unless itÂ’s assumed that thingsÂ’ weights, velocities, etc., can at least sometimes assume values given by irrational numbers, it follows that modern physics integrally depends on an assumption for which there cannot possibly be a strictly observational basis. This means that strict empiricism is inconsistent with the obvious fact that modern physics is a source of knowledge. 
Chapter 2 Properties and Non-Spatiotemporal Existence 
1.0 Why we must grant that there are non-spatiotemporal entities 
Not everything that exists is in space-time. Everything that is in space-time is an instance of at least one property, and properties are not themselves in space-time. I like to play tennis. I thus have the property of liking to play tennis and am thus an instance of that property. I am obviously in space-time, but that property is not. No matter how thoroughly one searches the universe, one will never encounter the property of liking to play tennis. One will, at most, encounter its instances. 
Many hold that, although property-instances exist, properties per se either donÂ’t exist or exist but only because theyÂ’re identical with spatiotemporal entities of some kind (e.g., aggregates of their own instances, ideas in peopleÂ’s minds). In this chapter, weÂ’ll discuss why this seemingly reasonable viewpoint cannot be sustained. WeÂ’ll also see why the negation of this viewpoint is, contrary to initial appearances, utterly consonant with commonsense. 
Properties themselves have properties. The property of being a square circle has the property of being uninstantiated. Properties of properties are higher-order properties. Properties that are not higher-order properties are first-order properties. The instances of higher-properties, being properties themselves, are not in space-time. The instances of first-order properties are in space-time. 
Everything that exists is either a property or is in space-time. NonÂ­spatiotemporal entities that seem not to be properties always turn out to be so. For example, propositions are not spatiotemporal and propositions do not initially seem to be identical with properties. (Propositions are the things that we affirm: so, setting aside cases of insincerity and linguistic incompetence, what one affirms in saying "snow is white" is a proposition, and in saying "schnee ist weiss", one affirms that same proposition.) But propositions turn out to be properties. (WeÂ’ll see why in Chapter 4.) Sets are not spatiotemporal, and sets do not initially appear to be identical with properties, 
but they too turn out to be properties.[117] 
(However, contrary to what many a philosopher has said, properties are not identical with the sets that contain their own instances. The property of being a bird is not identical with the set of all birds. ItÂ’s identical with a very different set, as weÂ’ll see at the end of the present chapter.) 
The doctrine that spatiotemporal things are instances of nonÂ­spatiotemporal things is known as Â“Platonism.Â” This is because Plato was the first person to advocate that doctrine. Sometimes Platonism is known as the theory of universals, and we will sometimes refer to it that way. The doctrine that properties donÂ’t exist, or do exist but only because they are identical with spatiotemporal entities, is sometimes referred to as Â“nominalism.Â” But weÂ’ll usually refer to it as Â“anti-Platonism.Â” 
Incidentally, nominalism is so called because some anti-Platonists held that universals are identical with word. (Â“NomenÂ” is the Latin word for Â“nameÂ” or Â“word.Â”) In Section 3.0, weÂ’ll see that this position, in addition to being false, is incoherent, the reason being that words are themselves universals.[118] 

1.1 Why we must grant that there are non-spatiotemporalentities (continued) 
Given that: 
(1) Sally and Fred are both intelligent, 
it follows that there is something that they have in common; that is, that: 
(2) There exists some property P such that Fred is an instance of P and Sally is an instance of P. 
Instances of intelligence are in space-time. Einstein was in space-time; so was Keynes. But intelligence itself is not in space-time. Â“But mightnÂ’t the property of intelligence be nothing other than some sort of aggregate of all its instances?,Â” one might ask. Â“MightnÂ’t there be some way of spatiotemporalizing that entity?Â” 
No. Consider the property of having a perfectly triangular shape. Nothing has this property. Are we to say that it doesnÂ’t exist? Were we to do so, weÂ’d be saying that, since there are no instances of the property of triangularity, that property doesnÂ’t exist. Which is the same as saying there exists a property, viz., that of triangularity, such that, because nothing has it, it doesnÂ’t exist. Which is absurd. 
Also, a consequence of identifying properties with Â“aggregatesÂ” of their instances is that properties that clearly arenÂ’t identical with each other must be seen as being identical with each other. (In this context, the word Â“aggregateÂ” can refer to any spatiotemporal entity that is composed, in any sense of the word Â“composed,Â” of other spatiotemporal entities.) There are no perfectly spherical objects; nor, as we just pointed out, are there any perfectly triangular objects. So, if we identify properties with aggregates of their instances, the aggregate of all the instances of the one property is identical with the aggregate of all the instances of the other, the reason being that each aggregate is a perfect nullity. 
1.2 Logic as property-based, not set-based 
Consider the clearly correct statement that: 
(1) Squareness is a form of rectangularity. 
On the face of it, (1) seems to make a statement about the property of squareness. So, if (1)Â’s appearance is to be trusted, then there exists a property (namely, squareness) that has another property (namely, rectangularity).Many philosophers[119] 
have tried to show that, despite its appearance, (1) doesnÂ’t really talk about properties per se and that it instead talks about their instances. TheyÂ’ve proposed that the real meaning of (1) is: 
(2) Everything that is square is a rectangle. 
And theyÂ’ve proposed that other statements, such as (1), that seem to refer to properties, be treated similarly. (So Â“green is a color,Â” they say really just means that everything green has a color.) 
But (1) doesnÂ’t mean the same thing as (2). If there were exactly two square things, x and y, and x and y happened to be green, the statement: 
(3) Everything that is square is green, 
would be true, but: 
(4) Squareness is a form of greenness, 
would be false (and so would other statements of its ilk; e.g., Â“squareness is a colorÂ”). 
Of course, the statement: 
(5) Everything that is square is for that very reason a rectangle, 
is true, whereas: 
(6) Everything that is square is for that very reason green, 
is false, even if the only two square things in existence happen to be green. What (5) says is that: 
(7) A thingÂ’s being a square is responsible for its being a rectangle, 
which is obviously correct; and (6) says that: 
(8) A thingÂ’s being a square is responsible for its being green, 
which is obviously false. 
But (5) collapses into (1). (5) says that, to the extent that everything square is rectangular, itÂ’s because the property of squareness bears a certain relation (that of being a form of) to the property of rectangularity. The relationship between a thingÂ’s being a square and its being a rectangle is, (5) rightly says, to be understood in terms of a relationship holding between squareness and rectangularity. But the relationship between a thingÂ’s being square and its being green is not to be understood in such terms. 
A thing is a rectangle in virtue of its being a square. But, given some object that is both green and square-shaped, it isnÂ’t in virtue of its being green that itÂ’s square-shaped. Whenever one encounters an expression like Â“in virtue of,Â” Â“ipso facto,Â” Â“to the extent that,Â” or Â“for that very reason,Â” one knows that one is dealing with a statement that is primarily about properties and only secondarily about objects. If I say that Â“copper things are ipso facto good conductors of electricity,Â” IÂ’m saying that the relationship between a given thingÂ’s being made of copper and its being a good conductor of electricity isnÂ’t fortuitous and is grounded in the natures of those two properties. In other words, to understand why an instance of the first property is an instance of the second, one looks to the natures of those properties. The connection goes from property instance (instance of being made of copper) to property (property of being made of copper) to property (property of being a good conductor of electricity) to property-instance (instance of being a good conductor of electricity). 
And the reason why Â“copper things are ipso facto in JMKÂ’s living roomÂ” is false is that, even though (so we will suppose for argumentÂ’s sake) every copper object happens to be in my living room, the connection between xÂ’s being made of copper and xÂ’s being in my living room isnÂ’t routed in that way through those properties. 
All principled connections are relationships between properties. This means that nomic[120] 
connections (e.g., the connection between a thingÂ’s being made of copper and its being a good conductor of electricity) and also all logical connections (e.g., the connections between a thingÂ’s having knowledge and its having a mind) are expressed by statements whose subjects are properties. The correct statement that: 
(9) For any x, the statement x has knowledge entails x has a mind, 
is another way of saying that: 
(10) Something that has knowledge for that very reason has a mind of some kind. 
And (10) is another way of saying that: 
(11) The property of having knowledge is a form of the property of having a mind. 
In conclusion, unless itÂ’s conceded that properties exist, there is no way to account for the fact that there are principled relationships of any kind. And in fact those who deny that properties exist tend not to grant that there exist any such relationships. Those who deny the existence of properties tend to be empiricists. Since empiricists cannot grant the existence of things, such as properties, that cannot be seen or otherwise known (more or less) directly on the basis of observation, they end up denying that anything has any bearing on anything. (See Chapter 18.) 
1.3 Logic property-based, not set-based (continued) 
Let S1 be the set containing the smallest number greater than zero that is divisible by two, and let S2 be FredÂ’s favorite number, which happens to be the number two. S1 and S2 are the same set, and the statement: 
(1) x is a member of S1, 
is therefore identical with the statement: 
(2) x is a member of the set that contains the number two and doesnÂ’t contain anything else; 
and both statements are identical with: 
(3) x is a member of S2. 
Thus, anything entailed by any one of those statements is entailed by each of the others, and anything that entails any one of those statements entails each of the others. Thus, (1) entails: 
(4) x is less than twenty, and so do (2) and (3). And: 
(5) x is a whole number greater than one but less than three, 
entails (1), as well as each of (2) and (3). But the statement: 
(6) x has the property of being FredÂ’s favorite number, entails: 
(7) x has the property that Fred is aware of its existence, 
but (1) doesnÂ’t entail this, and neither do (2) or (3). And 
(8) x has the property that it is a number that is preferred by Fred to every other number that Fred has considered, 
entails (6), but it doesnÂ’t entail (1) or (2) or (3). It follows that properties cannot be identified with sets of their instances without mutilating the most basic principles of logic. 
Â“But surely thatÂ’s wrong,Â” one will say. Â“(1) is the statement that x is a member of the smallest set that contains the smallest number divisible by two,Â” and (2) is the statement that x is a member of the smallest set containing FredÂ’s favorite number. So I donÂ’t see how (1) and (2) could entail, and be entailed by, the same things; nor do I see how (1) and (6) could entail, or be entailed by, different things.Â” 
If the expression Â“the set containing FredÂ’s favorite numberÂ” is taken in this wayÂ—in other words, if itÂ’s taken in such a way that (1) and (6) are equivalent, whereas (1) and (2) are notÂ—then the word Â“setÂ” is going proxy for the word Â“property.Â” If by Â“the set containing FredÂ’s favorite numberÂ” you mean, not Â“the set containing the number two,Â” but instead Â“any set, whatever its membership, that comprises FredÂ’s favorite number,Â” then what you mean by Â“the set containing FredÂ’s favorite numberÂ” is: Â“any set that is generated by the property of being FredÂ’s favorite number.Â” But in that case, when you make statements about Â“sets,Â” youÂ’re really talking about properties. 
1.4 The axiom of extensionality 
It may be obvious at this point that properties arenÂ’t identical with sets of their instances. But this now obvious point is easily extended to reveal the futility of attempts to show that properties, if existent, are spatiotemporal. But in order to make the needed extensions, we must take a very quick detour through a bit of set theory. 
Two very different properties can be co-extensive. Two properties are coÂ­extensive if any instance of the one is an instance of the other. But different sets cannot have the same members. This is known as the axiom of extensionality. Since different properties can generate the same set, properties arenÂ’t identical with sets of their instances. WeÂ’ll revisit this point later in this chapter. So if S1 is a set and S2 is a set, then S1 is identical with S2 
if and only if nothing is a member of the one that isnÂ’t also a member of the other. A set whose members are x, y, and z canÂ’t fail to have those members any more than it can fail to be itselfÂ—indeed, for it to fail to have those members would be for it to be fail to be itself. Thus, sets are individuated by their memberships. This principle is sometimes known as the axiom of extensionality. 
A corollary of this axiom is that a setÂ’s membership is frozenÂ—frozen, indeed, in two senses. First, itÂ’s temporally frozen. Sets donÂ’t gain members and they donÂ’t lose them. Second, itÂ’s modally frozen. If a setÂ’s actual members are x1...xn, it couldnÂ’t possibly exist without having exactly those 
members. 
This may at first seem patently false. Â“Surely the set of people changes from year to year; people are born; people die.Â” This is the wrong view. The right view is that some one propertyÂ—that of being a personÂ—generates different sets at different times. So really there is no such thing as the set of people. There is the set of people at 3:00 P.M. April[H2] 
28, 2009, the set of people at 3:01 P.M. April 28, 2009, etc. 
And if S is the set of peopleÂ—in other words, if itÂ’s the set that contains you, me, Barack Obama, etc.Â—S couldnÂ’t possibly exist in a universe in which one of us three didnÂ’t exist. Of course, there could be people in a world where one of us didnÂ’t exist. And, in that world, the property of being a person would generate a set. But that set wouldnÂ’t be S. It would be some other set. 
Â“But,Â” one might ask, Â“isnÂ’t the axiom of extensionality just a matter of convention? CouldnÂ’t we stipulate that sets could lose and gain members?Â” If we used the word Â“setÂ” in this way, it would become a proxy for the word Â“property.Â” To say that the Â“setÂ” of humans changes every time someone is born or dies is to say that, at any given time, this setÂ’s membership is determined by what it is that, at that time, has the property of being human. So, while thereÂ’s nothing wrong with using the word Â“setÂ” in this way, it isnÂ’t an option for somebody who wishes to replace properties with sets. 
Having taken care of these technical preliminaries let us move on to matters of substance. If some piece of copper happens, at a given time, to be conducting electricity, itÂ’s because of what is going on right then and there. The fact that there exists some other piece of copper in some remote galaxy is irrelevant. But if S is the set of all pieces of copper, the existence of that other piece of copper is relevant to SÂ’s existence. Sets are individuated by their memberships. (The set consisting of Smith, Larry, and Sally ceases to exist if Smith does.) So if, for some reason, the universe hadnÂ’t begotten that other piece of copper, then S wouldnÂ’t exist. But what difference would that make to the fact that this piece of copper is conducting electricity? None.[121] 

Any given thing belongs to many different sets. What those sets are is only as good an indicator of how that thing is as it is an indicator of what properties that thing has. If S is the set of people who actually exist, then S doesnÂ’t exist in a world W where Dick Cheney doesnÂ’t exist but is otherwise exactly like our world. But what difference does that make to my life-path in W? None. So far as you can learn anything about me from the fact that I belong to the set of humans, itÂ’s because, in learning this, you are learning that I have the property of being human. 
Everything just said about sets can be said of any entity that is constituted by property-instances. Suppose, for argumentÂ’s sake, that there is a Â“scattered objectÂ” consisting of all and only those human beings in existence. (This is a popular view among philosophers.[122]) Just replace each occurrence of Â“setÂ” in the argument just given with Â“scattered object consisting of all and only human beings,Â” and the resulting argument shows that the property of being a person isnÂ’t identical with that set. (Also, weÂ’ll see in the next section that, setting aside properties that have only one instance, there are no spatiotemporal entities that can be identified with a given propertyÂ’s instances. There are no Â“scattered objects.Â”) 
2.0 Arguments against Platonism 
It is seldom denied that there are instances of properties, but it has often been denied that there are non-spatiotemporal entities. But itÂ’s hard to see: 
(i) How there could be instances of properties without there being properties themselves, 
and it is also hard to see: 
(ii) How properties could be given spatiotemporal coordinates. 
Opponents of Platonism respond either by saying that (i) involves some 
sort of logical or linguistic trickery or by saying that properties can be 
identified with spatiotemporal entities. Let us now consider how anti-
Platonists defend their view. 
2.1. Argument #1 against Platonism 
Not every word in a sentence corresponds to some entity in the world. If I say Â“for the sake of all that is good, make sure you give at least some money to charityÂ” the word Â“sakeÂ” doesnÂ’t denote anythingÂ—there arenÂ’t such things as sakes, after allÂ—even though, being a noun, the word Â“sakeÂ” has the same syntactic function as words that do have denotations. 
We can develop this point by taking a brief tour through linguistic theory. It seems fairly clear that not all expressions refer to things. 
Consider words like Â“of,Â” Â“and,Â” Â“the,Â” Â“nonetheless.Â” ItÂ’s hard to believe that these words are comparable to Â“Smith,Â” Â“Jones,Â” and Â“cow.Â” The medievals referred to expressions like Â“SmithÂ” and Â“JonesÂ” as Â“categorematicÂ” expressions, and to expressions like Â“ofÂ” and Â“theÂ” as Â“syncategorematicÂ” expressions. A syncategorematic expression is one that doesnÂ’t refer to anything and whose linguistic function is strictly syntactical. Contemporary linguists make a similar distinction: they distinguish between Â“lexicalÂ” and Â“non-lexicalÂ” items: the former include Â“Smith,Â” Â“Jones,Â” Â“red,Â” and Â“cowÂ”; the latter include Â“the,Â” Â“of,Â” and Â“nonetheless.Â” A lexical item is one that has a referent; a non-lexical item is one that does not, and whose purpose is strictly syntactic. (In other words, the purpose of a non-lexical term is simply to facilitate the unification of lexical items to form larger lexical items.) 
Even though there are many expressions that appear to denote properties, they are really syncategorematic or non-lexical expressions. Words like Â“redÂ” or Â“the property of rednessÂ” donÂ’t refer to anything. This is not to say that they are not meaningful. Â“OfÂ” is meaningful, even though it doesnÂ’t denote anything, and the same is true of Â“the property of redness.Â”[123] 

This argument evaluated: If I know that: 
(1) x is red, 
is true, I can logically infer: 
(2) There exists some color or other that x has. 
If I know that: 
(3) 
Fred is smart but Larry is not, 

I can infer that: 

(4) 
There exists some property that Fred has that Larry lacks. 


These inferences are obviously valid. The view that Â“redÂ” and Â“smartÂ” are not syncategorematic invalidates them. Therefore, that view is false. So, just as the Platonist holds, Â“redÂ” and Â“smartÂ” pick out entities of some sort or other. To use the objectorÂ’s own (Medieval) terminology, those expressions are Â“categorematic,Â” not Â“syncategorematic.Â” 
When we make it clear just what these terms mean, it becomes clear that the objectorÂ’s argument not only fails, but fails relative to its own assumptions. A syncategorematic entity is one whose function is to form complex expressions out of other expressions. Thus Â“andÂ” is a syncategorematic entity since it enables complex expressions (Â“snow is white and grass is greenÂ”) to be formed out of other expressions (Â“snow is whiteÂ”,Â” Â“grass is greenÂ”). Â“OfÂ” is a syncategorematic expression for the same reason: given the expressions Â“pictureÂ” and Â“PaulÂ”, Â“ofÂ” yields the complex expression Â“picture of Paul.Â” 
Bearing this in mind, consider the sentence: 
(4) Â“snow is white and grass is green.Â” 
Although Â“andÂ” serves a purely Â“syntacticÂ” function, it does so, at least in part, by way of picking out a certain (Platonic) entity. This is because (4) entails: 
(5) There is some relation R such that the proposition that snow is white bears R with respect to the proposition that grass is green (and vice versa). 
What we said about the occurrence of Â“andÂ” in (4) is true of the occurrence of Â“ofÂ” in: 
(6) There is a picture of Paul on the mantelpiece. 
This is because (6) entails that: 
(7) There is some relation R such that there is a picture on the mantelpiece that bears R with respect to Paul. 
So even syncategorematic items sometimes have referents. Therefore, even if Â“redÂ” and other predicates were syncategorematic, it wouldnÂ’t follow that predicates didnÂ’t have referents. 
Gottlob Frege (1944-1925) put forth the following (italicized) argument, which some authors have taken to show that predicates donÂ’t refer to anything and, therefore, donÂ’t refer to properties (Â“NPÂ” is short for Â“No PropertiesÂ”). 
(NP) The expression Â“the property of whitenessÂ” refers to the property of whiteness, at least if anything so refers. So if the occurrence of Â“whiteÂ” in: 
(8) Â“snow is whiteÂ”, 
referred to that property, then (8) would have the meaning as: 
(9) Â“snow, the property of whiteness.Â” 
But (8) is meaningful, whereas (9) is meaningless; so they donÂ’t have the same meaning. 
Although Frege himself was an ardent Platonist, many have taken NP to show that properties donÂ’t exist. Here is their reasoning: 
(NP*) If there is any reason at all to posit the existence of properties, it is to explain the meaningfulness of predicates. Given that predicates donÂ’t refer to properties, as weÂ’ve just seen, but are still meaningful, there is no reason to suppose that properties exist. 
NP does show that Â“redÂ” doesnÂ’t only refer to the property of redness; it doesnÂ’t show that referring to that property is no part of what Â“redÂ” does. The expressions Â“Bill is a member of the species homo sapiensÂ” and Â“A member of the species homo sapiens, Bill is a scoundrelÂ” cannot be inter-substituted. But the former does say that Bill is a human. A given occurrence of Â“heÂ” can co-refer with a given occurrence of Â“him,Â” even though, supposing that each occurs in a grammatical utterance, neither occurrence can replace the other without turning a meaningful expression into a meaningless one. So NP doesnÂ’t show that Â“whiteÂ” doesnÂ’t refer to the property of whiteness. 
That said, NP does prove an important point: that not all meaning takes the form of reference. (9) is not a sentence. In general, a list of referring terms isnÂ’t a sentence. And, given a list of referring terms that isnÂ’t a sentence, adding referring terms to that list wonÂ’t turn it into a sentence. Adding Â“the relation of havingÂ” to (9) yields: 
(10) Â“snow, the property of whiteness, Â“the relation of having,Â” 
no permutation of which is a sentence. 
There is thus a kind of meaning that has nothing to do with reference. The inflections in (8) have this non-referring sort of meaning, the nature of which weÂ’ll clarify in Chapter 3. 
Unlike NP, NP* is a complete failure. There are many reasons to hold that properties exist, and most of them have nothing to do with language, as weÂ’ve already seen. 
2.2 Argument #2 
Although properties exist, they are identical with spatiotemporal entities. The property of being a rock is identical with the set of rocks. And the set of rocks is a spatiotemporal entity. After all, that setis simply a very spread out object that consists of rocks. 
This argument evaluated: Sets are abstract objects. They donÂ’t have space-time coordinates. The set of rocks is not some big rock and it isnÂ’t some big object consisting of rocks separated by stretches of empty space. If all the rocks in the world move to some new place, and none are destroyed, the set of rocks hasnÂ’t changed at all: it is the same as it was before. But, under those circumstances, any object consisting of all the rocks in the world has changed: it has acquired a new location (or, in any case, it has undergone an internal structural change). 
A set is a mathematical entity; it has no location and is defined entirely by its formal properties. Where its members are and what they are doing, is irrelevant (so long as its members donÂ’t cease to exist). But any object that is actually composed of all the rocks in the world is affected by the movements of their members, and thus cannot be identified with sets. (Of course, it is unclear whether there is such an objectÂ—an issue weÂ’ll revisit shortlyÂ—but what is clear is that if there is, then it is affected by movements of the kind just described.) Thus, sets arenÂ’t spatiotemporal entities. Consequently, they are themselves Platonic entities. So, one is conceding the truth of Platonism, not undermining it, by identifying properties with sets. 
Aware that, for the reasons just given, properties cannot be identified with sets, philosophers of an anti-Platonist bent have sometimes chosen to identify properties with what are referred to by contemporary philosophers as scattered objects. 
First of all, what exactly is a scattered object? Ordinary objects are geographically and dynamically cohesive. Consider your back-pack. If you move one of the straps ten feet across the room, you have moved the whole bag across the room (unless, of course, youÂ’ve damaged the bag in some way). And even though (at the microscopic level) the bag consists mostly of empty space, all of its parts occupy one, fairly compact, relatively continuous region of space-time. 
Now consider all the rocks in the universe. Those rocks clearly donÂ’t constitute a dynamically or geographically integrated unit. Supposing that those rocks collectively constitute any object at all, the object they constitute is a Â“scattered object.Â” In general, a scattered object is one that lacks the cohesiveness and dynamic integrity of ordinary objects. According to some anti-Platonists, properties are scattered objects. Is this correct? 
No. There are no scattered objects. The very concept of such a thing is an incoherent one. In Chapter 20, weÂ’ll see why. HereÂ’s an outline of what weÂ’ll say. ItÂ’s obvious that two objects that are spatially separated from each other can both be constituents of some third object. But if spatially disjoint entities are to constitute a single spatiotemporal object, their interactions must be characterized by a certain regularity and predictability. Dynamic cohesiveness must step into the breach opened by a lack of spatial cohesiveness. Since it cannot be known without doing empirical research whether the various rocks in the universe jointly constitute an entity have the requisite cohesiveness, it cannot be said on non-empirical grounds whether there is some Â“scattered objectÂ” consisting of all the rocks in existence. But, clearly, the property of being a rock does exist. So[H3] 
that scattered object, even if it does exist, isnÂ’t identical with that property. And that scattered object doesnÂ’t exist: given the empirical evidence at our disposal, there is no real chance that the various rocks in the universe, taken together, have the dynamic integrity that is a sine qua non for being a veritable object. 
But even if scattered objects do exist, properties arenÂ’t identical with them. Let R be some scattered object composed of all the rocks in the universe. If you destroy half of the rocks in the world, you have changed the just-mentioned scattered object. But you havenÂ’t changed the conditions that a thing must satisfy to be a rock. (For argument's sake, we'll suppose that to be a rock is to be hunk of matter with certain microstructural properties.) Therefore, you havenÂ’t changed what it is to be a rock or, consequently, the property of being a rock. So, by LeibnizÂ’s Law, that scattered object, if it even exists, cannot be identified with the property of being a rock. Given any other property, the same points mutatis mutandis show it not to be a scattered object. 

2.3 Argument #3: The third-man argument 
According to Platonism, any given spatiotemporal entity is an instance of at least one property, and for two spatiotemporal entities to resemble each other in some respect is for there to be some property of which each is an instance. Presumably, properties must resemble their instances. For example, the property of being triangular must itself be triangular. Bearing this in mind, let T be the property of being triangular, and let x be an arbitrary triangle. If Platonism is correct, it follows that there is some property T1 such that T and x are both instances of T1 and such that it is in virtue of their both being instances of T1 that they are triangular. Given that, according to Platonism, properties resemble their instances, it follows that T1 must resemble each of T and x. In other words, T1 must be a triangle. It follows that, if Platonism is correct, there must be some property T2 such that each of T1 and T and x is an instance of T2 and such that it is in virtue of their being instances of T2 that they are triangular. And so on ad infinitum. Were they to exist, properties would be useless, since the very questions that arise in connection with their instances arise in connection with them.[124] 

This argument evaluated: Consider the property of being spatiotemporal. If Platonism is right, that property is not itself spatiotemporal and, in the relevant sense of Â“resemble,Â” it doesnÂ’t resemble its instances. Here is another example. To be triangular is to have a certain shape. Only things that are in space have shapes. The property of triangularity is not in space and, therefore, doesnÂ’t have a shape and, therefore, isnÂ’t an instance of itself. TMA succeeds in showing that instantiation isnÂ’t resemblance. This means that it succeeds in proving nothing, given that itÂ’s inherent in Platonism that instantiation not be resemblance. 

2.4 Argument #4: The argument from the causal impotence of properties 
Properties lack causal powers. For this reason, they can serve no explanatory function. To explain something is to show how it came about. Being causally impotent, properties canÂ’t make anything come about. Therefore, there is no reason to posit them 
This argument evaluated: Properties do indeed lack causal powers. Causes are necessarily in space and time. To be a cause is to induce change. Changes and their causes are ipso facto in space-time. 
But this is no reason to think that properties are explanatory deadwood or, therefore, that thereÂ’s no good reason to believe them to exist. Not all explanation is causal explanation. Some explanation is what we call analytic or conceptual. There are as many even numbers as there are whole numbers. (This is a theorem of set-theory.) How is this to be explained? Even though the even numbers are a subset of the whole numbers, it is possible to put the two sets of numbers into a one-one[125] 
correspondence. Since, whenever two sets can be put into such a correspondence they have the same number of members, it follows that the set of even numbers has as many members as the set of whole numbers.[126] 

This explanation is not causal. It explains a truth not by identifying its causal antecedents, but by delineating the structures of concepts. Many explanations are like this. You ask me: Â“Why canÂ’t someone know something without having any form of awareness?Â” I answer (correctly) by saying: Â“because knowing something involves having a true belief, and a belief is a form of awareness.Â” This explanation identifies conditions that are conceptually, not causally, necessary conditions for knowledge. Like this explanation, PlatoÂ’s theory isnÂ’t a causal theory, and itÂ’s therefore irrelevant that properties arenÂ’t in space-time. 

2.5 Argument #5 (a variant of #4): The argument from the causal theory of knowledge 
For x to know of y, y must have causal effects on x. You can see the dog only because the dog has certain effects on youÂ—light bounces off its fur and hits your eyes. You can know about Socrates only because, long ago, Socrates made various noises, which were transcribed, and copies of those transcripts made their way to you. So it is only because there is a causal process linking Socrates to you that you know about him and are able to have thoughts about him. 
Properties donÂ’t have effects on anything. They donÂ’t initiate or otherwise participate in causal processes. So we canÂ’t know about them, even if they exist. So there is no good reason to suppose that they exist.[127] 

This argument evaluated: Seeing a dog does indeed involve the dog having effects on youÂ—it involves your eyes being disturbed by photons bouncing off of the dog. But, in and of themselves, those photonic disturbances are lifeless and informationally empty. If they were to hit a rock, vision wouldnÂ’t result. The photons responsible for those disturbances donÂ’t contain little dog images. You have to read such information into them. Your mind must extract such images from them; and to do this, your mind must have some way of interpreting those disturbances. The knowledge needed to interpret these disturbances cannot come from sense-perception, since that knowledge is itself a prerequisite for sense-perception. This entails that, in at least some cases, it isnÂ’t through a causal process that the knower becomes aware of the known. It also entails that a prerequisite for the very existence of sense-perceptions, or indeed of any mental activity that results from causal exchanges with the world, is knowledge of properties. Why does it entail this? Because, were it not for a grasp of what it is for a thing to have the property of having this or that shape (or this or that color or this or that location, etc.), one couldnÂ’t interpret the radiation-induced disturbances of oneÂ’s sensory receptors in the way needed to generate sense-perceptions. 
2.6. Argument #6: Conceptualism 
If they exist, properties are identical with mental representations of some kind or otherÂ—presumably, with thoughts about rocks or, in any case, with categories created by the mind that help it upload and process sensory information.[128] 

This argument evaluated: Since conceptualism is thoroughly evaluated in Chapter 13, IÂ’ll be brief. There were rocks before there people. And, back then, rocks were similar to one another in ways that they werenÂ’t similar to bats and stars and other non-rocks. For two things to be similar to one another in a certain respect is for there to be some property that they both have. So for two rocks to resemble each other in some respect is for there to exist some property that they both have. Thus, before there were human minds, there were properties. Therefore, properties are not products of human artifice. 

2.7 Argument #7: Resemblance nominalism (RN) 
Let x be some red thing. xÂ’s being red consists, not in its being related in some way or other to some non-spatiotemporal entity but in its resembling roses, spots of blood, stop-signs, and other such things. Being red is a relation, not between the spatiotemporal and the non-spatiotemporal but between the spatiotemporal and the spatiotemporal. In general, to have a property phi is to bear some relation to some other spatiotemporal entity; it isnÂ’t to bear some relation to some non-spatiotemporal entity.[129] 

This argument evaluated: For two otherwise dissimilar objects to have the same shape is for there to exist some shape, and therefore some property, that they both have. For two otherwise dissimilar red objects to be the same color is for there to exist some color, and therefore some property, that they both have. There is no such thing as mere resemblance; there is only resemblance in this or that respect. For two things to resemble each other in a given respect is for there to exist a property that they share, and resemblance nominalism therefore collapses. 

2.8 Argument #8: Conventionalism 
The only non-empirical truths are linguistic conventions (e.g., Â“there are three feet in a yardÂ”). Therefore, all non-conventional truths are empirical. Empirical truths register spatiotemporal facts. Conventions, whether linguistic or not, are obviously spatiotemporal entities. Therefore, all truths are spatiotemporal.[130] 

This argument evaluated: Since conventionalism is evaluated in Chapters 1 and 9, we can be brief.[131] 
Not all non-empirical truths are conventions. ItÂ’s a non-empirical truth that there are continuous functions that cannot be differentiated at any point. But itÂ’s not a convention. Given the symbolic conventions that govern our usage of the relevant words (Â“continuous,Â” Â“function,Â” Â“differentiated,Â” etc.), it follows that the sentence Â“there are continuous functions that cannot be differentiated at any pointÂ” expresses a truth. But this means that it holds in virtue of convention plus some various non-conventional facts. Those facts are not empirical; they donÂ’t concern the spatiotemporal world. Therefore, the fact described by that sentence is not spatiotemporal. Further, since that fact concerns logical structures of properties (e.g., the property of being differentiable), it follows that there are properties. Since, as we just noted, that fact is non-spatiotemporal, it follows that properties are non-spatiotemporal. 
3.0 Nominalism 
Many medieval philosophers, and some 20th century philosophers, held that properties are identical with words and, therefore, that properties are not spatiotemporal. 
But this position is incoherent, since words and linguistic expressions generally are themselves universals or properties. How many words are right below this sentence? 
Â“snowÂ” Â“snowÂ” Â“snowÂ” 
Is it one or three? The answer: there are three instances of one word. To put it another way, there are three tokens of one word-type.[132] 
Instances of an expression are expression-tokens and the expressions themselves are expression-types. 
No one utterance of the word Â“snowÂ” is identical with that word. ItÂ’s not as though the word-type Â“snowÂ” will disappear when the inscriptions of it in the lines above this are destroyed. That word-type is a property of certain deposits of ink (e.g., the ones above) and bursts of noise, and those ink-deposits and bursts of noise are therefore instances of that property. This shows that, even if the nominalist is right to identify the property of being a rock with the word Â“rock,Â” he has still conceded the truth of Platonism. 
Plus, that property isnÂ’t identical with that word. The Spanish word for rock is Â“piedra.Â” It would be arbitrary to identify that property with the word Â“rockÂ” but not with the word Â“piedra.Â” Since Â“rockÂ” and Â“piedraÂ” are obviously different words, the nominalist must say that the property of being a rock is not identical with itself, which is absurd. 
All of these points aside, it makes no sense to identify that property, or any other, with a word. A thingÂ’s being a rock has nothing to do with words; there were rocks before there were words. 

4.0 Properties demystified 
David Armstrong (1989) says that properties are Â“ways that things can be.Â” To be round is to be one way; to be square is another. ArmstrongÂ’s conception of what properties are is a fruitful one; and if it is kept in mind that properties are just ways that things can be, the resistances that we have to accepting their existence crumble. 
Nobody denies that there are ways things can be. To say that there are ways things can be is to say that there are possibilities as to how things can be. Not all of those possibilities are actualized. Not everything that could be the case is the case. Now, actualized possibilities are in space-time.[133] 
But unactualized possibilitiesÂ— possibilities that never Â“came trueÂ”Â—are surely not in space-time. So where are they? 
One could say that they donÂ’t exist. But that would be absurd. ItÂ’s one thing to say that a possibility wasnÂ’t (or wonÂ’t be) actualized; itÂ’s a very different thing to say that the possibility itself doesnÂ’t exist. ItÂ’s possible that you will you go to law school. But let's suppose that, even though, given our stellar grades and LSAT scores, there is clearly a sense in which law school is a possibility for you, you end up not going to law school. Does the fact that you wonÂ’t go to law school mean that it isnÂ’t an option? Surely not. Does the fact that this possibility isn't actualized mean that the possibility itself doesn't exist? Surely not. 
Your situation is very different from that of somebody (e.g., somebody on death-row) for whom it simply isnÂ’t an option. The fact that a path isnÂ’t taken doesnÂ’t mean that the path doesnÂ’t exist; and the fact that a possibility isnÂ’t actualized doesnÂ’t mean that the possibility itself doesnÂ’t exist. So, given that possibilities, even unactualized ones, do exist, we must again ask: where are they? TheyÂ’re not in space-time. The possibility of your going to law school is not in space-time. So that possibility, being outside of space-time and thus being without location, is nowhere. 
At first this may seem alarming, but it ceases to be so if we choose to see possibilities as properties and actualizations of possibilities as property-instances. It thus seems that the presumptive existence of unactualized possibilities provides support for the theory of universals. 
A story may help clarify the nature of properties. You are a meat inspector. YouÂ’ve just inspected all the meat in slaughterhouse X. None of it passes inspection. All of it was completely rotten. There is obviously a way something would have to be to be a piece of meat that passed inspection; and there is obviously a way something would have to be to be a piece of meat in slaughterhouse X that passed inspection. So when reporting to your supervisor, you say Â“none of the pieces of meat in X deserved to pass inspection,Â” youÂ’re saying: Â“none of those pieces of meat was the right way.Â” Which is the same as saying: Â“there exists a way that something would have to be in order to be a piece of meat in X that deserved to pass inspection; but nothing is that way.Â” Which is the same as saying: Â“the property of being a piece of meat in X that deserved to pass inspection is uninstantiated.Â” 
Thus, the property of being a piece of meat in X that deserves to pass inspection isnÂ’t a giant piece of meat in the sky. ItÂ’s simply a way something would have to be in order to be a piece of meat in X that passed inspection. 
The same is true of the property of being a pink elephant. There are no instances of that property, since there are no pink elephants. But there is a way that something would have to be to be a pink elephant. I know what that way is, and so do you. ThatÂ’s why we both know that, by going to the zoo and spray-painting one of the elephants there, we could make something be that way; and thatÂ’s why we also know that nothing is that way (or, in any case, that nothing weÂ’ve ever heard of is that wayÂ—maybe some prankster has spray painted an elephant). For something to Â“instantiate the property of being a pink elephantÂ” is simply for it to be that way. So that property isnÂ’t some pink elephant in the sky. ItÂ’s just a way something would have to be to be a pink elephant. And for there to be no instances of that property is simply for nothing to be that way. 
Properties can be thought of as conditions. The property of being a pink elephant is a condition a thing must fulfill in order to be a pink elephant. Lots of unfulfilled conditions exist. Mary wonÂ’t marry someone unless he fulfills the following condition: heÂ’s a genius who is always friendly and never sleeps and always dotes on her and has a billion dollars. That condition isnÂ’t fulfilled by anyone. But the condition exists. Thus, properties that arenÂ’t instantiated are just unfulfilled conditions. 
So given that there are unfulfilled conditions, it follows that there are uninstantiated properties. And given that properties exist, even when they have no instances, it follows that, when they do exist, they arenÂ’t identical with their instances. The property of being a pink elephant exists, but is currently uninstantiated. If there were to come into being a single pink elephant, which promptly died, the property wouldnÂ’t go out of existence. It would still be around. But if it were identical with instances, then it would go out of existence the moment its one instance did. 

5.0 Relations and higher-order properties 
We pointed out earlier that properties have properties. The property of being a bird has the property that there are more instances of it than the property of being a penguin. Actually, any statement can be interpreted as a statement about higher-order properties. Â“Smith has a dogÂ” is equivalent to Â“the property of having a dog has the property of being instantiated by Smith.Â” 
Higher-order properties are indispensable to scientific and ordinary discourse. If you say Â“true integrity is rare,Â” youÂ’re saying that the property of having true integrity has the property of being seldom instantiated. If you say that ambition is more important to success than ability, youÂ’re saying that the property of being ambitious has the property of comparing favorably with the property of having ability in respect to whether, in virtue of having it, its instances are likely to succeed. 
Gottlob Frege (1844Â–1925) discovered that statements about numbers are statements about higher-order properties. Â“There are zero penguins in the houseÂ” means: the property of being a penguin in the house has the property of being uninstantiated. Â“There are two penguins in the houseÂ” says that the property of being a pair of penguins in the house is instantiated. The number two may be defined as what all pairs of objects have in common. For x to be a pair of objects is for it to be a set S such that there are objects O1 and O2, distinct from each other, that belong to S and such that anything O2 that belongs to it is identical to either O1 or O2. The number two is the property of being such a pair. See Chapter 7. 
Relations may be identified with properties of ordered pairs. There is some property P such that x is taller than y exactly if the ordered pair <x, y> has P. This conception of what relations are may seem contrived. But itÂ’s an extremely useful one, since, without it, the logical forms of many inferences couldnÂ’t be identified. 

6.0 Sets and propositions identical with properties 
WeÂ’ve seen that properties are not identical with sets of their instances. The main reason for this, we saw, is that properties tend to be modally elastic, whereas sets are modally frozen. In other words, a given property (e.g., the property of being a poet) can generate different instances in different worlds, whereas the set of poets is frozen. If Smith is a member of the set of poets in this world, and S is the set of poets in this world, then S doesnÂ’t exist in any world where Smith does not (or where Smith does exist but isnÂ’t a poet). 
But sets still may be identified with properties. Suppose that Smith, Jones, and Brown are the only three poets in existence. Let S be the set of actual poetsÂ—that is, the set containing Smith, Jones, Brown, and nothing else. In that case, the statement: 
(1) x is a member of S, 
is equivalent with: 
(2) x is identical with Smith or Jones or Brown, 
and therefore, with: 
(3) x has the property of being identical with Smith or Jones or Brown. 
Thus, S may be identified with the property of being identical with Smith or Jones or Brown; and membership in S may be identified with possession of that property. 
Sets are non-spatiotemporal entities. Given that sets are really properties, it follows that, given only that sets are non-spatiotemporal, it doesnÂ’t follow that anything non-spatiotemporal isnÂ’t a property. 
Propositions are non-spatiotemporal entities. But they too are properties. The proposition JM is playing tennis at time t is true just in case certain properties are instantiated at certain times, and we may therefore identify that proposition with the set containing the relevant properties and identify that propositionÂ’s being true with the fact of all of that setÂ’s membersÂ’ being instantiated. (In Chapter 4, we clarify and defend this point.) Since sets can, in the way just described, be identified with properties, it follows that propositions are properties. 
Properties arenÂ’t mind-independent and neither (therefore) are propositions. But, of course, itÂ’s a popular belief, mainly among empiricists, that propositions, if existent, are human creations. Here is a reason, distinct from the one just given, to think otherwise. 
There are infinitely many propositions. (Since there are infinitely many locations, there are, for any given particle x, infinite propositions of the form x is in place y at time t.) We couldnÂ’t therefore have directly created every proposition there is. So, supposing that propositions are human creations, we must be only indirectly responsible for infinitely many of them, and it must therefore be supposed that we created some finite stock of propositions that somehow brought about the rest. But in that case there are true propositions, which weÂ’ll refer to as Â“intermediaryÂ” propositions, that describe how the ones we directly created brought about the others. But since there are infinitely many propositions that we didnÂ’t create, there are infinitely many intermediary propositions: one for each proposition not directly created. 
Suppose for argumentÂ’s sake that we didnÂ’t directly create the proposition 
that dinosaurs wore tweed, and also suppose that p1...pn are the propositions that we directly created. In that case, there is a true intermediary proposition to the effect that p1...pn brought about the propositions that dinosaurs wear 
tweed, another intermediary proposition to the effect that p1...pn brought 
about the proposition that either dinosaurs wore tweed or 1 + 1 = 2, and another to the effect that p1...pn brought about the proposition that itÂ’s possible that itÂ’s the case that either dinosaurs wore tweed or 1 + 1 = 2, and 
so on. 
We didnÂ’t create each of these individually many intermediary propositions. (Given that we didnÂ’t directly create the propositions that dinosaurs wore tweed, we also didnÂ’t directly create any proposition having it as a proper partÂ—e.g., the proposition that either dinosaurs wore tweed or 1+ 1 = 2.) We must therefore posit a second group of intermediary propositions that will mediate between the first group and the propositions that we directly created. 
But everything just said about the first group of intermediary propositions will hold of the second, and weÂ’ll be no further along. Thus, it cannot coherently be supposed that we directly created every proposition in existence. This might appear to leave open the possibility that some propositions, but not others, are human artifacts. But such a view would be arbitrary and implausible, like the view that some whole numbers are human creations while others are not. It would also be demonstrably false. WeÂ’ve seen that we donÂ’t directly or indirectly create the propositions describing how those that we do directly create, supposing that there are any, give rise to those we donÂ’t. Those that we donÂ’t directly create demonstrably entail those that we do. 
Suppose that we didnÂ’t create the proposition that dinosaurs wore tweed but that we did create the proposition that snow is white.
