In that case, we didnÂ’t create the proposition that dinosaurs wore tweed and snow is white. That proposition entails that snow is white and thus requires its existence. Therefore the proposition that snow is white doesnÂ’t need us to create it, since its existence follows from one that we didnÂ’t create. Therefore, we couldnÂ’t have created the proposition that snow is white, since one canÂ’t create what already exists. 
7.0 Concepts vs. properties 
Some authors distinguish properties from what they refer to as Â“concepts.Â” The sentence: 
(BS1) Â“Bill is a square circle,Â” 
is obviously meaningful. (ItÂ’s false; therefore itÂ’s meaningful.) But does the expression Â“square circleÂ” pick out a property? The right answer would seem to be Â“no.Â” Properties are Â“ways things can be.Â” (Or so IÂ’ve argued.) The laws of logic prohibit anything from being both a square and a circle. So the term Â“square circleÂ” doesnÂ’t pick out a way anything can be and therefore doesnÂ’t pick out a property. 
But itÂ’s meaningful. So we have a meaningful predicate that doesnÂ’t pick out a property. But this isnÂ’t possible, at least not relative to the reasonable assumption that at least part of the meaning of a predicate is a property. 
Some authors deal with this by saying that, although it doesnÂ’t pick out a property, the expression Â“square circleÂ” expresses a concept. What is the idea here? The sentence: 
(n1) Â“1 is one less than the whole number that immediately precedes 3,Â” 
doesnÂ’t have the same meaning as the sentence: 
(n2) Â“1 is one less than the unique even prime.Â” 
The property of being one less than the whole number that immediately precedes 3 is identical with the property of being one less than the unique even prime. Possession of either property is both necessary and sufficient for possession of the other. And there is no possible universe where this isnÂ’t the case. So possession of either property is necessarily necessary and sufficient for possession of the other. There is nothing that distinguishes a thingÂ’s having the one property from its having the other. 
So it would be foolish to contend] 
that we are dealing with two distinct properties. A better course of action would be to say that the predicates in question (Â“one less than the whole number that immediately precedes 3Â” and Â“one less than the unique even primeÂ”) pick out the same property but do so by way of different concepts. Hence the need to distinguish between properties and concepts. 
Part II Language 
Chapter 3 What Is a Language? 
1.0 The meaning of Â“meaningÂ” 
There would be no languages if there were no expressions (words, phrases, sentences, etc.). Nothing meaningless is an expression. For this reason, the concept of an expression must be understood in terms of the concept of meaning, the same therefore being true of the concept of language. 
But it isnÂ’t much use to be told that words and sentences Â“have meanings,Â” since the word Â“meaningÂ” has three different meanings, and only one of these directly relates to the nature of language. 
Incidentally, itÂ’s often said that there are linguistic expressions that are meaningless. For example, Chomsky famously said that Â“colorless green dreams sleep furiouslyÂ” is both meaningless and is a bona fide sentence, and therefore expression, of English. 
This reasoning is no good. Depending on how itÂ’s interpreted, Â“colorless green dreams sleep furiouslyÂ” either says (i) that there are dreams that are green and also colorless that sleep furiously, in which case itÂ’s false, or it says (ii) that there is nothing that is a colorless green dream that doesnÂ’t also sleep furiously, in which case itÂ’s vacuously true. 
WeÂ’ll develop this line of thought in next chapter. In the meantime, weÂ’ll operate on the assumption that nothing meaningless is a linguistic expression. Right now weÂ’ll identify the three different meanings of the word Â“meaningÂ” and weÂ’ll identify the sense in which linguistic expressions are meaningful. 









Meaning #1: The evidential meaning of Â“meaningÂ” 
In some cases, to say that x Â“meansÂ” y is to say that x is evidence of yÂ— that x and y are causally interrelated in such a way that, given x, it can reasonably be inferred that y. Â“SmithÂ’s hacking cough means that he has a violent lung infectionÂ” means Â“SmithÂ’s hacking cough is evidence that he has a violent lung infection.Â” And the latter means that coughs like SmithÂ’s are causally connected to violent lung infections in such a way that it may reasonably be inferred that Smith has a violent lung infection. 
SmithÂ’s violent lung infection is a cause of SmithÂ’s hacking cough. But for x to be evidence of y, it is neither necessary nor sufficient that y cause x. Why isnÂ’t it necessary? First of all, causes can be evidence of their own effects. (BillÂ’s current drunkenness is evidence of a poor performance on his upcoming economics exam.) Second, if some event or state of affairs z is a cause of both x and y, then x can be evidence of y without being a cause or an effect of y. (Suppose that Bill is slurring his words. This is evidence that heÂ’ll do poorly on the upcoming test. But his slurring his words is neither a cause, nor an effect, of his substandard test-performance. His drunkenness is a cause of (a) his slurred speech and (b) his imminent, substandard test-performance. And itÂ’s because his slurred speech has a causal ancestor in common with his poor test-performance that the former is evidence of the latter.) Why isnÂ’t it sufficient? Given only that the cause of BillÂ’s failing was that he was drunk, we canÂ’t infer from the fact that he failed that he was drunk. There are many reasons why a person may fail a test. Supposing that y caused x to occur, x is evidence of y only if it canÂ’t reasonably be supposed that anything other than y was the cause. (Only a violent lung infection could be responsible for SmithÂ’s hacking cough, that being why the latter is evidence of the former.) 

Meaning #2: The psychological meaning of Â“meaningÂ” 
When we use sentences, we mean things by them. Meaning in this sense is a psychological notion. You tell me that Sally is the most wonderful, decent person youÂ’ve ever known. I respond by saying Â“things arenÂ’t always as they seem.Â” What I mean is that Sally is devious. In other words, my intention in making this statement is to say that Sally is devious. Given that intentions are psychological entities, meaning in this sense is obviously a psychological notion. 

Meaning #3: The linguistic meaning of Â“meaningÂ” 
The sentence Â“snow is whiteÂ” says something about something; it attributes the property of being white to snow. Therefore, it means that snow is white. This kind of meaning is in a class by itself; it isnÂ’t identical with either of the two kinds mentioned so far; and there isnÂ’t any obvious way to understand it in terms of them. Let us now say why. 
Meaning in the psychological sense involves, but does not coincide with, meaning in the linguistic sense. Once again suppose that, in response to your telling me that Sally is a wonderful person, I say Â“things arenÂ’t always as they seem.Â” My meaningÂ—what IÂ’m trying to get acrossÂ—is that Sally is devious. But in my attempt to get this across, IÂ’m taking advantage of the fact that Â“things arenÂ’t always as they seemÂ” has an existing (linguistic) meaning. My meaning that Sally is devious is parasitic on my utteranceÂ’s meaning that things arenÂ’t always as they seem. Meaning in the psychological sense is therefore parasitic on meaning in the linguistic sense. 
1.2 Why meaning #3 . meaning #2 
Some philosophers and linguists have held that for: 
(1) Â“Snow is white,Â” 
to mean that snow is white is for it to be the case that, in uttering Â“snow is white,Â” what people mean is that snow is white. This view, duly generalized, is that for a sentence S to have meaning M is for it to be the case that, in 
[135] 

uttering S, people mean M. 
This position is false. There are many sentences that have determinate meanings even though theyÂ’ve never been uttered before and, therefore, no one as of yet has ever meant anything by them. The sentence: 
(2) Â“The cube root of three is Sir Lawrence OlivierÂ’s favorite irrational number between one and four,Â” 
has a determinate meaning, and it had a determinate meaning before any part of this book was written, even though, we may reasonably suppose, it had never previously been uttered or otherwise tokened. Thus, meaning in the linguistic sense is not in all cases identical with meaning in the psychological sense. 
But a stronger point is warranted. LetÂ’s say that P1 and P2 are the propositions meant by (1) and (2), respectively. In saying that (1) means P1 and that (2) means P2, we are not using the word Â“meansÂ” equivocally. Both occurrences of Â“meansÂ” in the last sentence denote the same relationship. Thus, the relationship that (1) bears to its meaning is the same as the relationship that (2) bears to its meaning. Given that, as we saw, (2)Â’s having P2 for its meaning isnÂ’t identical with P2Â’s being what people mean in uttering (2), it follows that (1)Â’s having P1 for its meaning isnÂ’t identical with P1Â’s being what people mean in uttering (1). Of course, what we just said about (1) and (2) can be said of any other sentence. So even if what people mean in uttering a given sentence happens to coincide with its literal meaning, what it is for sentence S to have proposition P for its literal meaning isnÂ’t for people to mean P in uttering S. 
Psychological meaning presupposes linguistic meaning. What a person means when uttering a given sentence is a function of, among other things, his beliefs as to what that sentence already means. You must believe that Â“snow is whiteÂ” means snow is white if, intending to speak sincerely and literally, you say Â“snow is whiteÂ” with the intention of getting it across that snow is white. If you think that Â“snow is whiteÂ” means grass is green, you cannot, if your intention is to speak sincerely and literally, believe that Â“snow is whiteÂ” means snow is white. 
Of course, you could know full well what Â“snow is whiteÂ” in fact means, but use that sentence to get across something that has nothing to do with the color of snow. Knowing what Â“snow is whiteÂ” actually means, you might utter that sentence with the intention of getting it across that the government is controlling our thoughts with alpha waves. And, depending on the circumstances, that could be precisely what an utterance of that sentence would convey. 
But whatever the message is that you wish to convey in uttering a certain sentence, you must believe that message to have some kind of relationship to the one meant by that sentence itself. Furthermore, if you are to succeed in saying what it is you wish to say, what you believe to be meant by the sentence you are using must be right. If, intending to speak sincerely and literally, you say Â“snow is white,Â” thinking that it means bananas are yellow, you will fail to say what you wanted to say. 
Thus, setting aside defective utterances, one cannot, in uttering a given sentence, mean anything by it unless one knows what it already means. So meaning in the psychological sense is parasitic on meaning in the linguistic sense, and the two kinds of meaning are therefore entirely distinct. 

1.3 Why meaning #3 . meaning #1 
The sense in which Â“snow is whiteÂ” means that snow is white isnÂ’t comparable to the sense in which smoke means fire. The fact that smoke means fire has nothing to do with conventions on the part of people.[ But the fact that Â“snow is whiteÂ” means what it does is, at least in part, a matter of convention. ItÂ’s a matter of convention that Â“snowÂ” doesnÂ’t refer to grass and, therefore, that Â“snow is whiteÂ” doesnÂ’t mean that grass is white; itÂ’s a matter of convention that Â“whiteÂ” doesnÂ’t mean green and, therefore, that Â“snow is whiteÂ” doesnÂ’t mean that snow is green. 
Although the whiteness of snow sometimes causes people to say Â“snow is white,Â” it doesnÂ’t do so in the way that fire causes there to be smoke. Fire happens; smoke happens as a result. The presence of smoke doesnÂ’t embody any judgment about anything. But, when caused by the whiteness of snow, utterances of Â“snow is whiteÂ” do embody judgments of various kinds. People see or otherwise come to believe that snow is white; and, since they know the relevant linguistic rules, they know that were they to say Â“snow is white,Â” they judge that theyÂ’d be making a correct statement. Thus, utterances of Â“snow is whiteÂ” embody judgments about the color of snow and about how, linguistic conventions being what they are, one can report the color of snow. Also, people donÂ’t say everything that occurs to them. Before deciding to utter a given sentence, people typically make context-based judgments about the appropriateness of uttering that sentence. So various judgmentsÂ—about snow, about language, and about human psychologyÂ—are involved in the causal connection between the whiteness of snow and a given personÂ’s saying Â“snow is white.Â” There is thus a normative dimension to language use that is absent where purely natural, non-conventional cause-effect relations are concerned. 
2.0 Sentences as proposition-isomorphs 
The meaning of a true or false sentence is a proposition. Propositions are not themselves sentences. That is why different sentences (e.g., Â“schnee ist weissÂ” and Â“snow is whiteÂ”) can express the same proposition. 
Propositions, when true, are truths. Thus, propositions have existed as long as there have been truths; which means that theyÂ’ve existed as long as there has been anything and, consequently, that propositions are not our creations. 
Though distinct from the sentences that express them, propositions are structurally similar to them. Two otherwise dissimilar sentences can share the word Â“John.Â” Â“John loves MaryÂ” and Â“Sally punched JohnÂ” are two such sentences. The meanings of those sentences obviously have something in common corresponding to the fact that they share the word Â“John.Â” Since they share no other constituents, the thing meant by Â“JohnÂ” must be capable of moving on its own from sentence-meaning to sentence-meaning. This would not be the case if the thing meant by Â“JohnÂ” in the proposition meant by Â“John loves MaryÂ” were incapable of being disengaged from the things meant by Â“lovesÂ” and Â“Mary.Â” It follows that propositions consist of discrete parts; it also follows that those discrete parts correspond to discrete parts of the sentences that express them. Taken together, these two points entail that sentences are structurally like the propositions they express. 

2.1 Propositions as digital structures 
Given that propositions consist of discrete, isolable entities, it follows that, like sentences and unlike visual perceptions and photographs, propositions are digital structures. The sentence Â“Sally punched BobÂ” has a unique decomposition into a certain Â“minimal units of significance,Â” or Â“morphemes,Â” these being Â“Sally,Â” Â“Bob,Â” etc. Given what we said in Section 2.0, it follows that something similar is true of the corresponding proposition. Sentences and propositions are digital structures, meaning that they have unique breakdowns into minimal significant units. 
A visual perception of Sally punching Bob doesnÂ’t have a structure comparable to that of Â“Sally punched BobÂ” or any other sentence. Unlike sentences, perceptions donÂ’t have to decompose into minimal significant units. Visual perceptions, unlike sentences and propositions, therefore have non-digital or analogue structures. Given that at least some thought involves the processing of perceptual information, it follows that thought 
at least sometimes has a structure very different from language. (See Section 5.4 for further discussion of this.) The nature of propositions is discussed in Chapter 4. 
3.0 The three branches of the philosophy of language: semantics, pragmatics, and syntax 
The study of language is typically divided into three sub-disciplinesÂ— semantics, pragmatics, and syntax. In addition to denoting a branch of linguistic study, each of these three words denotes dimension of language. So Â“semanticsÂ” refers to a certain discipline and also to a feature of expressions, the same being true of the other two expressions. 
3.1. Semantics 
The discipline of semantics attempts to make it clear what our utterances literally mean. It has no interest in what is conveyed through suggestion or innuendo. 
If a disappointed boss says to a substandard employee, Â“it might not be a bad idea for you to start thinking about finding a new position,Â” the literal meaning of his utterance is quite innocuous. But the message that is being sent is not innocuousÂ—that message is: youÂ’re fired; youÂ’re a disgrace; go away; etc. That utterance's semantics coincides with its literal (innocuous) meaning. 

3.2 Pragmatics 
Pragmatics studies the use of language. Sometimes language is used literally. Asked whether IÂ’m over thirty years of age, I say Â“yes, IÂ’m over thirty years of age.Â” What I mean coincides with what my utterance literally means. 
Language is often used non-literally. If, while addressing a pan-handler, I say Â“youÂ’ve made a fine life for yourself,Â” what I mean is the antithesis of what my utterance means. But usually the propositions literally meant by our utterances are neither opposed to, nor exhaustive of, the propositions we wish to affirm in producing those utterances. Asked whether thereÂ’s a place to get food, I say Â“thereÂ’s a McDonalds down the road.Â” The proposition IÂ’m affirming is: there is a nearby place to get food, the reason being that thereÂ’s a McDonalds down the road. Thus, the proposition literally meant by my utterance is only a part of what it is that IÂ’m saying. Thus, what a sentence literally means is only one of many factors governing what it is used to mean. The discipline of pragmatics tries to identify the remaining factors. 

3.3 Syntax 
The discipline of syntax studies the structures of the meanings of complex expressions. A complex expression is one that consists of other expressions. (Thus, Â“the man who ate my cookieÂ” is a complex expression, since it consists of Â“man,Â” Â“ate,Â” etc., each of which is meaningful. By contrast, Â“redÂ” is not a complex expression, since it doesnÂ’t have any meaningful proper parts.) The discipline of syntax tries to make it clear how the meanings of complex expressions depend on those of their parts. 
Thus, the discipline of syntax doesnÂ’t study the meanings of complex expressions per se. It studies the relationships that such meanings have to those of their constituents. Consider the sentence Â“Sally hates Bob.Â” The word Â“hatesÂ” occurs in that sentence. If that occurrence is replaced with an occurrence of Â“lovesÂ” or Â“is amused by,Â” the resulting sentence has a very different meaning from the first. This shows that what Â“Sally hates BobÂ” means depends on what Â“hatesÂ” means. 
Bearing this point in mind, consider the sentence Â“Larry loves Julie.Â” Obviously this sentence doesnÂ’t mean the same thing as Â“Sally hates Bob.Â” But the relationship borne by the meaning of Â“Sally hates BobÂ” to the meaning Â“hatesÂ” is identical with the relationship borne by the meaning of Â“Larry loves JulieÂ” to that of Â“loves.Â” Exactly similar points hold in connection with each of the remaining two constituents of each of those sentences. 
The discipline of syntax studies the relation that the meanings of complex expressions bear to the meanings of the simple expressions composing them. Thus, syntax doesnÂ’t study the semantics (meanings) of complex expressions. It studies the structures of the semantics of complex expressions. Syntax studies semantic structure. 
4.0 The need for the discipline of semantics 
Even though we all know what is meant by: 
(1) Â“John wants to catch a 20-pound striped bass,Â” 
we donÂ’t know what it is that we know in knowing this. Semanticists supply us with the missing meta-knowledge. Consider the sentence: 
(2) Â“John wants to punch Bob.Â” 
(2) attributes a certain property to JohnÂ—that of wanting to punch Bob. Given that (1) and (2) are grammatically isomorphic, itÂ’s natural to assume that there exists some 20-pound striped bass x such that the proposition expressed by (1) is: 
(3) John wants to catch x. 
But this isnÂ’t the right analysis. There isnÂ’t some one fish such that, if the desire ascribed to John by (1) is to be gratified, John must catch that very fish. There is thus no fish x such that, if (1) is to be true, John must want to catch x. 
The meaning of (1) is: 
(1R)[138] 
John wants it to be the case that: there exists some fish x such that x is a 20-pound striped bass and such that John catches x. 
Thus, (1) doesnÂ’t describe a relationship between John and some nonÂ­existent or quasi-existent fish. It affirms the existence of a relationship between John and a proposition. The proposition in question is one that, in English, is expressed by the sentence: 
(4) Â“There exists some fish x such that x is a 20-pound striped bass and such that John catches x.Â” 
If JohnÂ’s fishing-trip is a success, that proposition will be true; otherwise it 
will be false. But that proposition exists either way. 
But we still havenÂ’t solved the problem. In (4), the expression Â“some fishÂ” occurs. Grammatically, that expression is a noun-phrase. But, unlike other noun-phrases, it doesnÂ’t refer to anything. Â“Some fishÂ” doesnÂ’t refer to some fish. There is no fish x such that Â“some fishÂ” refers to x. ThatÂ’s why, given any particular fish F, if you say Â‹some fish is wet, but F is notÂ›, what you are saying isnÂ’t self-contradictory. So the problem we were trying to solve remains. 
But to solve the problem, we need only reword (4). The needed 
rewording is this: 
(5) "The property of being a 20-pound striped bass that John catches is instantiated." 
The property of being such a fish exists. So (1), which seemed to be about a non-existent fish, is about an existent property. (5) says of that property that itÂ’s instantiated. Thus, a complete analysis of (1) is given by 
(1CA) John wants it to be the case that the property of being a 20-pound striped bass that John catches is instantiated. 
So even though just about every English speaker understands (1), knowing what it is that one knows in understanding it isnÂ’t such a trivial thing. 

4.1 Semantics is needed to figure out what is literally meant and what is not 
Despite everything just said, there is clearly a sense in which every English speaker knows what (1) means. What the semanticist is doing in connection with (1) isnÂ’t comparable to what somebody who speaks both Spanish and English is doing in connection with it when he tells his monolingual Spanish speaking friend what it means. The semanticist is needed to clarify the structure of the meaning that (1) is already known to have, but he isnÂ’t needed to identify that meaning. The semanticist isnÂ’t a translator. But there are many cases where the semanticist is needed to identify literal meaning. In fact, as paradoxical as it may sound, there are cases where he is needed to identify the meanings of sentences that are perfectly well understood. 
First of all, we must distinguish what is literally meant by an utterance from what it is that the speaker wishes to convey. To give a trivial example: You and I are robbing a bank. I yell: Â“The cops are coming!Â” What I wish to convey is that we should hurry up. In this particular case, itÂ’s easy to distinguish what is literally meant from what is non-literally suggested, and semantics would therefore have no interest in it. But in other cases, itÂ’s exceedingly hard to do this, and itÂ’s with these other cases that semantics is concerned. 
A story will help us move forward. Somebody who is wearing a ski-mask, and who I therefore donÂ’t recognize, deftly snatches my wallet from my pocket. As heÂ’s running off, I point at him and yell: Â“That man is a thief!Â” Let U1 be this utterance. 
Before moving on, letÂ’s take a moment to make it clear what U1Â’s literal meaning is. Somebody just stole my wallet. I donÂ’t know who that person is. 
But whoever it is, I am attributing a certain property to him. If that person has that property, I have spoken truly; if not, I have not. U1 is correct if, and only if, the person referred to by Â“that manÂ” has the property expressed by Â“is a 
thief.Â” Thus, there is some individual x such that x has just stolen my wallet and such that what IÂ’ve just said is true exactly if x is a thief. (The italicized part is U1Â’s literal meaning.) 
The next day, my lovable office-mate Steve eats one of the cupcakes that was on my desk. I jokingly point at him and say: Â“That man is a thief.Â” Let 
U2 be this utterance. There is some x such that x just ate my cupcake and such that U2 is true exactly if: x is a thief. 
Unbeknownst to me, Steve is the pick-pocket, and there is some individual x, namely Steve, such that each of U1 and U2 is true if and only if x is a thief. Thus, U1 and U2 have the very same literal meanings.[140] 
But I donÂ’t know this, even though I speak English perfectly and, on each occasion, obviously 
understand perfectly well what it is that IÂ’m saying. 
How is this possible?[141] 
Our sense-perceptions describe things. My uttering U1 was a response to my being given a visual description of Steve. That description was to the effect that: 
(i) There is some man x such that x is wearing a ski-mask and such that x is running off into the distance. 
But U1Â’s literal meaning is not to that that effect. There is some man x such that x is a wearing a ski-mask (etc.), such that in uttering U1 I was saying that: 
(ii) x is a thief. 
The meaning of U1, being identical with (ii), is quite threadbare. But I 
grasped that threadbare meaning through my descriptively rich visual perception, whose content is given by (i). My uttering U2 was a response to my being given a different description of Steve. That description was to the 
effect that: 
(iii) There is some man x such that x is a portly amicable fellow who is sitting over in that chair. 
But U2Â’s literal meaning is not that that effect. There is some man x such that x is a portly amicable fellow (etc.) such that in uttering U2 I was saying that: 
(ii) x is a thief. 
Echoing what we said a moment ago, the meaning of U2, being identical with (ii), is quite threadbare. But I grasped that threadbare meaning through my descriptively rich visual perception, whose content is given by (iii). 
Because I grasped (ii) by way of different bodies of perceptual (descriptive) information, I didnÂ’t know, when uttering U2, that what I was affirming was the same thing I was affirming in uttering U1. Oftentimes, literal meaning is cloaked by the pre-semantic information through which it 
is grasped, and semanticists are needed to uncloak it. 

4.2 Semantics are needed to figure out what is literally meant and what is not (continued) 
Fido is the smartest dog on the planet. I know this well, but some of my friends donÂ’t yet know this. I point to Fido and say: Â“That dog is very smart.Â” 
The proposition that it was my intention to affirm and communicate is indeed true. For a dog, Fido is indeed smart. Of course, Fido is vastly less intelligent than a human being, such as my friend Timmy, who is of mediocre intelligence. But if I say Â“Timmy is very smart,Â” what IÂ’m saying is false. Judging by the words IÂ’ve used, the property IÂ’ve attributed to Timmy is identical with the property IÂ’ve attributed to Fido. Given that Timmy has that property to a vastly greater degree than Fido, it would seem to follow that, since Â“Fido is smartÂ” is true, Â“Timmy is smartÂ” must also be true. And yet Â“Timmy is smartÂ” is false. How can this be? 
Some deal with this by saying that Â“smartÂ” is ambiguous, like the word Â“dumb.Â” So Â“Timmy is smartÂ” and Â“Fido is smartÂ” have different meanings, like Â“Timmy is dumb [unintelligent]Â” and Â“Timmy is dumb [mute].Â” 
This solution is pretty clearly false. A more plausible one is that the property of being smart for a dog is distinct from the property of being smart for a human. Fido has the first but not the second. And many humans have the second, but almost all of those lack the first. 
A similar, possibly coincident, view is that Â“smartÂ” is implicitly relational. When, for some object x, you say Â‹x is smartÂ›, you are saying that x is smart relative to some benchmark, the identity of which the context makes clear. So Â“Fido is smartÂ” says that Fido is smarter than most dogs, which is true, and Â“Timmy is smartÂ” says that Timmy is smarter than most human beings, which is false. 
I published a paper[142] 
arguing that, for any degree-property phi, Â‹x has phiÂ› expresses a proposition of the form: the degree to which x has phi exceeds standard S, where S is some standard that, given the context, is clearly the relevant one. (A Â“degree propertyÂ” is one that can be had to varying degrees.) But even if this is right, it doesnÂ’t follow that such judgments are the literal meanings of such sentences. And there is no independent evidence that Â‹x is smartÂ› has the syntactic properties of sentences that clearly do have for their literal meanings propositions of the just-described kind. This suggests that, so far as Â‹x has phiÂ› communicates such a proposition, it isnÂ’t because it semantically encodes it. 
In any case, it is not obvious what Â‹x is smartÂ› means or, in general, what Â‹x has phiÂ› means, where phi is any degree property. Thus, the literal meanings of such sentences are sufficiently recondite that the intervention of professional semanticists is needed to identify them. 
See Chapter 4 for a thorough discussion of the points just made. 
5.0 Semantic rules 
The English language assigns a certain meaning to the sound Â“that dog has rabiesÂ”; and given the spectacle of a rabid dog, it furnishes one with a sentence with which to describe what one sees. In general, the English language assigns meanings to sentences and sentences to meanings. This is true of all languages. A language is a systematic way of pairing off sentences with meanings. Any rule that assigns a meaning to an expression is known as a Â“semantic rule.Â” Languages are sets of semantic rules. 
5.1. An important subtlety 
There are a couple of subtle but, in some contexts, important inaccuracies in what I just said. First of all, something isnÂ’t a sentence until a meaning has been assigned to it. In a world where there were no animate beings, but in which the forthcoming parenthetical ink deposit (1 + 1 = 2) was formed out of twigs, that twig deposit wouldnÂ’t be an expression of any kind. That twig deposit would be an expression if and only if it were endowed with meaning. This shows that something has to have meaning in order to be an expression. Thus, expressions arenÂ’t assigned meanings. They already have them and donÂ’t need to be assigned them. Therefore a semantic rule canÂ’t be defined as a rule that assigns a meaning to an expression. 

5.2 How meaning is assigned to hitherto meaningless, and, therefore non-linguistic, entities 
Thus, semantic rules assign meanings to non-expressions. But which non-expressions? A story will give us the answer. 
You and I want to invent a code that only we two know. We both know a guy whose real is name is Larry. We decide that our code name for Larry is to be Â“Ichabod.Â” So whatÂ’s going on is that weÂ’re creating a semantic rule: one that to the effect that Â“IchabodÂ” is to pick out Larry. How exactly is this rule enacted? 
In order to implement this rule, I say: LetÂ’s refer to Larry as Â“Ichabod.Â” The burst of noise that I produce is a sentence-token. And what you hear is some token of Â“IchabodÂ”Â—you do not, since one could not, hear the name type itself. 
When you hear this burst of noise, along with my proposal concerning our new name for Larry, you know that what IÂ’m saying is to the effect that any other physical object that is similar in the relevant ways to this burst of noise is itself henceforth to refer to Larry. Thus, I am in effect proposing that all and only those bursts of noise that are similar, in the relevant respect, to this particular burst of noise are to refer to Larry. (By implication, IÂ’m proposing the same thing mutatis mutandis to hold of all and only ink-deposits that, given certain conventions, are paired off with such bursts of noise.) The thing that, according to my proposal, is henceforth to pick out Larry is the thing of which all and only such bursts of noises (etc.) are instances. That thing, like anything else of which there are instances, is a property. It is the property had in common by all and only bursts of noise (etc.) of the relevant type. 
That property doesnÂ’t (yet) have a meaning; it isnÂ’t (yet) an expression. ItÂ’s a property that existed, and was instantiated, before either or any instances meant anything. So the semantic rule that IÂ’m proposing we adopt assigns a referent to a property that does not itself have a meaning. The same thing mutatis mutandis holds of any other semantic rule. 
Thus semantic rules assign meanings to properties of physical objectsÂ—to morphological or acoustical properties (in other words, to properties that a thing has in virtue of having a certain shape or sounding a certain way). A semantic rule is therefore something which assigns a meaning to a property, and language is a set of such rules. 
(Technically, this is only an approximation to the truth. The relevant qualifications are found in Section 7.5.) 

5.3 Semantic rules (revisited) 
Many believe that linguistic meaning is to be understood in function-theoretic terms. More precisely, they believe that semantic rules are mathematical functions. 
Let us start by defining the word Â“function.Â” Given any pair of whole numbers, the expression Â“+Â” assigns exactly one whole number to that pair. Thus, Â“+Â” denotes a function that assigns single numbers to pairs of numbers. In general, a function is a rule that, given some class of objects, assigns no more than one object to any given member of that class. 
Although the rule expressed by Â“plusÂ” assigns the number 8 to the pair <4,4>, it doesnÂ’t assign that number to that pair in the way in which a person assigns a task to an underling. In the one case, the word Â“assignsÂ” has a psychological meaning and it refers to something spatiotemporal; in the other case, it has a non-psychological, purely logical meaning, and it refers to something non-spatiotemporal. A related point is that the rule that assigns 8 to <4,4> isnÂ’t a social rule, and it therefore isnÂ’t something that can be obeyed or disobeyed. 
According to the function-theoretic view, semantic rules are rules in the same strictly logical sense in which F(x)=x+2 is function. The semantic rule for Â“SocratesÂ” is a function that assigns a certain individual (Socrates) to that word (or to occurrences thereof). The semantic rule for Â“snow is whiteÂ” is a function that assigns truth-conditions to that utterance (or to occurrences thereof). And so on.[145] 

5.3.1 Why semantic rules are not functions 
The just-described view is false. The rule denoted by Â“+Â” has always existed and always will. Of course, the expression Â“+Â” hasnÂ’t always existed. But thatÂ’s irrelevant, since things pre-exist the expressions we use to denote them. Â“SocratesÂ” is an Anglicization of the name by which Socrates was referred to by his contemporaries. Since Socrates lived well before the English language came into existence, Â“SocratesÂ” (the name, not the person) didnÂ’t come into existence until well after its referent went out of it. 
The semantic rule that assigns Socrates to ink deposits having certain shapes would exist even if the English language had never come into existence. Like the rule denoted by Â“+Â” that rule has always existed and always will. So has the rule that assigns Abraham Lincoln to such ink deposits. The mathematical function that assigns the proposition snow is white to ink deposits like the italicized one has always existed, as has the mathematical function that assigns the proposition all horses weigh 18,000 lbs. to those same ink deposits. 
But the English language hasnÂ’t always existed. Since the English language is a set of semantic rules, those semantic rules havenÂ’t always existed. They came into existence quite recently and thus cannot be mathematical functions. 
Also, if the semantic rules of English were such functions, there would exist a language in which Â“SocratesÂ” referred to Lincoln and in which Â“snow is whiteÂ” meant all horses weigh 18,000 lbs., the reason being that the corresponding mathematical functions exist. But there is no such language. Of course, there could be such a language. And maybe there will be; maybe somebody will invent a code in which those things have those meanings. But right now they donÂ’t. Such a language is merely possible, and therefore doesnÂ’t exist. Thus, semantic rules are not rules in the mathematical sense. 

5.3.2 The Gricean approach 
Understandably, many philosophers of language believe that semantic rules must be understood in psychological, not mathematical, terms. There are different versions of this view. I accept one version of it. But the version I accept bears little resemblance to the versions of it that are usually held, each of which is some variant of the view held by H.P. Grice. 
According to Grice (1957), for expression E to have literal meaning M is for it to be the case that, when they utter E, M is what they mean. So their answer to the question "why does 'snow is white' have the proposition that snow is white for its literal meaning?" is "because what people generally mean when they say 'snow is white' is that snow is white." Aware of some of the problems with Grice's view that we're about to identify, neo-Griceans concede that, although literal meaning cannot in all cases be identified with speakerÂ’s meaning, the former is parasitic on the latter in ways that are correctly described by modest liberalizations of Grice's view. 
Wittgenstein (1958) advocated a version of this view. Â“Roughly speaking,Â” he said, Â“meaning is use.Â” Expressions mean what we use them to meanÂ—they mean what we mean by them. Wittgenstein nowhere makes it clear what he means by the words Â“roughly speaking.Â” 
But it doesnÂ’t matter, since his statement isnÂ’t even roughly true. Literal meaning isnÂ’t identical with speakerÂ’s meaning and it isnÂ’t to be understood in terms of it. ItÂ’s the other way around. We saw why in Section 1.3. 
Also, GriceÂ’s theory fails to deal with the fact that the meaning of a subsentential expression isnÂ’t something that could possibly be meant. Â“Of Â” has a meaning; so does Â“skip,Â” Â“snorkel,Â” Â“or,Â” Â“gladly,Â” etc. But whatever it is that Â“orÂ” means, it cannot, at least not by itself, be what a person means by it. I cannot say "or" and mean it---my meaning cannot be its meaning. 

5.3.3 More problems with the Gricean approach 
If Grice were right, the meaning of the sentence: 
(SF) Â“Smith is now living in France,Â” 
would be fixed by the intentions people have in using it. 
But its meaning is not fixed by those intentions. It is fixed by the meanings of its parts (Â“Smith,Â” Â“France,Â” etc.), together with the way those expressions are ordered in that sentence. The semantic and syntactic rules of English being what they are, SF would have its current meaning even if it had never been used. So whatever the intentions of people using that sentence are, those intentions do nothing in the way of assigning it that meaning. In general, GriceÂ’s view is inherently incapable of accommodating the fact meaning is compositional. 

5.3.4 How some Griceans deal with the problem just described 
Some Griceans respond by saying that[146]: [H5] 

(GV) [147] 
Although speaker-meaning doesnÂ’t directly fix sentence-meaning, it does so indirectly. In uttering sentences of the form Â‹....France...Â›. our intention is to say thatÂ…FranceÂ… (For example, in saying "France is lovely,Â” one's intention is to say that France is lovely; and in saying "Jerry loves vacationing in France", one's intention is to say that Jerry loves vacationing in France.) It is in virtue of that fact that Â“FranceÂ” refers to France. 
For Â“FranceÂ” to refer to France is for Â‹....France...Â› to mean thatÂ…FranceÂ…So even though our linguistic intentions donÂ’t directly endow Â“FranceÂ” with meaning, they do directly endow sentences containing Â“FranceÂ” with meaning, and they thus indirectly endow Â“FranceÂ” with meaning. Therefore, GriceÂ’s core idea is right: What an expression means is to be understood in terms of what people using it are trying to say. 
[148] 

GV is a failure. Let P be the proposition meant by SF. So far as people utter SF with the intention of affirming P, itÂ’s because they believe (correctly, as it happens) that each of the expressions composing it already has a certain meaning. 
ItÂ’s irrelevant that how we use sentences of the form Â‹...France...Â› causally determines what Â“FranceÂ” means. There are many ways to cause meaningÂ­shiftsÂ—many ways to get a given expression to have a certain meaning. But the question weÂ’re asking isnÂ’t Â“how did Â‘FranceÂ’ acquire its current meaning?Â”, and is instead Â“whatever it is that Â‘FranceÂ’ means, what is it for it to have that meaning?Â” And itÂ’s no answer to this question to say that it may have acquired that meaning because of what, at some point in time, people meant by sentences of the form Â‹...France...Â›. 

5.3.5 Why GriceÂ’s theory is inconsistent with the normative nature of semantic rules 
A billiard ball isnÂ’t right to move after being struck; it just does. The relevant scientific laws merely register that fact; they arenÂ’t normativeÂ—that is, they donÂ’t characterize it as good or bad. Unlike scientific laws, semantic rules are normative. If, intending to affirm that Smith is female, you say Â“Smith is male,Â” youÂ’ve done something wrong. If Grice is right, literal meaning is speakerÂ’s meaning. This means that, if Grice were right, speakerÂ’s meaning wouldnÂ’t be accountable to existing semantic rules. Since it is, Grice is wrong. 


5.4 The psychological reality of semantic rules 
One view as to the nature of semantic rules is that they are idealized descriptions of the activities of speakers. Proponents of this view seldom if ever identify the facts about the speaker-behavior of which semantic rules are supposedly descriptions. The most natural assumption is that they are idealized descriptions of what people mean when they speak and write (etc.). If this assumption is right, then, given the points just made, the view in question is wrong. 
But even if this isnÂ’t what proponents of this view have in mind, their view is very clearly wrong. If semantic rules are just idealizations of speaker-behavior, then speaker-behavior must pre-exist the semantic rules embodied in it. But if thatÂ’s the case, then the activity described by semantic rules isnÂ’t guided by them. An awareness of those rules is no part of what leads people to say the things they do. Those rules are psychologically inert. They have no Â“psychological reality.Â” This view is held by Nathan Salmon (2007) and also by Scott Soames (2002). 
This view is inconsistent with some obvious facts. I know that Smith is now living in France. Wanting to tell you this, I say: Â“Smith is now living in France.Â” Why do I choose this particular sentence? Because, first of all, I know the relevant semantic rules (viz., that Â“SmithÂ” refers to Smith,that Â“livingÂ” refers to a certain property) and, secondly, because I believe that, given these facts about semantics, the sentence in question is the right one to express my belief. A knowledge of semantics underlies my speech-act and, by obvious extensions of these points, all non-defective speech-acts. 
Another problem with the Salmon-Soames view is that itÂ’s inconsistent with the normative character of semantic rules. If semantic rules merely describe existing semantic activity, then that activity isnÂ’t answerable to semantic norms. Semantic activity obviously is answerable to such rules. If, intending to tell you to take a break after jogging for another 100 yards, I say Â“jog continuously for another ten miles; therefore, do not take a break after jogging for another 100 yards,Â” IÂ’ve misspoken, given what it was that I intended to say, and IÂ’ve therefore violated the relevant semantic norms.) So the Salmon-Soames view is incorrect. 

5.5 Conceptual role semantics 
A little while ago, we briefly discussed WittgensteinÂ’s claim that Â“meaning is useÂ”; i.e., that for an expression to have a given meaning is for it to be used in a certain way. This doctrine is incoherent in many ways. WeÂ’ve already discussed one of those ways; now weÂ’ll discuss some of the others. 
Expressions have meanings. A meaningless burst of noise isnÂ’t an expression. If I cough or guffaw, the burst of noise IÂ’ve produced doesnÂ’t have the sort of meaning had by bona fideexpressions. It has, at most, meaning in irrelevant, purely evidential sense; e.g., the sense in which a cough may be evidence of a cold. Since anything that is a linguistic expression ipso facto has a meaning (in the relevant, linguistic sense), there are no expressions to be used before noises, ink-marks, etc., have been assigned meanings. So, since there can be no expression-use until after there is expression-meaning, it makes no sense at all to say that expression-use determines expression-meaning. Â“Meaningful expressionÂ” is a pleonasm.[149] 
So, contrary to what Wittgenstein said, meaning isnÂ’t use. 
Of course, how a given expression is used may well assign it a new meaning. But there is all the difference in the world between saying: 
(1) Expression EÂ’s having meaning M is causally determined by EÂ’s being used in such and such a manner, 
and: 
(2) Expression EÂ’s having meaning M is identical with EÂ’s being used in such and such a manner. 
(1) is a sterile triviality. And (2) is wrong. An expression EÂ’s having meaning M cannot possibly be constituted by its being used in such and such a manner since E isnÂ’t an expression, and therefore isnÂ’t an expression to be used until it has a meaning. 
According to a doctrine known as Â“conceptual role semanticsÂ” (CRS), whose exponents include Hartry Field (1977) and Robert Brandom (1994), for an expression to have a given meaning is simply for it to be used in a certain way. But this isnÂ’t correct as we just saw. 
CRS is incoherent for reasons other than the one just given. According to that doctrine, what a sentence means is determined by what people infer from it and what people infer it from. Whereas commonsense holds that one infers Â“an even number is less than fiveÂ” from Â“two is less than fiveÂ” because the latter already has a given meaning, advocates of CRS say that, on the contrary, itÂ’s because people infer Â“an even number is less than fiveÂ” and other similar statements from Â“two is less than fiveÂ” that the latter has the meaning it has. 
This is not a viable view. If we learn tomorrow that, contrary to what we previously thought, Aristotle wrote several plays, weÂ’ll infer Â“somebody who wrote several plays wrote the Nichomachean Ethics from Â“Aristotle wrote the Nichomachean Ethics.Â” But it doesnÂ’t follow that Â“Aristotle wrote the Nichomachean EthicsÂ” would have undergone some change in its semantic meaning. Changes in what we believe affect what we infer from statements; but they donÂ’t categorically change the meanings of those statements. CRS entails that every inference is an analytic inference. Once itÂ’s learned that Aristotle wrote plays, it becomes, according to CRS, constitutive of the meaning of Â“Aristotle wrote the Nichomachean EthicsÂ” that one can infer from it that a playwright wrote the Nichomachean Ethics. But surely the inference from Â“Aristotle wrote the Nichomachean EthicsÂ” to Â“a playwright wrote the Nichomachean EthicsÂ” isnÂ’t analytic.[150] 

What we may infer from a sentence is answerable to its existing meaning. CRS says that a sentenceÂ’s meaning is answerable to what we infer from it. If correct, that would have the consequence that one couldnÂ’t possibly draw a false inference from any sentence. This in its turn would have the consequence that no sentence would mean anything. Which, since nothing meaningless is a sentence, would have the absurd consequence that there neither are, nor could be, sentences. 
Consider the sentence Â“Bill plagiarized his first novel.Â” If one knows that sentence to be true, one can make inferences about BillÂ’s character, his past activities, his ambitions, his values, and so on, that one couldnÂ’t make if, other things being equal, one didnÂ’t know that sentence to be true. But itÂ’s only because of what the sentence already means that one can make those inferences. Given any other sentence, the same thing mutatis mutandis is true of it. CRS says that what a sentence means is determined by what we infer from it. Since itÂ’s the other way around, as weÂ’ve just seen, CRS is false. 
6.0 What is literal meaning? 
Where complex expressions are concerned, there is no limit to how much literal and understood meaning may diverge from each other. But where simple expressions are concerned, literal and understood meaning must coalesce. It makes no sense to suppose that people could be systematically wrong as to what Â“redÂ” meant. If people thought that Â“redÂ” meant what is in fact meant by Â“blue,Â” then Â“redÂ” would have that meaning. Systematic, widespread error is impossible where semantically simple expressions are concerned. This gives us a way of understanding what literal meaning is. 
Even though there can be widespread, systematic misinterpretations of sentences, those misinterpretations do not arise as a result of people failing to know what the simple parts of sentences mean. They arise as a result of people not knowing how to put those meanings together. So to the extent that its meaning is fixed by the fact that it has the form Â‹...Socrates...Â›, people (English speakers) do systematically understand Â“Socrates was more wise than Plato, but he was less sharp then AristotleÂ”; and to the extent that its meaning was determined by its having the form Â‹...wise...Â›, people do understand that sentence; and so on. So far as that sentence is systematically misunderstood, it is because people are having trouble putting the meanings of its constituents togetherÂ—it is because theyÂ’re having trouble figuring out how those meanings ought to be put together. 
What a simple expression literally means is determined by what it is that a sentence means by virtue of containing it. Since, where simple expressions are concerned, what people take literal meaning to be coincides with what it really is, a simple expressionÂ’s literal meaning coincides with what it is that, in virtue of containing that expression, sentences are taken to mean. So a simple expressionÂ’s literal meaning is given by a statement saying what it is that, by virtue of containing it, sentences are taken to mean; and a complex expressionÂ’s literal meaning is a function, in the mathematical sense, of the meanings of its parts. 
HereÂ’s an illustration. Â“SocratesÂ” is a simple expression. So what people think it means must ultimately coincide with what it actually means. So it refers to Socrates only because people think it refers to Socrates and, therefore, only because people think that Â“Socrates is intelligentÂ” attributes intelligence to Socrates and, in general, that Â‹...Socrates...Â› attributes...x...to Socrates. 
Of course, people donÂ’t always take utterances of Â‹...Socrates... Â› to be attempts to say that Socrates has...x... It might be clear from the speakerÂ’s tone that what he really meant when in saying Â“Socrates was wiseÂ” was that Socrates was not wise. But to the extent that their belief that Â“SocratesÂ” refers to Socrates is determinative of what people take the meanings of utterances of the form Â‹...Socrates...Â› to be saying, what they take it to be saying is that Socrates has...x... That is what it is for them to take Â“SocratesÂ” to refer to Socrates. And their taking Â“SocratesÂ” to refer to Socrates is for Â“SocratesÂ” to refer to Socrates, given that Â“Socrates,Â” being a simple expression, has the semantics that people think it has. The same thing mutatis mutandis is true of every other simple expression. 
Bearing these points in mind, let CE be any complex expression, and let e1...en be the simple expressions composing it. How people interpret CE may diverge from its literal meaning. But when this happens, itÂ’s because what it is taken to mean diverges from what people are disposed to take it to mean, given what people believe its simple parts to literally mean. 
Since what people take simple expressions to mean is what they mean, this is the same as saying the following. A divergence between: 
(i) 
A sentenceÂ’s literal meaning, 

(ii) 
That sentenceÂ’s understood meaning, 

(a) 
That sentenceÂ’s literal meaning, 


and: 
is the same thing as a divergence between: 
and: 
(b) What it is that, given their (correct) beliefs as to what its simple parts literally mean, people are disposed to take that sentenceÂ’s literal meaning to be. 
The literal meaning of a complex expression is a function of two things: 
(i) the meanings of its simple parts, and (ii) the order in which those parts are arranged. To say what literal meaning is in general, we need to say what it is for a simple expression to have a given literal meaning. Given the points just made, we can do this. Where simple expressions are concerned, literal and communicated meaning coincide (ultimately)Â—in other words, such expressions mean what people take them to mean. And where complex expressions are concerned, literal and communicated meaning may diverge, but literal meaning nonetheless coincides with what people are disposed to take it to mean, given what the simple components of the expression in question literally mean. 

7.0 Tokens vs. types: Some preliminary terminological points 
No word is identical with any utterance of it. My utterance of the word Â“snowÂ” lasts for a fraction of a second. But the word Â“snowÂ” itself endures. 
Utterances and inscriptions of expressions are referred to as Â“expressionÂ­tokensÂ” (or just Â“tokensÂ”). So there are three tokens of some one word to the right of the upcoming colon: snow, snow, snow. The things being uttered or inscribed are referred to as Â“expression-typesÂ” (or just Â“typesÂ”). 

7.1 Two-dimensional semantics[151] 

Some expressions appear to have a two-tiered semantic structure. For example, an occurrence of the pronoun Â“IÂ” has a referent, this being the person who uttered it, and it picks out that referent in a certain way (i.e., by way of a certain concept). 
Thus, the semantics of Â“IÂ” is given by the rule that an utterance of Â“IÂ” refers to a given person if and only if that person has the property of being the one that produced that utterance. 
So, if I say Â“I am tired,Â” the concept through which my utterance of Â“IÂ” refers to me is the concept person who produced the utterance in question. This, then, is the concept through which reference is secured; it is, as weÂ’ll henceforth put it, the mediating concept.[152] 
When Smith says Â“I am tired,Â” his utterance of Â“IÂ” refers to himself, not to me. But the mediating concept remains the same. 
If somebody points to me and says Â“that guy is tall,Â” the person picked out by Â“that guyÂ” is me. But in this case, the mediating-concept is different. The semantics rule for Â“that guyÂ” is given by the rule that, if Â“that guyÂ” is uttered in a context where there is a unique, salient guy, that utterance refers to that individual. 
Â“IÂ” and Â“that guyÂ” are context-sensitive expressions: What such an expression refers to depends in a systematic manner on facts about the context of utterance. (WeÂ’ll refine this vague statement shortly.) Such expressions are known as Â“indexicals.Â” Other examples of indexicals are Â“you,Â” Â“he,Â” Â“those animals,Â” Â“this monkey,Â” Â“tomorrow,Â” Â“yesterday.Â” Some indexicals are single words (e.g., Â“tomorrow,Â” Â“heÂ”); others consist of more than one (e.g., Â“that tall manÂ”). The latter are known as Â“complex 
indexicals.Â” 
7.1.1 Demonstratives vs. indexicals 
Some indexicals often cannot be successfully used without an accompanying demonstration on the speakerÂ’s part, the purpose of which is to eliminate any doubt as to what the intended referent is. If Jim and Larry are both equally salient in the context in question, an utterance of Â“that guyÂ” wonÂ’t single anyone out. But it will do so if an act of pointing accompanies it. Indexicals that fall into this category are known as Â“demonstratives.Â” Not all indexicals are demonstratives. For example, Â“tomorrow,Â” Â“now,Â” and Â“here,Â” arenÂ’t demonstratives. Given an utterance of Â“tomorrow,Â” no gesture is needed to make it clear what the intended referent is. If I say Â“tomorrow IÂ’m going hiking,Â” it is clear what the referent of Â“tomorrowÂ” is; no demonstrative act is necessary, and none could possibly do any good. 

7.1.2 Indexicals (continued) 
Indexicals have a Â“two-dimensionalÂ” semantic structure. Consider the expression Â“today.Â” If I say it right now, that utterance will refer to April, 27, 2009, since that is todayÂ’s date. If I say it tomorrow, that utterance will refer to April 28, 2009. But the rule that assigns April 27, 2009, to the first utterance is identical with the rule that assigns April 28, 2009, to the second utterance. That rule is this: if Â“todayÂ” is uttered on a given day D, that utterance refers to D. 
The meaning of an utterance Â“todayÂ” is the day it picks out. The meaning of the corresponding word-type is the rule just described. Given any indexical, the meaning of a token of that indexical is its referent; the meaning of the corresponding indexical-type is the rule that assigns that referent to that token. 


7.2 Definite descriptions 
If our pretheoretic intuitions are correct, definite descriptions are devices of reference.[153] 
ItÂ’s very hard to believe that Â“the whole number that comes right after oneÂ” doesnÂ’t refer to the number two. In this section we will operate on the assumption that, indeed, definite descriptions are devices of reference. (Later, in Section 9.0, weÂ’ll see good reasons to reject this way of understanding definite descriptions. But, for now, weÂ’ll operate on the plausible and, by the laity, universally held believe that they are what they are appear to be----that Â“the number twoÂ” refers to 2, that Â“the inventor of bifocalsÂ” refers to Benjamin Franklin.) [154] 

Definite descriptions, like indexicals, have a two-dimensional semantic structure. A given utterance of Â“the current U.S. PresidentÂ” refers to some individual. Right now such an utterance would refer to Barack Obama. A few years ago, such an utterance referred to Bill Clinton. 
But even though an utterance in 2009 of Â“the U.S. PresidentÂ” doesnÂ’t have the same referent as an utterance in 1999 of that same expression, both utterances are assigned their respective referents by the same semantic rule. The circumstances have changedÂ—hence the change in referentÂ—but the semantic rule has stayed the same. 
That rule is: if, at time t, x uniquely has the property of being a U.S. president, then an utterance at t of Â“the U.S. PresidentÂ” refers to x. 
7.2.1 Incomplete definite descriptions 
Some definite descriptions appear to be Â“incompleteÂ”Â—that is, they fail to pick out a single object. So, for example, Â“the bald guyÂ” could pick out any one of many different people. But, like all expressions, definite descriptions are not used in a vacuum; and the context usually supplies the information needed to enrich the mediating concept enough to enable it to single out a single person. So if you and I are in a room and I say Â“the bald guy is wealthy,Â” itÂ’s clear that, so far as I am making a determinate statement, what I mean is that the contextually salient bald guy is wealthy. 
If phi is a property that obviously has no more than one instance (e.g., the property of being the whole number successor of one or of being the U.S. President), phiÂ’s sole instance is contextually salient by default. 


7.3 The expressive limitations of indexical-free languages 
Indexical-free languages are expressively impoverished; much of what there is to say canÂ’t be said in them. The reason is that much information is perspectival, and nothing perspectival can be stated in a language that doesnÂ’t contain indexicals. 
Suppose that I spoke a language that didnÂ’t contain any indexicals, but was otherwise just like English. In order to express what I believe concerning the weather in my area, I couldnÂ’t say Â“it is now 60Â°.Â” IÂ’d have to say Â“it is 60Â° in Richmond on Feb. 07, 2009.Â” (And the Â“isÂ” couldnÂ’t be taken as the present tense of the verb Â“to be,Â” since, thus interpreted, it would be an indexical that picked out the time of utterance. The Â“isÂ” would have to be stripped of any temporal meaning and, thus, be downgraded to an empty grammatical place-holder, like the Â“itÂ” in Â“itÂ’s raining.Â”) But that utterance wouldnÂ’t necessarily express the belief I wanted to express. My believing that it is 60Â° in Richmond on Feb. 07, 2009, is different from my believing that it is now 60Â° here, even though I am in fact in Richmond at the time in question. I could have the one thought and not have the other. I could, after all, not know that I was in Richmond. And my believing either of those things is different from my thinking it is now 60Â° here. One could have any given one of those beliefs without having any of the others. Further, one could rationally have any given one of those beliefs without having any of the others. A person who is in Richmond at the time in question can rationally believe that it is now 60Â° here while believing it false that it is 60Â° in Richmond on Feb. 07, 2009. For the data at oneÂ’s disposal may warrant the first judgment, but not the second. 
So perspectival beliefs cannot be expressed without using an indexical. By a "perspictival" belief, I mean one whose truth depends, not only on the characteristics of the objects spoken about, but also on what coordinates those objects have relative to the speaker's framework. So an example of such a thought would be the one I express when, while pointing at some man in a van: 
(a) "Ever since I moved here, that guy has been stalking me, even though now it is clear to me how to deal with the situation, even though yesterday it was not." 
Supposing that Smith is the man in the van and that I utter those words on June 11, 1999, in Los Angeles, the belief expressed by: 
(b) "Ever since Kuczynski moved to Los Angeles, California, Smith has been stalking Kuczynski for two years; but on June 11, 1999, Kuczynski knows how to deal with that situation, even though he didn't know how to deal with it on June 10." 
The belief expressed by an utterance of (b) is true so the objects referred to have the properties attributed to them. But even if those very objects had those properties, an utterance of (a) might be wrong: for the speaker might be pointing at Jones, not Smith, and he might be in Richmond, Virginia, not Los Angeles, California, and so on. So, for the belief expressed by an utterance of 
(a) to be correct, it is necessary, not only that the objects referred to have the properties attributed to them, but also that those objects occupy certain positions within a frame of reference whose center is speaker himself. A language in which perspectival thoughts couldn't be expressed would have no practical value. For the individual's needs are, almost by definition, to be understood in terms of a frame of reference of which he is center. It might be thought that such a language could potentially have great theoretical value. But depending on how this thesis is interpreted, it's either false or trivial. The truths that a theoretician (operating in his capacity as a theoretician) aspires to identify are indeed non-perspectival, and such truths are expressed by sentences constructed out of expressions (e.g. "Alpha Centauri", "kiwi", "Earth", "electron") whose occurrences are not to be understood in terms of this or that person's frame of reference and are instead to be understood impersonally. But there is no way to endow such terms with meaning except through the use of terms (e.g. "here", "there", "now") whose occurrences must be understood in terms of specific frames of reference. Sentences like "this is planet Earth", "that is Alpha Centauri", "the animal we are now observing is a kiwi" are needed to give meanings to the terms "Earth", "kiwi", and "Alpha Centauri." Of course, such terms can, and usually are, defined by describing, as opposed to directly indicating, their referents. One can define "Alpha Centauri" by describing it as "the star nearest the Earth, apart from the Sun", and one define "Venus" as "the planet closet to the Sun, after Mercury." But such descriptive definitions would be impossible were it not for non-descriptive, purely demonstrative definitions, such as "this planet is the Earth" and "that thing is the Sun." 
Of course, one could imagine a language L that contained no perspectival terms (or "indexicals" as they're typically called) and whose expressions in terms of perspectival terms belonging to some other language L*. But this only proves our points, since it is only thanks to perspectival sentences belonging to some language other than L that L even exists to give those who speak it the means to state impersonal truths. So the relevant body of semantic rules, and thus, in effect, the relevant language, consists of those belonging to L as well as those belonging to L*. 
Also, theoretical truths are learned on the basis of the information embodied in one's sense-perceptions and post-perceptual beliefs; and that information is necessarily perspectival. So L would be completely useless except as a way of stating discoveries already made. The sentence-utterances involved in the process of making such a discovery would have to belong to a language, such as L*, that contained indexicals. Thus, the limitations of indexical-free languages are consequences of fundamental epistemological truths; and the study of indexicals needn't be the sterile, zero-sum enterprise that many investigations in semantics are generally believed to be.[155] 


7.4 Tokens, types, and context-sensitivity 
No sentence-type containing a context-sensitive component is either true or false; for no such sentence-type says anything. It is tokens of Â“I am now tiredÂ” that make statements; the corresponding sentence-type does not do so. What a token of Â“I am tired nowÂ” affirms depends on facts about the context of utterance. If SmithÂ’s the one whoÂ’s speaking, and itÂ’s 3:00 P.M., such an utterance is true just in case Smith is tired at 3:00 P.M. If Jones is the speaker and itÂ’s 4:00 P.M., such an utterance is true just in case Jones is tired at 4:00 
P.M. Thus the semantic rule that assigns a proposition to such a token does so on the basis of the facts about the context of utterance. And the rule in question is clearly this: Â“If, at time t, person p tokens the sentence-type Â“I am tired,Â” then the proposition thereby affirmed is true exactly if p is tired at t.Â” The same thing mutatis mutandis is true of all context-sensitive expressions. So the rule that assigns a proposition to an utterance of Â“that man is married to that womanÂ” is: if, in the context of utterance, x is a uniquely salient man and y is a uniquely salient woman, a token of the sentence-type Â“that man is married to that womanÂ” affirms a proposition that is true if and only if x is married to y. 
So context-sensitive sentence-types arenÂ’t true or false; they donÂ’t, in and of themselves, bear propositions. But they have an important semantic role: the identity of the proposition meant by a token of such a type depends on the identity of the type. A token of Â“I am tiredÂ” means one thing; a token of Â“you are tired,Â” uttered by the same person at the same time, means something else; and that difference obviously stems from the fact that, because different sentence-types were tokened, the semantic rule that assigns a proposition to the one token is different from the rule that assigns a proposition to the other. 
This can all be distilled into the following principle: where context-sensitive sentences are concerned, the meaning of a token is a proposition, and the meaning of type is a rule that assigns a proposition to one of its tokens on the basis of facts about the context in which that token occurred. 
Long story short: the meanings of sentence-tokens are propositions and the meanings of sentence-types are rules that assign propositions to their tokens, usually on the basis of facts about the context of tokening. 

7.5 Ambiguity and context-sensitivity (revisited) and the type/token distinction (revisited) 
Consider the sentence-type Â“that person is a professor.Â” Is that sentence true or false? No. Some tokens of it are true and some are false. This is because what a given token of that sentence says is a function of the circumstances. If I utter it while pointing at Bob, IÂ’m attributing the property of being a professor to Bob. If I utter it while pointing to Sally, IÂ’m attributing that property to Sally, not Bob. So what it is that IÂ’m affirming in the one case is different from what it is that IÂ’m affirming in the other case. But that isnÂ’t because the sentence Â“that person is a professorÂ” is ambiguous. That sentence is not ambiguous: it has just one meaning. But that meaning is not a proposition; it isnÂ’t something that is true or false. That meaning is a rule. That rule in its turn assigns meanings to tokens of that sentence. Those meanings are true or false; those meanings are propositions. 
Remember that expression-types are what result when properties per se, as opposed to their instances, are assigned meanings. Of course, the rules that assign meanings to properties are semantic rules, since anything that assigns meaning to anything is ipso facto a semantic rule. So the sentence-type of which the following ink depositÂ—Â“that guy is a professorÂ”Â—is a token is what results when some semantic rule assigns a meaning to some property. Let R1 be the semantic rule in question. Let R2 be the meaning that R1 assigns to the just-mentioned property. R2 is itself a semantic rule. But, whereas R1 assigns a meaning (a rule) to some property, R2 assigns meanings to instances of that property. So R2 assigns meanings to particular instances of the morphology had by the following ink deposit (Â“that guy is a professorÂ”). The meanings that R2 assigns to those tokens are not themselves rules; they are propositionsÂ—they are things that are true or false. 
There are thus very different sorts of semantic rules. There are those that assign meanings to properties, and there are those that assign meanings to instances of those properties. The meaning that was assigned to the property we were just discussing is itself a semantic rule. As weÂ’ll now see, every meaning that is assigned to a property (as opposed to a property-instance) is itself a semantic rule. Consider the following ink deposit: Â“Barack Obama.Â” There is a semantic rule that assigns a meaning to the property of having a morphology similar to that ink deposit. The meaning assigned to that property is itself a semantic rule. That rule assigns a meaning to each instance of the property in question. It assigns Barack Obama, the person, to any such instance. Thus, any such instance is an expression that picks out Barack Obama. 
In the previous section, we said that semantic rule is something which assigns a meaning to a property. ThatÂ’s correct, but incomplete. The right definition is this: a semantic rule is something which assigns a rule to a property that in its turn assigns meanings to instances of that property. Let us now move onto slightly less abstruse material. 

7.6 Do any expressions have one-dimensional semantics? 
The question arises: What about sentence-types that donÂ’t contain context-sensitive components? Where they are concerned, does token-meaning coincide with type-meaning? 
First of all, in natural languages, there are no such sentence-types. Every sentence contains a tense-marker. And in virtue of containing a tense-marker, a sentence is such that the proposition expressed by any given one of its tokens is a function of (inter alia) when that token occurs. If you say Â“the 
U.S. economy is fairly stable,Â” whether you are speaking the truth or not depends on when you say it. 
There are some apparent counterexamples to this. For all intents and purposes, any two tokens of: 
(IA)[156] 
Â“The interior angles of a Euclidean triangle add up to 180Â°Â” 
express the same proposition. But, from a strictly semantic perspective, IA is context-sensitive, and non-simultaneous utterances of it donÂ’t encode the same proposition. If it were believed that mathematical reality were as volatile as the stock-market, we would without hesitation regard IA as being in the same category as patently context-sensitive sentences such as: 
(BH) [157] 
Â“BillÂ’s holdings add up to $180,000,000.Â” 
And weÂ’d have no more temptation to regard the tense-marker in IA as inert than weÂ’d have to regard its counterpart in BH as inert. What this shows is that, to the extent that the tense-marker in tokens of IA are doing nothing, itÂ’s only because, our beliefs about mathematics being what they are, we choose to see such utterances as expressing atemporal propositions. 
Nonetheless, many semanticists hold that at the level of literal meaning IA is context-insensitive. In other words, they hold that IA is what Quine (himself such a semanticist) refers to as an Â“eternal sentence.Â” (S is an eternal sentence if there is some one proposition P such that any two of SÂ’s tokens express P.) If only for argumentÂ’s sake, letÂ’s suppose that there are eternal sentences. 
ItÂ’s tempting to hold that an eternal sentenceÂ’s meaning is identical with those of its tokens. After all, the distinction between type-meaning and token-meaning seems quite hollow except where context-sensitive expressions are concerned. 
But this reasoning is spurious. The tense-marker on the occurrence of Â“addÂ” in (IA) has the same semantics that it does in BH, where the tense-marker is obviously doing real work. ThatÂ’s why utterances of BH are true on Monday (before the market crashed) and false on Wednesday (after the market crashed). Therefore, different tokens of BH express different propositions. Therefore, the meaning of BHÂ—the sentence-typeÂ—isnÂ’t some proposition, and is instead the rule: 
(BHSR) If t is a token of BH that is uttered at time T, t is true iff, at T, BillÂ’s various holdings add up to $180,000,000. 
But, of course, for any time t, the meaning of a token of BH that is produced at t is a proposition that is true just in case. 
(BHT) At t, BillÂ’s various holdings add up to $180,000,000. 
Given that the occurrence of Â“addÂ” in any given token of IA has the same literal meaning as its counterpart in any given token of BHT, it follows that, from a narrowly semantic perspective, IA is quite as context-sensitive as BHT. To be sure, there is obviously a sense in which IA is, whereas BHT is not, context-insensitive. But IAÂ’s context-insensitivity, we must conclude, is a thoroughly pragmatics-based affair. 
Obvious extensions of this reasoning show that all expression-types have rules that assign meanings (or referents) to their tokens and, therefore, where any expression is concerned, type-meaning diverges from token-meaning. The meaning of the expression-type Â“that manÂ” is: a token of Â“that man,Â” uttered in context C, refers to x if, in C, x is uniquely a salient man. If, in a given context, Smith is such a man, then a token in that context of Â“that manÂ” refers to Smith; if instead Jones is such a man, it refers to Jones; etc. The same is true of Â“the current President.Â” In one context (the year 1992), tokens of that expression refer to Bill Clinton; in a different context (the year 2009) it refers to Barack Obama. 
Some would be tempted to say that, because they have fixed referents, proper names (e.g., Â“Bill ClintonÂ”) donÂ’t have a two-dimensional semantic structure. This would be a mistake. Expression-tokens are physical entitiesÂ— bursts of noise, deposits of ink, etc. Expression-tokens are therefore perceptible entities and are thus capable of transmitting information. Expression-types, on the other hand, are abstract entities and are thus inherently unsuited to be vehicles of communication. Let us develop these points. 
Expression-types are properties. Why are they properties? Tokens of a type are instances of it. Anything of which there are instances is ipso facto a property. So expression-types, unlike expression-tokens, are properties and are therefore non-spatiotemporal entities. And, as we just noted, it makes no sense to suppose a non-spatiotemporal entity could mediate information or, therefore, could in any significant sense be a symbol. Also, given the profound metaphysical differences between tokens and types, it would be theoretical arbitrariness of the worst kind to suppose that types could discharge the same semantic functions as their tokens. We must therefore assume that, whereas tokens of Â“Bill ClintonÂ” refer to Bill Clinton, the corresponding type does not refer to Bill Clinton; and we must also assume that Â“Bill Clinton,Â” the expression-type, has for its meaning a (constant) function that assigns Bill Clinton to any given one of its tokens. In general, proper names, no less than indexicals and definite descriptions, have two-dimensional semantics. 
The semantic rule corresponding to a proper name is a constant function, whereas the semantic rule corresponding to an indexical or definite description is not a constant function. All utterances of Â“Bill ClintonÂ” refer to Bill Clinton, but not every utterance of Â“the current U.S. President,Â” or of Â“that guy over there,Â” so refer. This has encouraged the erroneous view that Â“Bill ClintonÂ” itself, the expression-type, refers to Bill Clinton.[158] 


7.7 Ambiguity and context-sensitivity (re-revisited) and the type-token distinction (re-revisited) 
Remember that expression-types are what result when properties per se, as opposed to their instances, are assigned meanings. Of course, the rules that assign meanings to properties are semantic rules, since anything that assigns meaning to anything is ipso facto a semantic rule. So the sentence-type of which the following ink depositÂ—Â“that guy is a professorÂ”Â—is a token is what results when some semantic rule assigns a meaning to some property.
