Let R1 be the semantic rule in question. Let R2 be the meaning that R1 assigns to the just mentioned property. R2 is itself a semantic rule. But, whereas R1 assigns a meaning (a rule) to some property, R2 assigns meanings to instances of that property. So R2 assigns meanings to particular instances of the morphology had by the ink deposit (Â“that guy is a professorÂ”). The meanings that R2 assigns to those tokens are not themselves rules; they are propositions Â—they are things that are true or false. 
There are thus very different sorts of semantic rules. There are those that assign meanings to properties, and there are those that assign meanings to instances of those properties. Consider the following ink deposit: Â“Barack Obama.Â” There is a semantic rule that assigns a meaning to the property of having a morphology similar to that ink deposit. Let PBO be that property. The meaning assigned to PBO is itself a semantic rule. In other words, the meaning of PBO is given by the statement that: 
B1: Any given token of PBO refers to Barack Obama. 
Given some specific token t of Â“Barack Obama,Â” the semantic rule for t is: 
B2: t refers to Barack Obama. 
B1 and B2 are very different rules. Unlike B2, B1 doesnÂ’t say anything about any specific token of Â“Barack ObamaÂ” or any other expression. The need for a two-dimensionalist approach to semantics is embedded in the very concept of what an expression is. 
8.0 Logical form[159] 

Some statements that, given their grammatical forms, appear to be about objects are in fact about properties. We saw this in Chapter 1, and weÂ’ll see it again in Chapter 7 when we discuss FregeÂ’s ground-breaking insights into arithmetical statements (e.g., Â“2 + 3 = 5Â”). Frege was the first to see clearly that logical and grammatical form may divergeÂ—he was the first to grasp the very idea of such a divergence. This insight of his is embodied in his statement that the sentence: 
(WM) Â“Whales are mammals,Â” 
is not about whales. As paradoxical as it may seem, he was right. WM says that if an object is a whale, then itÂ’s a mammal. But there is no specific object x such that WM says that x is a mammal. A fortiori there is no specific whale x such that WM says that x is a mammal; and for any number n, no matter how high, there are no whales x1....xn such that WM says that xi (1 = i = n) is 
a whale. So just as Frege said, WM isnÂ’t about whales. 
WM makes a statement, not about whales, but about the property of being a whale. It says that: 
(WM*) the property of being a whale has the property of being instantiated only by mammals. 
WM* perspicuously represents WMÂ’s meaning. In other words, WM* represents WMÂ’s logical form. WM*Â’s grammatical form diverges from WMÂ’s grammatical form. (For a statement to be Â“perspicuousÂ” is for it to be clear in a logical, as opposed to a psychological, sense. The statement Â“if n is the number of Americans, and m is the number of cars collectively owned by American citizens, then n/m=2.2Â” makes it clear what is meant by Â“the average American citizen owns 2.2 carsÂ” and is thus a perspicuous affirmation of the proposition meant by the latter. But the latter is probably psychologically easier to absorb than the former.)_ 
The reason that WMÂ’s logical and grammatical forms pull apart is that WM contains a quantifier. (Examples of quantifiers are Â“all birds,Â” Â“no man,Â” Â“most whales,Â” Â“three birds,Â” and Â“some individuals.Â” WeÂ’ll define the term Â“quantifierÂ” in a moment.) Given any statement of English, (or any other non-artificial language) that contains quantifiers, the logical and grammatical forms of that sentence diverge. A quantifier is an expression having the property that, if a sentence contains it, that sentence is ipso facto to the effect that the extension of one property has a certain degree of overlap, ranging anywhere from no overlap to total overlap, with the extension of some other property. Â“All birds have beaksÂ” says that the extension of the property of being a bird is a subset of the extension of the property of having a beak. Â“Only birds have beaksÂ” says (falsely) that the extension of the property of having a beak is a subset of the extension of the property of being a bird. 
In virtue of containing a quantifier, a sentence is about properties, not specific objects. Of course, a quantified (quantifier-containing) statement can also be about individuals. But it isnÂ’t in virtue of containing a quantifier that a sentence concerns individuals; and it is in virtue of containing a quantifier that a sentence concerns properties. 
In natural language, quantified sentences are pseudo-objectual statements. They appear to be about objects, but are really about properties. That is why they must be reparsed if their logical forms are to be exposed. It immediately follows that a statementÂ’s grammatical form may diverge from its logical form. Frege discovered both facts and, therewith, created modern analytic philosophy. 

8.1 Contextual definition 
The fact that grammatical and logical form sometimes diverge is related to the fact that some expressions are to be defined contextually. To define an expression contextually is to show how, in virtue of containing it, a sentenceÂ’s meaning is affected. So, for example, Â“someoneÂ” doesnÂ’t refer to anyone. It doesnÂ’t refer to John or Sally or Jane. That is why, given any proper name N, the statement: 
(NS) Â‹N doesnÂ’t snore Â›, 
is compatible with:[160] 

(SS) Â“Someone snores.Â” 
Thus, the meaning of Â“someoneÂ” isnÂ’t given by some rule that pairs it off with this or that individual. In other words, there is no individual N such that the semantic rule for Â“someoneÂ” is: 
(WRS)[161] 
Â‹Someone has psiÂ› is true just in case N has psi. 
Rather, the meaning of Â“someoneÂ” is given by the statement that: 
(RS) Â‹Someone has psiÂ› is true just in case the property of being a psi is instantiated.[162] 

Thus, the logical form SS is clearly displayed by the sentence: 
(PS)[163] 
Â“The property of being a snorer is instantiated.Â” 
PSÂ’s logical form therefore coincides with its grammatical form. Since SS has a different grammatical form from PS, it follows that SSÂ’s logical form diverges from its grammatical form. The divergence between SSÂ’s grammatical and logical forms is obviously a consequence of the fact that Â“someoneÂ” must be defined contextually. 

8.2 Contextual definition: Its scope and limits 
Nonetheless, it would be an overstatement to say that whenever a sentence contains an expression that must be defined contextually, its grammatical form pulls apart from its logical form. As weÂ’re about to see, every expression is to be defined contextually. Obviously grammatical form doesnÂ’t always pull apart from logical form. Therefore, it isnÂ’t always the case that, in virtue of containing an expression that must be defined contextually, a sentenceÂ’s logical and grammatical forms diverge. 
How can it be said that all definitions are contextual definitions? ArenÂ’t there also denotative definitions? (A denotative definition of an expression E says what E means by saying what it denotes.) IsnÂ’t Â“SocratesÂ” defined denotatively? Yes, it is. There is some object x such that one says what Â“SocratesÂ” means if, and only if, one says that Â“SocratesÂ“ refers to x. 
But in saying of some object x that Â“SocratesÂ” picks out x, one is saying that, in virtue of having the form Â‹Socrates has psiÂ›, a sentence S is to the effect that x has psi. Â“SocratesÂ” refers to Socrates because, the remaining semantic rules of English being what they are, if you wish to attribute the property of being wise to Socrates, you can do so by saying Â“Socrates is wiseÂ”Â—because, in general, for any property psi, if you wish to attribute psi to Socrates you can do so by saying Â‹Socrates has psi.Â› If, in saying Â“Socrates was wise,Â” you were really saying that it was Aristotle, not Socrates, who was wise, then Â“SocratesÂ” wouldnÂ’t refer to Socrates, at least not in that context. In general, to say that E refers to O is to make a statement about effects that containing E has on a given sentenceÂ’s truth-conditions. More precisely, it is to say that, in virtue of having the form Â‹E has psiÂ›, a sentence attributes psi to O, for any property psi. 
To put this last point another way: it is say that, in virtue of having the form Â‹Â…EÂ…Â›, a sentence attributesÂ…xÂ…to E, whereÂ…x...may be any property. So Â“PlatoÂ” refers to Plato because Â“Aristotle admired PlatoÂ” attributes to Plato the property of being a thing x such that Aristotle admired 
x. If Â“Aristotle admired PlatoÂ” attributed the property of being hated by Mussolini to Gordon Brown, then, supposing the remaining semantic rules of English not to have been changed, Â“PlatoÂ” would (at least in that context) refer to Gordon Brown and Â“AristotleÂ” would (same qualification) refer to Mussolini. But the logical forms of sentences of the form Â‹E has psiÂ› donÂ’t necessarily pull apart from their grammatical forms. Since there is some object x (namely, Socrates) such that Â“Socrates is tallÂ” says that x is tall, and since Â‹x is tallÂ› has the same form as Â“Socrates is tall,Â” the fact that Â“SocratesÂ” is to be defined contextually does not entail that logical and grammatical form ever diverge. 
So it is only because certain expressions are to be defined contextually that such divergences occur. But which expressions? Those that cannot also be defined denotatively. Whenever an expression can be defined denotatively, a sentenceÂ’s logical form will not, by virtue of that sentenceÂ’s containing that expression, diverge from its grammatical form. (But, of course, that sentenceÂ’s logical form may diverge from its grammatical form for some other reason. Thus, the logical form of Â“Socrates saw someoneÂ” diverges from its grammatical form; but the reason for this is that it contains the word Â“someone.Â” The occurrence of Â“SocratesÂ” in that sentence isnÂ’t what induces that divergence.) 
Let E be an arbitrary expression that can be defined denotatively. In other words, suppose there to be some object x such that E is defined by saying that it refers to x. The logical form of Â‹E has psiÂ› is: x has psi. In general, to the extent that the logical form of a sentence containing E is determined by its containing that expression, that sentenceÂ’s logical and grammatical forms coincide. But, since such a sentenceÂ’s logical form isnÂ’t determined only by its containing E, and is also a function of the semantics of the other expressions occurring in it, its grammatical form may still diverge from its logical form. After all such a sentence may contain an occurrence of Â“someoneÂ” or Â“nobodyÂ” or some other expression that induces such a divergence. 

8.3 Scope, propositional attitudes, and the de dicto/de re distinction. 
A propositional attitude is an attitude towards a proposition. My wish that Smith would leave is an attitude (one of desire) towards a proposition (that Smith soon goes away). The sentence: 
(1) Â“John hopes that the current U.S. President will fix the economy,Â” 
ascribes a certain propositional attitude to John. The attitude: hope. The proposition: that the current U.S. President will fix the economy. So (1) can be thought of as having subject-predicate form, with Â“John hopesÂ” being the predicate (the expression that denotes the property being attributed to the subject) and the underlined expression being the subject. 
Â“Know,Â” Â“believe,Â” Â“hope,Â” Â“doubt,Â” Â“suspect,Â” Â“want,Â” and Â“wonderÂ” are examples of verbs that denote propositional attitudes. There are many other such verbs. Any verb whose complement (i.e., whose grammatical object) is an expression denoting a proposition falls into this category. 
It should be pointed out that, in the sentence: 
(2) Â“John wants to punch Smith,Â” 
the grammatical complement of Â“wantsÂ” is, despite appearances, an expression denoting a proposition. For (2) is a truncated form of the sentence: 
(2*) Â“John wants it to be the case that he punch Smith.Â” 
Oftentimes the sentential complements of verbs denoting propositional attitudes are compressed into expressions that very much do not appear to denote propositions. For example, in the sentence: 
(3) Â“John wants a boat,Â” 
the underlined part is an abbreviation of an expression denoting a proposition; for (3) is an abbreviated way of saying: 
(4) Â“John wants it to be the case that he has a boat.Â” 

8.3.1 The concept of scope 
In: 
(1) Â“John hopes that the current U.S. President will fix the economy,Â” 
the underlined expression falls within the scope of the expression Â“John hopes.Â” All this means is that, in (1), the property expressed by Â“John hopesÂ” is being attributed to the proposition denoted by the underlined expression. 
(1) says that a certain proposition, viz., the current U.S. President will fix the economy, has a certain property, viz., that of being such that John wants it to be true. 
In general, the scope of an expression E, occurring in a sentence S, is the largest expression E* such that, in S, the property expressed by E is being attributed to the proposition denoted by E*. 
If an expression E falls within the scope of an expression E*, E is sometimes said to Â“governÂ” E* In the sentence: 
(5) Â“It is possible that Jim has three cars,Â” 
the underlined expression falls within the scope of Â“it is possible that.Â” 
Â“It is possibleÂ” doesnÂ’t denote a propositional attitude. Thus, an expression may fall within the scope of an expression that doesnÂ’t denote a propositional attitude. 

8.3.2 De dicto vs. de re 
(1) is ambiguous. A story will make this clear. John lives next to the current (2010) President of the United States, namely Barack Obama. But John doesnÂ’t know that Barack Obama is the current President. John mistakenly thinks that Barack Obama is in charge of the Federal Reserve, and John hopes that he will fix the currently moribund U.S. economy. At the same time, John believes, for some strange reason, that the American system of government makes it impossible for a president to have any effect on the 
U.S. economy, and he therefore hasnÂ’t the faintest hope that an economic turnaround would have anything to do with the activities of anyone occupying the office of Commander in Chief. 
So there is some specific individual x such that, although John doesnÂ’t know it, x is the current President and such that (1) is true if it is taken as a way of saying that John hopes that x will fix the economy. But (1) is false if it is taken to mean that John hopes that an instance of the concept current U.S. President will fix the economy. 
Thus, (1) is true when read de re and false when read de dicto. De re means Â“about the individual,Â” and de dicto means about the concept. (1) is false if taken to concern JohnÂ’s attitude towards the concept current U.S. President, but itÂ’s correct if taken to concern the individual who happens to instantiate that concept. 
8.4 FregeÂ’s generalization of the concept of a function[164] 

As weÂ’ll see in Chapter 7, what made it possible for Frege to revolutionize logic was his insight that grammatical and logical form diverge; and what made the latter insight possible was his generalization of the concept of a mathematical function. 
A mathematical function is a rule that assigns no more than one object to each object falling in a given class. (So Â“+1Â” can be thought of as expressing a function or rule that assigns 2 to 1, 3 to 2, etc.) 
According to Frege, the occurrence of Â“snoresÂ” in: 
(PS) Â“Plato snores,Â” 
is best represented as the open sentence Â‹x snoresÂ›; and that open sentence 
is best thought of as expressing a function that assigns the truth-value true to each snorer and the truth-value false to each thing that doesnÂ’t snore. (For brevityÂ’s sake, IÂ’ll henceforth use the words Â“truthÂ” and Â“falsehoodÂ” instead of, respectively, Â“the truth-value trueÂ” and Â“the truth-value false.Â”) 
HereÂ’s the idea. A true sentence results if the variable in Â‹x is evenÂ› is replaced with an expression denoting an even number and false if itÂ’s replaced with a number that doesnÂ’t denote such a number. (Â“2 is evenÂ” is true and Â“3 is evenÂ” is false.) So we can think of Â‹x is evenÂ› as assigning truth to two, four, etc., and falsity to one, three, etc. For similar reasons, we can see Â‹x snoresÂ› as assigning truth to snorer Bob and falsehood to non-snorer Wilma, and so on. 
Frege sees the occurrence of Â“is taller thanÂ” in: 
(BTM) Â“Bill is taller than Mary,Â” 
as being identical with the open sentence Â‹x is taller than yÂ›, and he sees that open sentence as expressing a function that assigns truth-values to ordered pairs of objects. So Â‹x is taller than yÂ› assigns truth to the ordered pair <x, y> if x is taller than y and otherwise assigns falsehood to that pair. 
Frege treats: 
(BJMP) Â“Bill is standing between Mary and John,Â” 
as comprising the open-sentence Â‹x is standing between y and zÂ›; and he sees that open sentence as expressing a function that assigns truth to ordered triples of objectsÂ—as assigning that truth value to <Bill, Mary, John> just in case Bill is standing between Mary and John. 
In this way, Frege was able to assign a single form to all atomic sentences. An atomic sentence is one that, unlike Â“Bill is tall and Sally is smart,Â” doesnÂ’t consist of other sentences and that, unlike Â“someone snores,Â” doesnÂ’t contain quantifiers. Non-atomic sentences are molecular. A molecular sentence is one that either consists of other sentences or contains a quantifier. Frege was able to show that, ultimately, all atomic sentences have the form Â‹O has psi. Â› Contrary to first appearances, BTM has the form: the ordered pair <Bill, Mary> has psi, where psi is the property had by such a pair just in case its first member is taller than its second. 
Pre-Fregean logicians saw each of PS, BTM, and BJMP as having a different form from each of the other two, and this made it impossible for them to do anything meaningful in the way of formalizing inferences involving atomic sentences. But Frege didnÂ’t have this problem, since he, unlike them, wasnÂ’t made blind by grammatical surface structure to the underlying structural similarities. 
Chapter 4 What Are Propositions? 
1.0 The purpose of this chapter 
In this chapter, weÂ’ll provide abbreviated answers to the questions Â“what are propositions?Â” and Â“what is it for propositions to be true?Â”[165] 
HereÂ’s what weÂ’ll see. Propositions are sets of properties; and a proposition is true just in case the properties that are members of it are instantiated --so what it is for a proposition to be true is for the members of the set with which it is identical to be jointly instantiated. Roughly, truth is instantiatedness. Less roughly, truth is identical with the property of being a set (of a certain kind) all of whose members are instantiated. Aside from a few brief remarks, I will leave it open whether all sets of properties qualify as propositions (hence the parenthetical hedge in the last sentence). But a case will be made that only sets of properties are propositions. 
1.0 The Argument 
Consider the proposition: 
1. Tommy is smoking. 
Intuitively, this proposition seems to consist of at least three components: first, Tommy (or, in any case, something individuative of Tommy, that is, a property P such that anything having P is ipso facto identical with Tommy and Tommy alone; second, the property of smoking; and, third, some kind of Â“synthesisÂ” of the two Â– some complex constituent that involves TommyÂ’s smoking. (We will try to state precisely what this synthesis involves.) 
If 1 is true, then: 
A. The property of being identical with Tommy, 
is instantiated, and so is: 
B. The property of smoking. 
But, of course, those two properties could be instantiated in a world where Tommy is not smoking Â– in a world where, for example, Larry is smoking and a non-smoking Tommy is playing golf. We thus need a third property Â– a property such that, if a set S contains that property along with A and B, then 1 will be true just in case all of SÂ’s members are instantiated. That third property is not hard to identify. It is: 
C. The property of being identical with something that is smoking and is identical with Tommy. 
Before moving on, letÂ’s look at the apparatus that weÂ’ve been developing. Once again, let S be a set that contains all and only A, B, and C[166]; and remember that we have identified S with 1 (the proposition that Tommy is smoking). 
First of all, if C is instantiated, so are B and A. Further, if C, and therefore B and A, are instantiated, then, and only then, is 1 true. It follows that 1 is true if, and only if, each of A, B, and C is instantiated. This is consistent with, and even corroborates, the thesis that 1 is S that and that 1Â’s being true is SÂ’s membersÂ’ being jointly instantiated. 
Of course, that does not by itself show that 1 can be identified with S or that 1Â’s being true can be identified with SÂ’s membersÂ’ being jointly instantiated. After all, there are infinitely many distinct sets of properties such that 1 is true just in case their members are instantiated. For example, let Z be the set containing the following properties and nothing besides: the property of being identical with a smoking Tommy; the property of being an even number; the property of being three sided if a triangle. The second two properties are instantiated in every possible world, given that even numbers necessarily exist and given that triangles cannot fail to have three sides. But surely Z cannot be identified with 1, the reason being that ZÂ’s membership cannot, at least not in a sufficiently natural manner, be aligned with what we know about 1Â’s constituency. 
But SÂ’s membership does so align, as a brief look back makes clear. SÂ’s members are (or at least include) A, B, and C. 1Â’s constituents are (or at least include): 
(i) 
Something individuative of Tommy, 

(ii) 
The property of smoking, and 


(iii) Something that combines those two things. 
Obviously A is individuative of Tommy. (Only Tommy can have that property; and, what is more, he must have it.) So far, so good. (ii) and B are identical. So far, still so good. 
What about C? That property is instantiated exactly if A and B are both instantiated. So, in a very clear sense of the term Â‘combine,Â’ that property combines the property of smoking with (something individuative of) Tommy. (In the relevant sense of the term Â‘combine,Â’ one property Â‘combinesÂ’ n other properties exactly if the first is instantiated exactly if the other n properties are jointly instantiated.) And we know that, in some way or other, 1 combines (something individuative of) Tommy with the property of smoking. In at least one respect, then, CÂ’s relationship to A and B is suggestively similar to 1Â’s relationship to its parts. Moreover, C Â‘dominatesÂ’ each of A and B in a way suggestively similar to the way in which 1 dominates its constituents. AÂ’s being instantiated is necessary but not sufficient for CÂ’s being instantiated, the same being true of BÂ’s being instantiated. TommyÂ’s existing is necessary but not sufficient for 1Â’s being true, the same being true of somebodyÂ’s being a smoker. 
While none of this demonstrates definitively that 1 is identical with S or that 1Â’s being true is identical with SÂ’s being instantiated, we have, I believe, found enough of a match between 1/1Â’s being true and S/SÂ’s membersÂ’ being instantiated to warrant looking into the idea that they might be one and the same. 
3.0 The unity of the proposition 
How does 1 combine Tommy with the property of smoking? According to Frege, Tommy (or some concept thereof) saturates that property (or some concept thereof). (Henceforth, IÂ’ll omit the qualification Â‘or some concept thereof.Â’) But this doesnÂ’t help at all. For, as Davidson (1967) observed, the term Â“saturateÂ” is just another label for the operation in question. So while the Fregean statement: 
(FR) Â“1 is the result of TommyÂ’s saturating the concept of smoking,Â” 
may well be correct, we donÂ’t know what it means. 
We are in a position to give the meaning of FR and to say what this mysterious Â‘saturatingÂ’ amounts to. WeÂ’ve argued that 1 is a set whose members include the property of being Tommy, the property of smoking, and the property of being a smoking Tommy. 1 is the result of TommyÂ’s Â‘saturatingÂ’ the property/concept of smoking in the sense that 1 is identical with a set S that consists of those three properties. 
For any proposition X, to say that X is the result of YÂ’s Â‘saturatingÂ’ Z (for some Y and Z) is to say that X is a set whose members are the property of being identical with X, and Z itself, and also the property of being identical with something that is identical with X and also has Z. 
4.0 More on the decomposition of propositions 
It is indisputable that 1 is true just in case C is instantiated. So why not just identify 1 with C, and 1Â’s being true with CÂ’s being instantiated? Why go through the rigmarole that we went through? Why bother with A and B and, in general, any other properties other than C? Because if we identify 1 with C, and 1Â’s being true with CÂ’s being instantiated, our theory wonÂ’t accommodate the very reasonable presumption that 1 has discrete parts corresponding to Tommy and to the property of smoking. 
Consider an instance of the property of being a smoking Tommy. Obviously that instance will involve Tommy smoking. But it will not, at least in any obvious way, contain a discrete part corresponding to Tommy or a discrete part corresponding to smoking. And what is true of an instance of that property is, quite possibly, true of the property itself. It cannot be taken for granted that C has a discrete part corresponding to Tommy or to smoking or to anything else. In fact, being a non-spatiotemporal entity, C wonÂ’t have discrete parts in any straightforward sense at all. 
The impression that C is part-less, or at least lacking in the right kind of parts, is reinforced when we look at what an instance of C is like. Such an instance is, to adapt Kenneth TaylorÂ’s (1998) apt expression, a dent or ripple in the quantum; it is a shift in the movement of mass-energy. Of course, that mass-energy is (by hypothesis) sufficient for the existence of Tommy and of smoking and, indeed, of a smoking Tommy. But you would have a devil of a time isolating some part of that distribution that corresponded to Tommy, then distinguishing that from some other part corresponding to smoking, and then finding a third that fused those two, otherwise discrete, entities into a discrete instance of a smoking Tommy. 
By contrast, the proposition: 
1. Tommy is smoking, 
is, of its very nature, neatly parsed into Tommy, the property of smoking, and a third constituent that synthesizes the two just mentioned. The neat articulations found in 1 are found, in some form, in S. Those articulations, though found in SÂ’s membership as a whole, are not found in C taken by itself, making S, but not C, a suitable mirror for the decompositional structure of 1. 
States of affairs (or "facts," as they are sometimes called) do not, as Ian Hacking (1975) long ago put it, have the same kinds of Â“articulationsÂ” as propositions. The quantum-ripples on which the truth of a proposition supervenes donÂ’t have anything like the structure of that proposition. Whereas the proposition Tommy is smoking clearly has a unique, and relatively simple decomposition into Tommy (or some property/concept individuative thereof), the property of smoking, etc., the state of affairs in which TommyÂ’s smoking consists Â– the confluence of psychological, physiological, and, ultimately, sub-atomic disturbances Â– obviously doesnÂ’t uniquely decompose into Tommy and the property of smoking. In fact, it seems a stretch to suppose that it even has one such decomposition. 
4.1 A corollary 
Consider the proposition: 
2. Tommy is snoring. 
Let D be the property of being a snoring Tommy. It is obvious that: 
1. Tommy is smoking, 
and: 
2. Tommy is snoring, 
have much in common. They have in common the constituent Tommy (or, in any case, something corresponding thereto). They have in common the functions (or, if you prefer, properties) the property of being Tommy who is doing something and the property of being a something that is doing something. 
In light of this, consider some instance of D. In other words, consider the kind of property-instance, the kind of mass-energy distribution, on which the truth of 2 supervenes. That instance will, of course, suffice for the existence of Tommy, as will an instance of C. But will those instances, in virtue of that fact, have some discrete part in common? Unlikely. In neither case do we have Tommy simpliciter. We have Tommy smoking (while sweating profusely and worrying about his algebra test and his nascent nicotine addiction, all the while talking with his cousin Albert); in the other we have Tommy snoring (while having terrible dreams about his future as a second string pitcher on a mediocre team). There is no such thing, in either case, as Tommy simpliciter. There is only Tommy doing this or that, having this or that property. A corollary is that two situations that comprise Tommy do not, in virtue of that fact, have in common some discrete, isolable entity. So while it is true that C and D both comprise Tommy, the one does not, in comprising him, have a discrete constituent in common with the other. 
But now we must consider what weÂ’ve said about the composition of 1 and also what follows about 2, by obvious extensions of what weÂ’ve said about 1.1 is a set S whose members are: 
a: the property of being Tommy 
b: the property of smoking 
C: the property of being a smoking Tommy 
By similar reasoning, 2 is a set S* whose members are: 
a: the property of being Tommy, b*: the property of snoring, and 
D: the property of being a snoring Tommy. 
S and S* do have well-defined, discrete parts in common. Indeed, they have in common precisely what is had in common by: 
1. Tommy is smoking, 
and: 
2. Tommy is snoring. 
If we were to be really precise about it, weÂ’d say that each of S and S* comprised, not only a-c, but also: 
d. the property of being a Tommy that does something (i.e., the property being a Tommy that does something or, in any case, has some property), 
and also: 
e. the property of being a something that does something (i.e., the property being a something that does something or, in any case, has some property). 
LetÂ’s look at 1 for a second. It immediately and formally implies: 
i Tommy smokes; ii something smokes; 
iii Tommy does something; iv Tommy exists; v something does something. 
And 2 immediately implies: 
i* Tommy snores; ii* something snores; iii Tommy does something; iv Tommy exists; v something does something. 
Now letÂ’s look at S and at S*. The members of S are: 
I The property of being Tommy. II The property of snoring. III The property of being a Tommy that snores. IV The property of being a Tommy that does something. V The property of being a something that does something. 
The members of S* are: 
I The property of being Tommy. II* The property of smoking. III* The property of being a Tommy that smokes. IV The property of being a Tommy that does something. V The property of being a something that does something. 
Having identified 1 with S and 2 with S*, everything we know about those propositions Â– about what they entail, about what their components are, and about how their higher-level components are Â“forgedÂ” out of their lower level components Â– is accounted for. 
5.0 Another desideratum satisfied by our analysis 
Many semanticists today hold that Plato and Socrates are veritable objects are constituents of propositions that concern them. So according to Kaplan (1989), who is following and agreeing with Russell (1903), Tommy Â– the person, not some Fregean concept thereof Â– is a constituent of both 1 and 2. Other adherents of this view are Scott Soames (2003), Nathan Salmon (2005), and Robert Moore (1995). (Opponents are J. Searle (1983), M. Dummett (1973), and Â– with some very heavy reservations to be stated later Â– the present author.) 
There is a rather serious problem with this view. Consider, not 1 or 2, but rather: 
3. Plato snores. 
At this point in time, Plato doesnÂ’t exist. So if heÂ’s a (necessary) constituent of 3 Â– if, in other words, 3 exists only if Plato does --then 3 doesnÂ’t exist. Salmon and Soames, both of them hard-line direct reference-theorists, deal with this by taking a desperate measure, viz., by saying that 3 exists and that its existence constitutively depends on PlatoÂ’s existence and that these two positions can be reconciled with each other ---that, more specifically, they can be reconciled by saying that 3 exists, albeit as a nonÂ­existent proposition. 
This is not necessary or plausible or helpful. 3 exists. Plato does not. But the property of being identical with Plato, whatever it is, does exist. What is it to be Plato? To be Plato is, perhaps, to be a causal sequence that is initiated by the fertilizing of a certain egg by a certain spermatozoa. To be Plato is, perhaps, to have a soul or mind of a certain kind. What we know is that, if something is Plato, itÂ’s being Plato supervenes on something probably having to do with the mass-energy distribution in the cosmos Â– on its mode of origination, on the quotient of spiritual energy in the particle-interactions that constitute it, on who knows what. In any case, even though Plato does not exist, the property of being identical with Plato does. ThatÂ’s why I can meaningfully, not to mention correctly, say Â“I am not PlatoÂ” or, equivalently, Â“I donÂ’t have the property of being identical with Plato.Â” And itÂ’s also why we can meaningfully, and presumably correctly, say that Plato does not exist. For, in making such a statement, we arenÂ’t picking out a non-object---which would, having been picked out, ipso facto cease to be a non-object Â– and then saying of it that it doesnÂ’t exist. We are saying of an existing property, that of being identical with Plato, that it is uninstantiated. 
But our analysis is still consistent with the heart of direct-reference-theory, this being the idea that, for some x such that x is identical with Plato, the proposition meant by Â“Plato snoresÂ” is true just in case x snores, it being completely irrelevant what properties (other than being a snorer) x has. (The Fregean indirect-referentialist holds that for Â“Plato snoresÂ” to be correct it is necessary that, for example, a unique great philosopher to write The Parmenides snore.) It is clear why our analysis is consistent on this matter with the viewpoint of the direct referentialist. According to our analysis, 3 is true exactly if the following properties are instantiated: 
a. 
The property of being identical with Plato. 

b. 
The property of snoring. 

c. 
The property of being a Plato who snores. 

d. 
The property of being something that snores. 


e. The property of being something that does something (or has some property). 
It is readily seen that, on our analysis, there is some x, such that x is Plato and such that 3 is true exactly if x snores, it being irrelevant what other properties x has. This is exactly what the direct-referentialist holds. At the same time, our analysis guarantees the existence of the proposition that Plato snores --after all, the property of being Plato exists, even though it is now uninstantiated. So our analysis of Plato snores gives the direct-referenceÂ­theorist the truth-conditions that she wants and that (given certain compelling arguments due to Kripke, 1980; and Soames, 2003, 2004) she probably deserves. At the same time, our analysis doesnÂ’t put the direct-referenceÂ­theorist in the awkward, logic-bending position of having to say that the proposition that Plato snores exists despite the failure of existence of entities on whose existence its own existence is constitutively dependent. 
Chapter 5 Definite Dscriptions and the Nture of Rference 
1.0 An old puzzle 
Benjamin Franklin (BF) invented bifocals and he was also the first postmaster general. The semantic rules of English being what they are, it follows that: 
(CB) "The inventor of bifocals is identical with the first postmaster general," 
is correct and also that: 
(TB) "The inventor of bifocals is identical with the inventor of bifocals," 
is correct. 
But whereas TB is trivial, CB is non-trivial.[167] 

The non-triviality of CB is hard to explain if definite descriptions are supposed to be referring terms. As we saw in Section 1.2, the semantic rules of English being what they are, Â“the inventor of bifocalsÂ” refers to BF exactly if Â‹the inventor of bifocals has phiÂ› attributes phi to BF. So supposing that Â“the inventor of bifocalsÂ” does in fact refer to BF, it follows that CB attributes the property of being identical with the first postmaster general to BF. And supposing that Â“the first postmaster generalÂ” refers to BF, it follows that CB attributes the property of being identical with the inventor of bifocals to BF. And given both suppositions, it follows that CB says of BF that it has the property of being identical with BF. Which is trivial. 
Right now we'll consider Russell's solution to this problem, and we'll then consider Frege's solution. We're considering Russell's solution first because Frege's solution is more easily understood in terms of Russell's than vice versa. 
2.0 Russell's solution: The Theory of Descriptions 
According to Russell's Theory of Descriptions (TD) Â‹the inventor of bifocals has phiÂ› says that something uniquely invented bifocals and, moreover, that any such thing has phi. And, according to TD, Â‹ the first postmaster general has phiÂ› says that something was a unique first postmaster general and, moreover, that any such thing has phi. It follows that, if TD is right, CB says the same thing as: 
(CB3) "Something uniquely invented bifocals, and any such thing is a unique first postmaster general; and something was a unique first postmaster general, and any such thing is a unique inventor of bifocals.Â” 
It is readily seen that CB3 is more succinctly expressed as follows (the Â“RÂ” stands for Â“RussellÂ”): 
(CBR) "There is some one thing that uniquely invented bifocals and was also a unique first postmaster general.Â” 
To sum up, if TD is right, then CB means the same thing as CBR. It is easily verified that, indeed, CB is true exactly if CBR is true. TD thus seems to get the right result. (Why Â“seemsÂ”? See Section 11.1) Given that CBR is non-trivialÂ—given that historical knowledge is needed to know itÂ—TD readily explains why CB is non-trivial. 
3.0 An aside concerning the difference sentence-type logic and sentence-token logic 
On a first reading, go directly to Section 4.0; skip this section. 
Why do I say that TD "seems" to get the right result, and not that it does get the right result? CB is a sentence. Given only that CB is equivalent with CBR, it doesn't follow that the proposition meant by the one is equivalent with the proposition meant by the other. Strawson (1950) made this clear. (Strawson's insight was popularized by Kaplan (1989). Suppose for argument's sake that the semantic rule for "that person over there is" is: if, in a context C, somebody O is uniquely a salient person, then an utterance in C of Â‹that person over there is has phiÂ› has for its meaning some proposition equivalent (if not identical) with O has phi; and if, in C, there is no uniquely salient person, then such an utterance is neither true nor false (the reason being that the demonstrative doesn't have a referent). But, given that same supposition, the sentence Â‹that person over there is has phiÂ› would be true exactly if, in the relevant context, somebody x were uniquely a contextually salient person and, moreover, any such person had phi. 
Thus, given only that Russell's theory correctly models the logic of CB and other sentences containing definite descriptions, it doesn't follow that it correctly identifies the propositions meant by such sentences. My own view is that, indeed, TD is false. But I also believe, partly for the reasons given here, that Frege's view is false. My alternative to their analysis is put forth in my (2007) book Conceptual Atomism and the Computational Theory of mind. 
4.0 Frege's solution 
Here is FregeÂ’s solution to this problem[168][H6] 
: 
(FR)[169] 
Â“The inventor of bifocalsÂ” is a referring term. In other words, it picks something out. (Not all expressions do so. 
[170])That expression refers to a given thing if and only if that thing has the property of being a unique bifocal-inventor. If a given thing didnÂ’t invent bifocals then Â“the inventors of bifocalsÂ” doesnÂ’t refer to it. If lots of different individuals invented bifocals, then Â“the inventors of bifocalsÂ” doesnÂ’t refer to anything. (If 10 people collectively wrote War and Peace, it would be wrong to speak of the author of that book.) And if a given thing did uniquely invent bifocals, then Â“the inventors of bifocalsÂ” does refer to it. 
So there are two dimensions to the semantics of Â“the inventors of bifocals.Â” There is what it refers to: this is the referent of Â“the inventors of bifocals.Â” (Sometimes Â“referenceÂ” is used instead of Â“referent.Â”) And thereÂ’s the property that a thing must have to be its referent; this property is the sense of that expression. The referent is BF, and the sense is the property of being a unique bifocal inventor. 
Analogues of these points hold with respect to Â“the first postmaster general.Â” There is its referent (which is BF); and there is its sense (which is the property of being a unique first postmaster general). 
The reason that TB is non-trivial is that, although the definite descriptions in it have the same referent, they have different senses. A comparison may help. Imagine that youÂ’re looking at a certain person in the distance. That person is in fact Ralph, but you donÂ’t know it, because heÂ’s so far away and also, let us suppose, because he is (for reasons that arenÂ’t important) wearing a suit of armor. You see that he is doing jumping jacks. Later Ralph is standing right in front of you and, of course, you see him. HeÂ’s wearing a plaid shirt. Once again, heÂ’s doing jumping jacks. 
The first visual perception has the same object as the 
second. And each of those perceptions says of that object that he or she is doing jumping jacks. But those two perceptions pick out that object in different ways. In the first case, that object is presented to you as something that has one set of properties (itÂ’s far away, it's wearing a suit of armor, etc.); in the other case itÂ’s presented as having a different set of properties (itÂ’s nearby, it's wearing a plaid shirt, etc.). And thatÂ’s why, even though those perceptions have the same object, and even though both attribute the property of doing jumping jacks to that object, those perceptions tell you different things. 
Something similar holds of Â“the inventors of bifocalsÂ” and Â“the first postmaster general.Â” They have the same object (referent); but they pick that thing out through different bodies of information. ThatÂ’s why Â‹the inventors of bifocals has phiÂ› and Â‹the first postmaster general has phiÂ› tell you different things, even though they attribute the same property (phi) to the same object (BF).[171] 

4.1 Evaluating Frege's solution 
This all seems not only plausible, but practically self-evident. But, so far as what Frege says doesn't coincide with TD, what Frege is saying is false and, indeed, incoherent. 
LetÂ’s consider the two sense perceptions discussed in FR. The one perception tells you that there is something in the distance, that it's wearing a suit of armor, etc., and that, moreover, that thing is doing jumping jacks. So the sense in which Ralph is the object of that perception is that your perception describes Ralph. Your perception says: Â“something or other is over there, in the distance, wearing a suit of armor, (etc.).Â” Who (or what) fits that description? In other words, who has the relevant properties? Ralph. So Ralph is the object of that perception in the sense it describes him. 
The information borne by that perception has the form Â“something has such and such properties (itÂ’s wearing a suit of armor etc.), and any such thing is doing jumping jacks.Â” Thus, the content of that perception is given by an existence-claim (a claim of the form Â“something has phiÂ”). Ralph uniquely satisfies that existence-claim. (In other words, he and he alone has the relevant property.) And it is in virtue of his doing so that he is the object of the perception in question. 
The same thing mutatis mutandis is true of your second perception. The information borne by that perception is along the lines of Â“something has thus and such properties (itÂ’s standing nearby, is wearing a plaid shirt etc.), and any such thing is doing jumping jacks.Â” Ralph is the object of that perception by virtue of the fact that he and he alone has the relevant propertiesÂ—that he and he alone is a thing standing in the relevant place while wearing a plaid shirt, etc. 
In general, when a given thing x is picked out by way of descriptive information, whatÂ’s really going on is that some statement of the form Â“something has such and such propertiesÂ” is being affirmed (not necessarily verbally), and x is what fits the description. 
If we bear this point in mind, we find that, so far as it isnÂ’t totally incoherent, FregeÂ’s analysis collapses into RussellÂ’s. Consider the sentence: 
(IB)[172] 
Â“the inventor of bifocals is tall.Â” 
By FregeÂ’s own admission, Â“the inventors of bifocalsÂ” picks a given thing 
out if and only if that thing fits the relevant description (i.e., if and only if that thing is a unique inventor of bifocals). And if there is a unique inventor of bifocals, that thing, whatever it is, is the thing to which Â“the inventors of bifocalsÂ” refers. So supposing that there is such a thing and that x is it, IB describes x as being tall. 
It goes without saying that, if there is no unique inventor of bifocals, then there is no way that IB can be true. Frege himself emphasizes this last point. (And heÂ’s right to do so. ThereÂ’s no way that Â“the elephant in the corner is eating peanutsÂ” can be true, if thereÂ’s no elephant in the corner.) 
The upshot is that IB is true if and only if: 
(IB*) there is a unique inventor of bifocals and, moreover, that thing, whatever it is, is tall. 
But what does TD say about IB? According to TD, the meaning of IB is: something uniquely invented bifocals, and any such thing is tall. Which is precisely what FB says. So FregeÂ’s theory collapses into RussellÂ’s. 
By obvious extensions of this, it follows that, if FregeÂ’s theory is right, then CBÂ’s meaning is identical with that of CBR. So FregeÂ’s theory accounts for the non-triviality of CB in the same way as RussellÂ’s theory (as TD). 
4.2 Evaluating Frege's solution (continued) 
For argument's sake, suppose that the prettiest living woman is identical with the most evil living person. Given only that: 
(1) Â“Smith wants to marry the prettiest woman on the planet,Â” 
is true, it doesn't follow that: 
(2) Â“Smith wants to marry the most evil person on the planet,Â” 
is true. But why not? Because what (1) really says is that: 
(1*) Smith wants it to be the case that Smith is married to a woman who is prettier than anyone else, 
and what (2) really says is that: 
(2*) Smith wants it to be the case that Smith is married to somebody who is more evil than anyone else. 
Thus, if (1) is correct, Smith wants a certain proposition to hold, namely, that Smith is (or will be) married to a woman who is prettier than anyone else. And if (2) is correct, Smith wants some other proposition to hold, namely, that Smith is married to somebody who is more evil than anyone else. Since those two propositions are different, the fact that one of them has the property of being desired to be true by Smith, whereas the other lacks that property, does not constitute a violation of LeibnizÂ’s Law (if x=y, x has a given property iff y has that property). And the Â“substitution-failureÂ” whereby a truth (namely, (1)), is turned into a falsity (namely, (2)), corresponds to the innocuous fact that, whereas the grammatical complement in each of (1) and (2) of Â“marryÂ” is a singular term, the grammatical complement is an expression denoting a proposition (as opposed to a person). The occurrence in (1) of Â“the prettiest womanÂ” is an orthographic expedient Â—an orthographic stand-in for a more perspicuous but (for that very reason) unwieldy expression. And surely we shouldnÂ’t let orthographic expedients dictate our semantic beliefs. (Frege himself would be the first to admit this.) 
Few authors, if any, deny that apparent exceptions to Leibniz's Law are to be solved in this way. So given that, according to TD, the meanings[173] 
of (1) and (2) are given by (1*) and (2*), and given that, nuances aside, there's no other way to deal with the datum that (1) and (2) can simultaneously be true, it's odd that authors have continued to countenance Frege's system. 





4.3 Special compositionality in relation to Frege's theory 
There are other, related problems with that system. According to the principle of special compositionality (SC), what a referring term picks out is a function of what its parts pick out.[174] 
Bearing this in mind, let's suppose, as before, that the prettiest woman in existence is also the most evil person in existence. And let's also suppose, with Frege, that definite descriptions are referring terms. Given these suppositions, it would seem to follow that the underlined part of: 
(3) Smith believes that the prettiest woman in existence is identical with the prettiest woman in existence, 
refers to the same proposition as: 
(4) Smith believes that the prettiest woman in existence is identical with the most evil person in existence. 
But the underlined part of (3) very much seems not to co-refer with the corresponding part of (4)[175], that being why, even if the prettiest woman in existence is the most evil person in existence, (3) and (4) can differ in truth-value. 
There are only three ways to go here. (i) Deny SC. (ii) Deny that the underlined parts of 3 and 4 refer to different propositions. (iii) Deny that 4 is what results when a referring term in 1 is replaced with a co-referring term. 
Understandably, Frege rejects each of (i) and (ii) and thus accepts (iii). (To this extent, his semantics coincides with Russell's, give or take some technicalities relating to the fact that, according to TD, each of 3 and 4 is syntactically ambiguous.) Frege thus says that the definite descriptions occurring in 3 and 4 refer, not to some person, but rather to their "customary senses." What he means is that, in each of 3 and 4, "the prettiest woman in existence" refers, not to Sally or Betty or Ethel, but rather to the property (or concept) of being a woman who is prettier than every other (or some such[176]); and in 4, "the most evil woman in existence" refers to the property (concept) of being a person who is more evil than any other. 
An immediate consequence of FregeÂ’s theory is that the word Â“snowÂ” has three utterly distinct meanings in: 
(5) Â“Snow is white and Jerry believes that snow is white and Fred believes that Jerry believes that snow is white.Â” 
The first occurrence of Â“snowÂ” in (5) refers to snow. The second refers to the sense of the first occurrence. The third refers to the sense of the second occurrence. 
But surely all three occurrences of Â“snowÂ” in (5) mean the same thing. FregeÂ’s is clearly jumping through hoops to make his bankrupt theory work. 
Another immediate consequence of FregeÂ’s theory is that the word Â“snowÂ” doesnÂ’t refer to snow in: 
(6) It is true that snow is white. 
But thatÂ’s obviously false. (In any case, there's no independent support for this claim.) The occurrence of Â“snowÂ” in (6) clearly has the same meaning as its counterpart in Â“snow is white.Â” 
In any case, what does it even mean to say that, in (5), the third occurrence of Â“snowÂ” refers to the sense of the sense of Â“snowÂ”? If you say Â“Socrates was bald,Â” you are attributing baldness to SocratesÂ—not to Aristotle or Plato or anyone else who isnÂ’t Socrates. If you say Â“Socrates was intelligent,Â” you are attributing intelligence to Socrates and Socrates alone. Thus, Â“SocratesÂ” refers to Socrates because, the remaining semantic rules of English being what they are, Â‹Socrates has psiÂ› attributes psi to Socrates. By parity of reasoning, if the third occurrence of Â“snowÂ” in (5) really referred to a second-order sense, then it would make some statement about that senseÂ—it would attribute a property to it. But it doesnÂ’t. It doesnÂ’t say anything about such a sense. Whatever it is that it does in connection with such a sense, it isnÂ’t comparable to what Â“Socrates was intelligentÂ” does in connection with Socrates. 
Finally, to the extent that Frege's views concerning indirect reference are intelligible, they undermine his own semantics. According to Frege, the proposition meant by: 
(#) "The prettiest woman in existence is smart," 
is true just in case: 
(##) somebody who is smart is uniquely a woman who is prettier than any other. 
In general, the proposition meant by: 
(*) Â‹...the phi... Â›, 
is true just in case: 
(**) something x such that...x...uniquely has phi. 
Let "FR" (short for "Frege-Russell") be the principle ("hypothesis" might be a better word) that the meaning of (*) is given by some proposition that is equivalent (if not identical with) (**). It is to be emphasized that Russell and Frege both accept FR. 
Here's where they differ. According to Russell's system (TD), Â‹the phiÂ› is in the same category as "something," "everyone," etc. According to Frege's system, Â‹the phiÂ› is not in that category. 
Here's the problem. Let O be an occurrence of "the prettiest woman in existence" that falls within the scope of four epistemic (or modal) operators. So O might be the underlined expression in: 
(&) "Smith believes that Sally knows that Larry hopes that Mary is certain that the prettiest woman in existence is smart." 
A consequence of TD and of Frege's system is that the semantics of the occurrence in (&) "the prettiest woman in existence" is given by FR. But if Frege's system is correct, then that occurrence refers, not to Sally (who we'll assume is the prettiest woman in existence), but to the "customary sense" of the customary sense of the customary sense of the customary sense of the occurrence in (#) of "the prettiest woman.Â” (Let O# be the just-mentioned occurrence.) So, if Frege's system is right, then the semantics of each of O and O# is given by FR even though, whereas the one occurrence refers to Sally, the other refers to a fifth order property (or concept). Thus, a consequence of Frege's theory is that, in respect of their semantics, two expression-occurrences can be functioning in the very same way even though the one occurrence refers to an individual while the other refers to an nth order property (for any whole number n). So a consequence of Frege's system is that there can be reference-shifts where there haven't been semantic shifts. Which is obviously incompatible with the principle that, it is in virtue of how a given expression E affects the truth-conditions (or meaning) of sentences in 
which it occurs that E refers to this as opposed to that object.[177] 
We saw in Chapters 3 and 5, and will see in Chapter 6, we saw that for "Socrates" to refer Socrates is for Â‹....Socrates...Â› to be to the effect that ...Socrates...We saw that this condition's being satisfied is necessary and sufficient for that expression's referring to that individual. Thus, for a given expression to have a given referent is for it to have certain effects on the truth-conditions of the sentences in which it occurs. 
A corollary is that, where those changes haven't occurred, there hasn't been a shift in reference, a related corollary being that, where they have occurred, there has been such a shift. For any property phi, and for any whole number n, the semantics of an occurrence O^ that falls within the scope of n epistemic (or modal or otherwise intensional) operators of the phi is given by FR. Thus, so far as FregeÂ’s clearly contrived and ad hoc theory has any intelligible meaning, itÂ’s clearly false. 
Chapter 6 Slinging the Slingshot: How a famous argument of FregeÂ’s proves his conception of reference to be incoherent 
1.0 Is FregeÂ’s analysis of reference tenable? 
In this chapter weÂ’ll find that FregeÂ’s analysis of reference---which, on the face of it, is not only reasonable, but downright truistic---is indefensible. FregeÂ’s analysis has consequences too spurious for a reasonable person to accept (e.g., that nobody has thoughts about anything, that my typing this sentence is identical with your reading). But rather than rejecting FregeÂ’s analysis, philosophers chose to accept these consequences. Why did they do so? First, they couldnÂ’t come up with a viable alternative to FregeÂ’s analysis. Second, absurd though they are, these consequences supported positions that, independently of their views about semantics, these philosophers had made their lifeÂ’s work to develop and that desperately needed reinforcement. Third, FregeÂ’s analysis, preposterous though its consequences be, very much seems cogent. 
In this section, weÂ’ll identify the flaw in FregeÂ’s argument, thus stripping its credibility and preventing it from retarding philosophical progress any more than it already has. 
2.0 The Slingshot 
A "slingshot-style" argument is one to the effect that: 
(i) 
logically equivalent expressions canÂ’t have different referents, 

(ii) 
intersubstituting co-referring terms preserves truth-value, and 


(iii) given (i) and (ii), it follows that (iii) some class that would seem to comprise several objects (for example, the class of things that are referred to by true sentences) in fact only comprises one object (for example, the property of being true). 
In a moment we will present such an argument. That argument is based on the following four sentences : 
(1) Mozart was a composer. 
(2) 
The class of all things x such that Mozart was a composer and x is self-identical is identical with the class of all things x such that x is self-identical. 

(3) 
The class of all things x such that Bill Clinton was U.S. President in 1997 and x is self-identical is identical with the class of all things x such that x is self-identical. 


(4) Bill Clinton was U.S. President in 1997. 
Here is the argument (Â“SSÂ” is short for Â“slingshotÂ”) 
(SS[178]) (1) is logically equivalent with (2). Therefore, (1) and (2) must co-refer, supposing that either refers to anything. (It is being assumed, very reasonably, that logically equivalent expressions cannot have different referents.) 
(3) 
is what results when a referring term in (2) is replaced with a co-referring term.) (Â“The class of all things x such that Mozart was a composer and x is self-identicalÂ” refers to the class of all self-identical objects, and so too does Â“the class of all things x such that Bill Clinton was U.S. President in 1997 

and x is self-identical.Â”) Since intersubstituting co-referring terms preserves reference, it follows that (2) and (3) co-refer, supposing that either refers to anything. 

(3) 
is equivalent with (4). Therefore, (3) and (4) must co-refer, supposing that either refers to anything. Therefore, (1) and (4) must co-refer, supposing that they refer to anything. 


If the occurrences in (1)-(4) Â“Mozart was a composerÂ” and Â“Bill Clinton was U.S. President in 1997Â” are replaced with occurrences of any two true sentences, the argument that results is cogent. Thus, any two true sentences co-refer, supposing that any true sentence refers to anything. (For the same reason mutatis mutandis, any two false sentences co-refer, supposing that any false sentence refers to anything.) 
The property of being true is the one semantically significant thing that (1) and (4) have in common. So, supposing that sentences refer to anything, (1) and (4) must refer to the property of being true, and true sentences must in general be assumed to refer to the property of being true.[179] 

3.0 One problem with SS and with all other slingshot-style arguments 
Like all slingshot-style arguments, SS fails to establish its conclusion, the problem with it being that it embodies a spurious conception of reference--Â­one that, were it correct, would entail that reference was indistinguishable from quantification. 
Suppose for argumentÂ’s sake that Â“the class of all things x such that Mozart was a composer and x is self-identicalÂ” is functioning as a device of reference. In that case, itÂ’s picking out the class of self-identical objects, and what (2) is saying about that class is that itÂ’s identical with itself; in other words, (2), thus interpreted, says that: 
(2*) The class of self-identical objects is identical with the class of self-identical objects. 
But (2*) is not equivalent with (1). Therefore, if the definite descriptions in (1) and (2) are assumed to be referring termsÂ—which is precisely what they are being assumed to beÂ—(2) isnÂ’t equivalent with (1). For the same reason mutatis mutandis, (4) is not equivalent with (3) if Â“the class of all things x such that Bill Clinton was U.S. President in 1997 and x is self-identicalÂ” is taken to be a device of reference. 
In order for (2) to be equivalent with (1), the former must be taken to be to the effect that: 
(2#) There exists a class to which a thing belongs iff Mozart is a composer and that thing is self-identical; and there exists a class to which a thing belongs iff that thing is self-identical; and the first class is identical with the second class. 
But if (2) is interpreted in this way, the definite description occurring in it is a quantifier, not a referring term. And in that case (3) is not what results when a referring term is replaced with a co-referring term. (ItÂ’s what results when a non-referring term is replaced with a non-referring term.) 
So SS is a failure. 
Note: Some would disagree with our contention that, when read attributively, occurrences of definite descriptions are functioning as quantifiers not as referring terms. Some, in other words, hold that there is such a thing as "attributive" reference. This is the position of Frege and his followers (e.g., Church). In Section 7.0, we'll see why Frege's position is both indefensible and unnecessary. 
4.0 Is the conclusion of SS correct? Do true sentences refer to truth-values? 
In this section we'll see that, in respect of its semantic properties, Â“snow is whiteÂ” bears little resemblance to "the property of being true." And we'll see that, for this reason, it is implausible, if not incoherent, to hold that "snow is white" (or any other true sentence) co-refers with "the property of being true" (or "the True" or "the truth-value True"). 
LetÂ’s start with some platitudes about reference. To say that expression R refers to object O is to say that, for any property phi, Â‹R has phiÂ› attributes phi to O. If you want to say of Benjamin Franklin (BF) that heÂ’s bald, you can do so by saying Â“Benjamin Franklin is bald.Â” (Of course, BF is no longer with us. But to set aside some extremely intricate and, in this context, irrelevant issues relating to tense, let us pretend that Franklin is alive and that we can speak of him in the present tense.) And (the remaining semantic rules of English being what they are) if you couldnÂ’t attribute baldness to BF by uttering that sentence, then Â“Benjamin FranklinÂ” wouldnÂ’t refer to BF. If, in saying Â“Benjamin Franklin is bald,Â” one was attributing baldness to Aristotle, then, in that context at least, Â“Benjamin FranklinÂ” would refer to Aristotle. 
LetÂ’s generalize these points. For any property phi, Â“Benjamin FranklinÂ” refers to BF (and not to Aristotle, for example) because Â‹Benjamin Franklin has phiÂ› attributes phi to Benjamin Franklin; and if one couldnÂ’t attribute phi to Benjamin Franklin by saying Â‹Benjamin Franklin has phiÂ›, then Â“Benjamin FranklinÂ” would not refer to BF. Further, if, in uttering that sentence, one was attributing baldness to Aristotle (but not BF), then Â“Benjamin FranklinÂ” would refer to Aristotle (but not Benjamin Franklin). Thus, for Â“Benjamin FranklinÂ” to refer to BF it is both necessary and sufficient that Â‹Benjamin Franklin has phiÂ› attribute phi to BF. The fact that Â“Benjamin FranklinÂ” refers to BF is identical with the fact that Â‹Benjamin Franklin has phiÂ› attributes phi to Benjamin Franklin, for any property phi. 
In general, expression E refers to O if and only if, for any property phi, Â‹E has phiÂ› attributes phi to O. EÂ’s referring to O may be identified with EÂ’s being such that, in virtue of containing it, a sentence ipso facto attributes a property to O. 
Bearing these points in mind, let's revisit the question: Do sentences refer to truth-values? Does "snow is white" refer to the property of being true (which, in this context, we're assuming for argument's sake to be identical with the truth-value true)? No. In virtue of having the form, Â‹Â…the property of being trueÂ…Â›, a sentence is about the property of being true. (Â“Everything Bill says has the property of being trueÂ” says of the property of being true that it is instantiated by everything that Bill says.Â”) But it isn't the case that, in virtue of having the form Â‹Â…snow is whiteÂ…Â›, a sentence is about the property of being true. 
Of course, Â“if snow is white, then snow isnÂ’t greenÂ” can, like any other sentence, be interpreted as concerning the property of being trueÂ—it can be interpreted as saying that the property of being true is a characteristic of the proposition that snow isnÂ’t green if itÂ’s white. But given how artificial it is to paraphrase "if snow is white, then snow isn't green" in this way, it's clear that, in some respect that is deeply relevant to their semantics, "the property of being true" and "snow is white" aren't comparable. Which, in its turn, suggests that it isnÂ’t in virtue of its containing an occurrence of Â“snow is whiteÂ” that Â“if snow is white, then snow isnÂ’t greenÂ” concerns that property. 
But even if, in virtue of having the form Â‹Â…snow is whiteÂ…Â›, a sentence is about the property of being true, the way in which, in virtue of having that form, such a sentence concerns that property is obviously different from the way in which, in virtue of having the form Â‹Â…the property of being trueÂ…Â›, a sentence concerns the property of being true. A story may help make this clear. You are my philosophy professor and I am taking an exam that consists of just one question: I must identify at least one property that all propositions of the form x is even iff x is divisible by two have in common. I duly say (or write) "the property of being true." I pass. But I would have failed if I had instead said "snow is white" (or "grass is green"). In any case, you'd have no reason independently of Frege's argument for passing me. Which, taken together with the points made in the previous section, suggests that you'd have no reason at all for passing me. 
It's hard to find any reason, apart from Frege's argument to the contrary, to hold that "snow is white" refers to the property of being true. Which, given how far Frege's argument to the contrary falls short of being probative, suggests that "snow is white" does not so refer. 

4.1 Can sentences coherently be stipulated to have truth-values for their referents? 
Some (e.g., Church 1943) have stipulated that true (false) sentences refer to the property of being true (false). But some stipulations are incoherent, and this particular stipulation falls into that category. If I stipulate that "Gloxo" is to unambiguously refer to the number two, I cannot coherently stipulate that it is also to refer to the number of sides had by an arbitrary pentagon. 
Bearing this in mind, consider the following variant of the just-told story. You are my geography professor, and you've just given me a test containing just one question: identify the state that lies on the Northern border of California. Instead of saying "Oregon," which is the right answer, I say "snow is white." You duly fail me. 
Of course, if you and I had agreed that, by our stipulation, "snow is white" is to refer to Oregon, then "snow is white" would have been an acceptable answer. But to the extent that "snow is white" would, for that reason, have been an acceptable answer, it obviously wouldn't have been functioning in the same way as the homonymous sentence "snow is white." And it is thus incoherent to stipulate that "snow is white" is unambiguously both an English sentence (to the effect that a certain crystalline substance has a certain chromatic property) and is also an English expression that refers to the state of Oregon. For the same reason mutatis mutandis, it is incoherent to stipulate that the English sentence "snow is white" unambiguously refers to the property of being true. 

4.2 To what, if anything, do sentences refer? 
Given that "snow is white" doesn't refer to the property of being true, to what, if anything, does it refer? It seems to me that, if it refers to anything, that sentence refers to the proposition that snow is white. In virtue of having the form Â‹...snow is white... Â›, a sentence is ipso facto about the proposition that snow is white. Â“If snow is white, then snow isnÂ’t greenÂ” says that the proposition that snow is white entails (or otherwise has as a consequence) the proposition that snow isnÂ’t green. "It is not the case that snow is white" says that the proposition that snow is white has the property of being false. "Grass is green and snow is white" says that the proposition that snow is white has the property of being a thing x such that both x and the proposition that grass is green are true. So given the reasonable presumption that E refers O if, in virtue of having the form Â‹...E... Â›, a sentence is to the effect that...O..., it seems to follow that "snow is white" refers to the proposition that snow is white. 
And even if it doesn't follow, we'd be doing less damage to the concept of reference by saying that "snow is white" referred to the corresponding proposition than we would be if we said that it referred to its truth-value. 
A brief detour through the philosophy of science will clarify this last remark. It often happens that, in order for a discipline to move forward, the scope of a given term must be expanded. To be of use to science, terms such as "temperature" and "acid" must be given meanings that, although consistent with the pretheoretic judgments of laypersons, have a much wider sphere of application than do the concepts associated with those terms by the laity. By defining "temperature" as (I'm simplifying) "mean kinetic energy," the jurisdiction of the former term is increased even though its meaning is otherwise unchanged. Such redefinitions are sometimes referred to as precisifications or delineations. 
It's a distinct possibility that, in saying that sentences are referring terms, one is precisifying the term "reference," not identifying its existing meaning. Supposing this were true, it's still wrong (or, in any case, bad in some relevant way or other) to say that sentences refer to their truth-values, and it's less wrong to say that they refer to the propositions they express. In order to be a precisification of a given term T, as opposed to wholesale redefinition of it, an extension of T's jurisdiction must be consistent (for the most part) with T's existing meaning. (I say "for the most part" since pretheoretic judgments are sometimes revised in light of their own theoretical off-shoots. There are, or could be, objects x such that x is cold according to pretheoretic intuition even though, if temperature is identified with mean kinetic energy, x is extremely hot. ) What we know about the existing meaning of "refer" is that (the remaining semantic rules of English being what they are) it is in virtue of the fact that "Socrates" refers to Socrates that Â‹Socrates has phiÂ› attributes phi to Socrates; we also know (same qualification) that, if one couldn't attribute phi to Socrates by saying Â‹Socrates has phiÂ›, then "Socrates" would not refer to Socrates. In general, we know that to, the extent that, in virtue of having the form Â‹...E... Â›, a sentence is to the effect that...O..., then E refers to O and that E fails to refer to O to the extent that this condition isn't satisfied. Given this fact, it follows that we'd be horribly misprecisifying the term "reference" were we to say that sentences referred to their truth-values; it also follows that we would not be misprecisifying it as horribly were we to say that they referred to the propositions they meant. Give or take some niceties, if S is a sentence that has proposition P for its meaning, then, in virtue of having the form Â‹...S... Â›, a sentence S* is to the effect that...P...This suggests that, if sentences refer to anything, it is to the propositions they express and, moreover, that it is not to their truth-values. 
5.0 Davidson on facts 
Despite everything thus far said, Donald Davidson (1967) took it for granted that SS is cogent. And he argued that, given the (alleged) fact that SS is cogent, it follows that there is only one fact. His argument is simple. Put the expression Â“the fact thatÂ” in front of each of (1)-(4): an analogue of SS shows that the resulting expressions must co-refer. 
Instead of rejecting SS, Davidson concluded, absurdly, that these two facts are identical and that, by obvious extensions of this reasoning, there is, at most, only one fact. Having, in his mind, established that there is only one fact, he argued that, for this reason, mental states are not representations. Since there is only one fact, Davidson argued, no two mental states represent different facts. On this basis, Davidson concluded that differences between mental statesÂ—between, for example, my perception of the piano in my living room and your perception of the ink-marks in front of youÂ—are not representational differences. 
Why is this? Because, says Davidson, representations, supposing them to exist, are representations of facts; and, says Davidson, we've seen that there is only one fact. Therefore, Davidson says, my perception of the piano in my living room doesn't differ in respect of which fact it represents from your perception of the ink-marks in front of you. From this Davidson concludes (fallaciously, even relative to his own assumptions), that the one perception is representationally just like the other. Thus, the differences between those perceptions have nothing to do with any representational differences that there might be between them. This in its turn means that, if there are any such differences, they are innocuous: in other words, it is not in terms of those differences that the palpable differences between those perceptions are to be understood. This, in its turn, means either that: 
(i) Neither perception represents anything, 
or that: 
(ii) If either perception does represent something, it is irrelevant to how that perception differs from the other perception and, therefore, to what sort of thing that perception is. Which, give or take some unimportant nuances, means that 
neither represents anything. 

5.1 Evaluating Davidson's contention 
DavidsonÂ’s position is obviously false. The fact that I am typing this sentence is distinct from the fact that you are reading it. There is more than one fact. What could be more obvious? 
Of course, the word "fact" is a vague one; and, surely, it's at least partly for this reason that Davidson's position has been given any credence. In any case, there is no precisification of the term "fact" that validates Davidson's position. 
In some contexts, the word "fact" is synonymous with the word "truth." ("The fact that arithmetic is incomplete was unknown to Frege" is synonymous with "the truth that arithmetic is incomplete was unknown to Frege.") Since there are many truths, this interpretation of the word "fact" doesn't validate Davidson's view. 
In other contexts, the word "fact" seems to refer to (re)distributions of mass-energy---to the spatiotemporal conditions and changes in virtue of which certain propositions are true and others are false. Let M be the mass-energy (re)distribution in virtue of which the proposition x is now asleep (where x is any sleeping person) is true. Let N be the mass-energy distribution in virtue of which the Earth is now traveling at approximately 17,000 mph with respect to the Sun is true. M . N. That's just a fact. Pun intended. 
Are there other precisifications of the word fact? Probably. (For example, physical laws may qualify as "facts," at least on one interpretation of that word, even though it's not clear that physical laws are identical either with truths or with (re)distributions of mass-energy). But, apart from Davidson's argument to the contrary, there is no reason to expect any of the remaining precisifications to do a better job of validating Davidson's contention than those we've just considered. 

5.2 Evaluating Davidson's argument for his contention 
Davidson's argument fails for the same reason mutatis mutandis that SS fails. But DavidsonÂ’s argument involves a blunder of which SS is innocent. For a mental state to be representational is not for there to be some fact that it represents. It is for that mental state to be to the effect that there exists some fact. Suppose that I hallucinate that there is a pink elephant in my living room. (Assume that, in actuality, there is no such elephant.) My hallucination is representational. It isnÂ’t like a rock. But there is no elephant x such that my hallucination represents some pink elephant x such that x is in my living room. My hallucination is representational in the sense that it is to the effect that there exists some pink elephant x such that x is in my living room. For mental state M to be representational isn't (necessarily) for there to be some fact that M represents; it is (or can be) for M to be to the effect that there exists a fact having such and such characteristics. And the non-existence of such a fact is obviously compatible with the existence of erroneous propositional attitudes to the contrary. 
6.0 Neale on a variant of SS 
In his (ironically named) book Facing the Facts, Stephen Neale puts forth what he believes to be an improvement on SS.[182] 
NealeÂ’s argument involves the following four assumptions: 
G1: The sentence Â‹FaÂ› stands for the same fact as the sentence Â‹a = the unique thing x such that (x = a and Fx).Â› (In

2.

This result, if it is in fact true, is astonishing. But G2 allows us to go further. Let S and S* be any two distinct statements that are true. (So S and S* neednÂ’t have subject-predicate form.) According to G2, S can be put in subject-predicate form, and so can S*.
