And once that is granted, it follows, by the foregoing argument, that S and S* stand for the same fact. It follows that, given G1-G4, any two true sentences stand for

6.1 Evaluating NealeÂ’s argument 
The problems with this argument are very similar to the problems with DavidsonÂ’s. Consider line 4 of NealeÂ’s argument: 
4. Â‹a = the unique thing x such that (x = a and Fx).Â› 
If this sentence is read attributively (in other words, if the definite descriptions in them are treated as quantifiers, as opposed to referring terms), then it is logically equivalent with: 
1. Â‹FaÂ›, 
in which case those two sentences can therefore be seen as standing for the same fact. But if 4 is read referentially (in other words, if the definite descriptions in them are treated as referring terms, as opposed to quantifiers), then 4 stands for the same fact as:

in which case 1 and 4 cannot plausibly be seen as standing for the same fact. For exactly similar reasons, 5, 6, and 7 must be read attributively if there is to be any plausibility to the claim that they stand for the same facts as, respectively, 2, 3, and 4. In general, G1 is false if 4-7 are read referentially, 4Â­

7.0 A final note concerning SS 
SS assumes that: 
(i) Each of the two definite descriptions occurring in it is a singular term. 
SS makes the additional assumption that: 
(ii) Reference isnÂ’t changed by intersubstituting co-referring terms that have different senses. 
And, of course, SS assumes that: 
(iii) Referring terms can have both sense and reference (it assumes that the definite descriptions occurring in the second and third sentences have both sense and reference). 
(i) is innocuous. Even though, for reasons already discussed, some hold that definite descriptions are not singular terms, being instead quantifiers, we could obviously stipulate that the definite descriptions in SS are referring terms. We could stipulate that, for any property phi, and for any object O, Â‹the phiÂ› refers to O exactly if O uniquely has phi. 
But this wouldnÂ’t be enough to get SS to go through. For argumentÂ’s sake, suppose that Â‹the phiÂ› refers to O exactly if O uniquely has phi; and further suppose that, in virtue of having the form Â‹Â…the phiÂ…Â›, a sentence is true exactly ifÂ…OÂ…In that case, supposing that O were a unique phi, Â‹Plato thought highly of the phiÂ› would bear a proposition that was true exactly if Plato thought highly of O, it being entirely irrelevant what properties (other than being highly thought of by Plato) O had, and Â‹the phi was a great wrestlerÂ› would bear a proposition that was true exactly if O was a great wrestler, it being entirely irrelevant what properties (other than being a great wrestler) O had. 
Thus, supposing that Â‹...the phiÂ…Â› were defined in the way thus proposed, there is some x such that x = Socrates such that: 
(*) Â“Plato thought highly of the great philosopher who died 
of hemlock poisoning," 
would be true iff: 
(**) Plato thought highly of x. 
Thus, SS not only assumes that Â‹the phiÂ› is a singular term. It also assumes that, in virtue of having the form Â‹Â…the phiÂ…Â›, a sentence is true if and only if exactly one thing O has phi andÂ…xÂ… 
But even though each of those assumptions is perfectly defensible, they are incompatible with each other. Unfortunately, the essence of Frege's theory of reference is that both assumptions are correct. Thus, that theory is spurious, and so is SS, given that it relies, in a particularly brazen way, on both assumptions. Sadly, the obvious fact that sentences don't refer to truth-values wasn't taken to show that Frege's semantics was defective. Instead, it was assumed that Frege's semantics was non-defective that sentences therefore do refer to truth-values. For some reason, philosophers haven't been deterred by the fact that there is basis for this contention, apart from Frege's theory. This means that there's no basis for it at all, given that little credence should be given to a semantic theory according to which "snow" refers to an abstract object in "it is true that snow is white." But, in this case as in so many others, philosophers chose to hide their failure to see the obvious beneath a lot of gratuitous logic-chopping. 
Chapter 7 Some Puzzles Relating to Language and Logic 
1.0 Are there meaningless sentences? 
According to some, there are bona fide sentences that are meaningless. Among the various confusions underlying this totally erroneous position, three can be cleared up right away: 
(i) 
There are expression-like entities that, given their phonetic properties along with facts about the linguistic environments in which they occur, are easily mistaken for bona fideexpressions. Given what the words flanking it are and what it sounds like, the occurrence of Â“blerkoÂ” in Â“sometimes a blerko can be a manÂ’s best friendÂ” is likely to be mistaken for an actual word. But it has no meaning and is thus no word. 

In many lectures of his that I attended (as a student at UCLA), David Kaplan, a well known semanticist, insisted that the opening sentence of Lewis CarrollÂ’s Jabberwocky (Â“ Twas brillig, and the slithy toves/Did gyre and gimble in the wabeÂ”) was a bona fide sentence. It is not. It is a sentence-impostor. (Obviously Â“brillig,Â” Â“slithy,Â” Â“tove,Â” etc. are meant to bring to mind the words Â“brilliant,Â” Â“slimy,Â” Â“toad,Â” etc. But those two lines no more token a sentence than a man wearing a Richard Nixon mask is Richard Nixon.) 

(ii) 
According to Carnap (1932), Â“this stone is thinking of ViennaÂ” is literally meaningless, even though it is a bona fide sentence. Carnap is making the familiar mistake of confusing the property of having a meaning worth affirming with the property of having no meaning. That stone was not thinking of Vienna; so CarnapÂ’s sentence was false, and therefore meaningful. 


There is obviously a sense in which an utterance of Â“this stone is thinking about ViennaÂ” is Â“nonsense.Â” But in that sense of the word Â“nonsense,Â” a sentence's being nonsense consists in its having a meaning, albeit one that has no chance of being correct. 
Chomsky (1957) made the very same mistake, though in a 
less brazen way, when he famously said that Â“colorless green ideas sleep furiouslyÂ” is meaningless but that, since it has the right syntactic properties, is a bona fide sentence. On one of its two disambiguations, it says that there are ideas that are both colorless and green, all of them furious sleepers. Thus disambiguated, Â“colorless green ideas sleep furiouslyÂ” is meaningful, but its meaning isnÂ’t worth affirming. On its other disambiguation, it says that anything that is a member of the class of colorless green things that are ideas is also a member of the class of things that sleep furiously. In other words, it says that nothing that falls into the first class fails to fall into the second class. 
Thus disambiguated, that sentence is true but trivial: given that the first class is empty, it follows vacuously that there is no member of the first class that isnÂ’t also a member of the second class. ItÂ’s obvious that the first class cannot possibly have any members and therefore cannot possibly have any members in common with any other class. So, thus disambiguated, that sentence affirms a proposition that, being vacuously true and therefore devoid of significant information, is not worth affirming. 
Thus, contrary to what Chomsky says, Â“colorless green ideas sleep furiouslyÂ” is perfectly meaningful. In fact, itÂ’s hyper-meaningful, since it has two meanings. One of them is a correct (but trivial) proposition; the other is a false (and absurd) proposition. Triviality and falsity are properties of meanings. 
So ChomskyÂ’s contention is proven false---and not, contrary to what he seems to think, proven correct---by the very fact that, depending on how it is disambiguated, Â“colorless green dreams sleeps furiouslyÂ” is absurd or trivial. 
Russell claimed that Â“quadruplicity drinks procrastinationÂ” is a bona fide sentence that is meaningless. But that claim is false; the reasons for this are similar to those just given in connection with Â“colorless green ideas sleep furiously.Â” First of all, unless Â“quadruplicityÂ” has a meaning, this sentence of RussellÂ’s is no more a sentence than Â“drinks procrastination.Â” 
So it must be assumed that Â“quadruplicityÂ” has a meaning. According to Russell, whose word we can trust here, that word does have a meaning; it refers to the property of having four members. (So the smallest set consisting of the numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4 has the property of quadruplicity.) Given this fact, RussellÂ’s supposedly meaningless sentence is quite clearly false, and therefore meaningful. Being abstracts objects, quadruplicity and procrastination neither drink, nor are drunk by, anything. Russell seems to be committing the oft-made mistake of confusing absurdity, which is the property of having a meaning that is logically incapable of being true, with meaninglessness. RussellÂ’s belief that Â“quadruplicity drinks procrastinationÂ” was probably also motivated by his acceptance of the Theory of Types, which weÂ’ll discuss in Section 3.0 of this chapter and which, in agreement with every mathematical and philosophical logician alive, weÂ’ll find to be false. 
(iii) Oftentimes, a homonym of an actual word occurs in a context in which no semantic rule assigns any meaning to it and in which it therefore means nothing, even though the context in question is one that is otherwise just like a sentence. What occurs in Â“the absolute is oneÂ” is not the word Â“absolute,Â” but a mere homonym of that word. For the occurrence of Â“absoluteÂ” in Â“the absolute is oneÂ” to be a word, there would have to be some semantic rule that assigned it a meaning. Although there are semantic rules that assign meaning(s) to homonyms of that occurrence, that occurrence per se is assigned no meaning. Anything that is assigned no meaning is ipso facto not a linguistic expression. So Â“the absolute is oneÂ” is not a sentence, but a sentence-impostor, at least until it is said what "the absolute" refers to, or is supposed to refer to---at least, that is to say, until the semantic rule for it is identified. 
Anything to which no semantic rule assigns a meaning ipso facto isn't a linguistic expression. Because the logical positivists overlooked this humdrum fact, they sought some criterion by which to distinguish "meaningful sentences" (e.g., "the moon is made of cheese") from "meaningless sentences" (e.g., "the absolute is one"). But all of the meaningless so-called sentences that they identified weren't sentences at all; they were sentence-schemata, since they contained undetermined expressions (expressions to which no semantic rule assigned any meaning, at least not as far as occurrences in the sentence in question were concerned) and therefore no more qualified as bona fide sentences than does "x has property phi." 
Thus, in trying to explain the meaningless of pseudo-sentences as Â“the absolute is oneÂ”, the logical positivists were on a fools errant. In that pseudo-sentence, the term Â“the absoluteÂ” is a restricted variable, albeit one whose connotations constrict its range of possible values more than the range of the (almost entirely) non-connotative variable in, say, Â“x is extendedÂ” restricts its possible range of values. 
2.0 The liarÂ’s paradox 
WeÂ’ve found elementary blunders in each of the reasons already considered for holding that bona fide expressions can be meaningless. But there are other reasons for holding this that donÂ’t involve any obvious blunders and demand careful treatment. In the process of considering these reasons, weÂ’ll make some headway on some important, open questions in semantics and philosophical logic. 
There are sentences that, so initial appearances suggest, are true if theyÂ’re false and false if theyÂ’re true.[183] 
Consider the sentence: 
(LIE1) Â“I am now lying.Â” 
Given the law of excluded middle (Â“any proposition must be either true or falseÂ”), LIE1 cannot fail to be either true or false. Given the law of non-contradiction (Â“no proposition can be both true and falseÂ”), LIE1 cannot be both true and false. So if LIE1 expresses a proposition, that proposition is both true and false. Therefore, given that no such proposition exists, LIE1 doesnÂ’t express a proposition. But itÂ’s very hard to believe that Â“I am lyingÂ” is not a sentence. Exactly similar reasoning holds with respect to Â“I am lyingÂ” and Â“I am a Cretan and all Cretans are liars,Â” and each one of the infinitely many other sentences that are relevantly similar to those two. 
LIE1 is indeed a sentence. But itÂ’s not both true and false; itÂ’s just false. LIE1 is equivalent with: 
(LIE2) Â“There already exists some proposition P such that P is false and such that, by virtue of producing this very utterance, I am affirming P.Â” 
LIE2 thus entails that, existing prior to, and therefore independently of, any LIE2 or any utterance thereof, there is some proposition P such that (i) is false and, moreover, such that (ii) is true only if, for some utterance of LIE2, P is true only if that utterance is true. Since P pre-exists any such utterance, 
LIE2 is not false and true; it is simply false. Therefore, LIE1 is false. So we donÂ’t have in LIE1 a counter-example to our thesis that there are bona 
fideexpressions that are meaningless. 
2.1 The liarÂ’s paradox (continued) 
There is another way of dealing with the LiarÂ’s paradox, or at least with one version of it. Let UTF be a specific utterance of the sentence: 
(TF) Â“This sentence-token is false.Â” 
To what do the first two word-tokens constituting UTF refer? Â“They refer to UTFÂ”, it will be said. Â”In other words, that occurrence of Â‘this tokenÂ’ means Â“the sentence-token I will have produced by virtue of completing this sentence.Â” If only for argument's sake, letÂ’s suppose that this is so. In that case, TF is equivalent with: 
(TF*) There exists some proposition P such that there is exactly one sentence-token that I am now uttering such that my utterance affirms P (and is therefore true if, and only if, P is false).[184] 

A proposition is a truth or a falsehood. So P has been a truth or a falsehood as long as itÂ’s existed. (SinceÂ—see Chapter 2---propositions donÂ’t come into existence or go out of it, this means that itÂ’s always existed.) If P pre-dates TF*, then it was true or false before TF* ever came along. In that case, TF* is simply false. For TF* falsely says the truth of P is contingent on the truth of TF*, which is not the case. If P does not pre-date TF*, then TF is simply false; for it starts with the words Â“there exists a proposition P such that.Â” Even if that proposition pops into existence by the end of the TF*, TF* is false, since it affirmed the existence of some proposition that pre-dated TF*Â’s completion. 
3.0 RussellÂ’s Paradox and the Theory of Types 
Other sentences that are obviously comparable to Â“I am now lyingÂ” are Â“this sentence is falseÂ” and Â“IÂ’m a Cretan, and all Cretans are liars.Â” But there exist sentences that, it has been argued, are meaningless and that, unlike those two, are not in any obvious way modeled on Â“this sentence is false.Â” The best known example of such a sentence is[185]: 
(RP) K is a member of itself iff K is not a member of itself, 
where K is the class of all classes that are not members of themselves. (If K is a member of itself, then, since K includes only classes that arenÂ’t members of themselves, then K is not a member of itself; and if K is not a member of itself, then, since K includes every class that is not a member of itself, K is a member of itself.)[186] 

According to Graham Priest, a contemporary logician, RP is meaningful, 
i.e. there is some proposition that it affirms. According to Priest, since that proposition is both true and false, we must reject the law of nonÂ­contradiction.[187] 
In a moment, weÂ’ll see why PriestÂ’s reasoning is spurious. 
Unlike Priest, Bertrand Russell held that the law of non-contradiction is correct and, therefore, that there is no proposition that RP expresses. But Russell has a very different view from us as to why RP fails. 
RussellÂ’s view is embodied in his famous Â“Theory of TypesÂ” (Â“TTÂ” for short). According to TT, any given sentence belongs to a certain "type"; given any two types, one is higher than the other. The lowest type is Type1. 
Sentences of Type1 concern Â“individuals.Â” (An individual is anything spatiotemporal and, therefore, anything that isn't a set, property, sentence or proposition. In this context, for the sake of expediency, references to 
"classes" will be short-hand for references to classes and to properties and to propositions and to sentences.) Sentences of Type2 concern individuals and classes whose members are individuals. (Sentences of Type2 thus concern inter alia sentences of Type1.) Sentences of Type3 concern everything with which sentences of Type2 are concerned as well as classes of classes of individuals.[188] 
In general, for any whole number n, sentences of Typen+1 may concern everything with which sentences of Type n are concerned and, unlike sentences of Type n, sentences of Type n+1 may concern classes of Type n. 
A consequence of TT is that, if the free variable in Â“x is a member of class CÂ”, where C is of Typem, is replaced with an expression denoting a class of Typem or higher, the resulting sentence is meaningless, i.e. there is no proposition that it affirms and it is therefore neither true nor false. 
So, according to TT, Â“C is a member of CÂ” is meaningless, and so is its negation. TT entails that RP is no more meaningful than Â“blurka derka derk." Given his acceptance of TT, Russell understandably holds it to be a failing of the English language that it permits the construction of sentences like RP. 
3.1 Why the theory of types is false 
RP is ambiguous; there are two ways of disambiguating it. RP can be taken to be to the same effect as: 
(RP1) There exists some class K such that all and only those classes that are not members of themselves belong to K. 
Thus disambiguated, RP is false. There is no such class. A contradiction follows from the supposition that there is a class whose membership includes all and only those classes that arenÂ’t members of themselves. Therefore, there is no such class. 
The fact that no such class exists is to be established by a garden-variety indirect proof, just like the fact that there are no square circles.[189] 
Let x be a square circle. Being a square, x has four sides and therefore doesnÂ’t have a uniform curvature. Being a circle, x has a uniform curvature. Therefore, x both does and does not have a uniform curvature. This isnÂ’t possible. So x is a non-entity. K is a non-entity for the same reason mutatis mutandis. 
There is another way to interpret RP. We could take Â“KÂ” to be defined thus: 
(AI[190]) Assuming that there is some class O whose members include all and only those classes that are not members of themselves, then, in virtue of having the form Â‹ Â…KÂ…Â›, a given sentence S is true just in case O hasÂ…xÂ…(i.e., just in caseÂ…OÂ…); and, if that assumption is false, then Â“KÂ” picks out nothing, and Â‹Â…KÂ…. Â› bears no proposition and is thus neither true nor false. 
Thus taken, RP doesnÂ’t say anything. Since there is no class of the requisite kind, Â“KÂ” picks out nothing and, the semantic rule for Â“KÂ” being what it is, RP fails to encode any proposition. Thus disambiguated, KP is like an utterance of: (TPE) Â“That pink elephant is coming right at us,Â” 
made in a context where there is no pink elephant. So, thus disambiguated, RP requires neither an abandonment of the laws of classical logic nor an acceptance of TT. 
3.2 Two kinds of meaning: type-meaning and token-meaning (revisited) 
Here we must revisit an issue discussed in the previous chapter.[191] 
There seems to be some sense in which an utterance of TPE that is made in an elephant-free context is meaningful, notwithstanding that such an utterance bears no proposition. The sense in which such an utterance is meaningful is this: the semantic rules of the language to which it belongs determine what would have to be the case for that utterance to be meaningful. The semantic rule corresponding to TPE is this: 
(TPE*) If, in context C, there is some pink elephant E that is 
being indicated by some person P1, and P1 is indicating no 
pink elephant other than E, then an utterance on P1Â’s part, 
directed towards persons P2Â….Pn (2 = n), of Â“that pink 
elephant is heading towards usÂ” is true exactly if E is heading 
towards P1Â…Pn. If there is no such elephant, that utterance 
fails to encode any proposition. 
So, when uttered in an elephant-free environment, TPE is meaningful. ItÂ’s meaningful in the sense that it has well-defined truth-conditions. Whether those conditions are fulfilled has no bearing on whether TPE is meaningful. Nothing relating to the whereabouts of elephants redounds to the credit or the discredit of the body of rules that constitute the English language. 
Similar reasoning holds in connection with RP. RP has truth-conditions. Whether those conditions are fulfilled is irrelevant to whether RP is meaningful. "But there is a difference between RP and TPE,Â” it will be said. "Whereas tokens of TPE could be true, tokens of TT cannot possibly be true: the laws of logic prohibit it." Yes---but the laws of logic aren't coded into the semantic rules of English. One can master those rules without being a master-logician; one certainly doesn't need to know whether there exists a class of all classes that aren't members of themselves. So RP, though not proposition-bearing, is meaningful. 
To conclude: on neither of its disambiguations is RP a counterexample to our contention that all bona fideexpressions are meaningful. This is another instance of a philosopher failing to distinguish absurdity from 
meaninglessness. We discussed other such examples in Chapter 1. 
3.3 The theory of types revisited: More problems with it 
According to the Theory of Types (TT), no meaningful sentence occupies an order equal to, or lower than, the order occupied by any one of the sentences that it concerns. Since TT itself concerns statements belonging to every order, it concerns the order to which it itself belongs and, supposing it correct, is therefore meaningless and, being meaningless, is not correct. So TT is not correct if it is correct. Since, therefore, TT is inconsistent with itself, it is false. 
Also, TT has consequences too counterintuitive to accept. For example, according to TT, the sentence: 
(i) Â“Jim has three pairs of socks.Â” 
is of a lower order than the sentence: 
(ii) Â“The sentence Â‘Jim has three pairs of socksÂ’ is true," 
and (ii) is of a lower type than the sentence: 
(iii) Â“The sentence Â‘the sentence Â“Jim has three pairs of socksÂ” is trueÂ’ is true.Â” 
If TT is right, the property that one ascribes to (iii) by describing it as Â“trueÂ” is one that cannot possibly be had by (ii) or (i), and the property one ascribes to (ii) by describing it as Â“trueÂ” is one that cannot possibly be had by (i). So, if TT is right, there is no such thing as truth simpliciter. There is truth1, truth2, etc. 
By similar reasoning, if TT is right, the occurrence of Â“threeÂ” in: 
(iv) Â“Jim has three pairs of socks,Â” 
doesnÂ’t have the same meaning as its homonym in (i). (i) is to the effect that: 
(a) There are three true instances of the propositional-form x is a member of the class of pairs of socks had by Jim. 
The occurrence Â“threeÂ” in (i) denotes a property had by classes of individuals. (It denotes the property of being a three-membered class of individuals.) The homonymous occurrence in (iv) denotes a property of classes of classes of individuals. (It denotes the property of being a three-membered class of classes of individuals.) So the property denoted by the one occurrence is distinct from the property denoted by the other. Given how counterintuitive this is, TT must be presumed false. 
This presumption is easily verified. TT concerns all sentences. It isnÂ’t concerned with sentences belonging to this or that specific order. According to TT, any proposition that concerns all sentences is ipso facto meaningless. So if TT is true, then itÂ’s false; therefore, itÂ’s false. 
4.0 Vagueness and indeterminacy 
The word Â“indeterminateÂ” has two meanings. The sentence: 
(BW) Â“BillÂ’s whereabouts are indeterminate,Â” 
can be taken to mean either: 
(BW1) given the available information, it isnÂ’t possible to arrive at a principled judgment as to where Bill is. 
or 
(BW2) there is no fact as to where Bill is. 
BW2 cannot possibly be true. At any given point in time, some space-time region R is such that Bill is occupying R. Of course, half of Bill's body can be in the garage while the other half is in the drive way. But thatÂ’s because the region he is occupying is itself half in the garage and half in the driveway; it is not because there is no region that Bill is determinately occupying. The same points mutatis mutandis hold of any other proposition to the effect that the world per se is indeterminate in any respect. In any case, this is what the present author believes. 
But many disagree; and their reasons for doing so seem at first to be good ones. For there certainly seem to be cases of objects with vague boundaries. In fact, all spatiotemporal objects, it would seem, have vague boundaries. Given any person P, there are many particles x such that one cannot non-arbitrarily say that Â‹x is a part P's bodyÂ› is true or that it's not true. This apparent fact is one that has led many a philosopher to hold that there is objective indeterminacy.[192] 
But we'll now see that such philosophers havenÂ’t considered all the possible ways of modeling our intuitions. 
5.1 Non-epistemic indeterminacy 
Smith doesnÂ’t have a full head of hair; but there are a few tufts of hair on his head, in between which there is fuzz of varying degrees of thickness and density. Bearing this in mind, consider the statement: 
(SB) Â“Smith is bald.Â” 
is SB true or false? Many philosophers, probably most, would hold that: 
(OV)[193] 
There is no fact of the matter; and that fact has nothing to do with ignorance on our part. HereÂ’s whatÂ’s going on. There exists a certain property P that of baldness and a certain person x.(P = the property of baldness; x = Smith.) And x doesnÂ’t exactly instantiate P, but x doesnÂ’t exactly fail to instantiate P. There is no fact as to whether the proposition x has P is true. It isnÂ’t that we donÂ’t know whether itÂ’s true; itÂ’s that there is no fact of the matter. 
HereÂ’s the problem with OV. For argumentÂ’s sake, suppose that it is objectively indeterminate whether Smith is bald. Suppose, in other words, that the proposition (not the sentence):[194] 

(SB) Smith is bald, 
is true. And, let us also suppose, the reason SB is vague is that it is objectively indeterminate exactly what conditions a given thing must satisfy to be bald. 
Given these suppositions, it is ipso facto indeterminate what exactly SB entails and what is entailed by it. If it is objectively indeterminate exactly what features a thing must have to be bald, then it is for that very reason indeterminate, for any x, exactly what entails, and also what is entailed by, the proposition (notÂ—nota beneÂ—the sentence): 
(XB) Â‹x is baldÂ›, 
for any x. 
Thus, a consequence of the supposition that SB is objectively indeterminate is that it is indeterminate what SB entails and also what is entailed by it. 
But the very idea of such a proposition is not a coherent one. Propositions are individuated by what they entail. Different entailment relations, different propositions. So until the entailment relations of some sentence-like string of verbiage have been fixed, no proposition has been identified to that verbiage; and all we have is, at most, a sentence-schema. 
5.2 An objection to the argument just presented 
I have heard it said that: 
(ER)[195] 
Propositions are not individuated by their entailment relations. The proposition that 1 + 1 = 2 obviously isnÂ’t identical with the proposition that triangles have three sides. But a given proposition entails/is entailed by the one just in case it entails/is entailed by the other.Â” 
Obviously 1+1 =2 and triangles have three sides are different propositions. But contrary to what ER assumes, they don't coincide in respect of their entailment relations. The way [196] 
in which for some n, n + 2 follows from 1+1 =2 differsÂ—quite dramaticallyÂ—from the way (or, rather, any one of the infinitely many possible ways) in which for some n, n + 2 follows from triangles have three sides. A corollary is that, until it is settled what the entailment relations are of a given sentence, it ipso facto hasnÂ’t been settled which proposition is meant by that sentence. (This doesnÂ’t mean that one has to know what all of those relations are. No one knows what all of the entailment relations are of Â“1 + 1 = 2.Â” But, the semantic rules of the English language being what they are, it is indeed fixed what those entailment relations are.) 
What a sentence says---or, to be precise, what is affirmed by a non-abortive indicative token of that sentence ---is a function of exactly two things: first, what follows from that sentence-token (supposing it is true); second, how those things follow from it (same qualification). Given a sentence-token S, once what it entails and how it entails it is fixed, there is nothing left to be said about what it means. By the same token, if what S entails or how it entails it isnÂ’t fixed, it has yet to be fixed what S means. Thus, a sentence such that there is no fact as to what it entails, or as to how it entails what it entails, is a sentence to which no one proposition has been assigned. 
Bearing these points in mind, suppose the following. P is a true proposition. There are propositions P1Â….Pn such that, for each i, it is objectively indeterminate whether P entails Pi. Thus, P ipso facto leaves it open whether P is true. But if P leaves it open whether Pi is true, then P 
determinately fails to entail Pi. That doesnÂ’t mean that P entails the negation of Pi. (Snow is white doesnÂ’t entail grass is green or grass is not green.A proposition may be compatible with another proposition and with its 
negation.) 
The believer in indeterminacy has but one way of dealing with this argument. He is forced to say that, although there is no fact as to whether P entails Pi, nonetheless P does not leave it open whether Pi is true. But this 
position is tautologously false. 
5.2.1 An objection to the argument just presented (continued) 
Here is a similar argument. Suppose there to be some propositions P* such that (i), for any given proposition, it is determinate whether P* entails that proposition and therefore that it is determinate, for any i, whether P* entails Pi but such that (ii), with that qualification, P* entails a given proposition iff 
P also entails it. Is P identical with P*? It cannot be. For P* has, whereas P 
lacks, the property of being such that there is a fact as to whether it entails Pi, for some i. Thus, P is distinct from any proposition P% such that P%, supposing it true, settles whether or not Pi is true. So P fails to settle whether 
or not Pi is true and thus fails to entail it or its negation. So the statement Â“P entails PiÂ” is determinately false. 
Were there indeterminate statements; i.e., statements such that there was no fact as to whether what they affirmed was true, there would be pairs of statements such that there was no fact as to whether the one entailed the other (or, therefore, whether it entailed its negation). But given any such pair, the one ipso facto leaves it open whether the other is true and thus determinately fails to entail (the negation of the other), an immediate consequence being that there is a fact as to whether the one entails the other. So the concept of a proposition such that there is no fact as to whether it is true is an incoherent one and the same is therefore true of the concept of objective, as opposed to epistemic vagueness. 
6.0 The Sorites paradox 
Consider the following paradox. 
Paradox #1 (P1): A person with only one dollar is poor. If a person with n dollars is poor, then so is a person with n +1 dollars. It follows that a person with a billion dollars is poor. But, obviously, a person with a billion dollars is not poor. 
For reasons that are of no philosophical importance and that, in any case, will soon become clear, P1 is an example of what is known as the Â“Sorites ParadoxÂ” (a.k.a., the Â“Paradox of the Heap,Â” Â“SoritesÂ” being the plural of the Greek word Â“soros,Â” which, so I am told, means Â“heapÂ”). There are three different kinds of Sorites paradoxes, P1 being an example of only one of 
those three kinds. WeÂ’ll now outline solutions to all three kinds, beginning with the kind instantiated by P1. 
Here is an outline of the solution to P1: Like most predicates, Â“poorÂ” is a relational expression. Smith may be poor compared to Jones but wealthy compared to Green, or he may be poor relative to the standard set by some situation and wealthy relative to the standard set by some other situation. If Smith is a millionaire who needs to have a net worth of at least 50 million dollars to become a managing director of company X, he is poor relative to the standard of wealth that, given SmithÂ’s desire to become a managing director of X, is the relevant one. So an utterance of Â‘Smith is poorÂ’ is correct if made in a context in which the relevant standard of wealth is set by SmithÂ’s desire to become a managing director of X. For, in such a context, a "poor" person is one whose net worth is less than $50,000,000. For that very reason, it follows that, in such a context, there is a number n--namely, 49,999,999--Â­such that an utterance of Â‹x is poorÂ› is true if x has n dollars and false if x has n + 1 dollars. 
Bearing these points in mind, itÂ’s clear how to solve each member of the infinitely large class of paradoxes to which P1 belongs. Consider the following paradox: 
(P1#) If a personÂ’s top running speed is 1 mph, then that person is slow. For any number, if a person whose top running 
speed is n mph is slow, then a person whose top running speed 
is n + 1 mph is also slow. Therefore, a person whose top 
running speed is 75 mph is slow. 
A story, structurally similar to the one just told, will make it clear how to solve this paradox. At his best, Smith runs a 100 yard dash in 12 seconds. Smith tries to join track team X. In order to qualify for team X, one must run a 100 yard dash in no more than 10 seconds. Obviously Smith doesnÂ’t make the team. Smith then decides to join team Y. In order to qualify for team Y, one must run a 100 yard dash in no more than 100 seconds. Smith obviously qualifies for Y. 
If made in a context in which the relative standard of swiftness is set by SmithÂ’s desire to join X, an utterance of Â“Smith is fastÂ” is false. But such an utterance is true if made in a context in which the relative standard of swiftness is set by SmithÂ’s desire to join Y. In a context of either kind, there is some number n such that an utterance of Â‹x is slowÂ› is true if, at his best, xÂ’s average speed when running the 100 yard dash is n and such that an utterance of Â“x is fastÂ” is true if x is person whose average running speed when running 100 yards is n + 1. 
In a context of the first kind, n is any number such that if a person whose average speed when running a 100 yard dash is n and who, for that reason, runs the 100 yard dash in over 11 seconds but who, if his speed when running the 100 yard dash were n + 1, would run it in under 11 seconds. The same thing mutatis mutandis holds of contexts of the second kind. 


6.1 These points generalized 
To generalize these points, we must note a fact about languageÂ—more specifically, about predicates.[197] 
Some predicates are binary. P is a binary predicate if the property it expresses is one that cannot be had to varying degrees; it is one that a given thing either has or doesnÂ’t have. So Â“evenÂ” (as in Â“even numberÂ”) is a binary predicate. Sorites paradoxes always involve non-binary predicates (i.e., predicates that express properties that can be had to varying degrees), e.g., Â“fat,Â” Â“tall,Â” Â“smart.Â” A corollary is that Sorites paradoxes always involve properties that one thing can have to a greater extent than some other thing. One thing can be smarter than another. 
Bearing these points in mind, consider the following three sentences: 
(i) 
Smith is smart. 

(ii) 
Smith is more smart than Jones. 


(iii) Smith is smarter than Jones. 
(ii) and (iii) are synonyms. In effect, (iii) is just an abbreviation of (ii). Surely, the occurrence of Â“smartÂ” in (i) has the same meaning (picks out the same property) as the homonymous expression in (ii). This wouldnÂ’t be possible if, in (i), the occurrence of Â“smartÂ” picked out a binary (nonÂ­relational) property. This shows that Â“smartÂ” is always relational. This, in its turn, shows that tokens of (i) are elliptical for sentence-tokens that express-relational propositions---sentence-tokens having the form: 
(i#) Â“Smith is smarter than___,Â” 
or perhaps: 
(i*) Â“Smith is smart enough for__.Â” 
So tokens of Â“Smith is smartÂ” must be elliptical for sentences such as Â“Smith is smarter than JonesÂ” and Â“Smith is smart enough to solve the puzzle.Â” Exactly similar points hold of other non-binary predicates. The meaning of Â“x is fastÂ” is given by some sentence having the form Â“x is faster than yÂ” (e.g., Â“Smith is faster than JonesÂ”) or having the form Â“x is fast enough to satisfy standard SÂ” (e.g., Â“that plane is fast enough to make it to 
Pittsburgh by 3:00 P.M.Â”). 

6.2 A confusion side-stepped 
Here I would like to head off a source of serious confusion. I am not advocating the view that at the level of semantics Â“Smith is smart,Â” Â“Jones is tallÂ” etc. express relational propositions of the just-mentioned kind. It cannot be assumed that the philosophical insights needed to solve puzzles that turn on facts about language are themselves encoded in the semantic rules of English (or of whatever language happens to be the relevant one). So the just-stated analysis is not a semantic analysis; it is not an attempt to identify the semantic rules that assign meaning to sentences of the form Â“x is P,Â” where P is an arbitrary non-binary predicate. 
It makes no sense to say that some number is more even than some other number. But this has nothing to do with language; it has to do with the property of being even. The sentence Â“6 is more even than 8,Â” though absurd, does not run afoul of the semantic (or syntactic) rules of English. (Or, if it does, it is only because we have ex post facto projected our mathematical insights into the syntactic or semantic rules of English. And were some mathematician to show that evenness came in degrees, it would come to be grammatical---if it isnÂ’t already---to say Â‹x is more even than y.Â›) Clearly, Â“two is evenÂ” is not semantically or otherwise elliptical for some sentences of the form Â‹x is more even than yÂ› or Â‹x is even enough to satisfy standard S.Â› But unless we implausibly suppose that our knowledge that evenness doesnÂ’t come in degrees is coded into the semantic rules of English---unless we implausibly endow the semantic rules of English, which can be mastered by somebody who wrongly believes that evenness does come in degrees, with our mathematical knowledge---then Â‹x is evenÂ› is not, at the level of semantics, elliptical for Â“x is more even than yÂ” (etc.). 
This reasoning mutatis mutandis shows that at the level of semantics Â‹x is fastÂ› probably isnÂ’t elliptical for Â‹x is faster than yÂ› (etc.). For, were we to say otherwise, weÂ’d be endowing the semantic rules of English with our (extraÂ­linguistic) knowledge of the fact that, indeed, swiftness comes in degrees. Given that those rules can, at least in principle, be mastered by somebody who has the idiotic belief that swiftness does not come in degrees, we mustnÂ’t impute to the semantic rules of English our knowledge that swiftness does come in degrees; and we must therefore take the position, for which there is a vast amount of independent corroboration, that this knowledge of ours is nonÂ­linguistic. 
That said, the way to solve P1 is to take the view that in some way or other---probably through pragmatic implicature, not necessarily through literal meaning---tokens of (e.g.) Â“Bob is smartÂ” are elliptical for tokens of relational sentences of the previously described kind. 

6.3 A different kind of Sorites paradox 
Let us now move onto a different kind of Sorites paradox. Paradoxes of this kind are much harder to solve than those of the kind just discussed: 
P2: Let C be some cloud and let m be some water-molecule dead in center of C. Obviously m is a part of C. But letÂ’s suppose that m migrates towards the periphery of C. For a while, m will still remain a part of C. But if m travels, say, two miles away from C, then m will definitely cease to be a part of C. But whereÂ’s the cut-off line? Suppose that, for a while, m whizzes around CÂ’s periphery, sometimes bumping into molecules that are definitely a part of C, and never straying from CÂ’s periphery---i.e., from what definitely either coincides with or falls within CÂ’s periphery----by more than an inch. Under those circumstances, is m a part of C? What about if we continue to suppose that m intermittently bumps into C but we increase this margin from one inch to five inches? Is m still a part of C? And how infrequently can m collide with molecules that are clearly C-constitutive without itself definitely ceasing to be a part of C? If such collisions are frequent, weÂ’re inclined to consider it a part of C, even during those periods when itÂ’s not in contact with molecules that are clearly C-constitutive (provided that, during such periods, it doesnÂ’t veer off by too great a distance). By the same token, if such collisions are infrequent, weÂ’re inclined not to consider m a constituent of C, even if, in between such collisions, it remains fairly close to C. (The more frequent the collisions, the more m can travel away from C without ceasing to be a constituent of C.) But, once again, where is the cut-off line? Is it half an inch? Two inches? A foot? What is it? Any answer seems arbitrary. If I say: Â“itÂ’s exactly 3 inchesÂ”, IÂ’m making a stipulation; IÂ’m not identifying a pre-existing fact. (Technically, the right question is: where are the cut-off lines? For, whether or not m is a member of C seems to depend both on its average proximity and on the frequency with which it comes into contact with bona fideCÂ­constituents. But, for simplicityÂ’s sake, IÂ’ve chosen to abstract 
from this fact.) So here, quite indisputably, we have a case of indeterminacy. But, more interestingly, this indeterminacy has nothing to do with the representations of the world that we, or creatures of any other kind, have of the world. There could (and probably would) be clouds even if there were no sentient beings; and, in the absence of such beings, there would, given just about any cloud C, be molecules that were definitely parts of C and others that definitely werenÂ’t parts of C and, what is relevant, molecules x such that x is a constituent of C wouldnÂ’t exactly be true and wouldnÂ’t exactly be false---or, to make an equivalent point, such that xÂ’s constituency in C would not itself exactly be a constituent of the universe and also wouldnÂ’t exactly fail to be a constituent of the universe. 
6.3.1 A correct conception of thinghood the key to solving P2 
The solution to P2 is similar to the solution to P1. But there are some significant differences; and to solve P2, we must first make some substantive claims as to what is meant by the words such as Â“thingÂ” and Â“object.Â” (In this context, those terms are to refer only entities such as vases, rocks, windows, as opposed to abstracta such as numbers or possibilities.) For the reasons given in Sections 5.2-5.2.1 and now to be developed, I donÂ’t consider it an option to say that the world per se is indeterminate. Whatever the word "cloud" means, we gave it that meaning. So the corresponding cannot possibly contain the information needed to answer substantive questions concerning cloud-composition, given that we didn't built such knowledge into it. 
Semantic rules cannot know more than we do. So it's understandable, if not inevitable, that there should be arrangements of molecules that determinately don't deserve to be characterized either as "clouds" or as "nonÂ­clouds." and it's understandable, if not inevitable, the word "cloud" should fail to pick out any one property. 
We cannot expect our linguistic conventions to "cut nature at the joints." to use Francis Bacon's expression; we cannot expect them to be hewed to exactly those properties in terms of which the constitution of the world is to be delineated. A slight detour through legal theory will help make this clear. 
Laws created 200 years ago necessarily fail to address issues relating to the disposal of motor-oil. There's nothing mysterious about this, and it's obviously no reason for saying that the world is intrinsically vague. The same holds of semantic rules that were created over 200 years ago. And semantic rules, like laws, must be updated if they are to do what we want them do. So it isn't hard to make sense of the idea that semantic rules should sometimes be silent. 
But it is hard to make sense of the idea that properties should be indeterminate. What does it mean to say that the property of being a cloud is indeterminate? To which property are we referring? "The one had by those billowy things in the sky." Yes, but there are other objects that this person is not currently indicating. So, when confronted with some new object, by what criterion do we decide whether it is of the same ilk as those billowy things? Even if we could see the microstructural properties of those objects, we wouldn't necessarily know in virtue of which facts about their microstructures they fell into the same category as those billowy things. 
Until we can answer these questions, we don't have an answer to our original question, namely: which property is the relevant one? The information we have limits what a viable answer to that question could be. But it still leaves us with an infinitely large class of distinct properties to choose from. 
To sum up: attempts to identify properties that are objectively indeterminate can be interpreted as cases where no one property has been identified, suggesting that so-called cases of objective indeterminacy are nothing more than projections into the external world of the platitude that open scientific questions are not to be solved by studying semantic rules. 

6.3.2 A correct conception of thinghood the key to solving P2 (continued) 
In any case, P2 arises because we think about things in the wrong way. We think of things as being more thing-like than they really are! Right now IÂ’m looking at the pen on my desk. Let x be one half of my pen (the segment that includes the pen's tip and whose length is half the pen's), and let y be some region of the table immediately adjacent to x. Finally, let Z be the "entity", for lack of a better word, whose only two parts are x and y. Z is not a Â‘thing.Â’ If we were to list all the things in the world, my pen would be on the list, and so would the table on which it rests. But Z wouldnÂ’t be on the list. Why not? Because Z lacks the dynamic cohesiveness, and concomitant predictive and explanatory usefulness, that is had by the pen or the table or any other bona fideobject. 
Of course, tables donÂ’t last forever. They can be broken and burnt; and they all come to an end, in one way or another. But it is never by virtue of being a table that a thing ceases to exist. Qua table, a thing can be depended on and its behavior predicted. The fact that poorly constructed tables are not thus reliable only confirms this point; for, in virtue of being poorly constructed, and for that reason lacking causal and explanatory integrity, a thing fails as a table. This only confirms that it is never as a table that a thing lacks causal or predictive usefulness. 
These points mutatis mutandis hold of all objects. Things are ipso facto prediction-and explanation facilitators. One thing can be more prediction-and explanation-conducive than another. Because of its relatively high degree of causal integrity, a house made of bricks and mortar is more explanation-and prediction-conducive than a house of cards. We are independently inclined to say that, other things being equal, brick house is more of a thing, and thus more Â“thingy," than a house of cards. We now know what it is that weÂ’re saying when we say this. WeÂ’re saying that a brick house ceteris paribus has more structural integrity a house of cards. Thus, our analysis that things are prediction-/explanation-facilitators is consistent with our preÂ­theoretic intuition that (to switch examples) clouds, though things in some sense of the word, are less thingy than houses. 

6.3.3 A consequence of our analysis 
One consequence of our analysis is that a given aggregate of molecules may be a thing in one respect and fail to be a thing in some other respect. In a context where the interactions holding among molecules m1Â…..mn facilitate 
prediction and explanation, m1Â….mn constitute a thing. In a different explanatory context, one where they donÂ’t have the aforementioned virtues, they donÂ’t constitute a thing. A galaxy is a vast object. But a galaxy does, in some contexts, function as a single object; it has the requisite causal integrity and predictive fertility that, when trying to answer certain questions, one does well to consider the various microparticles of which a galaxy consists as constituting a single object. In other contexts, one is ill-advised to do this, for the same reason mutatis mutandis. 
To be sure, we believe that some aggregates of molecules (e.g., vases, rocks, pens) are just things; we believe, in other words, that their having the status of thing isnÂ’t relative to the dialectical context. This viewpoint reflects prejudices that, in their turn, reflect idiosyncratic facts about our lives. Supposing that m1Â…..mn are the molecules composing the vase on your coffee table, if we were much smaller, so that vases were to us what, in actuality, galaxies are to us now, whether m1Â…..mn constituted a single object would be a function of the explanatory context. Similarly, if we were much bigger and the rate at which we uploaded and processed information were much slower, we might see galaxies in much the same way that, in actuality, we see vasesÂ—we might see them (wrongly) as being as unconditionally thingy, since, relative to what weÂ’d need to know under such circumstances, it would (given certain additional assumptions as to what our interests and needs would be, were we such slow-thinking giants) only be in hypothetical or, at least, rather exotic contexts that they lacked the properties requisite for thing-status. 

6.3.4 The solution to P2 
These facts about the concept of thinghood help us solve P2. ItÂ’s meaningless to ask "how far can m stray from CÂ’s periphery---i.e., from the outermost layer of molecules that are definitely constitutive of C---without ceasing to belong to C?" The reason itÂ’s meaningless is that whether m is, or is not, a part of C depends on the explanatory context. Relative to certain questions about C, m would definitely fail to qualify as part of C were it so much as one tenth of an inch outside of the aggregate of molecules that definitely qualified as being identical with, or very close to, CÂ’s surface. (WeÂ’ll henceforth refer to that molecule-aggregate as Â“CSÂ”Â—short for Â“CÂ’s surface.Â”) In other contexts, m would definitely be a part of C if it were separated by a distance of 10 inches (or less) from CS. (Remember that, in this context, weÂ’re assuming, as to simplify the discussion, that mÂ’s distance from S is the only thing that matters, so far as mÂ’s being a constituent of C is concerned. In all likelihood, other things would matter, e.g. the manner in which m was moving, the frequency with which it collided with indisputably C-constitutive molecules and the manner in which such collisions occurred, etc. But analogues of the points weÂ’re making hold with respect to the questions Â“how often must m collide with molecules that are clearly C-constitutive?Â”, Â“with much force, and in what exact manner, must m collide with such moleculesÂ”, and so on.) 
In contexts of either of these two kinds, there would be some number n such that, if mÂ’s distance from S were n or less, m would determinately belong to C and such that if mÂ’s distance from S were n + 1, m would definitely fail to qualify as a member of C. In contexts of the third kind, this would not be the case. But that is because, in such contexts, Â“CÂ” would have no definite referent. It is not because, owing to some Â“objectiveÂ” indeterminacy---some gap or blank in the world---there was no fact as to whether or not m was a part of C. The real reason would be as follows. 

6.3.5 An objection to our solution 
Â“But arenÂ’t there contexts," will asked, Â“where, relative to the question whether m was or was not a constituent of C, it wouldnÂ’t matter by exactly how much m was separated from CS? And, supposing that such contexts exist, which they presumably do, doesnÂ’t that show that there is objective indeterminacy?Â” 
Each of these questions is to be answered with a Â“no.Â” Let m be some molecule that is on the periphery of some cloud C. We'll draw a blank if, without having any other questions in mind, we ask Â‹is m a part of C?Â›. The reason: the question is meaningless. Questions of the form: Â‹is x a part of y?Â› are seldom to be decided on strictly geographical grounds. Such far as such questions seem to be of a strictly geographical nature, a thing's causal liaisons to other things---what it affects, and is affected by, and in what manner---is obviously dependent on where it is. But, when we think that of the form Â‹is x a part of y?Â› is a strictly geographical one, the reason is almost certainly that, given where x is, it's clear that each of many different questions as to x's dynamic relations to other entities is inevitably to be answered in the affirmative. It is only in very artificial contexts that the question Â‹is x a part of y?Â› is to be answered on strictly geographical grounds. And given such a context, the question is meaningless unless the relevant geographical criterion is specified. But once it's specified, the question clearly admits of an affirmative or negative response. 
Whether x is a part of y depends what sort of organization y is and on how x contributes to that organization. My body is an organization. That's why an object lodged deeply in my body isn't necessarily a part of it. A penny that I've accidentally swallowed isn't a part of my body; it doesn't contribute to that organization in the right way. The United States is an organization. That's why a non-American can be in Delaware and an American can be in Nepal. He does little for the people of Nepal, and vice versa, and he expects little from them, and vice versa. Any responsibilities that he has towards them, and any expectations that he has of them, are likely to be of an ad hoc nature. Their laws don't protect him; his soldiers don't protect them. It's somebody in Washington who signs his paycheck and decides whether, this next year, he'll still have a job and, if so, what job will be. 
We naturally think of clouds as paradigm cases of things that are not organizations. So, given some molecule m and some cloud C, we assume that the question Â‹is m a part of C?Â› isn't remotely comparable to questions, such as "is Smith a U.S. citizen?" and "is Smith's right leg a very realistic looking prosthetic (in which case, it is not a part of his body) or is it actually his leg (in which case, it is a bona fidebody part of his)?," the answers to which clearly depend, not just on the relative locations of two objects, but on the ways in which the objects in question interact. We tend to believe that: 
(PP)[198] 
Instances of such relationships involve more than one object's being a part of another. Pure parthood is a strictly spatial relation. If x's being a so-called "part" of y involves x's being part of an organized system of entities, then x's relation to y isn't one of mere parthood. Consequently, an organized systems of entities is ipso facto such that its constituents cannot possibly bear that relation to it. Thus, anything whose constituents do bear this relationship to them is ipso facto nothing more than a disorganized heap or aggregate of entities. 
But PP is antithetical to the truth. Not only can organizations have parts, contrary to what PP alleges: they are the only things that have parts. The relation of parthood is always to be understood in organizational terms. Whether object x can fit into organization y often depends on where x is in relation to y. (Hence the illusion that parthood is sometimes a purely spatial relation.) But it's only if x's bearing a certain spatial relation to y suffices for its being appropriately integrated into y that x's location relative to y suffices for its being a part of y. 
So supposing that R is the space-time region occupied by some cloud, and some golf ball entered that cloud and, by some miracle simply hovered there for the duration of the cloud's existence, it would never cease to be a foreign object. The reason: the golf ball's structure doesn't permit it to behave in ways in virtue of which R's occupant interacts with other objects in distinctively cloud-like ways. 
Thus, even clouds aren't mere heaps of molecules. Nothing is a mere heap. Any group of objects that is organized in one respect is disorganized in some other. The very people who compose a highly organized law firm may compose a highly disorganized comedy troupe. The same particles that make up a highly organized work of art may make up a highly disorganized floorboard. 
There's nothing paradoxical about this. From a strictly syntactic standpoint, "organized" is a one-place predicate and thus denotes a property, not a relation. But, from a logical standpoint, "organized" a two place predicate and thus denotes a relation, not a property. For Smith to be organized when it comes to his responsibilities to his employer and disorganized when it comes to his responsibilities to his children is for Smith to bear some relation to the desiderata one must satisfy to be a good employee that he fails to bear to the desiderata that one must satisfy to be a good father. 
Before closing the argument, let's sum up. A moment ago, we saw that x's being a part of y consists in y's being a system of into which x has been integrated. But we just saw that "organized" is a relative term. A group of objects cannot just be organized; it must organized in this or that respect, a corollary being that a group of objects that is organized in one respect is necessarily disorganized in some other. 
So before we ask whether x is a part of y, there are a few questions that we must answer: 
(i) What kind of organization are we taking y to be? 
(ii) What conditions a given object must satisfy to belong to such an organization? How must a given object interact with a group of objects composing such an organization if it is to be one of them? 
(iii) Does x interact with the objects composing y in the requisite ways? 
These questions may be hard to answer. But they're answerable, at least in principle, and once they're answered there cannot possibly remain any reason to hold that there is no fact as to whether x is a part of y. 


6.4 A third kind of Sorites Paradox 
Let us now discuss, and attempt to solve, the so-called Â“Paradox of the 
Heap.Â”[199] 
Here is that paradox: 
P3: A single grain of sand is not a heap of sand. If n grains of sand donÂ’t jointly constitute a heap, then neither do n + 1 grains of sand. In other words, adding a grain of sand to a non-heap wonÂ’t yield a heap. Therefore, a billion grains of sand donÂ’t constitute a heap. 
As it stands, P3 isnÂ’t really a paradox. First of all, a billion grains of sand, even when taken jointly, donÂ’t necessarily constitute a heap. If a million 
grains of sand are dispersed through space---if they are Â‘scatteredÂ’---they donÂ’t constitute a heap. So for a given multiplicity of grains of sand to constitute a heap, any given grain must be (relatively[200]) contiguous with at 
least one other member of that multiplicity. But even though, for a multiplicity of grains of sand to form a heap, it is necessary that they fulfill that condition, it isnÂ’t sufficient. For a billion grains of sand that are arranged in a straight line, each contiguous with its neighbors (or, if itÂ’s the first or last grain, with its one neighbor) isnÂ’t a heap. For a multiplicity of grains of sand to qualify as a heap, it is necessary and (ultimately) sufficient that they satisfy the following requirements: 
(i) 
each member of that heap must be contiguous with at least one other such member; 

(ii) 
taken jointly, those grains of sand must form a 3-D entity; 


and 
(iii) the entity in question cannot be a structure, at least not 
in the same sense as a building or a ship in a bottle. 
(i) and (ii) are self-explanatory, but (iii) requires clarification. A sandÂ­castle is not a heap of sand. What is the relevant difference? Â“Sand-castles are products of human artifice, whereas heaps of sand are not.Â” 
First of all, heaps of sand are often products of human artifice; second of all, there are structures (e.g., plants) that are not the products of artifice that are definitely heaps and wouldnÂ’t be heaps if, other things being equal, they were made of sand. The difference between a heap of sand and a sand-castle seems to lie in the fact that there are quite strict conditions that a grain of sand must satisfy to become part of a sand-castle, whereas there are no conditions, apart from some very generic ones, that a grain of sand must satisfy to become part of a heap of sand. To become part of a given sandÂ­castle, a given grain of sand must be affixed to the sand-castle in such a way that it either (a) provides extra support for the walkway connecting the two towers or (b) completes some otherwise incomplete decoration on the castle, etc. But to become part of a heap of sand, a given grain of sand need only be adjacent with one or more of that heapÂ’s existing constituents. 
These points make it clear how to solve a paradox that is similar to P3 and that is to be solved in much the same way: 
(P3#) A single grain of sand is not a heap. If n grains of sand, no matter how they are arranged, donÂ’t jointly constitute a heap, then adding another grain to those grains wonÂ’t yield a heap, no matter how that extra grain is added to that heap. 
What makes it seem that (P3#) is hard to solve is that the word Â“heapÂ” 
hasnÂ’t been defined. I donÂ’t mean that it hasnÂ’t been precisified[201], but that it hasnÂ’t been disambiguated. If a Â“heapÂ” refers to a structure, as opposed to an amorphous mound, of a certain kind, then, depending on what sort of structure that is, adding one more grain of sand to a structure consisting of n grains of sand quite definitely will turn a non-heap into a heap. 
If by a Â“heapÂ” we mean an amorphous mound of some kind, then, given a few fairly innocuous points about language that weÂ’ve already made, weÂ’ve already solved P3. Let us (speaking as logicians, not as semanticists) regard Â“heapÂ” as a noun form of the adjective Â“heapy.Â” There are obviously degrees of heapiness---just as there are degrees of intelligence, tallness, etc. Whether a given mound of sand is Â“heapyÂ” is relative to the operative standard. Let A and B consist of n and n + 1 grains of sand, respectively, but otherwise be qualitatively identical. To an ant whose objective is make it over mound A, A may not be heapy---meaning that the ant can make it over. But B may be heapy to that same ant, given that, because B contains that extra grain of sand (as to whose position in B I am making definite assumptions, clearly), B is not surmountable. So relative to the antÂ’s objectives (and also, perhaps, relative to the ways it can think of surmounting a heap), B is, whereas A is not, heapy. 
6.4.1 Summing up 
P3 is dealt with in two steps. 
(1) 
Replace Â“heapÂ” with the corresponding adjective. 

(2) 
See that adjective as having (hidden) relational structure. 


7.0 ZenoÂ’s Paradox 
In order to travel a distance of n yards, it is necessary to travel a distance of n/10 yards. In order to travel a distance of n/10 yards, it is necessary to travel a distance of n/100 yards. In general, one cannot travel any distance at all without already having traveled some smaller distance. 
Consequently, 
(i) Any given motion presupposes a prior motion. A consequence of (i) is: 
(ii) There is no such thing as a stationary objectÂ’s beginning to move, 
Another consequence of (i) is: 
(iii) There is no such thing as an objectÂ’s ceasing to be in a given place. 
A consequence of (iii) is 
(iv) Nothing moves. 
Therefore nothing moves. But they obviously do! How to solve this paradox? 
7.1. Eugene MillsÂ’ solution to ZenoÂ’s paradox 
For any possible universe U, there is some distance D such that nothing in U can move at all without covering a distance of at least D. 
Explanation: Zeno has established that if any given motion presupposes another motion, then nothing can even begin to leave the place that it is occupying at a given time. Therefore, (i) must be rejected. 
Assuming that (i) is false, it is not possible for there to no minimum, short of nullity, to the amount by which a given object moves. Therefore, in any world where motion is possible, there is some finite distance such that anything that moves in that world moves by at least that distance. 
7 .1.1 Problems with MillsÂ’ solution 
If Mills is right, then any given universe U consists of discrete cells such that, for any occupant x of U, x moves by vanishing from one cell and then appearing in another. x cannot move from one cell to the next, since there would in that case not be a minimum distance that x had to travel in order to travel at all. 
A consequence of MillsÂ’ position is that nothing moves. The assertion that 
(i) x spontaneously appears in one cell and spontaneously reappears in an adjacent cell 
Is equivalent, logically and evidentially, with the assertion that 
(ii) x spontaneously ceases to exist and an x-like object that is not identical with x spontaneously appears in a cell adjacent to that occupied by x. 
If you are obliterated and some person who is exactly like you appears a moment later right next to where you were standing, that person isnÂ’t you. Let you2 be that person. Given that you2 came into existence spontaneously, 
there are no lines of transmission linking him to the past and thus no lines of transmission linking you2 to you. Therefore, you2 is not you; and youn (n>2) 
isnÂ’t identical with either you or with youi (1=i=n) any one of you-you n-1. If n is a sufficiently high number and there were a sufficiently small delay between youiÂ’s disappearance and youi+1Â’s appearance, it would certainly 
appear that you had moved from one place to another. But that is obviously irrelevant. 
In a Mill-universe, nothing has a past and, consequently, nothing has a future: everything that exists, exists for an instant and then vanishes. There would therefore be no possibility of mutual causal influence among occupants of a Mill-universe. 
But such a universe is no universe at all. Each of its occupants is isolated from each other such occupant. Therefore, each such occupant is in the very condition that it would be in if it were in a universe all by itself. Therefore, a Mill-universe is a non-universe. 
Also, relative spatial and temporal position are to be understood in causal terms. Events are simultaneous if neither can affect the other; otherwise non-simultaneous. Since there is no causation in a given Mill-universe U, no U-occupant x can have either a spatial or a temporal position relative to any other U-occupant y. Thus, a Mill-universe is one in which there are neither places nor times. 
In conclusion, Mill has given us a heap of absurdities, not a solution. 



7.2 Bertrand RussellÂ’s solution to ZenoÂ’s paradox 
In general, the sum of infinitely many positive numbers may be finite (e.g. 1+Â½+Â¼+Â…=2), and any finite number can be represented as such a sum. Therefore, the sum of infinitely many non-null motions may be a finite motion, and any given finite motion can be represented as such a sum. It is therefore no more of a mystery that any given motion should follow an infinite series of motions than it is that 2 should equal 1+Â½+Â¼+Â… 
7.2.1 Problems with RussellÂ’s solution 
This is not a good solution. Zeno is asking how a given object can take that first step. He is asking how an object that moves 2 inches can move inch, and then another Â½ inch, and then another Â¼ inch, and so on. Russell hasnÂ’t answered that question. He has only made the irrelevant point that if a given object can move that first inch, then it can, after an infinite series of further motions, move a second inch. 
Â“The first step is the hardest,Â” said Mao Tse Tung. Once an object moves that first inch, all of the remaining inches are a foregone conclusion. This is the conceit underlying both RussellÂ’s solution and MillsÂ’. But each of these solutions merely begs the question, given that the very thing Zeno is asking is how that first step can be taken. 
7.3 The solution to ZenoÂ’s paradox 
All position is relative position. Therefore, changes in position are changes in relative position. If x is the only occupant of a universe U, it cannot be said that x moves or a fortiori that x moves by a given amount. For there is nothing in relation to which xÂ’s position can change. 
Nor can it be said that x exists at a given time or for a certain period of time. For there is nothing that x either follows or precedes or with which it is simultaneous. 
Therefore, the universe occupied by x comprises no spatiotemporal positions, except such as are internal to xÂ’s proper parts. So far as there are relative positions or changes therein, they are strictly x-internal. 
x can equally be thought of as the sole occupant of U or it can be thought of as U itself, it being xÂ’s proper parts to which relative positions and therefore changes in relative position can be ascribed and it therefore being xÂ’s proper parts to which positions of any kind can be ascribed. 
The sole occupant of a universe is that universe. Contrariwise, a space-time manifold has no existence independently of its occupants. 
Position and change therein are multiply relative. Given only two objects, x1 and x2, it can be said that x1 and x2 are now further from each other, or closer to each other, than they were previously. But it cannot be said that either of them has changed its relative position by this or that specific amount. This is because, just as position is relative position, so distance is relative distance. If, in addition to x1 and x2, there is a third object x3, the distance between x1 and x2 can be compared with the distance between x1 and x3, and it can be said that the one distance either equals or exceeds the other. But unless there is a fourth object x4, it cannot be said by how much the one distance exceeds the other. 
The more objects there are in a given universe, the greater the number of distances with which a given distance can be compared. The more such distances, the higher degree the of precision with which a given distance can be meaningfully described. 
Therefore, if x1Â…xn are the occupants of a given universe, changes in xiÂ‘s position are capable of being small to the extent that n is large. It is the value of n that sets the metric. What we think of as a case of motion on the part of a given object xi is really a change undergone by x1Â…xn collectively. Seemingly system-internal changes are systemic changes. Therefore, to say that motion is continuous is to make the correct, if trivial, point that the class 
of changes capable of being undergone by a universe whose sole occupants are x1Â…xn is, for any number m, a proper subset of the class of changes capable of being undergone by an otherwise identical universe whose 
occupants are x1Â…xnÂ…xn+m. 
So when it is said that xi must move Â½ inch in order to move an inch, and Â¼ inch in order to move a Â½ inch, and so on, the point being made is this: 
(1) Given any change, however minute, in an objectÂ’s position, if the universe were better populated and otherwise more heterogeneous than it currently is, it would be possible for such a change to be even more minute. 
Given that xi moved .n inches is really an abbreviated way of describing a change collectively undergone by all of the universeÂ’s occupants. Therefore, the meaning of (1) is given by the truth that: 
(2) No matter how well populated and otherwise heterogeneous the universe is, the universe is capable of being even more populous and otherwise heterogeneous; and for this reason the class of possible states of the universe is a proper subset of the class of possible states of a more heterogeneous but otherwise identical universe. 
Let us consider the following two statements in light of (2) 
(a) 
Any given motion consists of other, smaller motion; there is no minimal unit of distance 

(b) 
If K is the class of possible states of the universe as it currently is and K* is the class of possible states of an otherwise identical universe that is more heterogeneous than others, K is a proper subset of K*. 


Given (2), it follows that (a) has nothing to do with the structure of motion, its real meaning being given by 
There is nothing paradoxical about (b). It is a truism, in fact. And there is no analogue of ZenoÂ’s paradox that holds in connection with (b). 
Systemic changes are too complex for us to understand with any precision. It is only by conceiving of them as system-internal changes that we can have any understanding of them. We should therefore expect contradictions to arise if take such approximations as bona fidetruths. 
Chapter 8 Do We Think in Words? 
1.0 Two different ways that knowledge of a language might enhance intelligence 
It is obvious that knowledge of a language makes one more intelligent in at least some respects. Consider the thought that authoritarian governments tend to be less responsive to the needs of their constituents than democratic governments. Could one grasp that thought without knowing some language or other? We have, I think, at least some inclination to say Â“no.Â” And, more generally, we are reluctant to regard creatures that cannot interact with reality through a language, or in any case through some sort of symbolic medium or other, as being capable of grasping, let alone delineating the consequences of, abstract principles or therefore of thinking about reality in a discursive manner. 
My own view, as weÂ’ll see shortly, is that this is falseÂ—that whatever one can grasp through language, one must be able to grasp independently of language. But this, I grant, is a counterintuitive view; and, speaking personally, it was only after trying to defend the negation of that view, and finding that it was impossible to do so, that I came to accept it. Still, our untutored intuitions do, I think, incline us to hold that, but for knowledge of a language (of some kind or other), a creature would be incapable of thinking discursively about the world. 
But untutored intuitions are not always probative. And sometimes they are inconsistent with one another, this being one of those cases. For, while we are reluctant to impute discursive thought to the language-less, we also strongly feel that we sometimes have thoughts of considerable sophistication that we donÂ’t know how to put into words; and, if that is right, then it seems to follow that not all discursive thought is language-dependent. 
The purpose of this chapter is to provide a brisk but relatively rigorous answer to the question: Do we think in language? 
2.0 Two different versions of the thesis that we think in language 
Do we think in language? No. But, before we can say why, there are two very different versions of the view that we think in language. 
Version #1: English speakers think in English; Albanian speakers think in Albanian; etc. In general, people think in the natural languages that they learn.[202] 
(A Â“natural languageÂ” is one that organically arises through human interactions. So English, Spanish, Arabic, Chinese, etc. are natural languages. A non-natural or Â“artificialÂ” language would be one that people inventÂ—for example, computer-programmers invent languages to serve their special needs, and so do mathematicians and philosophers. Philosophers invent special notations because natural languages often obscure important features of the logical structure of the meanings that their sentences express.) 
Version #2: We think in an innately known code, a Â“language of thought.Â” So although we think in sentences, those sentences donÂ’t belong to English or Spanish (etc.) but rather to some system of symbolism that is hard-wired into us from birth.[203] 

3.0 Why version #1 is wrong 
Do English speakers think in English, Spanish speakers in Spanish, etc.? No. (We will find that some of the arguments against Version #1 also apply to Version #2.) 
3.1 First reason 
We can obviously have thoughts that we are incapable of putting into words. This shows that we grasp those thoughts in some way other than by grasping the English sentences that express them. Also, there are occasions where, although we can put into words what we are thinking, doing so requires great effort: we have to think long and hard about which words to use. This shows that thinking is often a prerequisite to using language, which in turn shows that at least some thinking is non-linguistic. 
Astonishingly, many authors (e.g., Ludwig Wittgenstein, Simon Blackburn, John McDowell) deny that we know anything that we canÂ’t readily articulate. Â“If you canÂ’t say it, you donÂ’t know it,Â” they say. This presupposes that what we believe is expressed only in the words we utter. But thatÂ’s not the case. A given personÂ’s beliefs can be expressed in many ways, and many of them donÂ’t depend on that personÂ’s being able to use words. A personÂ’s knowledge of the differences between x and y may be expressed in that personÂ’s drawings of x and y; or it may be expressed in that personÂ’s movements while he is in the vicinity of x and y; or it may be expressed in some other non-linguistic manner. 
The way that authors such as Blackburn, McDowell, and Wittgenstein respond to this is to say that no bona fideknowledge is involved in my painting things accuratelyÂ—that what is involved is a kind of pseudo-knowledge.
