This is obviously false. It also overlooks the fact that, but for this Â“pseudo-knowledge,Â” we couldnÂ’t know anything about language, since it is only through our ability to differentiate noises, ink-marks, etc., on the basis of their perceptible properties that we can learn, or use, language. 
3.2 Second reason 
Some kinds of information (e.g., visual information) seem inherently incapable of being fully expressed by sentences of English or of any other natural language. Also, sentences have very different structures from pictures, even when the sentences and the pictures overlap in content. A visual perception of a man wearing a leather jacket has a very different structure from any sentence that describes that experience. For example, such a sentence decomposes into a finite number of distinct parts (words), whereas the sense-perception does not so decompose. (Sentences are digital structures, meaning that they consist of discrete entities. Sense-perceptions are analogue structures, meaning that they donÂ’t.) 
Also, any sentence must be interpreted to be understood. To understand the sentence Â“there is a man wearing a leather jacket over there,Â” you must know the relevant semantic rule (i.e., you must know the rules that assign meaning to that sentence). But you donÂ’t have to interpret a visual perception, at least not in the same way. Perceptions are Â“self-interpretingÂ” in a way that sentences are not.[204] 

3.3 Third reason 
In order to learn a language, one must already be able to think. To learn English is to learn that certain sounds have certain meanings; and in order to be able to do this, you already have to be able to synthesize informationÂ—to make judgments, on the basis of experience, as to what sounds have what meanings. So knowledge of a language presupposes the ability to think. 
3.4 Fourth reason 
Different sentences can have the same meaning, and a single sentence can have multiple meanings. What you think when you think that Bob loves Mary is identical with what you think when you think that Mary is loved by Bob. But the sentence Â“Bob loves MaryÂ” is different from the sentence Â“Mary is loved by Bob,Â” even though they mean the same thing. So if you thought in English sentences, then the belief youÂ’d have by virtue of accepting the sentence Â“Bob loves MaryÂ” would be totally different from the belief youÂ’d have by virtue of accepting the sentence Â“Mary is loved by Bob.Â” But the belief you have in virtue of accepting the one sentence is identical with the belief you have in virtue of accepting the other. 
Also, if you thought in language, you couldnÂ’t disambiguate ambiguous sentences. If your thinking Bob is dumb (i.e., unintelligent) were identical with there being an occurrence in your mind of the sentence Â“Bob is dumb,Â” then your thinking Bob is dumb (i.e., he canÂ’t speak) would be identical with there being an occurrence in your mind of that same sentence going off in your head, and those thoughts would therefore be identical. But they are not identical. So your thinking Bob is dumb (i.e., unintelligent) is not identical with your thinking Â“Bob is dumb.Â”[205] 

3.5 Fifth reason (similar to reason #4) 
People who speak different languages can have the same thoughts. Monolingual Spanish speakers believe that 1 + 1 = 2, and so do monolingual English speakers. But English and Spanish speakers use different sentences to express that truth, showing that thinking that truth cannot be identical with thinking a sentence of English or Spanish or, by obvious extensions of this line of thought, any other language. 
3.6 Sixth reason 
Understanding sentences involves thought. You must be able to think to understand what is meant by Â“if snow is cold, then snow is not hot.Â” This is because, in order to understand that sentence, you must be able to pair it off with the right meaning, and your pairing that sentence off with the right meaning is obviously different from an image of that sentence flashing through your mind. If I hear a sentence of a language that I donÂ’t understand, it may pass through my mind later (i.e., IÂ’ll remember the sounds later, just as songs that one has heard often flash through oneÂ’s consciousness), but I wonÂ’t know what it means. So understanding a sentence is different from its flashing through your mind. But if your thinking if snow is cold, then snow is not hot were identical with your thinking Â“if snow is cold, then snow is not hot,Â” then your having that thought would be identical with that sentenceÂ’s flashing through your mind. Since it isnÂ’t, we donÂ’t think in natural language. 
4.0 Why version #2 is false 
Do we think in some innate code? No. (Some of the arguments that we used against Version #1 obviously apply to Version #2. So we wonÂ’t repeat those.) 
4.1 First reason 
We often think in images (visual and auditory), and the contents of these images seem to have a structure that is fundamentally different from the structure of any sentence. Sentences are Â“digitalÂ” structures, meaning that they decompose into a finite number of distinct parts. Sense-perceptions are non-digital; they are Â“analogueÂ” structures, meaning that they donÂ’t decompose into discrete parts and are thus characterized by a kind of seamlessness that sharply distinguishes them from sentences. 
4.2 Second reason 
Knowing a language involves understanding the expressions belonging to it. Understanding such expressions involves knowing the rules that assign meaning to them. One canÂ’t understand any language, including an innately known one, without knowing such rules. But if oneÂ’s thought is entirely dependent on such a language, then one canÂ’t know those rules, or anything else for that matter, without understanding those expressions. Therefore it is viciously circular to hold that we think in an innately known code. 
4.2.1 How advocates of the view in question deal with this argument 
Advocates of the view that we think in an innate code deal with this problem by saying that, strictly speaking, we donÂ’t understand the sentences of our innate code. We are merely Â“built to conformÂ” to those sentences. In other words, although we donÂ’t understand those sentences, we are so neurologically structured that they cause us to act in ways that are appropriate to the meanings of those sentences. So if the sentence of my innate code that means fire is hot goes off in my head that fact will cause me to go near fire if IÂ’m cold and to stay away from it if IÂ’m hot (or some such). 
4.2.2 Why this move doesnÂ’t work 
If a sentence isnÂ’t understood by so and so, then from so and soÂ’s viewpoint it is not functioning as a sentence. If, as advocates of the viewpoint just presented maintain, nobody understands the sentences that mediate their thoughts, then those sentences arenÂ’t really functioning as sentences and, for all intents and purposes, they cease to be sentences. 
HereÂ’s an analogy. Suppose that you have a book, but that, instead of reading it, you use it as a weaponÂ—you throw it at your roommate, of whose antics you are growing increasingly tired. Even though the thing you are using as a weapon is a book, it is not in this context functioning as a book and, for all intents and purposes, is not a book. Similarly, if nobody understands the sentences that are, supposedly, identical with their own thoughts, then those sentences arenÂ’t really functioning as sentences anymore Â—theyÂ’re functioning more like the copy of War and Peace that, instead of being read, is being hurled at oneÂ’s roommate. 
Most importantly, the view that our thoughts are sentences that we donÂ’t understand is deeply implausible, if not tautologically false. 
So we may conclude that we donÂ’t think in language, even though, undeniably, knowledge of language enormously enhances at least some of our cognitive capabilities. 
5.0 Given that thoughts arenÂ’t identical with sentence-tokens, why is it that knowledge of language enhances cognitive ability and why does it feel as though we think in words? 
On your computer desktop, there are various Â“icons.Â” By manipulating these icons, you can perform various operationsÂ—you can close a document, open your email account, etc. But these icon-manipulations are but representations of changes in patterns of electrical activity to which they bear only an extremely schematic resemblance. 
When IÂ’m thinkingÂ—when, for example, IÂ’m trying to solve a problem (especially one connected to my work)Â—my thoughts often take the form of a voice. I have mental images of spoken words. This also happens when IÂ’m reading. Sometimes it happens that I read one book for a while (e.g., one by Frege) and then start reading another (e.g., one by comedian Dave Barry), and IÂ’m startled as to why Frege would say such things. Then I realize that IÂ’m no longer reading Frege and that I should therefore Â“switch voices.Â” 
And, of course, people think with the help of visual imagery. Many a student of calculus, or even of more advanced branches of mathematics, relies on mental images. I know I do.[206] 
But the images that go through my head when solving some problem arenÂ’t identical with the ratiocinative activities in which my problem-solving thought consists. Taken by themselves, those images are quite feeble. They donÂ’t specify the exact shape of the object IÂ’m thinking about. IÂ’ll use a five-sided figure to stand for a ten-sided figure, since I canÂ’t visualize the latter. But it doesnÂ’t matter, provided that I can find some mental icon that will stand for the relevant concept. The icon does not itself have to depict the concept or object it represents. It need only be sufficiently differentiated that I wonÂ’t confuse it with the image I am using to stand for some other concept of mine. 
But even if I were more visually adept and, for that reason, could produce more exact visual surrogates for the concepts IÂ’m thinking about, my ratiocinative activity couldnÂ’t possibly be identical with any sequence of images. For any given sequence of images, a creature that could experience those images wouldnÂ’t necessarily have any of the concepts that they represent in my thought processes. No matter how conceptually impoverished a creature is, little or nothing follows as to what sorts of images can go off in its head. 
But everything constitutive of consciousness seems to be image-like or, at the very least, to share with images the property of being phenomenologically pregnant.[207] 
Wittgenstein (1958) concluded from this that thinking isnÂ’t a private psychological act. For reasons that weÂ’ll discuss in the next section, he inferred that thinking consists of engaging in overt behaviors that involve symbols belonging to some public language.[208] 

WittgensteinÂ’s position is rank absurdity. HeÂ’s right, of course, that tickles, itches, etc., arenÂ’t thoughts.[209] 
But what follows isnÂ’t that thoughts arenÂ’t mental entities. What follows is that thoughts, unlike itches and tickles, arenÂ’t phenomenologically pregnant. 
Incidentally, the mistake Wittgenstein is making here is very similar to a mistake that David Hume makes in connection with the nature of personal identity. David Hume argues that there is nothing to oneÂ’s mind other than the conscious events that populate it.[210] 
His argument is that, when he introspects, he only encounters various tickles, pains, and other sensations. This argument assumes that everything there is to know about oneÂ’s mind is to be known in the same quasi-perceptual, phenomenology-drenched way in which we know of our sensations. But this assumption is blatantly false. I know that I believe that 2 + 2 = 4, and I know it in a relatively direct way. But it isnÂ’t because I experience some sensation or mental image or other phenomenologically pregnant entity that I know this. 
WittgensteinÂ’s view that thinking consists of manipulating expressions is inconsistent with the fact that, unless one can think, one cannot use expressions meaningfully. If I just bark out sounds, having no idea what they mean, IÂ’m not in any real sense using language. For my noise-making to be speech, it must be guided by a knowledge of what those noises mean. 
Wittgenstein is right that the sensations and images that pass through oneÂ’s mind when one is having a given thought do not constitute that thought. But heÂ’s wrong to conclude that thinking isnÂ’t a psychological process. (As previously stated, what he should have concluded is that not all psychological activity consists of images and sensations.) HeÂ’s also wrong to conclude that those images categorically have no significant cognitive function. Mental imagery facilitates thought. Thanks to it, we have thoughts that we otherwise simply couldnÂ’t have. 
Given this data, I would suggest the following. Though not themselves constitutive of thought, mental images allow us to manage thought-processes that we otherwise couldnÂ’t manage. Just as one can manipulate otherwise uncontrollable patterns of electrical activity by manipulating the icons on oneÂ’s computer desktop, so one can manipulate otherwise uncontrollable patterns of ratiocinative activity by manipulating cognitive imagery. 
There is another relevant point. Consciousness is a place where there are different streams of cognitive activityÂ—where otherwise mutually isolated streams of cognitive activity can meet. The processes that create an olfactory or auditory perception are isolated from those involved in reading music or understanding facial expressions. But, in consciousness, sense-perceptions meet with judgments and with intentions to act, and so on. Consciousness has the effect, and maybe the purpose, of integrating otherwise mutually isolated streams of cognitive activity and, therefore, of pooling otherwise discrete bodies of knowledge. Mental imagery improves thought because it enables otherwise compartmentalized ratiocinative activities to borrow information from other similar activities from which they would otherwise be sealed off. 
By virtue of knowing a language, one automatically has at oneÂ’s disposal a rich and easily operated system of icons by means of which one can manage oneÂ’s cognitive activities in the way just described. This, I would suggest, is why knowledge of a language does so much for thought. 
6.0 Wittgenstein on language, thought, and the relationship between the two 
Ludwig Wittgenstein (1889Â–1951) put forth several provocative contentions about language.[211] 
Perhaps the most celebrated of these is his contention that there cannot possibly exist such a thing as a private language. Human beings can devise private codes, he granted. But, Wittgenstein says, any such code must be a translation of an existing public language. It isnÂ’t even theoretically possible, Wittgenstein thought, for there to exist a language that wasnÂ’t created by several interacting individuals. 
Once such a language is created, Wittgenstein grants, a single person can use it on his ownÂ—he can go off into the woods and keep records with it. But any case of a single personÂ’s using a language for his own private use is, in WittgensteinÂ’s view, parasitic on there being, or once having been, a multiplicity of people using that same language. 
Wittgenstein isnÂ’t making the pedestrian point that, as a matter of psychological fact, it would be hard, maybe even impossible, for somebody to single-handedly create a language (other than one that was a translation of an existing language). HeÂ’s saying that itÂ’s logically impossibleÂ—that such a language is a surd, like a square circle. 
Wittgenstein also held that one canÂ’t think unless one knows a language. Wittgenstein seemed to grant that one could have mental states without knowing a language. But he pretty clearly thought that knowledge of a language was a prerequisite for any sort of reasoning. 
If Wittgenstein is right, one cannot think unless one is embedded in a society of some kind. It is not just psychologically, but also logically impossible, Wittgenstein thought, for a human being who isnÂ’t either a current or erstwhile member of a society to think. These contentions, along with WittgensteinÂ’s arguments for them, are put forth in his book The Philosophical Investigations. 
Wittgenstein provides an interesting argument for his view that there cannot be a private language, which is known, appropriately enough, as the Private Language Argument (PLA). WeÂ’ll discuss PLA in a moment. 
Wittgenstein provides two distinct arguments for the position that one cannot think without knowing a language. Because of the similarities between them, contemporary authors tend not to distinguish these arguments from one another, and they are collectively referred as to the Rule Following 
Argument. 
6.1 WittgensteinÂ’s first Rule-Following Argument 
(RF[212]) Not all ideation is ratiocinative. For ideation to be ratiocinative, it must be rule-governed. That is, it must be guided by a knowledge of the canons of logic. Thus, thinking involves following rules. 
But there is no psychological condition or event that necessarily accompanies an act of following a rule. To see this, go ahead and follow some rule. (Add two multi-digit numbers together; read some passage out loud.) When you introspect, you may find that you are experiencing these or those feelings or images. But you could obviously follow the rule in question without having such experiences. Thus, following a rule is not a psychological act. 
Contrary to what this argument assumes, not all mental states are images or sensations.[213] 
Your belief that 1 + 1 = 2 isnÂ’t such a thing; and your deploying that belief on some specific occasion isnÂ’t identical with your experiencing some image or sensation or series of images or sensations. 
Not everything in your mind is a fleeting conscious event. Much of what constitutes your mind consists of stable, enduring structures. Your belief that snow is white isnÂ’t a flash in the pan. ItÂ’s been there for a while, and will continue to be there for a while and though it gives rise to momentarily conscious events, it isnÂ’t identical with any such event or with any aggregate of such events. Contrary to what Wittgenstein alleges, given only that there is no tickle or itch or other fleeting mental event that necessarily accompanies an act of rule-following, it doesnÂ’t follow that rule following isnÂ’t a psychological act 
6.1.1 WittgensteinÂ’s second Rule-Following Argument 
(RF2) Consider the sentence Â“rabid dogs always foam at the 
mouth.Â” For argumentÂ’s sake, letÂ’s suppose that there exists 
some entity M that is the meaning of this sentence. LetÂ’s also 
suppose that, without grasping or operating with the sentence 
Â“rabid dogs foam at the mouthÂ” or any other expression, you 
behold MÂ—you grasp it. You see itÂ—through your Â“mindÂ’s 
eye,Â” or some such. Finally, letÂ’s suppose that you not only 
grasp M, but know it to be true. In other words, you know that 
rabid dogs foam at the mouth. 
If you canÂ’t see that, given M, Fido canÂ’t be rabid without 
foaming at the mouth, your grasp of M is, to that extent, 
useless and as good as non-existent. Thus, so far as you donÂ’t 
grasp how M bears on other meaningsÂ—so far as you donÂ’t 
grasp its significance, in other wordsÂ—your grasp of M is 
useless and might as well not exist. The problem we had with 
the sentence Â“rabid dogs foam at the mouthÂ” arises in 
connection with M. Wanting to explain what it is to understand 
that sentence, we posited M. But it turned out that M is just like 
that sentence: itÂ’s useless unless its meaning is grasped. M 
turned out to be just another symbolÂ—just another cognitively 
dead symbolic intermediary. 
Meanings are themselves symbols. So unless we already 
know what it is to understand symbols, positing symbol-
meanings doesnÂ’t help us understand the nature of symbol-
comprehension. Positing symbol meanings in the hopes of 
explaining symbol-comprehension is like positing little people 
inside peopleÂ’s heads in the hopes of explaining how people 
think.[214] 
Positing these little people is useless unless itÂ’s 
already understood how people think. Positing meanings is 
useless unless itÂ’s already known how symbols are understood. 
6.1.2 WittgensteinÂ’s second rule-Following agument criticized from a Platonic viewpoint 
This argument of WittgensteinÂ’s bears a striking resemblance to AristotleÂ’s Third Man Argument (TMA).[215] 
The purpose of TMA is to undermine PlatoÂ’s contention that spatiotemporal entities are instances of properties and, in addition, that the latter are not spatiotemporal. It will help if we take a moment to consider AristotleÂ’s argument (it will soon be clear why the third and fourth sentences are italicized): 
(TMA) For argumentÂ’s sake, suppose that there is such a thing as the property of being a triangle. Let T1 be that thing. If 
Platonism is right, T1 must itself be a triangle. Further, if Platonism is right, any case of two objectsÂ’ sharing some property is a case of there being some third object of which theyÂ’re both instances. Thus, if T2 is some triangle, there must 
be some third object T3 such that each of T1 and T2 is an instance of T3. But, by the same logic, there must be some fourth thing T4 such that each of T1, T2, and T3 is an instance of T4. And so on ad infinitum. 
AristotleÂ’s argument assumes that properties are instances of themselvesÂ— that the property of being a triangle is itself triangular. But thatÂ’s precisely what Platonism denies.[216] 
Platonism is the doctrine that spatiotemporal things are but instances of non-spatiotemporal things, the latter being properties. The property of being spatiotemporal is therefore itself nonÂ­spatiotemporal and, therefore isnÂ’t an instance of itself. And the property of being a cat obviously isnÂ’t a cat, since cats are spatiotemporal, whereas that property is not.[217] 

Just as, according to Aristotle, Platonism is struck with the problem of explaining why the property of being a triangle was itself a triangle, so according to Wittgenstein, those who believe in meanings are stuck with the problem of explaining how meanings are understood. 
But meanings are not themselves understood. TheyÂ’re no more understood than the property of being a cat is a cat. Consider the expression Â“I.Â” IÂ’m referring, not to specific occurrences (utterances, inscriptions) of that expression, but to that expression itselfÂ—the expression-type, in other words, as opposed to its tokens. The meaning of that expression is some rule that assigns referents to its tokens depending on the circumstances. More precisely, the meaning of Â“IÂ” is a rule to the effect that a token t of that expression that is uttered by x refers to x. My knowing that Â“IÂ” has that meaning is part of what enables me to understand utterances of Â“IÂ’m getting really bored,Â” Â“I really like snow-boarding,Â” etc. But that meaning is not itself understood. Meanings are either grasped or theyÂ’re not. ThereÂ’s no such thing as grasping a meaning but not understanding it. 
A consequence is that meanings donÂ’t have to be interpreted. ItÂ’s incoherent to suppose that Hoigaard (who, letÂ’s assume, is Norwegian) should be able to grasp this meaning, but fail to see that people were referring to themselves when they said Â“I." 
This isnÂ’t to say, what would clearly be false, that one automatically recognizes every consequence of every principle that one grasps. People fail to see the consequences of the principles they grasp. In fact, since any given proposition has infinitely many consequences, people fail to grasp infinitely many consequences of anything that they grasp. But to the extent that oneÂ’s grasp of a given principle is determinative of what one knows, there isnÂ’t a gap between grasping meaning, on the one hand, and applying it, on the other. And to the extent that one doesnÂ’t see the consequences of some meaning or principle that one grasps, it isnÂ’t because one has failed to interpret it. 
A story will clarify these points. Brown is a highly (but not superhumanly) intelligent person who not only speaks perfect English, but is exceptionally (but, again, not superhumanly) adept at understanding highly intricate sentences. XYZ is a sentence of English that is 100,000 words long but is otherwise normal. XYZ is grammatical, coherent, etc.[218] 
Even though Brown knows the relevant semantic rules, he obviously canÂ’t understand XYZ. But the problem isnÂ’t that Brown canÂ’t interpret the relevant semantic principles. The problem is that, because that sentence is so long, he canÂ’t deploy his semantic knowledge. In and of itself, that semantic knowledge is good to go. But, under the circumstances, itÂ’s weighed down by limitations on BrownÂ’s part that have nothing at all to do with his semantic competence. BrownÂ’s memory isnÂ’t perfect; he canÂ’t keep too many tasks going in his mind simultaneously, even if any given one of them is elementary. These arenÂ’t semantic limitations on BrownÂ’s part. The problem isnÂ’t that he doesnÂ’t know the relevant semantic rules. Nor is it that he hasnÂ’t adequately interpreted the semantic rules that he grasps. The problem is that his grasp of those principles is being inhibited by shortcomings that in no way detract from his semantic competence, even though they do limit his ability to deploy it. To the extent that what Brown knows is determined by his grasping those semantic rules, Brown does understand the expressions to which they assign meaning. But, of course, what Brown knows is a function of many things besides his grasp of those principles. 
WittgensteinÂ’s idea that meanings, if grasped, must be interpreted reflects his erroneous belief that, whenever one canÂ’t see a consequence of some principle that one grasps, itÂ’s because one hasnÂ’t adequately interpreted that principle. But principles arenÂ’t interpreted. TheyÂ’re grasped. And, if grasped, they guide judgments. And to the extent that oneÂ’s grasp of a principle is determinative of what one knows, those judgments are consistent with those principles. But, of course, oneÂ’s grasp of a given principle is but one factor among many determining the course of oneÂ’s thought-process; so oneÂ’s grasp of that principle may be prevented from eventuating in the judgments in which it would otherwise eventuate. But when that happens, it isnÂ’t because that principle wasnÂ’t adequately interpreted. 
6.2 The private language argument 
Neither of WittgensteinÂ’s attempts to show that thinking isnÂ’t a psychological act is probative. TheyÂ’re interesting arguments, if IÂ’ve interpreted them correctly; and if I havenÂ’t, itÂ’s an interesting question how they ought to be interpreted. But given what weÂ’ve seen, we have no reason to reject the plausible, if not self-evident, position that thinking is a psychological act. 
But, of course, Wittgenstein doesnÂ’t see it this way. Believing himself to have definitively established (the radically absurd principle) that rule-following and, more generally, thought arenÂ’t mental processes; he attempts to show that there can be no private languages. Here is his argument: 
(WA)[219] 
Imagine the following. Smith is alone on a desert island. HeÂ’s always been this way and, therefore, has never learned a language. But he wishes to create one. He thus decides to stipulate that the meanings of expressions X1...Xn are 
to be respectively, tree, berry, sand, sun, etc. (He also specifies how those symbols are to be written down. For some reason, he has a notebook and a pen.) He does this all on Monday. WeÂ’ll refer to the language Smith creates as Â“Smithese1.Â” One 
of the semantic rules for Smithese1 is to the effect that: 
X35: means that the berries on the dark side of the hill are poisonous. 
That same day, Smith sees some poisonous berries on the dark side of the hill, and writes X35 down in his notebook. (Let 
X35 be our symbol for that particular inscription.) On Tuesday, he reads what he wrote down. Question: is there any way that Smith can misinterpret what heÂ’s written? If he takes X35 to 
mean that the sun is out, his interpretation of X35 will be 
inconsistent with his Monday intentions. But so what? Smith is the only person who speaks Smithese1, so the expressions belonging to Smithese1 mean whatever Smith thinks they 
mean. It follows that there could not exist a language that, like 
Smithese1, is private. An English-speaker canÂ’t just decide that Â“snow is whiteÂ” means that grass is green. For it is the thoughts and practices of people in general, and not of this or that specific person, that determines what is meant by Â“snow is white.Â” But in this context, Smith is Â“people in general.Â” So his believing that X35 means that the sun is out is like everybodyÂ’s 
deciding that Â“snow is whiteÂ” means that grass is green. And just as Â“snow is whiteÂ” would mean that if everybody thought it did, so X35 means that the sun is out because, in effect, 
everybody thinks it does, the reason being that, in this context, 
Smith is everybody. 
Thus, the expressions of Smithese1 mean whatever Smith thinks they mean. This means that he canÂ’t be wrong as to what they mean. 
But a symbol that canÂ’t be used wrongly doesnÂ’t mean anything. What makes utterances of Â“John is a soccer playerÂ” meaningful is that they are used wrongly if John isnÂ’t a soccer player. If Â“John is a soccer playerÂ” couldnÂ’t be used wrongly, you couldnÂ’t conclude anything from the fact that such an utterance was correctÂ—you would be no less entitled to conclude that the moon was made of Styrofoam than you would be to conclude that the dog ate your wig. 
Thus, there are languages only where there are right and wrong ways to use expressions. Since it is only where several people are using a language that there are right and wrong ways of using its expressions, it is only where there are several people that there are languages: all languages are public. 
WA is spurious and establishes nothing. First of all, unless we can trust 
our sense-perceptions and our memories, the testimony of other people as to 
what words mean is worthless. If I canÂ’t trust the sense-perceptions involved 
in my being told what the word Â“grapeÂ” means, and if I canÂ’t trust the 
memories deposited by those perceptions, then I have no reason to give any 
credence to the testimony of the people who defined that word for me. So the supervision of others is useful only to the extent that I can trust my memories. But to the extent that I can trust my memories, I am competent to remember how IÂ’ve defined words belonging to a private language that IÂ’ve invented; and WittgensteinÂ’s argument implodes. 
But WittgensteinÂ’s argument involves other, equally profound blunders. The reason that expressions of English (or any other public language) are meaningful is that people remember what they mean. If everybody forgot what Â“snowÂ” meant, it wouldnÂ’t be of much use. To be sure, where English is concerned, no one personÂ’s forgetting the meaning of a word is going to strip of it meaningfulness, since there are millions of others who still know it. But that only means that English is causally more deeply entrenched than a language, such as Smithese1, that only one person speaks. This is not to 
mention that, if I forget the semantic rules for English, it will be as useless to me as Smithese1 would be to Smith if he forgets the semantic rules of Smithese1. By the same token, if Smith remembers the semantic rules for 
Smithese1, the expressions of that language will be useful for him. HeÂ’ll know not to eat the berries on the dark side of the hill; heÂ’ll know where the good-tasting aardvarks are; etc.[220] 

What about WittgensteinÂ’s point that the expressions of Smithese1 mean 
only what Smith thinks they mean? A language is a set of semantic rules. If, on Monday, X35 means that the berries on the dark side of the hill are poisonous, whereas on Tuesday that same inscription means that the sun is 
out, then the language Smith is using on Tuesday is ipso facto a distinct one from the language he is using on Monday. On Tuesday, heÂ’s speaking Smithese2, not Smithese1. Therefore, X35 means that the sun is out only if it 
isnÂ’t an expression of Smithese1. The expressions of Smithese1, then, donÂ’t 
mean whatever Smith thinks they mean. If his opinions assign new meanings to X1...Xn, those opinions are creating a new language that happens to be orthographically and phonetically coincident with Smithese1; those opinions arenÂ’t assigning new meanings to expressions constituting some existing 
language. So Wittgenstein is just wrong to say that the expressions of Smithese1 mean whatever Smith thinks they do.[221] 

Thinking seems to involve following rules. Wittgenstein grants that people think. But since he believes totally absurdly, that rule-following and, therefore, thinking arenÂ’t psychological acts, he is forced to come up with a different analysis of what thought is. He wrongly says that thought consists in the manipulations of symbols. Given his belief that there arenÂ’t private languages, he holds that to think is to manipulate symbols of public languages. 
Given that RF and WA are spurious arguments for false conclusions, Wittgenstein has given us no good reason to accept this position. In any case, we know it to be an erroneous one. A prerequisite for speaking a language is knowing its semantic rules and being able to operate in an intelligent and, consequently, thought-mediated fashion. 
Chapter 9 Modality and Non-Existence 
1.0 Necessity and possibility properties of statements, not objects 
A modal statement is one that says what could be the case or what must be the case. Here are some examples of such statements: 
(1) 
Triangles must have three sides. 

(2) 
ItÂ’s possible to make money without selling out. 

(3) 
ThereÂ’s no way anyone could have survived that fall. 


(4) 
Assuming that Bob has fifty cars, he must have at least some money. 

(5) 
JohnÂ’s becoming stronger was an inevitable consequence of his lifting weights all summer. 


For any proposition P, itÂ’s necessarily the case that P iff itÂ’s not possible that not-P; and itÂ’s possible that P iff itÂ’s not necessarily the case that not-P. (Â“IffÂ” is short for Â“if and only if.Â”) ItÂ’s necessarily the case that Jim is in the barn iff itÂ’s not possible that Jim is not in the barn; and itÂ’s possibly the case that Jim is in the barn iff itÂ’s not necessarily the case that Jim is not in the barn. 
There are no impossible objects (no objects that couldnÂ’t possibly exist). And there are no possible but non-actual objects (no objects that could exist but donÂ’t). Possibility and impossibility are properties of propositions, not of objects. For example: 
(6) "square circles cannot possibly exist," 
says that the proposition: 
(7) there are square circles, 
cannot possibly be correct. (6) doesnÂ’t make the self-contradictory claim that there exists some object x such that x is a square circle and such that x cannot exist. And: 
(8) "happiness is a possibility for Jim, even though heÂ’s still miserable," says that, even though Jim is now miserable, the proposition: 
(9) Jim is happy, 
could be true. (8) doesnÂ’t make the absurd claim that there exists some x such that x is JimÂ’s as of yet nonexistent happiness and such that x could exist. 
1.1 Existence and non-existence properties of propositions, not of objects 
The points just made concerning the concepts of possibility and impossibility are to be understood in terms of more general points concerning the concepts of existence and non-existence. 
Nothing doesnÂ’t exist. There exists no x such that x doesnÂ’t exist. Statements that, given their surface-structures, appear to attribute non-existence to objects in fact attribute falsity to propositions. A story will make this clear. 
An unscrupulous person claims to have been attacked. In reality, he wasnÂ’t attacked; but, for whatever reason, itÂ’s to his advantage for people to believe otherwise. He describes his non-existent assailant to a police sketch artist. The resulting sketch is distributed across the nation. If we say that the sketch depicts a nonexistent person, weÂ’re saying that there exists some person who doesnÂ’t exist who it depicts. But that would be absurd. The sketch is better thought of as saying: there is somebody having such and such features, these being the features that a person would have to have if he were to fit the sketch. Though false, that statementÂ—that existence-claim--obviously exists. 
Similarly, the cartoons that brought Fred Flintstone and Bart Simpson into our homes can be thought of as making false statements of a similar kind. In the case of Fred Flintstone, that statement is along the lines of: there exists a boorish man who has a pet dinosaur named Â“Dino,Â” a wife named Â“Wilma,Â” etc. In the case of Bart Simpson that claim makes a statement along the lines of: there exists a bratty boy who torments his oafish father with his loveable shenanigans, etc. 
All of these statements exist; theyÂ’re simply not true. Nothing answers the descriptions encoded in them. Therein lies the real meaning of Â“Fred Flintstone/Bart Simpson doesnÂ’t exist.Â” The real meaning is clearly not some absurd claim to the effect that there exists some entity that doesnÂ’t exist. 
2.0 Necessity does not come in degrees 
Here is a view about modality that is false, as weÂ’ll see in a moment, but is nonetheless a useful starting point[222]: 
(DN) There are different degrees of necessity. Â“Squares have four sides.Â” This is necessary in the strongest sense. The very idea of a squareÂ’s failing to have four sides is an incoherent one. 
Â“Metal expands when heated.Â” This is not as necessary as Â“squares have four sides,Â” since the idea of a universe in which metal didnÂ’t expand when heated is not incoherent. But, given that it describes a law of physics, and is therefore utterly unalterable, it clearly has a high degree of necessity. 
Â“After surgery, people are unusually prone to get infections and must be given antibiotics to stave them off.Â” There is clearly some sense in which this is necessarily true. An immunologically normal person who wasnÂ’t more prone to get infections after surgery is a medical impossibility. And, unless he qualified his point very heavily, a professor of medicine who denied this would be misleading his students. But this statement clearly isnÂ’t as necessary as the others. 
DN is false. There are only two degrees of necessity: having it completely and lacking it completely. When we say that P is Â“more necessaryÂ” than Q, weÂ’re saying something about the conditions that must hold for those statements to be true; weÂ’re saying that the conditions that must hold for the first to be true are weaker than those that must hold if the second is to be true. Â“Squares have four sidesÂ” is maximally necessary, because it holds unconditionally. In any universe at all, no matter how mass-energy is distributed in it, that statement is 
true.[223] 
So no condition has to be met for that statement to be true. Or, to think of it another way, the only conditions that have to be met are maximally weak: they could be thought of as limiting cases of conditions that are trivially satisfied by any distribution of mass-energy. To say that Â“metal expands when heatedÂ” is Â“less necessaryÂ” than Â“squares have four sidesÂ” is to say that the former could to be true in a wider class of circumstances than the latter; and to say that Â“after surgery, people are unusually prone to get infectionsÂ” is Â“less necessaryÂ” than Â“metal expands when heatedÂ” is to say that the former could fail in a wider class of circumstances than the latter. 
So there arenÂ’t really degrees of necessity. Something is either necessary or it isnÂ’t. But some statements (e.g., Â“two is bigger than oneÂ”) need less help from others to be trueÂ—those are the Â“highly necessaryÂ” ones. Others (e.g., Â“people who wear hats are bad driversÂ”) need a little more helpÂ—those are the Â“less necessaryÂ” ones. 
3.0 No necessary a posteriori 
In 1969, Saul Kripke gave a now famous series of lectures in which he 
argued that there are non-analytic necessary truths. Here, in my words, is 
KripkeÂ’s argument (Â“KAÂ” for short): 
(KA) The ancients referred to the last celestial body (besides the Sun) to disappear from the morning sky as Â“PhosphorousÂ” (or, to be precise, they referred to it with an expression whose Anglicization is Â“PhosphorousÂ”), and they referred to the first celestial body to appear in the evening sky as Â“HesperusÂ” (same qualification). The former is Venus and so is the latter, and the former is therefore identical with the latter. The ancients didnÂ’t yet know this; and they went for a very long time having no idea that some one celestial body appeared in the evening sky before any other, and disappeared from the morning sky after any other. But eventually they found this out. What they found out isnÂ’t trivial, of course; it isnÂ’t in the same category as the fact that Hesperus is identical with Hesperus. What they discovered is a non-trivial, empirical fact. 
Henceforth, Â“FESÂ” and Â“LMSÂ” will be our abbreviations for the predicates Â“first celestial body to appear in the evening skyÂ” and, respectively, Â“last celestial body (besides the Sun) to disappear from the morning sky.Â” 
Contrary to what it is extremely tempting to believe: 
(HIP)[224] 
Â“Hesperus is Phosphorous,Â” 
does not have the same meaning as: 
(S*) Â“the LMS is identical with the FES.Â” 
It will take a moment to make it clear why this is so. Let P be the proposition expressed by HIP. As we just saw, empirical investigation was needed to establish the truth of P; so P is an empirical truth and is therefore non-analytic. ItÂ’s important to keep the distinction between HIP and P in mind. The ancients didnÂ’t have any feelings about the English sentence Â“Hesperus is identical with Hesperus.Â” And, in making the astronomical discovery that weÂ’ve been discussing, what they found out had nothing to do with HIPÂ—or any other sentence. It was an astronomical, not a linguistic, discovery. This point is crucial. 
Moving on: If HIP has the same meaning as S*, then P is identical with the proposition meant by S*. And the latter is equivalent with the proposition that: 
(P*) exactly one thing is an LMS and exactly one thing is an FES, and nothing that has the one property lacks the other. 
[225] 

The same is true of P, supposing that S* and HIP express the same proposition. 
In light of these points, consider a world W* satisfying the following conditions. W* is semantically just like our world. (Two worlds or situations are Â“semantically identicalÂ” if the rules that govern word-usage in the one coincide with those that govern it in the other.) So, in W*, people speak English. But, in W*, Venus isnÂ’t the LMS or the FES. In W*, because of some cataclysm that didnÂ’t occur in our world, Mars is the LMS, and Mercury is the FES. So, in W*, Â“the LMSÂ” picks out Mars, and Â“the FESÂ” picks out Mercury. This follows from the fact that W* is semantically just like our world.(If John McCain had become President in 2008 instead of Barack Obama, Â“the U.S. PresidentÂ” would, given the semantic rules that we use, refer to McCain. But, given those very same rules, Â“Barack ObamaÂ” would still refer to Barack Obama. In other words, if x is the person who in our world is referred to as Â“Barack Obama,Â” Â“Barack ObamaÂ” would refer to x in W*. Similarly, if Mars were the LMS, as opposed to Venus, Â“the LMSÂ” would, given the semantic rules that we use, refer to Mars. But given those same rules, Â“VenusÂ” would still refer to Venus. In other words, if x is the planet that in our world is referred to as Â“Venus,Â” Â“VenusÂ” would refer to x in W*. 
Â“Venus,Â” like Â“Barack Obama,Â” is thus a rigid designator. If x is what Â“VenusÂ” in fact refers to, x is what Â“VenusÂ” would refer to in any world semantically like ours. But Â“the LMS,Â” like Â“the current U.S. President,Â” is not a rigid designator; it refers to different things in semantically identical situations. (It used to refer to Carter; now it refers to Obama. But the semantic rules governing that expression havenÂ’t changed in the least in the meantime.) 
In general, proper names are rigid designators. Â“HesperusÂ” and Â“PhosphorousÂ” are proper names. Therefore, unlike Â“the LMSÂ” and Â“the FES,Â” they are rigid designators. So as long as the semantic rules of English havenÂ’t changed, there is some one object x such that: 
(i) Â“HesperusÂ” refers to x, and so does Â“PhosphorousÂ”; 
and, consequently, such that: 
(ii) each of Â‹Hesperus has phiÂ› and Â‹Phosphorous has phiÂ› is true exactly if x has phi; 
a corollary being that: 
(iii) Â“Hesperus is Phosphorous.Â” 
It is obvious that, for any object x, the proposition x is identical with x is necessarily true. But itÂ’s equally obvious that the proposition expressed by HIP is empirical, and therefore non-analytic. Therefore, HIP expresses a non-analytic necessary truth. 
3.1 KripkeÂ’s argument evaluated 
This argument involves a massive non-sequitur. A story will make this clear. I meet a man. We shake hands. I obviously see what he looks like. He tells me that his name is Â“Hesperus.Â” (Without worrying about the details, letÂ’s assume that I know him to be telling me the truth.) In this context, there is some individual x such that I am learning that: 
(HX) Â“HesperusÂ” is xÂ’s name. 
But what I am learning must be distinguished from the information through which I am learning it. The information relayed to me by my senses isnÂ’t confined to HX. It would be absurd to think otherwise. That information is more along the lines of: 
(BHX) There is some individual x such that x is standing right in front of me (in my office in Richmond, VA) at this moment (3:00 P.M., March 13, 2009) and such that x has such and such characteristics (he has a mustache, heÂ’s over six feet tall, etc.) and such that I am being told, by x himself, that Â“HesperusÂ” is xÂ’s name. 
So there is some x such that Â“HesperusÂ” merely labels x. Â“HesperusÂ” doesnÂ’t have for any part of its meaning anything having to do with the property of being over six feet, having a mustache, being in this or that place at this or that time. But the information through which I learn whom Â“HesperusÂ” labels does concern such properties. That information is descriptive; a certain person x is visually represented, and thus described, to me as having certain characteristics (over six-feet tall, etc.); and, with the help of this information, it is also being made clear to me that Â“HesperusÂ” names x. But that descriptive information is not itself a part of the semantic rule that, with its help, I am learningÂ—that is to say, it is not itself any part of HX. HX is extremely threadbare; it merely puts a label on a certain object. So the just-mentioned descriptive information has no place in the semantics of Â“HesperusÂ”; its relevance is confined to the pre-semantic act of assigning it to the right object. That information isnÂ’t semantic; itÂ’s pre-semantic. 
The following evening, I receive a phone call. I donÂ’t recognize the callerÂ’s voice. The caller is obviously using a voice-modulation device, giving it a metallic, threatening sound. And threaten is just what he does; for he says Â“if you donÂ’t move out of town, IÂ’m going to kill you. By the way, my name is Phosphorous.Â” I look at my caller ID; and, sure enough, the call is from one Â“Phosphorous.Â” 
In this context, there is some individual y such that I am learning that: 
(PX) Â“PhosphorousÂ” is yÂ’s name. 
PX merely registers the fact that a certain name is associated with a certain object. It doesnÂ’t say anything (else) about that object. It doesnÂ’t say whether that object is tall or short, friendly or unfriendly. PX is exceedingly threadbare. But the information through which I am learning PX is very different from PX itself. That informationÂ—that pre-semantic informationÂ— is along the lines of: 
(BPX) There is some individual y such that, a moment ago 
(7:00 P.M., March 14, 2009), y called me; such that, using a voice-modulation device to disguise his voice, y is making threatening statements; and such that I am being told, by y himself, that Â“PhosphorousÂ” is yÂ’s name. 
Here must we repeat (mutatis mutandis) what we said a moment ago. There is some y such that Â“PhosphorousÂ” merely labels y. Â“HesperusÂ” doesnÂ’t have for any part of its meaning anything having to do with the property of talking on the phone with me at a certain time, or of using a voice-modulation device, or of making threats. But the information through which I learn whom Â“PhosphorousÂ” labels does concern such properties. That information is descriptive; a certain person y is perceptually represented, and thus described, to me as having certain characteristics (calling me at a certain time, making certain statements, etc.) and, with the help of this information, it is also being made clear to me that Â“PhosphorousÂ” names x. But that descriptive information is not itself a part of the semantic rule that, with its help, I am learningÂ—that is to say, it is not itself any part of PX. PX is extremely threadbare; it merely puts a label on a certain object. So the just-mentioned descriptive information has no place in the semantics of Â“Phosphorous,Â” its relevance is confined to the pre-semantic act of assigning it to the right object. That information is entirely pre-semantic. 
But such pre-semantic information can have an incalculably profound effect on what is (non-semantically; i.e., non-literally) conveyed by utterances. A continuation of our story makes this clear. Right after getting the upsetting phone call, the police call. For some reason, they know about the phone call. They say to me: 
(A1) Â“Phosphorous is a professor of political science.Â” 
There is some y such that A1 does nothing more than affirm the innocuous proposition that: 
(A2) y is a professor of political science. 
But under the circumstances, what will be conveyed to me is some much richer proposition along the lines of: 
(A3) There is some individual y such that, a little while ago (at around 7:00 P.M., March 14, 2009), y rang me; such that, using a voice-modulation device to disguise his voice, y is making threatening statements; such that I am being told, by y himself, that Â“PhosphorousÂ” is yÂ’s name; and, finally, such that y is a professor of political science. 
The pre-semantic information embedded in BPX affects what I take away 
from the policemanÂ’s utterance of A1, even though it is no part of its literal meaning. For exactly similar reasons, the pre-semantic information embedded in BHX affects what I would take away from an utterance of: 
(B1) Â“Hesperus is an avid tennis player.Â” 
There is some x such that B1 does nothing more than affirm the descriptively impoverished proposition that: 
(B2) x is an avid tennis player. 
But under the circumstances, what that utterance conveys to me is some much richer proposition along the lines of: 
(B3) There is some individual x such that, a couple of days ago (March 13, 2009) at about 3:00 P.M., x is standing right in front of me (in my office in Richmond, VA); such that x has such and such characteristics (he has a mustache, heÂ’s over six-feet tall, etc.); such that Â“HesperusÂ” is xÂ’s name; and such that x is an avid tennis player. 
We need only add one finishing touch to our story to see whatÂ’s wrong with KripkeÂ’s reasoning. The police arrest Phosphorous. They ask me to come down to the station to talk to them. They point to Phosphorous (who is handcuffed) and say: Â“thatÂ’s Phosphorous.Â” Phosphorous, I now see, is none other than Hesperus. The man I see is the mustachioed man I met a few days earlier. The police then say: Â“Phosphorous also goes by the name of Hesperus. His legal name is Â‘Hesperus Phosphorous.Â’ But he tends to introduce himself as either Â‘HesperusÂ’ or Â‘Phosphorous.Â’ In any case, Hesperus is Phosphorous.Â” The italicized sentence is none other than HIP, of course. 
Given what weÂ’ve already learned, itÂ’s obvious that there is some one individual z such that this utterance of HIP is true exactly if: 
(K) z is identical with z. 
Any proposition of that form is trivial. It is always trivial to say of an object that it is identical with itself. But by obvious extensions of what we said a moment ago, when I hear the policemanÂ’s utterance of HIP, what I take away from itÂ—what it (non-literally) conveys to me, given the pre-semantic information at my disposalÂ—wonÂ’t be at all trivial, as it will be along the lines of: 
(K2) There is some individual x such that, a couple of days ago (March 13, 2009) at about 3:00 P.M., x is standing right in front of me (in my office in Richmond, VA; such that x has such and such characteristics (he has a mustache, heÂ’s over 
sixfeet tall, etc.); such that Â“HesperusÂ” is xÂ’s name; and such that there is some individual y such that, a few hours ago (at around 7:00 P.M., March 14, 2009), y rang me; such that, using a voice-modulation device to disguise his voice, y is making threatening statements; such that I was told by y himself that Â“PhosphorousÂ” is yÂ’s name; and such that y is a professor of political science; moreover, I have just learned from the police that x is y. 
K2 is an empirical proposition; it isnÂ’t analytic; a fortiori it isnÂ’t trivial. But itÂ’s also a contingent truth. K, on the other hand, is a necessary truth. But itÂ’s also analytic. So we donÂ’t have anything that is both necessary and non-analytic. Kripke and many others have professed to find many examples of non-analytic necessary truths; but in each case, an exact analogue of the argument just given shows a confusion similar to the one just identified to be at work. In each case, semantics is being confused with pre-semantics. A defense of this claim is provided in Chapter 8 of my (2009) book Analytic Philosophy and in the first three chapters of my (2007) book Conceptual Atomism and the Computational Theory of Mind. 
4.0 Propositional necessity as microstructural truth: Some preliminary concepts 
The main modal concepts are necessity, possibility, impossibility, and contingency. All of these can be understood in terms of the concept of necessity. P is possible iff not-P isnÂ’t necessary. P is impossible iff not-P is necessary. P is contingent iff neither P nor not-P is necessary. 
Whether all modal concepts can be understood in terms of this one concept depends on how inclusive oneÂ’s conception of modality is. Like Bas van Fraassen (1989), I believe that the property of being probably true is a modal propertyÂ—that, indeed, for any number n, the property of being probable to degree n is a modal property. ItÂ’s an open question whether the concept of probable truth can be understood in terms of that necessary truth. IÂ’m inclined to think that it can be, given how natural it is to think of necessity as a limiting case of probable truth. But until this is resolved, it canÂ’t be said that all modal notions can be understood in terms of the concept of probability. But thereÂ’s no denying that necessity is the most important modal concept. 
But what is necessity? One plausible answer is this: necessary truth is analytic truth; necessity is analyticity. Â“Squares have four sidesÂ” is Â“analytic,Â” or Â“analytically true.Â” Indeed, all analytically true statements are necessarily true. So itÂ’s obviously worth looking into the idea that necessity is analyticity. Many deny this (for reasons that we've already discussed); but many, including the present author, hold it. But different authors use the word Â“analyticÂ” to mean different things, and we must make it clear how we will be using it before we can evaluate the proposal that necessary truth is analytic truth. 
Sometimes that word denotes a property of sentences; other times, it denotes a property of propositions. A sentence is analytic if, given only what it means, it must be true. So Â“squares have four sidesÂ” is analytic. Given only what it means, it couldnÂ’t possibly be false. A proposition is analytic if itÂ’s non-empirically true. So the proposition that squares have four sides is analytic. No conceivable state of affairs could make it false. We will use the word Â“analyticÂ” to denote a property of propositions, not sentences. 
When examining the concept of analyticity, one must make it clear at the outset whether one is talking about sentences or propositions. Otherwise one wonÂ’t be able to produce a coherent analysis of that concept. This is because there are analytically true sentences (or, strictly speaking, sentence-tokens) that have contingent propositions for their meanings. If, at this very moment, I were to say Â“I am here now,Â” my utterance couldnÂ’t fail to be true. Given the semantic rules that assign truth-conditions to that utterance, itÂ’s a logical impossibility that it should be false. But what it is that IÂ’m saying could very well be false. Given that I am JMK, that IÂ’m in Richmond, and that itÂ’s now March 13, 2009, I am, in producing such an utterance, attributing to JMK the property of being in Richmond, VA, on March 13, 2009. And, quite obviously, itÂ’s not a necessary truth that I have that property. Similarly, if I say Â“I am not here now,Â” my utterance is analytically false. Given its semanticsÂ—given what the semantic rules are that assign truths-conditions to itÂ—itÂ’s logically impossible that it should be true. But what it is saying could easily have been false; I might not, after all, have been in Richmond, VA, at this very time. It isnÂ’t in virtue of what itÂ’s saying that a given token of Â“I am here nowÂ” (Â“I am not here nowÂ”) must be true (false); it is in virtue of how it is saying it. But it is in virtue of what it is saying that a token of Â“any case of knowledge is a case of true beliefÂ” must be true. This shows that there are two very different kinds of sentence-analyticity. 
It also shows that sentence-analyticity diverges from proposition-analyticity and, more generally, that sentence-logic diverges from proposition-logic. In other words, the logical relations that propositions bear to one another donÂ’t always parallel the logical relation that the corresponding sentences bear to one another. The two sets of interrelations can diverge quite dramatically. (Credit for this astonishing insight goes entirely to P.F. Strawson.) So itÂ’s important to bear in mind that, in what follows, the word Â“analyticÂ” refers to a property of propositions, not sentences. (Later weÂ’ll discuss how it is exactly that analytically true (false) sentence-tokens can have contingent truths (falsehoods) for their meanings.) 
The word Â“analyticÂ” is ambiguous in another, equally important respect. As some philosophers use it, Â“analyticÂ” is synonymous with Â“trivialÂ” or Â“tautologous.Â” So Â“there are three feet in a yardÂ” is Â“analyticÂ” because itÂ’s trivial Â—because, basically, it says nothing. But as other philosophers use that word, analytic truths are often decidedly non-trivialÂ—for example, Â“a class is infinitely large exactly if it can be put into a one-one correspondence with a proper subset of itself.Â” When non-trivial truths are described as Â“analytic,Â” what is meant is that they are non-empirically true. (As previously stated, this is what we will mean by it.) 
There is one last ambiguity to deal with. As some philosophers use it, the word Â“analyticÂ” is synonymous with Â“formally true.Â” Formal truth is a property of sentences. ItÂ’s the property of being Â“syntacticallyÂ” true. A sentence is Â“syntactically trueÂ” if any sentence having the same syntactic form is true. So Â“either John is tall or John is not tallÂ” is formally true, and thus analytic (in one sense of the word), because every sentence having the form Â“either P or not-PÂ” is true. This obviously isnÂ’t how weÂ’ll be using the term Â“analytic,Â” given that, as previously stated, weÂ’re using it to pick out a property of propositions, not sentences. (Propositions donÂ’t have syntax. Syntax is a property of complex expressions. Propositions arenÂ’t expressions.) 
A final note: even though sentence-analyticity diverges from proposition-analyticity, the two ultimately coalesce. What does it mean to say that, although the proposition it encodes is synthetic, a given token of Â“I am here nowÂ” is analytic? It means that, the semantic rules of English being what they are, the proposition that any given token of Â“I am here nowÂ” is true, is analytic. (Given that any token t1 of Â“IÂ” refers to the person who utters t1, that any token t2 of Â“nowÂ” refers to the time at which t2 was uttered, and so on, it follows that a token t of Â“I am here nowÂ” couldnÂ’t be false.) 
4.1 Propositional necessity as microstructural truth (continued) 
Analytic propositions are true no matter what. The proposition: 
(GG) either grass is green or grass is not green, 
cannot fail to be true. It doesnÂ’t matter what happens or what natural laws govern what happens. Why is this? What is it about GG that makes it incapable of being false? A natural proposal is to say that GG is structurally true. In other words, given what its constituents are, along with how those constituents are put together, it cannot fail to be true. All structural truths are analytic truths. Analytic truth is truth in virtue of structure. 
This proposal is almost correct, but not quite. Analytic truth is truth in virtue not just of structure but also of substructure. It isnÂ’t merely in virtue of its structure that: 
(ACK) any case of knowledge is a case of true belief, 
is analytic; the structures of its constituents are involved. Some propositions structurally just like ACK are false (e.g., any case of knowledge is a case of false belief). At the same time, there are false propositions that are substructurally just like ACK (e.g., Â“any case of true belief is a case of knowledgeÂ”); and itÂ’s obviously because its structure differs from theirs that, unlike those propositions, ACK is analytically true. Analyticity is truth in virtue of structure along with substructure. Analytic truth is, as weÂ’ll put it, high-resolution structural truth. 
Before we can see what exactly this means, or why it holds, we must make a few non-controversial, but also non-trivial, points about language. The expressive power of a language is to be understood not only in terms of how many propositions can be expressed, but also in terms of how varied those propositions are. A language that can express the propositions snow is white, it is true that snow is white, it is true that it is true that snow is white, and so on, can express infinitely many propositions. But its expressive resources are minimal; and some other language that can express only a thousand propositions, not a single one of which entails a single one of the others, will grossly exceed the expressive capabilities of the first. And thatÂ’s why, when assessing the expressive potency of a language, the relevant question isnÂ’t so much Â“how many propositions can it express?Â” as it is Â“how much redundancy is there within the set of propositions that it can express?Â” 
These points may be obvious, but they have a non-obvious consequence, namely: as a rule, sentential structure mirrors propositional structure; propositions must have structures similar to those of the sentences that represent them. This doesnÂ’t mean that each propositionÂ’s structure is perfectly represented by those of all the sentences that express it. (In fact, this is impossible, given that sentences with different structures can express the same proposition.) It doesnÂ’t even mean that any propositionÂ’s structure is perfectly represented by that of any of the sentences that express it. What it means is that, to the extent that the sentences of a given language fail to mirror the structures of the propositions they express, that language is expressively frozen. So if L and L* are any two languages, then ceteris paribus LÂ’s expressive power exceeds L*s to the extent that the structures of L-sentences do a better job than those of L*-sentences of mirroring the structures of the propositions they represent. 
Let L* be a language that has only simple symbols. So the L*-sentence for Â“snow is colder than waterÂ” is some single, syntactically simple symbol, the same being true of every other L*-sentence. Obviously, thereÂ’s no limit to what L* can express, since thereÂ’s no limit in principle to how many primitive symbols can belong to a language. But, since each symbol belonging to L* is simple, itÂ’s necessary to add a new symbol to L* every time one wants to make a point that isnÂ’t the literal meaning of one of its simple expressions. Nothing could be said in L* that hadnÂ’t been said before: it would be impossible to express discoveries. Symbols would have to be added ad hoc to say anything new. But given a language L that has many ways of combining its primitive symbols into complex ones, itÂ’s expressive capabilities will dwarf those of L*, so long as the number of primitive expressions belonging to L rises above a certain, extremely small minimum number. L* is totally inflexible. L is highly flexible, and can do a lot with a little. Other things being equal, the extent to which one languageÂ’s expressive resources exceed those of another is directly proportional to the extent by which sentences of the one language exceed their counterparts in the other in respect of syntactic complexity. 
There is only one viable explanation of this last fact: Syntactic structure mirrors propositional structure. The syntactic devices that endow a language with expressive flexibility correspond to the relations by which propositions are constructed out of their constituents and, in particular, by which propositions are constructed out of other propositions. Thus, we can confidently say that the (syntactic) structures of sentences tend to mirror those of the propositions they express. 
4.2 Necessity as high-resolution structural truth 
We can now say what it means to say that analytic truth is high-resolution structural truth. Given the reasoning just presented, the sentence Â“either grass is green or grass is not greenÂ” must have a structure similar to GG. But, by that same reasoning, GGÂ’s structure probably differs from the structure of: 
(GA) Grass is green and grass is not green. 
But GA is not analytically true. (ItÂ’s analytically false.) Given that GA is false and has the same structure as GG, it cannot possibly be solely in virtue of its structure that GG is true. But we donÂ’t just want to give up on the idea that analytic truth is structural truth. An analytically true proposition is ipso facto true no matter what contingencies obtain. This entails, or strongly suggests, that it is always in virtue of something inherent in it that a proposition is analytically true, and itÂ’s hard to see how the relevant property could fail to be structural in nature. ItÂ’s obvious that, in the case of GA, whatÂ’s causing the trouble is that the concept of conjunction (the concept of and) is occupying the place that, in GG, is occupied by the concept of disjunction (the concept of or). Taken together, these points suggest that it is in virtue of its structure along with the structure of one of its constituentsÂ— viz., the concept of conjunctionÂ—that GG is analytically true. 
So itÂ’s not quite right to say that analytic truth is structural truth. At the same time, it isnÂ’t quite right to identify analytic truth with substructural truth. The proposition: 
(NG) itÂ’s not the case that grass is green or grass is green, 
is equivalent with the proposition that grass is not green. Thus, NG is contingently false. But it has the same constituents as the analytically true GG, and is thus substructurally identical with it, even though itÂ’s structurally very different. 
This suggests that for a proposition to be analytically true is for it to be true in virtue of its structural and its substructural properties. In other words, given a propositionÂ’s structure along with the structures of its constituents, itÂ’s settled whether or not that proposition is analytically true. Thus, a high-resolution representation of a propositionÂ’s structure settles whether or not itÂ’s analytic. (A Â“low-resolutionÂ” representation would be one that failed to disclose substructure.) Thus, analytic truth is high-resolution structural truth Â—and so, therefore, is necessary truth, given that itÂ’s identical with analytic truth. 
5.0 QuineÂ’s denial of informal analytic truth: preliminary concepts 
In this section, all references to Â“analyticÂ” truth are to sentential analytic truths; we will be discussing analytically true sentences, not analytically true propositions. 
W.V.O. Quine (1951) says that, with a few trivial exceptions, there is no such thing as sentential analytic truth. To understand exactly what it is that he holds, and why he holds it, we must first make some background points. 
Consider the following sentence: 
(ST) Â“if Smith is tall, then it is not the case that Smith is not tall,Â” 
Obviously you canÂ’t replace Â“SmithÂ” with Â“thereforeÂ” or Â“red.Â” The result would be syntactically ill-formed nonsense. Thus, such replacements would not be Â“grammatically admissible.Â” But you can replace Â“SmithÂ” with Â“JonesÂ” and Â“that person.Â” Such replacements would be grammatically admissible, that being why: 
(JT) Â“if Jones is tall, then it is not the case that Jones is not tall,Â” 
is a perfectly grammatical sentence. 
JT is what results when the occurrences of Â“SmithÂ” in it are replaced uniformly. In other words, JT is what results when not just one, but all of those occurrences are replaced with the same thing. The following sentence, by contrast, is what results when only one of the occurrences of Â“SmithÂ” in ST is replaced with Â“JonesÂ” (Â“NUÂ” is short for Â“not uniformÂ”): 
(NU) Â“if Jones is tall, then it is not the case that Jenkins is not tall.Â” 
Thus, a syntactically well-formed sentence S cannot be false if it is the result of uniformly replacing the occurrences in ST of Â“SmithÂ” (or, for reasons analogous to those just given, of Â“tallÂ”) with some other expression. 
In general, a sentence S is formally true if there is some expression E occurring in S such that no syntactically well-formed sentence S* is false if S* is what results when the occurrences in S of E are uniformly replaced with occurrences of some other expression. 
ItÂ’s generally heldÂ—and the present author himself holds thisÂ—that there are informal analytic truths. Consider, for example, the following sentence (Â“JTBÂ” is short for Â“justified true beliefÂ”): 
(JTB) Â“One canÂ’t know something without believing it.Â” 
JTB is analytically true. Given only a knowledge of what it means, one knows (or is in a position to know) that it is true. It isnÂ’t like Â“there are nine planets,Â” which, if true, can be established only on the basis of experimental data. NoÂ—JTB is inherently true. The denial of it (Â“one can know something without believing itÂ”) is prevented, by its very own meaning, from being true; and it (JTB) is required by its very own meaning to be true. 
But JTB isnÂ’t formally true. If you replace Â“knowÂ” with Â“doubt,Â” the result is a false sentence. In fact, given any expression in JTB, replacing it (in a uniform and grammatically admissible manner) with some other expression results in falsehood. For example, the sentence Â“one canÂ’t deny something without affirming itÂ” is a false sentence that results from replacements of the sort just described. 
It seems pretty clear, then, that there are informal analytic truths. And this is what most analytic philosophers hold, including the present author. But Quine denies it. Quine thinks that, apart from formal analytic truths, there are no analytic truths. This thesis of his is famous, and so is his argument for it. 
5.1 QuineÂ’s denial of informal analytic truth 
Here is QuineÂ’s argument. Consider the sentence: 
(B) Bachelors are unmarried men. 
If any sentence is analytic, (B) is one of them. According to Quine, supposing for argument's sake that (B) is analytic, the only possible reason is that Â“bachelorÂ” and Â“unmarried manÂ” are synonyms. Quine holds that all analytically true statements, supposing such things to exist, merely register synonymy-relations and, therefore, that all of them are as trivial as (B). 
Quine then asks the following question: What is it for two expressions to be synonyms? Quine gives the following (correct) response: It is for them to be such that intersubstitutions of them preserve meaning. Â“FoeÂ” and Â“enemyÂ” are synonymous because you cannot change sentence meaning by replacing Â“foeÂ” with Â“enemy.Â” Put another way, Â“foeÂ” and Â“enemyÂ” mean the same thing because, if a sentence S contains an occurrence of Â“foe,Â” and that occurrence is replaced with an occurrence of Â“enemy,Â” the resulting sentence has the same meaning as S. Consider the sentence: Â“Smith is a foe.Â” Now replace the word Â“foeÂ” with Â“enemy.Â” What results is Â“Smith is an enemy.Â” The sentence Â“Smith is an enemyÂ” has precisely the same meaning as Â“Smith is a foe.Â” 
This line of thought is easily extended. Let S and S* be any two sentences that are exactly alike except for the fact that, in the place where S contains the word Â“foe,Â” S* contains the word Â“enemy.Â” What we just said about Â“Smith is an enemyÂ” and Â“Smith is a foeÂ” is true of S and S*. That is why Â“foeÂ” and Â“enemyÂ” are synonyms. Inter-substituting synonyms doesnÂ’t change sentence-meaningÂ—and for two expressions to be synonymous just is for them to be such that inter-substituting them doesnÂ’t ever change sentence-meaning. 
But, Quine asks, what is it for two sentences to have the same Â“meaningÂ”? What is it for Â“Smith is an enemyÂ” and Â“Smith is a foeÂ” to mean the same thing? According to Quine, for two statements to have the same meaning is for them to be analytically equivalent. In other words, it is for them to entail, and be entailed by, exactly the same statements. Â“Smith is an enemyÂ” entails Â“Smith is somebody who would like to do me ill and will do so if given the opportunity,Â” and so does Â“Smith is a foe.Â” The statement Â“Smith is somebody whose sole objective in life is to make my life as unpleasant as possibleÂ” entails Â“Smith is an enemy,Â” and it also entails Â“Smith is a foe.Â” Given any statement S that entails Â“Smith is an enemy,Â” S also entails Â“Smith is a foeÂ”; and given any statement S* such that Â“Smith is an enemyÂ” entails S*, Â“Smith is a foeÂ” also entails S*. Thus, Â“Smith is an enemyÂ” and Â“Smith is a foeÂ” entail, and are entailed by, exactly the same statementsÂ—and that, according to Quine, is what it is for them to have the same meaning. 
But notice that we have gone in a circle. We defined analyticity in terms of synonymy. A recap will make this clear: 
1. (B) is analytic because Â“bachelorÂ” and Â“unmarried manÂ” are synonyms, and there is no analytically statements that isn't to be understood along similar lines: all such statements are sterile trivialities that hold in virtue of linguistic conventions. 
We then defined synonymy in terms of sameness of meaning: 
2. For two expressions to be synonymous is for them to be such that inter-substitutions of them preserve sentence meaning. 
But we then defined sameness of meaning in terms of analyticity: 
3. For two statements to have the same meaning is for them to be analytically equivalent. In other words, it is for them to entail, and be entailed by, exactly the same statements. 
1 defines analyticity in terms of 2 and, thus, in terms of synonymy. 2 defines synonymy in terms of 3, and thus in terms of analyticity. Thus, analyticity has been defined in terms of itself. We have gone in a vicious circle. Thus, Quine concludes, the concept of analyticity is viciously circular and therefore incoherent. Quine concludes that there is no such thing as analytic truth: all truths are synthetic. 
5.2 Evaluating QuineÂ’s argument 
First of all, Quine is wrong to hold that analyticity is to be understood in terms of synonymy. Consider the sentence: 
(T) The unique number n such that n = 2 if the interior angles of a Euclidean triangle add up to 180Â° and n =3 otherwise is identical with the unique number m such that 9n = 90 minus 9. 
(T) is analytic. No empirical knowledge, over and above such as is needed to know what meaning it bears, is required to know whether itÂ’s true. So itÂ’s true in virtue of what it means and is thus analytic. (To be sure, unlike some analytic sentences, it isnÂ’t formally true. But since the very thing that Quine is trying to show is that there is no informal analytic truth, he cannot, without assuming the truth of the very thing that heÂ’s trying to show, claim on those grounds that T is not analytic.) So if Quine is right, T holds in virtue of some synonymy relation. What, in this case, would the relevant synonyms be? Presumably they would be: 
(*) Â“the unique number n such that n = 2 if the interior angles of a Euclidean triangle add up to 180Â° and n =3 otherwise,Â” 
and: 
(#) Â“the unique number m such that 9m = 90 minus 9.Â” 
But even though they refer to the same thing (namely, the number two), * and # obviously donÂ’t have the same meaning; and Quine is therefore wrong to say that, if there are analytic truths, they always hold in virtue of synonymy relations. 
5.3 Analytic truth non-circularly definable as non-empirical truth 
QuineÂ’s larger point seems to be that there is no non-circular definition of the term Â“analytic truth.Â” But that is false: a sentence is analytic if (a) it is true and (b) it does not hold in virtue of empirical facts. Put simply: analytic truth is non-empirical truth. Â“Circles are figures of uniform curvatureÂ” is true and, moreover, it holds, not in virtue of empirical facts (i.e., not in virtue of how objects are in fact shaped), but in virtue of facts about the structures of the properties circle, curvature, and so on. Of course, being a nominalist, Quine would reject the idea that there are non-empirical truths. (After all, a nominalist believes that everything is spatiotemporal: there are no platonic entities and thus no properties.) But in attempting to establish that all truths are synthetic, Quine is, in effect, trying to establish that there are no empirical truths. For an empirical truth is, by definition, one that can be learned only through observation and therefore cannot be learned through any non-sensory modality such as conceptual analysis. So Quine would be guilty of begging the question were he to say that, since all truth is empirical, it is not an option to define Â“analyticÂ” as Â“non-empirically true.Â” 
5.4 QuineÂ’s position self-defeating 
Also, the view that there are no analytic statements is self-defeating.[226] 
The statement: 
(^) There are no empirical statements, 
is equivalent to the statement: 
(^^) for all values of S, the statement nothing follows from S follows from the statement S is a statement.
