This whole line of thought is preposterous. Any knowledge that we have about other universes is parasitic on our knowledge of modal truths. First, we know the counterfactuals. Only then do we know whatÂ’s going on in other worlds. ItÂ’s only thanks to our knowledge that 6 divided by 2 is 3, along with our knowledge that Smith is six feet tall, that we know that Smith would be three feet tall in a world where he were half his actual height. ItÂ’s only thanks to our knowledge that Kennedy was an enormously popular first-term President, along with our knowledge that popular incumbent Presidents win re-election, that we know that Kennedy would have won in 1964 had his life not been cut short. 
These pedestrian points show that other worlds are useless in the way of giving us modal knowledge. It also shows that modal truths donÂ’t hold in virtue of what goes on in other worlds. S is obviously correct. Whatever it is that makes it correct, we donÂ’t have to leave this world to have access to it. It follows that, given any true counterfactual statement S, it is in virtue of what happens in this world, and this world alone, that S is true. 
The real meanings of S and K are: 
(S*) The statement that Smith is six-feet tall entails that the statement, for all values of x,Â‹x is half SmithÂ’s heightÂ› entails Â‹x is three-feet tall.Â› 
and: 
(K*) Â“KennedyÂ’s assassination caused an otherwise unthreatened Kennedy not to be reelected.Â” 
For further discussion of the nature of counterfactual truth, see Chapter 7. 
7.0 Theoretical vs. observational knowledge 
It seems that much of what we can know comes directly from sense-perception. I open my eyes in a well-lit room, and I can just see that there are chairs and people there. 
But much knowledge is theoretical. We donÂ’t have direct knowledge of electrons or even of gravitational fields. We have direct knowledge of the effects of these things. (More accurately, we have relatively direct knowledge of such effects. WeÂ’ll see in a moment that our knowledge of these effects is itself indirect, even though itÂ’s obviously less so than our knowledge of electrons, etc.) But in characterizing something directly perceived as the effect of Â“gravitationÂ” or of the activity of Â“electrons,Â” we are going well beyond what we can literally see (or hear or touch, etc.), and we are assuming the existence of things whose existence can be justified only by theories of some kind or other. A theory is an explanation of what is directly experienced in terms of what is not directly experienced and whose existence is therefore not directly known.[243] 

Freud and others have posited the existence of mental activity that we are not directly aware of and of which we are therefore Â“unconscious.Â” One obviously canÂ’t be directly aware of unconscious mental activity. (Any mental activity that one is directly aware of is ipso facto conscious.) Thus, any knowledge that we have of the unconscious is inferential. In addition, such knowledge is also theoretical. But here we must take a moment to clarify the distinction between inferential and theoretical knowledge. 
A theory is an integrated set of statements that, if correct, describe some sector of reality that cannot be known strictly through sense-perception or introspection. All theoretical knowledge is inferential, but not all inferential knowledge is theoretical. If I see smoke, and I infer on that basis that there is fire, my inference isnÂ’t theoretical. It doesnÂ’t presuppose the truth of a theory. It assumes the truth of the statement Â“where thereÂ’s smoke, thereÂ’s fire,Â” which merely describes an observable concomitance, and therefore doesnÂ’t qualify as a theory. But, supposing for argumentÂ’s sake that there is unconscious mental activity and that we can have knowledge of it, the inferences that yield such knowledge do presuppose theoretical knowledge. If I infer from the fact that you are accident-prone that you have hostility towards yourself, I am obviously making several assumptions as to the nature of the psyche. Further, those assumptions donÂ’t merely register observable concomitances, and they arenÂ’t independent of one another. Thus, those assumptions jointly constitute a theory. It follows that any knowledge that we have of the unconscious is of a theoretical character. In Sections 8.2.-8.2.3 of the present chapter, weÂ’ll say more about the distinction between theoretical and inferential knowledge. 

7.1 Is all knowledge theoretical? 
Some epistemologists and cognitive scientists maintain that even perceptual knowledge is theoretical. This position may seem strange at first, but there is at least one reason to think that it may be true. 
Even though you donÂ’t have to do any work to generate your own sense-perceptions, your mind and nervous system certainly have to do a great deal of work. Consider the disturbances of your sensory surfaces that lead to your sense-perceptions. If the surface of a rock or a piece of wood were similarly disturbed, no sense-perception would result. What is the difference between you and a rock? Your mind can, whereas a rock cannot, process the relevant disturbances in the right way. ItÂ’s quite extraordinary that your mind is able to do this; for all it is given are various disturbances that, in and of themselves, bear no resemblance (or only an extremely abstract resemblance) to the things off of which the relevant photons (or whatnot) are bouncing. Nonetheless, on the basis of this meager information, your mind is able to generate perceptual representations that accurately depict those objects. The gulf between input and outputÂ—between, on the one hand, the surface-stimulations on the basis of which your mind generates its perceptions and, on the other hand, those perceptions themselvesÂ—bears a striking resemblance to the gulf between, on the one hand, the data on the basis of which a theoretical physicist posits the existence of a swarm of a certain kind of sub-atomic particle and, on the other hand, that particle-swarm itself. In the case of the theoretical physicist, that gulf can be bridged only by a theory. This suggests that the same is true of the gulf between disturbances of your eyes and the perceptions in which those disturbances eventuate.[244] 

7.2 A priori vs. a posteriori knowledge 
Thus, one must have knowledge in order to acquire perceptual knowledge. Given that even a newborn can have sense-perceptions, it follows that knowledge of some kind is coded into the innate structures of our minds. 
Such knowledge is referred to as a priori knowledge. Thus, knowledge is a priori if it is coded into the very structures of our minds and therefore preÂ­exists any perceptions that we have. 
If knowledge is not a priori, then it is referred to as a posteriori. Thus, a posteriori knowledge is acquired knowledge, and a priori knowledge is knowledge that is within us, in some form, from the outset. 
It is a matter of considerable debate whether there is a priori knowledge and, if so, precisely what it is that is known a priori. (My own strongly held view is that there is a priori knowledge.) Among those who believe that we have a priori knowledge are Plato, Leibniz, Kant, and Chomsky. Among those who deny it are Aristotle, Locke, and Quine. 


7.3 A second reason to think that perceptual knowledge is theoretical 
Suppose that X is some stop sign. If you look at X from a certain distance Â—from, say, a hundred feet awayÂ—it will appear a certain way to you. Given only how X appears to you from that distance, you cannot tell whether you are looking at an object that is around eight-feet tall and a hundred feet away or an object that is 1,000-feet tall and much further away or an object that is six inches tall and very nearby. Nonetheless, you know, when you are looking at X, that it is not 1,000-feet tall and far away or six-inches tall and very close, and that it is around eight-feet tall and about a hundred feet away. Given that XÂ’s appearance, by itself, does not reveal this to you, how do you know it? It is your background knowledge that, in conjunction with how X appears to you under the circumstances described, enables you to assign the right height to X. A continuation of our story may clarify this. Your friend Larry is right next to X. You can see the comparative heights of X and Larry; you can see that Larry is around three-fourths the height of X. So it is because of XÂ’s appearance plus this background knowledge that you are able to determine XÂ’s height. 
This must be understood correctly. You can just see how tall, approximately, X is. But, for the reasons just given, it seems that background knowledge of the kind just described seems to be involved in, and to some degree to constitute, your seeing this. 
An argument similar to that just given in connection with seeing XÂ’s size can be given in connection with seeing any objectÂ’s size. Indeed, similar arguments can be given in connection with seeing any fact about any object Â—in connection with seeing how fast an object is moving, what shape it has, how far it is from one, and so on. And extensions of those arguments suggest what is true of seeing facts about physical objects is true of any kind of perceptual awareness of any fact about them. 
7.4. Inferential vs. theoretical knowledge 
There is a reason to hold that not all knowledge is theoretical, namely that many inferences are involved in knowing a theory and, consequently, inferential knowledge is a precondition for theoretical knowledge. Some background points are needed to make it clear why, at least arguably, this holds. 
First of all, not all inferencesÂ—not even all inferences that lead to correct conclusionsÂ—yield knowledge. If I infer that Bob has cancer on the grounds that he has red hair, my inference doesnÂ’t yield knowledge, even if, by coincidence, Bob does have cancer. The reason my inference doesnÂ’t yield knowledge is that the Â“inference ruleÂ” implicit in itÂ—in other words, the principle that licenses itÂ—isnÂ’t a good one. That inference rule is: Â“if a person has red hair, he or she has cancer.Â” Since that rule obviously isnÂ’t Â“truthÂ­conduciveÂ”Â—since, in other words, that rule isnÂ’t likely to yield correct conclusions, given correct premisesÂ—no inference made on the basis of it is legitimate. So for an inference that yields a correct conclusion to yield knowledge, one must make that inference on the basis of a legitimate inference rule. 
Theories are systems of statements standing in various dependence-relations with respect to one another. (The word Â“statementÂ” here is not meant to have any linguistic overtones and should be taken as shorthand for Â“truth or falsehood.Â”) A dependence-relation holds between two statements if one of them supports the otherÂ—if, in other words, one of them provides some basis for inferring the other. Knowing that a dependence-relation holds between two statements involves either inferring the one from the other or, failing that, recognizing that such an inference could be legitimately made. For example, my recognizing that there is a dependence-relation between Â“there is fire at time t in place pÂ” and Â“there is smoke at t* in p*,Â” where t* and p* are neighbors of t and p, involves either my knowing one of them on the basis of the other or it involves my seeing that such inference would be legitimate. In either case, I have inferential knowledge. (Even if I happened to see the fire and the smoke, and thus didnÂ’t have to infer Â“fire at t in pÂ” from Â“smoke at t* in p*Â” or vice versa, my knowing that a dependence-relation holds between them involves my knowing that the one could be legitimately inferred from the other. And that knowledge, surely, deserves to be characterized as inferential.) Since, as we noted a moment ago, knowledge of dependence-relations precedes knowledge of theories, and since knowledge of such relations is inferential, it follows that inferential knowledge precedes theoretical knowledge. 
Of course, those who deny that all knowledge is theoretical donÂ’t have this in mind. Usually those who hold that there is Â“directÂ” knowledge mean that there is no inferential knowledgeÂ—they use the terms Â“inferentialÂ” and Â“theoreticalÂ” interchangeably and therefore, since theyÂ’re not interchangeable, loosely. 
7.4.1 Inferential vs. theoretical knowledge (continued) 
To be made cogent, the foregoing discussion must be qualified in a couple of ways. These qualifications will bring out some principles whose importance extends far beyond the points just made. 
I said that a dependence-relation holds between two statements just in case one of them can be legitimately inferred from the other. Some might object to this on grounds like the following: 
SmithÂ’s crashing the car might have resulted from his being drunk. So a dependence-relation holds between the truths expressed by the statements Â“Smith was drunk at tÂ” and Â“Smith crashed the car at t*.Â” Were it not for the first truth, the second wouldnÂ’t hold, and the second is therefore dependent on the first. But surely I cannot legitimately infer the second from the first. Given only that Smith is drunk, I canÂ’t infer that heÂ’ll crash his car. So, contrary to what you say, dependence-relations arenÂ’t always backed by legitimate inference rules. 
First of all, it wasnÂ’t merely SmithÂ’s being drunk that led to his crash. It was his being drunk while being behind the wheel. In fact, more than this is involved. He wouldnÂ’t have crashed had the car in front of him not slowed down or if he hadnÂ’t been talking on his cell phone when this happened. It was a confluence of factorsÂ—his drunkenness, the behavior of the driver in front of him, his own distractednessÂ—that led to the crash. Total causes are always confluences of circumstances. Thus, the dependence-relation in question holds, not between the two statements cited by the objector, but between Â“at t, Smith crashedÂ” and Â“at immediately preceding time t*, Smith was driving while drunk and talking on his cell phone, when the car in front of him suddenly slowed down.Â” The second statement does make it reasonable to infer that, at or around t, Smith crashed. 
Admittedly, the second statement doesnÂ’t make it certain that he crashed. This is because the presumption that, given the various factors at play (his drunkenness and distractedness, the sudden deceleration of the car in front of him, etc.) the imminent crash could still be headed off. Maybe the person in the passenger-seat of SmithÂ’s car wrenched the steering wheel to the right, just in time to avoid the crash. Not likely, but possible. Maybe Smith is somebody whose driving is enhanced by drunkenness. Not likely, but possible. But even though, given the operative conditions, SmithÂ’s crashing cannot be known with certainty to occur, it doesnÂ’t follow that the inference from Â“Smith was drunk and chatting on his cell phone (etc.)Â” to Â“Smith crashedÂ” isnÂ’t legitimate or, therefore, isnÂ’t licensed by a truth-conducive inference rule. What follows is that the inference rule in question is defeasible. An inference rule is defeasible if (i) it provides a reasonable presumption that, given certain premises, a certain conclusion holds, but (ii) that presumption may turn out to be false if other facts, not in evidence, happen to intercede. 
There is a big difference between an inference rule that is defeasible, on the one hand, and one that is simply bad (i.e., not truth-conducive), on the other. A bad inference rule provides no reason for inferring one thing from another. A defeasible inference rule (when good) does provide such a reason. It doesnÂ’t provide as good a reason as a non-defeasible inference rule. But that doesnÂ’t mean that itÂ’s not good at all; goodness (truth-conduciveness) comes in degrees. 

7.4.2 Rules vs. principles 
[245] 

ThereÂ’s also an important difference between rules and principles. Rules are about outcomes. Principles are about tendencies. Rules have the form: Â“if this, then that.Â” (If itÂ’s a raven, then itÂ’s black.) TheyÂ’re categorical. (All members of the category raven are members of the category black.)A rule that admits exceptions is false. (A single non-black raven falsifies the rule that all ravens are black.) A correct rule can be obtained by replacing a counter-exampled rule with one that is duly hedged with exception clauses. (So, supposing that Smith is the one non-black raven, then Â“all ravens other than Smith are blackÂ” is indeed a correct rule.) 
But a duly hedged rule is not a principle. Principles are not watered down rules. It is no accident that so many drunk drivers crashed; itÂ’s not a statistical fluke. Nor is it parasitic on some other, more robust connection. In a society where the government forced blond people to live near nuclear waste, there would be a connection between being blond and getting cancer. Drunk driving is to crashing what being exposed to radiation is to getting cancer. It is not what, in the just-described society, being blond is to getting cancer. 
As weÂ’ll see in Chapter 12, empiricists think of principles as being watered-down rulesÂ—as being expressed by categorical statements to which there are exceptions. This isnÂ’t the right way to think about them. Principles are better thought of as registering the existence of defeasible forces. Being drunk can be thought of as a car-crash-conducive force (or, more likely, confluence of forces) that, like most forces, can be overridden. Note that, whereas inference-rules are defeasible in a logical sense, forces are defeasible in a causal sense.[246] 

8.0 Knowledge of ourselves and others 
A personÂ’s knowledge of himself is obviously much better than his knowledge of others. You obviously have a much more accurate understanding of your own mind than you do of other peopleÂ’s minds. Nonetheless, we can, within limits, have some knowledge of what others are thinking. 
It is a matter of considerable dispute how we can acquire such knowledge. But here is a hypothesis that, I think, must surely be correctÂ—at least for some, though perhaps not all, instances of knowledge of others. 
We can, at least within limits, have direct knowledge of what is going on within our own minds. And we often know how we are likely to behave in response to an experience of a given kind. When others behave in a given way, I tend to ascribe to them the kind of mental state that accompanies instances of my behaving in that way. I know that when I am in pain, I tend to wince or clutch at the wounded part of my body (or some such). So when I see somebody else behaving in that way, I tend to assume that he or she is in pain. Comparable points hold with respect to our ascriptions of other kinds of mental states to others.[247] 

8.01 WittgensteinÂ’s attempt to refute this argument 
Wittgenstein (1958) rejects what we just said. He rejects the idea that one ever acquires knowledge of what is going on in another personÂ’s mind by assuming the latterÂ’s outward behavior to express a mental state similar the sort of mental state to which, in oneÂ’s own case, such behavior gives rise. Wittgenstein argues that: 
(WA)[248] 
A given person has direct knowledge of only one case---namely, his own---in which mental states of such and such a kind are followed by physical behaviors of thus and such a kind. Were one to conclude solely on the basis of oneÂ’s own case that, where bodies other than oneÂ’s own were concerned, such and such mental states eventuated in thus and such behaviors, one would, in so doing, be drawing conclusions that vastly exceeded anything warranted by the available information. 
WA is a text-book case of fallacious reasoning. In a celebrated passage, David Hume (1700-1776), though obviously not addressing WA specifically, made it clear why this is so.[249] 
Let us suppose that we discover some new kind of metal M, and we find that some one specimen m of M is conductive to a certain degree, malleable to a certain degree, has a certain micro-structure, and a certain melting point, etc. We know that, given any type of metal, its specimens are identical in respect of their microstructures, melting points, coefficients of expansion, etc. So if we assume, on the basis of what we know about m, that all specimens of M have such and such melting points, degrees of conductivity, etc., we are by no means over-drawing conclusions. For our inference is not based on m alone, but on m along with the previously mentioned background information. The other side of the coin is that, were m to differ in respect of its coefficient of expansion, etc. from other instances of M, then (supposing that we didnÂ’t decide on that basis to reclassify m) its thus differing would constitute a singularity of unprecedented proportions. It would thus be highly counterinductive to suppose that m might differ in these respects from other members of M. 
It would be similarly counterinductive to suppose that it was only in oneÂ’s own case that certain anatomical and behavioral phenomena had certain mental accompaniments. What Wittgenstein describes as abstaining from overdrawing conclusions is in fact positing singularities for whose existence the past, if itÂ’s evidence of anything, provides strong negative evidence. 
Also, to pick up on a parenthetical point made a moment ago, were one to discover that the bodies that one previously thought to be animated by minds like oneÂ’s own were not thus animated, one would ipso facto reclassify oneself. One would ipso facto cease to regard oneself as being of the same ilk as those mindless entities, oneÂ’s reasoning being: Â“they are zombies; I am not; so in at least one vitally important respect, I am not one of them.Â” 
Wittgenstein doesnÂ’t see this. He doesnÂ’t see that, if people other than oneself were to turn out to be zombies, they ipso facto wouldnÂ’t be Â“peopleÂ”, except in a narrowly biological sense. Wrongly assuming WA cogent, Wittgenstein believes there to be no choice but to deny the existence of minds. There is, he says, no Â“inner Cartesian theatre.Â” What he means is that there is nothing about oneÂ’s mind that is any more transparent to its owner than it is to any other person. 
This idea is, quite obviously, false. People can conceal much about themselves from others. Others may never be able to know about a given person what he can immediately know about himself. But Wittgenstein will have none of this. Â“The best picture of the mind is the body,Â” Wittgenstein famously says, meaning that there is nothing you know about yourself that I donÂ’t know by looking at you. Â“An inner state stands in need of an outward criterion," Wittgenstein says, meaning that the very idea of a mental state that doesn't involve overt behavior is absurd. So, if Wittgenstein is right, two soldiers, both of whom are standing perfectly still, cannot be in different psychological states. 
No argument could make the spuriousness of WittgensteinÂ’s position any more obvious than it already is. Nonetheless, in Chapter 22, we consider WittgensteinÂ’s position and, for what little itÂ’s worth, put forth arguments that make it clear that itÂ’s wrong. 

8.1 Self-knowledge 
People know much about themselves. I know that, right now, I have the intention of producing a helpful essay on the theory of knowledge. I know that, right now, IÂ’m in a pretty good mood. I know that I enjoy playing the piano. I know that I wish that I could play as well as Arthur Rubenstein; I also know that IÂ’m sad that I cannot play as well he could. All of you have comparable knowledge about yourselves. 
A striking feature of at least some of our self-knowledge is how direct it is. My knowledge that IÂ’m in a pretty good mood is even more direct than my knowledge that I am now typing on a computer. But how is this possible? IsnÂ’t my knowledge that IÂ’m now typing on a keyboard as direct as knowledge can be? 
No. My knowledge that IÂ’m typing on a keyboard is based on the sensory experiences IÂ’m having. These experiences are both visual and tactile. (Â“TactileÂ” means Â“having to do with the sense of touch.Â”) But, given only the nature of those experiences, it is a possibility, if only a theoretical one, that IÂ’m dreaming or hallucinating. 
My having accurate perceptions of the computer screen in front of me involves my bodyÂ’s being stimulated in very specific ways by causal processes that originate with that computer screen. (Light waves must bounce off of that computer screen and disturb my retinas.) Further, those light waves mustnÂ’t be distorted or altogether cut-off by intervening influences. If there were an uneven, thick piece of glass between me and the screen, those light waves would be distorted, and my perception of the screen would be inaccurate. If there were a piece of thick wood between me and the glass, those light-waves would be cut off, and I wouldnÂ’t see the screen at all. So my having an accurate perception of the screen involves more than just my having a certain visual experience: that experience must be caused in a very specific way by very specific events in the external world (i.e., the world outside of my body). 
A corollary is that I am not in any sense seeing the screen unless I am having a visual experience that is caused by events involving the screen. Even if I'm having visual experiences that are subjectively just like those involved in my actually seeing the screen, I'm not seeing the screen unless those experiences result from disturbances of my ocular surfaces caused by their being struck by light-rays bouncing off of it. So I'm not seeing the screen if light-rays responsible for those experiences are making their way to me from some other computer-screen. (In such a case, I'd be seeing that other screen, though I might think that I was seeing the screen before me.) Nor am I seeing the screen if those experiences are hallucinations. 
In this respect, sense-perceptions are like money. For a piece of a paper to be a dollar bill, it has to have a certain provenance. If it was created in somebody's basement, it's a counterfeit bill. Similarly, a given experience isn't a perception of X unless it has a certain provenance, even if, setting aside its provenance, it is indistinguishable from such a perception. 
Granting that I can have an experience just like that of seeing a computer screen even if IÂ’m not seeing a computer screen, could I have an experience just like that of experiencing intense pain if I werenÂ’t experiencing intense pain? No. An experience just like that of intense pain is an intense pain. The same thing mutatis mutandis is true of instances of any sensation of any kind. An experience like that of intense pleasure is one of intense pleasure. It's irrelevant how that experience was caused. Where sensations are concerned, the appearance is the reality. Anything like a sensation of a given kind is such an experience. 
Sensations aren't the only mental entities that have this property. Anything that, setting aside its mode of origination, is just like a belief that 2+2=4 is a belief that 2+2=4. To be sure, that belief is a psychological structure; it isn't a constituent of consciousness. And, although one can obviously be conscious of one's belief that 2+2=4, one's consciousness of it cannot be identified with, and is to no degree constitutive of, that belief itself. So how it appears to one is distinct from how it is, and it thus cannot be said that, where that belief is concerned, "the appearance is the reality." But what matters in this context is that its being a bona fidebelief that 2+2=4 has nothing to do with it how it came about. 
Whether that belief constitutes knowledge that 2+2=4 does so depend. It isn't knowledge if it has if the reasoning that led to it is spurious and, therefore, unless it has a certain provenance. So, just as our sensory experiences must have certain origins if they are to be bona fideperceptions, so beliefs must have certain origins if they are to constitute knowledge. 
This brings us to an important point. Words like "fake" and "real" are relative (in the sense that they denote relations, not in the sense that it is to any degree a "matter of opinion" whether a given usage of such a term is legitimate or not). A given piece of paper may not be a real dollar bill. But it's real in other respects. So it's fake relative to the standards that a thing must meet to be a dollar bill. But it's real relative to the standards that a thing must meet to have a certain molecular structure, shape, mass, and so on. 
A slight detour help clarify this points. To be a mother is for there to be a certain object x such that one bears a certain relation to x. But the word "mother" is syntactically very different from expressions, such as "to the north of" or "three feet from", that clearly denote relations, and syntactically it's exactly like expressions, such as "a sad person", that denote properties, as opposed to relations. So, whereas "New York is to the north of" is syntactically ill-formed and therefore isn't a sentence, "Mary is a mother" is a perfectly good sentence, and so is "Mary is a sad person." But logically "mother" is comparable to "to the north of," not "a sad person." For, whereas one can be a sad person all by oneself, so to speak, one can no more be a mother all by oneself than a place can to the north of all by oneself. Similar points hold of words such as "real", "bogus", and the like. Syntactically, those words are in the same syntactic category as expressions that denote properties. At the same time, they're in same logical category as words that denote relations, the reason being that "X is real" is, if meaningful, an abbreviated way of saying that X bears a certain relation to a certain set of standards. 
Thus, a conscious experience that is fake in one respect may be real in another. Even if all of the experiences that we believe to be perceptions are hallucinations and are therefore "fake" perceptions, as opposed to "real" ones, they are still real in other respects. Perceptions give us messages. They tell you that such and such is the case in certain places. Those messages happen to be correct. (In this context, I am using the word "perception" in the way that some authors use the term "accurate perception.") Hallucinations, and other pseudo-perceptions, also give you messages. Those messages are either false or coincidentally correct. A false statement is just as much of a statement as a correct one. So, considered as a messages, non-veridical hallucination and coincidentally veridical hallucinations are no less real than their (non-accidentally) veridical counterpart. So, even though, when considered as a perception, a given experience's reality doesn't merge with its appearance, its reality does so merge when it's considered as a message. 
To sum up, where some psychological conditions are concerned, the appearance and the reality merge. By contrast, where knowledge of the external world is concerned, the appearance and the reality are always distinct and are often (in fact, usually) separated by a large tract of space. Even where touch is concerned, the object touched is remote from the events in your central nervous system that mediate your experience of the object. So knowledge of at least some facts about oneÂ’s psychological condition is considerably more direct than knowledge of facts about the external world. 

8.2 Some limits to self-knowledge 
Notwithstanding what was just said, there are reasons to believe that, in many cases, self-knowledge is as difficult to obtain as knowledge of the external worldÂ—that, in fact, knowledge of some facts about our own minds is as theoretical and indirect as our knowledge of sub-atomic events. 
Before we can discuss these reasons, we must define a term and we must also make a distinction. The term to be defined is Â“consciousness.Â” In everyday speech, that word is ambiguous. Sometimes, it simply means Â“knowledgeÂ” or Â“awareness.Â” For example, in the sentence, Â“SmithÂ’s consciousness of the complexities involved in running a municipality is extremely limited,Â” the word Â“consciousnessÂ” seems to have more or less the same meaning as the term Â“knowledgeÂ” or Â“awareness.Â” 
In philosophical contexts, the word Â“consciousnessÂ” has a different and narrower meaning. In such contexts, it refers to oneÂ’s immediate experience. (Henceforth, we will use the term Â“consciousnessÂ” only in its narrow, philosophical sense.) 
This must be understood aright. The term Â“consciousnessÂ” does not refer to the objects of your experience. Right now, let us suppose, you are feeling a cool breeze. The cool breeze is something that you are conscious of. In other words, it is an object of consciousness. But that cool breeze isnÂ’t identical with your consciousness or with any part of your consciousness. What is a part of your consciousness is the sensation that the cool breeze causes you to have. What is also a part of your consciousness is your visual perception of the piece of paper that the cool breeze is blowing across your front lawn. But, to echo what we said a moment ago, the piece of paper itself is not identical with your consciousness or even with a part of it, even though it is something that you are conscious of (i.e., it is an object of your consciousness). 
Here we must make a delicate point. Many constituents of our minds exist even when we are sleeping and even when, more generally, they are not occupying our consciousness in any way. You believe that 1 + 1 = 2. But it is only on very rare occasions that this belief of yours is occupying your consciousness. Nonetheless, you obviously donÂ’t lose that belief when itÂ’s not occupying your consciousness. You still have that belief. This is made clear by the fact that it can readily make an appearance in your consciousness. For example, if I tell you that IÂ’ll give you an A in the class if you answer the question Â“what is 1 + 1?Â”, you will without any difficulty be able to draw on your belief that 1 + 1 = 2, even though, in all likelihood, that belief was remote from your consciousness prior to my asking you that question. 
So that belief, existing as it does when it is outside of consciousness, is not a part of consciousness. It is not, as we will henceforth put it, a constituent of your consciousness. 
Thus, there are instances of knowledge that are not consciousness. And there are instances of consciousness that are not knowledge. The euphoria induced by a drug is an instance of consciousness; it is a component of somebodyÂ’s immediate experience. But it isnÂ’t an instance of knowledge. (This is consistent with the fact that somebody experiencing such euphoria could, and probably would, have knowledge of that experience, just as you have knowledge of the piece of paper blowing across your lawn). 
8.2.1 An important fact about consciousness 
One feature of consciousness (as philosophers use that term) is that, if something has consciousness then there is Â“something it is likeÂ” to be that thing. If you are in pain, then there is Â“something it is likeÂ” to be you. So the presence of consciousness in something is sufficient for there to be Â“something it is likeÂ” to be that thing. Further, the presence of consciousness in something is necessary for there to be Â“something it is likeÂ” to be that thing. 
There is nothing it is like to be a pinecone, since pinecones are not conscious. But if, by some miracle, a pinecone were to become conscious, then there would be something it was like to be that pinecone. The presence of consciousness in something is thus both necessary and sufficient for there to be something it is like to be that thing. In fact, consciousness may be identified with a thingÂ’s having the property of there being something it is like to be that thing. 

8.2.2 An important fact about your belief that 1 + 1 = 2 
These points help clarify our earlier point that your belief that 1 + 1 = 2 is not a constituent of your consciousness (even though it may occupy your consciousness, just as the spectacle of litter blowing across a street may occupy your consciousness without, of course, being a veritable ingredient of that consciousness). Although there is something it is like to have a pain or a tickle, or to experience a sense-perception, there isnÂ’t anything it is like to believe that 1 + 1 = 2. 
Of course, that belief may have effects on your consciousnessÂ—in other words, it may generate constituents of consciousness (without itself being such a constituent)Â—and there is something it is like to experience those constituents. For example, your having that belief may lead to your getting an A on a test, which in turn may fill you with joy. 

8.2.3 A consequence of this important fact: the existence of the unconscious 
Thus, your belief that 1 + 1 = 2 is not a constituent of your consciousness. It is not like a pain or a tickle or a perception. But it is clearly Â“consciousÂ” in some sense of the word. (It is not buried in your subconscious; it isnÂ’t like the previously discussed processes by which your mind converts disturbances of your sensory surfaces into perceptions.) It is not a part of your consciousness. So in that sense it is unconscious. So to the extent that it is Â“conscious,Â” it is in the sense that you are conscious of it. 
What we just said about that particular belief is true of many, if not all, beliefs and, indeed, of many desires, aspirations, regrets, intentions, and emotions. Consider your intention to receive a degree from an institution of higher learning. That intention obviously has effects on what you do. (You choose to show up to class, take exams, and so on.) And it therefore obviously has effects on what is occupying your consciousness. (Because of that intention, you are now reading a book and are therefore having various perceptions and feelings that are constituents of your consciousness.) But that intention cannot be identified with any constituent of your consciousness. (That intention continues to exist even when you are asleep.) That intention is better thought of as a structural fact about your mind that underlies and regulates the events that populate your consciousness, without itself being such an event. Similar remarks hold with respect to (for example) your affection for certain people, your dislike of other people, your confidence in your ability to (for example) play tennis, your doubts about your ability to (for example) play the harmonica, and so on. 
These points give us insight into an issue of great importance. You donÂ’t have to be conscious of anything that you are in fact conscious of. You are now conscious of a piece of paper (or computer screen) in front of you. But you donÂ’t have to be, and in a few minutes you wonÂ’t be. You may, at a certain moment, be conscious of the fact that you believe that 1 + 1 = 2. But you obviously donÂ’t have to be conscious of the fact. In fact, most of the time, you are not thinking about that fact and therefore arenÂ’t conscious of it (though you readily become so). So the truth is that we donÂ’t have to be, and in fact are usually not, conscious of much of what is in our own minds. This shows that, contrary to what a number of authors have alleged,[250] 
there is at least some reason to accept the thesis, urged by thinkers in the psychoanalytic tradition, that we are not conscious of much of what is in our own minds. 
Of course, thinkers in that tradition hold not only that we arenÂ’t conscious of much of what occurs in our own minds, but also that emotional blocks may lead to our having very wrong and distorted and impoverished beliefs about our own minds. Whether that thesis is correct lies outside the scope of this book. But what seems reasonably clear is that there are good grounds for at least one contention of that school of thoughtÂ—namely, that we are, at any given time, unaware of many of the events that constitute our very own mental lives. And, once this is granted, it becomes a garden-variety empirical question whether, unless we take special measures to learn about ourselves, we have more than a superficial understanding of our own minds.[251] 

9.0 Knowledge by acquaintance vs. knowledge by description[252] 

At the beginning of this chapter, we distinguished between two kinds of knowledge. The one consists of awareness of people (or, more generally, objects); the other consists of awareness of truths. There is reason to think that up to a point, but probably not entirely, the first kind of knowledge collapses into the second. The reason for this is that, with certain very specific exceptions, awareness of objects is identical with knowledge of truths of a certain kindÂ—that, more specifically, it is identical with knowledge of truths to the effect that certain descriptions are in fact satisfied. 
A story will help clarify what it means to say that a description is Â“satisfied.Â” In order to collect insurance money, an unscrupulous store owner falsely claims that he is robbed. He gives a description of the (nonexistent) perpetrator of the (non-existent) crime. He goes to the police station and tells the police: Â“the person who robbed me was a tall male; he had a tattoo that said Â“I love momÂ” on his forehead; he had pointy gold teeth . . .Â” Here the store owner is really saying that there exists an object (a person) that has certain characteristics. To put it another way, he is saying that a certain description is satisfied, that description being Â“an entity that is a human being who robbed me and has pointy gold teeth and is male and . . .Â” Any statement to the effect that a description is satisfied is known as an existence-claim. So the store owner is affirming the following existence-claim: 
(1) There exists an object that is a person x such that x robbed me, x is a male, x has pointy gold teeth, x has a tattoo that says Â“I love momÂ” on his forehead . . . 
That existence-claim is false, of course, the reason being that the relevant description (the italicized part of 1) is not satisfied. But, of course, many existence-claims are true, the reason being that many descriptions are satisfied. For example, the following existence-claim is true: 
(2) There exists a person who is currently (in Feb. 2008) the 
U.S. President. 
And the reason that 2 is true is, of course, that the relevant description (the italicized part of 2) is satisfied. (It is satisfied by George W. Bush.) 

9.1 Theoretical knowledge as descriptive knowledge 
Whenever knowledge is theoretical or otherwise indirect, it is descriptive (i.e., it consists of knowledge of the truth of an existence-claim). We are aware of the existence of electrons. But we donÂ’t see them or otherwise sense-perceive them; and we certainly donÂ’t have the kind of direct experience of them that we have of some of our own psychological states (e.g., our joys and sorrows). So in what sense are we aware of electrons? The answer: we know the truth of various existence-claims that they satisfy, for example: 
(e) there exist various macroscopic, and therefore perceptible, phenomena that, given known physical laws, are most plausibly explained in terms of theories positing the existence of negatively charged particles orbiting around the nuclei of atoms . . . 
We are aware of electrons in the sense that we know the truth of existence-claims that they satisfy. Since, as we discussed, an existence-claim is a statement to the effect that a description is satisfied, our awareness of electrons is entirely descriptive in nature. 
Remarks similar to those just made about our knowledge of electrons hold with respect to our knowledge of anything theoretical or, indeed, anything whose existence is inferred, as opposed to known directly. 

9.2 Perceptual knowledge as descriptive knowledge 
Our knowledge of directly perceived objects is strictly descriptive. Consider your current visual perception. What it tells you is that a certain existence-claim is true, that existence-claim being along the following lines: 
(sp) There exists a piece of paper that is in such and such a location with respect to me, that has such and such a shape and color, that has such and such discolorations on it . . . 
Perception is description. It is inconceivable that one should have a perception that didnÂ’t describe the world in a certain way and that did not, therefore, say of the world that it contained an object having certain characteristics. (Even if you are looking into empty space, your perception is to the effect that the description stretch of empty space is satisfied by at least one entity in the world.) Thus, a given perception tells you that some existence-claim is satisfied, and perceptual awareness is therefore descriptive in nature. 
This shows that awareness of sense-perceived objects, and therefore of other people, is identical with knowledge of truths of a certain kind (existence-claims), vindicating our earlier suggestion that knowledge of objects at least sometimes collapses into knowledge of truths. 
Are there any cases where knowledge is not descriptive? The answer seems to be Â“yes.Â” If you have an intense pain, it seems that your awareness of that pain is utterly direct and doesnÂ’t involve your knowing that some existence-claim is satisfied. The pain is right there, so to speak, in the theatre of your consciousness, and it neednÂ’t be represented to you through the intermediary of some description. So, at least arguably, we have non-descriptive knowledge of at least some of our psychological states. But, for the most part, it seems that our knowledge is descriptive. 
Why, in the penultimate sentence, do I say Â“at least arguablyÂ”? Because having pain doesnÂ’t necessarily involving knowing that one is pain. Knowing that one is in pain involves more cognitive wherewithal than being in pain. And it may be that the steps one must take to go from being something that merely experiences pain to being something that knows itÂ’s in pain inevitably makes oneÂ’s knowledge of oneÂ’s pains indirect. I myself think that, all of this notwithstanding, one does have direct knowledge of oneÂ’s own conscious, phenomenal states; for I think that, unless we had direct knowledge of such states, we couldnÂ’t have any spatiotemporal knowledge. Nonetheless, given the distinction between experiencing pain and knowing that one is experiencing pain (or any other phenomenally pregnant, conscious condition), it is not a trivial question whether, indeed, oneÂ’s knowledge of the fact that one is in pain (same qualification) is direct. 
9.3 Procedural vs. declarative knowledge 
We have found that, at least arguably, there are some cases of awareness that are not awareness of truths. At least arguably, we can be directly aware of some of our own psychological states and can therefore be aware of them without being aware of truths that describe or otherwise implicate them. Are there other kinds of awareness or of knowledge that are not awarenesses of truth? 
Some philosophers and psychologists say Â“yes,Â” the reasoning being as follows: 
(KH)[253] 
We must distinguish knowledge-that from knowledge-how. I know that Paris is the capital of France. This is knowledge of a truth. It is knowledge-that. I know how to ride a bike. This is knowledge, but it isnÂ’t knowledge of a truth. It is knowledge-how, not knowledge-that. 
Any skill is a case of knowledge-how. ItÂ’s easily shown that knowledge-how and knowledge-that are fundamentally different things. No matter how much I know about the physics and geometry of bike-riding, I may not be able to ride a bike at all; and no matter how good I am at riding a bike, I may not be able to tell you the first thing about the geometry or physics involved. 
No amount of knowledge-that adds up to a skill, and no amount of skill adds up to knowledge-that. So knowledge-how is not knowledge-that, but it is, of course, knowledge of some kind or other. 
But itÂ’s a spurious argument for a false conclusion. Knowledge of a language is knowledge-how. To be able to speak English is to have a skill. But that skill involves having knowledge-that, for you must know various syntactic and semantic truths (e.g., the truth that Â“snowÂ” picks out snow) to speak English. Knowledge of a language is operationalized semantic and syntactic knowledge. In general, procedural knowledge is operationalized declarative knowledge. (By Â“declarative knowledge,Â” I mean knowledge of truths.) 
Of course, not all procedural knowledge starts out as declarative knowledge. (Your ability to ride a bike didnÂ’t start out as non-procedural knowledge. It was procedural all along.) Moreover, one has no conscious access to the declarative knowledge internal to oneÂ’s procedural knowledge. (One has conscious access only to analogues of that knowledge. A given piece of knowledge may be stored at many different cognitive levels. Knowledge is oftentimes Â“over-represented.Â” A baseball player who is also a physicist may have two distinct pieces of knowledge of some one fact.) Contrary to what Ludwig Wittgenstein (1889Â–1951) and John McDowell (1942Â– ) hold, the conclusion to be drawn from these facts is not that knowledge-that is no part of knowledge-how, and is instead that the mind is compartmentalized, and the right hand doesnÂ’t always know what the left is doing. 
10.0 Intuitive vs. discursive knowledge 
Whenever we know something without knowing how we know it, we have intuitive knowledge. Whenever we know something and we do know how we know, we have discursive knowledge. So to know something intuitively is to Â“just know it,Â” whereas to know something discursively is to know it while also knowing the grounds on the basis of which one knows it. 
Some stories will clarify these points. 
Story #1. Timmy, who is 10 years old, is in a classroom and he is looking at a figure on the blackboard. The teacher points to the figure and asks Timmy Â“what shape does that have?Â” Timmy correctly says Â“itÂ’s a circle.Â” The teacher asks: Â“how do you know? Why is it a circle as opposed to oval?Â” Timmy says: Â“I just know. ItÂ’s just obvious that itÂ’s a circle.Â” 
Story #2. Jones, who is a math major, is in a classroom and he is looking at a figure on the blackboard. The professor points to the figure and asks Jones Â“what shape does that have?Â” Jones says Â“itÂ’s a circle.Â” The professor asks: Â“how do you know? Why is it a circle as opposed to oval?Â” Jones says: Â“because, if x and y are any two arbitrarily short segments of that shapeÂ’s periphery, xÂ’s degree of curvature equals yÂ’s.Â” 
Commentary: Obviously both Jones and Timmy know that the figure on the board is a circle. But Jones knows something that Timmy does not know. But what, exactly? A possible answer is this: Â“Timmy doesnÂ’t know why the figure is a circle, whereas Jones does have that knowledge.Â” But surely TimmyÂ’s belief is based on the very fact about the figureÂ’s shape that Jones has described. It seems to me thatÂ—in some way, at some levelÂ—Timmy is aware of the fact about that figure that Jones is describing. He doesnÂ’t know it in the same way as JonesÂ—but he still knows it. So it is wrong, or at least very misleading, to say that Timmy doesnÂ’t know what it is about that figure that makes it a circle. 
10.1 How intuitive and discursive knowledge differ 
HereÂ’s what I think. Jones does, whereas Timmy does not, know on what grounds he himself is judging the figure to be a circle. Timmy and Jones both believe that the drawing is a circle, and (so we may assume) each believes it for the right reasons. But Jones knows, whereas Timmy does not know, what the considerations are that are moving him to make that judgment. The difference between Timmy and Jones is that Jones has a kind of self-knowledge that Timmy lacks. 
10.2 How intuitive and discursive knowledge differ (continued) 
HereÂ’s another hypothesis (which, I think, is compatible with the one just given). Even though both Jones and Timmy know that the drawing is a circle, Jones knows this in two distinct ways, whereas Timmy knows it in only one way. Timmy has a strictly visual (or, in any case, sensory) knowledge of this fact, whereas Jones has what might be described as propositional knowledge of this same fact. Let us now develop this point. 
First of all, a proposition is what is meant by a sentenceÂ—it is the information encoded in a sentence. The information provided by sentences has two striking features: first, it is very schematic; second, it is the kind of information that can be grasped only through an act of judgment, as opposed to perception. (These two facts are related, in ways that will now become apparent.) 
Suppose you see a certain man, whom you know to be Smith, next to a certain telephone pole, and you report that fact by saying: 
(SP) Â“Smith is next to that telephone pole.Â” 
Compare what you actually see to SP. You donÂ’t just see Smith. You see an individual with very specific characteristics (a specific shape, a specific posture or series of specific postures, wearing specific clothes, having hair of a specific color, and so on). And you donÂ’t just see a telephone pole. You see an object having a specific shape, in a specific location, with a specific color (and with specific discolorations on it), with wires of a certain kind attached to certain parts of it, and so on. Thus, the sentence provides a very schematic and abstract representation of the information provided to you by your visual perception. So, from one viewpoint, the sentence under-represents the content of your visual perception. 
But, from another viewpoint, the sentence over-represents the content of your perception. Given only what you seeÂ—given only what your eyes are telling youÂ—it could be that you are seeing somebody other than Smith; it could be that you are seeing somebody who looks just like him but isnÂ’t him Â—or even that you arenÂ’t seeing a person at all and are in fact seeing a robot. When you characterize that thing as Â“Smith,Â” you are making a judgment as to who and what that thing is; you are making a judgment as to the biological species and as to the specific identity of that individual. Though partially based on what your eyes are now telling you, that judgment incorporates information that is not derived from that specific perceptionÂ—information that is derived from past meetings with various individuals and from inferences drawn therefrom. 
And given only what your eyes are telling you, you donÂ’t know that you are seeing a telephone pole. A telephone pole is something that serves a specific function within a complicated network of social and physical relations. When you are staring at the telephone pole, you cannot literally see it performing these functions. Thus, implicit in your characterization of that thing as a Â“telephoneÂ” pole is a judgment as to its social function. And, though partially derived from your sense-perception, the grounds for that judgment have roots in past experiences of yours and also in inferences drawn therefrom. So, from that viewpoint, SP over-represents what your eyes are telling you on this occasion. 
Similar points hold with respect to the differences between Timmy and Jones. Jones isnÂ’t simply seeing a certain objectÂ’s shape; he isnÂ’t simply uploading perceptual information. He is making a judgment about that information. (So Jones is generating Â“meta-information.Â”) By contrast, Timmy is just uploading the information. 
A related point is that, although both Timmy and Jones know that the drawing is a shape, Jones knows this fact in more ways than Timmy. This can be understood in terms of our earlier point that knowledge is descriptive. Timmy knows that the drawing is a circle and so does Jones. But, in knowing of the existence of this one fact, Jones knows two different truths. He knows the truth embodied in some graphic (visual) description of that fact, and he also knows the truth embodied in some non-graphic representation of that fact. By contrast, Timmy knows the first truth but not the second. 
We thus seem to have two answers to the question Â“what does Jones know that Timmy doesnÂ’t?Â” First, Jones has a certain kind of self-knowledge that Timmy lacks: Jones does, whereas Timmy does not, know what the considerations are that led him to believe (rightly) that the drawing is a circle. Second, Jones knows the fact in question under two different descriptions (one pictorial, the other conceptual), whereas Timmy knows it only under one description. 
10.3 The paradox of analysis 
These points may give us some insight into an old philosophical dispute. Consider the statement: 
(CR) x is a circle if and only if x is a two-dimensional figure of uniform curvature. 
Obviously CR is informative. It isnÂ’t like the statement: 
(CC) x is a circle if, and only if, x is a circle. 
CR is an example of a conceptual analysis. A conceptual analysis is a statement that lays bare the structure of a concept. 
According to G.E. Moore, it is paradoxical to suppose that conceptual analyses can be informative. There is, he says, a Â“paradox of analysis.Â” MooreÂ’s reasoning seems to be this. The sentence Â“water is H2OÂ” expresses 
an analysis of water. In that sentence, the words flanking the Â“isÂ” refer to the same substance. If they didnÂ’t, that sentence wouldnÂ’t express a correct analysis. For the same reason, the expressions flanking the Â“iffÂ” in a sentence expressing a conceptual analysis must refer to the same concept. But if they did, then CR would be trivial, like CC, and thus fail to be an analysis. 
This is not good reasoning. TrueÂ—Â“water is H2OÂ” expresses a Â“chemical analysisÂ”; and, in it, the two words flanking the Â“isÂ” co-refer. TrueÂ—CR expresses a Â“conceptual analysis.Â” But it doesnÂ’t follow that, in it, the expressions flanking the Â“iffÂ” must co-refer. MooreÂ’s reasoning is comparable to that of somebody who thinks that, since so and so isnÂ’t interested in having Â“legalÂ” (law-related) discussions, so and so has no wish to have Â“legalÂ” (law-permitted) discussions. 
In any case, MooreÂ’s paradox is easily enough dissolved. The truth that one grasps in virtue of knowing that: 
(i) 
x is a circle, 

(ii) 
x is a two-dimensional figure of uniform curvature. 


is different from the truth that one grasps in virtue of knowing that: 
Both of those truths describe the same factÂ—the fact that a certain object has a certain shape. But a given fact can obviously be described in different, but equally correct ways. The fact that x is a triangle can be described by saying that x is the area bounded by three straight edges, any two of which intersect, but not all of three of which do so. And that same fact can be described by saying that x is a three-sided, straight-edged, closed, planar figure. And: 
(iii) x is a triangle iff x is the area bounded by three straight edges, any two of which intersect, but not all three of which do so iff x is a three-sided, straight-edged, closed, planar figure, 
is just another way of saying that there are three different ways of describing xÂ’s shape. 
Facts aren't truths. One can't know this without knowing how to solve the Paradox of Analysis. But Moore didn't know it. 
11.0 Justification vs. discovery 
The question: 
(1) What events in NewtonÂ’s mind led to his coming up with his theory of gravitation? 
must be distinguished from the question: 
(2) What merit does that theory have? 
One can know the answer to the one question without knowing the answer to the other. To know why Newton had such and such beliefs, I donÂ’t need to know whether those beliefs are correct or otherwise meritorious, and to know whether those beliefs are correct or otherwise meritorious, I donÂ’t need to know why Newton had them. 
Given a belief, the question Â“is it correct?Â” is to be distinguished from the question Â“how was it arrived at?Â” and knowing the answer to the one question doesnÂ’t necessarily involve knowing the answer to the other. 
Â“Justification isnÂ’t discovery.Â” Philosophers of science often say this. In so doing, theyÂ’re affirming the points just made.[254] 

11.1 The connection between justification and discovery 
Granting that an ideaÂ’s pedigree is to be distinguished from its merits, itÂ’s misleading to say that justification isnÂ’t discovery. To discover something is to come to know it. Knowing something involves having a justified belief in it. The justification for that belief will be encoded in the thoughts that led to that belief. No justification, no knowledge. No knowledge, no discovery. Thus, justification is discoveryÂ—or at least a good part of it. 
We must distinguish discovering something from merely coming to believe it. One cannot discover something without coming to believe it, but one can come to believe something without discovering it. Coming to believe something doesnÂ’t necessarily involve being justified in believing it or, therefore, in knowing it or, therefore, in discovering it. 
But to the extent that a personÂ’s thought-processes are expressions of intellectual ability, and not of prejudice or some other discovery-thwarting factor, that personÂ’s beliefs are likely to be justified and, consequently, that person wonÂ’t come to believe something without being justified in doing so. Given that the conjectures that led to great scientific and intellectual advances are obviously reflections of intellectual ability, as opposed to blind luck, it follows that oftentimes the justification for such a conjecture is to be found in its psychological antecedents. It follows that justification is inherent, not just in scientific discovery, but also in scientific proto-discovery. In other words, itÂ’s inherent not only in the processes that lead to advances, but in the processes that lead to the conjectures that lead to such advances. 
Great ideas often consist of many intricately interconnected subsidiary ideas. The odds of accidentally stumbling upon those ideas, as opposed to arriving at them on the basis of knowledge and insight, are exceedingly slim. Unless Newton and Keynes were just lucky, which is unlikely, the thoughts they had along the way to making their discoveries were driven by an understanding of how the evidence at their disposal ought to be interpreted. Those thoughts were therefore to the effect that, since such and such evidence justifies thus and such contentions, thus and such contentions ought to be accepted; therefore, thus and such contentions are true. So, setting aside cases where the discoverer was simply lucky, the psychology and the logic of discovery mirror each other. 
Pascal said Â“it is through intuition that we discover; it is through logic that we prove.Â”[255] 
This is wrong. It is through logic that we discover and it is 
through logic that we prove. For there is no discovery without justification. An unjustified intuition isnÂ’t a discovery at all. And if an unjustified intuition happens to be right, itÂ’s a matter of luck. While some non-trivial theoretical innovations may be made through luck, most of them are not. (I doubt that any of them are.) And a correct belief arrived at through intuition, as opposed to luck, is ipso facto justified. Proof is the identification of the logic embodied in discovery. 
11.2 Discovery vs. prediscovery 
Â“For all we know,Â” many a philosopher of science says, 
(BL)[256] 
It was NewtonÂ’s being hit on the head by an apple that led him to posit the inverse-square law. So, were we to know exactly what psychological processes led to Newton's putting forth this conjecture, we wouldn't necessarily find a justification for it; and should we find such a justification, our doing so would be a matter of blind luck. There's no point in poking around Newton's psyche unless you're interested in his relationship to his mother. If you're interested in physics, you'll find nothing. 
If you psychoanalyze great scientists, you'll find causes, not justifications. You'll find the cause of Einstein's belief that inertial and gravitational mass are the same thing. But you're no more likely to find a justification for that belief than you are if you look in Einstein's sock-drawer. Psychology isn't logic. Justification isn't discovery. 
BL is overstated. Not everybody who is hit on the head becomes an innovator in physics. So far as a blow to the head had anything to do with NewtonÂ’s discoveries, it was only by way of its triggering an intricate train of thought. We must distinguish the instigators of a thought process from the thought process itself. Being hit on the head was no part of NewtonÂ’s discovery process. It was, at most, a part of his discovery pre-process. The blow, supposing that it happened, merely activated the relevant processes and therefore wasnÂ’t constitutive of them.[257] 

11.3 The roots of the problem 
The connection between discovery and justification is easy to overlook if one doesnÂ’t bear in mind the following four points: 
(1) 
Having a justification for a belief doesnÂ’t always involve knowing what that justification is. 

(2) 
Knowing that justification doesnÂ’t always involve being able to say what it is. (One canÂ’t always articulate what one knows.) 

(3) 
Being able to articulate that justification is different from actually doing so and, in so doing, transmitting that justification to others. 

(4) 
Transmitting oneÂ’s own justification for a given belief is different from producing a general justification for it. (It is one thing for me to have certain experiences that give me an airÂ­tight justification for believing P. But given that those experiences may have occurred under singular circumstances, the likes of which are unlikely to be repeated, it is quite another thing for me to provide others with a way in which they can become justified in believing P.) 


11.3.1 (1) explained 
There is often a delay between having a justification for a belief and knowing what that justification is. My intuition tells me that so and so is ill-intentioned, even though, on the surface, he is behaving amicably; that a given sentence is grammatical, even though my grammar book classifies it as ungrammatical; that a given animal is about to attack, even though it isnÂ’t giving off any of the obvious signs. 
We trust our intuitions, and our confidence in them is usually vindicated. (Speaking personally, I always regret second-guessing my intuitions.) But when we have them, we donÂ’t know why they are to be trusted. If we did, they wouldnÂ’t be intuitions, since an intuition is, by definition, a belief whose justification, if it exists, is unknown to the person having the belief. Some have said that, for this very reason, intuitions are never knowledge. Â“If one has grounds for believing something,Â” it is said, Â“one knows what those grounds are.Â” 
This reasoning couldnÂ’t possibly be more off the mark. It is only to the extent that one hasnÂ’t fully internalized the relevant principles that oneÂ’s thought fails to be intuitive. It is only pedants and neophytes who rely on discursive thought. Good pianists donÂ’t have to think before they hit every note. Bad pianists do. Good pianists, unlike their bad counterparts, have internalized the relevant rules and, for that reason, donÂ’t need the crutch of conscious, discursive mentation. Relying on consciously executed operations to apply rules is like relying on an instruction manual. 
Discursive thought is remedial thought, and thought is non-remedial only insofar as itÂ’s intuitive. It doesnÂ’t follow that all non-discursive thought is truth-conducive. But it does follow that not all intuitive thought is bad. Given that knowledge is intuitive only in so far as its possessor doesnÂ’t know the justification for it, it follows that one can be justified in having a certain belief without knowing what that justification is. 
Nonetheless, philosophers of science tend to hold that one has a justification only when one states, or at least can readily state, oneÂ’s justification.[258] 
For this reason, theyÂ’re forced to say intuitions are never justified. Given that scientific breakthroughs result largely from intuitive thought and often themselves take the form of intuitions, philosophers of science have no choice but to see the generation of discoveries as having no connection, or only a fortuitous connection, to the eventual justification of 
them. 
11.3.2 (2) explained 
One can know oneÂ’s reason for having a given belief without being able to state it. A skillful interrogator may know why he believes that the suspect is lying but not be able to say why he thinks this. His judgments are made on the basis of subtle cues that he might have a hard time articulating. Articulating oneÂ’s knowledge may involve translating it from one medium into another. This is the case with the interrogator. His judgments are responses to visual information. Articulating those judgments would involve translating that information into a non-visual medium. 
Imagine the following. Max believes that metal usually expands when heated, and this belief of his is thoroughly justified. (HeÂ’s done numerous experiments, absorbed copious amounts of theory, and so on.) But for some reason Max refuses to state his reasons for having that belief. MaxÂ’s situation is very different from the interrogatorÂ’s. Unlike the interrogator, Max knows what the justification for his belief is. In any case, even though MaxÂ’s belief is thoroughly justified, it could be said that Max has Â“failed to justifyÂ” it. Thus, the expression Â“unjustified beliefÂ” is ambiguous. On the one hand, it can refer to beliefs that arenÂ’t justified. On the other, it can refer to beliefs the justifications for which, if they exist, havenÂ’t been stated. 
11.3.3 (3) explained 
Even though a given scientist has cogent reasons for accepting a given hypothesis, and makes every effort to communicate them to others, it doesnÂ’t follow that others know what those reasons are. Others may not understand what that scientist is sayingÂ—maybe his theories are too advanced for them. Maybe they do understand what heÂ’s saying but havenÂ’t yet had a chance to authenticate his results. Until they have good reason to accept the scientistÂ’s testimony, his justification for accepting the theory in question isnÂ’t yet theirs. 
When epistemologists say that a belief is justified, they mean that the person who has it is justified in having it. When philosophers of science say that a belief is justified, they mean either what epistemologists mean or, what is more likely, they mean that people in general are justified in having it. 
There was a time when many people believed that smoking causes lung cancer, but when only a few researchers actually knew it, since those researchers alone knew the relevant clinical data. During that time, it would have been correct to describe Â“the widespread belief that smoking causes cancerÂ” as unjustified. 
In general, there are many cases where the belief in such and such is unjustified and therefore isnÂ’t knowledge, even though specific scientists had already discovered such and such and therefore knew it, and were therefore justified in believing it. It thus happens that such and such is discovered before the belief in it is. 
Chapter 11 Skepticism and the Justification of Inductive Inference[H7] 

1.0 What is skepticism? 
A skeptic is a doubter, not a disbeliever. For me to be skeptical about SmithÂ’s assertion that heÂ’s an astronaut is for me to doubt that heÂ’s an astronaut. It isnÂ’t for me to disbelieve that assertionÂ—only to question it. If IÂ’m convinced that Smith is not an astronaut, IÂ’m not skeptical about his claim. Skepticism is doubt, not disbelief. 
But there is some tendency for skepticism to give way to disbelief. Even if I never definitively learn that Smith is not an astronaut, if I continue to find no good reason to believe that he is one, IÂ’m more likely than not to disbelieve it. We feel that, if a claim is true, some positive evidence for it will turn up: the mere absence of counterevidence isnÂ’t enough for us. 
Does our human tendency to transition from doubt to disbelief have any logical basis? Or is it just another case of emotion and instinct corrupting rationality? It depends on the case. In some cases, but not all, failure to find positive evidence is itself counterevidence; and, in such cases, our tendency to slide from doubt to disbelief does have a logical basis. But, as weÂ’ll see in this very chapter, unless some highly defensible forms of skepticism can be refuted, this claim of mine is simply wrong. 
Many important debates in philosophy concern the merits of some form of skepticism. Are there non-spatiotemporal entities? (Skepticism about platonic entities.) Do we have beliefs, feelings, etc., that we arenÂ’t aware of having? (Skepticism about unconscious ideation.) Could observation ever provide adequate grounds for believing in unobservables (e.g., electrons) or should we regard terms like Â“electronÂ” as referring to fictions of some kind or as not referring to anything at all? (Skepticism about theoretical entities.) 
As these examples indicate, philosophical skepticisms involve whole categories of truths. One doubts all truths affirming, or presupposing, the existence of non-spatiotemporal entities, unconscious emotions, theoretical entities, etc. 
In this chapter, weÂ’ll discuss what are probably the two most important forms of skepticism: skepticism about the external world and skepticism about inductive inference. 
To be a skeptic about the external world is to doubt that what our senses are telling us is accurate. One is a skeptic of this kind if one believes there to be no good reason to believe that oneÂ’s sense-perceptions are anything other than hallucinations. 
A bit of background is needed to say what it is for one to be a skeptic about inductive inference. Some knowledge is direct. One doesnÂ’t have to figure it outÂ—one just knows it. Somebody who is experiencing a searing pain knows it, and he didnÂ’t have to figure it out. But much knowledge is indirect. Einstein didnÂ’t Â“just knowÂ” that a bodyÂ’s mass increases as its speed increases; he had to figure it out. In other words, he had to infer it. So for knowledge to be indirect is for it to be acquired through inference. 
There are two parts to any inference: the premises and the conclusion. The conclusion is the belief arrived atÂ—the thing that, when the inference leads from the right premises to the right conclusion in the right way, is Â“figured out.Â” The premises are the pre-existing beliefs or assumptions on the basis of which one arrives at the conclusion. 
There are two kinds of inferences: deductive and inductive. An inference is deductive if, supposing oneÂ’s premises true and oneÂ’s reasoning non-faulty, it is impossible for oneÂ’s conclusion to be false. If my premise is that x is a square and my conclusion is that x has four sides, itÂ’s logically impossible for my conclusion to be false if my premise is true. So this would be a case of a deductive inference. An inference is inductive if, supposing oneÂ’s premises true and oneÂ’s reasoning non-faulty, it is possible for oneÂ’s conclusion to be false. If my premise is that, in the 35 years IÂ’ve been drinking tap water, I have never become sick as a result of doing so, and my conclusion is that I wonÂ’t become sick as a result of drinking the glass of tap water in front of me, my conclusion may be false, even though, so we may assume, that belief was generated in an utterly reasonable manner. So this would be a case of an inductive inference. 
A skeptic about inductive inference holds that it is impossible, as a matter of principle, to learn anything through non-deductive inference. He holds, in other words, that one cannot acquire knowledge through inductive inference. All knowledge is either direct or is arrived at through deductive inference. 
If this is right, then we know only an infinitesimally small fraction of what we think we know. This is because, for reasons thoroughly discussed in Chapter 10, no knowledge about the external world is direct, and only some knowledge of ourselves is direct. 
We will start by discussing skepticism about induction. 
2.0 Skepticism about induction 
David Hume made it clear why it may be doubted whether inductive inference ever leads to knowledge. Here is HumeÂ’s argument[H8] 
: 
(HA)[259] 
Consider some inductive inferenceÂ—for example, Â“the sun has always risen in the past; therefore, it will rise tomorrow.Â” First of all, this argument is not deductive, since, even if the premise is granted, itÂ’s a theoretical possibility that the conclusion will be false. The sun might explode, after all. So the conclusion is, at best, probable. ThatÂ’s step 1. 
HereÂ’s step 2. Given that the connection between premise and conclusion isnÂ’t deductive, we must ask: how does the premise warrant the conclusion? In other words, what reason does the (supposed) truth of the premise give us for accepting the conclusion? 
HereÂ’s an answer that seems tempting at first: Â“The past resembles the future; the known resembles the unknown. Nature is uniform. So given that such and such has been the case until now, we may infer that such and such will continue to be the case. Given that, until now, the sun has risen, pinewood has floated, water has quenched thirst, etc., itÂ’s reasonable to conclude that the sun will continue to rise, and so on. It is thus the principle that nature is uniformÂ—or, as weÂ’ll call it, the uniformity principle (UP)Â—that allows us to make rational, non-deductive inferences about the unknown on the basis of the known.Â” 
But this argument is no good. No one directly knows that UP holds for all places and times. At most, one knows that it has held for the fragments of nature with which one has personally been acquainted. One doesnÂ’t directly know that it held of past objects with which one was not personally acquainted; and one doesnÂ’t directly know that it will hold of future objects with which one wonÂ’t be personally acquainted. 
Thus, any knowledge that one has of UP must be inferential. The inference in question cannot be deductive. Given only that the ravens thus far known to one have been black, it doesnÂ’t follow deductively that ravens not (yet) known to one are also black. In general, given only that the phiÂ’s known to one are psiÂ’s, it doesnÂ’t follow deductively that the same is true of the phiÂ’s that arenÂ’t known to one. If it follows at all, it follows inductively, not deductively. But it follows inductively only on the condition that UP is granted. Since, however, a precondition for UPÂ’s legitimacy is the legitimacy of inferences of the form since known phiÂ’s are psiÂ’s, so are unknown phiÂ’s, it follows that UP is not legitimate and, therefore, that there is no way to justify inductive inference. 
[260] 

3.0 Problems with HumeÂ’s argument 
Nobody denies that inductive inferences are knowledge-conducive and, therefore, that the conclusion of HumeÂ’s argument is false. Even Hume said that, in his bones, he couldnÂ’t accept it. But thereÂ’s no accepted response to HumeÂ’s extremely clever argument. Nonetheless, HumeÂ’s argument is refutable and a refutation of it must lie in some argument not totally unlike the following.
