There are two serious errors in HumeÂ’s argument. First, it assumes that the primary form of non-deductive inference is induction by enumeration. In actuality, induction by enumeration is less important than, and subordinate to, a very different form of non-deductive inference known as inference to the best explanation. (The italicized terms will be defined shortly.) Second, Hume assumes that non-deductive inferences go through only if UP is granted (i.e., only if itÂ’s granted that nature is uniform.) But UP is not the relevant principle. The relevant principle, I propose, is that good explanations minimize causal anomalies. LetÂ’s refer to this principle as Â“MCÂ” (short for Â“minimization of causal anomaliesÂ”). Another way of stating MC is to say that, given two otherwise comparable theories, the one that does the most in the way of anomaly elimination is the better one. 
Unlike UP, MC is, I submit, analytically true: it is inherent in the concept of what an explanation is that, other things being equal, the theory that eliminates the greater number of unexplained explainersÂ—and, in particular, the greater number of unexplained causal connectionsÂ—is the one to be preferred. Because this principle, unlike UP, is analytically true, it doesnÂ’t have to be validated on inductive grounds. This makes it possible to validate inductive inference in a way that, unlike the way that Hume considers, is not viciously circular. 
3.1 Inference to best explanation vs. enumerative induction 
There are two forms of inductive inference: induction by enumeration and inference to the best explanation. (See Chapter 12.) An induction by enumeration has the form: every F that IÂ’ve ever known of was also a G; therefore all FÂ’s are GÂ’s. Example: All the balls that IÂ’ve thus far removed from the urn have been white; therefore, all the balls in (or removed by me) the urn are white. 
An inference to the best explanation has the form: Â“It is known that S; it isnÂ’t yet known that S*; but if S* were true, it would, without doing excessive violence to what we (think we) know about the world, explain why S is true; moreover, if S* werenÂ’t true, it would be hard to find a viable alternative explanation of S; therefore, S* is true.Â” 
For example: IÂ’m very careful with my credit cards (I never use them to make online purchases, I never let anyone besides reliable merchants see them, etc); and, before my friend Larry moved in with me, no unauthorized purchases were ever made with any card of mine. But after he moved in, my cards were used to make a series of unauthorized purchases. Moreover, the items bought were ones that, for work-related reasons, Larry desperately needs and that nobody outside of LarryÂ’s rather unusual profession would have the slightest use for. Knowing all of this, and not knowing any other way to account for the unauthorized purchases, I conclude that Larry made those purchases. 
ItÂ’s widely assumed among philosophers that induction by enumeration is the more fundamental form of inference. This is a mistake. All cases of induction by enumeration, when legitimate, are parasitic on cases of inference to the best explanation. There are, of course, many cases where one of my reasons for thinking that all FÂ’s are GÂ’s is that every F IÂ’ve ever known of was also a G. But, setting aside beliefs arrived at through spurious reasoning, there are no cases where that was my only reason for believing that all FÂ’s are GÂ’s. HumeÂ’s argument focuses entirely on induction by enumeration. Hume is right, I believe, that this form of inference is unjustifiable. But we donÂ’t use this form of inference. In any case, we donÂ’t use it in the way that Hume thinks. 
Moreover, we shouldnÂ’t use it and we neednÂ’t use it. In some cases we may think that weÂ’re doing straight induction by enumeration. But, in almost all such cases, a little probing always shows that many interconnected background assumptions are at work and that, when these are made explicit, what weÂ’re really trying to do is to produce an inference to the best explanation. And, although there are cases of straight induction by enumeration, they tend to occur in rather artificial contexts and that, when they do occur, theyÂ’re clearly spurious. 
There is a well-known inductive error known as the Â“gamblerÂ’s fallacy.Â” (Sometimes itÂ’s referred to as the Â“Monte CarloÂ” fallacy.) You are playing a game of roulette. (This game involves rolling a ball into a spinning wheel, which is divided into numbered slots.) [H9] 
You know that nothing about the game is in any way riggedÂ—that ball isnÂ’t weighted or otherwise propertied in such a way as to favor a particular outcome, and that neither the wheel nor the underlying apparatus were built or modified to favor any given outcome more than any other. And you thus know that, given only the physical properties of the game, the ball, once rolled, is no more likely to land in this as opposed to that slot. (How you know this is irrelevant; weÂ’ll just assume that you do.) You also know that, given any slot on the wheel, there is nothing about you that makes a ball youÂ’ve rolled more likely to land in that spot than in any otherÂ—nothing about your body, mind, or ball-rolling practices that favors this as opposed to that outcome. (Again, how you know this is irrelevant; weÂ’ll just assume that you do.) YouÂ’ve rolled the ball seven times. Each time, at least it has landed in slot #27. It must be stressed that you know there to be nothing about the game or about you that predisposed this to happenÂ—that you know this to be entirely a matter of luck. 
Under these circumstances, it would be natural to predict that youÂ’ll roll a 27 next time. But that prediction would be irrational: you have no more reason to believe that youÂ’ll roll a 27 than you will any other number. And if, by chance, you do roll a 27 next time, it will be natural to predict that youÂ’ll roll a 27 the following time. But this too would be completely irrational. So long as you know that thereÂ’s nothing inherent in the game or in yourself that favors this as opposed to that outcome, you are never any more entitled to bet that, with the next rolled, youÂ’ll roll a 27 than you are to bet that youÂ’ll roll any other available number. It doesnÂ’t matter how many consecutive 27s you rolled prior to that roll: it could have been ten, a thousand, or a million. 
By the same token, no matter how many consecutive 27s you roll, you are never any more entitled to bet that, next time, you wonÂ’t roll a 27 than you are to bet that you wonÂ’t roll any one of the other available numbers. It would be natural to think otherwise, of course. Given how improbable it is that you will roll five consecutive 27s, let alone 50, you may have an urge, when rolling for the 51st time, to think: 
This time, surely, IÂ’m even more unlikely to roll a 27 than I am to roll any other available number. The game isnÂ’t rigged. The likelihood of my rolling 51 consecutive 27s is infinitesimal and, therefore, is much smaller than 1/n (where n is the number of available slots). So a 27-roll is especially unlikelyÂ—more unlikely than a 5-roll or a 13-roll. 
But this is spurious reasoning. You are no more, and no less, unlikely to roll a 27 than you are to roll any other number. With every roll, the chances of rolling any one of the available numbers are identical with the chances of roll any one of the others. Since, by hypothesis, the conditions that obtain on any two occasions are identical, it would be irrational on any given occasion to think any given outcome more likely than any other given outcome. 
3.1.1 When is enumerative induction rational? 
When would it become rational to believe that, next time, youÂ’re more likely than not to roll this as opposed to that numberÂ—that, for example, you are especially likely to roll a 27? This belief becomes rational when, and only when, you have reason to believe that a 27-roll is favored by the structures involved in the game. And that belief, in its turn, is rational if you know that circumstances at all like the following obtain: 
*The ball is magnetically attracted to the 27-slot. 
*On any given occasion, you (unconsciously) intend to roll a 27, and you are so talented at rolling marble-sized balls that you can roll a 27 if it is your (unconscious) intention to do so. 
*The 27-slot is much bigger than any of the other slots. In fact, it takes up so much space on the roulette wheel that the remaining spaces are too small for the ball[H10] 
to fit into them. 
You are rational to believe that youÂ’ll continue to roll 27s to the extent that your having thus far rolled multiple 27s in a row gives you reason to believe there to be some underlying structure favoring that outcome. And to the extent that a long run of 27-rolls doesnÂ’t give you such a reason, you are irrational to believe that youÂ’re any more (or any less) likely to roll a 27 than you are any other number. So, no matter how many consecutive 27s you roll, if you know with complete certainty that nothing about either yourself or the set-up of the game favors that outcome, it is irrational to think that, next time, youÂ’re any more (or less) likely to roll a 27 than you are a 5 or a 32. Put pedantically, it is only insofar as you have reason to believe in such a structure that you have reason to expect something that has the property of being a ball rolled by you to have the property of landing in the 27-slot. 
3.1.2 Generalizing these points 
Your knowing of many phiÂ’s that are psiÂ’s and of none that are not doesnÂ’t necessarily give you any reason to believe that the next phi you encounter will be a psi; it gives you such a reason only insofar as it gives you a reason to believe in some structure or mechanism that disposes phiÂ’s to be psiÂ’s. If you know on independent grounds that there is no such mechanism, no run of phiÂ’s that are psiÂ’s, no matter how long, gives you a reason to think that the next phi will be a psi; and you are guilty of the gamblerÂ’s fallacyÂ—and thus, as we saw, of the most rank absurdityÂ—so far as you think otherwise. Thus, in and of itself induction by enumeration is worthless; itÂ’s a fallacious form of reasoning and falls in the same category as every other argumentative fallacy. Of course, if you know of many phiÂ’s that are psiÂ’s and of none that are not, you do have good reason to hold that, other things being equal, the next phi you encounter will be a psi. But this is because your having this knowledge gives you reason to believe there to be a principled or lawful connection between a thingÂ’s being a phi, on the one hand, and its being a psi, on the other. Here, then, is the real structure of inferences that are wrongly thought of as cases of induction by enumeration: 
(i) 
you know of many phiÂ’s that are psiÂ’s and of no phiÂ’s that are non-psiÂ’s; 

(ii) 
on the basis of step (i), you believe there to be some principled connection between a thingÂ’s being a phi and its being a psi; 


(iii) if you know of a given thing that is a phi, but donÂ’t yet know whether or not itÂ’s a psi, you know, given (ii), that itÂ’s likely to be a psi; therefore, 
(iv) you conclude (if only tentatively) that it is a psi. 
Thus, any case of induction by enumeration that isnÂ’t an instance of the gamblerÂ’s fallacy involves the positing of some mechanism or law that, were it to exist, would explain a certain concomitanceÂ—it involves, in other words, a case of inference to the best explanation. The best explanation of the fact that all known phiÂ’s are psiÂ’s is that, thanks to some mechanism or, in any case, principled connection of some kind or other, a thingÂ’s being a phi disposes it to be a psi; and as soon as such a mechanism has been posited, but not one second sooner, your knowing of a given thing that itÂ’s a phi is a reason for you to hold that itÂ’s a psi. So any non-fallacious Â“induction by enumerationÂ” is nothing other than a case of inference to the best explanation (or, more precisely, is a case of applying some theory that embodies an inference to the best explanation). 
HumeÂ’s argument assumes that it is only through induction by enumeration that the past is any guide to the future. It assumes that, so far as we have any reason to believe that future phiÂ’s will be psiÂ’s, it is that past phiÂ’s have been psiÂ’s. But this assumption is dead wrong. The fact that past phiÂ’s were psiÂ’s, is not, in and of itself, reason to hold that future phiÂ’s will be psiÂ’s; it is such a reason only to the extent that it suggests some mechanism that disposes phiÂ’s to be psiÂ’s. HumeÂ’s argument assumes otherwise and is thus guilty of assuming the legitimacy of the spurious form of inference involved in cases of the gamblerÂ’s fallacy. And, if it is to have a chance of going through, HumeÂ’s argument must be so reconstructed that it no longer embodies that assumption. 
4.0 The minimization of causal anomalies 
We havenÂ’t yet refuted HumeÂ’s argumentÂ—weÂ’ve only taken the first step towards doing so. Hume could defend his view against what weÂ’ve said thus far by saying the following: 
(HR)[261] 
Suppose that, to explain why all phiÂ’s thus far known are psiÂ’s, you posit some underlying structure or law that disposes phiÂ’s to be psiÂ’s. Unless you think that nature is uniform, you have no right to expect that connection to continue to hold. But if, in order to deal with this, you suppose that nature is uniform, then youÂ’re caught in the vicious circle that I described. 
HR is correct. One is indeed caught in a vicious circle if, in order to show the legitimacy of inductive inference, one assumes UP; and the reason is that, just as Hume says, UP can be known, if at all, only on inductive grounds. 
4.1. Why inductive inferences donÂ’t presuppose the truth of the uniformity principle 
But in making an inductive inference, one doesnÂ’t assume UP and, moreover, one doesnÂ’t assume anything that, like UP, can be known only on inductive grounds. What one assumes is that explanations are supposed to eliminate causal anomaliesÂ—that they are supposed to reduce the number of them and to limit the scope of those that arenÂ’t eliminated. What one assumes, then, is that it is inherent in the very concept of explanation that, other things being equal, T1 is a better explanation than T2 if T1 does a better 
job of eliminating causal anomalies than T2. 
The purpose of explanation is to minimize the breadth and depth of what must be taken for granted. The more a proposed theory requires you to say: Â“things just happen that way; thereÂ’s no explaining it,Â” the less successful an explanation it is. 
HereÂ’s an illustration. On Monday night, you park your car in the usual place, viz., right in front of your house, which is in a quiet residential neighborhood. As usual, you make sure that you lock the car and turn the car alarm on. You also put an almost, but not quite, indestructible device (popularly known as Â“The ClubÂ”) on the steering-wheel that locks it into place, making the car undriveable. Given where your home is in relation to where the car is parked, youÂ’d almost certainly hear the car alarm go off, were it to do so. In fact, unless you were fast asleep, youÂ’d even hear the footsteps of someone approaching the car. So even if the car alarm werenÂ’t on, you might well hear the approach of a would-be thief and youÂ’d certainly hear the noises made by somebody who, not having the keys needed to open the car or to unlock the steering wheel or to start the car, would have to jimmy the door lock, saw through the wheel lock, etc. 
As it happens, you hear nothing all night. And you know that you didnÂ’t sleep any more deeply than usualÂ—that, for example, you werenÂ’t in a particularly deep drug-induced slumberÂ—and, in general, that you werenÂ’t made less sensitive to noise than you usually are. (For argumentative purposes, weÂ’ll set aside the question of how you know this.) Nonetheless, on Tuesday morning, the car is gone. 
What are the various possible explanations of this? (By Â“possible,Â” I donÂ’t necessarily mean Â“worthy of consideration,Â” only Â“not ruled out by the laws of logic.Â”) There are infinitely many; but here are three. 
(E1) Using his or her super powers to bypass the security measures you took, some superhero-like creature made off with the car, making little or no noise and leaving few or no clues. 
(E2) As you were sleeping, the laws of physics changed in such a way that hitherto noisy processes (e.g., those that occur when car alarms go off) are no longer noisy. 
(E3) Your good friend LarryÂ—who, despite his numerous convictions for auto-theft, simply radiates trustworthiness and decency, and to whom, without so much as a touch of anxiety, you therefore gave copies of all your keysÂ—made off with the car. (For argumentative purposes, letÂ’s assume that, given that the car is gone, it had to have been stolen; it could not, we will suppose, have been towed or simply borrowed.) 
Each of E1 and E2 replaces the mystery of how your car could be 
noiselessly stolen with a far greater mystery. In fact, each creates a whole network of deep mysteries. E1, if correct, would generate a number of thorny questions concerning specific matters of fact and also concerning our 
knowledge of biological and physical law. (The features that weÂ’d have to ascribe to the superhero in question would be ones that, unless modern biology is very wrong, a life form is most unlikely to have.) And E2, if 
correct, would do nothing less than create the greatest scientific mystery of all time. 
E3 is not free from sin either. In general, you are a good judge of character. In any case, thatÂ’s what you believe and thatÂ’s what others tell you; and your judgments about people have generally been borne out by subsequent events. YouÂ’ve never been as convinced of anyoneÂ’s integrity as you are of LarryÂ’s. Without being morose or censorious, he exudes a decency and centeredness that youÂ’ve never even seen in a head of state, let alone a car thief. And although LarryÂ’s extensive criminal background is consistent with his stealing your car, it is not, you are convinced, as consistent with it as his current excellence of character is inconsistent with it. But, of course, E3 is hands down the best explanation. You may think youÂ’re a good judge of character; but that doesnÂ’t mean you are one. People proverbially overestimate their ability to read others. And even if you are a good judge of character, so what? Anybody can be fooled; everybody is fooled, at some point or other. And if Larry is a career criminalÂ—which, given his rap-sheet, he may well beÂ—then he has probably honed his skills as a con-man. 
This doesnÂ’t mean that E3 is completely innocuous. If correct, it raises the question of how somebody could seem so different from how they are. It also raises the question of how, despite being a crime expert, you could have been unwary enough to let yourself be seduced into trusting somebody who, given his background, was so obviously unworthy of trust. But these mysteries can be dealt with more easily than the mysteries created by E1Â–E2. 
All of this goes to show that ceteris paribus the best explanation is the one that leaves us with the fewest unexplained explainers. 
Of course, new theories raise questions of their own. For example: According to Freudian psychology, we repress distressing conceits. This raises the question: Â“Why donÂ’t holocaust survivors repress their memories of the horrors they went through?Â” But Freud didnÂ’t have to concoct an ad hoc answer to this question, since his theory of repression is itself an answer to it. According to that theory, one doesnÂ’t repress just any unpleasant conceit; one represses a conceit that is in conflict with values that one has that one believes to be integral to oneÂ’s psychological architecture. (One represses oneÂ’s hatred of oneÂ’s father because one also loves him and, in addition, oneÂ’s life is structured around oneÂ’s love for him, whereas, unless one is willing to overhaul the very structure of oneÂ’s existence, oneÂ’s hate for him is incapable of being acted on in a productive manner and, were it to remain conscious, would merely be a source of annoyance.) Data that seems to undermine a good theory turns out to support it when either (i) new data comes in or (ii) when what was previously implicit in that theory is made explicit. (Example of (i): Given what it known about the solar system, the trajectory of planet x is not what a certain theory says that it should be. But the discovery of a new planet y shows that x's trajectory is what the theory says it should be. Example of (ii): According to a certain theory, motion is relative and there is thus no difference between (a) my running around the bucket and the bucket's remaining station and (b) my remaining stationary and the bucket's rotating. But in situations of the first kind, but not the second, I become winded; and in situation of the second kind, but not the first, the surface of the water in the bucket comes to the have the shape of the interior of a bowl. This seems to suggest that motion is not relative. But when it's taken into account that, if motion is in fact relative, one must take into account, not just my spatial relation to the bucket, but also my spatial relation to the surface of the Earth, these changes prove to be logical consequences of the theory.[262]) In any case, whatÂ’s important in this context is that good theories tend get rid of causal gaps and they shrink the ones they canÂ’t get rid of. 
Before proceeding, we must make a certain distinction very clear. Little or nothing about the actual causal structure of the world is analytic. It isnÂ’t analytic that there arenÂ’t giant causal gaps in the causal structure of the world; that reality doesnÂ’t consist of one ex nihilo event after another; that superheroes donÂ’t suddenly pop into existence, steal cars, and then, without leaving a trace, vanish never to be heard from again. These things, if known, are known only on the basis of sense-experience. But it is analytic that, other things equal, good explanations are less dependent for their truth than bad ones on the existence of unexplained explainers. Given that E3 depends less for its truth on unexplained explainers than does either E1 or E2, it is analytic that, relative to the available data, E3 is the better explanation. 
But it isnÂ’t analytic that E3 is correct. ItÂ’s a possibilityÂ—maybe only a bare theoretical possibility, but a possibility no lessÂ—that the laws of physics changed overnight, that CIA super-agents have targeted you, that comic book 
characters now walk the Earth, etc. AnythingÂ’s possible. And so far as we know that E1Â–E2 are wrong, itÂ’s through sense-perception. So, I repeat, it isnÂ’t analytic that E3 is correct. But, given that it requires fewer unexplained explainers than others, it is analytic that ceteris paribus itÂ’s the better 
explanation. 
4.2 Correct explanations can be bad (or, rather, badly arrived at) explanations 
For an explanation to be good isnÂ’t for it to be correct. Sometimes the right explanations are bad ones. A story will make this clear. IÂ’m on a bus. The bus driver is smiling. A mystery! Â“What on Earth does he have to smile about?Â” I ask myself. His job is so boring, and his life must therefore be such a horror.Â” But then I remember that, just a minute ago, a disembarking passenger gave him fifty $100 bills as a tip. So I have my explanation: Â“he just came into a lot of money.Â” 
But here is the very different explanation tendered by my seatmate Gus, who, in addition to being unintelligent, is also completely insane. Â“The bus-driver is a CIA assassin. This morning he killed somebody who, by coincidence, had the name Â‘Benjamin Franklin.Â’ Benjamin Franklin (the statesman, not the murder victim) is on the $100 bill. So when the bus driver saw those bills, he immediately thought of that morningÂ’s murder. The murder was a particularly enjoyable one; the bus driver had a chance to try out some innovative techniques. So, on being given the fifty $100 bills, the bus driver was reminded of that happy experience.Â” That, my seat-mate believes, is why the bus driver is smiling. The bus driver is indifferent to the fact that he is now richer by $5,000 than he was before. (HeÂ’s not a materialistic man. Plus, the CIA pays him a huge salary. $5,000 is nothing to him.) 
Gus and I have access to the same empirical data. (Gus hasnÂ’t read the bus driverÂ’s diary; he doesnÂ’t know the bus driver any more intimately than I do; and so on.) And Gus doesnÂ’t have some sort of psychic gift that would give him access to otherwise unknowable facts about the bus driverÂ’s mind that would legitimize his explanation. Indeed, a belief that he has such a gift isnÂ’t even among GusÂ’s many delusions. Nor does he have any good reasonÂ—even if, for argumentÂ’s sake, one allows his delusions and hallucinations to count as good reasonsÂ—to believe that he has such a gift. So given the entirety of the data at our disposal, GusÂ’s explanation is a bad one. The only evidence in favor of GusÂ’s theory is that the bus driver started smiling upon being given the money. 
But Gus is right. His explanation is correct down to the last detail. 
Given that it turned out to be correct, should we say that, despite first appearances, GusÂ’s explanation is not a bad one? No! ItÂ’s a datum that itÂ’s bad. ItÂ’s a bad explanation that turned out to be correct. Thus, for an explanation to be a good one isnÂ’t for it to be correct. 
4.2.1 An objection to our analysis 
But a short extension of our story seems to illustrate the even stronger principle that for an explanation to be a good one isnÂ’t even for it to be likely to be correct. 
(NL)[263] 
Let W be the real world and let W* be a hypothetical world where we have the exact same experiences that we have in W, but in which the GusÂ’s of the world are always right.[264] 
In W*, itÂ’s because Santa Claus is personally delivering gifts to millions of people that they suddenly appear in living rooms round the globe; it isnÂ’t because hard-working parents purchased them. In W*, your keys are missing because stealthy gnomes took them; it isnÂ’t because you drunkenly threw them in the incinerator. And so on. In W*, the right explanations are the ones that, in our world, are extremely bad ones. The data on the basis of which those hypotheses are held in W* (so far as those hypotheses are held) is identical with the data on the basis of which theyÂ’re held here (same qualification). But in W* theyÂ’re right, and the good explanationsÂ—the logical, sane, well-supported explanationsÂ— that they compete with are always wrong. So in W* good explanations arenÂ’t even likely to lead to the truth. So thereÂ’s no inherent connection between an explanationÂ’s being good and its being true: goodness (in the explanatory sense) cannot be identified with, or even understood in terms of, truthÂ­conduciveness.[265] 

Causation and continuity are indistinguishable. (The most obvious, and the most important, sort of continuity is spatiotemporal continuity.) Continuous sequences of events (e.g., the sequence of events composing a single light-beam) are ipso facto a causal process. And where there is direct causation, there is ipso facto spatiotemporal adjacency. (That is why Newton rightly considered the idea of Â“action at a distanceÂ” to be an abomination.) Discontinuities constitute partial breakdowns of an otherwise unified space-time into separate space-times. Given two events, if neither can affect the other, or if there is no third event that both can affect or be affected by, it makes no sense to say that both events belong to the same space-time. So a Â“worldÂ” in which Gus is right isnÂ’t really a world at all: it is a collection of world-fragments. By the same token, to the extent that the data that one is trying to model represents a single world, it must be possible to show that continuous structures mediate between those data. So it is analytic, I would contend, that, given a single world, the GusÂ’s in that world are likely to be wrong. (A Â“singleÂ” world, as I am using this term, is to be contrasted with one that, because of discontinuities in it, and because of concomitant fissures in its causal structures, is, as it were, powdering into more than one world.) For, if correct, the hypotheses put forth by the GusÂ’s of a given world have the consequence that the data being modeled isnÂ’t to be understood in terms of the structure of a single, unified domain and thus isnÂ’t really capable of being explained at all---at least not in terms of any one set of principles.[266] 

4.3 Explanatory goodness is a relationship, not between explanations and reality, but between explanations and data 
The relations that hold in W* between theory and data coincide with those holding in W. ThatÂ’s why the ones that are wrong in W* are no less good on that account. What is it in W* that makes wrong explanations be good? In general, what is the relationship that good theories bear with respect to the data? 
First of all, Â“goodÂ” is a relative to term. An explanation is good relative to some body of data. No good explanation is inconsistent with the relevant data. And, of the various explanations consistent with a given body of data, the best one is the one that depends the least on unexplained explainers. 
HereÂ’s an illustration. I put an opaque plate on a table. I thus canÂ’t see the part of the table covered by the plate. Â“Given only this data,Â” says my sophist friend Smith, Â“itÂ’s a theoretical possibility that the moment you put the plate on the table, there suddenly came into existence a hole in the table the exact size of the plate.Â” Supposing that youÂ’re right, I ask Smith, why didnÂ’t the plate fall through the table? Â“Because,Â” Smith responds Â“when that hole came into existence, a special force was created that kept the plate in exactly the place that it would have occupied if there were no hole.Â” Why, I ask in response, did that force come into existence? Â“I donÂ’t know,Â” says Smith. Â“It just did.Â” 
Maybe this explanation is correct. WeÂ’ll never know for certain that it isnÂ’tÂ—at least not without presupposing the falsehood of various other, comparably ad hoc explanations. 
Be that as it may, itÂ’s a bad explanation. Why is it bad? Because it leaves us with more questions than answers. Why did the hole appear? Why did it happen to have just the right shape and size? Is it because the plate has special chemical properties? If so, why is it that, the moment the plate is whisked away from the table, the effects of any chemical interaction between the two are undone? Supposing that these questions can be answered, why did some force suddenly step into the breach left by the momentarily absent table surface? Why was that force just rightÂ—just enough to keep the plate on the table, but not so much that the plate rose above the table or trembled or did anything else inconsistent with its being on an ordinary table? And supposing that we have an answer to that question, why was there no independent evidence of the existence of that force? Why was its only effect to keep the plate in that very location, for that exact amount of time? Supposing 
that, for some reason or other, we have highly sensitive instruments of measurement underneath the table, why didnÂ’t any of them detect anything? 
With every answer, a new hole arises. It may be that, for each hole that pops up, there is a way to plug it up that is not only consistent with the laws of logic but is also consistent with our other empirical beliefs. Or, if there should arise a case where the hole cannot be plugged up without jettisoning some, or even all, of our remaining beliefs, maybe there is a way to revise those other beliefs in such a way that they remain consistent with the raw data and with the stopgap in question. 
It is generally said that a given body of data can be modeled by many different, mutually inconsistent hypotheses.[267] 
But even if this is true, which weÂ’ll soon see that it isnÂ’t, it doesnÂ’t follow that, for each hypothesis that models a given body of data in a way that has a given degree of success in the way of eliminating unexplained explainers, there is a logically incompatible way of modeling the data that also has that degree of success in that respect. 
4.4 Hypotheses must be capable of being evaluated in terms of benchmarks that can be identified independently of the realities those very hypotheses are meant to identity 
A continuation of our plate story will make it clear what this means and why it is true. Why doesnÂ’t the plate fall through the table? Because, says the conventional wisdom, the table didnÂ’t vanish. But, the skeptic will retort, maybe we can jettison that explanation; maybe thereÂ’s an alternative to it that is equally compatible with the perceptual data. 
But, I would respond, supposing for argumentÂ’s sake that there is such an alternative, it doesnÂ’t follow that it will create fewer holes to plug up than its predecessor did. It doesnÂ’t follow that itÂ’s comparable from a cost-benefit standpoint to the old oneÂ—that, in other words, it creates as few new mysteries as the old hypothesis while also eliminating as many existing ones. 
But not only does this not follow: the exact opposite holds. Consider the alternative explanation that we considered a moment ago (viz., when the plate is placed on the table, a hole opens up, etc.) The explanatory cost of that hypothesis (in other words, what it leaves us having to explain that we didnÂ’t have to explain before) was a thousand times greater than its explanatory value (in other words, what no longer has to be explained that did have to be explained before). 
It would be very hard to produce an explanation that was incompatible with the conventional one and, while remaining consistent with the relevant data, was as inexpensive from an explanatory viewpoint as the conventional one. I invite you to verify this for yourself. If there is any reason to believe that there exists so much as a single such hypothesis, it isnÂ’t that such a hypothesis has ever been produced or ever will be. That reason, if it exists, must be purely a priori. And, for reasons that will presently become clear, there can be no a priori reason to accept such a hypothesis. 
4.5 Correct explanations can be bad (not to say false) explanations (revisited) 
But there is an even more immediate problem for this (or, by an analogous argument, any other non-standard) substitute for the conventional view that the table, even when obscured by the plate, continues to support it. ItÂ’s far from clear that, once all the relevant data is taken into account, that hypothesis is even logically possible. LetÂ’s look at the statement: 
(*) Â“when the plate is placed on the table, a hole that coincides with the under-surface of the plate opens up. But a force field is suddenly created that keeps the plate exactly where it would have been if, other things being equal, that hole hadnÂ’t opened up.Â” 
Taken by itself, (*) describes a situation that could hold. That statement is a coherent one. ItÂ’s not in the same category as Â“squares are round.Â” 
But, while thatÂ’s obviously necessary for its being a logically feasible way of modeling the relevant data, itÂ’s far from sufficient. Think of the various physical laws that must be broken for the table section underneath the plate to vanish. Violations of natural laws, were they possible, would not be innocuous; there would be ripple effects. Think of the forces that (so we believe) actually prevent that plate-sized chunk of table from vanishing. Think of the various equilibriums that would be altered if those forces were immediately suspended. Think of the various energy transfers that would be changed or destroyed if, all of a sudden, those forces were put out of commission. 
Those forces donÂ’t only keep that chunk of table in place. Were they all to be suspended, there would be many consequences other than the disappearance of the requisite table chunk. In other words, there would be a lot of explanatory Â“collateral damage,Â” meaning that many events would occur other than the ones that, given that our objective is to validate (*), we want to occur. And thereÂ’s no guarantee that those other events would be consistentÂ—even in the narrowest, most emptily logical senseÂ—with the data that, supposedly, is modeled just as well by (*) as it is by the conventional explanation (viz., Â“the place doesnÂ’t fall because the table chunk doesnÂ’t disappearÂ”) that it replaces. 

4.5.1 Correct explanations can be bad explanations (continued) 
We might try to deal with this batch of problems by positing second-order suspensions of natural law. So in addition to suspending those laws involved in keeping the table chunk in place, we also suspend those laws that, given the first suspension, lead to the just-mentioned unwanted collateral events. 
The problem is that those second-order suspensions of law will be no more innocuous than their first-order counterparts. To counteract the unwanted effects of suspending the first set of forces, we have to suspend another set of forces. But just as the original forces did a lot more than keep the table intact, so these new forces will do a lot more than suspend the unwanted effects of suspending the first set of forces. And itÂ’s obviously of no use to try to deal with this problem by bringing in a third set of forces. 
Â“You may be right,Â” it will be said, Â“that if we hold onto our existing beliefs about physical law, then the disappearance of the table chunk would have all of this unwanted fall-out. But surely we could adjust those beliefs in such a way as to prevent this. Whatever those beliefs are, just get rid of them and replace them with ones that donÂ’t lead to all of this unwanted fall-out.Â” 
The very fact that this move must be made only proves my point, namely, that (*) is not consistent with what we know. In fact, it proves a stronger point, namely: (*) isnÂ’t consistent with any body of beliefs at all like the ones we now have. 
The objector is saying, rightly, that there is no way to square (*) with our existing beliefsÂ—that it is only what we believe minus many of our beliefs about natural law that can be so squared. But when our beliefs about natural law are subtracted, so to speak, from the totality of our beliefs, the resulting body of beliefs bears very little resemblance to our current beliefs. Our beliefs about natural law are not in all cases neatly separable from our beliefs about specific matters of fact; and if we were to strip away enough of the former to compatibilize (*) with our belief system, weÂ’d be biting off a lot more than we bargained for. This is because various beliefs about natural law are embedded in the concepts associated with expressions that, in order to say whatÂ’s on our minds, we must use every day (e.g., Â“microscope,Â” Â“telephone,Â” Â“radio,Â” Â“solar panel,Â” Â“cell phone,Â” Â“thermometer,Â” Â“thermostatÂ”). Theory-laden though they are, we need those terms to describe facts of everyday, pre-theoretic experience. We therefore need them to state the pre-theoretic data that our theories are to model. 
Â“But,Â” it will be said, Â“anything that can be described only by taking for granted some theoretical belief is ipso facto not a datum. A truth? Maybe. A datum? No.Â” 
That may well be true. But, if so, our belief-system is so overrun with theoretical beliefs that no belief system free of such beliefs would bear even the slightest resemblance to it. Also, it is incoherent to suppose that there could exist a belief-system that wasnÂ’t replete with theoretical content. The difference between a mere belief, on the one hand, and a belief-system, on the other, is that belief-systems are intended to be explanatory, whereas mere beliefs neednÂ’t have this property. I believe that itÂ’s raining because I see that itÂ’s rainingÂ—not because, in an effort to model various observational data, I at some point hypothesized that it was raining. But psychoanalytic theory constitutes a belief-system, as opposed to a mere belief, because it is intended to be explanatory. This suggests (though it doesnÂ’t establish) that Â“belief-systemÂ” and Â“theoryÂ” are veritable synonyms. (Why the parenthetical hedge? Â“Because there are belief-systems that arenÂ’t of a theoretical nature. Religious belief-systems arenÂ’t theories.Â” But even this is arguable.[268] 
Some would say, and I agree with them, that religious systems are proto-theories or paraÂ­theoriesÂ—structures that make heavy allowances to emotional factors and make insufficient allowances to considerations of logic and evidence, but are, within these parameters, as theory-like as they could possibly be.) If, indeed, belief-systems are ipso facto theories, it makes no sense to speak of what our Â“belief-systemÂ” would be like if it were stripped of theoretical content. Long story short: although itÂ’s obvious that, on its own, (*) is perfectly coherent, itÂ’s far from obvious that (*) is compatible with our belief system as a whole or with any belief system that isnÂ’t radically different from it. This was the very point we set out to establish. It goes without saying that what is true of (*) holds mutatis mutandis of each of many other Â“deviantÂ” hypotheses. 
But even if, for some reason, this last point is denied, there is no way to deny our main point, to wit: even if (*) is logically consistent with our belief system, or at least with some not-too-mutilated version of it, the explanatory benefits of countenancing (*) in favor of the conventional explanation are grossly outweighed by the explanatory costs. 
4.6 Synthesizing these points 
It will help if, before moving forward, we take a moment to synthesize the points thus far made. ThereÂ’s no difference between committing the GamblerÂ’s fallacy and performing an induction by enumeration. At the same time, knowledge of invariable concomitances is obviously an extremely valuable source of knowledge. But it isnÂ’t, or in any case shouldnÂ’t be, through enumerative induction that one transitions from (1) Â“all phiÂ’s that IÂ’ve known of were psiÂ’sÂ” to (2) Â“the next phi I come across will be a psi.Â” (In this context, it is to be assumed that that Â“x is a phiÂ” doesnÂ’t analytically entail Â“x is a psi.Â”) 
The actual bridge between (1) and (2), supposing that there is one, lies in the fact that, given (1), it is reasonable to believe there to be some mechanism or natural law that requires (or at least disposes) phiÂ’s to be psiÂ’s. By itself, (1*) Â“all metal known to me has expanded when heatedÂ” provides no good reason to accept (2*) Â“all metal expands when heated.Â” (1*) provides a good reason for accepting (2) only to the extent that (1*) provides a good reason for accepting (3*) Â“there is a lawful connection between a thingÂ’s being made of metal, on the one hand, and itÂ’s expanding when being heated, on the other.Â” 
4.6.1 Synthesizing these points (continued) 
Before we continue, itÂ’s crucial to note that none of this begs any questions against Hume. Hume is saying: Â“given only that every metal object that Smith has known of has expanded when heated, it doesnÂ’t follow that metal objects that Smith has yet to encounter will (or is even likely to) expand when heated.Â” We agree. Smith is guilty of the gamblerÂ’s fallacy so far as he thinks otherwise. All weÂ’re saying is this: SmithÂ’s experience thus far suggests that Â“xÂ’s being heated metal provides some kind of nomic basis for xÂ’s expandingÂ” has held for objects falling within the scope of SmithÂ’s experience. 
WeÂ’re not making the claim SmithÂ’s experience entails that some such connection has held. Such a claim would simply be false. And weÂ’re not making the claim that SmithÂ’s past experience gives him a good reason to think that metal objects not (yet) known to him will be more likely to expand or even that theyÂ’ll be more likely than not to expand. Such a claim would beg the question against Hume. Finally, weÂ’re not making the claim that SmithÂ’s past experience gives him a good reason to think that there continues to exist any nomic connection between a thingÂ’s being heated metal and its expanding. Echoing what we just said, such a claim would beg the question against Hume: for HumeÂ’s very point is that a thingÂ’s happening in the past is no guarantee of its continuing to happen in the future. And we cannot, without begging the question against Hume, assert that a lawÂ’s having held in the past is evidence of its holding in the future. 
So what are we saying? Only that SmithÂ’s experience gives him a reason to believe that such a connection has held, at least as far as metal objects falling within the scope of experience are concerned. And in making this obviously plausible claim, no questions have been begged against Hume. 
4.6.2 Synthesizing these points (continued) 
I propose that, armed only with this non-question-begging point along with the tautology that it is the purpose of explanations to eliminate unexplained explainers, we can show that Smith has reason to expect future metal objects to expand when heated. 
WeÂ’ve agreed that SmithÂ’s experience does give him some reason to think that, at least as far as objects thus far known to him are concerned, a thingÂ’s being metal provides some kind of causal or nomic basis for its expanding when heated. Let P be this causal principle. P is of doubly limited scope. It applies only to past objects and it applies only to past objects that Smith knows of. LetÂ’s suppose that Smith accepts P. 
Smith has two options. (I am not counting a refusal draw any inferences as an option.) 
(i) Hold that P provides no reason to believe that, outside SmithÂ’s past, personal experience, a thingÂ’s being a metal provides a basis of some kind for its expanding when heated. 
(ii) Hold that P does warrant some such generalization. 
One such generalization is: Â“that connection holds for all past objects, whether Smith knows of them or not; but it doesnÂ’t hold of future objects.Â” Another is: Â“that connection holds for objects that Smith will know of, but not for those that he wonÂ’t know of.Â” But, of course, the most natural, not to say the most rational, generalization is this: 
(P*) Â“That connection holds generally. It holds no less for objects not known by Smith than for those known by him, no less for future objects than for past.Â” 
LetÂ’s suppose that Smith chooses not to accept P* or any other generalization of P. How, in that case, would the world have to be for SmithÂ’s belief system to hold? Metal objects that Smith became aware of would suddenly undergo a profound change: they would go from being things that, when heated, didnÂ’t expand to being ones that did. And for this change to occur, each atom of every metal object known to Smith would have to change in fundamental ways. Given an acceptance of P, it may seem conservative not to accept any generalization of P. But itÂ’s the very opposite. If you accept P but reject any generalization thereof, youÂ’re saying that objects miraculously undergo profound microstructural changes whenever you know of them and undergo equally profound changes when you stop being aware of them. And that hypothesis is not a conservative one. 
And, quite clearly, itÂ’s a bad one. Why is it bad? Because it creates more unexplained explainers than it eliminatesÂ—because it creates more questions than it answers. 
4.6.3 Synthesizing these points (continued) 
Of course, not accepting a hypothesis isnÂ’t the same as rejecting it. Not accepting some generalization of P isnÂ’t the same as rejecting it. And itÂ’s obviously a good idea in many cases to hedgeÂ—to wait for evidence. But thatÂ’s irrelevant. The question is: given that there is enough information to warrant an acceptance of P, is there enough information to warrant acceptance of any generalization of P? If we answer by saying Â“no,Â” then weÂ’re saying that, given only the evidence at our disposal, itÂ’s no less likely than not that objects systematically undergo massive changes at the atomic level whenever they come or cease to be known by Smith. And that position, as we saw, creates more mysteries than it eliminates. So despite first appearances, thereÂ’s nothing conservative about refusing to countenance any generalization of P. And such refusal embodies acceptance of a principle that is straightforwardly false, namely: Â“thereÂ’s no reason to prefer explanations that explain a lot and create little that has to be explained to those that explain a little and create a lot to be explained.Â” 
4.6.4 Synthesizing these points (continued) 
These points are easily generalized. ItÂ’s no less absurd to suppose that, in the last nanosecond, all metal objects have undergone profound microstructural changes than it is to suppose that all metal objects known by Smith are microstructurally very different from those not known by him. This point provides the non-circular justification for UP that Hume sought but couldnÂ’t find. 
LetÂ’s suppose that Smith has reason to believe (i) that, where metal objects that he has known of are concerned, a thingÂ’s being heated provides some kind of basis for its expanding. LetÂ’s also suppose that Smith holds (ii) that this principle wonÂ’t hold for metal objects that he will encounter (i.e., for metal objects that he hasnÂ’t encountered but will and for those that he has already encountered and will encounter again). In holding (ii), he is ipso facto supposing that the laws of nature will abruptly change. And in positing this one change, he is positing innumerably many others, as we will now see. 
A metal objectÂ’s being heated involves innumerable microstructural changes, and so does its expanding. The macroscopic supervenes on the microscopic. Given two objects that are microstructurally alikeÂ—that consist of the same particles interrelated in the same wayÂ—there is no possibility, even a purely logical one, that those two objects should differ at the macroscopic level. By the same token, given two objects that differ at the macroscopic level, there is no possibility, even a purely logical one, that those two objects should fail to be microstructurally different. A metal objectÂ’s being heated thus consists in its undergoing many microstructural changes, and so does its expanding. And if a metal objectÂ’s being heated causes it to expand, it is in virtue of the fact that the first set of microstructural disturbances result in, or are themselves constitutive of, the second set. 
So given a lawÂ—even one that was confined to objects that Smith has encounteredÂ—to the effect that metal expands when heated, in order for that law to be annulled, each of innumerably many microparticles would suddenly have to undergo quite dramatic changes. So in assuming that, all of a sudden, a law that once held ceases to do soÂ—or, what is the same thing, in assuming that the future, starting now, is governed by different laws from the pastÂ— one is positing not one change, but innumerably many. For, in making that assumption, one is (implicitly) supposing that each of the innumerably many microparticles will, all of a sudden, stop being governed by one set of laws and will start being governed by another. And one is thus creating what, for practical purposes, might as well be infinitely many unexplained explainers. 
But not a single one of these unexplained explainers is created by the hypothesis that metal objects that we will encounter are governed by the same laws as those we have encountered. So given the truism that one explanation is better than another if, other things being equal, the first creates fewer unexplained explainers than the second, it follows that the rational move, at least until further evidence comes in, is to suppose that those microparticles will continue to be governed by the same laws that used to govern them. 
According to what is now the conventional wisdom, which coincides with the viewpoint that Hume bequeathed to us, the conservative move is the agnostic one: stick to the evidence; generalize as little as possible; donÂ’t assume that what you donÂ’t know resembles what you do know. But the so-called conservative view is really less conservative than the alternative. (The alternative is: Â“assume that what you donÂ’t know does resemble what you do know.Â”) The so-called conservative view posits giant schisms in the natural order and, therewith, masses of unexplained explainers. The alternative view does not. 
5.0 The goodness of hypothesis a function of its relationship to the data, not to the truth 
Earlier I said: 
(i) that explanatory goodness is a relationship between a given hypothesis and the available data. 
And I explicitly denied: 
(ii) that explanatory goodness is a relationship between a given hypothesis and the truth. 
Â“But surely this makes no sense,Â” it will be said. Â“Hypotheses are attempts to identify the truth. So surely for a hypothesis to be good is for it to be true; and for one hypothesis to be better than another, is for it to be closer to the truth than the other.Â” 
HereÂ’s the problem with this reasoning. Setting aside questions that can be answered directlyÂ—in other words, setting aside questions (if any there be) for which, without making any inferences, one can produce justified answersÂ­--it is through hypothesis, and only through hypothesis, that we have any way of identifying the truth. Often, when trying to solve a particular problem, we have many reasonable hypotheses to choose from. When seeking the truth, one must choose the best hypothesis available. This is a tautology. If, for any hypothesis H, HÂ’s being good was the same as its being true, weÂ’d have no grounds for accepting Hypothesis 1 as opposed to Hypothesis 2 unless we already knew what the truth was---unless, in other words, we already knew the very things of which it was the purpose of those hypotheses to apprise us. If hypothesis HÂ’s being good were identical with its being true, then weÂ’d have no way of knowing whether H was good until we knew whether it was true. But if we didnÂ’t know whether a given hypothesis was good until we knew whether it was correct, hypotheses would be useless in the way of helping us find the truth. For, by supposition, they couldnÂ’t be evaluated until their job had already been done. 
It follows that, when choosing between hypotheses, our choice cannot, if justified, be based on how accurate those hypotheses are. For if we knew how accurate they were, we wouldnÂ’t need them to find the truth and we thus wouldnÂ’t need them at all. Thus, when choosing between hypotheses, our choice (supposing it principled) must be based on something that, unlike the truth, is available to us. In other words, when trying to figure out to what extent a given hypothesis is worthy of our acceptance, the yardstick with respect to which we compare that hypothesis cannot possibly be the truth. For obvious reasons, that yardstick cannot be anything other than the relevant data. 
Let us sum up. The degree to which a given hypothesis is good is obviously something we consider when determining whether or not to accept it. The purpose of that hypothesis is to help us identify some as of yet unknown truth. Therefore, the degree to which a hypothesis is good is not identical with the degree to which it conforms to the truth. Therefore, the degree to which a hypothesis is good is identical with the extent to which it makes sense of the data. Therefore, explanatory goodness (i.e., the sort of goodness had by hypotheses qua hypotheses) is a relation between hypothesis and data, not between hypothesis and truth. 
A corollary is the point (which we stressed but which some philosophers of science deny[269]) that bad hypotheses can be correct ones. For the degree of goodness of a hypothesis, being the function of its fidelity to the data, not to the truth, a totally false hypothesis can be good and a completely accurate hypothesis can be bad; for the false one might model the available data, and thus satisfy the relevant desideratum, whereas a true one might fail to satisfy that desideratum.[270] 

6.0 Closing the argument 
We can now succinctly say why HumeÂ’s argument fails. 
Step 1: ItÂ’s an analytic truth that ceteris paribus the better explanation is the one that creates fewer unexplained explainers. LetÂ’s refer to this principle as Â“MCÂ” (short for Â“minimization of causal anomaliesÂ”). If UP can be known, it must be known on inductive grounds. But MC is not to be known on such grounds, since it's analytic and, unlike UP, is to be known on purely conceptual grounds. (It makes no sense to say that theory T1 is better than otherwise comparable theory 
T2 if T1 posits more causal anomalies than T2. It makes no sense to say that T1 posits fewer causal anomalies than T2 if T1 posits more unexplained changes than T2. It makes no sense to say that T1 posits fewer unexplained changes than T2 if T1 posits more unexplained breaches with the past than T2. And it makes no sense to say that T1 posits fewer unexplained breaches with the past than T2 if T1 posits more spatiotemporal discontinuities than T2.) Thus, MC, unlike UP, can be non-circularly assumed in the context of a defense of inductive 
inference. 
Step 2: ItÂ’s a datum that various concomitances are to be found among the objects known to one. ItÂ’s a datum that, so far as the objectÂ’s known to (say) Smith are concerned, putting a hand in boiling water causes intense pain, whereas putting that same hand in cool water causes intense relief. 
Step 3: One creates more unexplained explainers by assuming that the unknown differs from the known than by assuming that it does not. 
Step 4: If one remains agnosticÂ—if one refuses to say, one way or the other, whether the unknown resembles the knownÂ— 
one is committed to the incoherent position that thereÂ’s no reason to prefer a hypothesis that creates few unexplained explainers to an otherwise comparable one that creates many. (The reason this view is incoherent is that for one explanation to be preferable to another just is for it to do more in the way of explaining, and thus less in the way of creating unexplained explainers, than the other.) 
Step 5: Given MC, and given Steps 1Â–4, it follows that there is an analytic and therefore non-inductive reason to hold that, other things being equal, the unknown resembles the known. 
Conclusion: Hume is wrong. This is a direct consequence of Step 5. Contrary to what he says, it is rational to hold that, in its more general respects, the known is a good indication as to what the unknown, in its more general respects, will turn out to be like, supposing that we come to know it. Given the legitimacy of MC, it is obvious why skepticism about the external world is actually an extravagant and irrational position, though it may initially appear cautious and conservative. OneÂ’s sensory experience is replete with discontinuities. Every time you open your eyes or turn your head, you are flooded with sensory experiences that are totally unlike those that you were experiencing a moment earlier. According to the non-skeptic, these new experiences donÂ’t come into existence ex nihilo; they are merely links in chains of events whose other links you donÂ’t perceive. The skeptic says that itÂ’s no more rational to believe this about our sensory experiences than it is to believe that those experiences come into existence ex nihilo. In saying this, the skeptic is saying, in effect, that itÂ’s just as rational to accept a theory that creates more anomalies than it gets rid of than it is to accept an otherwise comparable theory that gets rid of more anomalies than it creates. Since itÂ’s an analytic truth that, given two otherwise comparable theories, the one that leaves us with fewer anomalies is the one that ought to be preferred, it follows that the skepticÂ’s position is analytically false. Of course, it isnÂ’t analytic that our sensory experiences are correct. But it is analytic that itÂ’s rational to suppose our sensory experiences veridical to the extent that doing so leaves us with fewer causal anomalies than weÂ’re otherwise left with. The skepticÂ’s denial of this embodies an analytically false conception of explanation. 
6.0 Skepticism about the external world 
Given what weÂ’ve said about induction, it is clear why, on the whole, it is rational to trust oneÂ’s senses---why, in other words, skepticism about the external world is not a rational view. There are two kinds of perceptions: those that have mental predecessors that they resemble and those that donÂ’t. If, while standing still and otherwise undergoing no changes relevant to your visual experience, you stare at a blank wall to which nothing is happening, the visual experience you have at any one instant will be very similar to its immediate predecessor. But, typically, there are discontinuities in oneÂ’s visual experience. The visual experience upon opening your eyes bears no resemblance to the visual experience you had before you opened your eyes. First, so your visual experience tells you, there is nothing. Then, so your visual experience tells you, there is a whole world of objects. And, supposing your visual experiences to be veridical, the states of affairs that you see after blinking are very similar to those that you saw just before blinking. 
Looked at from the skepticÂ’s perception, there are three possibilities as to what is going on when a person blinks: 
(a) 
During the instant that his eyes are shut, the situation he saw vanishes and, when he opens his eyes, there ex nihilo pops into existence a situation a numerically distinct from that situation but similar to it, if not qualitatively identical with it. 

(b) 
Before the person blinks, he isnÂ’t actually seeing anything. He is hallucinating. During the moment that his eyes are shut, he stops hallucinating. When he opens his eyes, there ex nihilo pops into existence a hallucination numerically distinct from the pre-blink hallucination but similar to it, if not qualitatively identical with it. 

(c) 
Before that person blinks, he is actually seeing various objects. His pre-blink visual experiences are caused by light-rays bouncing off of external (i.e., non-mental) objects. Information concerning those external objects and their interrelations is coded into the light rays that collide with his eyes; that structural information is transmitted to some part of 


his brain that produces visual experiences that themselves encode it. When the personÂ’s eyes close, light stops colliding with his eyes. During that brief period, nothing collides with his eyes that bears information about anything external. (Light that bears such information collides with his eyelids. But his eyelids donÂ’t in their turn transmit that information to the relevant part of his brain.) After he opens his eyes, light-rays bearing information collide with this eyes, leading by way of the previously described process to visual experiences that bear structural information concerning their external causes. So the reason that his pre-and post-blink visual experiences are so similar is that they have commensurately similar external causes. 
The non-skeptic accepts (c). The skeptic neither accepts nor rejects any one of (a)-(c). The skeptic says that, given any one of those hypotheses, it is no more rational to accept it than it is to accept either of the other two. So, according to the skeptic it is more rational to reject (a)/(b) in favor of (c) than it is to reject (c) in favor of either (a)/(b). 
Right now, weÂ’ll argue that (c) is preferable to (a). What we say in this connection will make it clear why (c) is preferable to (b). 
If one accepts (a), one has to explain two things that one doesnÂ’t have to explain if one accepts (c). One has to explain why, the moment one opens oneÂ’s eyes, anything comes into existence. Second, one has to explain why, despite any causal connection between the pre-and post-blink situations, the post-blink situation is so similar to the pre-blink situation. And, in having to explain each of these two things, the advocate of (a) has to explain innumerably many things that the advocate of (c) does not have to explain. The advocate of (a) has to explain the ex nihilo creation of each blade of grass that the person in question sees when he opens his eyes, and he must do the same for each other object post-blink object. Further, he must explain why (setting aside the odd post-blink object that doesnÂ’t have a pre-blink counterpart) every one of the objects that ex nihilo popped into existence is so similar, in so many respects, to one of the pre-blink objects that was annihilated. (These respects include, but are not limited to: color, shape, position, and state of motion.) If (a) is right, every one of these changes is a singularity---a breach in the fabric of space-time. (In fact, weÂ’ll see in Chapter 24 that, if (a) is right, the pre-and post-blink worlds are too disconnected from each other to be considered genidentical[271]--other words, that the occupants of the post-blink world are not even in the same space-time manifold as the occupants of the pre-blink world.) But if (c) is right, neither the differences nor the similarities between the pre-and post-blink worlds constitutes a breach in the fabric of nature. The differences correspond to continuous changes, and the similarities correspond to diachronic identities and thus themselves, for reasons that weÂ’ll see in Chapter 16, correspond to continuous changes. 
Chapter 12 Empiricism and Its Limits 
1.0 Empiricism vs. rationalism 
We obviously acquire a great deal of knowledge through Â“senseÂ­perceptionÂ” (i.e., through sight, hearing, touch, and so forth). According to a doctrine known as Â“empiricism,Â” all knowledge is derived from sense-perception. 
According to a view known as Â“rationalism,Â” some knowledge is acquired entirely through the use of oneÂ’s ability to reason. 
Rationalists almost never hold that no knowledge is acquired through sense-perception. They hold only that reason, as opposed to sense-perception, is the vehicle through which some knowledge is acquired. Rationalists typically hold that knowledge acquired in this way is very importantÂ—it isnÂ’t trivial. 
Some hold the view that there is knowledge that is acquired neither through the senses nor through reason. I donÂ’t wish to dismiss this view. Maybe itÂ’s correct. But there is an apparent problem with it. Any case of knowledge is a case of justified true belief. Given a belief that isnÂ’t acquired through the senses or through reasoning, the question arises: what could possibly justify it? And thereÂ’s no obvious answer. 
In any case, in this chapter, if only to simplify exposition, it will be assumed that the only viable sources of knowledge are reason and the senses, and therefore that the only viable options for epistemologists are rationalism and empiricism. But IÂ’m inclined to think that there is. Part of my reason for believing this is that we seem to have direct awareness of certain non-
empirical facts (e.g. the fact that green isn't orange)[272], and direct knowledge ipso facto is not obtained through analysis. Analysis is an operation that is carried out on pre-existing knowledge and, when properly executed, therefore yields meta-knowledge (knowledge about knowledge); and it is obvious that meta-knowledge cannot possibly be direct. We do therefore seem to have a faculty of divination, as it were, whereby we directly apprehend non-spatiotemporal truths. 
Those who believe that there exist non-spatiotemporal entities are rationalists (or at least must be rationalists, lest they be guilty of inconsistency.) Give or take a few nuances, empiricism is the view that you donÂ’t know it if you donÂ’t see it. We see property-instances, but not properties themselves. Therefore, empiricists either deny the existence of properties or they hold that properties are identical spatiotemporal entities. Those who take the latter view are forced to view properties as being composed of their own instances; so the property of being wet is identical with some object composed of all wet things, or some such. Therefore, empiricists donÂ’t believe in uninstantiated properties. Therefore, anyone who does believe in such properties, or who believes that properties are not spatiotemporal entities, is a rationalist. 
Those who believe that properties are non-spatiotemporal are Platonists. Therefore Platonists are rationalists. A Platonic metaphysics requires a rationalist epistemology. Plato himself accepted a very extreme form of rationalism. 
Being one that has deep roots in common sense, empiricism is a very old doctrine. But empiricism was first rigorously developed by John Locke (1632Â–1704), George Berkeley (1685Â–1753), and David Hume (1711Â–1776). The doctrines put forth by these authors form the basis of modern philosophy. HumeÂ’s beliefs about causality and inductive inference are outgrowths of his empiricism. These views are thoroughly examined in Chapters 12 and 17. 
BerkeleyÂ’s belief that objects are identical with our perceptions of them is an outgrowth of his empiricism. BerkeleyÂ’s ingenious arguments for this outrageous doctrine are examined later in this chapter. 
John LockeÂ’s plausible position that universals are Â“the workmanship of the understandingÂ”Â—that we create them, so as to make sense of the worldÂ— is a derivative of his empiricism. That doctrine is examined in the present chapter. (It is also examined in Chapter 2.) 
The first great rationalist was Plato (428 B.C.Â–348 B.C.). (PlatoÂ’s views are defended in Chapter 2.) Other rationalists are: Augustine (354Â–430), Descartes (1596Â–1650), Leibniz (1646Â–1716), and Gottlob Frege (1848Â– 1925). 
The first great empiricist was Aristotle (384 B.C.Â–322 B.C.), whose views, along with PlatoÂ’s, are also considered in Chapter 2. Other empiricists are 
J.S. Mill (1806Â–1873), Rudolph Carnap (1891Â–1970), and W.V.O. Quine (1908Â–2000). 
In this chapter, we will find that empiricism is not in its strictest form a defensible doctrine and that, consequently, at least some knowledge has a non-perceptual basis. 
There are, as we will see, two important corollaries. First, many commonsense-based views about the internal (psychological) and external (physical) worlds must be jettisoned. Second, sober scientific methodology actually demands an acceptance of principles that would strike common sense as decidedly unscientific. We will see that many concepts that cannot be adequately understood along strictly empiricist lines can nonetheless be correctly understood only in terms of what empiricism has to say about them. 
2.0 The particularist nature of sense-perception and the need for universals 
Sense-perception discloses only particulars to usÂ—particular objects having particular property-instances. But we understand and describe the world in terms of categories or, as they are sometimes called, Â“universals.Â” These can be thought of as natures, essences, or Â“ways of being,Â” that, although exemplified by the particulars that we encounter in sense-perception, are not themselves to be sense-perceived, and, though they presumably exist, do not exist in space-time. 
Because they are non-spatiotemporal, those of an empiricist mindset regard universals with extreme suspicion. In fact, empiricism is, nearly enough, the denial that such things exist. Why? The empiricists say: what we can legitimately believe is what we can sense-perceive or know on the basis of extremely conservative inferences on the basis of what we can sense-perceive. 
The problem is that there is no way to understand the world except in terms of universals. To understand things is to know how, in virtue of having such and such characteristics (i.e., in virtue of falling under such and such universals), they are subject to thus and such principles or laws. Â“Why did Max steal the money? Because Max is greedy and amoral and he believed it to be to his strategic advantage to steal the money.Â” MaxÂ’s behavior is explained by showing how, given the operative conditions, his having those characteristics makes it inevitable that he will act in that way. This explanation presupposes the existence of many different universals. (Among them are those denoted by the terms Â“greed,Â” Â“amorality,Â” Â“money,Â” and Â“theft.Â”) This explanation is not unique in this respect: all explanations presuppose the existence of universals. The very idea of an explanation that didnÂ’t do so is an incoherent one. 
Universals are outside of space-time. For this reason, they cannot have effects on anything. (Causal relations hold only among spatiotemporal entities.) One cannot sense-perceive an object without being affected by it. (It is only because your ocular surfaces are disturbed by light-rays bouncing off of the page in front of you that you can see it.) It follows that universals cannot be sense-perceived. It also follows that no evidence of them can be sense-perceived. This is because x is evidence of y only if x and y are causally interconnected in such a way that, given xÂ’s existence, yÂ’s may reasonably be assumed. (Smoke is evidence of fire because smoke and fire are causally connected in such a way that, given the presence of smoke, the presence of fire may be inferred.) It is therefore impossible as a matter of logic to find any observational basis for the existence of universals. This means that, if empiricism is correct, we cannot possibly have any good reason to posit the existence of universals. Given how endemic universals are to thought, language, and explanation, the right move is to reject empiricism. 
2.0 The shortcomings of empiricist attempts to deal with these problems 
Empiricists have responded by saying that, although instances of universals obviously exist, universals per se do not. (Remember that, in this context, Â“universalÂ” is synonymous with Â“property.Â”) 
The problem with this view is that, as previously noted, every sentence and every thought demands the existence of at least one universal. 
Also, some basic logic shows that universals exist. Consider the following inference: Â“Bob and Ted are both human; therefore, there is some characteristic that they have in common.Â” That is a valid inference; and the conclusion affirms the existence of a universal. (Â“CharacteristicÂ” is synonymous with Â“universal.Â”) 
Finally, many statements straightforwardly presuppose or affirm the existence of universals; and were it not for statements of this kind, many obvious truths couldnÂ’t be expressed. Consider the following statements: 
(i) Hitler and Stalin had a lot in common; 
(ii) Smith has what it takes to be a great pianist, but he doesnÂ’t have what it takes to be a great composer; 
(iii) Even though Smith is different from Jones, that has nothing to do with the fact that they donÂ’t like each other. 
The meanings of these sentences are, respectively: 
(i*) There are many properties such that, given any one of them, Hitler had it and so did Stalin; 
(ii*) There are properties such that, if one has them, one is a great pianist and such that, moreover, Smith has them; and there are properties such that, if one lacks them, one isnÂ’t a great composer and such that, moreover, Smith lacks them; 
(iii*) There are properties such that Smith has them and 
Jones does not, but this fact isnÂ’t responsible for the fact that 
they donÂ’t like each other. 
(i)Â–(iii) cannot be translated into statements that donÂ’t presuppose or affirm the existence of properties. So it isnÂ’t really an option to hold that properties donÂ’t exist. 
As soon as one grants that anything resembles anything, one must grant that universals exist independently of thought. For two objects to be similar in some respect is for there to exist some property that they both have. For two objects to have the same shape is for there to exist some morphological property such that each object is an instance of that property. ItÂ’s obviously possible for two objects to have the same shape in a world devoid of sentient beings. Therefore, there exist properties in worlds where there are no sentient beings. Therefore, properties arenÂ’t created by such beings and arenÂ’t otherwise dependent on them. 
2.1 More failings with empiricist attempts to deal with these problems 
Properties are identical with categories. For x to fall into a given category is for x to have a given property. (For x to fall into the category of round things, is for x to have the property of being round.) Given that properties exist independently of thought, the same is true of categories. Thus, contrary to what some empiricists (e.g., Locke) say, categories are not devices that human beings created in order to expedite thought. 
It is easy to find independent corroboration for this view. Let each of x and y be a pint of pure, clean glacial water, and let z be a pint of gasoline. The chef or chemist or auto mechanic who chooses to co-categorize x and z, as opposed to x and y, is in for some very unpleasant surprises. Why? Because his categories donÂ’t cut Â“nature at the joints,Â” to use Francis BaconÂ’s expression. In other words, there is some relevant property that x and y have in common that x and z donÂ’t have in common, and this personÂ’s system of categories embodies an ignorance of that fact. 
3.0 Non-perceptual knowledge a prerequisite for perceptual knowledge 
ItÂ’s not as though tables, rocks, trees, etc., create little images of themselves that they deposit in our hitherto empty crania. Our minds have to supply the Â“paint,Â” so to speak, with which our mental representations of those objects are painted. 
In fact, our minds must supply everything. External objects donÂ’t supply our minds with anything. All they do is tell our minds when to deploy what is already in them. External objects donÂ’t stock our minds; they activate whatÂ’s already in them. A rock will never experience an image. It doesnÂ’t matter how many light beams you fire at it. ThereÂ’s nothing in it to be brought forth; there are, so to speak, no images in there to begin with. For similar reasons, the acoustical disturbances that, in a human, would lead to knowledge of English or of philosophical principles will have no comparable effect on a rock. Knowledge is transmitted by being elicited, not by being deposited. A failure to see this is the most fundamental problem with empiricism. 
A precondition for sense-perceiving anything is that we be able to represent it as having a location (relative to us) in space and time, that we be able to represent it as having a certain shape, state of motion, color, etc. Although we learn a great deal through perception, what we donÂ’t learn through it are the conceptsÂ—space, time, motion, shape, color, etc.Â—out of which sense-perceptions are constructed. So those things, and all that having them involves, must be in the mind prior to sense-perception, as a necessary precondition for it.
