These considerations expose what I believe to be a deep confusion of which empiricism is guilty. Empiricists fail to distinguish between two very different roles that sense-perceptions can have: they can have a triggering role and they can also have an information-transmitting role. 
3.1 Sense-perception as transmitter of information about the external world 
You see a dog. On that basis you have the belief that there is a nearby dog. Here your eyes transmitted information to you about the external world. They Â“toldÂ” you, so to speak, that there was a dog in a certain place. You could not possibly have learned this fact through pure logic-chopping or conceptual analysis. You could learn it only through the senses (either by seeing the dog or by sense-perceiving some other sort of evidence of the dog). In this context, then, information about the external world is being transmitted to you through your senses. Your senses (specifically, your sense of sight) is thus functioning in what we might call an Â“information transmittingÂ” capacity. 
3.2 Sense-perception as trigger 
Sense-perceptions have a triggering role when they provide the recipient with new information not by telling him something about the external world, but by activating or Â“triggeringÂ” some already existing cognitive faculty. 
You are in a geometry class. The teacher draws something that is supposed to represent a triangle but only vaguely looks like one. He draws various lines through it, around it, etc. And from these diagrams you learn various facts about triangles. 
What did you actually see? What did your eyes show you? A triangle? No Â—only a few uneven lines that formed something that vaguely looked like a triangle. How did your seeing this non-triangle get you to know that, for example, the area of a triangle is 1/2 base times height? Since you didnÂ’t see any triangles, you didnÂ’t see any trianglesÂ’ height, base, or area. The things you saw were symbols for things that had to be supplied to you by something other than your sensesÂ—that had to be supplied to you by your intellect. 
This is not to say that the diagram was useless. Plainly it was not. It may be that, but for seeing it, you wouldnÂ’t have learned anything about triangles. But your seeing the diagram led to your knowing those truths about triangles not because any triangle, or any fact about triangles, was any part of the information imparted to you by your perception, but rather by triggering or activating certain conceptual faculties of yours. In this context, your senses are (to the extent that you are learning actual geometrical truths as opposed to mathematically irrelevant facts about the blackboard, chalk-marks, etc.) providing you with knowledge by getting you to acquire knowledge in some non-sensory way, viz., by getting you to grasp certain concepts to and to identify some of the relations holding among them. 
The proof that your visual perception of the diagram had only a triggering role, and that it did not itself contain any information relating to what you learned, is that, if you were to forget ever having seen that diagramÂ—were to forget what it looked like, who drew it, where you saw it, or even that you saw itÂ—it would have no effect on the geometrical truths that you learned that day. The reason is that those geometrical truths (e.g., area of a triangles = bh/2) were simply not part of the content of what your senses were telling you. 
By contrast, if you forget ever seeing the dog (described in the last section), you will forget the information that, on that occasion, your senses led you to have. The reason is that, in that context, your senses werenÂ’t serving the purpose of jogging your ability to acquire knowledge in some non-sensory way (viz., through rational insight) but were themselves the bearers of the information learned. 
3.3 An anti-empiricist consequence of the distinction between triggering and information transmitting 
According to strict empiricists, everything that is learned, including purely logical principles, is learned through sense-perception. When this appears to happen, itÂ’s because sense-perception is simply Â“turning onÂ” some non-sensory mode of knowledge acquisition. Â“Truths of reason,Â” as Hume called them, arenÂ’t learned through sense-perception, even though sense-perception may awaken the non-sensory faculty through which we do become aware of them. 
Some empiricists are aware of this objection, and they generally deal with it by saying one of two things: 
(1) 
Truths of reason really are truths about the irregular figures on blackboards, that truths of arithmetic really are truths about what happens when apples are put on top of other apples, etc. 

(2) 
The so-called Â“truths of reasonÂ” are just linguistic or typographical conventions. Â“1 + 1 = 2Â” is an empty, purely definitional truth. Â“2Â” is defined as Â“1 + 1,Â” and Â“3Â” is defined as Â“1 + 2.Â” Every other fact about mathematics can be reduced to definitions, linguistic conventions; and all of mathematics turns out to be typographical. (As a matter of typography, you can replace Â“1 + 1Â” with Â“2,Â” just as you can replace Â“fiveÂ” with Â“5.Â”) And all the so-called Â“truths of reasonÂ” that lie outside of mathematics are thought to be explained in the same way. 


3.3.1 Why (1) is wrong 
Your knowledge that 113 + 876 = 989 isnÂ’t empirical; you didnÂ’t see 113 pears being counted, then see 876 pineapples being counted, and then see the whole lot being counted. (And even if you did have such an experience in connection with those particular numbers, there are many other pairs of numbers whose sumsÂ—not to mention quotients, products, differences, etc.Â— you know, or could readily figure out, but in connection with which youÂ’ve never seen anything like the situation just described.) Your knowledge of arithmetical truths is based on a grasp of non-empirical principles. 
Even if (what we will find to be false) you learned that 1 + 1 = 2 from watching one thing be put on top of another, you still would not, on that basis alone, have any way of generalizing that knowledgeÂ—of inferring the other mathematical truths you know. To make the needed inferences, youÂ’d need access to rules of inference that you couldnÂ’t possibly know about if your knowledge were strictly sense-based. A rule of inference is given by a principle to the effect that, given such and such conditions, thus and such must be the case. Our senses donÂ’t tell us what must be the case; they tell us, at most, what is the case. Therefore, it cannot be strictly through sense-perception that we learn the inference-rules on the basis of which we can extract knowledge of a general and abstract kind from the, in all cases, hyper-specific information given us by our senses. 
3.3.2 Another reason why (1) is wrong 
Even oneÂ’s knowledge that 1 + 1 = 2 isnÂ’t empirical. As David Hume made clear, observation tells you how things are, not how they should be. It reveals facts, not norms. But oneÂ’s knowledge that 1 + 1 = 2 has normative force. If two people enter what you thought was an empty house, and three people leave, you donÂ’t reconsider your belief that 1 + 1 = 2. You take that belief as fixed and, in light of it, reconsider your belief that the house was in fact empty. If it turned out that, according to a certain scale, rocks R and R* had a collective weight of more than 2 pounds, even though you previously thought that each weighed no more than 1 pound, youÂ’d take your belief that 1 + 1 = 2 as fixed, and would revise some other belief of yours (e.g., your views concerning the rocksÂ’ individual weights or the accuracy of the scale, or possibly even the laws of physics). 
In fact, consequence of Relativity Theory is that if you add a rock weighing exactly 1 pound to a scale on which there is already a rock weighing exactly 1 pound, the collective weight of those two rocks will be 
over 2 pounds. Thus, weight is not a strictly additive property.[273] 
Neither, of course, is temperature. If you mix a quart of water with a temperature of 70Â° with a quart of water with a temperature of 90Â°, the result is not a body of water with a temperature of 160Â°. But we don't hold that 1+1>2 or that 70Â° +90Â°.160Â°. 
We interpret observations in light of the principle that 1 + 1 = 2, not vice versa, and the same holds for other 70+90=160 and, indeed, every other well-established precept of mathematics and, by obvious extensions of this reasoning, of logic. 
3.4 Why (2) is wrong: The falsity of empiricism, a corollary of the falsity of conventionalism 
First a terminological point. P and Q are consistent with each other if it's logically possible for both of them to be true; otherwise they're inconsistent with each other. So "grass is green" and "snow is white" are consistent with each other, as are "grass is black" and "snow is purple"; but "grass is green" and "grass has no color" are inconsistent with each other. A consistent set of propositions is one that doesn't contain any two propositions that are inconsistent with each other. 
Conventions are indeed arbitrary. But whether the conventions one adopts are consistent with one another is not itself a matter of convention. ItÂ’s a matter of convention that Â“1Â” denotes 1, that Â“+Â” denotes addition, that "snow" refers to snow, and so on. But, unless we changed those conventions, our linguistic conventions would form an inconsistent set if, without otherwise changing them, we added to them the convention that "1+1=3." For, our conventions being what they are, "1+1=3" entails that "1+1.2" is true; and, our conventions being what they are, "1+1.2" is false. So, even though it's up to us what our conventions are, it's not up to us, and therefore isn't a matter of convention, whether they're consistent with one another. 
At the same time, we can't know on empirical grounds whether those conventions form a consistent set. To say that P is inconsistent with Q is to say that P and not-Q cannot possibly be true; and observations apprise one only of what is, not of what isn't, let alone of what cannot be. So, our conventions being what they are, it is neither a matter of convention nor an empirical fact that "1+1.2" is false. It is a matter of non-empirical, non-conventional logical fact. 
Even if we stipulate that S means 1+1=2 and that S* means 1+1.2, it still isn't a matter of convention that those conventions are inconsistent with each other. There's nothing conventional about that fact that the number 2 cannot simultaneously have, and fail to have, the property of being the successor of 
1. There is nothing human beings could possibly do to make 2 not be the successor of 1. We'll revisit this topic below. 
The fact that consistency-relations are not a matter of convention means that there is nothing conventional about any body of statements that concern such relations. Mathematical principles are often, if not always, to the effect that some consistency-relation holds or fails to hold. Consider the proposition that: 
(ET)[274] 
Euclidean triangles have interior angles whose sum is 180. 
ET true. But there are no Euclidean triangles; the laws of physics prohibit it. So what is that proposition about? Non-existent triangles? No! Suppose that it were about such things. In that case, there would exist certain objects, viz. Euclidean triangles, that don't exist that it would be about. But that's absurd. 
ET is to the effect that if an object is a Euclidean triangle, then its interior angles add up to 180. So ET is to the effect that, for any x, x is Euclidean triangle is inconsistent with x's interior angles add up to 180. 
Even 1+1=2 concerns consistency-relations, since, according to it, if C and C* are non-overlapping one-membered classes, then the union of those classes is a two-membered class. 
Conventionalism is rooted in a failure to distinguish between two very different statements, namely: 
(A) Among our conventions is one to the effect that sentence S means P 
and 
(B) Our conventions being what they are, S means P. 
Our conventions being what they are, it's settled what is meant by the sentence: 
(RC)[275] 
"if Richard Nixon were stronger than the Hulk, then he'd be stronger than Chuck Norris, unless of course Chuck Norris were much weaker than he is in actuality." 
But there can't possibly be a convention concerning that very sentence. Before I wrote it down a few seconds ago, RC almost certainly wasn't even contemplated by anyone until just a moment ago, and even if a few people did contemplate it, their doing so didn't give it the meaning that it has. This what any given complex expression means is partly non-conventional. In a moment, we'll show that this is indeed the case. Right now, we'll show that, if it's true, conventionalism is incoherent in a way that we have yet to point out. 
"(p/q) 2 = 2" is a complex expression. So even though our linguistic conventions determine what is meant by "(p/q) 2= 2", they do not do so directly. Supposing that P is the proposition affirmed by that sentence, it is a non-conventional consequence of our conventions that "(p/q) 2= 2" has P for its meaning. Whether "(p/q) 2 = 2" is determined by what it means. (If it meant that snow is white, it would be true. But it doesn't, and it isn't.) So it isn't a matter of convention whether or not "(p/q) 2 = 2" is true. Since it therefore isn't a matter of convention what "(p/q) 2 = 2" means, it isn't matter of convention whether or not it's true. For whether a given expression is true is a function of what it means. "Snow is white" would be false if it meant that snow was black. 
We will now see why anything whose meaning is directly fixed by convention is ipso facto a simple expression. If we stipulate that "(p/q) 2= 2" has P for its meaning, then its having that meaning is no longer a function of what its parts mean. So, in that context, its parts are indistinguishable from things that don't have meanings and, in that context, are not functioning as expressions. Stipulating that a given expression has a given meaning strips its parts of meaning: those parts become meaningless homonyms of expressions with which, thanks to our stipulation, they have ceased to be identical. 
It should be pointed out that whether a given sentence is true is only partly 
a matter of what it means, given that it's also partly a function of nonÂ­linguistic facts. Ceteris paribus[276] 
"snow is white" would be false if snow were black, and ceteris paribus "snow is black" would be true if it meant that snow was white. given that snow is white. 
4.0 Why preperceptual and therefore non-empirical knowledge is a prerequisite for empirical knowledge 
Innate cognitive structures are needed to have sense-perceptions and also to learn from them. Having a sense-perception means having a certain kind of mental representation of an object. Not all mental representations of objects are sense-perceptions. Mental images arenÂ’t, even though they resemble them. Concepts arenÂ’t, and they donÂ’t resemble them. ItÂ’s a delicate matter exactly what kinds of representations are perceptual: a necessary condition, certainly, is that they be caused by their objectsÂ—your perception of Smith must be caused by Smith (by light bouncing off of him). It also seems necessary that (with certain qualifications) your perception Â“co-vary,Â” or be capable of co-varying, in real time with the thing perceived. If youÂ’re looking at Smith, and he moves, you see him move (provided certain conditions are met; e.g., the movement isnÂ’t infinitesimally small). ItÂ’s unclear whether there are other conditions that have to be met. (There probably are.) 
In any case, perceptions are mental representations. And they represent their objects in four dimensions, and as having various chromatic (color-related), kinematic (movement-related), dynamic (force-related, causal) properties. Unless we take the implausible view that no intelligence is involved in the processes mediating between the somatic disturbances that lead to sense-perceptions, on the one hand, and those sense-perceptions themselves, on the other, none of this would be possible unless your mind, at some level, had some kind of pre-perceptual understanding of what it is for two things to be spatially, dynamically, etc., interrelated. So, in all likelihood, sense-perception presupposes knowledge. 
4.1 Why non-empirical knowledge is a prerequisite for post-perceptual, inferential knowledge 
We couldnÂ’t do very much with the information that sense-perception gave us unless we had non-empirical knowledge. First of all, your senses operate in the present. You are not seeing, touching, etc., whatever youÂ’re not now seeing, touching, etc. At most, you are remembering it. In order to apply what you remember to a current situation, you must see how what you remember bears on your current situation. You remember seeing somebody turn the key in their car and then driving away. You are now in front of a car with a key in it, and you want to drive it. Obviously you can apply what you remember to this situation. Let us suppose that you do so. So you think: Â“on that occasion, turning the key started the car; so the same thing will happen on this occasion. So, given that I want to start the car, IÂ’ll turn the key.Â” Sense-perception (plus memory) has shown you that on the first occasion a certain car started after the key in it was turned. And, supposing that you turn the key in this car (the one in front of you), sense-perception will show you that another car started after the key in it was turned. 
But sense-perception did not show you, and could not possibly have shown you, that there was a relationship between these two situations; it could not show you that, because the car in the first situation started after the key was turned, the same would be true of the car in the second. Your senses apprise you of situations; they thus give you intra situational information. They donÂ’t give you inter situational information. You canÂ’t see or otherwise sense-perceive relations between situationsÂ—between an event you saw a week ago and one youÂ’re seeing right now. Thus, any knowledge that you have of intersituational relations is partly (though obviously not entirely) non-empirical. Therefore any knowledge of dependence-relations holding between distinct situations is, at least in part, not strictly sense-based. Since it is only by virtue of knowing of such relations that one can know anything other than what oneÂ’s senses are currently telling one, one can know extremely little if all knowledge is sense-based, and what one can know, one can know only for a fleeting instant. 
4.2 Why non-empirical knowledge is a prerequisite for post-perceptual, inferential knowledge (continued) 
Hume said that there is no legitimate inference from Â“that car (the one I saw two days ago) started when the key was turnedÂ” to Â“this car (the one IÂ’m looking at now) will start if the key is turnedÂ” and, in general, that there is no legitimate inference from any proposition concerning the past to any proposition concerning the present or future. Hume acknowledges, of course, that past experience makes people form certain beliefs. His point is precisely that those beliefs, lacking as they do any legitimate basis, are not knowledge; theyÂ’re just compulsions, albeit ones that, as he grants, have thus far served us well for the most part. (See Chapter 11 for a discussion of Hume's views concerning induction.) 
Although, unlike Hume, I believe that knowledge of the past does warrant beliefs about the present and future, there is an important truth in what Hume is saying. Hume has made it clear that if one permits oneself to use only such knowledge as one has acquired through the use of oneÂ’s senses, then one canÂ’t infer anything about anything from anything. Inferences are about bearing relations. (More precisely, if one legitimately infers Q from P, then (i) P supports Q, (ii) one knows that P supports Q, and (iii) oneÂ’s acceptance of Q, given P, is driven by oneÂ’s knowledge that P supports Q.) If something about situation X is inferred from something about situation Y, that inference, if legitimate, must accord with some principle that is concerned with relations holding between distinct situations. And such relations obviously cannot, at least not as a rule, be sense-perceived. 
To sum up, all knowledge that isnÂ’t strictly sense-basedÂ—and this means all knowledge that involves any element of inference and, therefore, all theoretical knowledge (all theoretical knowledge is inferential, but not vice versa)Â—one must have knowledge of intersituational dependencies; and, since they canÂ’t be sense-perceived, oneÂ’s knowledge of these dependences cannot be strictly sense-based. 
5.0 The biggest problem with empiricism: thoughts not pictorial (even though pictures may facilitate thought) 
What does perception give you? Images. (Not just visual images, of course, but also acoustical images, tactile images, etc.) If empiricism is right, this means that any thought that is not itself an image, or that contains information that cannot be encoded into an image, is unwarranted. But most thoughts, if not all of them, contain just such information. In other words, most thoughts, if not all of them, contain non-iconic information. For example, there is no image such that, in virtue of experiencing that image, one is thinking: 
(S) if Smith had fallen off the fence, he would have broken his leg. 
What sort of image would represent S? Obviously you could have an image of Smith falling from a fence, and you can have an image of Smith breaking his leg. But S is to the effect that SmithÂ’s falling would involve his breaking his leg; it affirms the existence of a certain dependence relationship. And nothing could be an image of such a relationship. There can be images of rocks, trees, explosions, fallings, and waterfallsÂ—but not of dependence relationships. 
5.1 No iconic representation of dependence relations 
Obviously there can be languages whose expressions consist of images. But so far as a given thing is functioning as an image, it isn't functioning as a linguistic expression. x is a linguistic representation of y only if x's representing y is a consequence of human conventions. Conventions can't make anything be an image of anything else. Conventions couldn't make a photograph of a waterfall be an image of a lion, even though such conventions could make such a photograph be a representation of a lion. 
Expressions can be created by juxtaposing simple expressions. By juxtaposing "tall" and "man" one creates a third expression ("tall man"). But juxtaposing two images doesn't create a third image. Let X be what results when an image of Smith falling off a fence is placed to the right of an of Smith with a clearly broken leg. X is not itself an image. Therefore it isn't an image of the fact that that Smith would have broken his leg if he had fallen off a certain fence. We could stipulate that it represented that fact. But to the extent that X's representing that fact was a consequence of that stipulation, it wouldn't be an image of that fact. 
True propositions are not responsible for their truth. (A proposition is any truth or falsehood.) If it's true, the proposition Smith is in Paris corresponds to some fact. If it isn't, it doesn't. We've seen that there cannot be images of the facts in virtue of which true conditional propositions hold. It follows that there cannot be images of disjunctive truths (those of the form P or Q). This is because, if true, a disjunctive propositions holds in virtue of the same fact as some conditional proposition. (P or Q holds in virtue of the same fact as if not-P, then Q. That is why the one cannot be true if the other is false.) It also follows that there cannot be images of the fact in virtue of which P necessarily true holds. (If true, P is necessarily true holds virtue of the same fact as if Q entails not-P, then Q is false, which is a conditional proposition.) 
If Mary is tall, then she's not short says that one proposition (Mary is tall) cannot possibly be true if another proposition (Mary is short) is false; so it says that the first proposition's being true is dependent on the second one's being false. Thus, conditional truths are propositions about propositions. They are meta-propositions. (We'll refer to propositions that are not meta-propositions as "first-order propositions.") 
Given any true meta-proposition, there can be no image of the fact in virtue of which holds. Snow is white attributes a color to snow. But it is likely that snow is white doesn't attribute any property to anything spatiotemporal. It attributes a property (that of being likely to be true) to a proposition (that snow is white). P is likely to be true if, supposing that L is a list of the propositions we know to be true, the additions that must be made to L if P is true are less extravagant than those that must be made if P is false. So P is likely to be true says that one class of propositions (the set consisting of L plus those propositions we'd have to add to it were P true) bears a certain relation (in some respect having to do with the desiderata that an explanation must satisfy to be good) to another set of propositions (the set consisting of L plus those propositions we'd have to add to it were P false); and the first set bears that relation to the second if the first one is less different from L (in that same respect) than the second. 
So the fact in virtue of which P is likely to be true holds involves the existence of instances of relations among relations among sets of propositions. Similar points hold fact in virtue of which any meta-proposition holds. So the reason such facts cannot be imaged is simply that nothing nonÂ­spatiotemporal can be imaged. Given that empiricism says that all knowledge is perception-based and therefore image-based, it's no wonder that empiricism has a hard time accommodating the fact that have knowledge of meta-truths. 
5.2 Iconic information too specific in some respects and also too unspecific in others 
First a terminological point: By a Â“generalÂ” thought, I mean one that concerns some unspecified thing (e.g., somebody or other cured cancer) or that concerns all things in a certain category without considering any one of them in particular (e.g., most people have at least some decency). 
Suppose you believe that the cat is on the mat. Any image of a cat on the mat will include information not included in that thought (e.g., it will include information concerning the catÂ’s shape or color, or concerning the matÂ’s shape or size). 
By the same token, any thought will contain information not included in any image. An image of a cat on the mat is indistinguishable from an image of a perfect cat-impostor that is on a mat. So if the thought that the cat is on the mat were identical with an image, it would be identical with the thought that a perfect cat impostor is on the mat. But those propositions are distinct.[277] 

Also, general thoughts couldnÂ’t possibly be identical with images. Suppose you think that something or other is on the mat. An image canÂ’t just be an image of something or other on the mat; it must be an image of some particular thing on the mat. So if the thought that something were on the mat were identical with an image, it would be identical with the thought that (say) Snoopy was on the mat. But those thoughts arenÂ’t identical. 
Similar arguments show that other general thoughts canÂ’t be identical with images. Consider the thought that all birds have feathers. An image of all birds Â—an image that depicted every single bird in existenceÂ—would be indistinguishable from an image of (say) 84 billion birds. But the thought 84 billion birds have feathers is different from the thought that all birds have feathers. So neither thought is an image. Obvious adaptations of this argument show that no image can be identical with the thought that most birds/many birds/all possible birds have feathers. 
So, really, no thought that can be expressed by a sentence is identical with an image. This shows that many thoughts arenÂ’t images and, since sense-perceptions are images, therefore have contents very different from those of any sense-perception. 
5.2.1 BerkeleyÂ’s unwitting anti-empiricism 
Ironically, it was that greatest of empiricists, George Berkeley, who made it clear that general thoughts cannot possibly be identical with images. BerkeleyÂ’s argument coincides with our own: any image is specific in ways that any one of those thoughts wonÂ’t be. (Berkeley didnÂ’t make the correlative point that thoughts are specific in ways that images are not.) Berkeley saw that if all thoughts are images, then there are certain thoughts we canÂ’t have. Berkeley also saw that, if empiricism is correct, thoughts must be images. Finally, Berkeley saw that, given these two points, empiricism is inconsistent with the presumption that we can have general thoughts. But instead of rejecting empiricism because it has this absurd consequence, Berkeley held that, indeed, we canÂ’t have general thoughts. This position, in addition to being obviously wrong, is self-defeating, since the thought that there are no general thoughts is itself a general thought. 
Berkeley qualified his position by saying that, although we couldnÂ’t directly grasp general propositions, we could grasp non-general propositions that we took to stand for general ones. But one canÂ’t take x to mean y unless one grasps 
y. So one canÂ’t take a non-general proposition to stand for a general proposition unless one grasps the latter. (See Sections 8Â–21 of BerkeleyÂ’s Â“Principles of Human Knowledge.Â”) 
5.2.2 BerkeleyÂ’s misuse of the term Â“ideaÂ” 
Some philosophers believe that we are aware of universals and, therefore, that we are aware of non-spatiotemporal entities. Berkeley denies this. Berkeley says that any given thought is in its entirety concerned with Â“particularsÂ” and that it is impossible to be aware of Â“universals." 
A couple of terminological points before we proceed. Berkeley uses the term Â“particularÂ” to refer to what, throughout this book, we have referred as Â“spatiotemporalÂ” entities, and he uses the term Â“universalÂ” to refer to what we have referred to as Â“propertiesÂ” (or Â“universalsÂ” or Â“characteristicsÂ”). So Â“particulars,Â” for Berkeley, are what we have referred to as instances of universals (or, to be precise, of certain universals (e.g., the property of being a dog), not all universals, since there are universals (e.g., the property of being an even number), whose instances are not spatiotemporal). And Berkeley uses the term Â“abstract ideaÂ” to refer to thoughts that (directly) concern universals or otherwise embody a (direct) awareness of them. Berkeley denies that we have abstract ideas. 
Given his acceptance of empiricism, Berkeley is right to deny this, and he supports his position with arguments that, relative to the assumption that empiricism is correct, are maximally cogent. But not only do those arguments fail to establish that we donÂ’t have abstract ideas: they establish that we do have such ideas. We must make a preliminary point concerning BerkeleyÂ’s use of the word Â“ideaÂ” before we see why the claims just made are true. 
As he uses the word Â“idea,Â” all Â“ideasÂ” are thoughts and all thoughts are ideas. (In this context, I am using the word Â“thoughtÂ” to refer to any case of anythingÂ’s being aware of anything, it being irrelevant whether the mode of awareness is perceptual or conceptual and it being irrelevant whether the object of awareness is spatiotemporal or non-spatiotemporal.) But, for Berkeley, the sentence: 
(i) Â“all thoughts are mental images,Â” 
expresses a substantive truth, not a linguistic convention. So, for Berkeley, 
(i) is in the same category as: 
(ii) Â“two is the unique number n such that n is an even prime iff it isnÂ’t possible for there to be a regular, 17-sided polygon,Â” and it is not to be in the same category as: 
(iii) Â“if Smith has ten fingers, then Smith has 10 fingers.Â” 
Berkeley says that we cannot form Â“indeterminateÂ” ideas. Here is his argument (Â“BAÂ” is short for Â“BerkeleyÂ’s argument[H11] 
Â”). 
(BA) All ideas (thoughts) are images. All images are Â“determinate.Â” In other words, given any object and any characteristic, any image either ascribes that characteristic to that object or it fails to ascribe that characteristic to that object, and if the property in question is one that can be had to varying degrees (such as height), there is some specific degree to which the object in question is represented by that image as having the characteristic in question. So an image cannot just be of a man. It must be of a man who has a mustache; and an image cannot just be of a man who is rotund; it must be one of a man who is rotund to some specific degree. Thus, the idea that one could have an idea of Â“manÂ” in general is preposterous. For such an idea would be an image of a man who had a beard and was clean shaven, who was six feet tall and five feet tall, who was standing and sitting, etc. 
One problem with (BA) is that not all thoughts are images. In fact, discursive thoughts are never images. Imagery is often a vehicle for thought. When I think about philosophical problems, I tend to think about shapes and surfaces. But my having those images is neither necessary nor sufficient for my having those thoughts. A person's experiencing this or that series of images is never either necessary or sufficient for his having this or that thought. One oftentimes uses imagery to direct the course of a discursive thought-process, but imagery is never itself constitutive of such a process. 
A consequence of empiricism is that a belief must be an image if is to be an instance of knowledge. According to empiricism, only beliefs that have a strictly observational basis are cases of knowledge. Observation gives us nothing images. So, if empiricism is right, information that cannot be embodied in an image has no place in any knowledge-conducive thoughtÂ­process. But no thought, and therefore no thought-process, consists solely of imagery. 
Let M be some mental image that you are currently having of our friend Smith. M, let us suppose, is not a sense-perception. But for argumentÂ’s sake, letÂ’s suppose that it is perception-like in that it is no less high-resolution or vivid than a sense-perception of Smith had under excellent conditions by somebody with excellent vision. In other words, M is about as Â“determinateÂ” as a (non-perceptual) mental image can be. 
Of course, if you know SmithÂ’s height, you are likely to take that image to one of somebody who is (let us suppose) six feet tall and relatively close by, and not as somebody who is six inches tall and very close by or 100 feet tall and far away. But it is only because you are reading background beliefs into it that M represents somebody who is six feet tall. 
In fact, nothing in M per se could possibly specify SmithÂ’s height. If M represents SmithÂ’s height as coincident with that of some object that you know to be six feet tall, it is only because you are reading into M your background knowledge as to that other objectÂ’s height. M per se leaves it open whether that object is six inches tall and very nearby or 100 feet tall and far away. 
In fact, M per se doesnÂ’t represent Smith at all. Let M* be a mental image that is qualitatively just like M but that occurs in the mind of somebody who doesnÂ’t know of SmithÂ’s existence and therefore isnÂ’t thinking about him. You are reading thoughts into M that this other person is not reading into M*. But that is the only relevant difference between the two images. Considered strictly as images, M and M* are indistinguishable. Obvious extensions of this reasoning show that, given any object, there is no image that by itself represents that object. Given some object x and some image M#, it is only if background information is read into M# that it represents x. 
No image by itself represents anything. Images are often integral parts of representations. But it is only when supplemented by mental activity that doesnÂ’t consist of imagery that any image manages to represent anything. There is no object such that any image per se represents that object. A fortiori there is no object such that any image attributes any characteristics to it. It is the thoughts behind an image that determine what that image represents and, though possibly to a lesser extent, what it says about what it represents. 
It is the thoughts behind an image that are determinate. Contrary to what Berkeley says, the image itself is completely indeterminate in respect of what 
it represents and largely indeterminate in respect of what it says about it. 
5.3 Knowledge is never wholly (or even partially) identical with mental imagery 
As we observed, if all knowledge is strictly sense-based, then any case of knowledge is a case of some sequence of images running through oneÂ’s mind. But no sequence of mental images is knowledge. Such a sequence may serve as a partial basis for knowledge (e.g., if the image-sequence is a series of visual perceptions of a dog, then, partly on the basis of that sequence, you may know that there is a dog near you); and one can have knowledge about that sequence (e.g., you can know that only a visually gifted person could experience such high-resolution mental images). Nevertheless, knowing something always involves grasping at least one thing in some way other than through an image and, therefore, in some way that, because sense-perception gives one nothing but images, empiricism cannot account for. 
ThereÂ’s a difference between an image, on the one hand, and that imageÂ’s being represented as true, on the other. (Philosophers use the word Â“veridicalÂ” to describe accurate perceptions, and they sometimes use the word Â“falsidicalÂ” to describe inaccurate ones. But IÂ’ll stick with Â“trueÂ” and Â“false.Â”) Consider some painting (e.g., a painting of a woman picking flowers). There is nothing in the image itself that says: this woman really exists, and she really is picking flowers. Images are not self-referential; so they donÂ’t say Â“I am trueÂ” or Â“I am false.Â” Thus, the image itself leaves it open to how it is to be taken. It could be taken as something true, something false, or something that is not meant to be taken as true or as false. 
A corollary is that there is no image such that, merely by virtue of experiencing it, one is grasping the concept of truth. To know something, one must believe it to be true. Believing something to be true thus involves grasping the concept of truth and, given what we just said, therefore involves grasping something that cannot possibly be grasped by experiencing an image. Since the senses provide us only with images, it follows that the concept of truth is one that is not grasped through the senses. And since a grasp of that concept is a prerequisite to knowing anything, it follows that, contrary to what empiricism says, not all knowledge is strictly sense-based. In fact, it follows that, although a great deal of knowledge is obviously largely sense-based, no knowledge is strictly sense-based. 

6.0 George Berkeley and the collapse of empiricism into idealism 
George Berkeley (1685Â–1753) argued that Â“to be is to be perceivedÂ” (esse percipi est). He held, in other words, that the things we believe to be revealed to us through sense-perception (e.g., rocks, trees) are sense-perceptionsÂ—or, more 
exactly, are collections of sense-perceptions.[278] 
So Berkeley held that the book that you see before you is identical with the perceptions you (and others) have of it. 
The view that physical objects are sense-perceptions is known as Â“idealism.Â” It is so named because it is the view that external objects are Â“ideas,Â” not because it embodies a spirit of optimism. 
Even though, if our intuitions are to be given any credence, idealism is an abomination, Berkeley had a very good reason for accepting it. Given an acceptance of empiricism, one must be an idealist if one is to avoid saying that we have no knowledge of the external world at all. Berkeley saw this; and, being an empiricist who wasnÂ’t also a skeptic, he duly accepted idealism. 
According to empiricism, if you donÂ’t know it through sense-perception, you donÂ’t know it. But what do you know through sense-perception? Â“I know that IÂ’m reading a book right now.Â” No you donÂ’t. You know that, if what your senses are telling you is the truth, youÂ’re reading a book. 
Your senses cannot themselves give you any good reason to believe that theyÂ’re truthful. Unless you already have some assurance that your senses are truthful, no attempt on their part to tell you this deserves any credence. So, supposing that you do know that youÂ’re reading a book right now, this knowledge, although largely based on sense-perception, isnÂ’t entirely so. 
In general, even if our senses are generally telling us the truth, this fact cannot itself be known through sense-perception. This doesnÂ’t mean that it cannot be known. (I believe it can be known that our senses are telling us the truth. See Chapter 11.) But it means that, if we are to come to know that our senses are telling us the truth, it cannot be entirely on the basis of what our senses themselves tell us. 
An analogy may help. Uncorroborated testimony is close to worthless. Smith is a suspect in a crime. He gives you an alibi. (YouÂ’re the detective assigned to the case.) You want to know whether SmithÂ’s alibi is correct. If you ask Smith Â“are you telling me the truth?Â” heÂ’ll obviously say yes. What you want is independent corroboration for SmithÂ’s testimony. No person can self-corroborate; and neither can anything else, including sense-perception. If we are to have any assurance that our senses are telling us the truth, that assurance must come from some non-sensory source. But empiricism says that nothing coming from any non-sensory source deserves any credit. Given this fact, there are only two (mutually exclusive) ways for empiricists, such as Berkeley, to go. 
(i) Deny that we know anything about the external world. 
(ii) Redefine the concept of an external object in such a way as to validate empiricism. 
(i) is self-explanatory. ItÂ’s skepticism. Some philosophers accept skepticism.[279] 
But for Berkeley, skepticism is not an alternative. He all but takes it for granted that itÂ’s false. (WeÂ’ll say why in a moment.) 
This puts Berkeley between a rock and a hard place. Berkeley refuses to stop being an empiricist. And he also refuses to accept skepticism. 
This leaves him with only one option. He must show that the presumption that our senses give us knowledge of the external world can be accommodated within the limits set by the belief that all knowledge is strictly observational. 
There is only one way to do this. One must reinterpret statements about the external objects as statements about oneÂ’s own perceptions. In other words, one must take the view that the statement Â“that rock weighs five poundsÂ” has the same content as some statement about oneÂ’s own perceptions. 
The position that statements about external objects can be translated into statements about perceptions is known as phenomenalism. Any attempt to translate a sentence about the external world into one about oneÂ’s perceptions is known as a phenomenal reduction. 
Phenomenalism entails idealism. If every truth about rocks, trees, etc., is a truth about perceptions, then rocks, trees, etc., are nothing if not perceptions. 
Phenomenalism is false. It simply isnÂ’t possible to translate statements about rocks (etc.) into statements about oneÂ’s perceptions. WeÂ’ll see why in Section 8.0. 
But phenomenalism must be accepted by any true empiricist who isnÂ’t also a skeptic. 

6.1 A systematic presentation of BerkeleyÂ’s argument [280] 

Step 1: If our senses are to be trusted, properties are observer dependent. A given elephant, at a given time, seems big to an ant and small to a giant. A given room, at a given time, seems cold to someone who just got out of a sauna and warm to someone who just came in from a blizzard. 
Step 2: The external world is totally unknowable unless we suppose that, typically, things are as they appear. 
Commentary on Step 2: This is a corollary of empiricism. Empiricism says: what we know, we know strictly on the basis of our senses. So if our senses tell us that x is big, then weÂ’re entitled to believe x is bigÂ—period. 
One cannot, in general, legitimately second-guess what oneÂ’s senses are telling one (at least not if one is an empiricist). One can throw out patently deviant perceptions (e.g., perceptions of suddenly appearing pink elephants). But this covers only an infinitesimal minority of our sensory experience. 
Step 3: Things are knowable. It would be absurd to say that we donÂ’t know anything about rocks, trees, etc. 
Step 4: Things canÂ’t have incompatible properties. A number canÂ’t be both even and odd. A thing canÂ’t be both big and small. A body of water canÂ’t be both hot and cold. 
Step 5: Suppose, if only for argumentÂ’s sake, that things exist independently of our perceptions of them. Suppose that, whether or not somebody perceives it, the vase exists (the same being true of the rock, the tree, etc.). In that case, things will have incompatible properties. 
Explanation of Step 5: Remember Step 3Â—we do know about external objects. They are not unknown. So they are as they appear. Well, they appear to have incompatible properties. One and the same thing appears both big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow, etc. 
Step 6: (this step is crucial to understanding Step 7, so bear with me): ThereÂ’s nothing incoherent in the idea that one and the same thing should 
appear both big and small, hot and cold. 
Clarification: Suppose I say Â“Bill is in Virginia right nowÂ” and I then say Â“Bill is not in Virginia right now.Â” Obviously there cannot be some one thing of which both statements are correct representations. But thereÂ’s nothing incoherent in the idea that both statements should be made. While it is incoherent to hold there is some one thing which they both correctly describe, itÂ’s obviously perfectly ok to hold that both statements (however badly they may fit together) were affirmed. Similarly, there is nothing incoherent in the idea that, at the same time, there should occur a perception to the effect that x has one temperature and also a perception to the effect that x has some other temperature. What is incoherent is the idea that there should be some thing of which both perceptions are correct representations. 
Step 7: If we say that our perceptions are representations of objects that lie on the other side of them, then (assuming, as we are, that our perceptions are accurate) things have incompatible properties. But if we say that our perceptions are not representations of such objectsÂ—if, instead, we say that perceptions are those objectsÂ—then things donÂ’t have incompatible properties. 
Clarification: Remember Step 6. It isnÂ’t possible for there to be two correct but incompatible representations of some one thing, even though itÂ’s obviously possible for two such representations to exist. Our perceptions give us incompatible messages (they say that one and the same thing is both big and small, is moving both quickly and slowly, etc.). So it isnÂ’t possible for our perceptions to be correct representations of things. But it is possible for our perceptions to exist. It is irrelevant that they are incoherent if taken to be representations of trans-perceptual entities. 
Step 8: It follows from Step 7 that our perceptions canÂ’t be representations of anything. 
Step 9: But remember Step 2Â—we do know about things. We do know their sizes, temperatures, etc. The way to make this all work is to say: things are our perceptions of them. We know our perceptions obviously. (So if we say that rocks, trees, etc., are our perceptions, then we can explain how we can know them.) And we also know that perceptions canÂ’t be representations of things. Thus, perceptions donÂ’t represent reality: they are reality. 
Conclusion: For something to exist is for it to be perceived. The perception doesnÂ’t represent the thing. The perception constitutes the thing. 
7.0 Evaluating BerkeleyÂ’s argument 
BerkeleyÂ’s argument fails. But the reason why it does must be understood in terms of a rather subtle point about sense-perceptionÂ—a point that will initially be hard to understand but that, after being stated abstractly, will be made clear with some examples. 
Our senses give us relational information. They tell us how things are in relation to one another and in relation to ourselves. They apprise us, not of absolute, but of relative heights, distances, velocities, temperatures, and masses; our eyes tell us, not that the car is going 35 mph, but that it is going faster than that other car; our muscles, when we exert ourselves, tell us not that the barbell weighs 215 pounds, but that it weighs more than the barbells we tried to move a moment ago. Our senses tell us, not that Smith is seven feet tall, but that he is much taller than Jones. And our senses tell us where things are, not in relation to some absolute coordinate system, but in relation to us. So the information given to us by our senses is relational in two senses: objects are related to one another; and they are also related to an egocentric, as opposed to universal, coordinate system. 
Once this is taken into account, it is clear why BerkeleyÂ’s argument crumbles. Consider a situation where X is walking at a rate of 1 mph, Y is driving at a rate of 30 mph, and Z is driving at a rate of 90 mph. (X, Y, and Z can see each other; they have good vision and normal cognitive capacities. So they know, at least approximately, what their relative velocities are.) 
According to Berkeley, XÂ’s perception of Y is simply this: Y is moving fast. And, according to Berkeley, ZÂ’s perception of Y is simply: Y is moving slowly. Berkeley rightly holds that both perceptions could be accurate. But he wrongly holds that the information embodied in the one perception contradicts that embodied in the other. This is because Berkeley has misrepresent both bodies of information. XÂ’s eyes donÂ’t tell him: Y is moving fast. They tell him: Y is moving faster than I am. And ZÂ’s eyes donÂ’t tell him: Y is moving slowly. They tell him: Y is moving more slowly than I am. 
So when we consider what XÂ’s eyes are telling him, and put it together with what ZÂ’s are telling him (Z), the result is: 
(i) Z is moving faster than Y, and Y is moving faster than X. 
There is nothing incoherent about (i). It does indeed attribute two 
properties to Y (namely, the property of moving slower than Z and the property of moving faster than X). But there is no reason why a thing canÂ’t simultaneously have both properties; for those properties are not incompatibleÂ—they arenÂ’t like the properties Â“squareÂ” and Â“circle.Â” (i) describes a state of affairs that can, without any incoherence or self-contradiction, be attributed to the external world. 

8.0 How we actually learn what properties things have 
As weÂ’ve noted, our senses give us only relational information; they tell us, not that the object x weighs 80 pounds, but that it weighs more than object y; not that object x is moving at a rate of 50 mph, but that it is moving faster than y; not that x has a temperature of 78Â°, but that x is warmer than y; and so on. At the same time, weÂ’re obviously capable of learning objectsÂ’ actual masses, temperatures, and such. But how is this possible if our senses give us only relational information? 
To answer this question, we must take a brief detour through the philosophy of science. Suppose you decide to measure time in terms of your own heart rate. YouÂ’ll find that, when you do vigorous exercise, everything in the universe (other than your heart rate itself) slows down. (Your heart rate does not itself slow down; for, being the standard of comparison, its rate is by definition constant.) And youÂ’ll find that, when you are calm and relaxed, everything in the universe speeds up. 
Here you can say one of two things. (i) Because of some strange law, your exercising causes the entire universe (except for your heart itself) to slow down (and your ceasing to exercise causes it to speed up). (ii) You shouldnÂ’t measure rates of change with respect to your heart rate, since doing so creates otherwise absent causal anomalies and demands that relatively simple physical laws be replaced with exceedingly complicated ones. 
Obviously (ii) is the right choice. You shouldnÂ’t regard your heart rate as a periodic process. You should say that itÂ’s your heart rate thatÂ’s changing, not the entire universe.[281] 

Comparable points hold with respect to all degree properties. (By a Â“degree property,Â” I mean one that can be had to varying degrees. So coldness is a degree property, since one thing can be colder than another. But the property of being divisible by two is not, since a number either has that property or it doesnÂ’t.) Suppose a consequence of taking object L to have a constant length is that, when L is put in a freezer, everything in the universe (except for L itself) expands and that, when L is put in boiling water, everything in the universe shrinks. In that case, obviously, you shouldnÂ’t take L to have an unchanging length; you shouldnÂ’t take it as your standard of comparison. The principle implicit in all this is that, if one learns that there has been a change in the difference between x and y in respect of how much they have degree property phi, one should regard the extent to which x has phi as having changed less than the degree to which y has phi if and only if doing so is less costly, from an explanatory viewpoint, than it would be to regard y as having undergone less change (in that respect) than x or to regard x and y as having undergone equal amounts of change (same qualification). So, if fewer causal anomalies are created by regarding y as having undergone less phi-change than x than are created by regarding x as having undergone more phi-change than y, then one should not regard x as approximating, to a higher degree than y, to a condition of phi-uniformity. And if fewer causal anomalies are created by regarding x and y as having undergone equal amounts of phi-change than are created by supposing one of them to have undergone more phi-change than the other, then one should regard neither x nor y as approximating a condition of phi-uniformity to a higher degree than the other. Otherwise one should regard x as approximating to a condition of phi-uniformity to a higher degree than x. 

8.1 How this last point relates to sense-perception 
Our senses constantly give us information about comparative rates of change. OneÂ’s eyes might tell one, for example, that the apparent size of the man is changing faster than the apparent size of the tree. The manÂ’s apparent size, so oneÂ’s eyes tell one, is shrinking faster than the treeÂ’s apparent size, even though the apparent size of each one is shrinking. Without in any way being untrue to this raw, pre-inferential, visual information, one could hold any one of the following: 
(i) 
OneÂ’s distance from the man remains constant, and so does oneÂ’s distance from the tree. But the man and the tree are both shrinking, and the man is shrinking faster than the tree. 

(ii) 
One is moving away from both the man and the tree. (Therefore, oneÂ’s distance from the man isnÂ’t constant, and neither is oneÂ’s distance from the tree.) But the distance between the man and the tree remains constant; and, whereas the man is shrinking, the treeÂ’s size remains constant. 


(iii) One is moving away from both the man and the tree. But the distance between the man and the tree remains constant. And even though both the man and the tree are shrinking, the man is doing so at a faster rate than the tree. 
(iv) The treeÂ’s size remains constant, and so does the manÂ’s. The man is moving away from the tree in one direction, and you are moving away from the tree in the opposite direction. 
Each of (i)Â–(iv) is consistent with the raw information contained in the previously described perception. But a world where any one of (i)Â–(iii) was correct would ceteris paribus be a world that was replete with causal anomalies absent from a world where (iv) was correct. This means that, if one were to countenance any one of (i)Â–(iii), oneÂ’s understanding of the world and the forces that govern it would undergo a weakening that it would not undergo were one instead to countenance (iv). It is for this reason, then, that ceteris paribus one countenances (iv), and not any one of (i)Â–(iii). It is for this reason, that, after exercising vigorously, one believes that oneÂ’s heart rate sped up and not that the rest of the world slowed down; that, after lifting weights for a year, one became stronger and not that everything became lighter; that, on leaving a steam room, oneÂ’s body has become warmer and not that the world that has become colder; and so on. 
So although it is obviously through sense-perception that we learn objectsÂ’ masses, speeds, temperatures, and so on, we donÂ’t sense-perceive them, at least not directly. Although it is through sense-perception that one learns that the water is 78Â°, one doesnÂ’t sense-perceive that the water has that temperature. What one sense-perceives is that the water is warmer than x and colder than y. 
Given this information, one is justified in believing that the waterÂ’s temperature is 78Â° just in case, in doing so, one is undermining the integrity of oneÂ’s understanding of physical reality less than one would be in not doing so. Basically, objectsÂ’ actual properties are inferred from sense-perceptions and not directly sense-perceived; and the relevant rule of inference is: Â“of the various ways of accommodating the raw, sensory data that youÂ’ve been given (and there will always be several such ways), the right one is the one that is the least ad hoc (that posits the fewest causal anomalies, that has the most explanatory fertility, etc.).Â” 
9.0 Primary vs. secondary properties 
Like John Locke, Berkeley distinguishes between primary properties and secondary properties.[282] 
Examples of primary properties are shape, size, density, liquidity, solidity, gaseousness, and state of motion. Examples of secondary properties are sweetness, smell, color, and timbre.[283] 

For a thing to have a given secondary propertyÂ—e.g., for it to have the taste of SnickerÂ’s barÂ—is for that thing to be prone to induce sensations of a certain kind in creatures of a given kind. 
For a thing to have a given primary property is for it to have an effect of a given kind on the conditions that objects must meet to occupy a certain region of space-time. By virtue of being round (or gaseous), a thing has certain effects on would-be occupants of its current location that, other things being equal, it wouldnÂ’t have were it square-shaped (or solid) instead. 
According to some, the essence of BerkeleyÂ’s argument for idealism is that primary properties are really secondary properties.[284] 
Thus interpreted, BerkeleyÂ’s argument is as follows: 
BerkeleyÂ’s argument (BA): For a thing to have a given secondary property is for it to taste, smell, feel, etc., a certain way. Some philosophers hold that, in this respect, shape, size, and other so-called primary properties are fundamentally different from secondary properties. But theyÂ’re wrong. Shape, size, etc., are quite as observer-dependent as taste, color, etc. When youÂ’re near the house, it looks big (weÂ’re assuming that your perception is accurate); and when youÂ’re far from the house, it looks small (same qualification). Of course, we could say that the size an object seems to have is different from the size it actually has. But in that case, weÂ’d be stuck saying that our senses tell us nothing, or next to nothing, about the external world, which is absurd. It follows (for the reasons given earlier) that the objects of sense-perception are identical with our perceptions of them. 
The problem with BA is that, contrary to what it says, your first house-perception is consistent with your second house-perception. The first perception doesnÂ’t say that the house is big. It tells you how its size compares with those of various objects. It tells you that itÂ’s shorter than the telephone pole next to it, but taller than the cactus in front of it, etc. The comparative information given to you by your second perception is consistent with it. The relative apparent sizes of the cactus, house, and telephone pole are the same. 
In the second perception, the house appears the way that small things appear when looked at from up close. And that is the one and only sense in which the house Â“looks small.Â” But youÂ’re not looking at the house from up close. YouÂ’re looking at it from far away. And your perception isnÂ’t telling you that the house is close by and looks that way. ItÂ’s telling you that youÂ’re far away from the house and it looks that way. So it isnÂ’t telling you that the house is small. ItÂ’s actually telling you that itÂ’s quite big. 
When youÂ’re near the house, your house-image hogs up your entire field of vision. It occupies more space on your visual map. When youÂ’re far from the house, your field of vision has to include a great many objects other than the house. So it doesnÂ’t eat up very much map-space. Thus, measured in terms of how much map-space they eat up, the first house-image is larger than the second house-image. 
But that doesnÂ’t mean that those perceptions make different statements concerning the size of the house. On a map the size of a postage stamp, the discoloration that represents Denmark will be miniscule. On a map the size of the side of a big house, the corresponding discoloration will be much bigger. But that doesnÂ’t mean that Denmark is small according to the small map and big according to the big one. Each of those maps tells you that DenmarkÂ’s actual size corresponds to the relative, not the absolute, size of the picture of Denmark on that map. The bigger that discoloration is in relation to the other nation-representations on that map, the bigger the size thereby attributed to Denmark. Thus, the size attributed to Denmark by the small map might be twice that attributed to it by the big map. 
The same thing mutatis mutandis is true of visual images. A big house no more Â“looks smallÂ” when looked at from far away than Denmark Â“looks smallÂ” on the tiny map. When the house is looked at from far away, the corresponding house-image is small (i.e., it eats up a comparatively small amount of visual space). But thatÂ’s consistent with that very perceptionÂ’s representing that very house as being huge. 

9.1 BA embodies a spurious understanding of what secondary properties are 
The health effects of eating a foul smelling cut of meat are very different from the health-effects of eating a wholesome smelling cut of meat that is otherwise observationally just like the first. The way a piece of meat smells is an indication of its ability to nourish. For this reason, otherwise hard to obtain causal knowledge is easily obtained and otherwise hard to make predictions are easily made. 
Differences in secondary properties always correlate with causal differences. In many cases, day-to-day experience makes it clear what causal properties are associated with possession of a given secondary property. (Day-to-day experience makes it clear that things with certain tastes and smells are not fit to drink.) In other cases, day-to-day experience doesnÂ’t do this. (Day-to-day experience doesnÂ’t make it clear how an object that is red differs in respect of its causal properties from one that is green but is otherwise identical.) But if a given object has a given secondary property, it ipso facto has some causal property that it wouldnÂ’t otherwise have. 
For this reason, secondary properties are not in any relevant sense Â“subjective.Â” The term Â“subjective,Â” as John Searle (1992) points out, has two very different meanings. To say that such and such is Â“subjectiveÂ” can mean that: 
(i) its existence presupposes that of some subject, 
or it can mean that: 
(ii) it embodies prejudices or other subject-specific idiosyncrasies that tend to inhibit the acquisition of knowledge. 
My belief that 2 + 2 = 4 is subjective in sense (i). That belief presupposes the existence of a subject. There canÂ’t be disembodied beliefs floating about. 
[285] 
But that belief isnÂ’t subjective in sense (ii). It is (so we will assume) based on rational consideration of the relevant information. By contrast, my intense fear of people who wear plaid shirts (which is based, not on rational consideration of the relevant data, but on childhood traumas that we neednÂ’t discuss) is subjective in sense (ii). In other words, it is rooted in peculiarities of my own person that make it harder for me than it would otherwise be to see things as they are. My olfactory perception that the maggot-infested meat in front of me smells awful is subjective in sense (i) but not in sense (ii). It is subjective only in the trivial and irrelevant sense in which any mental entity, even a coolly made judgment, is subjective: it is subjective in the same way as my rational and informed belief that 2 + 2 = 4 is subjective. But it isnÂ’t subjective in the same way as my prejudice-driven fear of people who wear plaid shirts. 
Bearing this in mind, suppose that, all of a sudden, the way things smelled was no indication as to whether they were rotten or not. So, for example, a putrid-smelling cut of meat might or might not be good to eatÂ—its smell would give you no information as to its fitness as a source of nourishmentÂ—the same being true of a wholesome-smelling cut of meat. In general, we wouldnÂ’t know anything about an objectÂ’s causal properties from the way it smelled. But we often know a lot about a thingÂ’s causal properties from the way it smells. Smells correlate extremely reliably with certain causal features of objectsÂ—sometimes much more reliably than other properties. Sometimes the way a thing smells is the only indication (short of eating it or sending it to a toxicology lab) that itÂ’s laced with poison or that itÂ’s completely rotten. 
Smells track primary properties; they track facts about microstructure that would otherwise be hard to detect. If a police-detective suspects that X is pure cocaine, he can verify his hypothesis by (i) snorting X, which would have various adverse consequences, (ii) sending X to a forensics laboratory, which would be extremely slow, or (iii) tasting it, which would be quick and easy. 
A relevant fact about method (ii) is that many scientific techniques would have been impossible to develop had there not been reliable correlations between microstructure and odor. This is true of secondary properties generally. 
There are some apparent counterexamples to our contention that secondary properties track microstructure. For example, a thingÂ’s color doesnÂ’t correlate reliably with its microstructure. From far away, the ocean water looks black; from up close itÂ’s transparent. Locke concluded from this that secondary properties are subjective. 
But this is not the only conclusion to draw. An objectÂ’s apparent color is a function both of that objectÂ’s microstructure and of the relevant observerÂ’s physical relation to that object. But so does an objectÂ’s apparent shape, apparent size, smell, etc. So the variability of apparent color no more entails the subjectivity of color than does the variability of apparent shape. And so long as the conditions of observation are held constant, an objectÂ’s apparent color does reliably correlate with its microstructure, just like its apparent shape (though not, it must be admitted, to as high a degree). 
The right conclusion to draw, I believe, is that what we refer to as an objectÂ’s color is an objective property, not of the object per se, but of the objectÂ’s relation to environment in which a given observer is perceiving it. Thus, color is neither subjective; nor is it an objective property of objects per se; it is an objective property of ordered triples. If O is some object, P is someone perceiving that object, and R is PÂ’s physical relation to O, then there is a property, to which we refer as Â“the color of O,Â” that, though not actually a property of O itself, is an objective feature of the world, being property of the ordered triple <O, P, R>. 
Setting aside people with visual defects, there is little or no variation between people in regards to how oneÂ’s physical relationship to a given body of water affects how that water appears. Given two people who are free of visual pathologies, if that object appears bright blue to the one person when he bears relation R to it, that object will appear bright blue when the other person bears R to it. Of course, the color that a given object appears to have to a given person is a function of changes in that personÂ’s physical relation to that object that havenÂ’t the slightest effect on that object itself. But an objectÂ’s apparent color does not vary, so long as the observerÂ’s physical relationship to it is fixed. A given objectÂ’s physical constitution doesnÂ’t determine its apparent color. But relative to an observer bearing a fixed relation to that object, that objectÂ’s apparent color is fixed. This suggests that what we refer to as an objectÂ’s color is a property of relations that observers may bear with respect to that object. Thus, colors are properties of ordered triples of the earlier-described kind. 
If this is right, then instances of color are mind-dependent but opinion-independent. In other words, there would be no instances of colors if there were no minds. But it isnÂ’t a matter of opinion what color such an instance has. There are many facts that are mind-dependent but opinion-independent. Right now, I am having various thoughts while standing within 20 feet from where Smith is standing. It isnÂ’t a Â‘matter of opinionÂ’ where I am at a given time in relation to Smith or what IÂ’m thinking at that time.[286] 
But (supposing that I couldnÂ’t exist without a mind) neither fact is mind-independent. 




9.2 BA embodies a spurious understanding of what secondary properties are (continued) 
Our perceptions of primary properties are very different from our perceptions of secondary properties. When one sees a porcupine, oneÂ’s visual image has a structural similarity to that of the porcupine; given any two features of the porcupine that are distinguished by image, there are corresponding 
differentiations in that image.[287] 
Perceptions of secondary properties are very different; they arenÂ’t internally differentiated, at least not in a way that at all corresponds to the objective facts to which they are hewed. 
This, presumably, is at least part of the reason why itÂ’s widely held that an objectÂ’s secondary properties are really properties of the subjectÂ’s experiences of that object, and not of that object itself. (ItÂ’s also why it seems more natural to speak of Â“sensationsÂ” of taste, smell, etc. than of Â“perceptionsÂ” of them.) But, I will now argue, an objectÂ’s secondary properties belong to it no less than its primary properties. I must warn that the forthcoming argument is quite intricate and that, for the first few paragraphs, it will seem as though IÂ’m arguing for the contention that an objectÂ’s secondary properties donÂ’t really belong to it. I must ask for a certain amount of patience on the readerÂ’s part. 
Let S be the smell that, in actuality, is had by extremely putrid meat; and let S* be the extremely pleasant fragrance that, in actuality, is given off by eucalyptus trees. There is no inherent reason why eucalyptus trees couldnÂ’t have S and there is no inherent reason why rotten meat couldnÂ’t have S*. In other words, if there occurred a smell-exchange between eucalyptus trees and rotten meat, we would not, at least not for that reason alone, forfeit the causal knowledge that we now have by virtue of knowing that a cut of meat has S or that a eucalyptus tree has S*. 
Of course, there would initially be a loss of knowledge. One would mistakenly think that the pleasant-smelling cut of meat one was about to eat was not rotten. But given some time to adjust to the new smell-situation, one would cease to make such mistakes.[288] 

9.3 BA embodies a spurious understanding of what secondary properties are (continued) 
There is another reason why, even though it wouldnÂ’t have any lasting effect on our ability to acquire knowledge through olfaction, that smell-exchange would initially compromise our ability to do so. This fact initially suggests that olfaction doesnÂ’t give us knowledge of the causal structure of the world. But, duly scrutinized, it turns out to entail that olfaction is, like vision and audition, does give us such knowledge. 
Much of the knowledge that we acquire through the sense of smell is based on the comparative properties of our olfactory sensations. Other things being equal, the more rotten a cut of meat is, the worse it smells. Other things being equal, the more pungent the fragrance of a eucalyptus tree is the richer that tree is in the chemical responsible for that smell. 
Bearing this in mind, suppose that S is the exact smell had (under a given set of circumstances) by a cut of meat that was rotten to degree n, and that S* is the fragrance (same qualification) of a eucalyptus having amount m of the relevant chemical. Because the previously described exchange hasnÂ’t occurred, given a cut of meat having S and some other, otherwise observationally identical cut of meat, with a much stronger (weaker) version of S, I know on that basis that ceteris paribus the latter cut of meat is more (less) rotten than the former. For this reason, if the exchange in question occurred but that other, compensatory changes didnÂ’t also occur alongside, our ability to acquire comparative knowledge of this kind would be diminished. 
But thereÂ’s no reason why any given set of causal properties should be associated with any given type of olfactory sensation. What is necessary is that, once the assignments are made, their mutual relations parallel the mutual relations of their objects. 
(SA) So you admit that its having this as opposed to that odor does not, in and of itself, diminish our ability to learn about the world through the sense of smell. You admit, in other words, that rotten meat doesnÂ’t have to have the smell it does. But in admitting this, youÂ’re admitting that it doesnÂ’t really have that smell. 
There are two problems with SA. 
Problem #1: When we say that a given cut of meat has a bad smell, weÂ’re talking about the cut of meat. If the word Â“smellÂ” referred to sensations, then sentences like Â“that meat has an awful smellÂ” wouldnÂ’t be about the meat. By the same token, so far as that sentence is about the meat, it isnÂ’t about sensations. Thus, to the extent that it really is about the meat, whether or not that sentence makes a true statement has nothing to do with anyoneÂ’s sensations. And to the extent that it isnÂ’t about our sensations, Â“that meat has an awful smellÂ” is about the meatÂ’s causal properties or, in any case, is about some other (probably related) mind-independent fact. 
Problem #2: SA establishes that smell is mind-dependent only to the extent that it establishes the obviously, or at least presumably, false conclusion that size and shape are mind-dependent. 
Look at the book in front of you. Let V be the visual sensation you are having. Under otherwise unchanged circumstances, you could have a visual sensation that, although very different from V, gave you either the very same information or that gave you much more information. In human beings, the set of sight isnÂ’t nearly as acute as it is where certain other species are concerned. Were they to look at the book in front of you, under conditions just like the ones that actually obtain, theyÂ’d have sensations very different from V that contained all the information contained in 
V, and then some.[289] 
You could have visual sensations very different from the ones you actually have without, for that reason, failing to know anything that you do know. 
But this doesnÂ’t entail that the facts of which vision apprises us are mind-dependent. V gives you a lot of information about the bookÂ’s location, its shape, and its size. And VÂ’s shape, size, etc., are quite definitely mind-independent. 
This reasoning is likely to meet with the following objection: 
(QB)[290] 
But arenÂ’t you begging the question against Berkeley in saying this? WasnÂ’t Berkeley arguing that, since (as you just pointed out) secondary properties are relevantly similar primary properties, to be is to be perceived? 
Berkeley does indeed argue that. But he also takes it for granted that secondary properties are mind-dependent. In other words, his argument has the form: (i) secondary properties are mind-dependent; (ii) secondary properties are relevantly similar to primary properties; (iii) therefore, primary properties are mind-dependent; (iv) it follows from (iii) that objects are mind-dependentÂ—are creatures of the mind. 
But I argued that secondary properties arenÂ’t mind-dependent. I reject step (i), and provided an independently plausible reason for doing so. Therefore, what IÂ’ve said doesnÂ’t beg any questions against Berkeley and QB thus fails. 
10.0 Is temperature a primary or a secondary property? 
Some properties that seem to be secondary turn out to be primary. A brief examination of one such property will clarify some of the points just made. 
For an object to have a certain temperature is for the particles composing it to have a certain mean kinetic energy. (Basically, itÂ’s for those particles to move around in a certain way. The faster the movements, the greater the temperature. [291]) But itÂ’s initially tempting to categorize temperature with sweetness and, thus, to see it as a secondary property. 
There are a couple of reasons for this. First, secondary properties are modality-specific. Sweetness can be tasted, but not heard, seen, touched. By contrast, primary properties are clearly transmodal. Squareness can be seen or touched. In fact, creatures with very good hearing (e.g,. bats), can hear shapes, just as we can see them; bats can detect an objectÂ’s shape through sonar. And creatures with a very olfactory keen sense (e.g., moles) can smell shape. 
According to some, including Locke and Berkeley himself, temperature can be known only through touch. But this isnÂ’t true, of course. Given what temperature is (namely, molecular motion), it is just as capable of being known through sight or audition as it is of being known through touch. But itÂ’s obvious why someone would think otherwise. 
ThereÂ’s another reason why temperature is often falsely regarded as a secondary property. There isnÂ’t anything inherently pleasant or unpleasant about seeing a square-shaped object or a fast-moving object.
