Under certain circumstances, it may be very unpleasant to see something move with a certain speed. But the connection is circumstance-specific. There is, however, something inherently unpleasant about certain odors, tastes, and timbres. In general, primary properties are not inherently associated with aesthetic propertiesÂ—any such association is circumstantialÂ—whereas secondary properties are non-circumstantially associated with such properties. Very high and very low temperatures are non-circumstantially associated with unpleasant sensations, and moderate temperatures are non-circumstantially associated with pleasant ones. 
Nonetheless, temperature is a primary property, since an instance of temperature is identical with various instances of motion. And, technically, temperature is transmodal; for one can learn a thing's temperature by figuring out how its parts are moving, which obviously need not, and often cannot, be established on the basis of the "feeling of temperature" on the basis of which 
one determines that one's beverage is warm or that it's too cold to go for a run. 
11.0 A second Berkeleyan argumentÂ—Â“to be is to be conceivedÂ” 
At one point, Berkeley argues that to be is to be conceived (Â“esse concipi istÂ”). In other words, things are the awarenesses that we, or other thinking beings, have of them. Here is his argument: 
(BA2) You cannot conceive of an unconceived object without its ipso facto being conceived. So it is literally inconceivable that there should be unconceived objects. (You canÂ’t conceive of an unconceived chicken, since, by virtue of your conceiving of it, it isnÂ’t unconceived.) Thus, the very idea of an unconceived object makes no sense, and unconceived objects no more exist than four sided triangles. 
If cogent, BA2 establishes that being conceived of is a necessary condition for existing, but not that itÂ’s a sufficient condition for it. (Given only that one canÂ’t conceive of a circle that isnÂ’t a closed figure, it doesnÂ’t follow that all closed figures are circles.) 
In any case, BA2 spurious. The problem with BA2 that, contrary to what Berkeley assumes, propositions, not objects, are the objects of conception. When one Â“conceives of a 50-pound chicken,Â” one is thinking about a proposition (namely, there exists a chicken that weighs 50 pounds). There isnÂ’t some specific chicken x such that x weighs 50 pounds and such that one is thinking about x. Similarly to conceive of an unconceived chicken isn't for there to be some chicken x such that one is conceiving of x and such that one is conceiving of x as being unconceived. Rather, one is thinking about the proposition: there is a chicken x such that nobody is conceiving of it, which one can grasp, and even know to be true, without there being any chicken x such that one is conceiving of x. So BA2 fails to show that to be is to be conceived. 
12.0 The phenomenal reductionÂ—some preliminaries 
First some terminological points. An object-statement is one that concerns mind-independent entities; e.g., Â“that statue is over 10 feet tallÂ” is an object statement. A perception-statement is one that concerns oneÂ’s own perceptions (e.g., Â“I am having an experience that, if it were veridical, would be of a statue that is over 10 feet tallÂ”). Two statements are observationally equivalent if there is no observation that (dis)confirms the one either more or less than it (dis)confirms the other. (All analytically equivalent sentences are observationally equivalentÂ—but not vice versa, as weÂ’re about to see.) Finally, a property or relation is observationally inert if no instance of it could possibly affect what anyone observes. 
12.1 The phenomenal reduction 
For the reasons given earlier, strict empiricism leads to either skepticism or to idealism. Skepticism and idealism are both deeply at odds with commonsense. Berkeley agreed that skepticism was at odds with commonsense. But he denied that idealism had this defect. He held, in fact, that idealism is the commonsense view. 
In an effort to vindicate this obviously false claim, Berkeley argued that any object-statement that we could have any good reason to believe correct can be reinterpreted as a perception-statement. 
Here is a modernized presentation of BerkeleyÂ’s reasoning: 
(BR)[292] 
A statement about the external world is meaningful only to the extent that, were it true, weÂ’d have observations that we wouldnÂ’t otherwise have. 
This entails that such a statement is meaningful only to the extent that it concerns observations. When the possible observations run out, so does the meaning. Thus, Â“Smith has a carÂ” is without meaning to the extent SmithÂ’s having a car is observationally inert, the same thing mutatis mutandis obviously being true of Â“Brown has a car.Â” And: 
(1) Â“SmithÂ’s car weighs twice as much as BrownÂ’s car,Â” 
is meaningful only to the extent that, for any objects x and y, if x weighs twice as much as y, there would ipso facto occur observations that would not otherwise occur. 
If we replace all of the constants in (1) with variables, what results is the sentence-form: 
(2) A bears R to B. 
A true sentence results if the variables in (2) are replaced 
with constants referring to classes of perceptions. Let K1 be the class of perceptions that one has in virtue of the fact that SmithÂ’s car exists. (K1 might include a perception of Smith pulling out of his garage.) Let K2 be the class of perceptions that one has when, and only when, there are objects x and y such that x weighs twice as much as y. And let K3 be the class of perceptions that one has in virtue of the fact that BrownÂ’s 
car exists. 
If a given observation O confirms (1) to a degree, it confirms: 
(3) K1 bears K2 to K3, 
to that same degree. (In this context, Â“confirmsÂ” is to be taken to refer to positive or negative confirmation.) If a given observation O* (dis)confirms any one of these three claims, it is ipso facto (not) a member of one of K1Â–K3. So there canÂ’t be 
an observation that (dis)confirms (1) more or less than it (dis)confirms (3). 
There is therefore no observation-based reason to prefer (1) to (3). So assuming, as we are, that empiricism is correct, and that all good reasons are observation-based, it follows that there is no reason at all. 
But the very fact that there is no such reason is itself a reason to prefer (3) to (1). (3) doesnÂ’t posit anything for which there is no observational evidence. (WeÂ’ll henceforth use the word Â“trans-observationalÂ” to describe entities for whose existence there is no observational evidence.) But (1), at least as many philosophers interpret it, does posit trans-observational entities.[293] 
And to the extent that a sentence demands the existence of trans-observational entities, it is meaningless. Why? Because sentences are meaningful only to the extent that, if true, they make a difference; and, given the truth of empiricism, a sentence makes a difference only if it makes an observational difference. 
12.2 The viability and significance of the phenomenal reduction 
In this context, IÂ’ll use the word Â“perceptionÂ” to denote any mental state that, if veridical, is an accurate sensory observation but that neednÂ’t be veridical. Thus, hallucinations are perceptions, as weÂ’ll be using that word, and so are veridical perceptions. 
Note: in what weÂ’re about to say, words like Â“seeÂ” and Â“perceiveÂ” are not to be taken as Â“success-verbs.Â” As IÂ’ll be using the word Â“see,Â” the fact that you Â“seeÂ” Smith driving a car doesnÂ’t mean that you really saw him driving a car. It means only that you had the sort of experience that would have been veridical had Smith actually been driving his car and had that in fact been what you were seeing. Given any other similar term----Â“perceive,Â” Â“perception,Â” Â“hear,Â” etc.---the same point mutatis mutandis holds with respect to it. Having cleared that up, letÂ’s consider the following hypothetical situation. 
You see Smith driving a car. Berkeley admits this. In other words, Berkeley admitsÂ—as he surely mustÂ—that, other things being equal, your having a perception of Smith driving a car gives some weight to the contention that Smith is driving a car. 
Question: How is P evidence of SmithÂ’s driving a car? ItÂ’s evidence of it because it says that Smith is driving a car. If your mother, who you trust, calls you up and says Â“Smith is driving a car (which he shouldnÂ’t being doing, since heÂ’s blind drunk),Â” youÂ’re likely to believe that Smith is driving a car, even if you didnÂ’t previously have any reason to believe it. The reason is that you regard your motherÂ’s testimony as evidence to the effect. You also regard your visual perception of Smith driving as (extremely strong) evidence to that effect. You do this because your eyes are telling youÂ—much as your mother might, but much more convincinglyÂ—that Smith (or, at any rate, somebody who looks a lot like him) is driving a car. 
Part of what your eyes (or, if youÂ’re hallucinating, the malfunctioning brain-centers) are telling you is that some spatially remote object (namely, Smith) bears a certain relation (namely, that of driving) with respect to some other spatially remote object (namely, the car Smith is driving). And in telling you that Smith and his car are spatially remote from you, your eyes are saying, or at least implying, that Smith isnÂ’t a part of you or, therefore, of your mind. 
It may be that P is wrong. It may be that youÂ’re hallucinating and that, when you come down from your acid trip, it will turn out that Smith wasnÂ’t driving at the time in question. But P still said that he was driving, and it still said that there exists some spatially remote object bearing a certain relation to some other such object. 
Any given perception is to the effect that objects that arenÂ’t a part of you bear certain relations to one another and/or individually have certain properties. So to the extent that our sense-perceptions are evidence of anything, they are evidence of trans-perceptual objects. And that is why statements about perceptions cannot possibly be equivalent with statements about objects. 
13.0 Two insights of BerkeleyÂ’s 
BerkeleyÂ’s argument for idealism does not go through, and neither does his attempt to reduce statements about objects to statements about perceptions. But, in the process of trying to establish idealism, Berkeley had two extremely profound and original insights, whose philosophical consequences are still being fathomed, to wit: 
(A) Many of the Â“statementsÂ” we make arenÂ’t really statements at all, and are instead statement-forms, 
and 
(B) A statementÂ’s grammatical form may not coincide with its logical formÂ—that, in other words, a statement must be reparsed if its meaning is to be made clear.[294] 

(A) explained: Â“The number five is oddÂ” is a statement. It attributes a definite property to a definite object. The expression "x is odd" is a statement-form, not a statement. An Â“interpretationÂ” of a statement-form is simply an assignment of constants to the variables. To model a statement-form is to identify an interpretation of it that yields a true statement. Here is a trivial example: 
(1) 
A bears relationship R to B. 

(2) 
If x bears R to y, y bears R to x. 


(3) Nothing bears R to itself. In other words, Â‹x bears R to xÂ› is false, for all objects x. 
Let R be the relationship that one bears to somebody else in virtue of being that personÂ’s next-door neighbor. Since (setting aside the odd person who owns adjacent houses) nobody is oneÂ’s own next-door neighbor, (3) comes out true. So does (2), since x must be yÂ’s next-door neighbor if y is xÂ’s next-door neighbor. Thus, supposing for argumentÂ’s sake that Smith and Jones are next-door neighbors, (1) comes out true if Â“AÂ” refers to Smith and Â“BÂ” refers to Jones. We have thus modeled (1)Â–(3). 
In conjecturing that (so-called) statements such as Â‘that rock weighs five poundsÂ’ can be reinterpreted as statements about perceptions, Berkeley was in effect saying that such statements arenÂ’t statements at allÂ—theyÂ’re statement forms. Though he didnÂ’t himself put it this way, he was saying (i) that the terms in them (e.g., Â‘rock,Â’ Â‘weighs five poundsÂ’) are really variables, and (ii) that true statements would result if those variables were replaced with constants referring to perceptions. 
Berkeley was wrong about (ii), as weÂ’ve already observed. But he was right about (i). There is no one microstructure that Rover must have if my current perception of him is to be accurate. There is, as we will now see, no one way anything must be if any given perception is to be correct. 
WeÂ’ve seen that our knowledge of the world is strictly comparative.[295] 
We know how fast a given thing is traveling only to the extent that we know how much faster it is traveling than some other thing. We know how heavy/hot/big/etc., a thing is only to the extent that we know how much heavier/hotter/bigger/etc., that thing is than some other thing. Spatiotemporal knowledge is comparative knowledge. 
That means that anythingÂ—no matter what itÂ’s parts are Â‘made ofÂ’Â—whose parts are appropriately interrelated is no more, and no less, consistent with what our sense-perceptions tell us than is any other thing whose parts are thus interrelated. This means that perception apprises us only of structure. 
Our perceptions (if correct) tell us the structure of the world, and our physical theories (if correct) apprise us of microstructure. Given any two things having the requisite structure, there cannot possibly be any observational basis for holding that it, and not the other thing, is what is really out there. 
This means that, if x and y both have the requisite structure but are qualitatively different in some non-structural respect, the supposition that x is what is really out there models the data exactly as wellÂ—no better, no worseÂ— than the supposition that y is what is really out there. 
This doesnÂ’t mean that there is no fact as to what is out there. There obviously is. Given any set of possible objects, each having the structure of the external world but each differing in some non-structural respect from the others, at most one of those objects can be the external world. But the supposition that any given one of them is what is actual does exactly as good a job of modeling the observational data as the supposition that any other given one of them is what is actual. And one of the claims embodied in BerkeleyÂ’s argument(s) for idealism is precisely that, to the extent that the probability of a hypothesis is a function of its congruence with observational data, anything that models the observational data ipso facto is no less likely to be whatÂ’s really out there than anything else that does so. Berkeley was therefore (so far as I know) the first model-theorist. 
(B) explained: To my knowledge, Berkeley was the first to recognize the distinction grammatical structure (surface structure) and logical form (deep structure[296]). To avoid getting caught up in technicalities, letÂ’s also suppose Smith is the only percipient being in existence. BerkeleyÂ’s idealism seems to entail that, if Smith closes his eyes (and is otherwise not in sensory contact with the world), the whole world disappears; and it also seems to entail that the whole world springs back into existence when Smith opens his eyes. This is deeply implausible. 
It also seems to undermine BerkeleyÂ’s claim that any object-statement that is presumed correct (e.g., Â‘the world doesnÂ’t disappear when I close my eyesÂ’) is equivalent with a statement stating the observational evidence for that claim. When I close my eyes, the observational evidence seems to suggest that the world has vanished. And itÂ’s only, so it is thought (or so I personally think), because one knows that oneÂ’s observations arenÂ’t the one and only relevant yardstick that one knows that the world hasnÂ’t disappeared. 
BerkeleyÂ’s response to this is brilliant. He says that the real meaning of: 
[H12] 

(1) Â“The world doesnÂ’t go out of existence when Smith (who, for argumentÂ’s sake, weÂ’ll assume to be the only sentient being in existence) closes his eyes,Â” 
is perspicuously[297] 
represented by a sentence whose surface-structure bears no resemblance to (1)Â’s. That other sentence is one along the lines of: 
(2) Â“If Smith closes his eyes for x minutes and then reopens them, the things he sees are where one would expect them to be, given that they are subject to the usual forces.Â” 
BerkeleyÂ’s own illustration of this principle is particularly effective. The stars are moving, Berkeley points out. A more precise way of putting it, as Berkeley himself makes clear, is that we are moving relative to the stars, and the stars are therefore moving relative to us. But, as Berkeley points out, we donÂ’t see the stars move. The blips in the sky that we see on a given night arenÂ’t in the same relative positions as the blips in the sky that we see on other nights. 
For this reason, we do a kind of Â“regression analysisÂ” on the blips that we see over the years. We try to connect the blips seen on night 1 with those seen on night 2, and we try to connect the latter with those seen on night 3, and so on. So if N1...Nn are nights in question, and n is some high number (e.g., 
500), we identify curves such that, if it is assumed that those curves are the trajectories of those blips, it follows that those blips obey well-defined, relative simple laws. So the logical form of: 
(A) Â“The stars are moving even when nobody is looking at them,Â” 
is perspicuously given by the grammatically very different sentence: 
(B) Â“If it is assumed that, when weÂ’re not looking at them, the stars obey certain laws and therefore have certain trajectories, we can make observationally accurate predictions that we couldnÂ’t otherwise make, and arrive at observationally correct explanations that we couldnÂ’t otherwise arrive at.Â” 
Berkeley said, as clearly as it can be said, that what sentences really mean isnÂ’t what, given their overt forms, they seem to mean. So setting aside some petty and insubstantial objections relating to the exact meanings of Â“grammaticalÂ” and Â“logical,Â” Berkeley was, to my knowledge, the first person to recognize the distinction between grammatical and logical form. 
Part IV Determinism, Causality, and Probability 
Chapter 13 Determinism, Randomness, and Unpredictability 
1.0 Determinism and indeterminism 
Determinism is the view that how the world is at any given point in time fixes how it will be in every respect at all later times. So given how the world is now, there is only one way it could possibly be in a thousand (or a billion) years. And given how the world was a minute ago (or a billion years ago), the world has to be the way it is now: things couldnÂ’t possibly be any other way. 
Indeterminism is the doctrine that determinism is false. So it is the view that, for at least one moment in time, how the world is at that time does not completely fix how the world will be at all later times. 
Indeterminism is not the view that the world is chaotic or lawless. Indeterminism is actually an extremely moderate doctrine. All it says is that, at some point in time (it could be past, present, or future), some event occurs that doesnÂ’t have to occur. So, technically speaking, for indeterminism to be true, there needs to be only one Â“renegadeÂ” event. 
Determinism is thus much harder to establish than indeterminism. After all, the determinist says that, for any time t, how the world is at t determines how the world will be in every respect at all later times. Which is a very strong claim. Indeterminism, on the other hand, only says that there is at least one counterexample to what the determinist says. Which is not a very strong claim. 
Nonetheless, even though determinism is a strong statement for which it is difficult to produce definitive grounds, we know that it is true or at least a very close approximation to the truth. It is an open question whether, at the sub-atomic level, the world is strictly deterministic. But whatever indeterminacies there are at that level seldom, if ever, percolate up to the molecular, cellular, biological, planetary, or astronomical scales. So, for most intents and purposes the world in which we operateÂ—the world of Â“medium sizedÂ” objectsÂ—is deterministic. 
To be sure, the world often seems to be indeterministic. But careful scrutiny of any such situation, with the possible exception of those at the subÂ­atomic level, tends to show that it is governed by deterministic mechanisms. 
2.0 Determinism vs. predictability 
Predictability and determinism are not the same thing. If a system is completely indeterministic, then it is indeed unpredictable (or only fortuitously predictable), since prediction requires regularity and there is regularity only where there are deterministic laws. But a deterministic system may be unpredictable. In fact, even if the world is completely deterministicÂ— even if the state of the universe at any point completely fixes how everything will be, in every respect, at all later pointsÂ—there are limits to how much any creature could predict about the course of future events. It doesnÂ’t matter how intelligent that creature is or how sharp its senses are or how good its technology is. For reasons of logic, no creature is able to predict everything that happens. There are four reasons for this. 
















2.1 Why predictability . determinism: Reason #1[298] 

We learn about the external world through sense-perceptionÂ—that is, through vision, hearing, touch, etc. LetÂ’s focus on vision for the moment. Suppose that youÂ’re seeing some rock. (LetÂ’s refer to that rock as Â“R.Â”) HereÂ’s whatÂ’s involved in your seeing R. Some light beam bounced off R. (WeÂ’ll refer to that light beam as Â“L.Â”) As a result of that collision, LÂ’s structure changed in such a way that RÂ’s structure is now coded in its (LÂ’s) structure. For this reason, L bears information about R. L hits your eyes, disturbing them. Those disturbances reflect LÂ’s structure. Given that L reflects RÂ’s structure, it follows that these disturbances of your eyes reflect RÂ’s structure. Those ocular disturbances therefore encode information about 
R. The resulting neural impulses transmit this information to some part of you that decodes this information. The results of this decoding are embodied in a visual perception that succeeds in representing R. 
Light is energy. Things change when bombarded by energy. They donÂ’t always change very much. But there is always some change. It takes time for light, or any other information-bearing process, to travel. During that time-interval, the changes in R that were initiated by L led to other changes in R. Since, for the time being, L is your only source of information about R, and since L gives you dated and otherwise inaccurate information about R, the information encoded in the visual perception that L caused you to have is itself inaccurate. 
Before we take the next step, IÂ’d like to clarify this point. Let t be the time that you have the visual perception of R that L caused you to have. Obviously t will happen after the time L hits your eyes and t is later than the time that L collided with R. During the time between that collision, on the one hand, and t, on the other, R has changed. Why has it changed? Because the just-mentioned collision made it change. That collision, as we just pointed out, set off processes because of which R changed. 
What you know, at t, about R is confined to what L tells you. And what L tells you is dated informationÂ—itÂ’s yesterdayÂ’s news. What you know, by virtue of having the sense-perception in question, is now dead and gone. What it tells you is how R was a little while ago; it doesnÂ’t tell you how R is now. 
Supposing that R is some rock in your backyardÂ—and not some rock in the depths of outer spaceÂ—the time lag is minimal. And, no matter where R is, L did extremely little to change it. The changes that L induced in R, by colliding with it, fall well below the limits of sensory discrimination. 
But mentally replace R with something smallÂ—something so small that the photons involved in its being bombarded with light do appreciably change it. In that sort of case, the thing you see at t is very different from the thing that is now out there in the world. 
You might be aware of this gulf between the perception and the reality. But any attempt on your part to narrow this gulf will only make it wider. If you try to learn more about RÂ—by, for example, shining more light on itÂ— youÂ’ll make it more unlike the thing it was initially. And youÂ’ll only compound the problem if you try to undo those distortions with counter-distortions. Setting aside the problem just discussed, thereÂ’s no point in trying to reverse the effects that L had on R by shining more light on R, since you donÂ’t know how R was before you bombarded it with light. Therefore, you donÂ’t know how R has changed and, consequently, you donÂ’t know what the needed corrections are. 
What is true of your seeing R is true, to some degree or other, of anythingÂ’s having any sense-perception of anything. It doesnÂ’t matter whether the percipient beings in question are super-brilliant aliens or iguanas or God Himself. As a matter of logic, perceiving a thing involves your being on the receiving end of causal process (e.g. a light-beam) that collided with that object and, as a result, was so changed that its structure came to reflect that of the object. Of course, that collision changed didn't just change that causal process: it also changed the object. But you can't possibly know what those changes were, since they occurred after the relevant information-transmitting process left that thing. (LetÂ’s assume that process to be a light ray.) For the time being, that light ray is your one source of information about that thing. So whatever that light ray did to that objectÂ—whatever changes, if any, it madeÂ—you canÂ’t know what they are. If no changes occurred, you canÂ’t know it; and if changes did occur, you canÂ’t know that either, and a fortiori you canÂ’t know the exact nature of those changes. So what you see is different from what is out there, in the relevant place, at the time of your perception. And, as we saw a moment ago, attempts to remove this margin of error by having more perceptions will only make it bigger. 
We are not talking about the limitations of human beings. WeÂ’re taking about the conditions that must, as a matter of logic, be fulfilled by any sense-perception on the part of anyone or anything. If itÂ’s said that God could Â“just knowÂ” what is out thereÂ—that He didnÂ’t have to be on the receiving end of some causal process starting with external objectsÂ—I would reply by saying: Â“rubbish!Â” If thereÂ’s no causal process, then, by definition, thereÂ’s no information for God to go off of. And if thereÂ’s no such information, then any image God comes up with is a hallucination. It might be a correct one. But, if so, it will only be an accidentally correct one, and it wonÂ’t be enough for knowledge of anything, and any belief He has in consequence of having that image will be nothing more than a guess. A correct guess, perhaps. Some guesses are lucky guesses. But lucky guesses arenÂ’t knowledge. (See Chapter 10 for an explanation of this.) 
If itÂ’s said that the laws of logic donÂ’t apply to God, I would say: Â“Yes they do.Â” If, in response to that, itÂ’s said that God, being omnipotent, canÂ’t be hemmed in by anything, even the laws of logic, I would reply by saying that this statement embodies a total failure to understand the nature of logical truthÂ—that GodÂ’s inability to create a square circle is no more an abridgment of His powers than an athleteÂ’s Â“inabilityÂ” to score a touchdown in a soccer match shows a lack of athletic talent. The idea that God could know of some event without having any causal connection is in the same category as the idea that a sufficiently good athlete could score a touchdown in the course of a soccer match. ItÂ’s simply incoherent. 
But why exactly is it incoherent? Only justified true beliefs are knowledge. Lucky guesses donÂ’t count. A justified belief is one for which there is evidence. One spatiotemporal thing is evidence of another if and only if the first is causally related to the second in such a way that, given the existence of the first, that of the second can be inferred. Therefore, oneÂ’s own mental states are evidence of a given external thing, and therefore give one a justification for believing that thing to exist, only if those mental states are effects of that thing. So the idea that God could know of some spatiotemporal entity without being causally connected to that entity is no more coherent than the abject absurdity that one event could be evidence of another even though the occurrence of the first event provided no reason to suspect the occurrence of the second. Since the latter idea is obviously a non-starter, which deserves to be put in the same category as Â“squares donÂ’t have four sides,Â” the same is true of the former.[299] 
For similar reasons, one would simply be redefining the terms Â“Â‘justificationÂ” and Â“knowledgeÂ” were one to say that unjustified beliefs were knowledge or that beliefs for which one had known evidence were justified. Nothing that follows from definitional truths can be false; anything that follows from a truth of logic is itself a truth of logic. So it is a truth of logic, since it follows from truths of logic, that God couldnÂ’t have knowledge of some spatiotemporal entity without being causally connected to that entity. ItÂ’s also a tautology that causal connections are disruptive and that tautology entails that GodÂ’s mental representations of the world must, in at least some cases, be discrepant with the corresponding realities. 
To sum up: Learning about the world involves changing it. A consequence is that the world is different from how it is represented to you as being. So even if the world is 100% deterministic, there is necessarily a gulf between the perception and the reality. 
Conclusion: Given the existence of the aforementioned gulf, any predictions one makes are necessarily slightly off. A prediction involves two things: first, knowledge of initial conditions (how things are at the momentÂ— or, in any case, how they were just a moment ago); second, what the relevant causal laws are. Given knowledge of those causal laws, one can predict what must occur, given those initial conditions. But since oneÂ’s knowledge of initial conditions is necessarily off, though sometimes not by very much, oneÂ’s predictions will be off. 

2.2 Why predictability . determinism: Reason #2 
What we know affects how the world is. Why is this? Because what we know affects what we do, and what we do affects how the world is. 
We canÂ’t know what it is that weÂ’ll know. Suppose that, right now, you know exactly what it is that youÂ’ll know in 10 years. (Let K be that body of knowledge.) In that case, what youÂ’ll know in 10 years will be K plus all the knowledge you pick up between now and then. And if you build that knowledge, viz., the knowledge you pick up along the way, into your definition of K, then youÂ’ll already know it and you wonÂ’t pick it up along the way anymore, and the knowledge that you do pick up along the way will be something else. So it makes no sense to say that you could know now what it is that youÂ’ll know in 10 years.[300] 

At the end of this chapter, weÂ’ll discuss some other reasons why a perfectly deterministic world is necessarily not one in which, for any time t, any creature, no matter what intellectual or sensory virtue it had, could possibly predict everything that would happen after t. 

2.2 Why predictability . determinism: Reason #2 (revisited and developed) 
Given a complex object, one part of it can be aware of another part; but, at any given time, no one part can be aware of itself. For a person to be Â“selfÂ­awareÂ” is for one part of his mind to be aware of another part of some other part of his mind. During a reflective moment, there must be a part of your mind that is not an object of reflection. It may be that you can be aware of a part of your mind that, in its turn, is aware of some third part of your mind. It may be that instances of Â“second-orderÂ” self-consciousness are possible. It may even be that, for any number n, self-consciousness of order n is possible (logically, if not psychologically). But, at any given time, there must be some part of oneÂ’s mind that one is not aware of. If, at a given time, some person were aware of everything in his mind, then heÂ’d be aware of his awareness of everything in his mind, and also of his awareness of that awareness, and also his awareness of that awareness, and so on ad infinitum. Such a mind is not only a psychological, but also a logical, impossibility. 
The part of oneÂ’s mind that one is not aware of is no less a determinant of future events than any other part of oneÂ’s mind. This means that there is necessarily a part of oneÂ’s mind, and thus of some determinant of future events, of which it is impossible that one should be aware. An obvious corollary is that oneÂ’s inability to be perfectly self-aware limits oneÂ’s ability to predict the future. 
2.2.1 Why predictability . determinism: Reason #2 (continued) 
A necessary condition for complete knowledge of the future is complete knowledge of the present. But if one had perfect knowledge of the present, one couldnÂ’t make predictions; indeed, one couldnÂ’t do anything. It is inherent in the concept of intentional conduct that the agent be ignorant of both some aspects of the future and some aspects of himself. 
If I know that, at time t, forces over which I have no control will force me against my will to go to the store, then I cannot possibly decide that, at t, IÂ’ll make a trip to the store. If I know that if IÂ’m at home on Tuesday forces over which I have no control will force me against my will to go to the store, I can decide to go to the store on Monday, so as to spare myself the trauma of a compulsory store-trip on Tuesday. But if I know that, at a given time, forces over which I have no control will transport to me to the store then I cannot possibly choose to initiate a journey to the store that begins that very time. One cannot possibly choose to make an event occur (at a given time) if one knows that (at that time) that event will occur anyway. 
At the same time, one cannot choose to try to prevent an event whose occurrence one knows to be inevitable. One can try to prevent an event whose occurrence one believes to be almost inevitable. I can try to make a hole in one as long as I think there is some chance of my succeeding. But if I know that there is simply no chance of my making a hole in one, I cannot, as a matter of logic, even try to make one. 
Thus, one can make choices only to the extent that one doesnÂ’t know what will happen. This by itself doesnÂ’t show that we canÂ’t have complete knowledge of the future. For it could be maintained that, when one makes a choice, one eliminates the very doubts concerning the future that one had to have in order to make that choice. (IÂ’m in doubt as to whether IÂ’ll go to the store before, but not after, I choose to do so.) 
But this move is to no avail. There are two reasons for this: a trivial one and a non-trivial one. The trivial one is that, in making a given decision, one seldom, if ever, eliminates all of the uncertainties that made that choice possible. We donÂ’t typically know that weÂ’ll manage to carry out the decisions we make, and we have little knowledge as to how, whether successfully carried out or not, those decisions will affect the world. 
The non-trivial reason is that one cannot possibly know what choices one will make. This is a corollary of the fact that one cannot try to do what one knows to be inevitable or to prevent what one knows to be impossible. Â“But surely thatÂ’s false,Â” it will be said. Â“I can know that, at some point tomorrow, IÂ’ll choose to smoke a cigarette.Â” In describing oneself as knowing that one will choose to smoke a cigarette tomorrow, one is saying, in a distorted way, that one has already chosen to smoke a cigarette tomorrow. To choose whether or not to smoke a cigarette is to make up oneÂ’s mind one way or the other. Knowing that tomorrow one will definitely make up oneÂ’s mind to smoke a cigarette is the same as having already made up oneÂ’s mind to smoke a cigarette tomorrow. So, although one can predict that one will smoke a cigarette tomorrow, that is only because one has already chosen to do so; it isnÂ’t because one has foreknowledge of some choice not yet made. Choices are ipso facto incapable of being predicted (by those who make them) and so, therefore, are their effects (to those who make them). 

2.2.2 Why predictability . determinism: Reason #2 (continued) 
The word Â“predictÂ” is ambiguous. Sometimes it means have a belief about the future and sometimes it means state a belief about the future. The fact that creatures have beliefs about the future entails that a perfectly deterministic world is not completely predictable, and so does the fact that creatures sometimes state their beliefs about the future. But statements about the future impose even greater limits on what can be known about the future than do unstated beliefs about the future, and the limits imposed by such statements are, up to a point, qualitatively different from those imposed by unstated beliefs. 
Two stories will illustrate these points. 
First Story: X is a company that specializes in medical research. It employs a team of brilliant scientists who will make many important discoveries if, and only if, X stays in existence. Billionaire Smith knows that heÂ’ll live another 20 years or so if company X stays in existence and that heÂ’ll soon die if it doesnÂ’t. Smith also knows that, unless he manipulates the market in highly illegal ways, X will instantly collapse. Without telling anyone of any of this, Smith manipulates the market in the needed ways, knowing that, as a result, heÂ’ll live another 20 years and also that otherwise never-to-beÂ­discovered cures will be discovered. Smith cannot possibly know the exact nature of what heÂ’ll learn in those 20 years, and XÂ’s research-team cannot possibly know what it will come to know. 
Second story: Smith correctly believes that heÂ’ll live another 20 years if X stays in existence and that heÂ’ll soon die if it doesnÂ’t. Smith correctly believes that X will make a speedy economic recovery if, and only if, he publicly announces that it will do so. (Such an announcement, as Smith knows, will stimulate investment in X, thus keeping it afloat.) Knowing that heÂ’ll make the announcement, Smith knows that X will prosper and that, as a result, heÂ’ll live another 20 years. Smith cannot know what heÂ’ll come to know in the time that, by making the announcement, he will buy for himself, and XÂ’s research-team (once it finds out that it wonÂ’t perish) cannot know what it will come to know in the time that Smith has bought for it. 
In the first story, knowledge of future events led to unforeseeable events. In the second story, somebodyÂ’s stating that he had such knowledge led to such events. Statements about the future make the future unpredictable in one way. Beliefs about the future make it unpredictable in a different way. Since the word Â“predictionÂ” sometimes means Â“belief about the futureÂ” and sometimes means Â“statement about the future,Â” the thesis that the future is Â“unpredictableÂ” is ambiguous; and even though both disambiguations are true, theyÂ’re true for very different reasons. 


2.3 Why predictability . determinism: Reason #3 
In this section, we will set aside the fact that, because of interference effects, there are limits to the degree of precision with which we can know what happens at the sub-atomic level. We will assume, falsely and strictly for argumentÂ’s sake, that there is a way to eliminate the gap between: 
(i) How the world is, 
and: 
(ii) How the world is represented to us that is the inevitable result of the fact that knowledge is acquired by interacting with the world. 
We will see that, even if this assumption is granted, a strictly deterministic world is still one in which there are limits to what any being---no matter how intelligent, no matter how unencumbered by fatigue, lack of acumen, limitations of memory and life-span, etc.---can know about the future. More specifically, weÂ’ll see that, for reasons inherent in the very concept of instantaneousness---i.e., of what an instant in time is----it cannot be known exactly what is happening at any given instant in time. 
If weÂ’re right about this, it obviously follows that we cannot know exactly what is happening at the present instant. Given that any knowledge we have of the future is based on our knowledge of current conditions, it follows that, for reasons having nothing to do with interference effects, there are limits, even in a strictly deterministic universe, to what it is theoretically possible to know about the future. 
2.3.1 Why predictability . determinism: Reason #3 (continued) 
What does it mean to say that the carÂ’s speed at instant t is 60 mph? Speed = distance/time. An instant is an infinitely short stretch of time.[301] 
The time-interval encompassed by an instant is nil. So the car cannot therefore cover any distance during that interval. It follows, so it would seem, that it makes no sense at all to speak of the carÂ’s speed at an instant. 
To say that the carÂ’s speed at t is 60 mph is to say that the carÂ’s speed during arbitrarily short stretches of non-null, t-inclusive time-intervals approximates to 60 mph to an arbitrarily high degree. If the carÂ’s average speed during t-inclusive interval S1 is 62 mph, there is some shorter t-inclusive interval S2 such that the carÂ’s average speed during S2 differs from 60 mph by less than 2 mph. And if S3 is some t-inclusive time-interval during which the carÂ’s average speed is 60.0001 mph, there is some shorter t-inclusive interval S4 such that the carÂ’s average speed during S4 differs from 60 mph by less than 1/10,000 mph. And so on. 
All statements about what obtains during a given Â“instantÂ” are elliptical for statements about what obtains during non-null stretches of time. If OÂ’s mass 
is constantly increasing, to say that, at instant t, OÂ’s mass is M is to say that, given any non-null t-inclusive time-interval S1, if OÂ’s mass deviates from M by a given amount, there is a shorter t-inclusive interval S2 such that OÂ’s mass deviates from M by less than that amount. 
Measuring an objectÂ’s speed involves seeing how much distance it covers during some interval of time. There is no other way---or, more precisely, no other direct wayÂ—of determining a given objectÂ’s speed. Given some object O whose speed at time t one wishes to ascertain, one cannot directly ascertain OÂ’s speed at t. (One can indirectly ascertain it, as weÂ’ll see shortly.) What one can directly ascertain is OÂ’s average speed during some t-inclusive interval. The smaller the interval, the better an approximation to OÂ’s speed at 
t. But---and this cannot be stressed enough---it is only by considering OÂ’s speed during (t-inclusive) stretches of time that one can determine OÂ’s speed. 

2.3.2 Why predictability . determinism: Reason #3 (continued) 
That said, there may be reason to believe that OÂ’s average speed during increasingly small t-inclusive intervals approximates without limit to 60 mph. (Put more precisely: there may be reasons to believe that, given any number x, no matter how small, there is some number y such that, if one considers a t-inclusive time-interval of length y, the difference between 60 mph and OÂ’s velocity at t is less than x.) Supposing for argumentÂ’s sake that one establishes that the smaller the t-inclusive interval that one considers the closer to zero is the difference between OÂ’s speed during that interval and 60 mph, then one has thereby established that OÂ’s speed at t is 60 mph. Indeed, the italicized claim is the meaning of Â“OÂ’s speed at t is 60 mph.Â” (See Section 2.5.1.) ItÂ’s not that, because of our scientific limitations, establishing the truth of the italicized claim is the best we can do in the way of establishing that OÂ’s speed at t is 60 mph. ItÂ’s that, for reasons inherent in the concept of what an instant is the two claims are identical, the former being but an abbreviation for the latter. 
Since any direct (non-inferential) measurement of an objectÂ’s velocity will be of an objectÂ’s velocity during some stretch of time, any judgments one makes as to that objectÂ’s speed during some instant will involve, as weÂ’ll now see, a heavy element of inference. Suppose that, during non-null, t-inclusive interval INT1. Bearing this supposition in mind, consider the following two 
statements: 
(i) OÂ’s average velocity is 60 mph. 
(ii) if INT1, INT2Â….are t-inclusive intervals such that, for any n, INTn is bigger than INTn+1, OÂ’s average velocity during INTn+1 is closer to 60 mph than it is during INTn. 
One is justified in accepting (i) if, and only if, one is justified in accepting (ii). 
But how could (ii) possibly be established? Not directly, obviously. Given any time-interval, one can measure OÂ’s average velocity during that interval but once. Speed isnÂ’t like length. One can measure an objectÂ’s length over and over again, since length is a property of enduring objects. But one canÂ’t do this with speed, since speed is a property of non-recurring events. So if one judges that OÂ’s speed at instant t is 60 mph, that is based partly on the fact that during the t-inclusive interval during which one measured OÂ’s average speed, that (average) speed was close to 60mph. 
Assuming that judgment to be made on good grounds, there is another, rather troublesome dimension to it. For, in making that judgment, one assumes that: 
(DI)[302] 
had one done the equivalent of performing the doubly impossible task of considering an infinitely long series of t-inclusive intervals, each smaller than its predecessor, one would have found that the limit of the series to be 60 mph. 
Why, incidentally, would the task mentioned in DI be Â“doubly impossibleÂ”? Because: 
(a) since an event only occurs once, one can measure an objectÂ’s speed no more than once, 
and: 
(b) for a variety of reasons, itÂ’s impossible to make infinitely many measurements. 

2.3.3 Why predictability . determinism: Reason #3---taking stock before closing the argument 
Before closing the argument, let us take stock. 
(i) 
one can directly ascertain average speeds, but one cannot directly ascertain instantaneous speeds. 

(ii) 
Fact (i) has nothing to do with our limitations as scientists; it has to do with the very meaning of statements of the form Â‘such and such was the case at instant t.Â’ (Why this is so will be clarified and defended in the next section.) 


(iii) For any time t and any object O, one cannot really know what OÂ’s speed at t is; one can, at most, make reasonable but highly theoretical, and therefore inherently tentative, inferences as to what OÂ’s speed at t is. 
(iv) The inferences mentioned in (iii) themselves involve assumptions as to the instantaneous speeds of objects and, unless those assumptions are constituents of a theory for which there is considerable independent evidence, are viciously circular. 

2.3.4 Why predictability . determinism: Reason #3---Closing the argument 
It is inherently impossible to know with what speed an object is traveling at a given instant. (Â“But doesnÂ’t the speedometer on my car indicate how fast my car is traveling at a given instant?Â” The speedometer on your car does (consistently, non-accidentally) tell you how fast your car is traveling at arbitrary instant t if various theories turn out to be right; e.g., theories correlating the carÂ’s speed at a given instance with the rate at which the engine turns over. Each of those theories is based on many a belief to the effect that, for some object x, velocity, and instant t, x is moving at v at instant t. Those beliefs donÂ’t register data; they embody judgments that are no less theory-dependent and no more secure than your judgment that OÂ’s velocity at t would coincide with its average velocity during the t-inclusive interval that you considered. 
In conclusion, setting aside anything having to do with interference effects and also with human intellectual and technological fallibility, it is impossible, for reasons inherent in the concept of instantaneousness, to know the state of the universe at any given instant. This means that we cannot have maximally precise knowledge of the present. And, given that we know both the past and the future on the basis of inter alia the present, this in its turn means that we cannot have maximally precise knowledge of the past or the future. 
What we just said about an objectÂ’s velocity at a given instant is true of its mass, length, color, and all of its other explanatorily significant properties. We cannot have direct knowledge of an objectÂ’s mass at an instant; at most, we can make reasonable inferences as to its mass at a given instance on the basis of our knowledge of its average mass during some interval that includes that instant. To be sure, there is an important difference between speed, on the one hand, and mass and length (etc.), on the other. Speed is a property of non-repeatable events involving objects. Mass and length (etc.) are properties of objects per se. But this makes no difference in the present context. Given some general truths concerning the nature of measurement, which weÂ’re about to state, along with the points already made, it will be clear why this is so. 
3.0 Determinism vs. randomness 
Â“RandomÂ” doesnÂ’t mean the same thing as Â“undetermined.Â” A deterministic world isnÂ’t necessarily one in which nothing random happens; and, give or take a few niceties, an indeterministic world isnÂ’t necessarily one in which anything random does happen. A story will make it clear why these points hold. 
Smith arrogantly insulted a high-ranking member of a particularly lethal criminal organization, and that person has thus sworn to kill him. For unrelated reasons, SmithÂ’s wife also wants him dead, and she has just hired a hit man to kill him. She has always wanted him dead; she just married him for his money. Plus, Smith has a serious heart condition, and his doctor is surprised that he didnÂ’t die years ago. You are a friend of SmithÂ’s, and you know all of this. But you donÂ’t know anything else that is relevant to an estimate of how much longer he is likely to live. Given that information, the right estimate is, of course, Â“not long.Â” 
But Smith beats the odds. Nobody kills him and nothing goes wrong with his heart. But one day, as heÂ’s making a sales pitch to some prospective clients, a ceiling-lamp comes loose and falls on his head, killing him. 
This was a Â“randomÂ” occurrence. But it wasnÂ’t uncaused. When a ceiling lamp falls, thereÂ’s a reason for it (e.g., the bolt wasnÂ’t screwed in tightly enough or the weight of the lamp was too much for the beam it was hanging from). It was Â“randomÂ” because, although caused, it wasnÂ’t the sort of thing that, given the information at your disposal, could reasonably be expected to do him in. Thus, it was Â“randomÂ” not because it was uncaused, but because it was independently caused, meaning that the causal sequence that led to his death was independent of the causal sequences that were under way that were reasonably believed, given the information available to you, to eventuate in his demise. So, in this context, Â“randomÂ” doesnÂ’t mean Â“uncaused,Â” it means Â“uncaused by anything that we had reason to believe would occur.Â” 
This is what Â“randomÂ” typically means. It may be that microphysicists deal with uncaused events. But the rest of us deal exclusively with things that are quite definitely caused. (As previously stated, the indeterminacies at the micro-level donÂ’t percolate up to the macrolevel, at least not enough to engage the structures that change human lives.) So the Â“randomÂ” things we deal with are things that have unforeseeable causes. 
A consequence is that randomness isnÂ’t a property of events; itÂ’s a relation that an event bears to a body of knowledge. Relative to what you know, it is unforeseeable, and therefore random, that a ceiling lamp will kill Smith. But relative to what Howard the building inspector knows, that same event is not random. (Howard knows that the plank in question will go at any time, and he sees Smith standing underneath it.) 
Thus, randomness isnÂ’t a property of events. ItÂ’s a property of statements Â—or, more accurately, of relations between statements. An event is random, relative to a certain body of information, if its occurrence couldnÂ’t reasonably be predicted on the basis of that information. So randomness is really a relation that holds between the statements describing some body of data and the statement describing some event; that relation holds if the former statements donÂ’t warrant acceptance of the latter. 
ItÂ’s obvious that there can be random events in a deterministic world. SmithÂ’s death was an inevitable consequence of pre-existing circumstances. But, relative to the information that you had, it was also quite random. 

3.1 Determinism vs. randomness (continued) 
Supposing that the world is indeterministic, would there for that reason be Â“randomÂ” events in it? The answer is Â“yes.Â” But the reasons are not what one would think; and the amount of randomness in such a world is not necessarily as great as one would expect it to be. 
For argumentÂ’s sake, suppose we know that, given the current state of the universe, itÂ’s causally completely undetermined whether, in five seconds, object O will move to the right or to the left. Each possible outcome is as likely as the other (theyÂ’re Â“equiprobableÂ”).ThereÂ’s no way, of course, to predict which way it will go. We could make that prediction only to the extent that we had reason to think one of the outcomes the more likely oneÂ— which we obviously donÂ’t. But when, at the moment of truth, it goes to the left, was that Â“randomÂ”? We couldnÂ’t predict it; but it isnÂ’t exactly random. On the contrary, itÂ’s consistent with our expectations of it. 
To see why, letÂ’s modify our earlier story about Smith. This time, he isnÂ’t killed by a ceiling lamp. The vindictive criminal kills him. Before Smith died, you knew that, in all likelihood, he would be killed either by that criminal or by his wife or by his heart-conditionÂ—but you didnÂ’t know which, since, given what you knew, they were all equiprobable. When the criminal gets him, that surely isnÂ’t random. Quite the opposite. Even though it could not itself be predicted with certainty to happen, it belonged to a class of events which, given the available evidence, was known to contain all and only the things that would kill him. 
The same is true of O. It is known that, in 5 seconds, O will either to go the left or to the right. So even though its going to the left as opposed to the right could not be predicted, its going to the left wasn't exactly random. So indeterminism doesnÂ’t entail randomness. 
But here we must make a subtle distinction. Relative to the knowledge that itÂ’s undetermined whether O goes to the left as opposed to the right (or vice versa), its going to the left is random. So OÂ’s going to the left is both random (relative to one body of knowledge) and non-random (relative to another). 
4.0 Why determinism, if true, is capable of being verified 
On hearing me say that the world is at least approximately deterministic, students of mine often respond by saying either that determinism is unverifiable or that itÂ’s simply false. Depending how itÂ’s meant, this statement is either false or vacant. With some trivial exceptions, any universal statement (i.e., any statement of the form Â“all xÂ’s are yÂ’sÂ”; e.g., Â“all birds have feathersÂ”) is incapable of being definitively verified. (The trivial exceptions concern cases where the generalization concerns only some very circumscribed class of objects; e.g., Â“all pencils on my desk are yellow,Â” or where some statement that, in terms of its content, is not a universal generalization but is turned into one through syntax-chopping; e.g., Â“all objects are such that, if they are identical with George W. Bush, they are mammals.Â”) Since determinism is given by the statement Â“all events have complete causes,Â” it is unverifiable, like Â“all metal expands when heated.Â” On this basis, it is concluded that determinism couldnÂ’t possibly be known to be true, and shouldnÂ’t be affirmed, even tentatively. 
But is it so clear that Â“all metal expands when heatedÂ” is unverifiable? So far as that is true, itÂ’s only in the trivial sense in which nothing other than analytic truths can be definitively verified. To be sure, Â“all metal expands when heatedÂ” couldnÂ’t possibly be verified on strictly observation grounds. After all, that statement concerns all metal, not just the metal you see. So no universal generalization, with the irrelevant exceptions noted a moment ago, can be verified on purely observational grounds; some element of inference is involved. Anything that can be observed to occur is, for that very reason, not general. And that is why, despite its syntactic similarity to Â“all metal expands when heated,Â” Â“all pencils on my desk are yellowÂ” is not substantively (as opposed to just syntactically) a universal generalization: one can observe that it is true. You can observe this or that metal bar expanding; but you canÂ’t observe the Â“general fact,Â” if there even is such a thing, that heated metal always expands. 
Also, if by Â“verificationÂ” you mean Â“observation-based verification,Â” then Â“all metal expands when heatedÂ” and Â“every event has a causeÂ” are incapable of verification, but only because Â“verificationÂ” has been so defined as to render that statement an empty truism. 
In any case, if one allows at least some inference-rules to be permissible sources of verification, then Â“all metal expandsÂ” is verifiable, depending on what those rules are. And if those rules are anything like those that laypersons and scientists permits themselves, then Â“all metal expands when heatedÂ” is verifiable. So it is only in some trivial sense that Â“all metal expands when heatedÂ” is unverifiable. 

4.1 Why determinism, if true, is capable of being verified (continued) 
Some say that Â“all metal expands when heatedÂ” is unverifiable in the sense that, no matter how many metal objects youÂ’ve seen expand when heated, the next one Â“couldÂ” fail to expand. But what does Â“couldÂ” mean in this context? There is a sense in which I Â“couldÂ” win the lottery, or even sprout wings, even though the latter and probably also the former are prohibited by natural law. (In fact, the former is definitely prohibited by natural law since, given who I am, it isnÂ’t psychologically possible for me to buy lottery tickets. I find the very concept of a lottery appalling.) To say that I Â“couldÂ” sprout wings is not to say that itÂ’s permitted by natural law, let alone that itÂ’s possible in some more robust sense. It is only to say that, given what I know, it isnÂ’t ruled out. But I would contend that I do know that I wonÂ’t sprout wings and, therefore, that what I know does rule it out. And you too, outside of a philosophy class, would say that you know that you wonÂ’t sprout wings. 
David Hume famously argued that inductive inference isnÂ’t rational. His argument is not easy to refute. (That said, we saw in Chapter 8 how to refute it.) But nobody accepts HumeÂ’s conclusion; and while itÂ’s one thing to say that we donÂ’t know how to justify a belief, itÂ’s quite another to say that it has no justification. Surely my belief that I wonÂ’t sprout wings in the next five minutes is not in the same category as a personÂ’s belief that tomorrow it will start raining gumdrops. And itÂ’s a veritable truism that the difference is that the former is justified, whereas the latter is not. 

4.2 An oft-heard argument as to why determinism, even if true, is incapable of being verified 
Here is an argument that several students, independently of one another, have presented to me, and that is also found in the work of C.S. Peirce (1839Â–1914): 
Let cell X be a Â“perfectÂ” clone of cell Y, and suppose that X and Y are kept under exactly similar conditions. (So, although they are kept in different Petri dishes, they are subjected to precisely the same forces.) X and Y will behave differently from each other. Therefore, the same initial conditions fail to lead to the same non-initial conditions. According to determinism, this isnÂ’t possible. (If two qualitatively identical circumstances are succeeded by qualitatively different circumstances, then neither circumstance completely determined what it would be succeeded by.) From this it follows that determinism is false. 
Given only that two cells are biologically exactly alike, it doesnÂ’t follow that theyÂ’re exactly alike in all other respects. It doesnÂ’t follow, in particular, that they are exactly alike at the atomic and sub-atomic levels. And the chances of their being thus alike are basically zero. There is no real chance that the micro-particles composing one organism will be moving in precisely the same way as the micro-particles composing any other organism. These sub-biological facts can and will have dramatic effects on what happens at the biological level. All this argument establishes, then, is the irrelevant point that different initial conditions may lead to different non-initial conditions. 

4.3 Another oft-heard argument as to why determinism, even if true, is incapable of being verified 
Many students of mine have put forth the following argument: 
Determinism says: Â“same initial conditions, same non-initial conditions.Â” But the conditions obtaining at any given time are different in at least some respects from those obtaining at any other time. For, between any two points in time, there has surely been at least one change; some particle has moved or rotated or vibrated.[303] 
So there is no way to verify determinism. 
Causal connections are discovered by seeing how differences in initial conditions correlate with differences in non-initial conditions. You allow initial conditions to change in one respect, but do your best to ensure that theyÂ’re unchanged in every other respect. This will guarantee that these other factors will at least tend to remain constant, even though, inevitably, theyÂ’ll never be perfectly replicated. If changes in that one factor reliably correlate with changes in the outcome, thereÂ’s probably a causal connection; and thereÂ’s probably no such connection if thereÂ’s no such correlation. 
You may not be able to establish a perfect correlation between your pushing the button and the elevatorÂ’s coming. But that doesnÂ’t mean that you canÂ’t have good reasons for positing the existence of a strictly deterministic connection between the first and the second. For there to be such a connection is not for the elevator to come without fail every time the button is pushed. It is for the likelihood that the elevator will come, given that the button was pushed, to approach 100% to the extent that other factors are held constant; that is, it is for there to be no limit to how close to 100% that likelihood can be made to be so by rooting out other factors that arenÂ’t constant. 
Your experience can easily give you good evidence that this condition is satisfied. If you find that itÂ’s always possible to make it more likely than before that the elevator will come, given that the button was pushedÂ—if, in other words, you find that, given enough tinkering about with the relevant circuitry and cables and so on, itÂ’s always possible to tighten this correlation Â—you ipso facto have evidence that the condition in question is satisfied and, therefore, that a strictly deterministic connection is at work. 
This doesnÂ’t show they can be definitively established. But it does show that, insofar as theyÂ’re incapable of being definitively established, itÂ’s only for the reason that nothing known through sense-perception can be definitively established. Your sense-perceptions make it probable that you have a television, but they donÂ’t make it certain. They make it probable that youÂ’re not a disembodied spirit, but they donÂ’t make it certain. They donÂ’t make anything about the external world certain. A fortiori they donÂ’t make the existence of any causal connections certain. But such connections are no less capable of being definitively established than anything else about the external world. Whatever shortcomings induction may have as a form of inference, theyÂ’re no more of a problem for attempts to establish causal connections than they are for attempts to establish that you have hands. 
We canÂ’t have perfect evidence of a perfect correlation.[304] 
But that doesnÂ’t mean we can only have evidence for imperfect correlations. ItÂ’s possible to have imperfect evidence for perfect correlations. IÂ’ve examined a million mammals, and they all had backbones. Here we have evidence of a perfect correlation. ItÂ’s imperfect evidence, but thatÂ’s the only kind thatÂ’s available. More precisely, itÂ’s imperfect evidence if by Â“perfect evidenceÂ” we mean definitive observational evidenceÂ—as opposed to observational evidence plus reasonable inference-rules. But if this is what we mean by Â“perfectÂ” evidence, then itÂ’s a sterile triviality that we canÂ’t have perfect evidence for the existence of transperceptual correlations. (By Â“transperceptual,Â” I mean Â“happening on the other side of the veil of perceptionÂ—out there in the world, as opposed to in our minds.Â”) 
We have similarly Â“imperfectÂ” evidence for deterministic laws. And such laws are no more incapable of being definitively established, and no less capable of being established with reasonable certainty, than biological concomitances of the kind just described. 
5.0 Some general, but often overlooked, principles concerning determinism 
A deterministic system may consist of parts that behave indeterministically. This is a consequence of a more general principle, to wit: the laws governing the parts don't necessarily govern the whole. (In Chapter 19, we'll see that attempts to reduce psychology to physiology involve a failure to grasp this principle.) 
A story may help make this clear. General Smith is in charge of Battalion 
A. The members of A are extremely disciplined, and none of them would dream of disobeying the command of a superior officer. SmithÂ’s commands determine how A as a whole will behave. But those commands donÂ’t micromanage every detail about every soldierÂ’s behavior. They donÂ’t determine the order in which Private Jones puts on his boots or exactly how the muscles in Private BrownÂ’s mouth move when heÂ’s eating. The forces that determinize (i.e., render deterministic) the behavior of A as a whole donÂ’t determinize the behavior of AÂ’s constituents. 
It may be that other forces determine the behavior of AÂ’s constituents. But, even if this is true, weÂ’re seeing some facts of profound importance. A system cannot just be deterministic; it must be deterministic in this or that respect. It makes no sense to say, without qualification, that a system is just deterministic---unless by that it is meant that itÂ’s deterministic in every respect. 
Also, weÂ’re seeing that the forces in terms of which the behavior of a system is to be understood donÂ’t necessarily coincide with those in terms of which the behavior of its parts are to be understood. So supposing for argumentÂ’s sake that our thoughts are brain-states (or changes therein) and, consequently, that they consist of microparticles, it doesnÂ’t follow that psychology is a branch of microphysics; it doesnÂ’t follow, in other words, that the principles in terms of which a personÂ’s thoughts and feelings (and so on) are to be understood coincide with those in terms of which the microparticles composing them are to be understood. 
In objection to this last point, it may well be said that: 
(MP)[305] 
YouÂ’re overlooking an important fact. The reason that Battalion AÂ’s behavior is determined by what General Smith says is that each individual soldier in A knows that his career would be over if he were to disobey the command of a superior officer. Were it not for Private BrownÂ’s knowledge that heÂ’d be court-marshaled if he decided to flout a C.O.Â’s orders, Brown wouldnÂ’t currently be hiking through a mosquito-infested jungle wearing a 70 pound pack. So, at the end of the day, itÂ’s the micro-mechanisms that do all the work. 
True. It is the microstructures that do all the work. ItÂ’s always the microstructures that implement the Â“higher-levelÂ” forces. For this reason, people advocate MP; in other words, they conclude that these higher-level forces donÂ’t really exist and also that everything that happens is to be explained and understood in terms of micro-(re)distributions of mass-energy. But theyÂ’re wrong. An extension of our story will make this clear 
Battalion A is but one of the many battalions that General Smith commands. Smith also commands Battalion B. A and B have the same structure: for each Captain in A, there is a Captain in B, and vice versa; and given any Captain in A, if that Captain is a fighter-pilot, so is his counterpart in B. A and B are perfect isomorphs of each other. 
But at the sub-structural level, A and B are very different. The members of A tend to be intellectual. Some of them are athletic, but their preferred sport is badminton. The members of B are anti-intellectual brutes; their favorite past-times are getting drunk and throwing sandbags at each other. But because of the way in which the members of each battalion are interrelated, these differences have no effect on how either Battalion acts as a whole. The principles in terms of which those Battalions behave, when taken as wholes, is to be understood in terms of principles that wonÂ’t be apparent, at least not for what they are, at the level of this or that particular soldierÂ’s personality or conduct. 
But surely if you knew exactly what each soldier in A was doing, and you knew exactly what his counterpart in B was doing, you could, in theory, deduce how A and B were behaving. And, by obvious extensions of this reasoning, you could easily explain the fact that A and B are, as wholes, qualitatively identical in terms of lower-level forces; i.e., in terms of the forces that govern the parts of A and B (and, ultimately, the parts of the parts [of the parts of the partsÂ…] of the parts of A and B). 
I agree. But these correct points leave out some truths that, given the context, shouldnÂ’t have been left out. Given a knowledge of how (say) A behaves as a whole, one can post hoc see that AÂ’s behavior was strictly determined by the behavior of its parts. (IÂ’m supposing for argumentÂ’s sake that acquiring the relevant information about AÂ’s parts wonÂ’t be a problem.) That micro-information would have been explanatory of AÂ’s behavior as a whole only to the extent that given similarly structured entities, whose parts may be very unlike AÂ’s parts, it also explains their behavior under circumstances similar to those in which A was operating. 
5.1. An illustration of this principle 
A story may clarify my meaning. There is some time t such that you know exactly what each member of A is thinking and doing at t and such that you know exactly what each member of B is thinking and doing at t. (How you know this isnÂ’t part of the story, since itÂ’s irrelevant to what weÂ’re talking about.) On this basis, you figure out what each of A and B, taken as a whole, is doing. So, at t, A and B are behaving in exactly the same way---despite the fact that, at t, there isnÂ’t a single soldier in either battalion who is acting just like his counterpart in the other battalion. Any battalion whose members are interrelated in the way in which, at t, AÂ’s members were interrelated will, under qualitatively identical circumstances, behave exactly as A behaved (and, therefore, exactly as B did). So supposing that A has organizational properties P1Â…Pn, anything else that has those properties will react to any 
given situation in exactly the way that A would, even if that other thingÂ’s parts are very different from AÂ’s parts. 
So, when asked Â“why did A do such and such at t?Â” the right answer is not: Â“because Private Green was doing such and such, and Major Max was doing thus and suchÂ…Â” That answer would leave out the information about AÂ’s structure that guaranteed that anything having that structure would have acted in the same way had it been in the same circumstances. That answer would have provided irrelevant information about the specific way in which that structure was implemented on this particular occasion. 
Micro-knowledge is knowledge of how the forces governing macro-structures are implemented. But it isnÂ’t knowledge of those forces themselves. To be sure, everything that happens at the macro-level is fixed by what happens at the micro-level: it is impossible, even in principle, for there to be two worlds that are micro-identical but macro-distinct. But it doesnÂ’t follow that the macro-world is not to be understood on its own terms; it doesn't follow, in other words, that the macro-world obeys laws that, although implemented by events governed by micro-laws, are altogether distinct from those laws. Thus, it doesn't follow that the truths provided by disciplines other than microphysics are merely low-grade microphysical truths. In Chapter 19, we'll find that the general principles about the structure of the world of which such a science apprises us are categorically incapable of being interpreted as (low-resolution) microphysical truths. At the same time, we will find that specific truths belonging to higher-level physical sciences (e.g., botany, astronomy) are capable of being interpreted as low-resolution microphysical truths. But, finally, we'll also find that psychological truths, whether general or specific, are categorically incapable of being interpreted as truths of microphysics or indeed of any science. At the same time, we'll see (in Chapter 22) that psychological truths are almost certainly identical with the (re)distributions of mass-energy that fall within the scope of microphysics. It will be made clear in Chapter 21 how all of these facts can be reconciled with one another. 

5.2 Ramsey's conception of physical law: an illustration of the vicious circularity inherent in hyper-empiricism 
A number of authors (e.g., Wittgenstein, Ayer, Ramsey, Davidson, 
Carnap) have said, in characterizing the world as Â“deterministic,Â” one isnÂ’t 
directly saying anything about that world. Rather, what one is saying is along 
the lines of: 
(AR)[306] 
Let T1Â….Tn 
be a list of truths that jointly describe everything that happens throughout the course of time. Let T be this giant list of truths. There will be ways of organizing T that enable you to compress it. There will be general propositions---propositions having such forms as: 
(*) anything that has phi also has psi, 
and: 
(**) if thereÂ’s an occurrence in a given space-region of an event having phi, there will be an occurrence in a neighboring region of an occurrence having psi, 
and the like. 
Your objective, let us suppose, is to compress T as much as possible. In other words, youÂ’re trying identify some truth T* such that: 
(i) 
T* is much shorter than T, the reason being that there many things that T explicitly says that T* does not say explicitly, 

but such that: 

(ii) 
T* contains all the information contained in T, the reason being that, for any truth that T but not T* states explicitly, T* states it implicitly----in other words, that truth can be deduced from the truths in T*. 


Some of the truths on T* will concern specific matters of fact---they will describe how, for at least one time t, mass-energy is distributed at t. (Given the points earlier made about instants, what this really means is that, for at least one time-period t, T will say how mass-energy is (re)distributed during t.) But it will provide as few truths as possible. The remaining members of T* be will general propositions that, given the remaining truths on T*, enable you to deduce all the truths that are not on T* but are on T. 
LetÂ’s suppose that T* is the most compact list of its kind. In other words, itÂ’s the shortest list of truths on the basis of which everything that is on T can be deduced. The general propositions on T* are what we call Â“the laws of nature.Â” 
Thus, the laws of nature are just abbreviatory devices. They spare us the trouble of having to know various individual facts; we need only know a few individual facts, along with a few general principles; and we can figure out anything else that we need to know as the occasion arises. 
There may be distinct, equally compact ways of compressing T; and given two such shortenings of T, they may not contain the same general propositions. That doesnÂ’t mean that one of them is wrong. It shows that the laws of nature arenÂ’t Â“out there,Â” in the world, and are rather Â“in here,Â” in our methods of describing the world.[307] 

HereÂ’s a Mickey Mouse example of the principle at work here. Let L be a list that says of each individual person how many cars he or she has. Now imagine adding another list to L that gives that same information, but does so indirectly: instead of saying Â“Bob has five cars,Â” this second list says Â“Bob has 3 
+ 2Â” cars. Now imagine a third list that gives that same information but in some third way. This third list says Â“Bob has the square root of 25 cars.Â” And letÂ’s suppose that we take 20 more lists such that: 
(a) 
no two of them are identical with each other or with any of the lists just mentioned, 

(b) each says how many cars any given person has, but 

(c) 
each does so by providing an expression that can be proven, on the basis of arithmetic, to refer to the relevant integer. 


Really, L provides no less information than this super-list. If you know that Bob has 2 cars, you donÂ’t need to know that, for some number n, Bob has n cars and n5 = 32. But, given this super-list, in order to see that it gives you the same information as L, you need knowledge of arithmetic. So the laws of arithmetic serve an abbreviatory function. Laws of nature are to be understood in much the same way. They are to be seen as abbreviatory devices, not as forces or structures that regulate the course of events. 
5.2.1. The spuriousness of AR and the uselessness of the Ramsey-sentence 
References to the laws of nature, if only implicit ones, are an ineliminable part of any description of any event. This is because, contrary to what AR assumes, space and time arenÂ’t vessels that happen not to be empty but could be.
