The concept occupancyÂ—as in occupying a certain space---is a causal concept. Smith wants to sit in chair x. By virtue of that Jones is already sitting in x, what must happen in order for Smith to sit in x will be very different from what ceteris paribus would otherwise have to happen. Even if Smith just walks over to x and sits down in it, JonesÂ’ body will serve as a buffer between him and x itself. It makes no sense to say that, while Jones is sitting in x, his presence there has consequences as regards what must ensue if, in the next two seconds, Smith is to be sitting in x. It makes no sense to say that, even though Jones is sitting in x, light is passing through the region he is occupying in exactly the way it would pass through that region were it unoccupied. And so on. 
Spatiotemporal relations are causal relations. (See Chapter 12 for a lengthy discussion of this.) It would make no sense to say that JohnÂ’s flipping the switch caused the light to turn on, but that the very instance of that lightÂ’s turning preceded that very instance of JohnÂ’s flipping that switch. If the latter caused the former, it ipso facto preceded it. According to Relativity Theory, if a light-beam, sent by event x at the time of its occurrence, reaches y, just as itÂ’s beginning to occur, then relative to any possible frame of reference, x precedes y in time. If a light-beam sent by x doesnÂ’t reach y, and a light-beam sent by y doesnÂ’t reach x, then x and y are simultaneous with each other relative to some frames of references and, relative to others, x precedes y, and relative to others, y precedes x. But, according to Relativity Theory, the causal order doesnÂ’t merely reflect the spatiotemporal order; it is the spatiotemporal order. 
A cause is a law at work. Setting aside exceedingly low-resolution descriptions of events, there is no description of an event that is nomically antiseptic. AR assumes that descriptions of the world can be neatly segregated into two groups, ones consisting of propositions that express laws, the other consisting of propositions none of which makes any assumptions as to what laws obtain, if any. But thatÂ’s not true. Once you set the facts, you ipso facto set the laws. The reason lies in the following two facts, taken jointly: 
(1) 
You canÂ’t say whether (relative to a given framework) A preceded, followed, or was simultaneous with B until you establish either that the one event is part of a causal series beginning with the other, in which case the latter was the first to occur, or that there is no such series, in which case theyÂ’re simultaneous. 

(2) 
Wherever thereÂ’s causation, thereÂ’s law. If e1 caused e2, then there is some law L, and some properties phi and psi such that e1 has phi, such that e2 has psi, and such that L is given by a proposition to the effect that anything having phi (occurring 


in a given region) precedes something having psi (occurring in some region related, in some specified way, to the first region). 
To sum up: AR naively assumes that there are anomic facts. (Â“NomicÂ” means Â“having to do with natural law. Â“Â“AnomicÂ” means Â“free from the influence of natural law and therefore capable of being understood independently of anything having to do with natural law.Â”) In fact, in describing something as Â“pinewoodÂ” or as Â“copper,Â” weÂ’re assuming that certain laws hold with respect to it. If it doesnÂ’t conduct electricity, is it copper? If it looks just like solid oak, but you can walk right through it, is it really solid oak? 
The terms that we use to pick out the objects that participate in the events and facts described by T are nomic terms. In describing something as copper, or water, or human, you are, in so doing, ascribing to it certain causal properties.[308] 
(You may not know what those causal properties are. There are certain properties P1Â…Pn such that, if I say that x is a puddle of mercury, 
the chemist to whom I am speaking will automatically know that, if my 
statement is correct, x has P1Â…Pn, so that, in effect, I was in some sense ascribing those properties to x. A derivative sense? Yes. An unimportant one? No.) Since AR assumes not just that some events can be understood in thoroughly anomic terms, but that all of them can be so understood, AR isnÂ’t 
even remotely close to the truth. 
6.0 The concept of measurement in relation to the concept of an instant 
Like the expression, Â“the average person," the word Â“instantÂ” refers to nothing, its function being to make it possible to abbreviate what would otherwise be long and cumbersome statements. There is no human being x such that the sentence: 
(AP)[309] 
Â“the average man owns 2.2 cars,Â” 
which says of x that he owns 2.2 cars. AP is an abbreviation of: 
(AP*) If x is the total number of cars that some person or other owns, and y is the total number of people, then x/y=2.2. 
Neither Â“the average personÂ” nor any synonym thereof occurs in AP*. Indeed, there is no isolable part of AP* that corresponds to the occurrence in AP of Â“the average man.Â” That expression refers to nothing. But Â“the average manÂ” is nonetheless meaningful. So, given that its meaning isnÂ’t given by saying what it denotes, how is its meaning to be given? 

6.1 The word Â“instantÂ” to be defined contextually, not denotatively 
Here a brief detour through the philosophy of language is in order. Â“The average manÂ” is in the same grammatical category as expressions that do refer to specifics; e.g., Â“the current U.S. PresidentÂ” and Â“the EarthÂ’s only moon.Â” For this reason, a sentence of the form Â“Â…the average manÂ…Â” ipso facto appears to concern some individual; it appears, to be more precise, to say of some individual O thatÂ….OÂ…(i.e., that O is a thing x such thatÂ…xÂ…) Since that is not what is meant by any given sentence E of the form Â“Â…the average manÂ…Â” and since any sentence E that states E*Â’s meaning in a non-elliptical manner has a grammatical structure that is to no degree comparable to EÂ’s, it follows that EÂ’s grammatical structure is at variance with its meaning. Thus, in virtue of having the form Â“Â…the average manÂ…Â” a sentenceÂ’s grammatical form is out of line with its logical form. The meaning of Â“the average manÂ” is given not by saying what it denotes, but by saying how, when given an arbitrary sentence E of the form Â“Â…the average personÂ…Â” to identify a sentence E* such that: 
(i) E and E* say the same thing, and 
(ii) E*Â’s grammatical form doesnÂ’t misrepresent its logical form in the way in which EÂ’s grammatical form, by virtue of the fact that it contains an occurrence of Â“the average manÂ” misrepresents its logical form.[310] 

Everything just said about Â“the average manÂ” is true of the word Â“instant.Â” There are no instants. If E is an arbitrary sentence of the form Â“Â…instantÂ…Â” E is but an abbreviation for some sentence E* that does not contain that word or any isolable part corresponding thereto. The meaning of the word Â“instantÂ” is not given by a rule of the form: the word Â“instantÂ” refers to entities having such and such properties. Rather, it is given by a rule to the effect, if E is a sentence of the form Â“such and such is the case at a given instant t,Â” E is an abbreviation for some sentence E* of the form[311]: 
(R1) Â“For any t-inclusive non-null interval S1, if the worldÂ’s condition during S1 deviates from such and such by amount M, 
there is some smaller t-inclusive interval S2 such that the worldÂ’s condition during S2 deviates from such and such by less than M.Â” 
Â“R1 is viciously circular and therefore fails,Â” it will be said, Â“as it defines Â‘instantÂ’ in terms of itself, given that a Â‘t-inclusiveÂ’ interval is one that includes instant t.Â” In Sections 7.5-7.5.3, it will be made clear why R1 is not viciously circular. For now, let us operate on the (soon to be discharged) assumption that R1 is non-circular and otherwise acceptable. 

6.2 The relevance of these semantic points to the concept instantaneity 
One cannot directly determine how quickly the car is moving at instant t. What is it to determine how fast the car is moving during some interval? First of all, measurement is comparison. Given some object O, to measure OÂ’s length is to determine how long it is relative to some object that is taken as a standard. (In a moment weÂ’ll discuss the criteria that an object must satisfy to qualify as such a standard.) It is determined that, for some object O* such that O*Â’s length is by definition one unit long, and for some number n, OÂ’s length is n multiplied by O*Â’s length. To determine OÂ’s mass is to determine how OÂ’s mass compares with that of some O* such that O* by definition has a mass of one; it is to determine, for some number n, that OÂ’s mass is n multiplied by O*Â’s mass. 
All magnitudes are relative; some objects are longer than others; some objects are more massive than others.[312] 
In order for a given object O* to be such that it can appropriately be taken as a standard, it is necessary and sufficient that that there be no object O# such that, if O# is taken as a standard, there are fewer causal anomalies than there are if O* is taken as a standard. 
Let O* be some inflatable raft that we stipulate to be one unit long, no matter what changes it undergoes. A consequence of this stipulation is that inflating O* would have the consequence that, apart from O* itself, every object in the universe shrinks, even though: 
(i) many of those objects are on the receiving end of any causal process initiated by O*Â’s being inflated, 
and even though: 
(ii) given virtually any object that is on the receiving end of processes initiated by O*Â’s being inflated, itÂ’s shrinking has nothing to do with that fact about it. 
Object-shrinkages of the first kind would be uncaused and, therefore, anomalous. Although theyÂ’d be consequences of O*Â’s being inflated, they would be logical, not causal, consequences of O*Â’s being inflated. So theyÂ’d be uncaused events. TheyÂ’d be anomalies. 
Object-shrinkages of the second kind would also be uncaused. It is irrelevant that those objects were on the receiving end of causal processes initiated by OÂ’s being inflated. The laws of physics being what they are, O*Â’s being inflated couldnÂ’t possibly have caused those objects to shrink. 
Also, O*Â’s being inflated would have the consequence that distances between objects became smaller. This consequence, it goes without saying, would be quite as inexplicable as the two just mentioned. 
Of course, in order to validate our decision to take O* as having an unchanging length, we might posit physical laws that would explain why O*Â’s being inflated led to such consequences. But those physical laws would themselves be inconsistent with well-established laws (e.g., that radiation travels at a finite speed), and we couldnÂ’t eliminate those well-established laws from our system of physics without ceasing to understand what we previously understood and without also ceasing to be capable of understanding both what we already understood and what we did not yet understand but were capable of understanding. 
To sum up, a consequence of taking O* as having an unchanging length would be that, to a large extent, the world would cease to be intelligible to us. Given any object that we intuitively regard as being highly alterable in some respect, an analogue of this argument shows, were that object stipulated to be unchanging in that respect, the results would be comparably devastating to our ability to understand the world. 

6.3 The relevance of these semantic points to the concept instantaneity (continued) 
Now suppose that one takes as oneÂ’s yard-stick, as it were, some titanium object that is kept in an environment in which, speaking intuitively, it doesnÂ’t undergo any (relevant) changes---that it is kept in a temperature controlled room, that it isnÂ’t subject to forces that would disfigure it, etc. Taking that object as having an unchanging length wonÂ’t lead to anomalies of the just-discussed kind and wonÂ’t strip the world of whatever causal and explanatory integrity it has. 

6.4 How measurements of speed are, in the relevant respects, comparable to measurements of mass 
Speed, like mass and volume, is to be understood in relative terms. Consider the statement: 
(1) During time-interval T, xÂ’s average speed is such and such. 
The meaning of (1) is to be understood in terms of the concept of a periodic process. A periodic process is a repetitive sequence of events. More precisely, it is a series of events each of which is of the same kind as its neighbor(s) in that sequence (all of those members have two neighbors except for the terminal members). The series of rotations of the Earth around the Sun, during an interval long enough for more than one such rotation to occur, is a periodic process, and so, during such an interval, is the series of rotations of the Earth on its axis. A personÂ’s heartbeat is a periodic process, and so is the series of round-trips made by a beam of light bouncing between two mirrors whose distance from each other remains constant. 
In some cases, direct comparisons of speed are possible. If x and y are engaged in a foot race, then if x makes it to the finishing line before y, xÂ’s average speed during the interval when x was running exceeded yÂ’s average speed during that same interval. (We are assuming that, for the duration of the race, xÂ’s trajectory was the same as yÂ’s and, therefore, that neither covered a significantly greater distance than the other.) 
6.4.1 How measurements of speed are, in the respects that are relevant here, comparable to measurements of mass (continued) 
But direct comparisons of speed are not always possible. Suppose that runners x and y both travel from points A to B, whose distance from each other is held fixed, but that they do so at different times. xÂ’s trajectory, we will assume, is the same as yÂ’s. 
Given those circumstances, how is it to be established who ran faster? One must first identify some periodic process; e.g., a light-beam bouncing between two mirrors held at a fixed distance from each other or ticks on a properly functioning clock. If fewer installments of that process occur during xÂ’s journey from A to B, then xÂ’s average speed during that journey exceeded yÂ’s. 
Bearing this in mind, suppose that the periodic process in question is one that, speaking intuitively, weÂ’d describe as highly variable. Suppose that SmithÂ’s heart rate is this process and that Smith suffers from a heart-problem that involves his suffering from both extreme tachycardia and bradycardia. (Speaking intuitively----in other words, speaking as though it made sense to speak of absolute speeds---Â“tachycardiaÂ” and Â“bradycardiaÂ” may be defined, respectively, as Â“hyper-accelerated heart rate,Â” as when one is having a heart attack, and Â“hyper-decelerated heart-rate,Â” as when one is in a coma.) In that case, even if x is an Olympic sprinter who is performing at his best during his journey from A to B, and y is an arthritic who couldnÂ’t even make it onto his school track team, SmithÂ’s heart may beat more times during xÂ’s journey than during yÂ’s. 
Let us generalize this point. Suppose that we take SmithÂ’s heart-rate as being unchangingÂ—that, by our stipulation, it doesnÂ’t change and that, serving as it does as a Â“standardÂ” process, we determine the speeds at which objects are traveling in terms of it. In that case, weÂ’ll end up with counterintuitive results, such as the one just described, and weÂ’ll also end up with rampant anomalies, comparable to those described earlier in connection with mass and volume. Every time that Smith has a heart-attack, everything in the universe will slow down; and every time Smith falls asleep, everything will speed up. For reasons analogous to those described earlier, this will have two consequences: 
(i) There will be otherwise non-existent causal anomalies, 
and: 
(ii) There will be (otherwise non-existent) nomic anomalies (i.e., there will be laws of physics that are inconsistent with other, better corroborated laws of physics). 
To sum up, by stipulating to be non-erratic a periodic process that we intuitively regard as erratic, we strip the universe of much of its causal and explanatory integrity. 

6.4.2 How measurements of speed are, in the relevant respects, comparable to measurements of mass: closing the argument 
But now suppose that, given some period process that we do intuitively regard as non-erratic (e.g. the series of round-trips made by a light-beam between two mirrors whose distance from each other remains fixed), we stipulate that it is indeed non-erratic. This practice will have none of the just-mentioned consequences; it will not have the result that Olympic sprinter x is a slower runner than arthritic, non-sprinter y; it will not have the result that the rate at which a given object O is traveling will change depending on the vicissitudes undergone by some object O* to which O is not (relevantly) causally connected. By the same token, if we stipulate that a process of the just-discussed kind is erratic, the consequences will, by now familiar reasoning, resemble the consequences of stipulatively regarding as non-erratic some process that, intuitively speaking, is erratic. 
Thus, given two periodic processes P and P*, P is less erratic than P* iff ceteris paribus there are fewer causal and nomic anomalies if P is taken as a standard than if P* is taken as a standard. Thus, a given periodic process P is perfectly non-erratic if there is no periodic process P* such that ceteris paribus fewer anomalies would result if P* were taken as a standard than if P were taken as standard. 


6.5 Why RI is not viciously circular 
RI may initially appear circular. But it appears that way only so long as one holds onto the demonstrably false idea that position in time is non-relational. Consider the sentence: 
(S) Â“Event x occurs at 3:00 P.M. on April 21, 2010.Â” 
S says that x occurs simultaneously with some event y such that y is an installment in a certain kind of periodic process that is assumed to be unchanging, the reason being that not making this assumption leads to a proliferation of anomalies that would otherwise be easily explained. To say that JMK sneezed at a given time is to say that his sneezing was simultaneous with, let us say, the coincidence of some needle on some clock with some mark on that clockÂ’s face or, more realistically, with the collision of some light-ray with some surface. 
Â“But,Â” some will say, Â“to say that two events are Â‘simultaneousÂ’ is to say that they occur at the same instant; so your analysis is still viciously circular.Â” 
Not true. To say that two events are simultaneous is to say that the laws of physics prohibit either eventÂ’s having an effect on, or a hand in, the genesis of the other. (For an explanation of this statement see Chapter 19, Section 8.0.) Thus, the statement Â“x and y occurred simultaneouslyÂ”[313] 
means that x cannot have any effect on y or vice versa.[314] 
Given an arbitrary event e, let E be the smallest class containing all and only events e* such that e cannot affect e* or be affected by it. In that case, the statement Â“x is a member of EÂ” is equivalent with Â“x occurred at the very same instant as eÂ” or, alternatively, Â“there is some instant t such that x and e both happened at t.Â” Thus, an instant is the least inclusive class of events all of whose members are incapable of affecting or being affected by some given event; and an eventÂ’s happening at that instant is identical with its being a member of the aforementioned class. Given any class C such that, for some event e, C is the least inclusive class containing e and every event that e can neither affect nor be affected by, let us say that C is an I-class. 
Instants are I-classes. There is no way to pick out an I-class except by picking out one of its members. The reasons for this are of a strictly logical 
nature; they have nothing to do with anyoneÂ’s limitations.[315] 

7.5.1 Why RI is not viciously circular (continued): A penultimate preliminary point 
An interval of time is a class C of I-classes such that: 
(i) 
The (distal) cause of any event that is a member of the last member of C is a member of the first member of C. 

(ii) 
if x is any given member of CÂ’s terminal I-class and y is any given one of the members of CÂ’s initial class that is causally responsible for x, then, for each event z such that z was one of the events that was a link in the chain of events whereby y affected x, there is some I-class that belongs to C to which z belongs. 


Given any series of I-classes satisfying these requirements, let us refer to them as S-classes.[316] 


7.5.2 Why RI is not viciously circular (continued): final preliminary point 
There is one last point to make before closing the argument. We assign numbers to instants. The higher the number, the later the instant. So Â“tÂ” is a variable, the constants corresponding to which are numbers. There must be some one relation R such that if e is a member of some I-class X, that I-class must be assigned a number that bears R to that assigned to any I-class to which one of eÂ’s effects belongs. (We use the relation Â“lower than,Â” since it has the right properties and since, unlike some of the other relations that have the right properties, itÂ’s psychologically easy to manage. So if e (somebodyÂ’s birth) happens before e* (that personÂ’s beginning to sneeze on his second birthday), then e is assigned a lower number (say, 06:45, June 8,1970) than the one assigned to e* (09:45, June 8,1972). 
Each event is (in principle) assigned a number. But the number it is assigned is not based on the Â“positionÂ” in time that it occupies. There is no such position. It is, since it must be, based on its causal relations to other events.[317] 
e is given a higher number than e# if e is incapable of affecting e#; e is given the same number as e# if neither can affect the other. Given some event e, our conventions assign it a number on the basis of a procedure consistent with the guideline just described; and given oneÂ’s knowledge as to the identities of the numbers assigned by the same procedure to other events, one knows (within limits) what is (simultaneous with something that is) the effect of what. 

7.5.3 Why RI is not viciously circular: closing the argument 
Bearing all of this in mind, letÂ’s revisit the question: what does it mean to say that a given time-interval is Â“t-inclusiveÂ”? t is an I-class. t is assigned a number. (Or, what comes to the same thing, each member of t is assigned a number, and that number is then assigned to t itself.) For argumentÂ’s sake, let 34 be that number. t is a member of an S-class, which weÂ’ll call Â“X.Â” This means only that any given member of t is either the cause (not necessarily the immediate cause) or the effect (same qualification) of at least one member of at least one of XÂ’s terminal I-classes. 
So to say that a given interval is t-inclusive is just a very encrypted way of saying that a certain event (it could be a bolt of lightning, a hiccup, or the ringing of an alarm clock) is a member of a class no two of whose members can affect each other but any given one of whose members is the cause or the effect one of the events marking either that intervalÂ’s inception or its cessation. It follows that occurrence of Â“t-inclusiveÂ” in RI is eliminable, being 
but an abbreviated way of making a causal claim of the kind just described. 
Chapter 14 Causality 
1.0 The basics 
Events cause other events to occur. Smith pulls the trigger, causing the gun to fire. Jones throws the vase against the wall, causing the vase to break. There are causes and there are effects. 
Astonishingly, some philosophers have denied the existence of causation. Why? Because many philosophers are empiricists, and given an empiricist outlook, it is hard to accommodate the presumption that events make events happen. According to empiricism, all knowledge is strictly observation based. Thus, if you know it, one of two conditions is met: (a) you observed it (in other words, you saw it, heard it, felt it, etc.); or (b) you inferred it from what you observed, provided that you used no inference rules other than those of whose legitimacy direct observation apprised you. (See Chapter 12.) According to many empiricists, we cannot see or otherwise observe causal ties. We see events, but not forces. We see rocks strike windows, and we see windows shatter upon being thus struck. But we donÂ’t see anything that, given such a collision, compels the window in question to shatter. Since we donÂ’t observe causal connections, we donÂ’t have good reason to believe them to exist. 
But this argument involves a major non-sequitur. We donÂ’t observe electrons or quarks, but we have good reason to believe them to exist. How are causal ties different? Given that itÂ’s methodologically permissible to posit unobservable viruses and particles, why isnÂ’t it equally permissible to posit unobservable causal ties? 
Â“Because,Â” we are told, Â“the concept of a causal tie, unlike that of a proton or a virus, is an incoherent one. For that reason, it wouldnÂ’t do any good to posit causal ties. Causal ties, if they exist, are occupants of space-time, like rocks and vases and chairs; and they are therefore just as incapable as chairs and rocks of being the Â“glueÂ” that, supposedly, keeps the universe from powdering into so many renegade events.Â” But notice that the second argument, unlike the first, isnÂ’t an empirical argument at all. ItÂ’s a strictly logical one. It is to the effect that forces are in the same category as square circles and therefore couldnÂ’t possibly exist and, therefore, couldnÂ’t possibly be observed. Thus, the first empirical argument against the existence of causal ties is parasitic on a non-empirical, purely a priori argument, and is therefore only as good as the latter. (An a priori argument is one that has its basis, not in observational data, but entirely in considerations of coherence and logic.) 
Moreover, the latter argument isnÂ’t a good one. The concept of persistence is itself a causal notion, and anything that persists is, for that very reason, a causal sequence. Thus, we observe causal sequences whenever we observe anything. And we knowingly observe them. In other words, we donÂ’t merely observe what are in fact causal sequences; we observe such sequences to be causal sequences. This line of thought will be substantiated in Section 5.3. 
Much of this chapter will be spent evaluating the contention that we donÂ’t see or otherwise observe causal ties. Although it has been enormously influential, itÂ’s of doubtful accuracy, as weÂ’ve just seen. And the more itÂ’s scrutinized, the more incoherent it proves to be. For example, the very notion of spatial occupancy is a causal notion, since a given thingÂ’s occupying a given region R ipso facto alters the trajectories and velocities of other would-be and soon-to-be occupants of that region. 
These points generalize. A Â“steelÂ” object that lacked the requisite degree of malleability or thermal conductivity would ipso facto not be steel. Malleability and conductivity are causal properties. x is more malleable than y if, other things being equal, less force is needed to cause xÂ’s shape to change than is needed to cause yÂ’s shape to change. x has a higher degree of thermal conductivity than y if, other things being equal, less energy is needed to raise xÂ’s temperature by a given amount than is needed to raise yÂ’s temperature by that same amount. Thus, to describe a given object as being of made of steel is to say that, other things being equal, it will react to situations in ways in which it wouldnÂ’t otherwise react. 
In describing something as Â“self-identicalÂ” or as Â“being such that 1 + 1 = 2,Â” one is not making a causally loaded claim. But those characterizations say nothing about anything. In being told that x is Â“self-identical,Â” one isnÂ’t being told how x is different from, or similar to, water or steel or the planet Neptune or anything else. The same is true of all causally sterile characterizations. For that reason, anything that says anything about anything in the spatiotemporal world has causal content. 
2.0 Causation a relation between events, not objects 
But before we enter these stormy and controversial waters, let us make some non-controversial points about the logic of the concept of causality. 
First of all, it is only events that can be causes. Objects are not causes. The rock is not a cause. The rock didnÂ’t cause the window to break. What did so was some event involving the rock (e.g., the rockÂ’s striking the window at a certain time). 
Sometimes the way we speak suggests that, in our view, objects are causes. For example, people say Â“Carter was the cause of the recession in the late Â‘70s,Â” Â“Hitler was the cause of World War II.Â” But these statements are elliptical for Â“such and such events involving Carter (Hitler) were responsible for the recession in the late Â‘70s (World War II).Â” 
In connection with this, we must distinguish between somethingÂ’s being a cause, on the one hand, and its having causal properties, on the other. Non-causes may have causal properties. The rock isnÂ’t a cause, as we discussed, but it has causal properties. The rockÂ’s having a certain mass is among its causal properties, meaning that its having that mass is, or can be, a (partial) cause. (Not every property of the rock is a cause. The rock is such that it either is or is not identical with the number 2. But the rockÂ’s having that property doesnÂ’t cause anything to occur.) 
2.1. Conditions vs. events 
We must also distinguish conditions from events. A condition is a relatively persistent state (e.g., the roomÂ’s having a certain temperature). An event is a change in conditions. But conditions themselves seem to be causes. For example, the waterÂ’s having a certain temperature is what caused the spaghetti in it to soften. At the same time, conditions appear not to be events. An event is, by definition, a change, whereas a condition is, it would seem, the absence of change. So if conditions are non-events and are also causes, then, contrary to what we earlier said, it isnÂ’t events alone that are causes. 
This argument overlooks the fact that conditions consist of events. The waterÂ’s having a given temperature consists in its containing particles that have certain kinetic properties. There is no heat where there are no events. A personÂ’s being healthy (i.e., being in a condition of health) consists in that personÂ’s body doing what it should. There is no life, and therefore no health, where there are no metabolic events. And although events do necessarily constitute changes, those changes may be, and often are, internal to conditions of changelessness. For the waterÂ’s temperature to remain at 101Â° for 5 minutes is for the changes undergone by its constituent molecules to remain within certain limits; it is for their mean kinetic energy to stay within certain bounds. For the waterÂ’s temperature to change is for their behavior to exceed those limits. What we call Â“conditionsÂ” are patterns of constant change (i.e., of change that occurs in a uniform manner). 
What we call Â“eventsÂ” are changes in the manner of change. When the waterÂ’s temperature increases, the way its constituent molecules move about changes. When the waterÂ’s temperature stays the same, they still move about Â—they still undergo changeÂ—but the way they do so doesnÂ’t undergo change: those changes fall within certain limits. So conditions can be causes. But since conditions, far from being the absence of events, consist of them, this is in no way inconsistent with our contention that it is events, and events alone, that are causes. 
2.2 All causes ipso facto spatiotemporal 
There are causes only where there are changes, and changes happen in time. So universals, if they exist, are causally impotent. Many have concluded that, for this reason, they cannot be known and, therefore, that there is no legitimate reason to grant their existence. The idea is that there must be some kind of a causal connection between two things if one of them is to know of the other. For me to see the rock, it is necessary that light rays bouncing off of it affect certain sensory surfaces of mine. For me to know of SocratesÂ’ existence, I must be on the receiving end of testimony, the vehicle for which is always some causal process (noises, light rays bouncing off of ink marks), that can be traced back to some state of affairs involving Socrates. One obvious way to generalize this line of reasoning is to say that there is never awareness where there isnÂ’t a causal nexus. 
For reasons given in Chapter 12 of this book (and given in greater detail Chapters 8 and 9 of my (2009) book Analytic Philosophy and in Chapters 6-9 of my (2007) book Conceptual Atomism and the Computational Theory of Mind), this conception of conception is erroneous; under no circumstances does a causal connection between two things by itself mediate the oneÂ’s having an awareness of the other. There is always a non-causal component to awareness, even to sense perception, which, of all the many forms of awareness, is the one in which a causal connection between subject and object is most obvious. Further, for reasons given in Chapter 2, we do have good reasons to countenance the existence of universals, and no good reasons not to. 
3.0 Causes as INUS-conditions 
The things we describe as Â“causesÂ” are really partial causes. Supposing it correct, the sentence Â“SmithÂ’s drunkenness is what caused the accidentÂ” must really be elliptical for Â“SmithÂ’s drunkenness is a part of what caused the accident.Â” Had he been driving a car with new tires on an open country road, instead of a car with bald tires on a busy city street, Smith might not have crashed even if heÂ’d been drunker than he actually was. So it wasnÂ’t SmithÂ’s drunkenness or any other one thing that caused the crash, and was instead a confluence of circumstances. In some contextsÂ—for example, those of a legal or ethical or psychological natureÂ—the relevant partial cause might well be SmithÂ’s drunkenness; and that seems to be what we mean when we say that it was the cause.[318] 

The complete cause of anything is very hard to identify. It is a matter of philosophical and scientific debate whether, given an event E happening at t, anything other than the entire state of the universe just prior to t can be the complete cause of E. So for all intents and purposes, the expression Â“the cause of occurrence EÂ” never refers to a sufficient condition for E. 
Â“Even though SmithÂ’s being drunk wasnÂ’t sufficient for his crashing the car,Â” it will be thought, Â“it was necessary for it. Had he not been drunk, he wouldnÂ’t have crashed.Â” This is false. SmithÂ’s being drunk wasnÂ’t necessary for his crashing. If he had been sober, but had been driving too fast on an icy road, he might well have crashed. 
J.L. Mackie (1917Â–1981) made it clear what is meant by Â“the cause of E,Â” as this expression is typically used. SmithÂ’s being drunk wasnÂ’t a necessary condition for his crashing.[319] 
He could have crashed if sober. But his being drunk was a necessary condition for his crashing under the circumstances. Given that he wasnÂ’t driving a high-performance car on a country road during a clear day, and given that he was driving a low-performance car on a rainy night on a busy street, SmithÂ’s being drunk was, we may suppose, a necessary condition for his crashing. For it could be that, had he been sober, Smith would have narrowly avoided crashing, despite the rain, darkness, and faulty steering mechanism, and that it was only these things plus SmithÂ’s drunkenness that led to the crash. So, if it is to be correct, the statement Â“SmithÂ’s drunkenness was the cause of the crashÂ” must be taken to mean that, under the operative circumstances, SmithÂ’s being drunk was necessary for his crashing. 
There are just a few more points to make. First, given that Smith did crash the car, it follows trivially that a sufficient condition for his doing so was fulfilled. Second, whatever that sufficient condition was, it wasnÂ’t necessary. Suppose that what led to the crash was SmithÂ’s driving a low-performance vehicle on a dark, rainy night, while drunk. Even though, by hypothesis, that confluence of circumstance was sufficient for his crashing, it wasnÂ’t necessary. Smith might have crashed even if heÂ’d been driving a high-performance vehicle in broad daylight while stone cold sober. 
Thus, SmithÂ’s being drunk was an insufficient but non-redundant part of an unnecessary but sufficient condition for his crashing. SmithÂ’s being drunk was thus an Â“INUS-conditionÂ” for his crashing. For this reason, Mackie says that if it is to express a true statement Â“E was the cause of event E*Â” must be taken to mean that E is an INUS-condition for E*. In a word, Â“the causeÂ” of an event is an INUS-condition for that event. 
4.0 Aristotle on causality 
Aristotle (384Â–322 B.C.) distinguished between four different kinds of causality: efficient, final, material, and formal.[320] 

(AC)[321] 
x is the efficient cause of y if x makes y happen. 
x is the final cause of y if y is an action on the part of some creature and x is that creatureÂ’s objective in performing y. Final causes are goals or objectives. 
x is the material cause of y if x is the material that y is made of. 
x is the formal cause of y if x is yÂ’s form. (To expedite discussion, weÂ’ll henceforth omit the obvious qualifications relating to the fact that Aristotle didnÂ’t use English words.) Sometimes Aristotle uses the word Â“formÂ” to refer to shape. But sometimes he uses it to refer to what he elsewhere refers to as Â“essences.Â” Those properties that are essential to a given thing jointly constitute its essence; and a property is essential to a given thing if that thing could not lose that property without for that very reason ceasing to exist. The italicized phrase is intended to indicate that the dependence-relation in question is not of a causal nature, and is instead of a logical or constitutive nature. In other words, that relation is comparable to the dependence that triangles have on being three sided, not to the dependence that mammals have on air. 
Setting aside a few trivialities, pretty much nothing Aristotle has to say about causality has any merit. Aristotle incoherently believes that objects simpliciter---as opposed to objectsÂ’ having these or those properties---have essences. This belief, as weÂ’ll soon see, is an incoherent one, and along with the more general coherence of which it is but one instance, it vitiates AristotleÂ’s views on causality. 
It is essential to a thingÂ’s being triangle-shaped that it have three sides. But a given triangle-shaped objectÂ’s continued existence neednÂ’t depend on its continuing to have three sides. Things change shape. It is essential to a thingÂ’s being water that it consist of H2O molecules. But a given puddleÂ’s 
continuing to exist neednÂ’t depend on its consisting of such molecules. 
Things undergo chemical changes without ceasing to exist. 
Contrary to what Aristotle thought, dependence-relations donÂ’t hold between objects. They hold between events or between statements, depending on whether theyÂ’re of a causal or a logical nature. To say that xÂ’s having three sides is essential to xÂ’s being a triangle is to say that Â“x is a triangleÂ” entails that Â“x has three sides.Â” To say that xÂ’s consisting of H2O molecules is 
essential to its being water is to say that Â“x consists of waterÂ” and Â“x doesnÂ’t 
consist of H2O moleculesÂ” are incompatible statements. To say that treating children with kindness is essential to their becoming sane adults is to say that treating a child unkindly prevents him from becoming a sane adult. 
So-called formal causes donÂ’t hold between events (or states of affairs) or statements; they hold between things. Thus, the concept of a formal cause is an incoherent one. So, for the same reason, is the concept of a material cause. 
The concept of efficient causality clearly is a coherent one. There is such a thing as efficient causality. WeÂ’ll see in the next section that it isnÂ’t the only bona fideform of causality. But itÂ’s the most fundamental one. 
What about (so-called) final causes? If, as Aristotle seems to think, final causes are goals per se, heÂ’s wrong to describe them as causes. Goals per se do nothing. Goals are abstract objects and therefore do no causal work. What does do causal work is a given personÂ’s having a given goal. My having the goal that: 
(*) I, JMK, get in shape; 
obviously does causal work; it causes me to jog around the block for hours on end. But (*) per se does nothing. Like all other goals, (*) is a proposition. My having that goal is my intending to make that proposition come true. But my having a goal is a garden-variety efficient cause. In general, goals per se, being propositions, arenÂ’t causes at all. A given personÂ’s (or creatureÂ’s) having a given goal is a cause. But itÂ’s a garden-variety efficient cause. So in saying there are such things as Â“finalÂ” causes, Aristotle is either making the trivial point that a personÂ’s having a goal can have effects or he is making the deeply confused point that goals per se can have effects. 
4.1 The importance of the expression Â“in virtue ofÂ” in causal discourse 
The expression Â“in virtue ofÂ” has an important place in philosophical discourse. (I will use Â“in virtue ofÂ” and Â“by virtue ofÂ” interchangeably.) Without this expression, or some equivalent, it would be very hard to say anything meaningful about causal explanationÂ—or about non-causal explanation, for that matter. The meaning of this term is to be understood in terms of two parallel points, namely: 
(i) It is states of affairs (or events), not objects, that have effects; 
and: 
(ii) it is propositions, not objects, that stand in dependence-relations. 
For reasons that will become apparent, (i) and (ii) can be condensed into: 
(iii) dependence-relations hold between propositions, as opposed to objects. 
A story will help us explain what (i)Â–(iii) mean and why theyÂ’re true. Despite being intellectually mediocre, Smith never loses an argument. He wins arguments, not by addressing points with counterpoints, but by bullying his opponent into submission. In this way, Smith recently won an argument with Jones, who is SmithÂ’s superior intellectually. Thus: 
(A) even though Smith won his argument with Jones, he did so not by virtue of making good points, but by virtue of bullying Jones. 
What (A) means is that the cause of SmithÂ’s winning was his being a bully, and not his being smart. (Cause: SmithÂ’s being a bully. Effect: SmithÂ’s winning. Smith wasnÂ’t the cause of anything.) Thus, the occurrence of Â“by virtue ofÂ” in (A) is a way of encrypting a statement about states of affairsÂ—of making them seem about objects, when in fact they are about states of affairs. 
Even if Smith did make good points in the course of the argument, it doesnÂ’t follow that he won by virtue of making good points. It could be that his making good points had nothing to do with his winning and that it was his bullyism that was responsible for it. In that case: 
(A*) even though Smith won his argument with Jones, and even though he made good points in the course of that argument, Smith won by virtue of his being a bully, and not by virtue of his making good points. 
Importantly, Smith could have won both by virtue of being a bully and by virtue of making good points. In other words, his bullyism and his making good points could have been co-factors. 
Let us now discuss (ii). Suppose that there are only three triangular objects in the world, x being one of them, and also that these three objects are the only green objects in existence. In that case, although Â“every triangle is greenÂ” is true, Â“x is green by virtue of its being triangleÂ” is false. The right statement is: 
(B) Â“x is a triangle by virtue of its having three co-planar sides, each of them straight, such that any two of them intersect and such that not all three of them intersect.Â” 
What (B) means is: 
(C) The proposition that x is a triangle entails, and is entailed by, the proposition that x has three co-planar sides, each of them straight, such that any two of them intersect and such that not all of three of them intersect. 
In what follows, I will use the term Â“factÂ” to mean Â“spatiotemporal state of affairs.Â” So a Â“fact,Â” as IÂ’ll be using this word, is a distribution of mass-energy.[322] 

Suppose that, for reasons of physical law, nothing could be triangular without being green, and nothing could be green without being triangular. In that case, given some green/triangular object x, the fact in virtue of which x is greenÂ—in other words, the distribution of mass-energy in virtue of which x was greenÂ—would be spatially and causally indistinguishable from the fact in virtue of which x was triangular. Nonetheless, it wouldnÂ’t be in virtue of its being a closed three-sided (etc.) figure that x was greenÂ—it would be in virtue of its having certain reflective properties. And it wouldnÂ’t be in virtue of its having those reflective properties that x was triangularÂ—it would be in virtue of its being a three-sided, straight-edged (etc.) figure. This shows that the meaning of (B) is (C). When occurring in statements affirming logical (as opposed to causal) dependencies, Â“in virtue ofÂ” denotes a relationship holding, not between things or even facts, but between propositions. 
Given that the occurrence in (A) of Â“by virtue ofÂ” does denote a relationship holding between states of affairs, what are we to say? One response, of course, is to say that itÂ’s ambiguous. But, in addition to appearing very wrong, this response is unnecessary. (A) doesnÂ’t express an entailment. But it does express a dependence-relation holding between statements. The truth of Smith won the argument is, in this context, dependent on the truth of Smith bullied his opponent. In general, Â“in virtue of,Â” when occurring in causal contexts, can be interpreted as denoting a form of interpropositional dependence; and we may therefore condense (i) and (ii) into: 
(iii) Dependence-relations hold between propositions, as opposed to things. 
4.2 Functionalism, content-externalism 
According to a doctrine known as Â“functionalism,Â” it is wholly in virtue of what its causes and effects are that a given brain-state (or physical entity of any kind) falls into a given mental category. Anything that has certain causes and certain effects is ipso facto a belief that snow is white or a desire for a world peace or a vitriolic dislike of a certain piece of music.[323] 
Functionalism is discussed at length in Chapter 22. But a few words on it here are appropriate. 
Functionalism has no plausibility when it comes to sensations or, more generally, anything that has phenomenal content. (For a mental state to have Â“phenomenal content,Â” or Â“phenomenology,Â” is for there to be a certain kind of consciousness such that, having that form of consciousness is necessary and sufficient for being in the state. So feelings all have phenomenal content; so do all perceptions. But enduring mental structures---judgments, attitudes, values---lack phenomenology. Of course, they give rise to conscious events that have phenomenal content. But they themselves lack it, for there is no specific kind of consciousness such that having it is necessary and sufficient for believing that 1 + 1 = 2 or being suspicious of oneÂ’s neighborÂ’s intentions.) But functionalism is widely taken to be correct when it comes to so-called Â“dispositionalÂ” mental entities such as beliefs and objectives. (I put the word Â“dispositionalÂ” in quotes, because, for reasons that IÂ’ll now give, I reject this way of characterizing the mental entities in question.) 
4.2.1 Why, even thus restricted, functionalism is indefensible 
Thus restricted, functionalism may initially sound plausible. But it has some grisly problems that a story will help to expose. While standing right in front of you, Jones, a demented acquaintance of yours, puts what is clearly arsenic in a glass of water. He then tries to make you drink the water. Jones is very strong and is also a trained martial artist; so while holding the glass in one hand, without spilling any of it, he puts you in a joint-lock and tries to pour the contents of said glass down your throat. You shut your mouth, and you twist and squirm. Miraculously, you break free and run out the door. 
What caused all of this behavior? A good part of it was your belief that Smith was trying to make you drink arsenic. Another part of it was your belief that, were Smith to succeed in making you drink arsenic, youÂ’d suffer some adverse consequence. Yet another part was your wish to not die. And, of course, other propositional attitudes of yours were determinative of your behavior. Supposing that x is the part of your brain that comprises the various physical structures and events that mediate these different propositional attitudes, it isnÂ’t just x that makes you squirm and fight, and so on. Rather, itÂ’s xÂ’s being a belief that Jones is about to make you drink arsenic. 
But functionalism cannot accommodate this obvious fact. According to functionalism, it is in virtue of what x causes and what causes it that x is a belief that Jones is about to do that. The causal relations fix the content, not the other way around. This means that, if functionalism is right, xÂ’s being a belief that Jones is about to make you drink arsenic does nothing. In general, given any entity O that mediates mental state M, OÂ’s being an instance of M is causally inert. But this means that, if functionalism is correct, then the mental does nothing; it has no causal powers at all. Of course, functionalism is consistent with, and in fact depends on, the presumption that the brain-states that mediate mental states have causal powers. But since functionalism is inconsistent with the fact that in virtue of being mental states, brain-states are powerless, functionalism amounts to the denial that the mental (qua mental[324]) has any causal powers at all. Given the fact that anything spatiotemporal ipso facto has causal powers, the reason being that occupancy of a time or a place is a form of causality, it follows that functionalism denies the very existence of minds. 
4.2.2 Content-externalism: another popular but indefensible doctrine 
According to a doctrine known as Â“content-externalism,Â” two people, Smith and Twin-Smith, who are exactly the same, leaving aside the remote causes of their current conditions, can have thoughts with different contents. So, because SmithÂ’s current visual perception was caused by light that bounced off of Mary, whereas Twin-SmithÂ’s current visual perception was caused by light that bounced off of Twin-Mary, otherwise identical Smith and Twin-Smith are now having thoughts with different truth-conditions and, therefore, different contents. (Smith is thinking that personÂ—viz., MaryÂ—is tall. Twin-Smith is thinking that personÂ—viz., Twin-MaryÂ—is tall.) 
To appreciate just what the content-externalist says, we must distinguish causal from constitutive necessity. Obviously people have different thoughts. And obviously differences in peopleÂ’s personal pasts create many of the cognitive divergences between them. But the content-externalist is saying that, given two people who, like Smith and Twin-Smith, are now atom-forÂ­atom duplicates of each other, and whose respective pasts havenÂ’t so much as made a dent in the one person that they havenÂ’t made in the other, those two people will think different things. TheyÂ’ll have thoughts with different contents. One of them will think about Mary (gold, water, etc.), while the other thinks about Twin-Mary (foolÂ’s Gold, faux-water, etc.) 
Content-externalism is incoherent. If Smith and Twin-Smith were to switch places, but everything else were held constant, neither would behave or think differently from how he would otherwise do so. Thus, to the extent that SmithÂ’s mental content is fixed by factors that arenÂ’t operative in TwinÂ­SmithÂ’s case, SmithÂ’s thinking isnÂ’t at all different from Twin-SmithÂ’s. Any differences between SmithÂ’s and Twin-SmithÂ’s thoughts have some basis other than the differences in their distal causes. So to the extent that mental content is to be understood along content-externalist lines, it is without any causal powers at all, and therefore doesnÂ’t exist. 
As for the content-externalistÂ’s contention that Smith is thinking that Mary is tall, whereas Twin-Smith is thinking Twin-Mary is tall, that is a non-starter. What SmithÂ’s eyes tell him isnÂ’t that Mary is tall. They tell him that a person who has certain features is tall. Given only what his eyes are telling him, Smith doesnÂ’t know whether heÂ’s seeing Mary or some Mary look-alike. To be sure, he may well know that heÂ’s looking at Mary. But that knowledge wonÂ’t be based strictly on the content of his visual perception. It will be based also on background knowledge that he brings to the present context. 
Content-externalism embodies a failure to appreciate the concept meant by the phrase Â“in virtue of.Â” True-Smith and Twin-Smith arenÂ’t doing the same things. Smith is in one place; Twin-Smith is in another. Smith is looking at one person; Twin-Smith is looking at another. But it isnÂ’t in virtue of any differences in their respective mental contents that Smith and Twin-Smith diverge in these respects. Since, therefore, no differences between Smith and Twin-Smith, or by obvious extensions of this argument, between any two people, are to be understood along content-externalist lines, mental content is causally impotent, and therefore non-existent, to the extent contentÂ­externalism is the right theory about it. 
Tyler Burge (1946Â–), a leading exponent of content-externalism, deals with this by arguing that the notion of causality should be revised, so as to accommodate content-externalism. Were two qualitatively identical objects x and y to switch places but everything were held constant, this switch would be experimentally undetectable. Burge acknowledges this but says that, nonetheless, x and y have different causal properties. By thus reanalyzing the concept of causality, he safeguards content-externalism from the objection to it just considered. 
In addition to being brazenly ad hoc, this is incoherent, since it says, quite straightforwardly, that there can be distinctions without corresponding differences. 
Also, the relevant data is easily modeled without stooping to such lows. To see why, see Chapters 6, 8, 9, and 18 of my (2009) book Analytic Philosophy, as well as my (2010) article Â“Intensionality and Modality,Â” published in the Journal of Pragmatics, and, finally, pages 207Â–507 of my (2007) book Conceptual Atomism and the Computational Theory of Mind. 
4.3 Program-causality[325] 

We obviously know of many cases of one eventÂ’s causing another. We are inclined to think that, in each such case, the one event is the efficient cause of the other. Working jointly, Frank Jackson (1943-) and Philip Pettit (1945Â–) have shown this to be false. Given almost any known instance of one eventÂ’s causing another to occur, the one event is the program-cause, not the efficient cause, of the other. 
What does the term Â“program causeÂ” mean? Some scenarios will help us answer this question. There is a kettle on the stove. You turn on the gas. The resulting flames underneath the kettle cause it to heat up and thus cause the water to boil. Let F be the flame. WeÂ’re inclined to think that F caused the kettle to heat up. 
(i) F (or, in any case, FÂ’s having a certain temperature) caused the kettle to heat up. 
But only a tiny part of FÂ’s surface was in contact with the underside of the kettle. Had the events at those contact points been present, the effect on the kettle would have been the same, even if the other flame-constitutive events were absent. 
Another example: Statements such as: 
(ii) high-inflation led to crime, which, coupled with xenophobia on the part of the populace, gave the government a powerful incentive to scapegoat a foreign nation and go to war with them. 
But causes are much more specific than (ii) suggests. Crime doesnÂ’t do anything, and neither does xenophobia. Things are caused by specific people, performing specific criminal or xenophobic acts. 
One last example: 
(iii) The impact of the rock on the window caused the window to shatter. 
This case is similar to the first. Only a small part of the surface of the rock came into contact with the windowÂ—and, in fact, those parts of the rockÂ’s surface came into contact with specific parts of one of the windowÂ’s two surfaces. Had the events at those contact points happened, the effect on the window would have been the same, even if no rock had struck the window. 
But if we say that (i)Â–(iii) are just wrong, our grounds being that a Â“causeÂ” of an event E can only be an event that is directly responsible for EÂ’s occurrence, then just about every single causal statement anyone makes will be wrong. But statements like (i)Â–(iii) obviously convey valuable 
information. So rather than say that theyÂ’re all just wrong, we should look for an interpretation of the word Â“causeÂ” that validates those statements.[326] 

Jackson and Petit have done just that. The form of causality mentioned in (i)Â–(iii) is program-causality. x is a program-cause of y if x consists of events that, in their turn, are directly responsible for y. A countryÂ’s being poor consists of various specific states of affairsÂ—various specific people being without funds in various specific situations. The specific situations that constitute a condition of wide-spread poverty will directly cause crimes. And so on. F heats up the pan in the sense that among the events constitutive of F are those that heat up the pan; and it is in the same sense mutatis mutandis that the impact of the rock shattered the window. Thus, Jackson and Pettit have successfully validated ordinary causal statements. 
They make other important points. One would think that high-resolution causal information is better than low-resolution causal information. But this isnÂ’t always so. What caused the house to burn down? 
(SA)[327] 
Arson on SmithÂ’s part was the cause. He threw several Molotov cocktails at the house and up in flames it went. 
SA obviously doesnÂ’t give us the micro-story. For argumentÂ’s sake suppose that some long sentence MS does give us the micro-story. MS will be worthless in terms of giving us information about SmithÂ’s character, and it will be equally worthless in other, comparable respects. There are many principled regularities of which this particular incident is an instance, and we blind ourselves to all but a few of them if we reject any story that isnÂ’t the micro-story. So the macroÂ­storyÂ—or, rather, the various different macro-storiesÂ—arenÂ’t inferior versions of the micro-story; they arenÂ’t precursors to it that weÂ’ll chuck when we have it. They expose regularities, structures, and counterfactual truths omitted by the micro-story. This shows that biology isnÂ’t just bad physics, that psychology isnÂ’t just bad physiologyÂ—it shows that different disciplines are dealing with different program-causes, and therefore distinct and very possibly sui generis nomic connectionsÂ—that happen at least sometimes to be instantiated by the same efficient (micro) causes. 
Predictions are almost always made on the basis of a knowledge of program-causes. To predict whatÂ’s going to happen, one must know of structures that can be depended on to yield certain outputs, given certain inputs. So far as one lacks such knowledge, one must make predictions on an ad hoc basis, and there are two reasons why this is a problem. First, sub-structural facts tend to be smallÂ—literally small. (Something is a structure only to the extent that itÂ’s a cohesive aggregate of events. Something fails to be a structure only to the extent that itÂ’s an isolated event. Thus, lone events tend to be smaller than structures by orders of magnitude.[328]) And when they can be known, the process of learning about them tends to disrupt them in prediction-foiling ways. (See Chapter 14.) 
Also, structures comprise back-up mechanisms that ensure a certain outcome even if, because of some hidden variable, some rogue, structure-unfriendly event makes it through the gauntlet. If a salesperson working for megacorporation X unexpectedly quits, another takes his place. If one police officer doesnÂ’t report for duty, another steps into the breach. ItÂ’s of the essence of structures that a certain amount of causal redundancy be incorporated into them. Where there isnÂ’t such redundancy, predictions are easily foiled, since there is nothing to absorb the ripple-effects created by some rogue occurrence. 
Given the dependence of predictive knowledge on structures and, therefore, on program-causes, it follows that knowledge of explanations is comparably dependent. The reason is that explanation is reverse-prediction. One predicts X when one identifies current conditions that, given known mechanisms, make XÂ’s occurrence likely. One explains X when one identifies past conditions that, given known mechanisms, resulted in XÂ’s occurrence. The concept of a program-cause, which was, so far as I know, first clearly analyzed by Pettit and Jackson, is therefore central to the concepts of prediction and explanation and, thus, to the theory of knowledge. 
Chapter 15 HumeÂ’s First Analysis of Causality 
1.0 HumeÂ’s counterintuitive analysis of causality supposedly de rigueur, given his acceptance of empiricism 
According to David Hume, nothing makes anything happen. There are no forces or structures underlying the various events that occur. There are just the events. 
Why does Hume think this? Because he accepts a very strict form of empiricism, this being the doctrine that what is known is either (i) directly observed to be the case, or (ii) is inferred from what is directly observed in accordance with inference-rules of whose legitimacy direct observation has apprised one. 
Do we observe connections between events, Hume asks? NoÂ—we only observe the events. Thus, Hume believes, so far as you have empirical grounds for saying that the collision of billiard balls B1 and B2 caused previously stationary B2 to start moving, itÂ’s because you know the following three conditions to be fulfilled (let E1 be the collision and let E2 be the subsequent displacement of B2): 
(HC)[329] 
(1) E1 immediately preceded E2; (2) E1 and E2 are adjacent; and (3) any event similar to E1 immediately precedes, and is adjacent with, some event similar to E2. 
Conditions (1) and (2) explained: If there were a spatial or temporal gap between the two events, weÂ’d be unjustified in believing the first to be a direct cause of the second. Hence conditions (1) and (2). Condition (2) explained: If events similar to E1 werenÂ’t typically adjacent with, and immediately followed by, events similar to E2, weÂ’d have no reason to think that E1Â’s occurring had anything to do with E2Â’s occurring. 
Hume thus proposes the following analysis of causation: 
(HC1)[330] 
E1 causes E2 to occur if E1 immediately precedes and is adjacent with E2, and any event similar to E1 immediately precedes and is adjacent with some event similar 
[331] 

to E2. 

2.0 Problem #1 with HumeÂ’s analysis: It doesnÂ’t distinguish between actual causation and pseudo-causation 
This analysis is untenable. A story will help us identify one of the reasons why. Your dog Fido is an infallible earthquake detector. Whenever an earthquake is about to strike, he senses it, and barks hysterically and runs around in circles. One day, Fido starts barking hysterically and running around in circles. Sure enough, an earthquake strikes right then and there. 
HumeÂ’s analysis entails that FidoÂ’s antics caused the earthquake to strike. FidoÂ’s antics immediately precede the earthquake. (So condition (1) is satisfied.) FidoÂ’s antics are adjacent with it. (So condition (2) is satisfied.) And such antics on FidoÂ’s part are always adjacent to an immediately ensuing earthquake. (So condition (3) is satisfied.) Given that FidoÂ’s antics obviously didnÂ’t cause the earthquake, HumeÂ’s analysis is wrong. 
The real cause of the earthquake presumably created some disturbance that Fido detected, that being why he engaged in his antics. Thus, some one thing was responsible both for FidoÂ’s antics and for the earthquake. The two effects fulfilled the conditions described by Hume. For this reason, the sequence they formed mimicked a bona fidecausal connection. 
When some one thing E1 has two effects E2 and E3 that appear to be 
related as cause and effect, respectively, we say that the sequence consisting of E2 and E3 is a Â“pseudo-causal processÂ” or, alternately, a case of Â“epiphenomenal causation.Â” HumeÂ’s analysis cannot distinguish 
epiphenomenal causation from actual causation. 
3.0 Problem #2: HumeÂ’s analysis entails that events canÂ’t be space-time neighbors without one of them causing the other to occur 
If E1 and E2 are any two spatiotemporally adjacent events, itÂ’s easy to find categories K1 and K2 such that E1 and E2 belong to K1 and K2, respectively, and such that any instance of K1 immediately precedes, and is adjacent with, some instance of K2. Though he doesnÂ’t know it, Bob is due for a heart attack. Right before the heart attack, Sally gently hugs him. Given the almost certainly correct supposition that nobody who is exactly SallyÂ’s height has ever hugged anyone who is exactly BobÂ’s height, it follows that any hug involving people with heights m (SallyÂ’s height) and n (BobÂ’s height) immediately precedes and is adjacent with a case of somebody of height n having a heart attack. (So if K1 is the category of hugs involving people with heights m and n, and K2 is the category of people with heights n having heart attacks, any event E1 that belongs to K1 immediately precedes and is adjacent with some event E2 that is a member of K2.) So HumeÂ’s analysis has the false consequence that the hug caused the heart attack. Given any two spatiotemporally adjacent events x and y, a similar argument shows that, if HumeÂ’s analysis is right, x caused y. Since not all such pairs of events are related as cause and effect, HumeÂ’s analysis is false. 
3.1 Problem #2 (continued): No way to fix HumeÂ’s analysis without making it viciously circular 
In response to this it will be said that: 
The categories in question must be relevant ones. K1 and K2 wonÂ’t do. TheyÂ’re the wrong ones. All youÂ’ve shown is that HumeÂ’s analysis must be modified. Instead of: 
(HC1) E1 causes E2 to occur if E1 immediately precedes and is adjacent with E2, and any event similar to E1 immediately precedes and is adjacent with some event similar to E2, 
Hume should have said: 
(HCI#) E1 causes E2 to occur if E1 immediately precedes and is adjacent with E2, and any event relevantly similar to E1 immediately precedes and is adjacent with some event relevantly similar to E2. 
This proposal doesnÂ’t work. Given any two spatiotemporally adjacent events, each of those two events will belong to many different categories. HumeÂ’s analysis is powerless to tell us whether the one caused the other until we select the relevant categories. But we canÂ’t select the relevant categories until we have the very knowledge that HumeÂ’s analysis is supposed to give us. It is only because we already know that the hug isnÂ’t what caused the heart attack that we know that K1 and K2 arenÂ’t relevant categories. 
A related point is that HC1# is viciously circular. Supposing that E1 directly causes E2, for K1 and K2 to be the Â“relevantÂ” categories is for it to be the case that itÂ’s because E1 and E2 belong to them that those events are related as cause and effect. Thus, HCI# collapses into the viciously circular 
statement that: 
(HC1+) E1 causes E2 to occur if E1 immediately precedes and is adjacent with E2, and anything like E1 causes something like E2 to occur. 
4.0 Problem #3: HumeÂ’s analysis falsely assumes that spatiotemporal position is non-relative 
According to Hume, x is a cause of y only if x and y are space-time neighbors. Thus, Hume analyzes the concept of causality in terms of the concepts of space and time. Were it to turn out that the concepts of space and time are themselves to be understood in terms of the concept of causality, HumeÂ’s analyses would be viciously circular. HeÂ’d be analyzing causality in terms of itself and thus not analyzing it at all. 
In fact, the concepts of space and time are to be understood in terms of the concept of causality, and HumeÂ’s analysis is viciously circular for this reason. According to modern physics, E1 precedes E2 iff itÂ’s possible for a signal beginning with E1 to be sent to E2. E1 and E2 are simultaneous iff it isnÂ’t possible for a signal beginning with either to be sent to the other. Order in time is thus to be understood in causal terms.[332] 

So is order in space. Events happen in different places if, and only if, something can affect the one that cannot affect the other. If x and y are in coincident places, nothing can affect the one without affecting the other. If x and y are not in coincident places, something can affect the one without affecting the other. Thus, x and y are in different places exactly if something affecting the one may fail to affect the other. So if one says that x and y occupy distinct but adjacent places, or that they occupy some one place, one is ipso facto making a causal statement. Thus, HumeÂ’s analysis of causality is circular, given that it analyzes Â‹x causes y to occurÂ› in terms of Â‹x is spatiotemporally adjacent with y.Â› 
4.1 Problem #3 (continued) 
Here is a similar line of thought. It would be meaningless to say that object x moved but that its causal liaisons to other objects didnÂ’t change for that very reason. If I approach you, my causal relations to you change, and so do your causal relations to me. After those changes are set aside, there is nothing left: there is no Â“pureÂ” change in position underlying all the causal changes. 
Also, the concept of spatial occupancy is a causal concept. What is it for me to be occupying this place? It is for it to be harder than it would otherwise be for you to enter this place. It makes no sense to say: Â“x is occupying spatial region R, but xÂ’s occupancy of R has no effect on what things other than x must do to occupy R.Â” To occupy a place is to make it harder, other things equal, than it would otherwise be for other things to enter that place. 
Hume analyzes causality in terms of the concept of spatial occupancy. E1 causes E2 only if they occupy adjacent, or coincident, spaces. But since E1Â’s (or E2Â’s) occupancy of a place is itself to be understood in causal terms, HumeÂ’s analysis analyzes causality in terms of itself and therefore doesnÂ’t 
analyze it at all. 
A corollary of the fact that spatiotemporal relations are causal relations is that, contrary to what Hume alleges, we do see causal processes and, moreover, we see them as causal processes. We see nothing instantaneous. Everything we see persists, if only for a short while. Anything that persists is, for that very reason, a causal process; and anything that is seen as persisting, which is everything that is seen, is, for that very reason, seen as a causal process. 
4.2 Two conceptions of spatiotemporal position 
There are two views as to what space and time are. According to the one view, space and time are not empty containers. Spatiotemporal positions are relations between events, and there thus couldnÂ’t be a space-time empty of events. If this view is right, itÂ’s meaningless to say some object just approaches some other. For x to precede y isnÂ’t for xÂ’s position to bear a certain relation to yÂ’s position. Given any spatiotemporal relation R, for x to bear R to y is not for xÂ’s position to bear R to yÂ’s position. There are no event-independent positions. Relations between positions are mediated by relations between events, not vice versa. It thus makes no sense to suppose that there could be bare spatiotemporal interrelations or, therefore, bare changes in such interrelations.[333] 

According to the other view, space and time exist independently of events. A consequence is that spatiotemporal positions exist independently of the events that might (or might not) occupy them. Spatiotemporal relations holding among events are to be understood in terms of spatiotemporal relations holding among positions in space-time. This means that there are absolute positions in space-time. If this view is right, it does make sense to say that one event just precedes some other event, or that one event just happens to be equidistant between two other events, and so on.[334] 

Bearing these points in mind, consider the statement that: 
(IP)[335] 
x immediately precedes and is adjacent with y, 
and suppose IP to be true. If the first view is the right one, there are no event-independent positions. In that case, xÂ’s being adjacent with y is a relation that holds directly between x and y, and to say that some position bears a certain relation to another position is to say that some event bears a certain relation to some other event. 
If the second view is the right one, the fact described by IP consists in xÂ’s occupying some position that bears a certain relation to a position that is, in turn, occupied by y. In other words, it is only because the positions they occupy are adjacent that x and y are adjacent. Thus, the second view presupposes that there are event-independent, and thus absolute, spatiotemporal positions. 
Since HumeÂ’s analysis presupposes the correctness of the second view, HumeÂ’s analysis is refuted by the very empirical and philosophical arguments that show the concept of absolute position to be an untenable one. (Further argumentation to the effect that the relational conception of space-time is the right one will be provided in this chapter, in Sections 4.2.2-5.0, and in Chapter 20, Section 8.0.) 
4.2.1 Continuity identical with causality 
Ball A crashes into previously stationary ball B, whereupon B lurches into motion. This is Hume's paradigm of an instance of causality. This change in B's condition appears discontinuous. It would not seem that way were we to have a more high-resolution understanding of the exchange of energy that is actually constitutive of the collision. 
In general, the more accurate our knowledge of what is involved in any apparently discontinuous change of state, the more we find that no discontinuities were involved. Given information about the aforementioned collision that is slightly more high-resolution than the sort of information about collisions that was available to Hume, it proves to be no more discontinuous than was A's pre-collision state of motion. I now hope to show that Hume was very much led astray, so far as his understanding of causality was concerned, by the technological limitations of his time. 
4.2.2 Continuity identical with causality (continued) 
Hume's paradigms led him to see discontinuity as a sine qua non for causality. Let event E be the aforementioned collision, and let E* be the subsequent change in B's state of motion. For Hume, E's being the cause of E* doesn't involve E*'s being the continuation of some process initiated by E. There is no torch that A is passing to B. 
"How,Â” it will be asked, Â“can you say that, for Hume, discontinuity is essential to causality? For the very opposite is clearly true. In HumeÂ’s view, cause and effect must be spatiotemporally adjacent. So for Hume, the essence of causality is continuity." 
Discontinuity takes many forms. Like Hume, the objector is focusing on only one of the many relevant forms of continuity. For Hume, E's causing E* to occur involves B's lurching into motion spontaneously. True---this sudden lurch into motion is spatiotemporally adjacent with the place where A stops moving. But the two events are otherwise disconnected. Also, A's suddenly ceasing to move is, on Hume's view, just as spontaneous as B's starting to move. So, on Hume's view, we have two discontinuities: B's starting to move and A's ceasing to move. So, for Hume, a causal nexus is a regularity whose instances are spatiotemporally adjacent discontinuities. 
Also, Hume's conception of what it is for two events to be spatiotemporally adjacent is not a coherent one, a corollary being that, if Hume is right, E's being the cause of E* doesn't in any significant way require that one of those events be continuous with the first. x and y are two objects that are relatively near each other. x and y are spatiotemporally remote from x* and y* but are otherwise just like them. Moreover, x* and y* are spatiotemporally interrelated in exactly the same way as x and y: so x*'s movements "track" x's (so, for example, if x approaches y, x* approaches y* by the same amount), and y*'s movements track y's. But one day this changes. On that day, during interval t, x moves one foot closer to y than it was before 
t. during that same interval, x* moves one foot closer to y* than it originally was.[336] 
Otherwise, x's relation to y is, with one important qualification, just like x*'s relation to y*. 
But there is a difference. Because x is now one foot closer to y than it was previously, x's causal relations to y have changed; but, despite being one foot closer to y than it used to be, x*'s causal relations to y* haven't changed at all. The amount of time that ceteris paribus[337] 
it takes light to travel from x to y has decreased, as has the amount of energy[338] 
that ceteris paribus is needed to transport a given amount of grain from x to y has decreased; and x's degree of gravitational attraction to y has increased. But the amount of time it takes light to travel from x* to y* has not decreased and neither has the amount of energy required to transport a given amount of grain from x* to y*; and x*'s gravitational attraction to y* hasn't increased at all. So there is nothing to indicate that x* has gotten one foot closer to y* than it was before: the amount of time it would take x* to travel to y* hasn't changed; since x*'s optical relationship to y* can't have changed, the way x* appears to somebody on y* hasn't changed; there would be no reason of any kind--Â­optical, kinematic, dynamic---to regard x* as having undergone a change in position relative to y*. 
Spatiotemporal changes that aren't marked by causal changes are surds. But if spatiotemporal relations were more fundamental than causal relations, they would not be surds: bare (causally antiseptic) changes in relative position would be perfectly possible. Since they're not, it makes no sense to speak of changes in relative spatiotemporal position except as supervenient on changes in relative causal relations.
