Statements about spatiotemporal relations, we must conclude, are very generic, very low-resolution statements about causal relations. 
So, in saying that E and E* are just adjacent to each other, Hume is speaking incoherently. It makes no sense to speak of mere adjacency. Adjacency is a causal concept. The way in which E and E* must be adjacent if Hume's analysis is to be free of vicious circularity must have no causal meaning: it must not be different, so far as E's causal relation to E* is concerned, from the relationship that E bears to some event that happened eons earlier, in some remote galaxy. But this eviscerates Hume's analysis, since that analysis obviously fails unless E's relationship to E* is relevantly different from its relationship to some long gone event in a distant galaxy. Since the relevant difference lies in E's causal relations to E*, Hume's analysis is doomed to vicious circularity. So, since Hume's concept of adjacency is hollow, his insistence that cause and effect be spatiotemporally adjacent is without any real meaning and doesn't undermine our contention that, for Hume, the occurrence of various discontinuities (of a certain kind) are a sine qua non for one event's causing another. 
What Hume thought is the antithesis of the truth. The essence of causality is continuity. So far as Hume's belief to the contrary had any support, it lay in 
the limited state of microphysical knowledge in his day. 
4.2.3 Continuity with causality (continued) 
Newton rightly said that the concept of "action at a distance" was "abhorrent" to anyone of any intelligence. These days, the conventional wisdom would be to say (i) that Newton's suspicion that causal influences must be propagated by intervening media was vindicated by later developments in physics but (ii) that there is nothing absurd in the supposition that there should be action at a distance. 
I agree with Newton. The sentence "there could be action at a distance" is tautologously false. To say that A is a given distance from B is to say that it takes a certain amount of time for events occurring on (or next to) A to have an effect on B. To say that an event on A "instantaneously" affects B is to say that A and B are adjacent. So it is nonsense to say that, even though A and B are remote from each other, events on A could instantaneously affect B. 
4.2.4 Continuity identical with causality (continued) 
Suppose that object A disappears in place P and, at that instant, some perfect duplicate of A, which we'll call "B,Â” appears in some place P* that is remote from P. What grounds have we for saying that B is identical with A? 
"What if we find out that A's disappearance is what caused B to appear, seemingly ex nihilo, in P*?" 
But what conceivable grounds are there for saying that A 's disappearance caused B to appear? There was no lapse in time between those two events and thus no possibility of anything being transmitted from P to P*. 
"What if we find out that these two events---A's disappearance and B's sudden appearance elsewhere---is an instance of a general regularity? Wouldn't that be evidence of some causal connection?" 
It would be evidence of epiphenomenalism causation, not of causation proper. It would be evidence that, underlying both A's disappearance and B's appearance, was some structure that, by way of continuous series of events, led to both. 
Â“But, assuming, if only for argumentÂ’s sake, that weÂ’ve definitively established that there is no such structure and a fortiori that there are no such series, what we are to say then?Â” There are two ways to answer this. The first is to say: Â“We're dealing with a brute fact.Â” The second is to say: Â“A and B are adjacent; and in stipulating that P and P* are disjoint places, we were prejudicially ruling out a viable way of explaining the concomitance in question: we must rethink what it is to say that two events are spatiotemporally adjacent.Â” 
Strange as the second response may seem, it is, I believe, de rigueur, so long as we refuse to see the concomitance in question as an unexplainable, brute fact and so long as we know there to be series of events mediating between AÂ’s disappearance and BÂ’s appearance. We must remember what we said a moment ago about the concept of action at a distance. Newton believed this concept to be incoherent. Newton, we suggested, was right. One eventÂ’s being adjacent with some other event is identical with the oneÂ’s being able to have immediate effects on the other. 
Assuming the truth of the assumptions within which weÂ’re currently working, I would propose that adjacency is a relative concept. Two events, x and y, may be adjacent relative to certain forms of causal influence and nonÂ­adjacent relative to other forms. It makes no sense, as we saw, to say that, by virtue of changing its position relative to B, AÂ’s causal relation to B failed to change. And the reason it makes no sense is that changes in position are causal changes. There are different ways in which one event can affect another. Let E and E* be two different forms of energy, and let x and y be two events such that E takes a finite amount of time to travel from x to y and such that E* takes no time at all to travel from x to y. Nothing can travel faster than light. (So E* cannot travel faster than light.) Light takes a non-null amount of time to travel along any path whose length is greater than zero. So if it was by transmitting E* that AÂ’s disappearance brought about BÂ’s appearance, then those two events were adjacent. That is, they were adjacent relative to E*, even though they were also non-adjacent relative to E. In general, if we are forced to operate with the framework within which our adversary insists that we operate, the right way to model this data is to say: Â“Relative position is itself a relative notion. Given two events x and y, they may be adjacent relative to certain forms of energy and non-adjacent relative to others.Â” 
This model is a coherent one. It seems incoherent only if one assumes that there is event-independent spatiotemporal position. But judgments as to spatiotemporal position cease to have meaning the moment they cease to do anything more than register causal relations between the events in question. Let events x and y be such that: 
(i) xÂ’s distance from y is non-null, given the amount of time that it takes causal process K to start with the one event and end with the second, 
and such that: 
(ii) xÂ’s distance from y is null, given the amount of time that it takes causal process K* to start with the one event and end with the second. 
Given (i) and (ii), weÂ’d have to say that, relative to processes of the same kind as K, x is not adjacent with y, but that, relative to processes of the same kind as K*, x and y are adjacent. It is logically possible that (i) and (ii) should both be true. And, by doubly relativizing spatiotemporal position in the way just described, we can hold onto the fecund principle that nothing travels 
faster than light. 
5.0 Problem #4: HumeÂ’s analysis isnÂ’t strictly empirical 
We donÂ’t see light; we see illuminated surfaces. Similarly, we donÂ’t see space; we see spatially separated objects. Look around youÂ—at your desk, at the painting hanging on the wall, on the door on the opposite side of the room, etc. These things are spatially separated from one another. And there is no doubt that you know this through observation. But do you observe the space that separates any two of these items? 
You do not. You observe the items. On the basis of their appearances, along with background knowledge (e.g., the intensity, duration, and nature of the effort involved in your walking from your desk to the painting), you infer that the desk is separated by (say) a distance of approximately 10 feet from the painting. 
The sense in which one perceives space and time is not comparable to the sense in which one perceives the objects in them. One perceives events. Those events all have various properties. Among them are properties that spatiotemporally order them. You abstract the concepts of space and time from your knowledge of these properties (or property-instances, rather). But you no more perceive space or time than you perceive propertyless substances. In fact, the concepts of an empty space and an empty time belong in the same category as the concept of such a substrate, and all three concepts belong in the same category as the concept of a square circle. Compare the statement: 
(1) A day has just passed since I last experienced gastrointestinal pain, and during that day not a single event occurred in the entire universe, 
with: 
(2) I just experienced gastrointestinal pain. 
In a world in which (1) was true literally nothing would have happened to affect the speaker's relation to his last episode of gastrointestinal pain. There would be nothing in the condition of any constituent, no matter how big or how small, that would distinguish a world where (1) was true from one where 
(2) was true. 
To speak meaningfully of there being a passage of time, there must be events. Otherwise I'd be perfectly in my rights to say that between the time at which I began to type this very sentence and the time at which I stopped typing the previous one there was an interval of a day, or of a billion years, when in actuality the interval was less than one second. 
Statements about the "passage of time" are very abstract statements about events; they're statements about the events one has experienced that register such generic properties of events that one can assume the events in one's interlocutor's experience to have relevantly similar properties. 
It is thus through conception, not perception, that we grasp time per se. And this feat of conception is a misguided one, since there is no such thing as time per se. (Some events happen before others; but this isnÂ’t because those events occupy certain positions in some event-independent order.) 
For similar reasons, it is through conception, not perception, that we grasp space per seÂ—it being events in space, not space itself, that we perceiveÂ— and the concept of a space devoid of events (for reasons slightly subtler than, but basically parallel to, those just stated in connection with time) is a broken one. 
To sum up: the concepts of space and time are theoretical concepts. So, in trying to analyze causality in terms of the concept of spatiotemporal position, Hume is trying to understand causation in terms of two highly theoretical concepts. Thus, HumeÂ’s analysis of causality, like so many other analyses of his, is not empirical; for that analysis assumes that what are in fact constructs are givens. More importantly, that analysis is false; for, in taking those constructs as givens, it assumes, falsely and incoherently, that there exists an event-independent spatiotemporal order. 
6.0 HumeÂ’s supposedly empirical analysis a foil for a non-empirical analysis[H13] 

Hume says that we donÂ’t observe forces. But this seems false. When you are trying to lift a heavy suitcase or trying to arm wrestle a much stronger person, you are, so it would seem, observationally aware of a force. 
Hume considers this very point. In response to it, he says that what you are aware of is a mere sequence of events. You have various perceptions. Some are visualÂ—you see your opponentÂ’s sweaty, determined face. Some are tactileÂ—you feel your opponentÂ’s increasingly sweaty hand. Some are kinestheticÂ—you feel your arm moving the wrong way. But Hume says you donÂ’t perceive any force in all thisÂ—even though, because you are in the grips of some wrong theories, you think you do. 
But this seems very wrong. ItÂ’s a datum that you feel your arm being forced to move in a way you donÂ’t want it to be. That doesnÂ’t mean that this feeling is accurate. Maybe itÂ’s a hallucination, like oneÂ’s visual perception of a pink elephant. But itÂ’s a datum that you have such a feeling, even though it isnÂ’t a datum that itÂ’s accurate; and in denying that itÂ’s a datum, Hume isnÂ’t being true to his own empiricism. 
Plus, this response of HumeÂ’s is decidedly contrived. If, in describing your arm-wrestling experience, you left out the part about how you felt as though your arm was being moved the wrong way, youÂ’d be seriously under-describing your experience. 
Thus, if the observational evidence is to be taken at face value, forces do exist. This doesnÂ’t mean that the observational evidence should be taken at face value. But it means that HumeÂ’s denial of causality cannot, if legitimate, be based on strictly empirical grounds. And this means that his supposedly empirical argument against causation (a) isn't empirical and (b) is only as good as some other, purely a priori argument. 
That other argument, it will be recalled, is as follows (what follows is not a quotation): 
(NF)[339] 
The very concept of a force is an incoherent one. Were they to exist, forces would just be more constituents of the physical world. They would thus be no more capable than vases and rocks and so forth of constituting the cement of the universe. The idea of a force that wasnÂ’t that sort of cement is a contradiction in terms. Therefore the concept of force is an incoherent one.Â” 
We saw that vases and rocks are such cement. Any given physical object is a series of events any two of which are Â“cementedÂ” together. Therefore, NF is no good. Therefore HumeÂ’s analysis of causality is no good. 
Chapter 16 HumeÂ’s Second Analysis of Causality 
1.0 The counterfactual analysis 
Hume gives two analyses of causation. WeÂ’ve just discussed the first. According to the second, 
(CF)[340] 
For E1 to cause E2 to occur is for it to be the case that E2 wouldnÂ’t have occurred unless E1 had occurred. 
This is known as the counterfactual analysis of causality. 
Why advocate CF? The elevator comes because somebody pushed the button. If the button hadnÂ’t been pushed, the elevator wouldnÂ’t have come. The gun went off because somebody pulled the trigger. If the trigger hadnÂ’t been pulled, the gun wouldnÂ’t have gone off. No cause, no effect. Hence CF. 

1.1 CF easily confused with a weaker position 
CF must be distinguished from the related, but weaker claim that: 
(CF*) Given any two events E1 and E2, such that E1 precedes E2, E1 caused E2 to occur just in case E2 wouldnÂ’t have occurred unless E1 had occurred. 
What is the difference between CF and CF*? A story will help us answer this question. Smith is mathematically omniscient---there is no mathematical truth that he doesnÂ’t know. But he knows nothing that isnÂ’t a mathematical truth. (So he doesnÂ’t know that Paris is the capital of France or that snow is white.) Thus, given any mathematical truth T, Smith knows T, and that given any non-mathematical truth T*, Smith does not know T*. ItÂ’s therefore true that: 
(SM*) T is a mathematical truth iff Smith knows T. 
But it isnÂ’t true that: 
(SM) For T to be a mathematical truth is for Smith to know T. 
Similarly, given only that CF* is true, it doesnÂ’t follow that CF is true. But if CF is true, it does follow that CF* is true. 
CF and CF*, though different statements, are extensionally equivalent. In other words, given any two events E1 and E2, if CF entails that E1 caused E2, so does CF*, and vice versa. If CF is to be correct, it must be extensionally correctÂ—that is, it must entail E1 caused E2 just in case E2 wouldnÂ’t have occurred unless E1 had occurred. Given that CF and CF* are extensionally equivalent, the one is extensionally correct iff the other is as well. 
2.0 Why, even if itÂ’s extensionally correct, CF is false 
Jones drinks poison and as a result dies at time t. (From now on, weÂ’ll leave the Â“at tÂ” implicit.) It may well be true that: 
(SB) Jones wouldnÂ’t have died if he hadnÂ’t consumed poison. 
SB seems to entail that: 
(WB) Given any world W in which Jones doesnÂ’t drink the poison but is otherwise just like our world (or, in any case, is as much like our world as JonesÂ’ not consuming poison in it allows it to be), Jones doesnÂ’t die in W. 
Question: Why doesnÂ’t Jones die in W? Because nothing in W causes him to die. No cause, no effect. In our world, the cause is present. In W, it isnÂ’t. WBÂ’s truth is thus to be understood in terms of the fact that, in our world, JonesÂ’ drinking the poison is what killed him. So SB no more constitutes an analysis of the statement Â“Jones died because he drank the poisonÂ” than Â“Smith (the mathematical prodigy mentioned in the previous section) believes that there are no regular, 17-sided polygonsÂ” constitutes a proof or an explanation of the fact that there are no regular, 17-sided polygons or of any other mathematical truth. And just as SmithÂ’s believing that there are no regular, 17-sided polygons is to be understood in terms of the truth of that statement, not vice versa, so WB is to be understood in terms of the truth of SB and thus in terms of the fact that JonesÂ’ drinking poison is what killed him, not vice versa. In general, Â“E2 wouldnÂ’t have occurred where E1 did not,Â” when true, is to be understood in terms of the fact that E1Â’s occurring is what caused E2. So even if CF is extensionally correct, itÂ’s no analysis of the concept of causality. 

3.0 The vicious circularity of CF, and an outline of a positive analysis of counterfactual truth 
CF assumes that the concept of counterfactual truth is not itself to be explained in terms of the concept of causality. But that may well be false. The statement: 
(SB) If Smith hadnÂ’t fallen off the building, he wouldnÂ’t have died, 
seems to be equivalent, or nearly so, with: 
(SB*) Falling off the building caused an otherwise unthreatened Smith to die. 
But not all counterfactuals register causal facts. For example: 
(SH) If six-feet tall Smith were half his current height, heÂ’d be three-feet tall, 
is equivalent, or nearly so, with: 
(SH*) Smith is six-feet tall entails that anything that is three-feet tall is half SmithÂ’s height. 
Notice that SH is analytically true, whereas SB is non-analytically true. It thus seems to me that counterfactuals are just disguised causal or logical assertions and that, consequently, alternative worlds have no place in any decent analysis of them. In any case, these cases provide us with evidence that counterfactual truth is itself to be understood in terms of causality and that CF is therefore guilty of vicious circularity. 

4.0 Why CF isnÂ’t even extensionally correct 
CF assumes that that thereÂ’s no causal redundancy in the worldÂ—that, were a given mechanism to fail, nothing would step into the breach. But sometimes there are back-up mechanisms. If, for some strange reason, electrocuting condemned criminal Smith didnÂ’t kill him, the state would have found some other way to do so. Thus, the statement Â“the cause of SmithÂ’s death was electrocutionÂ” isnÂ’t equivalent with Â“if Smith hadnÂ’t been electrocuted, he would not have died.Â” And this seems to show that CF is wrong. 
Admittedly, CF has little trouble dealing with this case, and with many others of its ilk. Smith didnÂ’t just die; he died in a very specific way. And he wouldnÂ’t have died that way if, instead of being electrocuted, heÂ’d been shot. This suggests that itÂ’s only when events are seriously under-described that there appear to be counterexamples to CF. 
But this maneuver doesnÂ’t always work. A and B are both trying to push the same doorbell button. Since neither is aware of the otherÂ’s presence, each acts exactly as he would have in the other manÂ’s absence. The button only has room for one finger. Both fingers get there at the same time, but AÂ’s finger, being the bigger one, crowds out BÂ’s. The requisite electrical signal is sent at time t. Had A been absent, BÂ’s would have struck the same doorbell; and, given the rapidity with which BÂ’s arm was moving, the electrical signal would have been sent at precisely t. 
It may be that, were it not for AÂ’s presence, B wouldnÂ’t have pushed the doorbell in exactly the same way as A. (Our story may even require this.) But the signal is sent at the right time, and thatÂ’s all that matters. It doesnÂ’t matter how exactly B pushed the doorbell. Doorbells are binary systems. The signal is either sent or it isnÂ’t. 
4.1 An objection 
In response, it might said that: 
(LF)[341] 
Â“Perhaps the laws of physics donÂ’t validate your point,Â” one might protest. Â“Maybe itÂ’s a matter of physical law that nothing happens in quite the same way in a world where its actual cause is absent and some stand-in has to take its place[H14] 
.Â” 
If correct, LF is a complete disaster for CF. First of all, LF is an empirical point. Empirical investigation might or might not bear it out. But even if it did bear it out, the mere fact that empirical research was needed to verify LF is enough to show that LF has no place in a philosophical analysis of counterfactuals. Such an analysis is supposed to identify what, as a matter of logic, is meant by statements like SB. ItÂ’s obviously an interesting question what the correct physical analysis of SB is. But here weÂ’re doing logical, not physical, analysis; weÂ’re making it clear what SB means. And surely what SB means doesnÂ’t include some as-of-yet undiscovered laws of physics. 
We may conclude that the counterfactual analysis of causation is a failure. 
Chapter 17 Counterfactuals 
1.0 David Lewis on counterfactuals 
Should it turn out that the concept of counterfactual truth has no logical integrity, it would follow that CF had no logical integrity. But we canÂ’t know whether that concept has any integrity until we have an answer to the question: What does it mean to say that, if P had been the case, Q would have been the case? In the next chapter weÂ’ll examine the orthodox answer to this question and, having found fault with it, replace it with one of our own. 
The most famous analysis of counterfactual truth is due to David Lewis (1941Â–2001).[342] 
His analysis is beautifully clear and straightforward. According to Lewis, the meaning of[H15] 
: 
(KN)[343] 
Â“if kangaroos didnÂ’t have tails, they would fall overÂ” 
is: 
(OK)[344] 
Given any world W where kangaroos donÂ’t have tails, kangaroos fall over, provided that W is as much like our world as is permitted by the fact that, in it, kangaroos donÂ’t have tails. 
In general, the right analysis of counterfactual truth, according to Lewis, is this: 
(LA)[345] 
Â“given any world W where P is the case, Q is the case, provided that W is as much like our world as is permitted by the fact that, in it, P is the case.Â” 
2.0 The role of other worlds in LewisÂ’ analysis 
LewisÂ’ analysis obviously assumes that other Â“worldsÂ” exist. This raises the question: What does Lewis mean by the term Â“worldÂ”? There are two options. 
Option 1: Like our world, these other worlds are space-time manifolds that are populated by objects and events. 
Option 2: These other Â“worldsÂ” are representations of some kind or other (sets of statements, presumably). 
LetÂ’s consider each option. For argumentÂ’s sake, assume that these worlds are sets of statements. In that case, if LA is correct, counterfactuals merely register interpropositional relations. In other words, KN merely registers the fact that the statement Â“kangaroos donÂ’t have tailsÂ” bears some sort of relation (presumably, one of confirmation) to the statement Â“kangaroos fall over.Â” But if thatÂ’s the right analysis, then until this relation is identified, LA fails to say what counterfactuals are. And once it does identify that relation, it wonÂ’t be necessary to talk about other worlds at all. 
Lewis sees this and, for this very reason, he holds that the worlds in question are real worldsÂ—space-time manifolds populated by events and objects. Lewis is thus a realist about other worlds. 
3.0 Some consequences of modal realism 
As you might predict, the standard objection to LewisÂ’ analysis is as follows: 
(SO) We donÂ’t know if there are other worlds. What we do know is that, even if there are other worlds, we donÂ’t know anything about them. So nothing happening in these other worlds, if they even exist, provides the basis for our counterfactual knowledge. 
[346]SO is obviously true. In any case, weÂ’ll argue for it in Section 5.0. 
But letÂ’s start out by granting LewisÂ’ assumption that counterfactuals, when true, hold in virtue of states of affairs that obtain in veritable alternative worlds. If we show that given this assumption, LA fails, then weÂ’ve shown that it fails relative to its own terms and that there is thus no hope for it. 
Let W be our worldÂ—the real world. In W, Smith intentionally shoots Jones, killing him. There were no other threats to JonesÂ’ life; therefore: 
(SK) If Smith had not shot Jones, Jones would be alive. 
If LA is right, SK means the following: 
(LASK): Let W* be a world where Smith doesnÂ’t shoot Jones but that is as much like our world as that fact lets it be: in W*, Jones is alive. 
In W, Smith doesnÂ’t just shoot Jones. That event has a cause. (It actually has a plurality of causes. But for the sake of simplicity, weÂ’ll just speak of Â“the causeÂ” of that event.) Let E be that cause. Presumably one of E's components is an intention on Smith's part to kill Jones. But whatever E is, it canÂ’t occur in W*, at least not in its entirety. So, in W*, either Smith doesnÂ’t intend to kill Jones and therefore doesnÂ’t shoot Jones; or he does shoot Jones, but Jones is wearing a bulletproof vest. It could be anything. To fix our ideas, letÂ’s suppose that, in W* SmithÂ’s hand seizes up just before he pulls the trigger, the gun drops, Jones gets away. Let E* be the event that, in W*, makes SmithÂ’s hand seize up. 
What we said about E is true of E*. E* didnÂ’t just come out of nowhere; it 
itself had a cause. Let E*2 be that cause. And E*2 had a causeÂ—and E*2Â’s cause had a cause, and so on. So, in W*, we have a long chain of events (E*1....E*n) not a single one of which occurs in W. Depending on how far 
back this chain has to go, it could make W* very different from W. In fact, W* might be so different that it might not be able to contain a Smith or Jones to begin with; and even if it did, thereÂ’s no guarantee that Smith would shoot Jones or that, if he did, Jones wouldnÂ’t be wearing a bulletproof vest, etc. 
Events have causal roots. Two worlds cannot differ with respect to a single event unless they differ with respect to all of the causal antecedents of those events. But, given that those go back to the beginning of time, that means that theyÂ’ll differ so much that the one world becomes unable to validate the counterfactuals of the other. 
It may be that some events are completely and entirely uncaused. But, in W, that happens only where micro-events are concerned. SmithÂ’s shooting Jones (in W) is an extremely complex event, involving innumerably causally cohesive parts and having deep roots in the past. So even if some events in our world are uncaused, SmithÂ’s shooting Jones isnÂ’t one of them. 
And even if it is one of them, itÂ’s useless as far as LA is concerned. A logical analysis of LASK canÂ’t assume the results of empirical facts not in evidence and therefore cannot assume that SmithÂ’s shooting Jones is totally uncaused. In fact, such an analysis, being of a logical as opposed to an empirical kind, canÂ’t make any empirical assumptions. 
3.1 Some consequences of modal realism (continued) 
But even if it could assume this, LA would still be in trouble. First of all, we canÂ’t say that, in W*, SmithÂ’s not shooting Jones is just as uncaused as the event of his doing so in W. In other words, we canÂ’t say that, in W*, SmithÂ’s hand just seized upÂ—that, in other words, there was no causal basis for it. For, to the extent that this event was uncaused, any other event could have happened instead of it. We could, of course, just stipulate that, in W*, SmithÂ’s hand seizes up. But that wonÂ’t help. If, in W*, SmithÂ’s hand just seizes up, then there will be at least one other worldÂ—call it W#Â—such that W# is just like W* except that, in W#, SmithÂ’s hand didnÂ’t seize up or, if it did, something else happened that led to Jones being killed. In which case, LASK will be false. For, contrary to what LASK says, there would be a world satisfying the relevant conditions in which Jones dies. ItÂ’s not a good idea, in general, to posit causal slack in the worlds we want to validate our counterfactuals, since that same policy makes those very worlds unreliable in the way of validating our counterfactuals. 
LewisÂ’ own way of dealing with the problem is different from those just considered. In his view, some miracle happens in W* that prevents E from occurring there. So even though the natural laws in W* demand that E happen there (or, at any rate, demand it no less than the laws of our world demand it here), a Â“miracleÂ” suspends these laws, and Jones lives. 
Lewis is saying that, if a world validates LASK, there is some miracle in it (at a certain time, in a certain place). So W*, by virtue of being able to validate LASK, also validates the following counterfactual: 
(MLASK) If Smith had not shot Jones, then a miracle would have happened. 
W* is, by hypothesis, a world where Smith doesnÂ’t shoot Jones but is otherwise maximally like our world. 
In W*, thereÂ’s a miracle (at a certain time and a certain place). So W* makes MLASK true if it makes LASK true. But MLASK isnÂ’t a true counterfactual. And, of course, if a miracle is needed to validate MLASK, then a miracle will be needed to validate any counterfactual. What we just said about MLASK is true of Â“if Jones hadnÂ’t driven drunk, he wouldnÂ’t have crashed his car,Â” Â“if Brown hadnÂ’t been so diligent in college, he wouldnÂ’t have gotten into a reputable graduate program,Â” and so on. So assuming these counterfactuals were true, the same would hold of (e.g.): Â“if Brown hadnÂ’t been so diligent, a miracle would have happened,Â” which is obviously a preposterous counterfactual. 
Also, SmithÂ’s (actually) shooting Jones is an enormously complex event, involving trillions upon trillions of mass-energy displacements. In W*, those events canÂ’t happen. Which means that, in W*, it isnÂ’t just one miracle that has to happen: itÂ’s trillions upon trillions of them. Which, in its turn, makes W*Â’s relevance in this context extremely questionable. WeÂ’re finding that, in order to get W* to validate LASK, we have to doctor itÂ—to mutilate it. But the very fact that we have to tamper with itÂ—that we must employ such artifices to find a world that, in keeping with LA, can validate LASKÂ— practically proves that LA is wrong. A theory that only doctored data supports is a bad theory, and LewisÂ’ analysis of counterfactuals is untenable or, at the absolute least, grossly under-supported. 

4.0 How LewisÂ’ realism about possible worlds almost saves the day for the Humean 
If weÂ’re right, counterfactuals are identical with causal statements. According to David Hume, nothing makes anything happen. If Hume is right, itÂ’s hard to see how anything could, in any real sense, cause anything to happen. But this seems a little strange. 
David Lewis accepts HumeÂ’s analysis. This is because, like Hume, Lewis is a hardcore empiricist and, for the same reasons as Hume, rejects the idea that there are forces. But Lewis rightly thinks that denying the existence of causality is going too far. He sees that, given a realistic attitude towards other worlds along with an acceptance of the counterfactual analysis of causality, the presumption that events cause other events to occur can be reconciled with Humeanism. (By Â“HumeanismÂ” I mean the view that nothing makes anything happen.) For these reasons, Lewis says that: 
(LC)[347] 
In our world, event x causes y to occur if, given any world W where x doesnÂ’t happen but is otherwise as much like our world as that fact permits, y doesnÂ’t occur. 
But weÂ’ve already seen why this stratagem fails. Given that x occurs in our world, a world in which x doesnÂ’t occur will bear so little resemblance to our world that it wonÂ’t be able to validate the target-counterfactual (viz., Â“if x hadnÂ’t happened, y wouldnÂ’t have happenedÂ”). 
5.0 The basic problem with LewisÂ’ analysis (LA): revisiting SO 
We obviously canÂ’t see or otherwise sense-perceive what is going on in other worlds; nor can we sense-perceive evidence of what is going on in such worlds. Any knowledge that we have of what is going on in them is parasitic on our knowledge of counterfactual truths. So even if: 
(i) had x not happened, y wouldnÂ’t have either, 
is true, just in case: 
(ii) given an x-free world W that is otherwise just like ours, y doesnÂ’t happen in W, 
our knowledge of (i) has nothing to do with other worlds. This shows that we know (i) to be true because we know of some fact in our world that coincides with the fact registered by (i). This, in its turn, shows that other worlds have nothing to do with counterfactual truth. Which shows that LA is false. 
Chapter 18 Explanatory vs. Statistical Probability 
1.0 Humeanism and probability statements 
In keeping with common sense, I believe that statements about the past confirm statements about the future and, more generally, that statements about the known confirm statements about the unknown. 
It is hard to reconcile this belief with Humeanism. David Lewis is the only Humean who has even come close to succeeding in showing Humeanism to be compatible with the presumption that statements about the known can confirm statements about the unknown. To understand his argument, we must make a few preliminary points about probability. 
LetÂ’s suppose that: 
(BU)[348] 
At time t, there are 10 balls in the urn. Nine are white. The other one is black. And, at t, thereÂ’s nothing in the urn besides these 10 balls. You know all this. But this is all you know thatÂ’s relevant to the probability of your pulling a white as opposed to black ball out of the urn. 
BU isnÂ’t analytic. Nor are the statements composing it. But it does seem to be analytic that: 
(BB)[349] 
Given a single chance to pull a single ball out of the urn, the probability that youÂ’ll remove a black ball from the urn is 1 in 10. 
It thus seems obvious that, given BU, it is analytic that BB holds. 
But it isnÂ’t analytic. It isnÂ’t even true. Given only BU, you are no more entitled to think that youÂ’ll withdraw a white ball than you are entitled to think that youÂ’ll withdraw a black ball or a green ball or an iguana. 
It may be that, given BU along with some reasonable assumptions (e.g., that it isnÂ’t a law of physics that white objects cannot be displaced or that, at time t, all white balls in urns turn into black balls or green balls or iguanas), BB is analytic. 
But if any one of the parenthetical assumptions is false, you have no chance, given BU, of pulling a white ball out of the urn. Since these assumptions arenÂ’t analytically true, BB doesnÂ’t analytically follow from BU. 
In general, when words like Â“probableÂ” (and Â“probability,Â” etc.) refer to statistical probability they must be taken in a strictly non-temporal sense. The statement: 
(*) Given that, at time t, there are 10 apples in the barrel and only three oranges (and no other objects), your chances at later time t* of selecting an orange are 3 in 13, 
is false. What is true is: 
(*1) Given that, at time t, there are 10 apples in the barrel and only three oranges (and no other objects), your chances at time t of selecting an orange are 3 in 13, but only if the term Â“selectingÂ” is used metaphorically. 
More precisely, (*1) is true only if it coincides with the trivial claim that, if three out of the 13 objects in the barrel are oranges, then three out of the 13 objects in the barrel are oranges. 
Of course, even a Humean can grant the truth of trivial probability statements, such as (*). So if, by some remote chance, it could be shown that non-trivial probability statements (e.g., given that in the past all metal has expanded when heated, it will probably continue to do so) could be identified with trivial ones, then the Humean would be able to accommodate the presumption, so crucial to thought and scientific explanation, that non-trivial probability statements are correct. David Lewis makes a noble effort to do just this. 
2.0 Why for this reason Humeanism canÂ’t explain explanation 
LetÂ’s start by describing the viewpoint of common sense. In saying that Smith will probably disgrace himself at his job interview, given that he drank an entire bottle of gin right before, you are saying that he all but guaranteed an unacceptable performance at the interview. In saying that BrownÂ’s victory is probable, given that he drugged his opponentÂ’s water, youÂ’re saying that he all but necessitated his opponentÂ’s defeat. In these contexts, the word Â“probablyÂ” doesnÂ’t have the emptily statistical meaning borne by its homonym in statements like: 
(NC) Given that better than nine out of 10 people donÂ’t own a pogo stick, a person chosen at random probably wonÂ’t own one. 
If common sense is right, statistical probability isnÂ’t explanatory probability (even though statistical probability is sometimes a consequence of explanatory probability: other things being equal, explanatory probabilities are expressed by statistical probabilities; and itÂ’s from this fact that the Humean conception of probability derives what little credibility it has). 
The Humean denies all this, since he thinks that nothing makes anything happen. But this means that he can't explain the fact that anything can be explained. A world where nothing makes anything happen is one where nothing has any rootsÂ—where, no matter what the conditions are, any outcome is just as likely as any other. 
The Humean has three choices: 
(i) reject the presumption that some things can be explained; 
(ii) stop being a Humean, since Humeanism is inconsistent with this presumption; 
or: 
(iii) try to reconcile Humeanism with this presumption. 
Obviously Humeans choose (iii). 
They defend this choice by saying that, contrary to what we said a moment ago, the concepts expressed by words like Â“causeÂ” and Â“probableÂ” are of a strictly statistical kind. Â“Given E1, E2 is probableÂ” means Â“most events of the same kind as E1 are accompanied by events of the same kind as E2.Â” And, as previously discussed, Â“E1 causes E2 to occurÂ” means Â“given any event of the same kind as E1, there occurs an adjacent, subsequent event the same kind as E2.Â” 
The latter claim is a complete failure. There is no way to say what it is for events to be Â“of the same kindÂ” as E1 or E2 that doesnÂ’t render HumeÂ’s theory of causality viciously circular. (We saw in Chapter 15.) The very same argument mutatis mutandis holds in connection with the Humean theory of probability. But Lewis chooses to argue for this theory; and he does so very cleverly. So letÂ’s hear him out. 
3.0 LewisÂ’ argument[350] 

WeÂ’ve just seen that, even within a Humean framework, probability judgments are rational when they merely redescribe statisticsÂ—that, for example, (#) may be rationally accepted if itÂ’s just a way of saying that, at a given time, one person out of two weighs more than 50 pounds. Probability judgments are irrational, given a Humean framework, when they involve extrapolations. LewisÂ’ metaphysical apparatus gives him a way of sidestepping this problem. 
Bearing all of this in mind, letÂ’s suppose that, up until time t, whenever a rock with a mass of m or more, moving with a velocity of v or more, has collided with a window of thickness t or less, the window shattered upon impact. In that case, presumably, itÂ’s reasonable to judge that, the next time such a rock strikes such a window, the window will shatter. The non-Lewisian Humean is stuck; he has no way to validate this presumption. The Lewisian isnÂ’t stuck. HereÂ’s what he says[351]: 
(LA): Let C1 be the class of worlds where, before time t, such windows shatter when struck by such rocks and where, after time t, such windows continued to shatter when struck by such rocks; and let C2 be the class of worlds where, before 
time t, such windows shatter when struck by such rocks and 
where, after time t, such windows didnÂ’t shatter when struck by 
such rocks. C1 has more members than C2. 
For the non-Lewisian Humean, judgments about what is likely to happen next time are great leaps into the unknown. For the Lewisian Humean, such judgments merely redescribe what is already there. To say that next time such a collision occurs the window is likely to break is to say that there are more worlds where it does break than where it doesnÂ’t. If itÂ’s given that exactly one of the cards in the deck is a King of Spades, it follows trivially that, given an arbitrary card, it has a 1 in 52 chance of being a King of Spades. Our judgments about what will happen to windows in future collisions are equally trivial. 
3.1 Why LA fails 
Any knowledge we have of what happens in other worlds after t will be at least as uncertain as our knowledge of what happens in our own world after t. There are two reasons for this. Any knowledge that we might have about anything in other worlds will be at least as uncertain as any knowledge that we have about anything in our own world. Moreover, any knowledge that we have of what happens after t in other worlds will be based on our knowledge, so far as we have any, of what happens after t in our world. So LA goes through only if itÂ’s assumed, question-beggingly, that we know what will happen in our own worldÂ’s future. 
3.2 Why LA fails (continued) 
But there are deeper problems with LA. Here we must remember what Hume said about inductive inference: 
(HA)[352]: Given only that such and such has happened, it canÂ’t be assumed that such and such will continue to happen Â—unless itÂ’s assumed, question-beggingly, that what has happened will continue to happen. In general, given only that such and such is true of the known, it canÂ’t be assumed that it also holds of the unknownÂ—unless itÂ’s assumed, questionÂ­beggingly, that the unknown resembles the known. 
An analogue of what HA shows concerning inductive knowledge holds with respect to knowledge of other worlds. Given only that, in other worlds, such and such happens after time t, it canÂ’t be assumed that such and such happens after t in this worldÂ—unless itÂ’s assumed, question-beggingly, that what holds in circumstances already known to us also holds in circumstances not yet known to us. So LA goes through only if itÂ’s assumed, questionÂ­beggingly, that inductive inference works. 
In objection to these points, one might say that: 
You, the author, are missing the very point of LA. Supposing that there are 10 balls in the urn, and only one of them is white, the statement (Â“WBÂ” is short for Â“white ballÂ”): 
(WB) the probability of an arbitrary one of them being white is 1 in 10, 
holds as a matter of definition and, therefore, can be affirmed without begging the question against HA. The beauty of LA is that it assimilates apparently non-innocuous probability judgments into the class of trivially true, totally innocuous probability judgments, such as WB. LA shows that: 
(UB) the probability that future unsupported objects will fall is extremely high, given that all such objects (apart from helium balloons, etc.) have fallen so far. 
UB, which is non-trivial and (in this context) objectionable, is in the same category as WB, which is trivial and unobjectionable. 
This line of thought embodies a confusion that has vitiated the efforts of epistemologists and philosophers of science for centuries. This confusion is of such importance that it deserves a section of its own. 

4.0 Statistical vs. explanatory probability and the solution to the lottery paradox 
The second word in WB is nothing more than a homonym of the second word in UB. In WB, the word Â“probabilityÂ” has a purely statistical meaning. In UB, it has an explanatory meaning. Philosophers have tried to assimilate explanatory probability to statistical probability. And, while this may initially seem like good sense, itÂ’s as misguided as trying to show that a bank (financial institution) is a certain kind of bank (riverÂ’s edge). This is made clear by the following paradox, commonly referred to as the Â“lottery paradoxÂ” (Â“LP,Â” for short): 
(LP) ThereÂ’s a lottery. One million tickets are sold. ThereÂ’s one winner. So, given any one ticket, the probability of its losing are 999,999 in 1,000,000. You buy a ticket. Let x be this ticket. You know that (Â“LTÂ” is short for Â“losing ticketÂ”): 
(LT) the probability of ticket xÂ’s losing is 999,999 in 1,000,000. 
But do you know that itÂ’ll lose? No. It may even have been rational for you to buy the ticket. Given what you stand to lose by buying the ticket and given what you stand to gain in the remote chance that you win, it may have been in your interest to buy it, even after you take into account that the chances of your losing is 999,999 in 1,000,000. But this decision couldnÂ’t possibly have been rational if you knew that your ticket would lose. 
In general, thereÂ’s no knowledge where there isnÂ’t certainty. If, given the information at your disposal, there is any chance, no matter how small, that P isnÂ’t the case, then you donÂ’t know P. We all know (or so let us suppose) that: 
(UB) the probability that future unsupported objects will fall is extremely high, given that such objects have fallen so far. 
Is there any chance that, all of a sudden, unsupported objects will no longer fall? Yes. (The statement Â“all of a sudden, unsupported objects will no longer fallÂ” isnÂ’t ruled out by the laws of logic. So it could, theoretically, be true.) Therefore, you donÂ’t know that they wonÂ’t fall; and, by obvious extensions of this arguments, you donÂ’t know anything about the future (apart from sterile trivialities; e.g., Â“whatever happens, happensÂ”). The very concept of Â“probableÂ” knowledge is incoherent. The merely probable is ipso facto not known. To know it to be 99.9999% likely that unsupported objects will continue to fall is to not know that theyÂ’ll fall. 

4.1 The problem with LP 
LP uses word Â“probabilityÂ” in an equivocal manner. Once this is seen, LP loses any appearance of cogency that it might otherwise have had. 
LetÂ’s take another look at: 
(LT) the probability of ticket xÂ’s losing is 999,999 in 1,000,000. 
LT says that there are one million tickets but only one winner. ThatÂ’s all it says. But UB doesnÂ’t say anything of the sort. UB doesnÂ’t make a statistical point. It doesnÂ’t say: Â“nine times out of ten, unsupported objects fall.Â” It doesnÂ’t say anything at all like that. UB makes a point about the relative merits of two competing hypotheses, these being: 
(H1) unsupported objects will continue to fall, 
And: 
(H2) unsupported objects will not continue to fall. 
UB is true if, given the data that we have, H1Â’ s being true would undermine the integrity of our belief system to a lesser degree than H2Â’ s being true. Given the information that we have right now: 
(SB)[353] 
there is only an extremely low probability that walking on stilts for an hour while wearing a beanie with a propeller on it is a foolproof cure for cancer. 
Does SB say that better than nine cases of cancer out of 10 arenÂ’t cured in this way? No. It doesnÂ’t make any sort of statistical claim. SB is a claim, not about statistics, but about explanatory integrity. It says that more damage will be done to our belief system if it turns out that cancer can be cured in that way than if it turns out that it cannot. If, by some remote chance, cancer can be cured in that way, everything we Â“knowÂ” about medicine and pathology is false. But the damage wouldnÂ’t end there. Our medical beliefs are rooted in general assumptions about the causal structure of the world. (For example, given the information that Smith has gone into anaphylactic shock whenever heÂ’s eaten peanuts or anything with peanuts in it, even cutting-edge medical researchers will assume that Smith will go into anaphylactic shock if he eats peanuts that have been painted green. This assumption is rooted in generally held causal beliefs. No inside information is involved.) Were it found out that SB was false, many of the commonsense-based underpinnings of our medical beliefs would have to be reconsidered. But all of those beliefs remain intact if cancer cannot be cured in that way. It is improbable that walking on stilts (etc.) cures cancer to the extent that our current beliefs depend on its not being a cure. And itÂ’s probable that walking on stilts (etc.) isnÂ’t a cancer cure to the extent our beliefs depend on it. 
In general, P is probable to the extent that our beliefs depend on it, and improbable to the extent that they depend on its negation. 
5.0 Two kinds of probability 
Counterstatistical events are innocuous, but counter-explanatory events are not. Smith rolls double-sixes five times in a row. Statistically unlikelyÂ— yes. ImportantÂ—no. Must we change our belief system because of it? No. Need we reconsider our assumptions about the basic structure of the world? No. And it makes no difference whether itÂ’s five double-sixes in a row or a billion. The improbable sometimes happens, and thatÂ’s the end of it. When it happens, we have a nice anecdote for cocktail parties; we donÂ’t have a situation worthy of scientific scrutiny. But we do have such a situation if it turns out that Smith is using telekinetic powers to make the dice come up sixes. For, in that case, some deeply held convictions of ours have to be revised. 
In describing SmithÂ’s rolling double-sixes five times in a row as Â“improbable,Â” what one is saying is very different from what one would be saying in describing SmithÂ’s having telekinetic powers as Â“improbable.Â” In the first case, one is affirming a mere statistical improbability. One is saying only that such things donÂ’t often happen. In the second case, one isnÂ’t saying anything of the sort. One is saying SmithÂ’s having such powers is inconsistent with some fundamental beliefs of oursÂ—with beliefs that, if jettisoned, would take a lot of other obviously (or at least presumably) correct beliefs with them. 
Given any event, there is a way of describing it that makes it improbable in the statistical sense. In fact, any given event, described at all precisely, has a statistical probability of vanishingly close to zero. I flip a coin and it lands somewhere nearby. Nothing improbable about this. But itÂ’s a safe bet that no coin has ever moved in exactly the way this one did after I flipped it. 
Described as a case of my flipping a coin, the event isnÂ’t improbable at all. But that same event is extremely improbable if described as a case of an objectÂ’s moving in manner M, where M is the exact way that it did move. But even though nothing apart from that coin has ever moved in manner M, that coinÂ’s doing so isnÂ’t a matter that deserves the slightest scientific scrutiny. Its moving in that way is consistent with everything we know about the world, and there is therefore nothing to be explained. But there is something to be explained if Smith turns out to have telekinetic powers, since his having such powers is improbable in the explanatory sense. ItÂ’s irrelevant that it is also improbable in the statistical sense. Every event is improbable in the statistical sense. 
My winning the lottery is improbable in the statistical sense, but not in the explanatory sense. And thatÂ’s why, before the winner is announced, we canÂ’t say that we know it wonÂ’t win: my winning is consistent with everything we know about the world. My sprouting wings in the next five minutes is improbable in the explanatory sense. And thatÂ’s why we can say that we know it wonÂ’t happen. ItÂ’s inconsistent with everything (or much, at any rate) that we know about the world. 
6.0 Â“GrueÂ” and the problem of counterinduction 
A puzzle devised by Nelson Goodman[354] 
will clarify, as well as support, what weÂ’ve said: 
(GA)[355]: LetÂ’s invent a new word: Â“grue,Â” to be defined as follows. Something is grue if it is green before Jan. 1, 2010, or blue thereafter. So a shirt thatÂ’s green on Oct. 12, 2007, is grue, as is a shirt thatÂ’s blue on Nov. 11, 2012. LetÂ’s assume that, before Jan. 1. 2010, all emeralds have been green. (From now on, weÂ’ll abbreviate Â“Jan. 1, 2010,Â” as Â“2010.Â”) In that case, all emeralds have been grue prior to 2010. Anything that is greenÂ­and-examined-before-2010 is also grue. So the fact that all emeralds examined before 2010 are green means that all emeralds examined before 2010 are grue. We are assuming for argumentÂ’s sake that, given the fact that all emeralds examined before 2010 were green, we are inductively warranted in believing that all emeralds examined after 2010 are green. By that logic, it follows that, given the fact that all emeralds examined before 2010 were grue, we are inductively warranted in believing that all emeralds examined after 2010 are grue. But anything examined after 2010 that is grue is blue, not green. So, given that all emeralds before 2010 were green, our inductive grounds for believing theyÂ’ll be blue after 2010 are as strong as our grounds that theyÂ’ll be green. 
The degree to which a given fact is statistically improbable depends on how it is described. Given some emerald x that was examined before 2010 and found to be green, Â“x is grue after 2010Â” is, from a strictly statistical viewpoint, equiprobable with Â“x is green after 2010Â” and also with Â“x is blue after 2010.Â” But thatÂ’s no cause for alarm. Statistical improbability is innocuous. ItÂ’s explanatory improbability that you have to worry about. But the explanatory probability of Â“x is green after 2010Â” dwarfs that of Â“x is grue after 2010Â” and, therefore, Â“x is blue after 2010.Â” The supposition that objects donÂ’t change color (except under conditions that emeralds donÂ’t satisfy, at least not in virtue of making it to 2010) is deeply embedded in scientific theory and also in the commonsense underpinning of scientific theory. If itÂ’s wrong, then science is in serious trouble, and so is human knowledge in general. 
In response to this, it will be said that: 
(OA)[356] 
If GA is right, emeralds that Â“turn blueÂ” at the beginning of 2010 donÂ’t change color. They stay the same colorÂ—grue. And emeralds that Â“stay greenÂ” do change color, since they go from being grue to having some other color. (Or, to be more precise, emeralds do change color at the beginning of 2010Â—but only relative to one set of color-terms [Â“red,Â” Â“green,Â” etc.]. But emeralds stay the same color relative to different color terms [Â“grue,Â” Â“bleen,Â” etc.].) 
OA simply isnÂ’t true. Pictures of green emeralds (taken before 2010) show them not to have the same color as blue things after 2010. Grueness and greenness are different properties. But theyÂ’re not different colors. Grueness isnÂ’t a color at allÂ—itÂ’s a color-related property. 
Chapter 19 The Raven Paradox[H16] 

1.0 An illustration of the brokenness of Hume-based conceptions of causation and explanation: The raven paradox 
Because they donÂ’t grant the existence of causality, except of a degraded and reduced kind, Humeans are categorically incapable of producing viable theories of confirmation.[357] 
One sign of this is that Humean theories of confirmation always have paradoxical consequences. 
The most famous of these famous paradoxes is the so-called Raven paradox. This was discovered by C.G. Hempel[358], who was himself a hardcore Humean. WeÂ’ve already considered HempelÂ’s unsuccessful, Humean analysis of explanation, and weÂ’ll soon consider HempelÂ’s equally unsuccessful, Humean attempt to solve the raven paradox. 
In any case, here is that paradox: 
(RP) Logically equivalent sentences are confirmationally equivalent. 
This means that, if P and Q are logically equivalent, then not only does evidence E confirm P just in case it confirms Q, but E confirms P to degree n just in case it confirms Q to that same degree. The sentence: 
(1) Â“All ravens are black,Â” 
is logically equivalent with: 
(2) Â“All non-black things are non-ravens.Â” 
The existence of non-ravens (e.g., pianos, pants, carpet fibers) that are pink or green confirms (2), but does not, unless our intuitions are very wrong, confirm (1). So, impossible though it must be, (1) and (2) are logically, but not confirmationally, equivalent. 
An analogous paradox is associated with each of many other pairs of logically equivalent sentences. For example: 
(i) Â“If itÂ’s made of metal and is being heated, then itÂ’s expanding.Â” 
is logically equivalent with: 
(ii) Â“If it isnÂ’t expanding, then it isnÂ’t both made of metal and being heated.Â” 
(ii) is confirmed by the fact that the non-expanding Tupperware in my freezer is not made of metal (or a fortiori of metal that is being heated). But, unless our intuitions are very wrong, that fact provides no support for (i). 
Some, including Hempel himself, have argued that, our intuitions notwithstanding, the existence of pink pianos does confirm (1) to degree n exactly if it confirms (2) to that same degree and that the existence of non-expanding Tupperware in freezers does confirm (i) exactly as much as it confirms (ii). Others have argued that the paradox should be solved by advocating non-standard logics, relative to which logical equivalence doesnÂ’t guarantee confirmational equivalence. 
WeÂ’ll evaluate these solutions after we put forth our own. ItÂ’s clear that, whatever merits these solutions have, they are counterintuitive. And the very idea of logical equivalence not guaranteeing confirmational equivalence is of questionable coherence. But even if it can be shown that an internally consistent logic could be invented relative to which logical and confirmational equivalence pull apart, it seems excessive to throw out classical logic to solve this one problem. Fortunately, the paradox can, I will argue, be solved without going to such lengths. 
2.0 Inductions by enumeration identical with crypto-inferences to the best explanation 
In this context, (i) may be treated as saying the same thing as: 
(MH) For any x, if x is made of metal and x is being heated, then x is expanding. 
And (ii) may be treated as saying the same thing as: 
(HM) For any x, if x isnÂ’t expanding, then x isnÂ’t made of metal that is being heated. 
MH can be taken either to express an Â“accidental generalizationÂ” or to express a principled relationship. Taken in the first way, it does nothing more than affirm a purely de facto concomitance of two properties (viz., the property of being heated metal and the property of being something that expands). Taken in the second way, MH seems to say that all heated metal expands, the reason being that a thingÂ’s being heated metal provides some kind of nomic basis for its expanding. In this section, we will focus on the first, strictly extensional, reading. In the next, we will focus on the second, nomically committed reading. 
Let us paraphrase MH, when it is taken as a purely de facto generalization, as follows: 
(MHA)[359] 
For any x, if x is made of metal and is being heated, then, by happenstance, x is expanding. 
So, in this context, take the operator Â“by happenstanceÂ” to be short for Â“not because xÂ’s having the first property provides a causal or nomic basis for its having the second.Â” We donÂ’t need to worry about whether this corresponds to the usual meaning of Â“as a matter of happenstance,Â” since we are using this expression in a stipulative manner. 
If we take MH in this wayÂ—if we take it to mean the same thing as MHA Â—does HempelÂ’s paradox arise? No. Let phi and psi be any two properties such that x has psi isnÂ’t an analytic consequence of x has phi, or vice versa. If I know that there is no causal or, more generally, nomic connection between xÂ’s being a phi, on the one hand, and xÂ’s being a psi, on the other, then I have no reason to infer, from xÂ’s being a phi, that x is also a psi. Even if, thus far, every ball withdrawn from the urn has been black, unless I have reason to believe that this concomitance has some basis in natural law or in some causal mechanism (e.g., the presence of a force field surrounding the urn that allows entry only to black balls, or some personÂ’s resolute intention to allow no non-black balls into the urn), I must ipso facto regard it as nothing but coincidence that, thus far, every ball withdrawn has been black; and I must therefore not think it more likely than not that the next ball withdrawn will be blackÂ—for to think otherwise would be to commit the Monte Carlo fallacy. 
[360] 
Thus, supposing that, in fact, this concomitance is mere coincidence, the generalization all the balls in the urn are black fails to receive any positive confirmation from its instances.[361] 
For the same reason mutatis mutandis, the statement all non-black things are not balls in the urn, unless read as having nomic force, fails to receive support from its instances. 
Of course, it also follows that HM, if read as doing nothing more than affirming a de facto concomitance, doesnÂ’t receive support from its instances. Thus: 
(HMA) For any x, if x isnÂ’t expanding, then, by happenstance, x isnÂ’t made of metal that is being heated, 
doesnÂ’t receive support from the fact that the non-expanding Tupperware in my freezer isnÂ’t made of metal that is being heated. 
So, if MH and HM are read as having no nomic contentÂ—if they are read as doing nothing but expressing de facto concomitancesÂ—then, once it is seen that de facto generalizations donÂ’t receive support from their instances, HM doesnÂ’t even appear to receive support from the fact the non-expanding Tupperware in my freezer isnÂ’t made of heated metal, and MH doesnÂ’t even appear to receive support from the fact that the metal pan I put in the oven is expanding. A fortiori the former fact doesnÂ’t even appear to confirm HM more than it does MH, and the latter fact doesnÂ’t even appear to confirm MH more than it does HM. 
And we therefore donÂ’t get the kind of (apparent) confirmational nonÂ­equivalence that gives rise to HempelÂ’s paradox. For that paradox depends precisely on its being the case that, despite the (alleged) fact that HM and MH are logically equivalent, they are not, or at least appear not to be, confirmationally equivalent. And they appear to be confirmationally nonÂ­equivalent only in so far as (e.g.) the existence of a heated, expanding metal objects confirms MH but not HM, and only in so far as (e.g.) the existence of non-expanding, non-heated, non-metal objects confirms HM but not MH. But once it is made clear that de facto generalizations donÂ’t receive support from their instances, it follows that, if MH and HM are read as free of nomic content, nothing even appears to give more support to the one than to the other. And the paradox fails to arise. 
2.1 Inductions by enumeration identical with crypto-inferences to the best explanation (continued) 
So if HempelÂ’s paradox is to arise, at least one of MH and HM must be taken as doing more than affirming a de facto concomitance. And it seems that, thus taken, MH is to the effect that all heated metal expands for the reason that a thingÂ’s being metal that is being heated provides some kind of nomic or causal basis for its expanding. Let us paraphrase MH, when it is taken in this way, as follows: 
(MHN)[362] 
For any x, if x is made of metal and is being heated, then, as a matter of principle, x is expanding. 
So, in this context, take the operator Â“as a matter of principleÂ” to be short for: Â“because xÂ’s having the first property provides a causal or nomic basis for its having the second.Â” Echoing what we said earlier, it is irrelevant this may not correspond very well to the usual meaning of Â“as a matter of principle,Â” since we are here using this expression in a stipulative manner. 
At this point, we have a choice. We can take HM as having no nomic contentÂ—as taking it to have the same import as HMA. Or we can take it to have nomic content. LetÂ’s consider both options, starting with the first. 
Given that MH is taken to do more than affirm a de facto concomitance, if MH is taken to affirm nothing but a de facto concomitance, the two will, quite trivially, not be equivalent. For obviously MHN is not equivalent with HMA. The first is committed to its being the case that inter alia a thingÂ’s being made of heated metal provides some kind of nomic basis forÂ—or, in any case, is nomically or causally connected in some way withÂ—that thingÂ’s expanding. The second isnÂ’t committed to there being any kind of nomic, or otherwise not purely extensional, connection between the property of not expanding and the property of not being made of heated metal. MHN is true only if certain nomic connections hold; HMA can be true in the absence of those connections. So there is no equivalence, or even the appearance of equivalence for that matter. 
WeÂ’ve just seen that, if we take MH to have nomic force (which we must Â—see aboveÂ—if HempelÂ’s paradox is to arise), HempelÂ’s paradox doesnÂ’t arise if we donÂ’t take HM to have nomic content. In other words, if we take HM to do nothing more than affirm a de facto concomitance, then it wonÂ’t, as weÂ’ve just seen, even appear to be equivalent with MHN, and nothing even resembling HempelÂ’s paradox arises. So if that paradox is to arise, then we must take HM to have nomic content. 
In light of this, consider the sentence: 
(HMN) For any x, if x isnÂ’t expanding, then, as a matter of principle, x isnÂ’t made of metal that is being heated. 
HMN says that a thingÂ’s not being an expander provides some kind of (partial) nomic basis for its not being heated metal. Of course, the relationship that HMN bears to HM is analogous to the relationship that MHN bears to MH. But what is most important here is that HMN would be the right wayÂ—or, in any case, the (or, at least, a) natural wayÂ—to take HM if the latter were taken to do more than affirm a de facto concomitance between two properties. 
To clarify this last point, suppose that you are speaking to a friend who is about to drink a large quantity of arsenic but who doesnÂ’t realize that consuming arsenic in large quantities leads to death. You tell him, warningly, Â“people who consume large quantities of arsenic die soon thereafter.Â” Here you are obviously not affirming a purely extensional connection between, on the one hand, the property of being a person who drinks large quantities of arsenic at a given time and, on the other hand, the property of being something that dies soon thereafter. What you are saying is that a person xÂ’s drinking large quantities of arsenic at a given time leads to, or in any case provides some kind of nomic foundation for, xÂ’s dying soon thereafter, that being why there is a concomitance between the property of being a person who drinks arsenic, on the one hand, and the property of being dead soon thereafter, on the other. That this is the right interpretation is made clear by the fact that you would be failing to warn your friend not to drink the arsenic if you had instead said: Â“All people who have drunk arsenic died soon thereafter. But that had nothing to do with their drinking arsenic. You see, it turns out that the only people whoÂ’ve ever drunk arsenic belong to religious sect X; moreover, all of those people were about to be executed. One of the precepts of X is that, if you are about to be executed, you must drink arsenic in order to get into heaven. And thatÂ’s why, thus far, each person whoÂ’s consumed arsenic died soon thereafter.Â” 
The most natural way to take HM to have nomic force is to take it to mean that a thingÂ’s being a non-expander provides some kind of causal or nomic basis for its not being heated metal. And that is precisely the reading of HM that is embodied in HMN. 
HMN is clearly not equivalent with MHN. Suppose, if only for argumentÂ’s sake, that a thingÂ’s being made of heated metal causes it to expand. So suppose that: 
(MHC) Â“as a matter of natural law, xÂ’s being heated metal causes x to expand,Â” 
which would certainly be sufficient for the truth of MHN. In light of this, consider the statement that: 
(HMC) Â“as a matter of natural law, xÂ’s not expanding causes x to not be metal that is being heated.Â” 
Suppose it is a law that xÂ’s being a human who drinks arsenic at t causes x to be dead at some later time t*. This very reasonable and (give or take a few nuances) correct statement obviously doesnÂ’t entail, and therefore isnÂ’t equivalent with, the false and incoherent statement that xÂ’s not being dead t* causes x to be a human who doesnÂ’t drink arsenic at earlier time t. 
For similar reasons, MHC is not equivalent with HMC. So, since MHC and HMC are sufficient for the truth of, respectively, MHN and HMN, it follows that MHN and HMN are not equivalent: they donÂ’t hold in the same models, the same possible worlds. In fact, whereas MHN, or something similar to it, does hold in our world, the same doesnÂ’t go for HMN or anything at all like it. 
2.2 Inductions by enumeration identical with crypto-inferences to the best explanation (continued) 
WeÂ’ve seen, first, that MH must be read as having some kind of nomic content if HempelÂ’s paradox is to arise (i.e., if there is to even be the appearance that MH is logically, but not confirmationally, equivalent with HM). And weÂ’ve also asserted that, if MH read as having nomic force, its meaning is given by MHN, and we made the same assumption mutatis mutandis about HM. 
But, it must be admitted, we have provided no argumentative basis for this assertion, our grounds for it being purely intuitive. There is another possible nomic reading of MH: 
(MHW)[363] 
Â“Thanks to the existence of some kind of nomic (or causal) connection between the two properties about to be mentioned (viz., the property of being heated metal, on the one hand, and the property of expanding, on the other), for all x, if x is heated metal, then x is expanding.Â” 
How is MHN different from MHW? MHN says pretty much the same thing as: 
(*) For all x, if x is heated metal, then x is expanding, and this is because xÂ’s being heated metal provides a nomic basis for xÂ’s expanding. 
By contrast, MHW says that: 
(^) For all x, if x is heated metal, then x is expanding, and this is because either xÂ’s being heated metal provides a nomic basis for xÂ’s expanding or xÂ’s expanding provides a nomic basis for xÂ’s being heated metal. 
To be sure, the expression Â“provides a nomic basis forÂ” is an obscure one, which IÂ’ve done little or nothing to clarify; and it might therefore seem that there is no difference between (*) and (^). But, obscure though that expression may be, (*) and (^) are demonstrably different, and nonÂ­equivalent, statements. 
ItÂ’s true (or so let us suppose, for argumentÂ’s sake) that all people who consume large quantities of arsenic die soon thereafter. And this is not an accident: human biology being what it is and the chemical properties of arsenic being what they are, thereÂ’s a nomic connection between consuming arsenic and dying. Vague as the expression Â“provides a nomic basis forÂ” is, would it be correct to say that being a dead human at 3:10 P.M. Â“provides a nomic basis forÂ” being a person who drinks arsenic at 3:00 P.M.? More generally, supposing that xÂ’s having psi at t* is an effect of xÂ’s having phi at earlier time t, does it make sense to say that xÂ’s having psi at t* provides a nomic basis for xÂ’s having phi at t? No. My being obese provides a nomic basis for my having a heart-attack. But surely my having a heart attack doesnÂ’t provide a nomic basis for my being obese. And thatÂ’s 
all we need to know in this context about what it means to say that one thing provides a Â“nomic basisÂ” for another. So let us proceed. 
Suppose that, in possible world W, all things made of heated metal expand. Further suppose that, in W, xÂ’s being something that is expanding causes x to turn into something that is metal whose temperature is continuously rising and whose volume is constantly increasing. And, to make things simple, suppose that, in W, all things made of heated metal got that way by, at some point in their histories, being things that were expanding. In that case, MHW would be correct in W: for there would, in that world, be a nomic connection between a thingÂ’s being heated metal, on the one hand, and its being something that expands, on the other; moreover, the fact that, in W, all heated metal expands would have a basis in this nomic connection. But it would not, at least not on that account, be correct to say that, in W, a thingÂ’s being made of heated metal provides a nomic basis for its expanding. In W, things expand before they become expanding heated metal. So, in W,a thingÂ’s being heated metal obviously cannot cause it to expand. 
But there is a further point: in W, a thingÂ’s expanding is not to be understood in terms of its being heated metal. It is the other way around. In W, a thingÂ’s expanding is causally and explanatorily more basic than itÂ’s being heated metal. In any case, just as (see above) it would be wrong, or at least very odd, to say that being dead at t* provided a nomic basis for drinking arsenic at earlier time t, it would, for parallel reasons, be wrong to say that, in W, being heated metal provided a nomic basis for being a thing that expands. And this entails that, however vague the expression Â“provides a 
nomic basis forÂ” is, * and ^ are, very clearly, not equivalent. 
3.0 This argument concluded 
First of all, MHW obviously isnÂ’t logically equivalent with HMA: the former does, whereas the latter does not, allege the existence of certain nomic dependencies. More importantly, MHW isnÂ’t equivalent with: 
(HMW) Â“thanks to the existence of some kind of nomic (or causal) connection between the two properties about to be mentioned (namely, the property of not expanding, on the one hand, and the property of not being heated metal, on the other), for all x, if x is not expanding, then x is not heated metal.Â” 
Given only that there is a nomic connection between a thingÂ’s having phi and itÂ’s having psi, it doesnÂ’t follow that there is a nomic connection between a thingÂ’s not having psi and itÂ’s not having phi. There is a causal, and therefore a nomic, connection between SmithÂ’s falling off of tall building X at t, on the one hand, and his being dead at a later time t*, on the other. SmithÂ’s falling off of X is an event. It is something that makes things happen (e.g., various bones of SmithÂ’s being shattered); and, what is probably a more general notion, it is something in terms of which things can be explained. 
Compare SmithÂ’s situation with BrownÂ’s. Brown does not fall off X, or any other building, at t; and Brown is alive and well at t*. Obviously BrownÂ’s not falling off X at t doesnÂ’t cause Brown to be alive at t*. More generally, BrownÂ’s being alive at t* is not, except perhaps in some extremely derivative sense, to be explained in terms of BrownÂ’s not falling off of X. Whereas SmithÂ’s falling off of X is an event, BrownÂ’s not falling off of X is not an event, and it doesnÂ’t consist of events. A chair consists of events (various miniscule displacements of mass-energy), and so does a corporation (various actions on the part of sentient beings); and so, indeed, does any enduring entityÂ—any structure, any Â“object,Â” any non-instantaneous event. But BrownÂ’s not falling off X isnÂ’t identical with an event and isnÂ’t constituted by events. 
Of course, since itÂ’s a truth, and therefore a Â“fact,Â” that Brown did not fall off of X, we might say that the (negative) Â“factÂ” of his not falling off of X exists no less than the (positive) fact of SmithÂ’s falling off of X. But that doesnÂ’t undermine our point that BrownÂ’s not falling off of X isnÂ’t identical with, or constituted by, events. 
While it is a matter of intense debate what nomic relations are, it is pretty clear they hold only among occupants of the space-time manifold. They clearly hold among events (my pounding the table causes it to break). Maybe they hold among things other than events. Maybe, for example, they hold among conditions. And maybe they hold among objects. But while it is unclear whether all spatiotemporal entities stand in nomic relations, it is clear that nothing non-spatiotemporal stands in them. My pounding the table is nomically connected to the tableÂ’s breaking. But my not destroying Jupiter isnÂ’t nomically related to anything. 
My pounding the table is an event; it makes things happen; things can be explained in terms of it; it has a place in the tapestry that constitutes the spatiotemporal world. My not destroying Jupiter is nowhere in that tapestry, and therefore isnÂ’t fit to be nomically related to anything. There is no event of my not destroying Jupiter. There is thus no condition or object that is constituted to any degree by that non-event. Therefore, it isnÂ’t identical with, or constitutive of, anything that falls within the scope of natural law. It isnÂ’t, therefore, nomically connected to anything. 
A thingÂ’s being composed of metal that is of a certain temperature is, in the relevant respects, like my pounding the table. Things are to be explained in terms of it. And, though not itself an Â“event,Â” it is constituted by various interacting events, all of which occupy space-time. So the skilletÂ’s having a certain temperature, at a given time, is something that can, and indeed obviously must, stand in nomic relations. And the same is true of the skilletÂ’s expanding during a given interval. 
But a thingÂ’s not expanding is, in the relevant respects, like my not destroying Jupiter, and so is a thingÂ’s not being heated metal. So, whereas a thingÂ’s being heated metal is, or at least could be, nomically related to its expanding, it doesnÂ’t follow, and it isnÂ’t the case, that a thingÂ’s not expanding could be nomically related to itÂ’s not being heated metal. 
These points make it clear why MHW isnÂ’t logically equivalent with HMW. A thingÂ’s being heated metal can (and, in fact, must) be nomically related to other things, and the same is true of a thingÂ’s expanding. But a thingÂ’s not expanding, like my not destroying Jupiter, isnÂ’t nomically related to anything, and neither is a thingÂ’s not being heated metal. Which is why, even though MH and HM are equivalent when they're read as merely affirming de facto concomitances they cannot always be intersubstituted salva veritate. In particular, they cannot be so intersubstituted in contexts governed by the operator that begins each of MHW and HMW (viz., Â“Â‘thanks to the existence of some kind of nomic (or causal) connection between the two properties about to be mentionedÂ”). There is nothing mysterious about this. Many operators donÂ’t permit intersubstitutions of logically equivalent expressions.
