Logically equivalent sentences can be truth-preservingly intersubstituted in contexts governed by (e.g.) Â“it is true that,Â” but not, at least not categorically, in contexts governed by Â“Timmy believes that.Â” The operator Â“there is a nomic connection between the facts expressed by the antecedent and consequent of the following statementÂ” doesnÂ’t tolerate intersubstitutions of logically equivalent sentences. For, even if: 
(T1) Â“There is a nomic connection between the facts expressed by the antecedent and consequent of the following statement: if x is heated metal, then x is expanding,Â” 
is true, it doesnÂ’t follow that: 
(T2) Â“There is a nomic connection between the facts expressed by the antecedent and consequent of the following statement: if x isnÂ’t expanding, then x isnÂ’t heated metal,Â” 
is also true. In fact, T2 is false, for the reasons just given. 
4.0 Hume-internal solutions to the raven paradox: QuineÂ’s solution 
QuineÂ’s (1977) solution is to say that logical equivalence doesnÂ’t guarantee confirmational equivalence. This idea is totally incoherent. P and Q are equivalent if they are true in exactly the same worlds. Thus, supposing that P and Q are equivalent, it immediately follows that, given any proposition R, the likelihood of RÂ’s being true in a world where P is true is identical with the likelihood of RÂ’s being true in a world where Q is true. QuineÂ’s proposed solution is thus a non-starter. 
4.1 Hume-internal solutions to the raven paradox: HempelÂ’s solution 
Hempel proposes a more plausible solution. It obviously seems as though the existence of a pink piano provides less support for: 
(1) Â“All ravens are black,Â” 
than does the existence of a black raven. And it obviously seems as though the existence of pink pianos provides more support for: 
(2) Â“All non-black things are non-ravens," 
than it does for (1). But, says Hempel, these intuitions are misleading. Under ordinary circumstances, if we know that something is a piano, we almost certainly already know that it isnÂ’t a raven. 
But imagine the following. You have bet your friend Smith $1,000,000 that all ravens are black. There is some object x such that, although you and Smith donÂ’t yet know it, x is a piano. All you know about x is that itÂ’s pink. In that case, when you discover that x is a piano, and thus a non-raven, you (but not Smith) will breathe a sigh of relief; and your confidence in (1) will surge, and so, of course, will your confidence in (2). 
Now imagine a different scenario. You have bet your friend Smith $1,000,000 that all non-black things are non-ravens. There is some object y such that, although you and Smith donÂ’t yet know it, y is black. All you know about y is that itÂ’s a raven. When you discover that y is black, you will breathe a sigh of relief; and your confidence in (2) will surge, and so, of course, will your confidence in (1). 
Thus, to Hempel, the confirmational disparities between (1) and (2) are illusory. When we imagine ourselves trying to confirm (2), we assume that we are looking at things that we already know to be non-ravens, but we donÂ’t make the same assumption mutatis mutandis when we imagine ourselves to be trying to confirm (1). 
HempelÂ’s solution is better than QuineÂ’s, but itÂ’s still no good. The problem is that, if itÂ’s known that there is no nomic or causal relationship between a thingÂ’s being a raven on the one hand, and its being black on the other, then there is ipso facto no reason to believe that the next raven you see will be black. Maybe youÂ’ve seen a million ravens, all of them black. ItÂ’s doesnÂ’t matter. Unless you have reason to believe that a thingÂ’s being a raven is connected somehow to its being black, youÂ’re guilty of the gamblerÂ’s fallacy if, on the basis of that data, you believe that the next raven you see is (likely to be) black. But if you do believe that a thingÂ’s being a raven is connected in some way to its being black, then your confidence in (1) is derivative of your confidence in: 
(1*) A thingÂ’s being a raven provides a basis of some kind for its being black. 
WeÂ’ve already seen why. And weÂ’ve already seen why (1*) isnÂ’t equivalent with: 
(2*) A thingÂ’s being non-black provides some kind of a basis for its being a non-raven. 
If the existence of a black raven is to provide any legitimate support for (1), there must be a causal or nomic connection between ravenhood and blackness. Once this is realized, two things immediately become obvious. First, HempelÂ’s solution is spurious, since it presupposes that black ravens can confirm (1) without there being any connection of the sort just described. Second, (1) must be read as having nomic force. Since, thus read, it is no longer equivalent with (2), the paradox vanishes. 
5.0 Summary of this chapterÂ’s main points 
If read as doing nothing more than affirming de facto concomitances: 
(MH) if x is made of heated metal, x expands, 
And: 
(HM) if x isnÂ’t expanding, x isnÂ’t made of heated metal, 
donÂ’t receive support from their instancesÂ—and donÂ’t even appear to receive support and are therefore vacuously confirmationally identical. So they are logically and confirmationally identical when read in this way, and HempelÂ’s paradox doesnÂ’t arise. If they are read as doing more than affirming de facto concomitances, they must be read as alleging, or at least being committed to there being, some kind of nomic connection between the properties in question. But, no matter what nomic readings we give these sentences, they donÂ’t even appear logically equivalent. (This is, to put it very crudely, because logically equivalent sentences cannot, at least not in general, be intersubstituted salva veritate in contexts governed by nomic operators; e.g., Â“there is a nomic connection between the following statements.Â”) Bottom line: once it is realized that accidental generalizations donÂ’t receive support from their instances, this being the prerogative of principled generalizations, it isnÂ’t possible for HempelÂ’s paradox even to arise. 
Part V Explanation 
Chapter 20 Scientific Explanation 
1.0 Hume's regularity analysis of causation: The awkward constraints it places on would-be explainers of explanation 
According to Hume, for x to cause y is for the sequence consisting of x and y to be an instance of a regularity (provided that x immediately precedes y and is also adjacent with it). We found there to be not so much as a sliver of truth in this view. But philosophers to this day accept it. Presumably, this is only because no significant alternative to it has been put forth. Given how wrong HumeÂ’s analysis seems to be (Â“youÂ’re pulling the trigger had nothing to do with the gunÂ’s firingÂ”), itÂ’s hard to believe that anyone would accept that analysis unless they felt they had no other choice. 
In any case, supposing it correct, HumeÂ’s analysis of causality has very definite consequences as to what it is to explain events. As a result, there is no shortage of Humean theories of explanation; in fact, such theories still predominate. Echoing what we said a moment ago, this is presumably because no viable alternatives to those theories have been proposed, given how wrong those theories seem to be (as weÂ’re about to discover) and given how wrong they are easily proven to be (as weÂ’re also about to discover). 
1.1 Two preliminaries: The nature of scientific truth and the Duhem-Quine thesis 
Statements are either true or they arenÂ’t. There are no Â“scientificÂ” statements, and there are no Â“unscientificÂ” statements. 
To the extent that an utterance lacks a clear meaning, it constitutes a failed attempt to make a statement and therefore isnÂ’t a statement. And to the extent that an utterance has a clear meaning, itÂ’s either true or false, and therefore cannot meaningfully be described as Â“scientificÂ” or Â“unscientific.Â” If T is true, science has to accept it; if T is false, science has to reject it. Period. 
That said, there are distinctly scientific ways of generating statements. Given some statement S, assuming that: 
(SS) Â‹S is a scientific statementÂ›, 
doesnÂ’t say the very same thing as: 
(OS)[364] 
Â‹S is a statementÂ›. 
SS must say S was generated in a certain wayÂ—that it was generated in accordance with procedures whose truth-conduciveness has been definitively established, or some such. 
Nonetheless, a number of philosophers have argued that there is some property that all and only Â“scientificÂ” statements have. For example, in his (1931) book The Logic of Scientific Discovery, Karl Popper (1902Â–1994) argued that a statement is scientific iff it is falsifiable. To say that a statement S is falsifiable is to say that it could in principle be shown to be false on strictly observational grounds. (The sort of falsificationism that Popper advocated is not to be confused with the very different doctrine, discussed in Chapter 1, according to which a statement is meaningful iff it is falsifiable.) 
To be sure, some theories can be falsified on strictly observational grounds. Suppose that, according to theory T, anyone who takes medication M will be acne-free within five hours. Given that acne-ridden Smith took M at noon, it follows that T is false if Smith still has acne at 5:00 P.M. Given that Smith does still have acne at 5:00 P.M., and given that this fact is painfully obvious to anyone who looks at Smith, it follows that T can be falsified on strictly observational grounds. 
But T is not representative of most theories in this respect. Whether or not a given theory has a given observable consequence is likely to depend on whether each of various other theories is correct. (To confirm a given astronomical theory, one must assume the truth of various theories concerning the behavior of light. In making this assumption, one is assuming that the instruments used to authenticate those theories were reliable ones. In making this assumption, one is, for reasons similar to those just given, assuming the truth of physical theories additional to those already mentioned. And so on and so forth.) So given only that some observable event hasnÂ’t occurred, itÂ’s not likely to follow that this or that specific theory must be false. 
1.1.1 The Duhem-Quine thesis 
Aware of the fact that theories canÂ’t typically be falsified on strictly observational grounds, W.V.O. Quine (1908Â–2001) took the position that any theory is consistent with any body of observational data. Given any theory and any set of observations, Quine says, there is way of modeling those observations that is consistent with that theory. Quine refers to this thesis of his as the Â“Duhem-Quine thesis.Â”[365] 

The so-called Duhem-Quine thesis is an extremely facile one and is easily refuted. As before, suppose that, according to theory T, anyone who takes medication M will be acne-free within five hours. Given that SmithÂ’s acne is going strong six hours after taking M, thereÂ’s nothing we can say that isnÂ’t brazenly ad hoc and that doesnÂ’t create vast numbers of otherwise nonÂ­existent anomalies. Should an opponent of M point out this fact, his attempt to refute M would be a success, as it would have met the relevant standards of proof. For, when evaluating a scientific theory, the relevant standard of proof isnÂ’t given by the question Â“given the sensory data at our disposal, is it logically impossible for that theory to be correct?Â”, and is instead Â“given the sensory data at our disposal, would countenancing that theory require us to renounce fruitful theories which there are no independent reasons to reject and which, therefore, we couldnÂ’t reject without repopulating the universe with anomalies that we had long since solved?Â” 
ItÂ’s obvious and trivial that, given any theory T that concerns the external world, no matter what observations weÂ’ve had; itÂ’s logically possible that T is false. For, as Quine points out, itÂ’s theoretically possibly that everyone is always hallucinating and, therefore, that the data on which any given scientific theory is based is spurious. But, since this platitude is all Quine gives us in the way of substantiating his thesis, heÂ’s effectively done nothing to substantiate it. 
In any case, unless itÂ’s completely hollow, the Duhem-Quine thesis canÂ’t just say that, for any theory T that concerns the external world, no body of observations analytically entails that T is false. It must therefore be to the effect that, given any body of observations and given any theory T, the explanatory costs of accepting T are no greater and no smaller than the explanatory costs of rejecting T. 
But that statement is very obviously false. The data being what it is, the explanatory costs of holding onto T far outweigh the explanatory gains of doing so. If we hold onto it, weÂ’re stuck with various anomalies that we wouldnÂ’t otherwise be stuck with. If we reject it, weÂ’re not stuck with those anomalies; nor are we stuck with any other anomalies that we werenÂ’t already stuck with. So depending on how itÂ’s interpreted, the Duhem-Quine thesis is either trivial or false. 
2.0 Scientific explanation: HempelÂ’s theory 
Let us now turn our attention to Carl HempelÂ’s important theory as to the nature of scientific explanation. HempelÂ’s theory is important because it is the clearest, purest expression of the Humean conviction that all probability is statistical probability and also because of the consequent fact that, given the enormously powerful hold of Humean ideas on methodological thought, all theories of explanation can be understood in terms of HempelÂ’s theoryÂ— either as versions of it or as reactions to it. HempelÂ’s theory is known as the Â“deductive nomologicalÂ” account of explanation: 
(DN) To explain an event E is to show that its occurrence is a logical consequence of the statement formed by conjoining statements describing known natural laws with statements describing the conditions under which E occurred.[366] 

I drop an otherwise unsupported object. The laws of physics being what they are, the object must fall, given the circumstances. And to explain that event is to identify known natural laws that, when conjoined with a correct description of the circumstances, entail that the object will fall. 
2.1 HempelÂ’s analysis evaluated 
What is meant by the term Â“lawÂ”? One possible answer is: A law is what is described by any true universal generalizationÂ—that is, by any statement of the form Â“all phiÂ’s are psiÂ’s.Â” Few have explicitly given this answer. But weÂ’ll now see that Hempel has no choice but to accept that answer, ridiculous though it is. 
If the word Â“lawÂ” is taken in this way, DN has the consequence that the following counts as an Â“explanationÂ” of the fact that the pencil on my desk is yellow[367]: 
(NE) Premise #1 (description of the relevant natural law): Everything is such that itÂ’s either yellow or it isnÂ’t a pencil on JMKÂ’s desk. 
Premise #2 (description of initial conditions): x is a pencil on JMKÂ’s desk. Conclusion (thing being explained): x is yellow. 
But NE isnÂ’t an explanation of the fact that my pencil is yellow. The problem, of course, is that[368]: 
(YP) Everything is such that itÂ’s either yellow or it isnÂ’t a pencil on JMKÂ’s desk, 
doesnÂ’t express a natural law. But why not? Because, says Hempel, it doesnÂ’t support counterfactuals. The statement: 
(ME) Metal expands when heated, 
expresses a law of nature because a piece of metal that isnÂ’t being heated would expand if it were heated. Nothing comparable holds of YP. Given an arbitrary pencil, YP doesnÂ’t entail that it would be yellow if it were on my desk. In general, says Hempel, laws are expressed by universal generalizations that support counterfactuals. 
Hempel is surely right that a statement must support counterfactuals if it is to express a natural law. But DN collapses if laws are understood in this way. Let m be some unheated metal object. Why is it that m would expand if it were heated? Because, the laws of nature being what they are, heating m would cause it to expand. So the fact that m would expand if heated is to be understood in terms of the fact that ME expresses a natural law. 
Remember what we said earlier about counterfactuals: they are thinly veiled causal statements. Â“Smith would be alive if he hadnÂ’t jumpedÂ” means: Â“jumping is what caused the death of an otherwise unthreatened Smith.Â” So far as that causal claim is warranted, it is because there is known to be a law that, given the circumstances, demanded SmithÂ’s death. The counterfactual claim is to be understood in terms of a causal claim, and the causal claim is to be understood in terms of a statement describing a natural law. DN thus becomes viciously circular if Â“lawÂ” is defined as Â“what is expressed by a counterfactual-supporting universal generalization.Â” 
Causal claims are themselves explanations. In being told that lung cancer is what led to SmithÂ’s death, IÂ’m being given an explanation, albeit an incomplete one, as to why he died. Counterfactuals, as we know, are identical with causal claims. It is only where explanations are already available that counterfactual claims are warranted. 
By the same token, if we donÂ’t know that it was arsenic consumption that killed SmithÂ—or, if not Smith, then somebody elseÂ—we have no basis for affirming the counterfactual that Jones, who isnÂ’t consuming arsenic, would die were he to do so. 
Thus, we are warranted in affirming counterfactuals only where we already have explanations. So to understand the concept of law in terms of the concept of counterfactual truth is to understand the law in terms of the concept of explanation. Thus, if laws are understood in this way, DN is analyzing the concept of explanation in terms of itself. 
So long as the concept of law is understood in terms of the concept of explanation, DN is viciously circular. Is there some other way to understand the concept of law? This question exposes a serious problem with DN. Hume tried to show that laws are mere concomitances. He denied the existence of causal ties; so he couldnÂ’t take laws to be descriptions of such ties. And he therefore couldnÂ’t take Â“metal expands when heatedÂ” to describe the connection that we presume to hold between xÂ’s being heated metal and xÂ’s expanding. He had only one option: the law isnÂ’t some structure or metaphysical glue underlying the fact that the property of being heated metal is always found in conjunction with the property of expanding; the law is that regularity. Laws are the regularities that non-Humeans typically regard as their expressions. 
The advocate of DN is forced to take this position. So long as he thinks of laws as being given by statements that describe structures of some kindÂ—the structures that are manifested by regularitiesÂ—the advocate of DN is analyzing the explanation in terms of itself. For it isnÂ’t until there are explanations, that there can be any good reason to posit such structures. The structure is posited to validate preexisting explanations. This makes it viciously circular to understand laws in terms of causality. This, in turn, makes it viciously circular to understand laws in terms of counterfactual truth, given that counterfactual truths are to be understood in terms of causality. If his position is to be free of such circularity, the advocate of DN must take laws to be mere concomitances. In his view, the law that all metal expands when heated is the regularity that, in the eyes of a non-Humean, merely expresses that law. In general, for the advocate of DN, laws are regularitiesÂ—nothing more. 
But in that case, any true universal generalization expresses a law. YP (Â“everything is such that itÂ’s either yellow or it isnÂ’t a pencil on JMKÂ’s deskÂ”) describes a regularity. It correctly states that nothing has the property of being a pencil on JMKÂ’s desk on March 11, 2009, unless it also has the property of being yellow. But it doesnÂ’t express a law. 
If laws are identified with regularities, as opposed to the structures that (so non-Humeans think) underlie them, then DN ends up having the same problems as HumeÂ’s analysis of causation. People often know what caused what, even though they couldnÂ’t for the life of them identify the relevant generalizations. It often happens that, in order to identify the relevant generalization, one must know what caused what, and therefore that one must already have an explanation of the event in question, if only a crude one, if one is to identify the relevant generalization. Jones turns the ignition in his car, and his car explodes. Smith witnesses this and wants an explanation for what he just saw. He thinks about the sequence of events that he just witnessed. Jones got into his car; he put the key in the ignition and then turned it; the engine turned over a few times; at that point, the car exploded. If Smith falsely believes that well-known evil person Brown used his telekinetic powers to blow up the car, SmithÂ’s search for covering laws will be futile. It is only if Smith does have a correct explanation (JonesÂ’ starting the engine set off a bomb that, presumably, somebody deliberately installed in the car), if only an extremely low-resolution one, that he can even begin to search in a meaningful way for the relevant law. 
Laws are hyper-explanations.[369] 
They are explanations of the explanations. First there are the anomic explanations. (Â“NomicÂ” means Â“involving or having to do with natural law.Â” Â“AnomicÂ” means Â“not involving natural law.Â”) The explanations that we come up with in everyday life are anomicÂ—Â“heating it caused it to expand,Â” Â“falling caused him to break his leg,Â” Â“drinking arsenic caused him to die,Â” Â“being made of pinewood caused it to float when placed in water.Â” The laws explain these explanations. Â“There is an underlying structure that guarantees that a thing will expand if itÂ’s made of metal that is being heated/that a person will break his leg as a result of such and such a fall/that a person dies if he consumes arsenic/that a thing floats if itÂ’s pinewood in water.Â” 
So Hume and Hempel have it backwards; for they believe that the event is to be explained in terms of the law. To be sure, once the law is in place, new and better explanations are possible. But those higher-level explanations stand on the shoulders of lower-level ones that model the data without the help of statements describing laws. Hypotheses concerning laws are distillations of existing, low-level explanations. 
In conclusion, DN is viciously circular and is therefore a failure. 
2.2 More on the circularity inherent in the Hempel-Hume analysis of explanation 
To explain an event is not to show that it is an instance of a general regularity. First of all, given any event E, itÂ’s possible to contrive regularity of which E is an instance. Right now, my pencil, which is yellow, is occupying region R on the surface of my desk. No other object has ever occupied that exact region; and, we will suppose, no other ever will occupy it. So every object that ever has or will occupy R is yellow. 
Consider the following three pairs statements: 
1. x is yellow. 
2. x occupies R; every occupant of R is yellow; i.e., it is a regularity, to which there are no exceptions, that every occupant of R is yellow. 
a. x just expanded. 
b. x is made of metal and all metal objects expand when heated. 
i. x is floating. 
ii. x is made of pinewood and pinewood floats. 
Bearing these three statement-pairs in mind, consider the following three questions: 
1*: Why is x yellow? a*: Why did x expand? i*: Why is x floating? 
2 is clearly not an answer to 1*. But why? Because the regularity indicated by the italicized part of 2 is obviously of the wrong kind. But why is it of the wrong kind? Because a thingÂ’s being in region R obviously doesnÂ’t cause it to be yellow.[370] 

Obviously 2 isnÂ’t the sort of explanation that advocates of DN have in mind. They have in mind explanations of the form: 
2#: x has phi and every instance of phi is yellow, 
where the italicized part indicates a relevant regularity. But, as weÂ’ve just seen, the underlined part indicates a relevant sort of regularity only if a thingÂ’s being phi causes it to be yellow. But if we know that a thingÂ’s being a phi causes it to be a psi, then we ipso facto already have a wealth of explanations, if only crude ones, at our disposal. For if we know that O is causally responsible for O#, then we ipso facto have an explanation of O#. 
So relevant regularities---regularities of the sort that DN-advocates obviously have in mind (Â“DNÂ” being short for Â“deductive nomological analysis of explanationÂ”)---presuppose the existence of explanations. Thus, DN is either viciously circular or, at best, it provides a correct analysis only of explanations of a derivative and therefore relatively unimportant kind. 
The exact significance of these remarks will become clear, as will the justification for them, when we consider a* and i*, which we will do right now. The italicized part of 2 obviously does correspond to the sort of regularity that advocates of DN have in mind---but only because itÂ’s already known that a thingÂ’s being made of heated metal causes it to expand. Somebody who doesnÂ’t already know that xÂ’s being made of heated metal caused it to expand wonÂ’t be able to identify the relevant covering law. But somebody who does know that xÂ’s being made of heated metal caused it to expand will have no use for that law. Such a person already knows that xÂ’s being made of heated metal caused it to expand; so such a person already knows that a thingÂ’s being made of heated metal causes it to expand. So unless a person already knows why x expanded, he wonÂ’t be able to find the right covering law. But if he knows why x expanded, he already knows the relevant covering law. So a person canÂ’t identify the sort of explanation that advocates of DN have in mind unless they already have an explanation of the fact for which an explanation is needed and unless, therefore, they have no use at all for the DN-explanation of that event. 
3.0 Psychological explanation: the glaring failure of Hempel-Hume conception of explanation to provide a reasonable account of it 
Some explanations concern psychological events: they concern thoughts, feelings, intentions, etc. along with the overt behaviors in which they result. When we consider such explanations, it becomes clear that what Hume and Hempel have to say about explanation fails, in a very ugly and obvious way, to give a correct account of psychological explanation; and, in the process of seeing why this is so, it will become even more clear than before why exactly that analysis fails to give a correct account of any sort of explanation. 
Consider the following two statements, both of which we'll assume to be correct: 
Statement#1: Smith goes to church every Sunday. Statement#2: All people as devout as Smith go to church every Sunday. 
Here is what advocates of DN say[371]: 
(VDN) To explain the fact that Smith goes to church every Sunday is to identify some pair of characteristics, phi and psi, such that it is already known every instance of phi is an instance of psi and such that Smith is already known to be a phi. Smith is already known to be devout, and itÂ’s already known that people as devout as Smith go to church every Sunday. Therefore, Statement #2 (henceforth Â“S2Â”) provides an 
explanation for the fact described by Statement #1 (Â“S1Â”). 
VDN is obviously not the right explanation of Smith's behavior. The right explanation is this: heÂ’s devout; his being devout, along with some beliefs of his as to how a devout person ought to act, prompt him to go to church every Sunday. Supposing that everyone as devout as Smith goes to church every Sunday, that regularity is a consequence of facts about the causal structure of the world. Far from being something in terms of which Smiths behavior is to be explained, that regularity is itself to be understood in terms of the behavior of people like Smith. The fact that devout people regularly attend Church is parasitic on the fact that SmithÂ’s being devout causes him to go to church every Sunday, along with the fact that BrownÂ’s being devout causes him to go church every Sunday, along with the fact that JohnsonÂ’s being devout causes her to go to church every Sunday, etc. So, in effect, one explains S1 in 
terms of itself, and thus explains nothing, if one explains S1 in terms of S2. For exactly similar reasons, one explains heated copper object xÂ’s expansion in terms of itself, and thus doesnÂ’t explain it at all, if one explains it in terms of the fact that copper objects expand when heated. 
4.0 The beginnings of an explanation of explanation 
One principle always underlies the search for answers (here I am referring exclusively to attempts to answer empirical questionsÂ—questions concerning the spatiotemporal): 
(MC)[372] 
causal anomalies must be minimized. 
For everything to be explained is for every cause to be known. 
Â“But surely that isnÂ’t true,Â” it will be said. Â“I can know what killed Tim (he ate fish) without knowing how it did so. (Was the fish rotten? Was it poisoned? Was Tim allergic to fish?)Â” Yes, but knowledge of the how is knowledge of the what. How-knowledge is high-resolution what-knowledge. If all you know about the cause of TimÂ’s death was that it was brought on by his eating fish, then you donÂ’t really know what caused his death. Your not knowing the Â“howÂ” consists in your not knowing the specific mechanisms involved; and your not knowing those mechanisms consists in your not knowing the Â“what.Â” 
That having been settled, let us turn to the question: How are causal anomalies minimized? The answer: 
(ED)[373] 
The elimination of causal anomalies consists of the elimination of discontinuities. 
You see a red ball roll in one end of a tunnel with opaque walls. A moment later, you see a similar ball roll out the other end. Given this information, it is natural to suppose that: 
(H1) The ball you saw entering the tunnel rolled from one end of it to the other and then exited it. 
ItÂ’s a theoretical possibility that H1 isnÂ’t the right explanation. Maybe what you saw is part of a magic-trick. But other things being equal, H1 is almost certainly correct. And even if it isnÂ’t correct, itÂ’s obviously a very reasonable hypothesis. The reason is that it eliminates the discontinuities in the events that you observed by supplementing them with events that you did 
not observe. Your observations tell you that some ball was instantaneously annihilated and that some other ball instantaneously popped into existence a few feet away. But if H1 is correct, none of these apparent discontinuities is 
an actual discontinuity. At least part of what makes H1 a good hypothesis is that, to the extent that itÂ’s correct, reality is continuous. This suggests that to explain is to eliminate discontinuities. Explanation is discontinuity-elimination. In response to this, it will be said that: 
(OH)[374] 
We can use your own example to prove that, contrary to what you are alleging, explanation is not the same thing as discontinuity-elimination. A ball rolls into one end of a tunnel and a similar ball rolls out the other. But the second ball isnÂ’t identical with the first. The first was obliterated the moment it was completely inside the tunnel. At that instant, an iguana suddenly materialized in the place previously occupied by the ball. That iguana ran from one end of the tunnel. But just before it would have emerged from the other end of the tunnel, the iguana hit a force field. Because of that collision, the iguana turned into a ball just like the one that entered the tunnel and, in addition, that ball rolled out of the tunnel. 
Let H2 be this hypothesis. H2 eliminates each of the discontinuities eliminated by H1. But whereas H1 is a good hypothesis, H2 is rubbish. So youÂ’re wrong: to explain is not to eliminate discontinuities. 
OH is misguided. Supposing that H2 is correct, a red ball suddenly vanishes and is replaced with an iguana that, although continuous with the ball in respect of its position, is discontinuous with it in respect of its morphological, chromatic, and chemical properties; and, a moment later, that iguana suddenly vanishes and is replaced with a ball that, although 
continuous with the iguana in respect of its position, is discontinuous with it in respect of its shape, color, and chemical properties. Thus, merely H2 replaces observed discontinuities with unobserved discontinuities. H1 doesnÂ’t posit any of the discontinuities posited by H2. So contrary to what OH says 
there are many discontinuities that H1 eliminates that H2 fails to eliminate. Moreover, there are discontinuities that H2 creates that H1 does not create. These facts are not only consistent with, but strongly support, our thesis that 
explanation is discontinuity-elimination. That said, there is a gap in our defense of that thesis: 
(OH*) Clearly erroneous hypotheses can do just as good a job as correct ones of eliminating discontinuities. Here is an example. You see a ball roll into an opaque tunnel. Immediately upon entering the tunnel, the ball quickly but continuously turns into an iguana. The iguana runs to the other end of the tunnel. Once at the other end, the iguana quickly but continuously turns back into a ball; and that ball rolls out the other end of the tunnel. 
Let H3 be this hypothesis. Even though itÂ’s obviously unacceptable, H3 does as good a job of eliminating discontinuities as H1. Thus, contrary to what you are saying, discontinuity-elimination cannot be the essence of 
explanation. 
Contrary to what OH* alleges, H3 does not do as good a job as H1 of 
eliminating discontinuities. First of all, even though it seems, at least initially, to do as good a job as H1 of eliminating spatiotemporal discontinuities, H3 creates a number of theoretical discontinuities that H1 does not create. There is no independent evidence that balls turn into iguanas or vice versa. So, in 
supposing that H3 is correct, weÂ’re supposing either (i) that the physical laws governing this one situation are very different from those governing other situations or (ii) that the observational data that weÂ’ve had thus far, which strongly suggests that iguanas donÂ’t turn into balls or vice versa, is very misleading as to the nature of reality. If (i) is the case, the laws of nature, and 
therefore the very structure of reality, had to undergo an abrupt and unprecedented change in order for the changes described by H3 to be possible. (And given the reasonable, though debatable (not to mention vague), supposition that the laws of nature are veritable spatiotemporal 
structures, it follows that H3 fails to eliminate discontinuities in a particularly egregious way.) If (ii) is the case, there is so little conformity between the data of observation and the structure of reality that we have no good reason to expect any of our observation-based beliefs, including our belief in (ii) itself, to be correct. Given obvious extensions of these points, itÂ’s clear that H2 
creates similar theoretical discontinuities. But H1 doesnÂ’t have any of these problems. It doesnÂ’t create any of the 
theoretical (or spatiotemporal) discontinuities that either H2 or H3 creates, and it eliminates each of the discontinuities eliminated by either. All of which suggests that, just as we proposed, discontinuity-elimination is the essence of explanation. 

5.0 Probability as an explanatory, not a statistical, concept (revisited) 
At time t, a prominent medical researcher says: 
(S1) Â“itÂ’s probable, but not certain, that Socrates had four kidneys.Â” 
Given all of the data available up until time t, S1 is the rational thing to say. 
More data becomes available. The researcher considers it. And, at time t*, that same researcher says: 
(S2) Â“Socrates only had two kidneys.Â” 
Given all of the data available up until time t*, S2 is the rational thing to 
say. 
Question: Given that S2 is true, does it follow that S1 was false? No. Given the data available to the researcher at t, it was probable that Socrates had four kidneys. Like all probability statements, S1 describes a relationship (one of bearing) that holds between some body of data and some hypothesis. S1 does not describe some state of affairs. If it did, it would be to the effect that Socrates had two kidneys to a certain degree, in which case it would be meaningless. 

5.1 Probability a property of statements, not of events or states of affairs 
Probability is a property of statements, not of states of affairs.[375] 
ItÂ’s a property of statements to the effect that a certain hypothesis is given a certain amount of support by a certain body of data. So itÂ’s a property of statements that describe bearing-relations. True probability statements correctly describe such relations; false ones incorrectly describe them. 
An illustration: Smith tells his friend Brown that heÂ’s going on a tour of Europe. But heÂ’s vague about where heÂ’s going to go, and when. But heÂ’s not completely vague; he gives Brown some relevant information. A month after Smith leaves, Brown tells a friend of his that: 
(PS1) ItÂ’s probable that Smith is in France right now. 
PS1 is correct. ItÂ’s correct because, given the data available to Brown, itÂ’s 
far more reasonable to believe that Brown is in France than it is to believe that he isnÂ’t. And PS1 is correct even if, at the time, Brown is Spain. It doesnÂ’t matter whether Brown is in France or not. What matters is that, given 
the available data, itÂ’s more reasonable to believe that he is than it is to believe that he isnÂ’t. 
PS1 says that, given such and such data, itÂ’s probable that Smith is in France. ItÂ’s irrelevant that, from a phonetic viewpoint, thereÂ’s no expression of the form Â“given such and such data.Â” From a logical standpoint, there is such an expression (unless PS1 is completely meaningless). 
In general, probability is inherently relational. For this reason, the words Â“P is probably the caseÂ” may be correct when they come out of one personÂ’s mouth and false when they come out of some other personÂ’s mouth. This will happen if the data available to the one person makes P more belief-worthy than not-P and the data available to the other makes not-P more belief-worthy than P. 
A complete description of the universe would contain no probability statements. Given any statement S (that isnÂ’t a probability statement), such a description would contain either S or not-S. Thus, probability is but Â“a measure of ignorance,Â” as Laplace put it. Somebody who knew everything could never correctly describe a proposition as probable but not certain. 








5.2 Probability not subjective 
Probability is a mind-independent logical relationship holding among statements. The degree to which a given body of data D confirms a given statement S has nothing to do with anyoneÂ’s opinion about anything: D confirms S to that degree whether or not anyone knows itÂ—whether or not anyone exists. Probability statements are useful only to the ignorant. (An omniscient being wouldnÂ’t have to bother with them.) But that doesnÂ’t mean itÂ’s only insofar as people are ignorant that theyÂ’re true. It means the opposite. TheyÂ’re useful to the ignorant because, when correct, they describe relations that actually hold between what (little) they know and what theyÂ’d like to know. 
Given a certain body of data, itÂ’s more reasonable to believe P than it is to believe not-P, even though, given that same data, it is not reasonable to believe P. To believe P is to be certain that P is correct. The data one has may make P more worthy of belief than not-P without making P worthy of belief. Given the data available to me, itÂ’s more reasonable to believe that my friend Sally is in Washington than it is to believe that she isnÂ’t. But since, given that data, itÂ’s only marginally more likely than not that sheÂ’s in Washington, it would be irrational of me to believe that she he is. 

5.3 Is there such a thing as non-epistemic probability? 
According to some, probability is sometimes a property of events, as opposed to statements. HereÂ’s the idea. At time t, electron e jumps to a higher orbit. Though the laws of nature didnÂ’t require it to jump, or not to jump, at that time, they did dispose it to jump. Here, it is said, we are dealing with a case of intrinsic, as opposed to evidential, probability. Supposing that one knew everything there was to know other than the fact that e jumped orbit at t, one could not on that basis predict with any certainty that e would jump at that time. Under these circumstances it might be said, it would be correct to say, that for reasons having nothing to do with ignorance on anyoneÂ’s part, the statement Â“it is more probable than not that e will jump at tÂ” is correct. 
Suppose for argument's sake that there are indeed undetermined eventsÂ— events that donÂ’t have to happen but do---one could argue that intrinsic probability is a kind of evidential probability: 
(IP)[376] 
Let S be a true statement alleging the occurrence of event E. S has an Â“intrinsicÂ” probability of greater than 50% iff S1. . . . Sn make it more likely than not that S, where S1... Sn is 
a list of every true statement that doesnÂ’t logically entail S. The idea is that, if you knew everything there was to know other than the fact that E jumps orbit at t, you could not learn more that was relevant to whether E would jump without actually learning whether E would jump. But, it will be said, the story is very different with statements that as a matter of natural law either must happen or cannot happen. Let S* be a true statement falling into this category. No matter how small the likelihood that S* is false, there are true statements that, if conjoined with the truths already known, will shrink that likelihood even further without eliminating it. (It may be that, because of interference effects, itÂ’s impossible to acquire more information that is relevant to whether S* is correct or not without actually learning whether S* is correct or not. But that would only be because those interference effects made it impossible to learn the truths that would enable you to shrink your margin of doubt.) Thus, intrinsic probability is a kind of evidential probability. One is dealing with intrinsic probability when, setting aside problems relating to interference effects, 
there is a limit to how much, short of learning whether the 
target statement is true or not, oneÂ’s margin of error can be 
reduced, and one has non-intrinsic evidential probability if 
there is no such limit. 
Nonetheless, IÂ’m not convinced that intrinsic probability is, in fact, a form of evidential probability. As before, let S be a true statement alleging the occurrence of some event E that has an intrinsic probability of greater than 50% but less than 100%, and let S1... Sn be a list that contains every true statement other than those that entail S. The statement Â“given S1... Sn, S is more probable than notÂ” does not say that, given S1... Sn, weÂ’re stuck with more questions than answers if we deny S. Were it supposed true that Hamlet was written by a levitating cat that, despite being incapable of self-consciousness, was deeply neurotic, all manner of beliefs concerning physics, biology, and psychology would have to be revised. But, assuming the truth of S1. . . Sn, it doesnÂ’t much matter whether S is accepted or rejected. It is, by 
hypothesis, a free wheel. I must therefore conclude that intrinsic probability, if it exists, is not evidential probability. 
I leave it to the reader as an exercise to say why intrinsic probability is not, contrary to what some might hold, identical with statistical probability; and I also leave it to the reader to say what exactly intrinsic probability is. 

5.4 Explanatory vs. statistical probability (revisited) 
In this section, weÂ’ll put forth some more reasons to think that explanatory (evidential) probability is not statistical probability. It will help if we start with a summary of our findings thus far. 
Other things being equal, a hypothesis is to be preferred to its negation if and only if more causal anomalousness is created by rejecting it than by accepting it. The degree to which a hypothesis is to be preferred to its negation is directly proportional to the degree to which it does a better job than the other of minimizing the net amount of causal anomalousness in the world. 
Probability is not a statistical notion. The word Â“probabilityÂ” has a statistical meaning. This is the meaning that it has in the statement: Â“the chances of a person whoÂ’s picked at random having red hair are one in eight.Â” All this means is that one person in eight has red hair. 
But this isnÂ’t the sort of probability that is relevant to explanations. When you say (Â“SNSÂ” is short for Â“Smith no showÂ”): 
(SNS) Â“Given that Smith hasnÂ’t shown up yet, heÂ’s probably not going to show up at all,Â” 
you are not making a statistical statement; you are not saying that in more than 50% of situations like the present one Smith doesnÂ’t show up. SNS could be true even if Smith has never failed to show up to anything in his life. And it could be false even if, in the past, heÂ’s failed to show up to 90% of his appointments. 
Statements affirming the probability of hypotheses seldom even appear capable of statistical interpretations. You can know that x is likely to do y in circumstances z without ever having seen x, or anything much like it, do y, or anything much like, in circumstances z, or anything much like them. For example, we have a pretty good idea of what at least some of the consequences of detonating a hydrogen bomb over the South Pole would be, even though nothing much like that has ever occurred. 
Â“But thatÂ’s where youÂ’re wrong,Â” contemporary Humeans say. Â“You see, itÂ’s only if itÂ’s interpreted in an absurdly narrow way that that the statistical conception of explanation has any of these problems.Â” And they defend this position by saying that (Â“SEÂ” stands for Â“statistical explanationÂ”): 
(SE) If a hydrogen bomb were detonated over the South Pole, it would by no means be unprecedented. True, we havenÂ’t detonated hydrogen bombs over the South Pole. In fact, we havenÂ’t detonated hydrogen bombs anywhere. But weÂ’ve detonated weapons similar to hydrogen bombs over places similar to the South Pole. Given this information, we have a pretty good idea of what the consequences would be of detonating a hydrogen bomb over the South Pole. 
And while youÂ’re right that SNS may be correct even if Smith has never missed an appointment in his life, youÂ’re wrong to conclude that explanation is not to be understood in statistical terms. If one is to be justified in accepting SNS, one doesnÂ’t need to know that Smith ever failed to show up to anything; and one doesnÂ’t need to know that what the relevant individuals, whoever they might be, failed to do was to show up. One need only know that people similar (in some respect relevant in the present context) to Smith failed to do something similar (same qualification) to showing up. One need only know that people like Smith (e.g., people who have serious drug problems) failed in some way that would be comparable to SmithÂ’s failing to show up (e.g., those people did not keep their promises). 
ItÂ’s easy to ridicule the statistical conception of explanation by showing that events exactly like the one being explained havenÂ’t occurred. But the situation being explained neednÂ’t be a perfect replication of any past situation. It need only be like past situations in some very abstract respect. 
The problem with this response is that there is no way to understand the 
concept of Â“relevant similarityÂ” in statistical terms; and in deciding what is 
relevantly similar to what, the advocate of SE is drawing on hypotheses that 
canÂ’t possibly have received any confirmation of a purely statistical kind. Any two things are similar in some respects and dissimilar in others. Some 
of these similarities are explanatorily significant, and others are not. It often 
happens that, despite our not having first conducted context-specific research, 
we can distinguish the relevant from the irrelevant forms of similarity. For example, itÂ’s obvious that, when trying to figure out what the consequences would be of detonating a given bomb over the South Pole, it doesnÂ’t matter whether that bomb is green as opposed to red, but it does matter whether itÂ’s a nuclear as opposed to a non-nuclear bomb. So itÂ’s obvious that, in the relevant respects, a red hydrogen bomb would be much more similar to a green hydrogen bomb than it would be to a red non-nuclear bomb. 
But this wouldnÂ’t be obvious at all if our evidence for it were strictly statistical. Given that, for any two things, one can contrive some respect in which they are similar, it follows that, with a few trivial qualifications, anything can confirm anything to any degree. 
This is what Nelson GoodmanÂ’s argument shows. (See Section 7.3). Find a respect in which green emeralds are similar to blue emeralds, and the fact that, thus far, all emeralds have been green confirms that, after this point, theyÂ’ll all be blue. (All green emeralds examined before the present are similar to blue emeralds examined in the future in that theyÂ’re all Â“grue.Â”) 
Another example: Find a respect in which herbivorous brontosauruses resemble cars that arenÂ’t affected in any adverse way by high-speed collisions, and the fact that all brontosauruses were herbivorous confirms that a speed collision wonÂ’t damage your car. (Herbivorous brontosauruses are similar to cases of your crashing your new, as of yet unscathed, car in that they are both Â“carbivorous.Â” Something is Â“carbivorousÂ” if itÂ’s either an herbivorous brontosaurus or a car driven by you after the present time thatÂ’s involved in a high-speed collision and isnÂ’t damaged by it.Â”) 
We know that terms like Â“grueÂ” and Â“carbivoreÂ” pick out explanatorily hollow properties, and thatÂ’s why we donÂ’t base our driving habits on our beliefs about the dietary habits of dinosaurs. We know what to infer and what not to infer only insofar as we know what kinds of similarity count. A precondition for making the right inferences is knowing what the relevant kinds of similarity are. 
Thus, thereÂ’s no way that judgments as to what the relevant forms of similarity are could have a strictly statistical basis. (That said, they obviously can and do have a partly statistical basis. But thatÂ’s not enough to make a go of the statistical model.) The concept of probability is to be understood in terms of the concept of explanatory integrity, not that of statistical frequency. The concept of explanatory integrity is to be understood in terms of the concept of causal integrity. The concept of causal integrity is to be understood in terms of the concept of continuity of change. One very important kind of change is change of position (motion). But not all change is change of position. Changes in temperature arenÂ’t changes in position. Nor are changes in color, shape, or structure. That said, at least some of these forms of change are to be understood in terms of the concept of change of position. But the same canÂ’t be said of other explanatorily important kinds of change. It canÂ’t be said of higher-order changes (changes in the manner of change), since higher-order changes arenÂ’t spatiotemporal changes at all. (A second-order change is a change in a spatiotemporal change; it is not itself a spatiotemporal change, and the same is obviously true of all other higher-order changes.) Earlier we considered some clearly erroneous hypotheses that seemed at first to do just as good a job of preserving continuities as some clearly worthy hypotheses. Had these initial impressions been correct, our analysis of explanation would have been in trouble. But they werenÂ’t correct. When we took a second look, we found that the clearly wrong hypotheses did a much worse job than their meritorious counterparts of dealing with higher-order continuities. And the continuities in question were ones that we already knew to be explanatorily important; they werenÂ’t contrived ad hoc to buttress our theory. 
6.0 A crucial fact about scientific explanation: Reality-description methodologically subordinate to data-modeling. 
There is more to explaining an event than showing it to be continuous with events in its vicinity. Let M1 and Mn be two mental events. M1, weÂ’ll 
suppose, is SmithÂ’s suddenly realizing that heÂ’s not a good composer and Mn, we will suppose, is SmithÂ’s realizing that his compositional efforts over the last 20 years have been in vain. There are, as we know, good reasons to believe that M1 and Mn are identical with brain events---let B1 and Bn be 
those events. But weÂ’ll see that, in order to explain Mn in terms of M1, it is neither necessary nor sufficient that we show, for each i (1 = i = n), that Bi is continuous with the brain-events in its spatiotemporal vicinity. Scientific 
disciplines (e.g., psychology, physics) are individuated, as weÂ’ll see, not (merely) by what they study, but by the data in terms of which the objects of their study are given to them. Those data are expressed by propositions. 
The same is true of events: they too are known to us through propositions. 
[377] 
Propositions consist of concepts. Disciplines model data. It isnÂ’t the event per se that is explained; it is some proposition describing its occurrence. Any given event---in other words, any (re)distribution of massÂ­energy---can be correctly described in many ways. There are many true propositions describing it. 
A consequence of these points is that, for any given (re)distribution of mass-energy, there are many possible objects of explanation. Given some event E, let T be some proposition describing EÂ’s occurrence that we wish to explain. Remember that it is T, not E per se, that we are trying to explain. It would be meaningless to say Â“IÂ’m explaining event E---but there is no truth that I am explaining.Â” It is (alleged) truths that are explained. Facts and events are explained only in the indirect sense that true propositions about them are explained. 
Moving on: Unless the continuities that we posit in the hopes of explaining T are expressed by propositions consisting of concepts belonging to the same family of concepts to which those constituting T belong we havenÂ’t established continuity within our models of events. And since it is only through these models that we know what the transphenomenal facts are, and thus what the transphenomenal continuities are, we havenÂ’t, under the circumstances described, succeeded in establishing any sort of continuity that is of any use in discovering the facts that lie on the other side of the data. 
So the essence of explanation lies not merely in the discovery of continuities, but in the discovery of propositions that, because of the structures of the concepts out of which they are constructed, establish what we might refer to as Â“model-internalÂ” (or Â“data-internalÂ”) continuities. We will clarify, illustrate, and demonstrate the truth of these points in the upcoming chapter. Moreover, we will do this in connection with our discussion of why it is that recent attempts to Â“scientizeÂ” the discipline of psychology are broken and ab initio doomed to failure. 
Chapter 21 Psychological Explanation and Interdisciplinary Reduction 
1.0 Some introductory remarks 
"The brain is an organ just like another." This is a popular saying among contemporary psychologists, especially among those who claim to be doing psychology in a "scientific" manner. So far as this slogan means anything, it means that psychology should be studied physiologically, not psychologically. 
In addition to being tautologically false, this position embodies a failure to grasp certain basic truths about knowledge and scientific methodology. It will be the purpose of this chapter to state those truths and to draw attention to some of their more obvious consequences. One of those consequences is that the mind must be understood on its own terms. So long as psychologists treat psychological truths as low-resolution physiological truths, and so long as they don't treat the class of psychological truths as sui generis, psychology will be a broken and incoherent discipline. 
Before we can substantiate these claims, we must make some general points concerning the nature of scientific inquiry. 
2.0 What it is to be a datum 
In this context, any references to intentions are to intentions that donÂ’t embody any incoherent beliefs. 
Even though, when framing a hypothesis, oneÂ’s ultimate objective is to identify the realities with which that hypothesis is concerned, that cannot possibly be oneÂ’s immediate objective. For it could be oneÂ’s immediate objective to describe those realities only if one knew what they were and therefore didnÂ’t need the help of hypotheses to acquire this knowledge. Thus, oneÂ’s immediate objective must be to model the data, not to describe data-transcendent realities. 
A related point is that it is truths that are explained. Not objects. Not events. Rocks aren't explained. Neither are migraines. Â“But surely explain events," it will be said. "A few years ago, my husband had a seizure. We went to a physician, looking for an explanation, and we got one." If the truth that your husband had a seizure had the same spatiotemporal boundaries as the seizure itself, it would have ceased to exist the moment the seizure ended, and it wouldn't have existed outside the place where the seizure occurred. Thus, the physician you later saw would have been explaining a non-existent truth. In other words, there would have been no truth that he was explaining. But there was such a truth, and there still is. That said, is no place that it is occupying. It isn't propping up a tent or heating up water otherwise behaving like things that occupy places. There isn't some place such that, by virtue of being in it or right next to it, one is better able to see or touch or hear or otherwise be affected by that truth. So it makes no sense to say that it has a location. So that proposition, just like its negation, is a non-spatiotemporal entity. But that event did have a location. So what the physician explained was a truth, not an event, and the same is true of everything that can possibly be explained. We'll see that this seemingly technical point must figure prominently in any decent explanation of explanation. 
2.0.1 What it is to be a datum (continued) 
Data are not raw facts. Data are propositions. Propositions are not raw facts. 
When trying to say what distinguishes a given discipline from every other discipline, the relevant question is not "which things and which events does that discipline study?" but rather "which propositions does that discipline assume to be true and which propositions is it trying to model?" 
Of course, there are some very generic propositions that all disciplines take for granted (e.g., if a thing is, in its entirety, in a given place at a given time, it cannot, in its entirety, simultaneously be in some other place that is a million miles awayÂ”). But given any discipline, there will be some class of propositions that it alone assumes to be true; and the subject matter of that discipline is identified when this class's membership is identified. 
There is a plausible objection to this position: 
(PO)[378] 
But astronomy studies stars; geology studies landmasses; zoology studies animals. Surely, contrary to what you say, disciplines are individuated by what they study. Disciplines are therefore not individuated by which propositions they assume to be true. They are individuated, I repeat, by which objects and events they study. 
Much of this is correct. For example, the facts studied by astronomy clearly don't even overlap with the facts studied by zoology. 
But we mustn't let these truths lead us astray. Astronomical facts are microphysical facts. Any movement of a star is nothing but a giant constellation of microphysical facts. Two universes that are indistinguishable at the microphysical level are necessarily indistinguishable at the astronomical level. Two such universes, indeed, are indistinguishable tout court. But astronomy is not a department of microphysics. In fact, those disciplines are disjoint, or nearly so. 
Similarly, even though all zoological facts are microphysical facts, zoology is disjoint from microphysics, or nearly so. Also, all of the facts studied by zoology are microphysical facts, and so are all of the facts studied by astronomy. 
To be sure, there is no specific fact that falls within the scope of both disciplines. But that's irrelevant. At the microphysical level, a dog is not so different from a comet. The general principles instantiated by the one class of microphysical facts overlaps heavily, if it doesn't coincide with, those instantiated by the other class. But that does nothing in the way of causing zoology to merge with astronomy. The fact that the class of things studied by astronomy is disjoint from the class of things studied by zoology is, we must conclude, a consequence of the fact that there are no raw facts described by data belong to both disciplines or by theoretical extensions thereof. 
Thus, disciplines are individuated primarily, and sometimes solely, by the bodies of data that they are trying to model. Disciplines are individuated only secondarily, and sometimes not at all, by the facts that they describe. 
PO embodies a failure to take into account that it is truths, not raw facts, that are explained. The raw facts in virtue of which astronomical facts hold are of the same ilk as those in virtue of which zoology holds. So, were it raw facts (and raw events), that were the foci of scientific explanation, astronomy would be zoology. But astronomy isnÂ’t zoology. 
Â“But,Â” it will be said, Â“when explaining star-constitutive events, one must sometimes apply microphysical principles in ways in which one neednÂ’t apply them when explaining animal-constitutive events.Â” True, but irrelevant. The way in which one must apply architectural principles to build a 33-story building doesnÂ’t precisely coincide with the way in which one must apply those same principles to build a 29-story building. But it would be absurd to say on that account that, if X designs a 29-strory building, he is not an Â“architectÂ” in the same sense as someone who builds a 33-story building. 
Â“But," it will also be said, Â“the classes of specific raw facts studied by those disciplines are disjoint.Â” True, but irrelevant. Given two medical researchers X and Y, itÂ’s unlikely that they study precisely the very same tissue samples. But it would be absurd to say on that account that X and Y are practitioners of different disciplines. It could very well be that X and Y are studying the very same problem, in the very same way. 
2.1 What it is to be a datum: conclusion 
Given only that somebody studies what is in fact a plant, it doesnÂ’t follow that heÂ’s a botanist. If his interest in those plants extends only as far as their ability to furnish him with information as to the structure of a certain kind of particle, then they are just heaps of particles to him, and it is as a physicist, not a botanist, that he is interested in them. Similarly, given only that somebody studies heaps of molecules, it doesn't follow that heÂ’s a microphysicist; for if his interest in those heaps extends only as far as their ability to furnish him with distinctly botanical knowledge, he is a botanist, not a microphysicist. 
By parity of reasoning, given only that somebody studies what are in fact neurological events, it doesn't follow that he's a neurologist. And given only that somebody studies what are in fact mental events, it doesn't follow that he's a psychologist. What determines whether somebody is a psychologist as opposed to a neurologist is a function of which truths he's trying to explain, not which raw facts those truths describe. 
3.0 Psychological explanation vs. non-psychological explanation 
We thus have the following facts to work with: 
(i) 
Science tries to eliminate anomalies. (Anomalies are not irregularities. Anomalies are discontinuities. It is in terms of concept of continuity that the concept of an explanatorily significant regularity is to be understood. See Chapter 17.) 

(ii) 
Science doesnÂ’t directly deal with the realities it aspires to describe. (If it did, it wouldnÂ’t have to aspire to describe them.) Science deals directly with data. 


(iii) What distinguishes discipline A from discipline B is that the class of propositions whose truth A assumes doesnÂ’t coincide with the class of propositions whose truth B assumes. 
Bearing these three facts in mind, consider the following situation. Barry is a botanist. Barry leaves plant X in a place where, for hours on end, it is exposed to blistering sunlight. Unbeknownst to Barry, X belongs to a species whose members can live only in cool, shady places. After a few hours, X dies. 
It's clear to Barry's supervisor that the cause of X's death was overÂ­exposure to sunlight. But the supervisor knows Barry to be a brilliant scientist and he is more interested in learning from Barry than in reprimanding him. The supervisor thus asks Barry to produce a maximally thorough botanical explanation of X's death. 
Assume (per impossibile) that Barry has complete knowledge of the microphysical activity constitutive of XÂ’s being placed in the sun, remaining in the sun, and then eventually dying, and also that everything Barry says is correct. 
Barry gives a thorough and precise description of each and every last micro-event involved in the series of particle-flurries mediating between, and including, X's being placed in the sun and X's dying. He uses no botanical or biological terms. The only non-generic terms that he uses belong to microphysics and mathematics. 
Did Barry explain X's death? No. We must remember that it is truths that are explained, not (re)distributions of mass-energy. Things aren't explained. Rocks cannot be explained. Propositions about rocks are explained. Events aren't explained. Truths that hold in virtue of events are explained. 
Barry did an excellent job of describing the (re)distributions of mass-energy mediating between X's being put in the sun and X's dying. True---the first particle-flurry happened to be identical with a certain, still-living plant; and the last particle flurry happened to be identical with a genidentical, recently-deceased plant.[379] 
So Barry successfully explained a microphysical truth that happened to hold in virtue of the same raw fact as the botanical truth that he was asked to explain. But he did not explain that botanical truth itself. So he failed to explain what he was asked to explain. 
3.1 An objection 
Some will feel that, by virtue of giving a maximally precise and thorough account of the microphysical activity involved in X's death, Barry has given a maximally good explanation of X's death. Such thinking is off the mark. 
The botanical changes that mediated between XÂ’s once healthy state and its eventual demise can be realized by infinitely many different microphysical changes. So Barry's excursion into microphysics may have explained why this plant died. But it did nothing in the way of explaining the deaths of plants whose situations were botanically indistinguishable from XÂ’s. Had Barry given a cogent botanical explanation of X's death, he would ipso facto have explained why events botanically similar to X's being moved lead to events botanically similar to X's dying. And by failing to give a cogent botanical explanation of XÂ’s death, Barry failed to say anything about why plants botanically similar to X, when placed in botanically similar situations, end up dying. Therefore, Barry failed to provide a botanical explanation of the death of even this one plant. 
3.2 Why concomitances are not enough for explanation 
If there turned out to be a way to characterize botanical concepts in microphysical terms, then Barry's answer might constitute a bona fidebotanical explanation of XÂ’s death. 
But there is no such way; nor could there be. The relevant distributions of micro-particles couldnÂ’t be described without using botanical terms. A given type of botanical event can be realized by infinitely many different events, no two of which have anything in common at the microphysical level. Let K be the least comprehensive class containing every instance (past, present, future, and possible) of some pine-tree's dying. 
Obviously K's membership is infinitely large. But that isn't important. What is important is that, from a microphysical perspective, K's membership is infinitely diverse. In other words, there is no one microphysical property (or finitely large set of microphysical properties) had by everything in K and by nothing not in K. 
But let's set aside talk of the merely possible; let's focus on the class of all actual pine-tree deaths. Let K* be that class. The likelihood that there is some microphysical property had in common by all and only K*'s members is small (but not zero). Obviously pine trees have similar cellular structures. But cells don't fall within the scope of microphysics. One reason for this is that, although cells are small in absolute terms, they are enormous relative to electrons, quarks, etc. Another far more important reason is that the concept of a cell no more helps the (micro)physicist discover principles relevant to his field than does the concept of a theocratic dictatorship.) But even if this slim possibility materialized, Barry still would have failed to explain X's death. Some science fiction will make it clear why this is so. 
Imagine a world in which round objects were green and square ones were red and in which we knew that colors and shapes were thus coordinated. In such a world, our knowledge of the truth that x is a green wheel could be very useful, as could our knowledge of the truth that y is a red wheel: weÂ’d know that, other things being equal, x would be a much better wheel than y. And, supposing that we lived in a world in which the microphysical truths Â“trackedÂ” botanical truths in a way similar to the way in which, in the world just described, chromatic truths Â“trackedÂ” geometrical truths, our knowledge of that fact could potentially be very useful. 
Knowledge of concomitances. But it mustn't be thought that knowledge of concomitances is anything more than a surrogate for genuine understanding. The next section will develop what we've already said in defense of this claim. 
4.0 The concept of psycho-physical reduction 
In this context, when talking about the Â“physical condition" of some object X, I mean what would be given by a description of the constellation of micro-particles composing X that was put forth by an infallible physicist who was acting in his capacity as a physicist. 
A plantÂ’s botanical condition supervenes on its physical condition. In other words, given two plants that are physically indistinguishable, it is impossible, as a matter of logic, that they should be botanically distinguishable. Since any given plant is composed of nothing but micro-particles, everything that happens to a plant coincides with a change in the inter-relations, if not the individual compositions, of those micro-particles. So where there are no micro-physical changes, there are no botanical changes; and where there are identical micro-physical changes, there are identical botanical changes. 
It has been assumed that, because the botanical supervenes on the microphysical, it must be possible to "reduce" botany to microphysics---that is, to show that what botany has to say about the world could, at least in theory, be said (and said more thoroughly and precisely) by microphysics. 
We're now going to find that: 
(i) Botany couldn't possibly be reduced to microphysics. 
(ii) Psychology couldn't possibly be reduced to microphysics (or any other physical science). 
And 
(iii) The reasons why psychology cannot be reduced to microphysics (or any other physical science) are distinctive. The sense in which psychology cannot be reduced to (micro)physics is more robust than the sense in which botany (or any other physical science) cannot be reduced to microphysics (or any other physical science). 
Let's start by considering the classical answer to the question: "what is it to 
reduce one discipline to another?Â” or, to put the question more precisely, Â“what are the conditions the fulfillment of which is both necessary and sufficient for the reduction of one discipline to anotherÂ”? Here is that answer[380]: 
(CA) LetÂ’s say youÂ’re trying to reduce botany to microphysics. There are many bridges you must cross. Let b be an arbitrary botanical concept. So b, let us suppose, is the concept pine-tree. (A consequence of this supposition, of course, is that x is an instance of b is (to the same effect as) the proposition x is a pine-tree.) You must, at the very least, identify certain microphysical concepts m1Â….mn such that any 
instance of the concept pine-tree is an instance of m1Â….mn. In other words, you must, to use HempelÂ’s (1965) expression, produce an accurate Â“microphysical characterizationÂ” of the concept pine-tree. Needless to say, given any botanical concept, you must do the same thing mutatis mutandis in connection with that concept that we just did (or, rather, described doing) in connection with the concept pine-tree. But that is not all you must do. Let p be any law of botany. (If, for whatever reason, you deny that there are laws of botany, replace the word "law" with the word "principle" in what follows.) p is presumably to the effect that, if a botanical truth of a certain kind is true, then so (probably) is a botanical truth of a certain other kind. To reduce botany to microphysics, you must show that, whatever it is about the universe in virtue of which that general botanical truth holds there is a micro-physical characterization of it. 
Let us clarify this last point. Let B be an arbitrary botanical law. B demands that, if botanical concept b1 is instantiated in space-time region R, then in all likelihood botanical concept b2 be instantiated in space-time region R*. (It is irrelevant in this 
context whether or not R and R* are distinct regions.) Given these assumptions, this is what you must do to reduce botany to microphysics: you must identify two sets of 
microphysical concepts, m1Â…mk and m*1Â…m*j, such that (i) b1 is instantiated in R iff m1Â…mk are instantiated in R and such that (ii) b2 is instantiated in R* iff m*1Â…m*j are instantiated in R*. 
To sum up: to reduce botany to microphysics you must provide microphysical characterizations of all botanical concepts and all microphysical laws. Doing this involves showing (1) that, for each botanical concept b, there are microphysical concepts m1Â…mn such that the proposition b is 
instantiated in R is true if and only if the proposition m1Â…mn are (jointly) instantiated in R is also true; and (2) that for each botanical principle B there is a microphysical law M such that an instance of B occurs in a given region, at a given time, only if an instance of M occurs in that same region, at that same time. 
Of course, given any two disciplines D1 and D2, the points 
just made in connection with the reduction of botany to microphysics are true mutatis mutandis of the reduction of D1 to D2. 
4.1 Concomitances require explanation and donÂ’t provide it (revisited) 
Right now, weÂ’ll evaluate CA. First point: The laws governing an entity are not necessarily identical with those governing its parts. Here are some illustrations of this. A and B are two distinct battalions. General Smith is in charge of both of them. The GeneralÂ’s orders determine how each battalion as a whole behaves. The soldiers composing A are psychologically very different from those constituting B. So, in effect, the soldiers in A are not governed by the same psychological forces (laws) as the soldiers constituting 
B. Nonetheless, the forces that determine the behavior of the battalion as a whole coincide with those determining the otherÂ’s behavior as a whole. So the laws, and therefore the principles, in terms of which the behavior of A's (collective) is to be understood coincide with those in terms of which B's behavior is to be understood. 
For the same reason mutatis mutandis, even if the parts composing a thing are governed by the same laws as the parts composing some other thing, it doesn't follow that, taken as wholes, those two things are governed by the same law or, therefore, are to be understood in terms of the same principles. There is considerable evidence that, even though medium-sized objects (e.g., basketballs) are themselves governed by deterministic laws. (More precisely, the sub-atomic parts of the atoms composing them are not governed by deterministic laws.) If this is right (and even if it isnÂ’t, in fact), the laws governing basketballs donÂ’t coincide with those governing their parts. (To clarify the parenthetical qualification: the laws governing basketballs coincide with those governing the behavior of objects having radically different microstructural compositions. As a result, the laws governing the micro-activity constitutive of basketballs donÂ’t coincide with those governing other objects that, as wholes, are governed by the same laws by which basketballs, as wholes, are governed.) 
Thus, two different objects could be governed by precisely the same botanical laws, even though the microactivity constitutive of the one is governed by entirely different laws from the microactivity of the other; and two things could be governed by different botanical laws, even though the microactivity constitutive of the one is governed by the very same laws as the microactivity constitutive of the other. 
4.1.1 Complying with laws vs. being governed by them, being governed by them; being governed by them vs. being explainable in terms of them 
Â“Your reasoning involves a serious fallacy," it will be said. Â“The laws of physics govern everything. Therefore, two different things cannot, at least not in the final analysis, be governed by different laws.Â” 
There are several points to make in response to this. We must start by distinguishing between Â“constitutionÂ” and Â“identity.Â”[381] 
Given a statue made of clay that is still soft, one can destroy a statue (by balling up the clay) without destroying the clay. Thus, the statue and clay donÂ’t have the same properties. The one has, whereas the other lacks, the property of being destroyed when balled up. For this reason, we say that the clay constitutes the statue without being identical with it 
For similar reasons, a plant is not identical with the aggregate of particles constituting it. For, by redistributing those particles (without scattering them), one can destroy the plant without destroying the aggregate. And itÂ’s probable, for the same reason mutatis mutandis, that mental states are not identical with the various physiological structures and patterns of physiological activity constituting them.
