For itÂ’s a theoretical possibility that the part of a given personÂ’s brain responsible for some psychological function is so altered that the brain-part not only continues to exist, but remains alive, even though, because of that alteration, that brain-part no longer performs F. 
The laws of physics clearly govern and explain the behavior of the particle-aggregate constituting the plant. But do they govern the plant itself? No. Before we explain this answer, we must put it in context. Two microphysically identical objects are ipso facto botanically identical. (If neither object is a plant, theyÂ’re still botanically identical; for neither has any botanical property not had by the other.) A corollary is that ceteris paribus identical microphysical changes realize identical botanical changes. 
But the laws of physics donÂ’t govern plants; they govern the particle-aggregates on which the behaviors of plants supervene. In order for the laws of physics to govern plants it is necessary, but not sufficient, that they govern plant-constituting particle-aggregates. Thus must govern plants per se. But, as far the laws of physics are concerned, there are particles, particle-swarms, etc.---but not plants. The right position, then, is to say that the laws of physics donÂ’t govern plants, but that the laws of physics govern the entities that constitute plants and that implement all of the changes undergone by them. Plants cannot violate the laws of physics, since a plantÂ’s condition supervenes on that of the physics-governed particle-heap of which it is composed. But those laws donÂ’t govern plants per se. 
Here is another way of thinking about. You could coherently imagine a universe botanically identical with ours----in which plants reacted in the same way to the same stimuli and, at the cellular and super-cellular levels, were structurally just like plants in our world---but in which the laws of physics were different. In such a world, the principles in terms of which plant-behavior was to be understood would coincide with the principles in terms of which plant-behavior is actually to be understood. So the laws of botany in that world, to the extent that there is such a thing as a law of botany, would coincide with the laws of botany our world.[382] 
Given that the laws of physics in that world donÂ’t coincide with the laws of physics in our world, it follows that, in our world, the laws of botanyÂ—the laws that govern plants--Â­arenÂ’t laws of physics. For exactly similar reasons, the laws of psychology in our world are not the laws physics. 
So, although everything that happens to a plant is determined by the laws of physics, it is misleading to say that the plants themselves are governed by such laws. For laws donÂ’t govern entities whose existence they donÂ’t countenance, and the laws of physics donÂ’t countenance the existence of plants. The physicistÂ’s world is plant-free. The laws of physics govern particle-heaps on whose properties those of plants supervene but with which plants are not identical. But only the laws of botany govern such heaps qua plant-constituting entities. Only the laws of botany acknowledge the existence of plants. So only the laws of botany can be said to govern botanical activity. And, for the same reason mutatis mutandis, only the laws of psychology can be said to govern psychological activity: the laws of physics donÂ’t govern it and neither do the laws of physiology. 
4.2 Concomitances require explanation and donÂ’t provide it (revisited) 
The conventional wisdom among philosophers of science is to say that, for the reasons just given, it's an open empirical question whether botany (or any other discipline) can be reduced to microphysics (or any other discipline)[383]: 
(CW) It cannot be known a priori whether or not botany is reducible to microphysics. In other words, given only that the microphysical laws govern the parts composing plants, it doesnÂ’t follow that such laws govern plants themselves. So supposing that all we know about plants is that such and such laws govern the microactivity constitutive of plants, it is an open empirical question---which, in light of future findings, might or might not turn out to be answered affirmativelyÂ— whether the laws of botany coincide with, or can be derived from, the laws governing the microphysical activity composing plants. 
CW is false. To say that botany can be reduced to microphysics is to say that microphysics can say whatever botany can say (and, possibly, say it better). WeÂ’ve seen that the laws governing the micro-particles composing plants could be different from those governing plants themselves. That means that, even if two objects are botanically indistinguishable, it could be that the one plantÂ’s microstructure has many a property that otherÂ’s microstructure lacks. To put it another way: even if, for any botanical property phi, x is phi is true iff y is phi is true, it could be that there exists many a microphysical property psi such that xÂ’s microstructure has psi is true and yÂ’s microstructure has psi is false. This, in its turn, means that, for any two plants x and y, even if it turns out that: 
(a) for any botanical property phi, x is phi is true iff y is phi is true, 
and it also turns out that: 
(b) for any microphysical property psi, x is a psi is true iff y 
is a psi is true, 
microphysical statements about a given plant would still not be analyses, or high-resolution versions, of botanical statements about that plant. 
So even if botanical truths about plants Â“trackedÂ” microphysical truths about them---even if, for any given plant, a perfect concomitance could be established between its botanical and its microphysical properties---those microphysical truths would have altogether different contents from those botanical truths. Those microphysical truths would not be high-resolutions of those botanical truths; those microphysical truths would not explicate or clarify or precisify the contents of those botanical truths. 
There would thus be no reduction of botany to microphysics. The relationship of the one set of truths to the other would not be a relation of content. We would, under such circumstances, learn no more about botanical truths from microphysical truths than, were we in a world in which all round objects were green and all square ones were red, we would learn about geometrical truths from color-truths. 
4.3 The sterility of brute concomitances in relation to psychophysical reduction 
Bearing this in mind, let MA be a passage that is exactly like CA except that, in each place where CA contains a reference to botanical truths, MA contains a reference to psychology (that is otherwise just like the reference to botany that it supplanted). For reasons exactly analogous to those just stated, even if the conditions described by MA were fulfilled, then psychology would still not be reduced to microphysics. ItÂ’s easy to extend this point. Let BA be a passage that is exactly like MA except that, in each place where MA contains a reference to microphysical truths, BA contains a reference to physiology (or neurology or brain-science, or whatnot). It follows for obvious reasons that psychology would not have been reduced to physiology (or whatnot). Thus, even if it turns out that physiological truths Â“trackÂ” psychological truths, the former provide not one shred of insight into the content of the latter. 
Of course, should it turn that there existed some such concomitance between the physiological and the psychological, that fact could be tremendously useful. In fact, it has turned out that (with some qualifications that, although heavy, arenÂ’t relevant here) there is such a concomitance between the neurological and the psychological; and it has turned out that knowledge of this fact has been of tremendous use. (It has made it possible to invent psychoactive medications and, more generally, medical procedures that dramatically improve peopleÂ’s lives.) But, contrary to what people generally infer from this, this does not entail that truths about the mind are to be sought in facts about the brain. I benefit enormously from the fact that certain things happen to my computer just in case certain buttons on my computer-keyboard are struck. But the truth that such and such keys are struck on the keyboard provides not the slightest wisp of insight into the truth that, thus and such images are showing up on the monitor. 
4.3.1 A variant of the point just made 
Imagine a world W that is just like ours, except that, in it, penguins were the only animals on the South Pole and also, in that world, there were no penguins that were not on the South Pole. In such a world: 
(i) x is an animal on the South Pole, would be true just in case 
(ii) x is a penguin 
was also true. Given that, in W: (HP)[384] 
all and only penguins were animals on the South 
Pole, it follows that, in W, for any given x, (i) and (ii) would be equivalent. But, in W, (i) and (ii) would mean exactly what they mean in the real world and theyÂ’d thus have very different meanings. Thus, in W, the meaning of: 
(1) Smith is an animal on the South Pole, would be very different from the meaning of: 
(2) Smith is a penguin. 
Thus, in W, the truth of (2) would not, except perhaps in some very attenuated sense, be explainable in terms of the truth of (1), or vice versa. Suppose that, at time t, Smith is the only person in place p and also that Smith is the only person wearing a black shirt. Under those circumstances, Smith is in p at t and Smith is wearing a black shirt at t are equivalent. But neither proposition to any degree explains the other. 
The relationship between (1) and (2) is, in the relevant respects, identical with the relationship between the just-mentioned propositions about Smith. 
Since, apart from the fact that HP is true in world W but not in our world, W is governed by the same laws as our world. So it is just as possible in W as it is in our world for something to be a penguin that is not on the South Pole. That is why, even in W, (1) doesnÂ’t explain (2), or vice versa; it is why, for any x, (i) doesnÂ’t explain (ii), or vice versa. 
5.0 The sui generis nature of psychophysical explanatory gap 
One of the ways in which psychology cannot be reduced to any one of the physical sciences is comparable to the way in which botany cannot be reduced to physics. But there is a way, weÂ’ll now argue, in which psychology cannot be reduced to any other discipline that is distinctive. The irreducibility of the psychological is distinctive; the sense in which truths of psychology are anomalous with respect to truths of any one of the physical sciences is deeper than the sense in which the truths of botany (or any other physical science) cannot be reduced to those of physics (same qualification). 
5.1 Type-type vs. token-token reduction 
The irreducibility of botany to microphysics lies in the fact that botanical concepts are not co-extensive or a fortiori co-intensive with microphysical concepts. So there is no microphysical concept that is co-extensive with the concept of a pine-tree. Indeed, there is no botanical concept that is coÂ­extensive (or, therefore, co-intensive) with any micro-physical concept, that being why no microphysical principle can replace any botanical principle. 
Nonetheless, given any specific botanical truth B (e.g., plant x died on Tuesday), it is theoretically (though not practically) possible to show B to be a consequence of some microphysical truth. (I am using the term Â“microphysical truthÂ” to cover truths consisting of enormously long conjunctions of true microphysical propositions.) A metaphor may be of use here. If you know how the various bricks composing some building are interrelated---if you know, for any two such bricks, how they are spatially interrelated---then you can, in principle (if not in practice), figure out the shape of the structure that those bricks jointly constitute. 
For exactly similar reasons, supposing for argumentÂ’s sake that you knew, for some time t, exactly how, at t, any two of the micro-particles composing some object O were interrelated, you could on that basis figure out OÂ’s overall structure (at least in principle). [385] 
Given a knowledge of OÂ’s overall structure (at a given time), along with a grasp of the conditions that an object must satisfy to fall under the concept pine-tree or blade of grass or any other botanical concept, you could determine what, if any, botanical properties O had. 
So even though botanical types canÂ’t be identified with microphysical types, botanical tokens (i.e., instances of botanical types) can be identified with microphysical tokens (i.e., instances of microphysical types). Moreover, even though botanical principles are not identical with, and cannot be derived from, microphysical laws, any given non-general botanical truth can (in principle, setting aside interference-effects, though not in practice) be shown to be a consequence of some non-general microphysical truth. And this shows that, even though the principles of botany cannot be derived from those of microphysics and even though, therefore, botanical explanations cannot be replaced by microphysical explanations, it is not anomalous that there should be botanical data in a world all of whose denizens are governed by (micro)physical laws. In other words, it shows that, even though botany cannot, even in principle, be absorbed into microphysics, there is no reason in principle (setting aside interference-effects and other problems relating to the acquisition of knowledge of micro-particles) that, in a world all of whose constituents are composed of objects governed by microphysical laws and must themselves comply with such laws, there should nonetheless be truths that defy microphysical explanation. 
5.2 Type-type vs. token-token reduction (continued) 
But psychology is, in this respect, not to be put in the same category as botany. Not only is it not possible to reduce psychology to microphysics (or any other physical science): given any non-general biological truth, there is no microphysical truth such that---even after every possible allowance is made for interference-effects, human limitations, etc.---knowledge of that microphysical truth could possibly make it at all clear why that psychological truth should hold; there is no microphysical truth such that (even after all the usual allowances are made) makes it at all clear why any given psychological proposition should hold. 
HereÂ’s why. The data modeled by any physical science---by physics, zoology, botany, etc.---is perceptual data. The data modeled by psychology is (for lack of a better word) Â“introspectiveÂ” data. What does this mean? First of all, the Â“raw dataÂ” modeled by botany (for example) doesnÂ’t consist of experiences; it consists of things known (or believed to be known) through experiences. That raw data concerns plants, trees, etc. Botanists donÂ’t talk about their experiences; they talk about the things that are the objects of their experiences---the plants, etc. that they see. The same is true of physicists. They donÂ’t talk about their experiences; they talk about the things they see and touch---the needle-displacements, the discolorations on photographic-plates, etc. 
By contrast, experiences themselves constitute the data modeled by psychology. A physicist may refer to an experience that he has (Â“I suddenly saw a blinding explosion and momentarily couldnÂ’t seeÂ”) but only because he is attempting in so doing to describe some phenomenon known through experience (through perception); the experience is of interest only in so far as it gives one information as to some trans-experiential entity---as to something that, although the object of experience, is not itself an experience. 
Psychology is interested in the experience itself, and itÂ’s interested in the object of experience only in so far as knowledge of the latter may help one acquire knowledge of the former. Psychology is interested in what I felt on such and such an occasion; in order to make it clear how I felt, I must inevitably refer to external events (Â“so and so took my wallet; I punched him; I was arrested; my lawyer was five hours late,Â” etc.). In fact, descriptions of external events are constitutive of descriptions of the experiential data in which the psychologist is interested. (The contents of oneÂ’s experiences are given by Â“thatÂ”-clauses. Â“I felt that I had been cheatedÂ”; Â“I saw that he was foaming at the mouth.Â” The exceptions to this prove spurious. Â“I saw a dogÂ” is really elliptical for Â“I saw that there was a dog in a certain place.Â” Grammatically, the object of a verb such as Â“see,Â” Â“feel,Â” or Â“knowÂ”---the sort of verb that would be integral to any description of oneÂ’s experience---Â­may either be a Â“thatÂ”-clause or an ordinary noun phrase. One can say Â“I know that snow is whiteÂ” or Â“I know Charlie.Â” But we have seen that, ultimately, what one believes, feels, or otherwise experiences is given by a Â“thatÂ”-clause.) But it is those experiences per se, not their objects, which the psychologist tries to model. 
This is easily shown. Given two people who are atom-for-atom duplicates and whose experiences are qualitatively identical, those people are ipso facto identical as far as a psychologist is concerned, even if one of them is a brain in a vat whose experiences are caused, not by photons bouncing off of the things he thinks he sees, but by stimulations of nerve-endings, whereas the other has veridical experiences. Setting aside the irrelevant, technical issue of how the disembodied brain would make its sentiments known to anyone, the disembodied brainÂ’s experiences are, from a psychoanalytic or psychological perspective, 100% comparable to the other personÂ’s experiences. But to a physicist (or botanist or geologist, etc.), the fact that the one personÂ’s experiences are hallucinatory ipso facto disqualifies them: they are no longer viable sources of information. 
5.3 Weak vs. strong reduction and the reason why mental truths are both weakly and strongly irreducible to physical truths 
Any physical science models things known through perception. Psychology does not model things known through perception. It models our experiences. Of course, our perceptions are among our experiences. But psychology studies the perceptions themselves. Other sciences study the things known through them. Astronomers study stars, not perceptions of stars; psychologists study perceptions of stars, not stars. 
Because experiences are the subject-matter of psychology, two people whose lives are experientially indistinguishable are psychologically indistinguishable, even if one of them, during his waking life, experiences nothing but hallucinations, whereas the other has never had so much as a single hallucination. 
Of course, psychologists are interested in the fact that a given person has had a hallucinationÂ—but only in so far as that fact indicates some psychological malfunction on that personÂ’s part. The hallucinations had by the aforementioned brain-in-a-vat are not (necessarily) so indicative, at least not necessarily, and therefore do not (necessarily) interest the psychologist except in so far as, and in the same way as, their veridical counterparts interest him. 
5.3.1 Weak vs. strong reduction and the reason why mental truths are both weakly and strongly irreducible to physical truths (continued) 
Given a building composed entirely out of bricks, if one knew how any two of those bricks were spatiotemporally interrelated, one could in principle figure out the structure of that building. Similarly, by knowing how any two atoms composing a given plant were spatiotemporally interrelated, one could in principle (though not in practice, given how many atoms would be involved) figure out what that plantÂ’s macro-characteristics were---its morphology, its mass, etc. 
Further, supposing that one had such macro-knowledge and that one had a knowledge of the concepts of botanyÂ—concepts such as plant, pine-tree, cactus, leaf, etc.---and, therefore, that one knew what morphological, dynamic, etc. properties a thing had to have to qualify as (say) a Venus flyÂ­trap, the aforementioned microphysical propositions would, given the propositions embodying that persons knowledge of the concepts of botany, entail (for example) that such and such was a Venus fly-trap that had thus and such distinctively botanical properties; and the same thing mutatis mutandis would be true of any other given botanical propositions. 
So the truths of microphysics, taken together with truths describing the concepts of botany---truths that, since they merely delineate those concepts and donÂ’t say anything as to whether theyÂ’re instantiated or by what, are analytic---entail the truths of botany. In other words, if B1Â….Bm is the least inclusive list containing every botanical truth, and M1Â….Mn and Cb1Â…Cbo are the least inclusive lists containing the truths of microphysics and the truths concerning the structures of botanical concepts (the analytic truths of botany, in other words), then, given M1Â….Mn and Cb1Â…Cbo, it is 100% probable that B1Â….Bm are true. Put yet another way, the way in which the conjunction of M1Â….Mn and Cb1Â…Cbo entails B1Â….Bm is comparable to the way in which x is a triangle entails x has more than two sides. WeÂ’re dealing with deductive, not with inductive, inference. So given any one (non-general) botanical truth (e.g., x is a Venus fly-trap), there is some microphysical truth (which, in all likelihood, is a long conjunction of microphysical truths) with respect to which that botanical truth is completely non-anomalous. 
5.3.2 Weak vs. strong reduction and the reason why mental truths are both weakly and strongly irreducible to physical truths (continued) 
So there is a sense, albeit a weak one, in which botany is reducible to microphysics. Botany is reducible to microphysics in the weak sense that, for any given botanical truth, there is some microphysical truth with respect to which the former is non-anomalous. Botany is irreducible to microphysics in the sense that the system of botanical truths that botany puts forth, containing as it does botanical principles alongside the specific botanical truths it contains, cannot be deduced from, or otherwise understood in terms of, the truths of microphysics. In fact, we have seen that, contrary to what Hempel (1965) assumed, even if we happened to live in a world in which botanical-types happened to be co-extensive with microphysical types, botany still couldnÂ’t be reduced, at least not in this robust sense, to microphysics. 
As weÂ’ve seen, a consequence of the irreducibility, in this strong of sense, of botany as a whole to microphysics is that what is said by any given botanical proposition is different from what is said by any given microphysical proposition, even if both truths concern the same displacement of mass-energy. Nonetheless, any given botanical truth is non-anomalous with respect to some microphysical truth. 
5.3.3 Weak vs. strong reduction and the reason why mental truths are both weakly and strongly irreducible to physical truths (continued) 
Bearing this in mind, letÂ’s suppose that Smith has a thorough knowledge of the concepts of psychology (desire, anxiety, intention, etc.). LetÂ’s further suppose that Smith is given a thorough and accurate description of the microphysical events composing BrownÂ’s brain over some period of time. 
By reasoning analogous to that just put forth, Smith could in principle infer everything there is to know about BrownÂ’s brain. But, given only that data, he could infer not one single psychological truth about Brown. Psychological truths (about Brown) are not given by propositions to the effect some external object has some property or has been displaced in a certain way. Whatever information psychological truths do contain, that information is not to the effect that brains or physiological or otherwise sense-knowable entities have (undergone) some sense-knowable property (change). That information is about the experiences through which such changes are known, not the changes themselves. Which, as weÂ’ve said twice before, is why the psychologist qua psychologist regards persons x and y as psychologically indistinguishable if the propositions describing the one personÂ’s mental states coincide with those describing the other personÂ’s, it being irrelevant from his viewpoint whether there is any divergence between those two people in respect of how accurately their experiences depict the world. (Â“But doesnÂ’t the psychologist care whether somebody is hallucinating or not?Â” Yes, but only because hallucinations are typically symptoms of psychological disturbances. The envatted brainÂ’s experiences are not thus symptomatic.) 
So if M*1Â….M*n is the least inclusive list of all of the microphysical truths describing the thing constituting BrownÂ’s brain, and P1Â….Pm is the least inclusive list of all of the truths concerning the concepts of psychology (i.e., is the least inclusive list of all analytic psychological truths), the conjunction of those two lists of propositions does not, by itself, entail (or, indeed, otherwise confirm) so much as a single psychological truth about Brown. 
5.3.4 Weak vs. strong reduction and the reason why mental truths are both weakly and strongly irreducible to physical truths (closing the argument) 
In order for Smith to make any inferences about what is going on in BrownÂ’s mind, we must add to what Smith already knows. So, granting that Smith knows M*1Â….M*n and also P1Â….Pm, Smith would have to know that 
when thus and such microphysical propositions (about the heap of particles constituting BrownÂ’s brain) held, then thus and such psychological truths (about Brown) also held. In other words, in order for Smith---even if given the vast amount of information embodied in M*1Â….M*n and P1Â….Pm ---to 
acquire knowledge of so much as a single psychological truth about Brown, he has to know of psycho-physical correlations. 
What this shows is that the best one can do in the way of absorbing psychology into physiology is to establish correlations between them. But this means that what psychology says about the world cannot even in principle be deduced from, or otherwise understood in terms of, what physiology says about the world. Even if psychological types were coÂ­extensive with physiological types, the very fact that psychological types are not necessarily coextensive with physiological types entails what psychological truths say about the world is altogether disjoint from what physiological truths say about the world. 
Even in a world W where all red objects were round, and no non-round objects were red, the information provided by the proposition x is red would be different from that provided by x is round. For it would be true, in W, that, even though the redness and roundness were co-extensive types, they werenÂ’t necessarily so. Even in W, that is to say, the proposition x is red but not round would make sense, as would the proposition x is round but not red, even though theyÂ’d be false for all values of x. This shows that, even in a world where two properties P and P* are co-extensive, unless x is P entails x is P*, or vice versa, those propositions, if true, reveal different facts about the world. 
In our world, psychological types are not identical with physiological types. (A given ability on somebodyÂ’s part; e.g., that personÂ’s ability to drive or speak English, can migrate. It often happens that, if brain-center A, which thus far has mediated SmithÂ’s ability to drive, is damaged and can no longer do its job, some other brain-center B takes over AÂ’s job---notwithstanding 
that A and B are neurologically very different. There are a lot of different neurological ways to skin a given psychological cat.[386]) 
5.4 A similar line of thought 
The truths that it is the purpose of psychology to model are such that, unless one has had some kind of non-perceptual encounter with those things or with things of the same kind, one couldn't possibly understand them. I obviously canÂ’t have your experiences. But unless I myself had experienced sadness, frustration, etc., I wouldnÂ’t understand what you were saying when you spoke about your own feelings of sadness, etc. (For argument's sake, we'll suppose that, so far as anyone has knowledge of what is going on in any other person's mind, I have knowledge of what is going on in your mind.) So even though I cannot possibly have the direct, intuitive knowledge of your mental states that you can have of them---even though I can do no better than to have "knowledge by description" of them, whereas you can have knowledge "by acquaintance" of them[387]---my knowledge of your mental states isnÂ’t purely formal; it is informed by a knowledge of relevantly similar states in myself, my knowledge of which is completely non-perceptual. 
Moreover, the types of things in which the psychologist is interested are such that their instances are always known in a way that is at least partly non-perceptual. Their instances in the conscious or preconscious parts of one's mind are known in a wholly non-perceptual way.[388] 
Their instances in other people's minds are known in a partly non-perceptual way, as are nonÂ­(pre)conscious instances in one's own mind. 
So even though the specific things in which the psychologist is interested are often such that he cannot know them through sense-perception, there are three fundamental differences between the subject matter of astronomy, or any other physical science, and the subject-matter of psychology: 
(i) 
The things in which the psychologist is interested, though known to him in a partly sense-based way (except when he is studying his own mind), are known (to the patient) in a non-sense-based way. 

(ii) 
By virtue of knowing those things in a non-sense-based way, the patient has a more robust knowledge of them than could be had by anyone who knew them in a sense-based way. 


(iii) The types of things studied by the psychologist are such that, unless one has had direct, non-sense-based knowledge of them, one cannot even have descriptive, second-hand knowledge of their occurrence in others. 
Given (i)-(iii), it follows that oneÂ’s knowledge of another personÂ’s mental states is partly, though obviously not entirely, based on knowledge of oneÂ’s own mental states and, therefore, that knowledge of another personÂ’s mental states is partly, though obviously not entirely, not sense-based. 
5.4.1 Why there is a sense in which psychology is anomalous with respect to the physical that is deeper than the sense in a given physical discipline could possibly be anomalous with respect to another physical discipline 
Botany, astronomy, microphysics, zoology, and geology, though very different from one another, model data to the effect that the structure of the external world is such and such; that things are spatiotemporally interrelated in such and such a way; that the things thus interrelated have such and such properties; and that those properties themselves are such that their instances are inherently constitutive, or at least dispositive, of instances of certain kinds of spatiotemporal interrelations or changes in such relations. Consider the sorts of properties in which a physical scientist is interested: temperature, conductivity, gravitational pull, acidity, malleability, density, migration patterns, physical morphology, way of reproducing, way of obtaining nourishment. It is easily shown that, for any concept C such that C is one of the concepts which is the object of (non-psychological) scientific study, x is an instance of C holds in virtue of the way in which mass-energy is (re)distributed . 
But, for any concept C such that C is one of the concepts which is the object of psychological study, x is an instance of C is not to that effect. The proposition Sam is sad is not to the effect that some (re)distribution of mass-energy holds. It may be---indeed, the present author firmly believes it to be--Â­that SamÂ’s sadness is mediated by physiological events and therefore by (re)distributions of mass-energy. But Sam is sad is not to the effect that anything having any motion-constitutive or motion-conducive properties is occupying, or likely to occupy, any position relative to anything else. Sam is sad registers a truth that is known to Sam in a thoroughly non-perceptual way and that cannot be known to anyone other than Sam except on the basis of his own experience of sadness and therefore cannot be known to anyone other than Sam in a way that is in part (though not entirely) non-sense-based. 
5.5 Donald Davidson's failed attempt to demonstrate the anomalousness of the mental with respect to the physical 
Like us, Donald Davidson held that psychological truths are anomalous 
with respect to physical truths. He presents his argument for this in his 
celebrated (1970) paper Â“Mental Events.Â”[389] 
Here is that argument: 
(DA)[390] 
Suppose the following. x is some event in SmithÂ’s brain. x also constitutes a desire on SmithÂ’s part to become a lawyer. 
Question: Why does x constitute such a desire? Answer: Because, given the thoughts and deeds on SmithÂ’s part that x follows and given the thoughts and deeds on SmithÂ’s part that x precedes, it makes sense to see x as a desire on SmithÂ’s part to become a lawyer. It is analytic that a desire on somebodyÂ’s part to become a lawyer has certain causes and also certain effects. It is analytic that, given certain circumstances, a desire to become a lawyer leads one to study for the LSAT, apply to law school, and so on. And itÂ’s analytic that, given certain circumstances, a desire to become a lawyer be the result from oneÂ’s belief that lawyering is the best way to promote the interests of justice (or whatnot). 
Before we take the next step in our argument, we must generalize these points. Let P be an arbitrary physical event and let M be an arbitrary mental category. (An example of a mental category would be belief that snow is white, desire to become a senator, regret at never having learned to play a musical instrument. So for x to fall into the category desire to become a senator is for x to be a desire to become a senator.) If P is to fall into M, it is necessary and sufficient that, given what PÂ’s owner thought and did prior to PÂ’s occurrence, and given also what PÂ’s owner thought and did after its occurrence, it makes sense to suppose that P is an instance of M. In other words, for P to fall into M is for P to be such that it can be reasonably interpreted as falling into M. To be a belief that 1 + 1 = 2 is to be interpretable as being such a belief. 
This must be understood aright. Supposing that P is a belief 
that 1 + 1 = 2, there isnÂ’t anything other than PÂ’s being interpretable as being such a belief that makes it be such a belief. It being thus interpretable isnÂ’t a consequence of its being such a belief: it is its being such a belief. In general, there isnÂ’t anything to anythingÂ’s being an instance of mental category M other than its being such that it can reasonably be seen as being such an instance. 
To move forward, let us continue to suppose that P is a belief that 1 + 1 = 2. Let us also suppose that P is a brain-event and, in addition, that P falls into physical category C. 
For P to fall into C isnÂ’t for P to be such that it can reasonably be interpreted as falling into C. It isnÂ’t in virtue of what PÂ’s owner does or thinks before or after PÂ’s occurrence that P falls into this as opposed to that physical category. If P falls into a given physical category, it is in virtue of its chemical structure, or some such, it being irrelevant whether so categorizing P has the consequence that PÂ’s owner is rational or not. 
It follows that, even though mental events are identical with brain-events, the reasons for which a given event is mental are different from those in virtue of which itÂ’s physical. Moreover, the former reasons cannot be understood in terms of the latter. Thus, there is an explanatory gap. 
Although we've seen reason to agree with Davidson that there is an explanatory gap, DA utterly fails to establish this. This is because it depends on two false assumptions. 
The first is the assumption that to be a belief that 1 + 1 = 2 (or a desire to lose weight or an intention to buy a car, etc.) is to be interpretable as being such a belief (or desire or wish, etc.). In addition to being deeply counterintuitive, DavidsonÂ’s Â“interpretivistÂ” view of the mental is demonstrably false. According to DavidsonÂ’s interpretivism, for brain-event x, had by person A, to fall into mental category M is for it to be the case that, if x is assumed to fall into M, then A is, to that extent, rational. If this were right, nobody could possibly make any erroneous inferences; nobody could ever think or act irrationally. For, by DavidsonÂ’s lights, if x doesnÂ’t have the consequences that a belief that 1 + 1 = 2 should have, it ipso facto isnÂ’t a belief that 1 + 1 = 2. But people make erroneous inferences from their beliefs; people arenÂ’t always rational. (See Chapter 19 for a more thorough refutation of DavidsonÂ’s interpretivism.) Therefore, Davidson is wrong. 
Also, DavidsonÂ’s argument assumes the truth of a doctrine known as "functionalism,Â” which, in Chapter 22, Section 7.1, weÂ’ll find to be false. 

6.0 Duly modifying our earlier claim that to explain x is to show x to be continuous with other events in its neighborhood 
Sciences model data. Hopefully these models yield truth. But, since truth is known only through the models we construct, it cannot be a scientistÂ’s immediate intention to describe the truth; his immediate intention must be to construct a model. More specifically, his immediate intention is to construct a model that, although hoped to be truth-conducive, is intended to satisfy some desideratum that can be identified without already knowing the relevant truth: some model, that is to say, that is Â“goodÂ” in a way that can be defined independently of the concept of truth---but that, because it is good in that way, hopefully leads to the truth. 
The body of data at a personÂ’s disposal isnÂ’t homogenous. It automatically differentiates itself into sub-classes of data. These sub-classes comprise propositions that share certain key concepts and that, if accepted, tend to lead one to accept other propositions that share those concepts. If the subject makes a sufficiently intelligent and concerted effort to delineate the consequences of these propositions, they can be organized into an system of propositions whose natural tendency is to become more organized and more comprehensive. 
As we've said many times, a scientist's immediate intention is to model the data, not to identify the truth. Given this fact, along with the fact that to explain is to show the apparently discontinuous to be continuous, it follows that a scientist's immediate intention to establish data-internal continuity, not among in reality per se---not in the data-transcendent reality to which, if all goes well, his models will lead him---but in reality in so far as it can be described using the concepts definitive of his discipline. 
So a botanist wants to avoid botanical discontinuities. In his effort to explain how plant X's not being watered on Monday led to its dying on Tuesday, he'll posit botanical continuities, not microphysical continuities. From his viewpoint, the propositions by which microphysical continuities are described are data-transcendent. Thus, those propositions are meaningless from a botanical perspective, since they are constructed out of concepts that are external to those out of which botanical propositions are constructed. He'll thus posit botanical continuities. True---propositions describing such botanical continuities are exponentially more low-resolution than those describing microphysical continuities. But former propositions, unlike the latter, are data-internal and can describe continuities that help him model the relevant data. 

7.0 The concept of a datum (revisited) 
We began this chapter by outlining an answer to the question: "What is a datum?" WeÂ’ll end this chapter by filling in that outline. 
You believe many things. Some of your beliefs are true. Some of your true beliefs are cases of knowledge. Consider the smallest set containing all of those beliefs of yours that are cases of explanatorily robust knowledge. A given piece of knowledge is Â“explanatorily robustÂ” if the proposition thereby known is explanatorily robust, and a proposition is Â“explanatory robustÂ” if it leads to explanations that lead to the truth. (So Â“Smith is a person who just consumed large quantities of cyanideÂ” is explanatorily robust, since it naturally leads to an explanation of the fact that Smith is now dead.[391]) Let S* be the smallest set containing all of the propositions that you accept by virtue of having those pieces of knowledge. 
S* can be divided into sub-classes. Some of those sub-classes are not explanatorily unified. An example of such a class would be the one whose only members are the propositions two is even, Neptune is a planet, and ketchup is not a vegetable. But some of those sub-classes are explanatorily unified. An example of such a class would be the one all and only those propositions concerning numbers that you know to be true. 
Any given class corresponds to a concept.[392] 
The class of all plants corresponds to the concept plant. (This concept may be identified with the property of being a plant, at least for the purposes of this discussion, and the same thing mutatis mutandis is true of every other concept.[393]) The class of all things that are either dogs or numbers corresponds to the concept thing such that x is either a dog or a number. 
7.0.1 The concept of a datum: Concepts that have explanatory value vs. those that donÂ’t 
The concepts in terms of which we instinctively understand the world tend to have considerable explanatory and predictive value. The world is so structured that, given that x is a plant, it follows that it will thrive under certain conditions and die under others; that x cannot talk; that x reproduces in certain ways but not others; that x has certain organelles but not others; and so on. Given this information about x, along with a modicum of knowledge concerning xÂ’s physical surroundings, it can be explained why x died/why, despite previously being on the brink of death x is thriving/whether x will reproduce/and so on. Thus, the concept of a plant picks out an explanatorily unified class of entities. 
Not all concepts are comparable in this respect to the concept plant. Let a dogber be something that is either a dog or a number. Even when taken together with considerable zoological and mathematical knowledge, oneÂ’s knowledge that x is a dogber is useless from an explanatory viewpoint. 
Of course, given the knowledge that x is a dogber that isnÂ’t a number, or that it is a dogber that isnÂ’t a dog, one can, given a modicum of knowledge about xÂ’s circumstances, make many a correct statement as to its structure and (supposing that it is a dog and therefore that, unlike numbers, things will happen to it) as to what is likely to kill it, cure it, etc. But this shows that any value had by the concept dogber is stolen, as it were, from some virtue had by the concept number or the concept dog. 
The value of the concept plant is not thus derivative. The fact that x is a plant by itself has many ramifications as to xÂ’s structure, etc. Of course, the fact that x is a rose is, in some contexts (not all), richer in predictive and explanatory information than the fact that x is a plant. But, in and of itself, the fact that x is a dogber is without any insight-or prediction-conducive ramifications. By contrast, the fact that x is a plant is replete with such ramifications. 

7.0.2 Final preliminaries 
Of those beliefs of ours that are cases of knowledge, some have explanatory value, whereas others do not. (Knowledge of a truth of the form x is a plant has explanatory value. Knowledge of a truth of the form x is a dogber does not.) Let Smith be an arbitrary person, let S be the set whose members include all and only those propositions that: 
(i) Smith knows to be true, 
and: 
(ii) have explanatory value. 
SÂ’s members can be divided into different sub-classes. Some of those subÂ­classes are explanatorily unified; others are not. Given any one of the explanatorily unified sub-classes, there is some set of concepts such that: 
(a) Each of the members of that sub-class contains at least one of those concepts, 
and such that: 
(b) Given any two members of that sub-class, the one bears on the other by virtue of the fact that each contains one or more of those concepts. 
If S# is an arbitrary one of those sub-classes, S# can be divided into two groups of propositions: those of whose truth Smith has direct knowledge and those of whose truth Smith has indirect (inferential) knowledge. 
[394] 



7.1 Â“DatumÂ” defined 
A proposition P is a datum, relative to S#, if SmithÂ’s knowledge of it is Â“directÂ” (in the just-described) sense. 
In general, D is a datum, relative to some class C of propositions known by a given person to be true, if (1) C is explanatorily unified, (2) D is a member of C, and (3) that knowledge of D is direct (in the previously described sense). 

7.2 "Datum" a relative term 
We've just seen that the property of being a datum is inherently relational. In this section, we'll find that this property is relative in more ways than one. 
Patient Z dies. For the attending physician, thatÂ’s a datum. (LetÂ’s refer to this datum as Â“DP.") It isnÂ’t a conjecture. It's known directly, not through inference or a fortiori through theory. 
But for the microphysicist, ZÂ’s being dead isnÂ’t even a fact, let alone a datum. Terms like Â“deadÂ” and Â“illÂ” have no microphysical meaning. So DP is a datum for medicine, but not for microphysics. 
So the concept of a Â“datumÂ” is a relative notion. Something is a datum relative to one discipline but not relative to some other discipline. In fact, itÂ’s a doubly relative notion, since what is a datum today for a given discipline may come into question tomorrow. 
7.2.1 "Datum" a relative term (continued) 
Also, there are degrees of datumhood. ItÂ’s more of a datum that I am having such and such visual and tactile sensations than it is that I am now typing on a keyboard. But it is, surely, a datum that I am typing on a keyboard. Indeed, it is much more of a datum than are the so-called data on which many scientific theories are based. For those data often presuppose the accuracy of instruments that, unless highly elaborate theories are correct, are quite erroneous. 
The right reaction to this last fact isnÂ’t to say that those so-called data arenÂ’t really data. If one used the term "datum" only to refer to things known in a thoroughly theory-innocent manner, that term would refer to nothing. The right reaction is to say what we've been saying---that the concept of a datum is a relative one. 
To sum up: whatever properties a piece of information must have to qualify as a datum, some pieces of information have it to a greater degree than others. At the same time, most, if not all, of those things that we describe as "data" fail to have those properties to such a high degree that there is no context in which that piece of information is a non-datum. The class of things that have those properties to that degree is either empty or highly restrictive. 
[395] 

Part VI Mind, Body, Self 
Chapter 22 Different Views as to the Relation Between Mind and Body 
1.0 Some important terms and concepts 
Beliefs, hopes, tickles, pains, aspirations, dreads, intentions, fantasies, and longings are mental entities. Chairs, explosions, rocks, gusts of air, and quagmires are physical entities. 
How is the mental related to the physical? Here are the different views: 
(1) 
Dualism: mental entities are not physical entities.[396] 


(2) 
Materialism: mental entities are physical entities.[397] 



(3) 
Dual aspect theory: the mental and the physical are different aspects of the same thing.[398] 


(4) 
Mental eliminativism: there is no such thing as the mental. There are brain-statesÂ—but no beliefs, tickles, etc.[399] 


(5) 
Idealism: there is no such thing as the physical. There are experiences, hopes, etc.Â— but no chairs, rocks, etc.[400] 



Right now, let us focus on (1) and (2), since they are, pretty obviously, the only two of these five views that have any real chance of being correct. Later weÂ’ll discuss why, despite their obvious falseness, people have held (3)Â–(5). 
First of all, (2) is not the view that mental entities donÂ’t exist. (2) must be distinguished at all costs from (4). According to (2), perceptions, beliefs, doubts, and so on, all existÂ—but they are identical with brain-states. The materialist says that, just as water is H2O, so your belief that 1 + 1 = 2 is 
identical with some pattern of neural stimulation (or some such). Just as the physical chemist isnÂ’t denying the existence of water in identifying it with H2O, so the materialist isnÂ’t denying the existence of the mental in 
identifying it with physical entities. Although there may be some tendency on the part of materialists to be dismissive of certain features of the psychological realm, they donÂ’t have to be thus dismissive: Chomsky is a materialist, as was FreudÂ—and those two were nothing if not great believers in the psyche. 
Advocates of (2) typically (but not universally) hold that mental entities 
are identical with brain-events and brain-structures. For obvious reasons, they donÂ’t usually hold that mental entities are identical with trees or rocks or anything else that is not a part of oneÂ’s body (or, more specifically, oneÂ’s central nervous system). 
I have published some papers arguing for dualism. I am now a materialist. But I am still fundamentally open on this issue. 
Here are my own views. I believe (as I just said) that materialism is correct. Second, I believe (very strongly) that functionalism (a very popular form of materialism: to be defined later) is wrong. Third, although I believe that materialism is correct, I donÂ’t think (paradoxical though it may sound initially) that it can ever be explained why the mental is identical with (some aspects of) the physical. 
Right now, let us focus on some of the basic arguments for and against (1). (In the process of discussing these arguments, we will find that there are different versions of both materialism and dualism.) Of course, since (1) is the negation of (2), any argument for (1) is an argument against (2), and any argument for (2) is an argument against (1). 
2.0 Two arguments for dualism 
Setting aside arguments that are patently fallacious, there are, ultimately, two arguments for dualism. (The arguments considered in sections 4.0-4.5 are, it is easily seen, variants of these arguments.) 
2.1 The first argument for dualism 
The mental obviously has properties not had by the physical. For example: mental entities are representational; they are purposive; they have Â“phenomenologyÂ” (i.e., there is something it is like to have them). Since physical events obviously donÂ’t have those properties, physical events arenÂ’t mental. (This argument was given by Franz Brentano in Psychology from an Empirical Standpoint.) 
2.1.1 This argument evaluated 
Though it has force, there is a problem with this argument. The materialist can say that physical events do have these properties, but that this simply isnÂ’t obvious to introspection. For example, physical events have lots of properties that arenÂ’t obvious. When you look at a chair or a rock or a pool of water, your perception doesnÂ’t tell you anything about the microstructural properties of what you are seeingÂ—but it would obviously be absurd to conclude that what you were seeing didnÂ’t have invisible (to the naked eye) microstructural properties. Similarly, says the materialist, when you introspect a pain or a tickle or a belief, your introspection doesnÂ’t tell you anything about the neural properties of what you are introspectingÂ—but it would be absurd to conclude, on that basis alone, that what you were introspecting didnÂ’t have neural properties. 
2.1.2 A counterargument 
Some mental entities seem to be appearances. Consider your perception of (e.g.) some nearby table. Your perception is just the event of somethingÂ’s appearing to you. It doesnÂ’t make sense to say that there is more to an appearance than meets the eye. After all, what doesnÂ’t meet the eye is ipso facto not an appearance. Your perception of the table obviously doesnÂ’t seem to consist of lots of neural events. So, if it did consist of such events, they are beneath the surfaceÂ—they donÂ’t Â“meet the eyeÂ” of introspection. But given what we said a moment ago, this would mean that such events arenÂ’t part of that perception. 
2.1.3 This counterargument evaluated 
IÂ’m genuinely open as to whether this argument is a good one. I believe (for reasons to be stated) that materialism is correct. But I cannot find any errors in the just-stated counter-response (though others claim to be able to do so). If you can identify some consideration that resolves the matter, or that gives some weight to a certain (attempted) way of resolving the matter, I would be extremely interested in what you have to say. 
2.2 The second argument for dualism: the explanatory gap 
Consider some psychological statement, for example: 
(P) Last year I was very sad, because I completely failed in my efforts to write a best-selling novel. 
(P) is obviously the kind of statement that could be true. But can the truth of (P) be understood in terms of facts about neural-firings? Can we conceive of some statement about a personÂ’s body that made it clear why (P) was true? Of course, we can imagine discovering that people feel sad when, and only when, certain neurons in their brains are firing. But would such a discovery really give us any insight into the nature of the dependence (if any there be) of that psychological fact on the existence of those neural states of affairs? 
Let us generalize this point. There is no denying that we can discover psycho-physical concomitances; that is, that we can discover truths of the form mental phenomenon m occurs when, and only when, physical phenomenon p occurs. But there always seems to be a Â“gapÂ” between the neural event and the associated psychological event. Permit me to clarify this last point. 
Water is H2O. Of course, when you look at a glass of water, you cannot see that it consists of H2O molecules. But suppose that you could shrink yourself down to the size of such a molecule. In that case, you could literally 
see the molecules with which physical chemists identify water. 
When you look at a brain, you see beige tissueÂ—you donÂ’t see emotions, beliefs, etc. If you were to shrink yourself down the size of a molecule, you still wouldnÂ’t see emotions, beliefs, etc. In other words, you still wouldnÂ’t see the entities that the materialist identifies with brain-states.[401] 
You would see the entities with which the physical chemist identifies with brain-states (atoms, molecules of various kinds) but not, as we just said, those with which the materialist identifies such states. This suggests that psychophysical identifications (e.g., Â“pain is c-fiber stimulationÂ”) are not comparable to typical scientific identifications (e.g., Â“water is H2OÂ”); and this makes it 
questionable whether psychophysical identifications are correct. Also, the fact that you could coherently imagine seeing water molecules (even though, for many reasons, our ability to see such things is limited) 
seems to be bound up (in a way that isnÂ’t easy to articulate) with the fact that identifications such as Â“water is H2OÂ” are explanatory. The identification of 
water with H2O renders explicable otherwise inexplicable facts about water (e.g., that the amount of space occupied by a frozen gram of water is larger than that occupied by a liquid gram of water). But, at an intuitive level at least, it doesnÂ’t seem that a comparable gain of insight into the nature of pain is gained as a result of the identification of pain with c-fiber stimulation. Imagine somebody who, because of some defect, didnÂ’t feel pain. If that person were to learn everything there was to know about the structure of the neural events underlying pain, he would still be ignorant of what pain was. 
[402] 
By the same token, somebody who has no idea what a neuron is can know exactly what pain is. 
This suggests that psychophysical identifications are, in a fundamental way, not comparable to garden-variety scientific identifications. Somebody who knows what water tastes like, looks like, etc., doesnÂ’t necessarily know what water is. But somebody who knows that water consists of H2O 
molecules really does know what water isÂ—it doesnÂ’t really matter what other knowledge he has or lacks. It thus becomes very hard to sustain the idea that (A) Â“pain is c-fiber stimulationÂ” is in the same category as (B) Â“water is H2O.Â” There is a clear sense in which somebody who knows (A) may not 
know what pain is but in which somebody who knows (B) cannot possibly fail to know what water is. In connection with this, there is reason to think that there is an explanatory gap between the mental and the physicalÂ—to believe, in other words, that there is no way to understand the mental in terms of the physical. And if this is the case, then it would seem to follow that the mental is not the physical. 
2.2.1 This argument evaluated 
Even if the mental cannot be understood in terms of the physical, it doesnÂ’t follow that the mental isnÂ’t identical with the physical. Even if the fact that Jerry is sad cannot be understood in terms of the fact that JerryÂ’s brain is in such and such a condition, it doesnÂ’t follow that JerryÂ’s sadness isnÂ’t identical with his brainÂ’s being in that condition. 
We know that biological phenomena (e.g., digestion, respiration) are identical with interactions of atomic and sub-atomic parts. But there would be no way to translate a biological statement (e.g., Â“Smith is now breathingÂ”) into a statement about atoms bouncing off of one another. Because statements belonging to biology involve concepts (e.g., respiration) that arenÂ’t found in physics, it is to be expected that the former are not going to be capable of being translated into, or otherwise understood in terms of, the latter. Biology talk isnÂ’t physics talk, even though all biological events are physical events. Similarly, psychology talk isnÂ’t physics talk (or chemistry talk or biology talk) even though psychological events are physical events. Because psychology uses concepts not found in any physical science (e.g., chemistry or physics), it is to be expected that statements belonging to the former are not going to be capable of being translated into, or otherwise understood in terms of, statements belonging to the latter.[403] 

2.2.2. A counter-response 
Although this argument obviously has merit, and is widely accepted, I don't accept it. There seems to me to be a significant difference between the relationship that holds between statements belonging to physics and statements belonging to biology, on the one hand, and the relationship holding between statements belonging to psychology and statements belonging to physics (or chemistry or biology . . .) on the other. This viewpoint is defended in Chapter 21. 
2.2.3 A counter-response to the counter-response 
The mental can be understood in terms of the physical. There is no more of an explanatory gap between the mental and the physical than between the biological and the chemical. In other words, there is no explanatory gap. Right now weÂ’ll discuss why, according to many, there is no such gap. 
2.3 Is there an explanatory gap? 
So far as advocates of the view just described provide clear grounds for it, those grounds lie in two doctrines. Right now, we will discuss just one of them. (In a moment, weÂ’ll discuss the other.) 
Some hold that to explain why one state of affairs accompanies or follows another simply to show that, taken together, those two events instantiate a general regularity.[404] 
To explain why, in this one instance, smoke follows fire is simply to identify some comprehensive regularity of which this particular sequence of events is an instance. If it is shown that fire is always followed by smoke, it has ipso facto been explained why, in this case, fire was followed by smoke. By parity of reasoning, were we to establish perfect concomitances between mental events and physical events, we would ipso facto have explained the mental in terms of the physical. 
2.3.1 A counter-response to the argument given 
HempelÂ’s conception of explanation is erroneous. The basic problem is that itÂ’s too liberal: if it were right, anything could be said to be the cause of anything. The reasons for this are given in Chapter 17. But hereÂ’s the basic idea. 
I grab my phone, so as to pick it up and make a call; just after I do so, it rings. By coincidence, IÂ’m getting a call at that exact moment. HempelÂ’s theory has the obviously false consequence that my grabbing the phone is what caused it to ring. Let E1 be the event consisting of my grabbing the phone, and let E2 be the event consisting of the phoneÂ’s ringing. Obviously E1 will be unique in many respectsÂ—no other event will involve exactly the same mass-energy distributions that it does. It follows that E1 uniquely has some property P1. The same thing mutatis mutandis is true of E2; and E2 therefore uniquely has some property P2. Thus, the sequence of events consisting of E1 and E2 is a unique instance of the true universal generalization that any instance of P1 is immediately followed by, and adjacent to, an instance of P2. If HempelÂ’s analysis were right, then my grabbing the phone would have caused it to ring. Since it didnÂ’t, HempelÂ’s 
analysis is wrong. 
2.3.2 Another counter-response 
Setting this aside, it isnÂ’t widely held that mind-brain concomitances (other than obviously contrived, explanatorily irrelevant ones similar to the one just described in connection with E1 and E2) are to be found. The reason: 
it is widely believed that the mental is Â“multiply realizable.Â” Instances of any kind of mental category can, it is alleged, be constituted by physical events of very different kinds; and for this reason, there are no true statements of the form Â“events having such and such biochemical properties occur iff events having thus and such psychological properties occur.Â” 
2.3.3 How the functionalist tries to eliminate the explanatory gap 
But, even though, for the reason just given, the alleged multiple realizability of mental states seems to eliminate one way of closing the explanatory gap between mind and matter, it actually opens what many (myself not included) claim to be a promising way of closing that gap. As previously noted, almost all contemporary materialists hold that mental entities are multiply realizableÂ—that, for example, a belief that snow is white could be composed of any material capable of having the causal liaisons had by a belief that snow is white. For X to be such a belief, it is said, is not for it to be composed of this or that material, but is for it to have certain causes and effects. They hold, in general, that given any mental category M, for a given physical entity P to fall into M simply is for P to have certain causes and certain effects. This doctrine is known as functionalism. 
In Sections 7.1-7.1.2 of the present chapter, it will be argued that functionalism is false, the reason being that it collapses into the obviously false view that there are no mental entities. It goes without saying that, if itÂ’s false, functionalism does nothing to close the explanatory gap. In any case, IÂ’d now like to put forth a positive reason to believe that there is no way to close the explanatory gap. 
3.0 The reason there is an explanatory gap 
For argumentÂ’s sake suppose that every mental event is identical with (or realized by) some physical event. In that case, my feeling remorseful that I stole my sisterÂ’s cookie is identical with some brain-event of mine. Let M be my feeling of remorse, and let B be the corresponding brain-event. Suppose that I sincerely and accurately express my remorseÂ—taking care to discuss its origins, its exact content, etc. Let SM be this statement. And suppose that I see an accurate image of B on a giant monitor, and I thoroughly and accurately describe what I see. Let SB be this statement. 
SM describes the very same event as SB. But the data of which SM is a synthesis doesnÂ’t even overlap with the data of which SB is a synthesis. Even if mental events are identical with physical events, the data of which mentalistic statements are syntheses doesnÂ’t even overlap with the data of which physicalistic statements are syntheses. This means that, given the data of which any mentalistic statement is a correct synthesis, it is epistemically possible that none of the data of which any given physicalistic statement is a correct synthesis even exists. Mentalistic statements donÂ’t model the same data as physicalistic statements, or vice versa. So even though the facts described by the former probably are identical with (a subset of) the facts described by the latter, any statement belonging to the one category leaves it completely open whether any given statement belonging to the other is correct or not. 
The purpose of Chapter 18 is to show that there is an explanatory gap. In that chapter, we will examine Donald Davidson's attempt to establish that there is an explanatory gap; we will find Davidson's attempt to be a failure. 
4.0 DescartesÂ’ arguments for dualism 
Descartes provided a straightforward and, at an intuitive level, compelling argument for (1). Here it is. I can believe that x is a feeling (or belief or intention) without believing that x is a brain-state. Therefore, x cannot be a brain-state if x is a feeling (or belief or intention). 
4.1 This argument evaluated 
This argument is guilty of the so-called Â“intensionalÂ” fallacy. Remember what we said about intensional contexts: Given only that Â“Smith thinks that the inventor of bifocals invented bifocalsÂ” is true, it doesnÂ’t follow that Â“Smith thinks that the first postmaster general invented bifocalsÂ” is true, even though the first postmaster general is identical with the inventor of bifocals. Similarly, given only that Â“Smith thinks that x is a beliefÂ” is true, it doesnÂ’t follow that Â“Smith thinks that x is a brain-stateÂ” is true, even if beliefs are in fact brain-states. 
4.2 A refinement of DescartesÂ’ arguments for dualism 
Here is an improved version of DescartesÂ’ argument that, so its proponents believe, isnÂ’t vulnerable to the points just made. 
I can coherently think: 
(*) Â“x is a feeling, but x is not a brain-state.Â” 
In other words, (*) is not analytically false. 
All necessary truth is analytic truth. In other words, if a statement is necessarily true, that is because it holds entirely in virtue of the concepts composing its meaning (i.e., it is analytic). Therefore, given that (*) is not analytically false, it follows that it isnÂ’t necessarily false and, therefore, that it could be true. So feelings could be distinct from brain-states. 
Next-step: identity holds necessarily if it holds at all. If x and y are identical, then they are necessarily so. Proof[405]: Suppose that x and y are identical, but only contingently so. Obviously x cannot be contingently identical with itself. So if x and y are contingently identical, then y has a property that x lacks: y has the property of being contingently identical with x, whereas x does not have that property. Thus, contrary to our supposition, x is not identical with y, showing that it is incoherent to suppose that there is such a thing as Â“contingentÂ” identity. 
Thus, given that (*) could be true, and given that identity holds necessarily if it holds at all, it follows that feelings (and, for exactly similar reasons, beliefs and pains) are not brain-states. 
4.3 This argument evaluated 
First of all, it is easy to adapt what we said about (i) and (ii) to this argument. So this refinement of DescartesÂ’ argument is, like the first, guilty of the intensional fallacy. 
But thereÂ’s another reason to question that argument. According to many contemporary philosophers, not all necessity is analytic. The sentence Â“water is identical with H2O,Â” it is said, expresses a proposition that, although non-analytic, is necessarily true. There is no possible circumstance where water is anything other than H2O. There are circumstances where liquids that, in terms of their macroscopic properties, resemble water but are not H2O. But there are no circumstances where water is not H2O. 
Why is this? The categories in terms of which science explains the world are known as Â“natural kinds.Â” Examples of natural kinds are zebra, metal, proton, water, emotion, human being, acid, base, star, and penguin. Natural kinds are generated by properties that are predictively and explanatorily fecund. Properties that donÂ’t have those virtues (e.g., person who drives a green car, edible substance on LarryÂ’s table) donÂ’t generate natural kinds. The property of being H2O generates a natural kind. Two things that are 
explanatorily and predictively very different can be indistinguishable in respect of their macro-characteristics, at least within the narrow horizons within which non-experimentalists typically operate. For this reason, that the property of having such and such macro-characteristics does not determine a natural kind. 
But two things that are indistinguishable in respect of their micro-characteristics (e.g., their chemical compositions) cannot be explanatorily and predictively different. Thus, the property of having such and such micro-characteristics generates a natural kind.[406] 
It canÂ’t be known a priori what chemical composition water has. But, for the reasons just given, its having that composition, whatever it turns out to be, is essential to it. Supposing that x is some body of water, xÂ’s being water is identical with xÂ’s having that composition. Since, therefore, water necessarily has that compositionÂ—and, therefore, is necessarily H2OÂ—and since it cannot be known a priori that it has that composition; Â“water is H2OÂ” expresses a necessary, but non-analytic truth. 
4.4 Evaluating this counter-response 
This is a prima facie very compelling line of thought, and it is almost universally accepted. For reasons that I state in Chapter 9, I do not accept it (even though I accept some parts of it; e.g., the part about how natural kinds are individuated by their microstructures or by whatever it is about them that makes them explanatorily and predictively useful). In any case, these reflections naturally bring us to KripkeÂ’s compelling argument for dualism. 
4.5 KripkeÂ’s argument for dualism 
All identities hold necessarily, and some identities are indeed a posteriori. Nonetheless, dualism can be established by means of an argument not entirely unlike DescartesÂ’. Consider some (alleged) necessary, non-analytic truth; for example: 
(WH) water is H2O. 
First of all, the sentence "water is H2O" must be distinguished from the corresponding proposition. Once we take into account the information on the 
basis of which one determines the identity of the proposition literally meant by that sentence, it becomes de rigueur to se "water is H2O" as encoding either a proposition that is synthetic but non-necessary or necessary but non-
synthetic. I state my reasons for holding this in Chapter 9. I state my reasons for holding this. But, for argument's sake, we'll assume the truth of the orthodox and prima facie plausible position that WH is both synthetic and necessary. 
The reason that WH is non-analytic is that something that appeared, visually and otherwise, to be just like water might not be water, as it might have the wrong micro-structure. In general, whenever a statement of the form x=y is non-analytic, it is because objects that arenÂ’t x can appear just like x. But it makes no sense to say that something that appeared (felt) just like a pain wasnÂ’t actually a pain. Anything that feels just like a pain is a pain. Â“Pain is identical with brain state XÂ” would be non-analytic, if it were true. Thus, since what makes it possible for it to be non-analytic that water is H2O 
is that appearing like water is different from being water, and the same thing mutatis mutandis being true of all non-analytic necessities, it follows that Â“pain is identical with brain state XÂ” is not true. 
5.0 The arguments for materialism 
There are several powerful arguments for materialism. But there is one line of thought that lies at the core of these various arguments. 
5.1 The primary argument for materialism 
It is obvious that mental events create, and otherwise affect, physical events; and it is obvious that physical events create, and otherwise affect, mental events. A hot iron is pressed to your skin (physical event); as a result, you feel pain (mental event). You intend to go to the store (mental event); as a result, you end up going to the store (physical event). You feel nervous (mental event); as a result, your heart races (physical event). 
There is extremely strong evidence to the effect that any physical event is the result only of other physical events. To explain why a personÂ’s body moves a certain way, it is necessary only to know what the strictly physical (neural, muscular, etc.) antecedents of that event are, and it is not necessary to know what its psychological antecedents are. The behavior of a personÂ’s body is no more in need of Â“mentalisticÂ” explanation than is the behavior of a brick. (Of course, a knowledge of a personÂ’s psychological condition is often sufficient, given knowledge of easy-to-ascertain facts about the external world, for a knowledge of what that person is going to do next. But such knowledge is not necessary: such predictions can, in principle, be made without having any knowledge as to the relevant personÂ’s psychology.) 
Given that every fact about a personÂ’s bodily behavior can be explained in strictly physical terms, we can take one of two positions. We can say either: 
(i) The mental does not, contrary to appearances, have any effects on the body, 
or: 
(ii) The mental does have such effectsÂ—and the mental is identical with the physical events that we know to have those effects. 
Since it is very hard to believe that the mental is without effect on the physical, (i) is almost certainly false. Hence (ii) is the right view.[407] 

Evaluating this argument: My own personal view is that this argument is pretty solid; that being why I am a materialist. Others have responded (or, given their positions, would respond) differently to this argument. 
For example, according to epiphenomenalism, even though the physical affects the mental, the mental does not affect the physical. 
But epiphenomenalism is clearly wrong. ItÂ’s an empirical datum that the mental affects the physical and vice versa. Should it be denied that this is a datum, or even that itÂ’s true, I would respond by showing that epiphenomenalism is at odds with a fundamental fact about the nature of causation. 
Causation is bidirectional. If my hand affects the table (e.g., if my hand pushes the table), then the table affects my hand. So if, as the epiphenomenalist believes, the physical affected the mental, then the mental would affect the physical. But in that case, epiphenomenalism is false. 
The epiphenomenalist might counter-respond by saying that there are exceptions to the principle of bi-directionality that IÂ’ve been advocating: physical situations create, and have effects on, shadows; but shadows donÂ’t have effects on anything. 
But this move is a non-starter. Mental entities, unlike shadows, really do have causal powers. Even the epiphenomenalist doesnÂ’t deny that they affect one another. Given this fact, along with the fact mental events result from physical events, it follows that some of the energy associated with physical states of affairs is transferred to them. So unless energy is implausibly assumed to vanish from the physical world, never to return, we must assume that the mental can, so to speak, spit it back into the physical world and, therefore, that the mental can affect the physical.[408] 
And, as weÂ’ve seen, once it is granted the mental can affect the physical, it must be granted that the mental is physical. 
5.1.1 Another argument for materialism 
As weÂ’ve seen, the mental clearly affects the physical. If mental entities are subject to physical laws, they are ipso facto physical. (After all, what would it be to be physical, if not to obey physical laws?) And if something obeys physical laws, it is ipso facto physical. What would it mean to say Â“X obeys the laws of physics Â—but it isnÂ’t physicalÂ”? X is physical iff X obeys physical laws. 
Thus, if mental entities are not physical, they are not subject to physical laws. So if mental entities were non-physical, things that didnÂ’t fall within the scope of physical law would constantly have effects on the physical world, resulting in physical events that couldnÂ’t be explained in terms of physical lawsÂ—physical events that were, in fact, violations of physical law. But such violations do not occur. In any case, there is no evidence that they occur, and certainly no evidence that they occur with anything even approaching the frequency with which, if dualism were correct, they would occur.[409] 

5.1.2 A counter-response 
Surely we could imagine physical objects breaking physical laws. We can imagine people sprouting wings and flyingÂ—even though, given the structures of our bodies, such events would be violations of physical law. 
5.1.3 A counter-counter-response 
Bertrand Russell said that objects are sequences of events that are governed by physical law. I agree with him.[410] 
If Russell is right, it makes no sense to speak of a physical object that is in violation of all physical laws. So when we imagine a person sprouting wings we are imagining something that is subject to physical laws (albeit laws that are different from those that are actually operative). Second, so far as the objects of oneÂ’s thoughts arenÂ’t law-governed, those thoughts involve incoherent or otherwise impoverished views as to the nature of physical law. A defense of this controversial point of view lies outside the scope of the present book. 
5.2 The third argument for materialismÂ—FodorÂ’s argument[411] 

The mental obviously affects the physical. Anything that affects the physical is ipso facto physical itself. What is there to be physical other than being able to displace mass-energy (or whatever it is that events consist of)? 
5.2.1 Evaluating this argument 
I personally find this argument compelling, and have yet to hear a cogent response to it. 
6.0 The Problems with dual aspect theory, idealism, and eliminativism
