Supposing that the mental and the physical are two aspects of the same thing, we must ask: what is that thing?[412] 
It canÂ’t be mental; for surely the mental is not an aspect of the mental. (My belief that snow is white is not an aspect of itself or of any other mental thing.) And it canÂ’t be physical; for surely the physical is not an aspect of the physical. (The chair is not an aspect of itself or of any other physical thing.) So (3) is either incoherent or it presupposes that there is something spatiotemporal that is not either physical or mental. But it is incoherent to suppose that there is anything spatiotemporal that is not either mental or physical. It follows that (3) is simply incoherent. 
It seems to me that so-called Â“dual aspectÂ” theorists are really just materialists who have misstated their view. So far as thatÂ’s correct, we can forget about (3), and focus on (2). And since weÂ’ve already discussed (2), we can move on to (4). 
(4) is obviously a non-starter. But, for what extremely little itÂ’s worth, hereÂ’s the argument behind it. Scientific hypotheses are supposed to deal with things that can be publicly verified. Suppose that scientist Smith insisted that he, and he alone, were able to see (or otherwise sense-perceive) the data that confirmed some hypothesis of his. Obviously Smith wouldnÂ’t be taken seriously. My pains, tickles, etc., cannot be witnessed by anyone other than myself. For this reason, some psychologists who were attempting to scientize their discipline said that such things had no place within science and therefore had no place in a scientific world-view. Given this position, it is a short step to saying that pains, tickles, etc., donÂ’t exist at all. In a word, science deals with what is objective; mental states are subjective; therefore, mental states donÂ’t exist. 
There are many fallacies in this argument. One of them is that, in actuality, the existence of pains, tickles, etc., is easily verified. Of course, you cannot have my pains. But you can have your pains, and you can therefore confirm that pains exist. 
Also, as Searle (1992) points out, that argument involves a failure to distinguish two meanings of the term Â“subjective.Â”[413] 
Sometimes, when we describe something as "subjective,Â” we mean that it is influenced by personal biases. (So and soÂ’s reaction to the incident was extremely subjectiveÂ—it wasnÂ’t impartial and logical.) But when we say that mental entities are Â“subjective,Â” we meanÂ—not that they are biasedÂ—but that they must be had in order to exist. There canÂ’t be orphan pains and beliefs floating around: a belief must be somebodyÂ’s belief. Mental states thus have, as John Searle puts it, a Â“first-person ontology.Â” Obviously science mustnÂ’t be Â“subjectiveÂ” (i.e., it mustnÂ’t be biased); but it doesnÂ’t follow that it mustnÂ’t deal with the subjective (i.e., with things having a first-person ontology). In any case, itÂ’s a plain fact that mental entities exist, and eliminativism is a hideous monstrosity to which we shall give no further thought. 
(5) 
is not a view that anyone really holds (even though a fewÂ—e.g., George Berkeley, William James, Bertrand RussellÂ—have claimed to do so). 

(5) 
is really more of an epistemological view than it is a view about the relation between body and mind: so far as philosophers advocate (5), it is on the grounds that it is the only viable response to skepticism about the external world. (Skepticism is the focus of Chapter 11 and also of Sections 6.0Â–8.0 of Chapter 12.) 


7.0 The different versions of materialism: behaviorism 
There are different versions of materialism. Let us now consider them, starting with behaviorism. According to the behaviorist, to believe that 1 + 1 = 2 is to only have a disposition to respond with certain overt behaviors to certain physical stimuli. If when asked Â“what is 1 + 1?Â” you say Â“2Â”Â—if, in general, you respond to sensory inputs in ways that are characteristic of a belief that 1 + 1 = 2Â—then in virtue of that very fact, you believe that 1 + 1 = 
2. In other words, according to the behaviorist, behaving in the right way is believing that 1 + 1 = 2. It isnÂ’t a consequence of such knowledge. It is such knowledge.[414] 

The general definition of behaviorism is this. If M is any mental category, P is an instance of M just in case P is a disposition on the part of some individual to respond with certain overt behaviors to certain sensory inputs. 
Behaviorism is false. How a person reacts to a given sensory input is a function, not only of what that input is, but also of what that personÂ’s existing mental states are. If you donÂ’t speak English, an utterance of Â“what is 1 + 1?Â” will not cause you to say Â“2.Â” It is only in people who have various pieces of background knowledge (e.g., knowledge of linguistic conventions) that such a disposition corresponds to the knowledge that 1 + 1 = 2. What we said about that particular disposition is true (mutatis mutandis) of any other. By itself, no disposition to engage in a certain kind of overt behavior, given certain stimuli, corresponds to any mental state: what does so is such a disposition plus various pre-existing mental states. So, mental states cannot be reduced to behavioral dispositions. At most, they can be reduced to behavioral dispositions plus various mental states. But this means that they canÂ’t be reduced to behavioral dispositions. 
Aware of these problems with behaviorism, but still wanting to holding onto the idea that mental entities could be dispositionalized (identified with tendencies to respond with certain overt behaviors to certain inputs), many philosophers of mind responded to this by adopting functionalism, which weÂ’ve already discussed and will now discuss further. 

7.1 Functionalism 
Consider the kinds of situations that characteristically give rise to a belief that snow is white (e.g., visual perceptions of white snow), and consider all the thoughts and behaviors that characteristically result from such a belief (e.g., oneÂ’s forming the belief that snow is not green). According to the functionalist, for a brain-state to be a belief that snow is white just is for it to have the right causes and effects. So if brain-state B has the right causes and effects, B is ipso facto a belief that snow is white (or a desire to become president or a pain or a feeling of euphoria). According to the functionalist, BÂ’s having those causes and effects isn't evidence of B's being such a belief; nor is it a consequence of B's being such a belief. It is B's being such a belief. 
The functionalist says that, for any mental type M, mental entities are among the characteristic causes and effects of instances of that type. So the functionalistÂ—unlike the behavioristÂ—allows that among the causes of (e.g.) a belief that snow is white are other mental entities (e.g., perceptions of white snow); and that among the effects of such a belief are other mental entities (e.g., a belief that snow is not green). 
Remember that behaviorism falsely supposes that a person who had no linguistic knowledge would react by saying Â“2Â” to an utterance of Â“what is 1 
+ 1?Â” and, in general, that behaviorism identifies mental states with dispositions that can be understood in strictly behavioral terms. Functionalism doesnÂ’t run into this problem. Unlike behaviorism, functionalism can (supposedly) accommodate the fact that among the causes and effects of a mental entity are other mental entities. (Why Â“supposedlyÂ”? Keep reading.) 
For something is (e.g.) a belief that snow is white wholly in virtue of its causal role. In general, for any mental category M, there is some causal role C such that x falls into M if and only if x has C. (This statement may not be easy to follow, but there is no simpler, but equally accurate way of saying what functionalism is.) 
7.1.1 Problems with functionalism 
For something to be a pain is for it to feel a certain wayÂ—its causal role is secondary. It is true, of course, that pains are likely to have certain causes (kicks to the shins) and certain effects (screaming loudly). But for something to be a pain isnÂ’t for it to have a certain causal role; for something to be a pain is for it to feel a certain way. 
Since it says otherwise, functionalism is wrong. 
There is a related point. Supposing that P is some pain, PÂ’s having a given causal role is a consequence of its being a pain; its being a pain is not a consequence of its having that causal role. Supposing that P is some pain of yours, your writhing and screaming is an effect of PÂ’s being a pain and, contrary to what the functionalist alleges, it thus cannot be constitutive of its being a pain. 
Functionalism says that x is a belief that snow is white iff x has the right causal role. That causal role involves other mental entities. Functionalists know that. So it sounds as though functionalism analyzes the mental into causal role plus the mental. It thus seems questionable whether functionalism really is a form of materialism. 
If cogent, this criticism of functionalism is devastating, given that the whole raison dÂ’Ãªtre for that doctrine is that it supposedly explains the relationship between mind and body. Functionalists respond by saying that, through judicious use of a technical device known as the Â“Ramsey sentence,Â” it can be shown that functionalism does reduce the mental to the physical, while at the same time doing justice to the fact that, given any arbitrary mental type M, instances of M may have other mental entities for their causes and effects. Here is their reasoning (this is a paraphrase, not a quotation): 
(RS)[415] 
We must distinguish the concept of all from the concept of any. Among the causes and/or effects of practically every given mental entity are (a) other mental entities and (b) strictly physical inputs (e.g., photons striking oneÂ’s retinas) and strictly behavioral outputs (e.g., oneÂ’s reaching for the glass). But even though any given mental entity is to be understood in terms of other mental entities, nonetheless the totality of a personÂ’s mental entities can be understood entirely in terms of strictly physical inputs and strictly behavioral outputs. Let MS (short for Â“mental sentenceÂ”) be a single, very large sentence that says, for any given mental kind (e.g., belief that snow is white, dread of visiting oneÂ’s mother in law, etc.), what the causes and effects of instances of that kind are. MS is going to contain Â“constantsÂ”: it will contain expressions, such as Â“dread of going jogging in the morning,Â” that refer to kinds of mental entities. Given any such expression, replace it with a variable. The result will be an open sentence (an expression that contains a free variable but is otherwise just like a sentence). Bind the occurrences of that variable in that open sentence with an existential quantifier. Do the same thing mutatis mutandis for each occurrence of any expression that refers to a mental kind. But donÂ’t do it for any of the expressions that refer to physical kinds. The result will be a sentence that completely describes the causes and effects of instances of each mental kind, but that does so without using any expressions that refer to anything mental. The mental will thus be completely described in terms of the physical. But that sentence will do justice to the fact that mental events cause other mental events to occur, and it will do justice to the precise way in which they do so. 
By saying that causal role fixes content, RS makes content too brittle: any deviations of any kind between any two mental states ipso facto amount to differences in content. No two mental entities have exactly the same causal roles. (There isnÂ’t anything in your mind that has exactly the same causal role as my belief that 2 is an even prime. There isnÂ’t anything in any personÂ’s mind that has exactly the same causal role as anything in anyone elseÂ’s mind.) It follows that, if RS is right, no two people can believe that 1 + 1 = 2 or that Mongolia is in Asia, etc. Since that is obviously false, so is RS. 
A story may clarify this point. Both Smith and Jones believe that snow is white. Smith is a physicist who focuses on the reflective properties of white surfaces. Jones doesnÂ’t know anything about physics. Obviously the functional role of SmithÂ’s belief that snow is white will be very different from that of JonesÂ’ corresponding belief. But if, as functionalism holds, a brain-stateÂ’s being a belief that snow is white just is its having a certain functional role, then presumably one personÂ’s belief that snow is white shouldnÂ’t be able to differ, at least not too drastically, from another personÂ’s belief that snow is white. 

7.1.2 The main problem with functionalism 
It is not objects, but states of affairs, that have causal properties. What shatters the window is not the rockÂ—it is rather the rockÂ’s moving with a certain velocity, in a certain direction, etc. Similarly, if B is the brain-state that realizes your belief that (e.g.) water quenches thirst, it isnÂ’t B that causes things to happenÂ—it is BÂ’s having these or those properties. According to functionalism, BÂ’s being identical with a belief that water quenches thirst is identical with BÂ’s having certain causes and effectsÂ—it is identical with (e.g.) its causing you to drink water when thirsty. But if BÂ’s being identical with that belief is identical with BÂ’s causing you to drink water (when thirsty), then BÂ’s being such a belief cannot cause such behavior. Cause and effect must be distinct: if x causes y, then x is not identical with y (and neither is a part of the other). So if functionalism is correct, then the fact that you believe that water quenches thirst cannot cause you to do things like drink water when thirsty. Thus, if functionalism is right, then your belief that water quenches thirst does nothing. 
Given any other behavior that we know to be caused by the existence of a certain kind of mental entity, an analogous argument shows that, if functionalism is right, such an entity cannot possibly cause that behavior. Setting aside cases of linguistic incompetence and insincerity, utterances of Â“snow is white" are caused by, among other things, beliefs to the effect that snow is white. Functionalism says that there is some brain-state B such that that BÂ’s being a belief that snow is white is identical with, among other things, BÂ’s causing that person to utter those words. But if BÂ’s being such a belief is identical with its causing that utterance, then BÂ’s being such a belief cannot cause that utterance to occur. So functionalism strips the mental of any causal powers. Given that the mental does have causal powers, it follows that functionalism is wrong. 
8.0 Conclusion of this Chapter 
The main argument for materialism: Mind and body interact. Such interactions seem not to involve violations of physical law. Given these two facts, it seems likely that materialism is correct. 
The main argument for dualism: Our experiences don't seem to be anything like brain-states or physical entities of any other sort. So, if they are brain-states, it is because we experience them as being very different from how they really are. But it makes no sense to suppose that we experience our experiences; and it therefore makes no sense to suppose that we experience them as being different from how they are. So, given that we experience them as being totally unlike physical entities, they must really be totally unlike physical entities. 
The argument for materialism strikes me as being slight more compelling than the argument for dualism. But second argument is hard to dismiss. It seems to show that there is something distinctive about the relationship between mind and body---that the former is not to the latter what the biological is to the chemical or what the chemical is to the physical. Given these facts, I conclude that materialism is correct, but also that the truths described by psychological statements are, for some reason other, completely and utterly incapable of being understood in terms of the truths described by physicalistic statements. In Chapter 21, I tried to explain exactly why this is so. 
Chapter 23 The Computational Theory of Mind: Progressing Towards a Scientific Psychology or Regressing to Pre-Scientific Animism? 
1.0 Introduction 
These days, a doctrine known as the Â“Computational Theory of MindÂ” (CTM) is very popular, both among scholars (especially philosophers and computer scientists) and among the laity. CTM is a form of materialism, for reasons that will become clear. 
Because of its liberal and confident use of words such as Â“computeÂ” and Â“algorithmÂ”, CTM has an impressive sheen of rigor, and one would think that this doctrine would be informed by the same intellectual progressiveness that led to the creation and subsequent development of computer science. But we will find that, ironically, CTM involves a regression to archaic, animistic forms of thought and, more specifically, that it represents the recrudescence of the primitive and obviously spurious thinking that the grumbling of thunder represents the wrath of the gods. 
Speaking more philosophically and less psychoanalytically, weÂ’ll find that CTM involves some basic ratiocinative failings. For example, CTM embodies an ignorance of the fact that it is not objects, but events that have effects. These events often involve objects. But objects per se cause nothing. The rock didn't break the window; what did so was the rockÂ’s striking the window. Also, weÂ’ll find that, if CTM were true, we couldnÂ’t know it to be true and couldnÂ’t have any legitimate reason to advocate it. 
1.1 What is CTM? 
According to CTM, to think is to compute. Thoughts are computations. A computation is a formal inference. So CTM is the view that any instance of thought is identical with the making of a formal inference. 
But what is a Â“formalÂ” inference? To qualify as Â“formal,Â” a case of reasoning must be identical with a reaction, on the part of some creature or other, to symbolic-inputs. But not all such reactions qualify as cases of formal reasoning: only those reactions so qualify that arenÂ’t to any degree driven by the knowledge of the meanings of the symbol-tokens in question and are driven entirely by a sensitivity to their forms. So CTM is the contention that thought consists of responses to symbol-tokens that are driven entirely by the formal properties of those tokens and therefore embody no knowledge of what those symbol-tokens mean. In Section 1.2, weÂ’ll give some examples of such responses, thereby eliminating any obscurity from the statement just made. 
Why advocate CTM? Two reasons. First, CTM, if correct, solves the mind-body problem. When you add two numbers, you are ipso facto thinking. Computers presumably add numbers. (Computers presumably compute.) Therefore, computers, when adding numbers, are ipso facto thinking. We know how a computerÂ’s software is related to its hardware. So CTM, if correct, solves the mind-body problem. (In other words, CTM, if correct, makes it clear how brains are responsible for the mental activity that they mediate.) 
Second, CTM, if correct, solves the Â“tracking problemÂ” (or so CTM-advocates say and so weÂ’ll momentarily assume). Brain-activity, though clearly 100% physics-driven, is also logic-driven (or, in any case, logic-consistent), at least to the extent that it mediates rational thought. So, to the extent that itÂ’s constitutive of rational thought, brain-activity, though governed by descriptive laws, embodies sensitivity to prescriptive laws: where such activity is concerned, the descriptive Â“tracksÂ” the prescriptive. Nothing that is obeying the laws of physics is, in virtue of that fact, doing anything that can be evaluated---that can be described as Â“correctÂ” or Â“validÂ” or Â“false.Â” (In moving hither as opposed to thither, the billiard ball isnÂ’t doing anything right or wrong, valid or invalid.) And, it seems to follow that nothing that can be so described could be constituted by brain-activity. But brain-activity does constitute activity that can be so described. 
CTM (supposedly) solves this problem. ItÂ’s possible to create an environment in which there occur symbol-tokens whose logical properties are hewed to their physical properties in such a way that, within that environment, symbol-tokens occur in sequences that are consistent with the requirements of logic. In fact, not only is it possible to create such environments: we routinely do create themÂ—and employ them. We call them Â“computers.Â” So it would seem that CTM, if correct, explains how activity that falls within the scope of physics can, at the same time, embody a sensitivity to the demands of logic and, more generally, of normativity. 
1.2 Mentalese: the Â“language of thoughtÂ” 
According to CTM-advocates, those symbol-tokens mediating our thoughts are held to belong to a hypothetical language. This hypothetical language is generally referred to as Â“Mentalese.Â” 
According to CTM, one doesnÂ’t have to learn Mentalese. Brains are computers. Computers donÂ’t function until theyÂ’ve been programmed. Therefore, our brains donÂ’t function until theyÂ’ve been programmed. Mentalese is that program. Thus, Mentalese must be programmed into a brain before that brain can mediate cognitive activity, and therefore before that brainÂ’s owner can learn a language or, indeed, do anything that involves having any awareness of anything. Mentalese is to a functioning brain what a computerÂ’s operating system is to that computer. Thus, just as your IBM came Â“bundledÂ” with DOS, so your brain came Â“bundledÂ” with Mentalese. 
In light of what weÂ’ve said, it might seem reasonable to say that, according to CTM, one innately knows Mentalese. But if CTM is right, one doesnÂ’t know Mentalese at all, let alone innately. Knowing a language involves being able to correlate linguistic with non-linguistic entities. If I couldnÂ’t correlate snow (the powdery substance) with Â“snowÂ” (the word), I couldnÂ’t possibly know what Â“snowÂ” meant. In order to correlate Â“snowÂ” with snow, I must have some way of being aware of snow that doesnÂ’t involve knowing what Â“snowÂ” means. Knowing Mentalese would involve being able to correlate the expressions belonging to it with non-linguistic entities. According to CTM, thoughts are identical with Mentalese expression-tokens, and such expressions must therefore be operational if one is to make correlations or, therefore, to know a language. 
So if CTM is right, a precondition for one's being aware of anything is that one's brain be stocked with already operational Mentalese symbol-tokens. So it isnÂ’t by virtue of oneÂ’s knowing Mentalese that expression-tokens belonging to it mediate oneÂ’s thoughts or otherwise do what CTM-advocates allege them to do. So nobody knows Mentalese and nobody understands the expressions belonging to it. Therefore, it isnÂ’t by being understood that such expression-tokens facilitate thought. 
In this respect, Mentalese is radically different from English and every other non-hypothetical language. Expression-tokens belonging to English, Urdu, etc. do not facilitate thought except by being understood. By contrast, the symbol-tokens of Mentalese, supposing such tokens to exist, need not be understood to facilitate thought. Indeed, it is inherent in what Mentalese expression-tokens are that they be able to discharge all of their duties without being understood to any degree by anyone or anything. 
Because Mentalese, were it to exist, would differ in this respect from English, Spanish, and other bona fidelanguages, it follows (for reasons to be discussed in Section 4.0) that the very concept of a Â“language of thoughtÂ” is not a coherent one. Given that CTM assumes there to be a language of thought, and given that (for reasons to be disclosed in Section 4.0) no doctrine that doesnÂ’t assume this bears any resemblance to CTM, it follows that CTM is incoherent. 
1.3 The concept of a formal inference: Some illustrations 
WeÂ’ve seen, if correct, CTM explains much. But is it correct? We canÂ’t answer that unless we make it clear what, in this context, the word Â“computeÂ” means. And we canÂ’t make that clear unless we make it clear what, in this context, it means to say of symbolic activity that it is Â“form-driven.Â” 
The following three stories will help answer these questions. 
Story #1 (not an example of computation): Smith, who speaks English, is told: Â“Jones has two yachts.Â” On the basis of this information, along with his knowledge of the English language, Smith concludes that the following sentence is correct: Â“the number n such that Jones has n yachts is such that n has no rational square root.Â” 
Commentary on Story #1: SmithÂ’s reasoning is cogent. But it is not in any sense Â“formal.Â” SmithÂ’s thought process was a driven by an understanding of inter alia the meanings of the words he was hearing. 
Story #2 (an example of a kind of computation): Wooden tokens of the expressions Â“2,Â” Â“+,Â”Â“9,Â” and Â“=Â” are fed, in that order, into wood chipper W. Driven solely by the morphological properties of those symbol-tokens, W cranks out a wooden Â“11.Â” And given any wooden-token of a sentence-fragment beginning with an operator flanked by two numerals and ending with the sign for equality, W does the same thing mutatis mutandis. 
Commentary: There would seem to be a sense in which W can compute sums. It is typically this sense of the word Â“computeÂ” that advocates of CTM have in mind when they say that to think is to compute. Why only Â“typicallyÂ”? Why not Â“alwaysÂ”? Because sometimes what they have in mind is the prima facie quite different sense of the word Â“computeÂ” that is illustrated in the following section. 
Story #3 (an example of a different kind of computation): Smith has no idea what Â“1,245,Â” Â“241,Â” Â“1,486,Â” etc. mean. But Smith has been told by a source whose testimony he rightly trusts that, when given ink-marks having such and such shapes, a correct sentence results when another ink-mark, having thus and such a shape, is placed in a certain position relative to the original ink-marks. In particular, Smith knows that, given their respective shapes, the ink-marks Â“1,486Â” and Â“1,245 + 241 =Â” form a correct sentence when (some isomorph of) the former is placed to the right of (some isomorph of) the latter. It must be emphasized that Smith has no idea what any of these ink-marks mean. Smith knows nothing of relevance to this situation other than the rules as to how certain shapes ought to be manipulated or complemented. Those rules in fact describe how to do sums involving multi-digit numbers. But Smith doesn't know that. He knows only that, when given ink-marks having such and such a shape, another ink-mark must be placed beneath them if a true statement (as to whose identity he is quite ignorant) is to result. 
Commentary: What Smith is doing seems to be different from what W is doing. SmithÂ’s applying the just-mentioned rule involves his having various sense-perceptions (e.g., he sees various ink-deposits) and various beliefs (e.g., he believes that those ink-marks are symbols of some kind or other, and he believes that a correct statement, albeit one of whose meaning he is ignorant, will result if, underneath them, he produces an ink-mark having a certain shape); and his having such beliefs involves his making quite delicate judgments (e.g., he must judge that the ink-deposits in question were produced by sentient beings with certain intentions---he would not see those ink-deposits as tokening the sentence-fragment Â“1,245 + 241 =Â” were he to learn that their existence was the unintended result of some explosion involving an ink-filled urn). 
Nothing comparable holds of W. It isnÂ’t because of any sense-perceptions or beliefs or intentions on its part that, having been fed a wooden token of the sentence-fragment Â“2 + 9 =Â” W spits out a wooden Â“11.Â” So what Smith is doing in writing a Â“1,486Â” seems not to be comparable to what W is doing in spitting out a wooden Â“11.Â” 
And, while there is certainly a sense of the word Â“computeÂ” in which Smith is computing a sum, this cannot possibly be the sense in which, according to CTM, to think is to compute. A precondition for SmithÂ’s performing the just-described computation is his already being able to upload and process information. So CTM would be guilty of vicious circularity were it given by the thesis that, in this sense of the word Â“computeÂ” to think is to compute. So, supposing CTM coherent, the sense in which to think is to compute is the sense in which W computes, and the sense in which Smith computes is irrelevant. 
We will now see that CTM is indefensible and that no doctrine at all similar to it can possibly be correct. There are five reasons for this. These reasons will given in Sections 2.0-6.0. 
2.0 CTMÂ’s failure to distinguish between shape and syntactic form 
A story will help expose one reason why CTM is false. You shout the following at me: Â“if your nose starts to bleed in the next ten seconds, IÂ’ll give you a million bucks.Â” Let T be the sentence-token in question. As a result of TÂ’s being uttered, I do start to bleed out of my noise, and you duly give me $1,000,000. But it wasnÂ’t because of what T meant that I had a nose-bleed; nor was it because of TÂ’s syntax. It was TÂ’s being loud that caused my noseÂ­bleed. 
My reaction here wasnÂ’t symbolic. Even though T is a symbol (or, to be precise, a symbol-token), TÂ’s being a symbol did nothing. For exactly similar reasons, WÂ’s spitting out an Â“11Â” isnÂ’t symbolic, even though its doing so was precipitated by events involving symbol-tokens. 
2.1 This line of reasoning generalized 
WeÂ’ve just seen that CTM is a non-starter if a symbol-tokenÂ’s Â“formÂ” is identified with its shape. But sometimes, when referring to a symbol-tokenÂ’s Â“form,Â” advocates of CTM are (so they say) referring to its syntactic form. Given this use of the word Â“form,Â” CTM becomes the contention that thoughts are syntax-driven operations on symbols. 
This contention is easily refuted. Syntax is semantic structure. Â“Smith loves MaryÂ” and Â“Sally hates GregÂ” have the same syntax because the semantics of the one has the same structure as the semantics of the other. 
To be sure, those sentences have very different meanings. But theyÂ’re semantically isomorphic. Each constituent of the one sentence corresponds to exactly one constituent of the other (Â“Smith,Â” Â“loves,Â” and MaryÂ” correspond to Â“Sally,Â” Â“hates,Â” and Â“Greg,Â” respectively); and the relationship borne by the semantics of any given constituent of the one sentence to the semantics of that sentence as a whole coincides with the relationship borne by the semantics of that constituentÂ’s counterpart in the other sentence to the semantics of that sentence as a whole. So the relation borne by the semantics of Â“SmithÂ” with respect to the proposition that Smith loves Mary coincides with the relation borne by Â“SallyÂ” to the proposition that Sally hates Greg. 
Given that syntax is semantic structure, syntax-driven operations are ipso facto meaning-driven. Being the contention that Â“formalÂ” operations are not meaning-driven, CTM is therefore completely incoherent if taken to be the contention that Â“formalÂ” operations are syntax-driven operations. 
At the same time, CTM is incoherent, as we saw, if Â“formalÂ” operations are taken to be shape-driven operations. There is no third way to interpret the word Â“formal.Â” So CTM is incoherent. 
2.2 Shape vs. syntax (revisited): The equivocation that lies at the heart of CTM 
Here is the thinking embodied in CTM: 
Form-driven responses to symbolic inputs are ipso facto cases of thought. W has form-driven responses to symbolic inputs. Therefore, W is thinking (it is adding numbers). 
But when this argument is stated in a clear and non-elliptical manner, it becomes clear that it involves an equivocation and is invalid for that reason: 
Form-driven responses to symbolic inputs are ipso facto cases of thought. (In other words, syntax-driven responses to symbol-tokens are ipso facto cases of thought.) W has form-driven responses to symbolic inputs. (In other words, WÂ’s responses to its inputs are morphology-driven.) Therefore W is thinking. 
The second argument is clearly spurious. Presumably because they are aware of this, advocates of CTM typically hold that, even though a symbolÂ­tokenÂ’s shape isnÂ’t identical with its morphology, syntax can be Â“codedÂ” into morphology---that syntax can be Â“morphologizedÂ” in much the way that geometry can be arithmetized. This is both false and irrelevant. 
ItÂ’s false because anything, no matter what its shape, can have any syntactic structure, and anything, no matter what its syntactic structure, can be tokened by anything, no matter what its shape. (In other words, given an arbitrary shape, and given an arbitrary syntactic structure, there is a possible language to which there belong expressions having that syntactic structure that are tokened by objects having that shape.) ItÂ’s irrelevant because, even if syntax can be morphologized, it isnÂ’t, as weÂ’ve already seen, in virtue of its having this as opposed to that shape that a symbol-token has this as opposed to that syntax. So in so far as one is responding to an objectÂ’s shape, oneÂ’s behavior is, to that extent, not the effect of, or otherwise to be understood in terms of, that objectÂ’s shape. 
To be sure, one knows what syntax an object has on the basis of its shape. A large part of the reason that I know the syntax of the following sentenceÂ­token---Â“John is tall and grass is greenÂ”---is that I know what shape that ink-deposit has. But sentence-tokens with precisely the same syntax can be tokened by hand-movements or by noises; and hand-movements and noises have no strictly morphological resemblance at all to any ink-deposit. (No ink-deposit that tokens Â“John is tall and grass is greenÂ” bears much resemblance to a stream of noises, or a series of hand-movements, that also tokened that same sentence, except relative to rules of projection that were contrived ex post facto to establish such a resemblance.) 
Also, the relationship that holds between (a) my knowledge of that inkÂ­depositÂ’s shape and (b) my knowledge of its syntax is of a causal, and not of a constitutive, nature. I see that it has that shape. Given that knowledge, along with my background linguistic knowledge, I judge that it has a certain syntax. 
To be sure, from an experiential (phenomenological) perspective, it may seem as though in knowing that it has that shape I ipso facto know that it has that syntax. But thatÂ’s not the case. What we have is one bit of knowledge (knowledge of shape) leading, by way of (rapid) judgments, to some other bit of knowledge (knowledge of syntax). 
Echoing what we just said, these two bits of knowledge may seem, at the level of consciousness, to come into existence simultaneously. But that appearance is misleading and, even if not misleading, irrelevant. ItÂ’s misleading because any knowledge of an objectÂ’s syntax must follow knowledge of its physical properties. To clarify these last two statements: If I judge that youÂ’re angry, itÂ’s on the basis of your facial expression, or some such. My judgment as to your emotional state may immediately follow my awareness of your expression. But given that the former is based on the latter and is also caused by it, the one awareness follows the other, however quickly. Exactly similar points hold of the relationship between my knowledge of a given objectÂ’s physical shape and my subsequent knowledge of its syntax: it isnÂ’t possible for me to have the latter knowledge without having the former; it is possible for me to have the former without having the latter; and my knowledge of the former is the sole foundation for, and is also what leads to, my knowledge of the latter. 
Plus, itÂ’s irrelevant that, speaking from a strictly experiential (phenomenological) perspective, the occurrence of the one bit of knowledge seems to coincide with the occurrence of the other. It is the purpose, or at the very least the effect, of consciousness to condense the intricacies of the cognitions underlying it into a single, seemingly homogeneous Â“experience.Â” 
If every articulation of pre-conscious cognition were faithfully represented in consciousness, if phenomenology faithfully duplicated every joint in the intricacies of the cognitions of which our conscious judgments are the outcomes, then consciousness would be so overburdened with information that it would cease to be able to perform the executive functions with which it is tasked. When seeing a rabid dog run towards me, my consciousness would present to me a richly articulated mosaic of judgments, whose consequences for my well-being would take much more time to figure out than was available to me. Fortunately, however, my consciousness presents me with a homogenous feeling that causes me to bolt into action. Instead of giving me the psychological equivalent of a two-hundred page state-department report, consciousness gives me the equivalent of an electric cattle-prod in my back. And because the rich cognitive back-story is telescoped into that unpleasant burst of phenomenology, I do the right thing. (I run to the mini-van, lock the doors, roll up the windows, and so on.) And I do it in real time. 
In general, it is precisely because consciousness represents as homogenous Â“feelingsÂ” what are in fact intricate networks of judgments that the contents of consciousness, unlike their cognitive underpinnings, are actionable. It is, I would conjecture, the very purpose, or at least one of the purposes, of consciousness to condense cognitive intricacies into affective simplicities. Therefore, it is inter alia its purpose to condense distinct, albeit adjacent, stages of intricate thought processes into a single, action-causing, survival-ensuring feeling. 
In any case, if this is at all on the mark, then itÂ’s of no relevance that my recognition of the ink-depositÂ’s shape seems to be temporally coincident with my recognition of its syntax. It is to be pointed out that, if this isnÂ’t on the mark, then much work in psychology crumbles. 
3.0 A related point: CTM incompatible with the fact that distinct thoughts can be part of some one thought-process 
If CTM is right, my thinking 2 is a prime number and 2 is less than three cannot be responsible for my later thinking some prime number is less than three. According to CTM, if B1 is the totality of brain-events constitutive of 
my thinking 2 is a prime number and 2 is less than three, and B2 is the 
totality of brain-events constitutive of my thinking some prime number is less than three, it cannot be B1Â’s being such a belief that brings about B2. So it cannot be B1Â’s being such a belief that leads me to believe that some prime number is less than three. 
So, if CTM is right, B1Â’s being such a belief has nothing to do with B2Â’s existence or a fortiori with B2Â’s being constitutive of a thought to the effect that some prime number is less than three. Thus, my believing that two is even and is less than three cannot, if CTM is right, have anything to do with my later believing that some even prime is less than three. So, if CTM is right, T1 has nothing to do with T2, notwithstanding that the brain-events 
constitutive of T1 brought about those constitutive of T2. 
So even though B1 occurs right before B2 and is causally responsible for it, and even though B1 and B2 are constitutive of, respectively, T1 and T2, nonetheless T1 and T2 cannot, if CTM is right, be installments in some one thought-process. 
In general, CTM is incompatible with the fact that distinct thoughts can be part of some one thought-process. CTM is thus incompatible with the fact that thought-processes occur---with the fact that there are sequences of thoughts (setting aside such thought-sequences whose constituents have no thematic coherence, having at best the content-free coherence had by a series of domino-fallings). 
4.0 CTMÂ’s dependence on the false assumption that syntax can mirror logical form 
Context-sensitivity drives a wedge between syntax and logical form. If I say: 
(1) "it is snowing now and it is not snowing now," 
what I'm saying might be true---it might stop snowing before I utter the second conjunct---even though it has the same syntax as: 
(2) 
"n is even and n is not even." Similarly, if I say: 

(3) 
"that guy is identical with that guy," 


what I'm saying might be false, even though it has that same syntax as 
(4) "n is identical with n." 
If our thinking were syntax-driven, we couldn't recognize the differences in respect of logical form between (1) and (2) or between (3) and (4). We can recognize those differences. So our thinking is not syntax-driven. So CTM is wrong. 
Here is a similar line of thought. If, on July 1, 2010, in Richmond, VA, I say: 
(i) "right now, Jim is three thousand miles from here," 
the information encoded in my utterance is very different that encoded in an utterances of: 
(ii) "On July 1, 2010, Jim is 3,000 miles from Richmond VA." 
The information encoded in (i) doesn't follow from the information encoded in (ii), or vice versa. In general, when the context-sensitive expressions in a true statement are replaced with context-insensitive expressions, the result is a statement that, although true, neither entails the first statement nor follows from it. 
For an expression to be context-sensitive is for its referent to vary with the context. What an expression refers to is determined by its semantics, not its syntax. CTM says that thought is to no degree semantics-driven. If that were true, we couldn't grasp perspectival truths, such as that expressed by (i). Since we can grasp such truths, CTM is false. 
5.0 CTMÂ’s reliance on the erroneous assumption that there are minimal units of thought 
First a definition: a Â“morphemeÂ” is an expression that cannot be decomposed into others. Bearing this in mind, letÂ’s suppose that, just as CTM says, we think in a language. In that case, our concepts are identical with expressions. Linguistic expressions consist of morphemes. (Any given complex expression; e.g., Â“the cat is on the mat,Â” decomposes into expressions that cannot, in their turn, be further decomposed; (e.g., Â“cat,Â” Â“matÂ”). So in contending that our thoughts are identical with (tokens of) Mentalese symbols, CTM is, in effect, assuming that we have simple concepts: concepts that cannot be decomposed in others. So CTM, if correct, entails that any given thought that one has can be decomposed into Â“simpleÂ” concepts. CTM thus has the radically implausible consequence that we have Â“simpleÂ” concepts. In other words, CTM has the consequence that some of our concepts are no more capable of being decomposed into other concepts than a morpheme (e.g., the word Â“catÂ”) can be decomposed into other expressions. If this consequence of CTM is correct, it follows, as weÂ’ll now see, that some of our concepts would be such that one could have them without also having other concepts. 
Let T be the token of the Mentalese word for Â“snowÂ” that went off when, just a moment ago, I thought to myself that snow is white. We may assume that T is a morpheme. (If, for some reason, you reject that assumption, just map what we say about T onto some Mentalese expression-token that, in your judgment, is a morphemeÂ—and you must, if you grant that we think in a language, grant that there is some such token, since morpheme-less language is a surd---and everything that we say about T will hold mutatis mutandis of this other expression-token.) Not being decomposable into other expression-tokens, T presumably exists independently of such tokens. Given any simple expressionÂ—given any morphemeÂ—belonging to a language L, you can remove that morpheme without removing other morphemes. Of course, in removing that morpheme, youÂ’ll remove all of the expressions of which it is a constituent. (And, if you choose a non-lexical item; e.g., Â“andÂ” or Â“of,Â” you may thus do a lot of damage to L.) But you wonÂ’t, in removing that morpheme, be removing other morphemes. 
Supposing that CTM is right, some of our concepts must be identical with morphemes of Mentalese. Taken together with the points just made, this entails that 
(i) If you strip Mentalese of the word-type of which T is a token, the only other expressions which, in so doing, youÂ’ll be removing from Mentalese will be other morphemes, 
and also that: 
(ii) Some of our concepts are such that one can have them without having others. This means that, if CTM is right, your concept of snow is primitive, the same being true of your concept of Smith, Jones, and Brown (assuming, for argumentÂ’s sake, that the Mentalese expressions for these individuals are morphemic). 
5.1 CTMÂ’s reliance on the erroneous assumption that there are minimal units of thought (continued) 
But there are no primitive concepts. I couldnÂ’t possibly have a concept of snow, or of Barack Obama, or (to take a more tendentious example) of the number three without having a network of other concepts---extension, spatiotemporal location, surface-area, sentience, etc. 
Concepts are necessarily contrastive; in order to have a concept of a thing, one has to be able to distinguish that thing from other things. A prerequisite for distinguishing a given rock from a given tree is my being aware of some property had by the rock that isnÂ’t had by the tree. And a prerequisite for my having such knowledge is my already having concepts. 
5.1.1 How some contemporary philosophers would response to this argument 
Many contemporary theorists---some of them CTM-advocates, some of them notÂ—reject this line of thought, saying that, to have a Â“fix,Â” on the rock (or the tree), I need only be on the receiving end of a causal series beginning with it. Their view is that concepts are mental photographs. The relationship borne by my concept of Socrates with respect to Socrates himself is identical with the relationship borne by a photograph of Barack Obama with respect to the events (the impact of certain light-rays with Barack ObamaÂ’s body) that, in due course, led to that photograph. 
The position just described involves a failure to distinguish between: 
(i) awareness of some entity, 
and: 
(ii) information that, if known, would lead to such awareness. 
I see discolorations of a certain kind on a photographic plate. Given that information, along with other pieces of background information that I have, I can make various inferences. I can infer that, at some point, light bounced off of a person who was bald and was wearing a toga (and so on). So the photographic plate is information in the sense that, to a creature with the requisite background and the requisite intelligence, its existence warrants the making of an inference that will eventuate in knowledge of some entity (e.g., a person) or state of affairs (e.g., one consisting of a person wearing a toga) that might otherwise have remained unknown. (Why Â“might otherwise have been unknown,Â” instead of Â“would otherwise have been unknownÂ”? Because I might have been the one who took the picture and might therefore have already known of the person and the corresponding state of affairs.) The discolorations on the photographic plate are Â“informationÂ” in the sense that, to a suitably endowed creature, they warrant the making of inferences that, in due course, lead to concepts. 
In any case, it is massively to CTMÂ’s discredit that it presupposes that there are representational atoms. 

5.2 A similar argument 
Sentences are digital structures. Setting aside cases of ambiguity, any given sentenceÂ—any given complex expression, in fact---has a unique decomposition into minimal units of significance. This means, as previously pointed out, that our thoughts decompose into minimal representational units. Which is radically implausible. 
In any case, sense-perceptions donÂ’t have a digital structure, and neither, it would seem to follow, does the information that sense-perceptions encode. Given which, it would be very artificial to maintain that all post-perceptual cognition was digital or, therefore, sentential in nature. 
But, for argumentÂ’s sake, letÂ’s suppose that the contents of our sense-perceptions can, as some advocates of CTM maintain, be Â“digitized.Â” Supposing this hypothesis correct, all the problems previously posed for CTM by perceptual content are now posed by the post-perceptual thoughts involved in this (alleged) digitization-process. If IÂ’m translating from Albanian to English, I must speak both Albanian and English. Moreover, supposing that IÂ’m translating competently, I have some way of evaluating the degree to which my English outputs match my Albanian inputs. If my thinking is entirely mediated by English sentences, I wonÂ’t be able to do either of these things: I wonÂ’t be able to translate from Albanian into English; and, if per impossibile I were able to do so, I couldnÂ’t verify the accuracy of my translations. By analogous reasoning, if the aforementioned post-perceptual thoughts were themselves entirely digital, they would ipso facto be blind to the benchmarks relative to which their own translations were to be evaluated, supposing for argumentÂ’s sake that they could produce such translations to begin with. 
Of course, one could say that those processes are purely causal; i.e., that they donÂ’t embody any awareness of what, given the relevant perceptual inputs, the relevant digital outputs ought to be. But in that case, our post-perceptual thoughts are ex hypothesi merely the results of, and are in no way justified by, the contents of our perceptions. But that is surely too absurd a position to take seriously. 
6.0 The regress-problem 
If CTM is right, then: 
(ARS)[416]anything that represents anything is a symbol. 
If, as CTM says, our thoughts are sentence-tokens, then surely we understand those tokens. But understanding a sentence involves being able to pair it off with its meaning. This means that one must be able to compare that sentence with something that isnÂ’t a sentence, which wouldnÂ’t be possible if all of our thoughts were sentences (or sentence-tokens). 
Â“That doesnÂ’t follow," it might be said. Â“Suppose that you think that snow is white, and that your thinking this consists in there being an occurrence of some Mentalese sentence. Your understanding that sentence could consist in there occurring, in your mind-brain, various sentences of some languageÂ— call it Mentalese2---such that, given those sentence-occurrences, you can duly interpret the original (Mentalese) sentence.Â” 
Yes, but by that logic, Mentalese3 sentences must occur in one's mind before one can understand those Mentalese2 sentence-occurrences, and Mentalese4 sentences must occur in one's mind before one can understand 
those Mentalese3 sentence-occurrences, and so on ad infinitum. So itÂ’s viciously regressive to hold, as CTM does, that symbol-tokens mediate our thoughts. More precisely, itÂ’s viciously regressive given the reasonable assumption that we understand those symbols. 
6.1 How advocates of CTM deal with the regress-problem 
Aware of this line of thought, advocates of CTM say that we donÂ’t understand the symbol-tokens that mediate our own thoughts. As William Lycan (1984, p. 217) puts it, we are simply Â“built to use those symbolsÂ” in the Â“rightÂ” ways, much as computers are Â“builtÂ” to use the symbols (or, rather, the things which are tendentiously and, we have seen, wrongly called Â“symbolsÂ”) on which it operates. 
6.2 The problem with the way advocates of CTM deal with the regress-problem 
But, so far as a given thing isnÂ’t understood, it isnÂ’t functioning as a symbol. A story, similar to one told earlier, will make this clear. On my desk, I have a wooden sculpture, which weÂ’ll call Â“WS," that tokens the sentence Â“haste makes waste.Â” Even though WS tokens three words, all three word-tokens are carved from the same block of wood. So WS consists of one, solid object, not of a lot of letter-or word-blocks. WS is heavy; itÂ’s made of solid oak, not pine or plywood or any other cheap sort of wood. It would thus serve as an excellent cudgel. A student of mine comes into my office. He reads it, understands it, and accordingly changes his, hitherto impetuous ways. In this context, WS is functioning as a symbol. In other words, if E1Â…En are the 
just-mentioned effects on the student, it is WSÂ’s being a symbol (of quite a specific kind, in fact) that leads to E1Â…En. Later that afternoon, a colleague, whom I detest, comes into my office. He doesnÂ’t read WS. Because of his myopia, he sees a brown blur in the place that WS occupies. Gripped by a non-tenure-conducive rage, I strike my colleague with WS. If E1*Â…Em* are 
the subsequent bruises and fractures suffered by my colleague, it is WSÂ’s having a certain mass, moving with a certain velocity, etc. that brings about E1*Â….Em*. WSÂ’s being a symbol is utterly irrelevant. Why? Because WSÂ’s 
being understood is essential to its functioning as a symbol. 
Let us sum up. Languages are sets of semantic rules. Where there are no such rules, there are no languages; and where there is no knowledge of such rules, there is no linguistic activity. The idea that there is a Â“language of thoughtÂ” is incoherent, given that it is inconsistent with these basic truths, and so is CTM, given that it assumes that there is a language of thought. 
7.0 CTM self-refuting. 
CTM says that we think in sentence-tokens. CTM also says that, qua proposition-bearing entities, those sentence-tokens do nothing. For reasons that weÂ’ll now see, it follows that, if CTM is correct, it cannot be known to be correct or even rationally accepted. 
We must start by remembering that no thing is a cause. The rock isnÂ’t what breaks the window. What does so is the rockÂ’s striking the window with a certain amount of force. Bearing this in mind, let B be the brain-structure that encodes my belief that 1 + 1 = 2. Nobody denies that B has causal properties. But if CTM is right, BÂ’s being (or constituting) a thought to the effect that 1 + 1 = 2 does nothing. The same thing mutatis mutandis holds of any content-bearing brain-state. If CTM is right, even if a given brain-state bears content C, its bearing that content is causally inert. This entails that, if a given person accepts CTM, it isnÂ’t because of the contents of any of his thoughts that he does so; and, consequently, it isnÂ’t because he knows of any reason to accept CTM. So, if CTM is correct, there is ipso facto no way that a person could be justified in accepting CTM (or, by obvious extensions of this reasoning, anything else). Which, while not showing that itÂ’s false, does show that one cannot coherently advocate it. 
Chapter 24 Personal and Objectual Identity 
1.0 Identity-related expressions ambiguous 
We often make statements of the form Â‹x is identical with yÂ›. Examples are 
Â“IÂ’m the guy in the photo,Â” Â“water is H2O,Â” Â“Superman is Clark Kent,Â” Â“thatÂ’s the eraser I was looking for,Â” and so on. Statements of this form are known as Â“identity statements.Â” 
Identity statements donÂ’t always, or even typically, use the terms Â“identityÂ” or Â“identical with.Â” Usually, they just use some form of the verb Â“to be.Â” So Â“thatÂ’s the guy who took my moneyÂ” is an identity statement, even though the terms Â“identityÂ” and Â“identical withÂ” are nowhere to be found in it. 
1.1 Identity-related expressions ambiguous: Predicative vs. non-predicative uses of such expressions 
This brings us to a fact that confused many pre-20th-century thinkers. The verb Â“to beÂ” is ambiguous. As just noted, it sometimes means Â“identical withÂ” (Â“he is GeorgeÂ” means Â“he is identical with GeorgeÂ”). But sometimes it has an entirely different meaning. When you say Â“Smith is tall,Â” you are not saying that Smith is identical with tallness; you are not making an identity statement. So oftentimes Â“isÂ” (and Â“are,Â” Â“am,Â” etc.) doesnÂ’t denote the relation of identity and instead denotes the relation of having (as in having an attribute). In other words, Â“isÂ” sometimes has a predicative meaning: it is used to predicate a property of an individual. (To predicate a property of an individual is to attribute that property to that individual.) But in this context we will focus on the concept of identity, not on the concept of attribute possession. 
That said, it should be pointed out that, although it is generally clear what is meant by statements involving the term Â“isÂ” (or some other form of the verb Â“to beÂ”), there are cases where it is functioning in both waysÂ—where it both indicates identity and attributes a property to somebody (or something). If you say Â“Smith is the guy who washes my windows,Â” that seems both to identify Smith with a certain person and to attribute various properties to him (e.g., the property of a window washer). We will find that these borderline cases expose important facts about the concept of identity. 
1.2 Metaphorical uses of identity-related expressions 
Identity statements are often used in a loose, figurative fashion. One often says things like Â“George isnÂ’t the person he used to beÂ—having money has changed himÂ” and Â“IÂ’m not myself today.Â” These statements are not meant literally. Although having money may have changed George, since he now has unsavory character traits that he used not to have, George hasnÂ’t literally become a person distinct from the person he used to be. It isnÂ’t as though GeorgeÂ’s brain was replaced with that of an alien. Similarly, when one says Â“IÂ’m not myself today,Â” one isnÂ’t saying that one is literally not identical with oneselfÂ—such a statement would be nonsensical. One is merely saying that, because of fatigue (or some such), one isnÂ’t doing as well as one would like (or some such). Henceforth, we will disregard non-literal sentences like Â“George isnÂ’t himself todayÂ” and will concern ourselves only with what is literally meant by Â“identical with,Â” Â“identity,Â” etc. 
1.3 Numerical vs. qualitative identity 
Terms such as Â“identical,Â” Â“identity,Â” etc. sometimes refer to Â“strictÂ” or Â“numericalÂ” identity, and sometimes refer to Â“qualitativeÂ” identity. 
For x and y to be qualitatively identical is for them to have the very same features (or, in any case, for them to be as similar to each other as is possible given the one is not the very same entity as the other). x and y can be qualitatively identical even if they are not literally the same thingÂ—even if, in other words, x and y are two things, not one. If you are cloned, you and your clone are qualitatively identical, meaning that you and your clone are very similar. But there are still two of you. 
In philosophy, we are concerned with the other kind of identity, which we will henceforth refer to as numerical identity. This is the kind of identity involved in statements such as Â“water is identical with H2O.Â”.Â” This doesnÂ’t 
say that water and H2O are merely very similar. It says that water and H2O are but one thing. Other examples of statements affirming strict identity are Â“the square of 4 is identical with 16,Â” Â“Clark Kent is Superman,Â” and Â“light is electromagnetic radiation.Â” 
1.3.1 Numerical identity entails qualitative identity, but not vice versa 
If x and y are literally the same thing, then x resembles y to the highest degree possibleÂ—after all, x cannot, under that circumstance, have any attribute that y lacks. But x and y can be qualitatively identicalÂ—that is, they can resemble each other a great deal, without being numerically identical, as we noted when discussing the possibility of cloning. 
1.3.2 Correction: Numerical identity does entail qualitative identity and vice versa 
Strictly speaking, qualitative identity entails numerical identity. If x and y are truly exactly the sameÂ—if there is no characteristic that the one has that the other lacksÂ—then they must be the same. For, at any given time, they must occupy the same place and must be doing the same things. 
It can be proven formally that qualitative identity entails numerical identity. If x and y are numerically identical, then, by hypothesis, neither has any property lacked by the other. x has the property of being identical with x. Therefore, y has the property of being identical with x as well. So y = x. 
The principle that genuine qualitative identity entails numerical identity is known as the Identity of Indiscernibles (if x and y have the very same properties, then x is numerically identical with y.) This principle is to be contrasted with the Indiscernibility of Identicals, better known as LeibnizÂ’s Law (if x is numerically identical with y, then x and y have the very same properties). 
A few remarks on these two principles are in order. Though it has been disputed, the Identity of Indiscernibles is clearly correct: if x and y have the same properties, then, given that x has the property of being identical with x, y also has that property. And, though it is seldom disputed, Leibniz's Law is not correct. When I was three, I weighed less than 100 pounds. I now weigh more than 100 pounds. So that three year old lacks some property that I have. But there is surely a sense in which I am that very person. Wrongly thinking that, if LeibnizÂ’s Law were jettisoned, logic as we know it would crumble, philosophers have responded to facts such as this one by proposing highly artificial and, more importantly, demonstrably false ways of holding onto LeibnizÂ’s Law. WeÂ’ll discuss these misguided efforts later in this chapter, and weÂ’ll propose an alternative to them. 
2.0 Objectual identity 
Sometimes identity statements concern people or other animate beings, and sometimes they concern inanimate objects. Examples of the first kind are Â“Clark Kent is SupermanÂ” and Â“Einstein is the physicist who invented Relativity Theory.Â” Examples of the second kind are Â“thatÂ’s the shirt I just bought,Â” Â“the car sitting in my driveway today is the very one I drove back in the Â‘70s,Â” and Â“the liquid in your glass is the water that you poured into it a moment agoÂ—I havenÂ’t switched it with poison.Â” 
If an identity statement concerns an inanimate object (or substance), then it affirms a case of objectual identity. Â“ObjectualÂ” is the adjective form of Â“object.Â” If an identity statement concerns people or other animate beings (e.g., dogs, Martians), then it concerns personal identity. (The term Â“personalÂ” is used even if the animate being in question is not a personÂ—even if it is, for example, a dog.) 
2.1 Objectual identity more fundamental than personal identity 
My guess is that most people would find the topic of personal identity more interesting than that of objectual identity. A bit of autobiography may make it clear why I say this. 
What is it for meÂ—a middle-aged professor who rarely drives over the speed-limitÂ—to be the same person as the guy who, 20 years ago, was out partying every night? I have changed so much in the meantime that it almost defies comprehension how I could ever have been some young roustabout. My musical horizons, for example, extend no further than the easy-listening channel on my radio, and I no longer have any tolerance for the cacophony of Â“rock music,Â” which used to be my lifeÂ’s blood. I spend my evenings either working or reading. And when IÂ’m not engaged in one of those two activities, itÂ’s probably because I am hobbling (or, more likely, using my Â“RascalÂ”Â—a motor-powered personal locomotion device for the decrepit) at a rate of around 1/2 mph, from my desk to the easy chair in which I watch television shows targeted for senior citizens (e.g., Â“Murder She WroteÂ”). Not a single one of these statements would have applied to the person I was when I was your age. 
This is not to mention that my once supple joints are frozen with arthritis, and my once pink and healthy vital tissues are now an oxygen-starved gray, thanks to the scourges to oneÂ’s health brought on by middle age. In high school I was a creditable athlete, playing on three different teams. These days, even a game of shuffleboard pushes me to my limits; and IÂ’m even considering giving that up, since thereÂ’s no Rascal-parking anywhere near the local shuffleboard court. 
It thus defies comprehension how, given my current condition, I could possibly be identical with the party animal of two decades ago. This problem, and others like it, are very interestingÂ—much more interesting than the question of why the chair IÂ’m sitting on now is identical with the chair I was sitting on 10 minutes ago, when I first started writing this section. In other words, personal identity seems more interesting than objectual identity. 
The problem is that personal identity must be understood in terms of objectual identity. Why is this? There are two dimensions to the concept of personal identity, the reason being that people have both minds and bodies, and statements about personal identity often therefore depend for their truth on both bodily and mental facts. By contrast, objects (chairs, rocks, etc.) 
donÂ’t have mindsÂ—they are pure body. So identity statements concerning them (in other words, objectual identity statements) depend for their truth only on physical facts. Identity statements that concern human or animal bodiesÂ—for example, Â“this is the hand that signed that piece of paperÂ”Â— concern objectual identity. And the reason, of course, is that bodies are objectsÂ—like rocks and trees. They are not subjects, like you and me. Statements about personal identity are often concerned both with physical and with mental facts. Since they concern physical facts and objects, such statements are concerned, at least in part, with the concept of objectual identity. One must therefore understand objectual identity before one can understand personal identity, just as one must understand single-variable calculus before one can understand multivariable calculus. 
2.2 One kind of objectual identity: diachronic objectual identity 
A story will help clarify the nature of statements concerning objectual identity. At 11:00 A.M. I make myself a sandwich. But I donÂ’t eat it; I just place it on the kitchen counter. Let X be the object that at 11:00 A.M. I place on the kitchen counter. At 1:00 P.M. I see my roommate, Smith, holding and apparently intending to consume the sandwich that I made. (There is no doubt that itÂ’s the same sandwich.) Let Y be the object that at 1:00 P.M. Smith is holding. 
Under these circumstances, the statement: 
(*) X is identical with Y, 
is true. 
But exactly what does this mean? X doesnÂ’t have the same properties as Y. First of all, X is on the kitchen counter, whereas Y is in SmithÂ’s hands. X, having just been made out of refrigerator-stored ingredients, is nice and cool. Y, having been sitting on the counter for two hours is warm and yucky. Given how different X and Y are, what sense can it make to say that they are identical? 
Here we have to take a brief detour through a bit of physics and metaphysics. X is not a simple entity. It has various partsÂ—it consists of two slices of bread, a leaf of lettuce, etc. But each of those parts consists, ultimately, of a vast swarm of incessant displacements of mass-energy. Given any macroscopic physical objectÂ—a rock, a bar of soap, a plantÂ—not a single micro-constituent of that object will stay in the same place for any amount of time. Given any one of the atoms composing any macroscopic object, that atom will move (it will rotate, vibrate, and altogether change its location) if you give it so much as a trillionth of a second. And all the objects that we deal with in everyday lifeÂ—our cars, our clothes, our toothbrushesÂ—are composed of these incessant movements of micro-particles. So, really, all of those objects are collections of events. The seeming changelessness of the poster on your wall is an illusion: At any given time, that poster consists of nothing but movements and exchanges of mass and energy. 
We must make two final points before we can say what (*) means. First, in some cases, events are causally related to one another, and in some cases theyÂ’re not. I brushed my teeth this morning and you put on your shoes. The one event didnÂ’t cause the other. But my brushing my teeth did cause various particles on my teeth to dissolve or change location. 
When events are causally related to each other, they satisfy one of two conditions: either they are adjacent in both space and time or, if they are not adjacent, they are connected by a series of events each of whose links is adjacent with at least one other event in that same series. The event of my dragging the toothbrush across the bit of cereal stuck to my tooth occupied the same approximate place as the event of the bit of cerealÂ’s leaving my tooth, and the first event came right before the second. So, in this case, the cause (my moving the toothbrush over my tooth) and the effect (the bit of cerealÂ’s being dislodged from my tooth) are adjacent in space and time. 
Not all causes are related to effects in such a direct way. I turn on a flashlight by pushing a button on it. The event of my pushing this button causes a light beam to travel from my flashlight to some distant planet. So one event (my pushing a certain button) causes another event (a certain spotÂ’s appearing on an otherwise dark, planetary surface). These two events are separated in space and also in time (it takes time for light to travel, and the larger the distance, the more time is needed). Nonetheless, the cause and the effect are connected by a series of events each of which is adjacent, in space and time, with another event in that same series. Let t be some period before the light beam reaches the planet but after it has left my flashlight. Suppose that, at time t, the tip of the light beam is in place p. The eventsÂ—the swarm of photonsÂ—in place p at time t cause there to be similar photon-swarms at the place right next to p at the time right after t. So if p* is some place right next to p, and t* is some time right after t, then the photon-swarms in p at t cause there to be similar photon-swarms in p* at t*. In their turn, those photon-swarmsÂ—the ones in p* at t*Â—cause there to be other, similar photon-swarms in some third place (one that is right next to p*) at some third time (one that is right after t*). So even though my pushing the button is remote, in both space and time, from the resulting spot of light on the distant planet, those two events are connected by a continuous series of events each of whose installments is caused by its predecessor and causes its successor. Any such series is known as a Â“causal sequence.Â” Light beams are causal sequences; but so, for the reasons given earlier, is every object. X (the cool 
11:00 A.M. sandwich on the counter) is part of the same causal sequence as Y 
(the warm 1:00 P.M. sandwich in SmithÂ’s hands). In light of these points, we can say what (*) means. (*) says that the events that constitute X and Y are both parts of some one causal sequence. To generalize this point, many statements of the form a is identical with b say that some object is causally connected in a certain way with some other object. 
HereÂ’s another example. Let B be the person who is, at this very moment, writing this handout; and let A be the earlier described wild man from many years ago. The statement A is identical with B is true because B is the result of a continuous series of changes the first of which was undergone by A. For reasons that I give in Chapter 14, I hold that, where there is continuity, there is causality. So the sequence just described is a "causal series," meaning that any given event in it is a cause of any later event in it. 
To sum up, in some cases, x is identical with y says that x and y are different installments in some one causal sequence. (For reasons that I give in Chapter 14, I hold that, where there is continuity, there is causality. So the sequence just described is a "causal series," meaning that any given event in it is a cause of any later event in it.) 
2.3 Another kind of objectual identity: synchronic objectual identity 
But sometimes x is identical with y has a very different meaning. Suppose that the worldÂ’s most valuable diamond is the only diamond in the Hawthorn Museum. In that case, the following identity statement is true: 
(#) Â“The worldÂ’s most valuable diamond is identical with the only diamond in the Hawthorn Museum.Â” 
But # isnÂ’t saying anything about causal sequences. This becomes clear when we replace # with the (let us suppose) true statement: 
(#t) Â“The most valuable diamond in the world at time t is identical with the only diamond that is in the Hawthorn Museum at time t.Â” 
#t concerns a single instant. It doesnÂ’t concern a stretch of time; and it therefore doesnÂ’t concern causal sequences, since those, by definition, take up more than an instant of time. What # and #t are saying is that there is some one object that has two different properties. So # is saying that: 
(##) there exists a certain object that is a diamond that is more valuable than any other diamond in the world and that, at this time, is in a certain museum (the Hawthorn museum) that contains no other diamonds. 
Thus, #t is saying that there is some property P and some property P* such that some one thing uniquely has P and also uniquely has P*. Many identity statements are of this kind. Consider: 
(SC) Â“Superman is Clark Kent.Â” 
This doesnÂ’t tell you that two different things are one. Two things canÂ’t be one. If SC said otherwise, it would not only be false but absurd. SC makes a non-absurd statement about properties. It says of the property of being a super-hero who lives in Metropolis and has a domicile on the North pole (etc.) that exactly one thing has that property; and it says that anything that has that property also uniquely has the property of being a wimpy reporter at the Daily Bugle who is the butt of Lois LaneÂ’s derision (etc.). 
Similar remarks hold of: 
(WH) Â“Water is H2O (or, rather, any body of water is identical with some collection of H2O molecules).Â” 
WH doesnÂ’t make the absurd statement that two different thingsÂ—water, on the one hand, and H2O, on the otherÂ—are the same thing. WH makes a statement about properties. One of those properties is that of being the liquid that we drink, bathe in, etc. The other is the property of having a certain chemical composition. WH says that the first property is uniquely instantiated and, in addition, that anything instantiating that property also uniquely instantiates the second. 
To sum up: a=b says one of two things: (i) there is some causal sequence of which a and b are different installments or (ii) there is some one thing that has a number of different properties. 
3.0 Personal identity 
Suppose that each of Â“aÂ” and Â“bÂ” is an expression referring to a person. In that case, of course, Â“a = bÂ” is an identity statementÂ—but it is one that concerns personal identity, and not merely objectual identity. Nonetheless, the principles in terms of which personal identity is to be understood are pretty much the same as those in terms of which objectual identity is to be understood. For even when it is a statement about personal identity, Â“a = bÂ” says either (i) there is some causal sequence of which a and b are different installments or (ii) that there are properties P and P* such that each is uniquely instantiated and such that nothing instantiating the one doesnÂ’t instantiate the other. 
Consider the statement: 
(IB) Â“The inventor of bifocals is identical with the first postmaster general.Â” 
IB says that there is some one person (Benjamin Franklin, as it happens) who, in a world otherwise bereft of bifocal-inventors and first post-masters general, both invented bifocals and was a first postmaster general. (To avoid philosophically empty technicalities relating to tense-markers, weÂ’ll assume that BF is still with us.) So IB says that somebody has a number of different properties. So, in this respect, IB is SC, #t, and WH. 
Now consider the statement: 
(OF) Â“The old fogy who, at this very moment is writing this chapter (which no one will ever read and whose comedic excellence will therefore go unappreciated) is identical with the guy who, many moons ago, drove from Los Angeles to New York. 
OF says that one set of eventsÂ—the events constituting a person who, right now, is writing about personal identityÂ—is an installment in a causal sequence of which an earlier installment was some set of events that constituted some personÂ’s driving from Los Angeles to New York. So OF is like our earlier statement (concerning the sandwich): (*) X is identical with Y. 
Each of OF and (*) affirms that two different, non-simultaneous events (or sets of events) are installments in some one causal sequence. 
So the logical structure of statements concerning personal identity is not different from the logical structure of statements of objectual identity. 
3.1 Personal identity: the mentalistic conception 
Human beings have both physical and mental (i.e., psychological) characteristics. I have a certain weight. This is a physical characteristic. I have certain beliefs and interests. These are psychological characteristics. Human existence thus has a dual nature. 
It is vigorously debated how the mental and the physical are related to each other. A related, equally vigorous debate concerns the nature of the events that must occur if a person is to continue to exist. 
A story will clarify these points. Smith is in an accident and all of his brain is destroyed, except for the parts that regulate involuntary functions (e.g., breathing, digestion, etc.). So Smith is Â“brain-dead.Â” Question: Does Smith still exist? My own view is Â“no.Â” Legally speaking, of course, Smith exists as long as his heart is beating. But legal categories are of little use when it comes to settling philosophical issues[417], and it seems to me that Smith went out of existence the moment his mind did. 
Why do I have this view? Because I have what is referred to as a Â“mentalisticÂ” conception of personal identity. This is the view that you are your mind. People are identical with mental entities of some kind. This doesnÂ’t mean that people arenÂ’t also identical with physical entities. It means that if people are identical with physical entities (e.g., with their brains or certain parts thereof), it is only because those entities are themselves identical with mental entities. If, for example, it turns out that the mental entities with which people are identical are also brain-structures or patterns of brain activity, what follows, the mentalist believes, is not that people are non-mental entities but that people are mental entities and that mental entities, in their turn, are also physical entities. 
According to mentalism, the statement Â“I weigh 200 poundsÂ” really means Â“my body weighs 200 poundsÂ” and therefore doesnÂ’t really say how much I weigh.
