And given that I am identical with purely mental entities, I weigh no more than they doÂ—which isnÂ’t very much, since they weigh nothing if theyÂ’re non-physical, and next to nothing if they are physical (the reason being that, if theyÂ’re physical, theyÂ’re patterns of neural activity that have little or no mass). 
3.2 An important fact about the mentalistic conception: a materialist can have a mentalistic conception of personal identity 
One can believe that mental events are identical with certain kinds of physical events and still have a mentalistic conception of personal identity. So, for example, if you believe that feelings, intentions, and mental events in general are patterns of neural activity, and you believe that a body that doesnÂ’t house such patterns of activity ipso facto doesnÂ’t house a person, then you have a mentalistic conception of personal identity. So even if you believe that mind facts are identical with body facts, you still have a mentalistic conception of personal identity so long as the relevant body facts are those that mediate mental phenomena. Most contemporary mentalists fall into this category, and I myself am inclined, with some reservations (which I discuss in Chapter 22), to think that this is the right view. 
4.0 Personal identity: The non-mentalistic (or physicalistic) conception 
Many philosophers these days would disagree with much of what IÂ’ve just said. For these days, non-mentalistic, Â“bodilyÂ” conceptions of personal identity are dominant. So many contemporary philosophers would say that brain-dead Smith still exists. 
Why say this? There are some obvious reasons. First of all, we can truthfully say, while pointing to SmithÂ’s thought-free body Â“that person is brain-dead.Â” It seems a simple fact that we can describe people as Â“brainÂ­deadÂ” or even as just plain dead. Of course, dead people donÂ’t have anything going on in their minds. But we can still correctly say, while pointing at a corpse, Â“that person is dead.Â” 
Further, the (brain-)dead person of whom weÂ’ve been speaking is identical with some bodyÂ—not a body, like yours or mine, that mediates thoughts and feelings, but just a plain old body. 
HereÂ’s a rundown of the relevant facts: 
(1) 
Statements such as says Â“that person is (brain)deadÂ” are often true. 

(2) 
Such statements must be about people. Otherwise, it would be inappropriate to use the word Â“person.Â” When pointing at (brain)dead Smith, one would have to say Â“that non-person is dead.Â” 

(3) 
The (brain)dead Smiths of this world donÂ’t have psychological characteristics. Therefore, the right conclusion is: 

(4) 
A thing can be a person without having thoughts or any other psychological attributes. 


The argument just given, though accepted by many, involves a gross overestimation of what our linguistic practices can give us in the way of philosophical illumination.[418] 
ItÂ’s true that we refer to certain (brain)dead objects as Â“people.Â” But, it seems to me, that could well just be a verbal convention. We refer to scooters of a certain kind as Â“rascals.Â” But theyÂ’re not really rascals. (A rascal is a mischievous young person.) 
I also think that our tendency to describe (brain-)dead bodies as Â“peopleÂ” has emotional roots. At some level, we are holding onto the idea that, deep within that ravaged body, is a mind. In any case, the present author puts no stock in arguments such as (1)Â–(4). 
4.1 A better argument for the physicalistic view 
But there is a much better argument for the physicalistic conception of personal identity. A story will help us state this argument. 
Smith is a normal adult with a vigorous mind. One day heÂ’s hit by a bus. There is a complete cessation of all mental activity. SmithÂ’s stream of mental activity has been snipped. But SmithÂ’s body doesnÂ’t die. It goes into a vegetative coma for 20 years. During that time, there is no mental activity at all in what was once SmithÂ’s brain. The brain centers regulating automatic functions (e.g., respiration, digestion) work just fine, but the parts involved in mental activity are totally inactive. No thoughts, no dreams, no sensations. Nothing. After 20 years, the body wakes up, and the hitherto inactive brain centers spring back to life. The occupant of that body is obviously in complete command of his faculties. His personality traits are just like those of the pre-accident occupant of that same body, as are the values, the memories, the cognitive aptitudes, and so on. Let X be the person who occupied that body before the accident and let Y be the person whoÂ’s been occupying it since the accident. 
Is X the same person as Y? Is the post-coma person Smith? Or is it somebody who is psychologically a lot like Smith, but isnÂ’t actually him? 
Surely it really is Smith. ThatÂ’s what weÂ’d say, anyway. ItÂ’s very hard to believe that Y is a brand-new person (albeit one who has the psychological characteristics ordinarily had only by adults). 
This is a serious problem for the mentalistic view of personal identity. According to the mentalist, Smith is his mind. No mind, no Smith. Whatever his mind is exactly, it would make no sense to say Â“his mind is fineÂ—but thereÂ’s not so much as a flicker of mental activity going on in that head of his.Â” Thus, no thoughts, no mind. So if the mentalist is right Â“no thoughtsÂ” means Â“no mindÂ”; which means Â“no SmithÂ”; which means that the minute SmithÂ’s mental stream was cut off, Smith ceased to exist.[419] 

4.1.1 An unsuccessful mentalistic rejoinder 
Â“But so what?Â” a mentalist might ask: 
Â“Smith went out of existence 20 years ago. And he came back into existence a few days ago. The same happens to everyone every day. You go to sleep. During that time, except when youÂ’re dreaming, your mind is gone, and so, therefore, are you. You wake up, and your mind is back, and so, therefore, are you. People go away. They come back. WhatÂ’s the problem?Â” 
My response: Nothing that goes out of existence comes back into existence. Ever. No exceptions. Therefore, if you can survive interruptions of your mental existenceÂ—if you can awaken from a sleep, or a coma, during which there was no mental activity at all in your craniumÂ—then you are not a stream of mental activity. And if you are not such a stream, itÂ’s a little hard to see how you could be your mind. So if you can wake up from thought-free slumber, then you arenÂ’t your thoughts or, therefore, your mind; and since it was your body, and your body alone, that existed uninterruptedly during sleep-time, you must be your body. 
By way of anticipation, I myself reject one of the steps in this argument. Although I do think that one is oneÂ’s mind, I donÂ’t think that oneÂ’s mind is oneÂ’s thoughts. (I believe, for reasons to be discussed, that oneÂ’s mind is a structure that gives rise to thoughts but does not itself consist of them.) But right now, instead of saying why, in my view, this argument is objectionable, I want to make it clear why it is such a powerful argument. 
4.1.2 An unsuccessful mentalistic rejoinder (continued) 
What most people will disagree with in this argument is the assumption that nothing that goes out of existence comes back into existence. 
Â“But surely that isnÂ’t right,Â” it will be said. Â“What about reincarnation? Teleportation? CanÂ’t things take breaks from existence? CanÂ’t they, so to speak, go on holiday, and then come back later?Â” 
No. A story will make this clear. Using your laser gun, you vaporize some rock. So what was once a very sturdy, solid rock has now been dispersed into various atoms. But you manage, through some miracle of technology, to locate all of these atoms, scattered throughout space though they are, and then to reassemble them into a rock that is qualitatively just like the rock you vaporized. Question: is the new rock numerically identical with the one you vaporized? In other words, is it the very same rock? Or, instead, is it a distinct rock that is extremely similar to the old one? 
Answer: itÂ’s a distinct rock thatÂ’s very similar to the old one. They are, apart from their spatiotemporal properties, qualitatively but not numerically identical. 
Another, similar story will reinforce this conclusion. Rock R is vaporized Â—but not by a human or anything else that can act deliberately. The blind, uncaring hand of nature is what does the vaporizing. RÂ’s atoms are dispersed through the cosmos. But, by some extraordinary coincidence, they all reconvene a million years later and they attach themselves to one another, thereby forming a new rock. Let R* be this new rock. Of course, R* consists of exactly the same particles as R. Moreover, R*Â’s structure is exactly like RÂ’s. Finally, each of the atoms composing R* has exactly the same role within R*Â’s structure that it had within RÂ’s structure. So, setting aside their spatiotemporal differences, R and R* are qualitatively identical. But theyÂ’re not numerically identical. 
4.2 Continuity a sine qua non for diachronic identity 
Continuity is necessary for identity (i.e., for genidentity/diachronic identity). ItÂ’s only a slight exaggeration to say that it is identity. If, on the other side of the world, atoms were to collect and form a creature exactly like youÂ—same physical and psychological characteristicsÂ—it wouldnÂ’t be you. (YouÂ’re here. That other person is over there.) Should you predecease this doppelganger, he obviously wonÂ’t become you; he wonÂ’t take over your identity any more than he did when you were alive. ItÂ’s irrelevant that qualitatively heÂ’s just like you. He doesnÂ’t pick up where you left off. Supposing that you die at time t, pre-t you doesnÂ’t flow uninterruptedly into post-t him. 
LetÂ’s change the story a bit. Right now, thereÂ’s no doppelganger of you. You pass on (sadly). So, for a period, thereÂ’s no one in existence who has exactly your characteristics. But, by some extraordinary coincidence, various atoms come together and form a creature qualitatively just like you, who weÂ’ll call Â“new-you.Â” Is new-you you? No. Does it make any difference whether the atoms composing you are the ones composing new-you? No. Once youÂ’re gone, youÂ’re gone. 
4.3 Why the concept of teleportation is an incoherent one 
On Star Trek, people were routinely teleported. Any case of teleportation has three phases. Phase 1: the disintegration phase. The teleportation candidate is decomposed into small particles. Phase 2: the movement phase. Those particles are moved at or near the speed of light to another place. Phase 
3: the reintegration phase. At the new place, those particles are reassembled into a being that is qualitatively just like the one that, moments earlier, was disintegrated. So the Phase 3 entity is exactly similar to the Phase 1 entity. 
Is the Phase 3 entity numerically identical with the Phase 1 entity? No. Once Captain Kirk has been disintegrated, heÂ’s gone. What shows up on the Enterprise isnÂ’t him; it is, at most, a doppelganger. 
4.3.1 Structure-preserving continuity, as opposed to mere continuity, as the essence of identity 
My students often object to this. HereÂ’s their argument: Â“Teleporting Capt. Kirk involves transforming his energy into a new form, and then, at the target location, converting that same energy back into the old form.Â” 
I agree with the first part: Teleporting Capt. Kirk would indeed involve transforming his energy into a new form. But so would dropping a one million ton weight on him or dispersing his atoms across the cosmos. Â“Same energyÂ” doesnÂ’t mean Â“same object.Â” IÂ’ve been around for three-and-a-half decades. My energy has been around a lot longer than that. Thirty five years ago that energy came to be embodied in a structure that, through a series of piecemeal, continuous, and structure-preserving changes eventuated in the structure that is writing this sentence. 
The changes in question had to be Â“structure-preservingÂ” because, as weÂ’ll see in Sections 7.0Â–7.5, a continuous causal process that mediates drastic structural changes may not be enough for identity. The person currently typing this sentence arose, by a continuous series of changes, from a certain tadpole-like creature. But, structurally, IÂ’m sufficiently different from that tadpole that it would be a stretch to say that I used to be it. But IÂ’m structurally enough like the blobby infant in the picture that, given my causal connectedness to him, I can say that I used to be him. 
4.4 Once gone, always gone 
LetÂ’s map these points onto our points about teleportation. The Phase 2 atom-scatter has no meaningful structural resemblance to the Phase 3 human who, when these atoms are integrated, appears on the deck of the Enterprise. The degree of structural resemblance between me and the zygote that eventually turned into me is far greater than the structural resemblance between the Phase 2 atom-scatter and the Phase 3 Enterprise occupant. We thus have no choice but to say that Kirk was obliterated the moment his atoms were scattered. Whatever it is that Â“beams aboardÂ” isnÂ’t Kirk: it is, at best, a good imitation of him. 
4.5 The physicalistÂ’s high-card: the ice-man 
Of course, certain aspects of existence can be interrupted. You can temporarily shelve your career as a hockey player. But you cannot be shelved. Â“But what if IÂ’m frozen and kept in ice for a thousand years, and then thawed out and reanimated? Would that be me?Â” Yes, it would (or so I think). But what that means is that, when you were on ice, you were still in existence. If, instead of being frozen, you had been disintegrated and, a thousand years later, the atoms composing you were reassembled into a creature just like you, we would not say that you had come back; weÂ’d say that, although you were gone, somebody just like you popped into existence. 
So, returning to our ice-man story, if post-thaw you is identical with preÂ­thaw you, thatÂ’s because the years of frozen stillness didnÂ’t interrupt your existence. Â“But,Â” you protest, Â“my mind was frozen during that time. No dreams. No thoughts. Nothing (in the way of mental activity). So, clearly, my existence was interrupted.Â” 
Your mental life was interruptedÂ—but not your existence tout court. Â“But,Â” you respond, Â“you agreed that the post-thaw person is really meÂ—that the pre-thaw person and the post-thaw person are identical, just as the person typing this sentence is identical with the person who typed the sentence before it.Â” 
Yes, I do agree. Â“But that makes no sense, given the reasonable supposition that (i) I am my mind and given that (ii) my mental existence was severed.Â” YesÂ—it makes no sense given those two assumptions. (By way of anticipation, weÂ’ll find that (ii) is false.) 
But it does make sense given a different supposition, namely, that you are your body. Your body remained in existence during the freeze years. There was no interruption. To be sure, certain forms of activity were interrupted. Everything associated with mentation was on hold. But itÂ’s a datum that your body was aroundÂ—that, in fact, it was kept more intact during that period than most living organisms are kept for a period of more than a day. But, evidently, you were around. 
Bottom line: a sentient creature can survive interruptions of its mental existence, but not its physical existence. Interrupted existence is nonÂ­existence. So a sentient creature is identical with its body. 
That is the main argument on behalf of the physicalistic theory of personal identity. And itÂ’s a good one. To refute it, the mentalist would have to show either (a) that existence can be interrupted or (b) that cessation of mental activity isnÂ’t the same thing as cessation of mind. (a) is a non-starter; establishing it would be like trying to establish that squares could have five sides. But (b) is quite defensible. 
4.6 A defense of (b): the mentalist strikes back 
People have relatively stable personality traits and beliefs. Yesterday I believed that snow is white. I still believe it, and IÂ’ll believe it tomorrow. This holds of countless other beliefs of mine, as well as attitudes, aspirations, values, fears, etc. 
People change, of course. The deepest changes happen in oneÂ’s early years. But the change never entirely stops, even though it does become increasingly internal to established structures. 
Throughout all this change, however, there is a great deal of stability in oneÂ’s beliefs, attitudes, etc., and also in oneÂ’s basic personality architecture. And the change itself is, in its broader outlines, continuous. It doesnÂ’t typically happen in fits and starts; it is typically more evolutionary than revolutionary. Of course, there are revolutionsÂ—sudden epiphanies or transformations. But they are internal to a larger, continuous structure whose integrity they donÂ’t undermine. 
Where there is regularity, there is typically an underlying structure; and where there is irregularity, there is typically a lack of structure. A person who has a job tends to act in the same ways over and over. This is because his activities must be internal to a certain organizational framework. By the same token, a person who doesnÂ’t have a job doesnÂ’t have to behave in those ways. Other things being equal, a person without a job behaves more erratically than one who doesnÂ’t. 
In light of this, letÂ’s consider some humdrum facts about my psychology. When I woke up today, I believed that 1 + 1 = 2. When I went to sleep last night, I believed it. I obviously wasnÂ’t thinking 1+1 =2 the entire time I was asleep. (And even if, by some remote chance, I was, there are many other beliefs that I have that werenÂ’t coursing through my psyche during sleep. So just let my belief that 1 + 1 = 2 represent any one of those.) If that belief simply ceased to exist when, upon my falling asleep, it became inactive, it would be a miracle that, on waking up, I resumed having that belief. That would be a causal anomaly, a case of creation ex nihilo. That belief, therefore, must have its basis in some kind of structure that endures even when it isnÂ’t active. 
In fact, beliefs are structures. Beliefs must be distinguished from the use to which theyÂ’re put. At any given time, most of your beliefs are inactive. YouÂ’re not drawing on them, arguing for them, reconsidering them, or emoting about them. But during these lulls the beliefs themselves no more cease to exist than a sheriffÂ’s gun ceases to exist when heÂ’s not firing it. 
Beliefs are not happenings. They are not, as philosophers say, Â“occurrent.Â” A searing pain is occurrent. So is any sense-perception or act of thought, whether conscious or unconscious. But beliefs arenÂ’t processes. Nor are attitudes or intentions or aspirations. 
No individual belief changes. For a personÂ’s beliefs to change is for that person to shed some old beliefs or acquire new ones. I used to be convinced that Platonism is false; now IÂ’m convinced that itÂ’s true. But that change was a case of one beliefÂ’s being obliterated and replaced by a different one; it wasnÂ’t a change that was internal to the persistence of some one belief. Whenever a belief is Â“modified,Â” whatÂ’s going on is that itÂ’s being replaced with another, possibly related belief. The belief itself is a stable structure; it isn't an event; it isn't an occurrent phenomenon. What is such a phenomenon is the process by which a belief is jettisoned and replaced with another. 
The same is true of personality traits and of propositional attitudes. (A propositional attitude is an attitude towards a proposition: a desire that it will rain, an intention that one make a lot of money, a fear that one's plane will crash, etc.) What is occurrent isnÂ’t the intention itself; itÂ’s the process of acquiring it or of dumping it. 
OneÂ’s beliefs, attitudes, etc., are an important part of oneÂ’s mind. Since these things are structures, it immediately follows that there is much to oneÂ’s mind that isnÂ’t a process of any kind. What about the occurrent processes that are associated with mind? The pains, the pleasures, the sense-perceptions, the waves of doubt, the conscious acts of deliberation? These, it seems to me, are mental actions and are thus no more constitutive of your mind than a bodily action (e.g., oneÂ’s jumping over a fence) is constitutive of your body. 
OneÂ’s mind isnÂ’t oneÂ’s stream of mentation; it is the structure that mediates this mentation. We saw reason to believe this earlier. So the slogan Â“no thought, no mindÂ” is false. The right slogan is: Â“no thought-enabling structure, no mind.Â” 
This slogan suggests another one: Â“mind = thought-enabling structure (as opposed to stream of thought).Â” When one is in a deep sleep or even cryogenically frozen, the structures responsible for thought are inactive, but they donÂ’t cease to exist on that account. (An elevator that isnÂ’t being used still exists.) 
4.7 An objection 
LetÂ’s consider an objection to the argument just presented: 
But arenÂ’t those structures brain-structures? Ice-man survives his thousand-year ice coma only because those brain-structures remain intact. Those structures are obviously physical; theyÂ’re part of oneÂ’s body, like oneÂ’s heart or gallÂ­bladder. So your theory of personal identity (viz., oneÂ’s self is oneÂ’s mind and oneÂ’s mind consists of the structures underlying oneÂ’s thoughts) collapses into a physicalist, and therefore a non-mentalistic, analysis of personal identity. 
Mentalists usually hold that mental entities are physical entities. A mentalist who holds that thought-structures are brain-structures will hold that, when those brain-structures go, so will the corresponding person, the reason being that those brain-structures are identical with that personÂ’s mind. 
The physicalist, on the other hand, holds that, no matter what happens to the parts of brain mediating sentience, a given individual survives provided that his heart, lungs, gall-bladder, etc. are still working. His reason is that oneÂ’s self is oneÂ’s body and itÂ’s a fact that oneÂ’s body can remain alive, and certainly exist in some form or other, well after oneÂ’s mind is gone. 
The difference between physicalists and mentalists isnÂ’t that the former do, whereas the latter do not, believe the minds are brains (or brain-structures). The difference is that mentalists, unlike physicalists, believe the only parts of the mind to be directly responsible for personal identity are the parts that are identical with oneÂ’s mind. 
4.8 McMullin's position: things are more basic than events 
Ernan McMullin, a respected historian of science, read an earlier version of this chapter. His response, which I will quote verbatim, is penetrating: 
I read your discussion of Hume on personal identity. It seems right. But I have two questions. One is about your identification of "things" as "swarms of events", with a causal connection holding the events together. That seems to me a much more Humean conception than is warranted. For me, events happen to things: things are what undergird events. No things, no events! The reason that this issue seems crucial in your response to Hume is that you point out (correctly) that when someone is asleep, there is still a "stable mental structure" that persists, one that is not a "mental happening". Is that structure a swarm of events (happenings)? Is your point that these are not mental but physical (?) happenings? I would find your response to Hume more persuasive if the "stable" mental structure were taken to be a thing to which events occur. 
Dr. McMullen is making two distinct points: 
(i) 
things are more basic than events. Things happen to things. My contention that everything is either an event or a swarm of events is incoherent. 

(ii) 
my position that events are the ultimate constituents of the spatiotemporal world is inconsistent with belief that the mind consists of stable structures, as opposed to the fleeting will o' the wisps that populate consciousness. 


I sent a response to Dr. McMullin in which I responded to both questions and which, because it expresses my current views, I will quote verbatim: 
The brain-structures that give rise to fleeting mental occurrences, and that constitute the self, do consist of swarms of events; but those structures don't consist of mental events. Consider, for example, your ability to speak English. Presumably, that ability is constituted by some brain-structure. The neurons (or whatever) that, in their turn, constitute that structure are, in their turn, constituted by (I'm skipping some intermediate levels of description) minute displacements of mass-energy. Those displacements are not themselves mental, even though, ultimately, they're mind-constitutive. (No contradiction here: the atoms that compose cells are not themselves biological entities, even though those cells are such entities.) 
In connection with your question about mental structures, you make an important point that, if correct, undermines much of what I say but that, I will now try show, is not correct. (In what follows, IÂ’ll use the word Â“thingÂ” in the narrowest possible sense. So, as IÂ’ll be using it, rocks, apples, and trees are Â“things,Â” but neither non-spatiotemporal entities, e.g. possibilities, nor spatiotemporal but intangible entities, e.g. gravitational fields, qualify as Â“things.Â”) 
Just as you say, my position is that events are the ultimate constituents of the spatiotemporal world and, therefore, that: 
(i) Although there could be events in the absence of things, there couldn't be things in the absence of events. 
Your position is that things (substances), not events, are the ultimate constituents of the spatiotemporal world and, therefore, that: 
(ii) Although there could be things in the absence of events, there couldn't be events in the absence of events. 
The first question to ask is: what do you believe Â“thingsÂ” to 
be? There are three possibilities: 
(a) 
Things consist entirely of property-instances. Consider the rockÂ’s weight, shape, color, etc. There is nothing underlying those property instances; there are just the property instances. 

(b) 
Things are identical with entities---or, as theyÂ’re traditionally called, Â“substancesÂ”---that underlie property-instances but do not themselves consist of such instances. 

(c) 
Things consist partially of property-instances and partially of substances. 


For argumentÂ’s sake, letÂ’s suppose that either (b) or (c) is correct. In that case, underlying a given rockÂ’s shape, mass, color, position, etc., there is something that has no shape, mass, color, etc., i.e. there is something that, although it underlies properties, is itself featureless. A featureless thing is a surd. Nothing can have no properties. Thus, both (b) and (c) are false. 
So (a) must correct. But if (a) is right, then events are the most basic constituents of spatiotemporal world. HereÂ’s why. First of all, for an event to occur is for some property to either come to be instantiated or to cease to be instantiated. (In this context, Â“propertyÂ” is short for Â“property or multiplicity of properties.Â”) 
There would be no events if there were no changes, and there would be no changes if there were no cases of properties coming or ceasing to be instantiated. Further, there would be no passage of time if there were no events. To say that it's been a year since you've seen Smith is to say that certain periodic processes have happened a certain number of times since you last saw Smith. Thus, period during which absolutely nothing happens cannot possibly last for more than an instant. 
It follows that any case of a property-instance's existing for a non-null period of time is parasitic on cases of change and, therefore, on events. Since, as weÂ’ve established, Â“thingsÂ” are wholly constituted by property-instances, it follows that any case of a thingÂ’s enduring for more than instant is parasitic on the existence of change. 
The concept of a thing that exists for no more than an instant is incoherent. Things necessarily consist of property-instances, as weÂ’ve seen. So a thingÂ’s existing for a mere instant would involve there being some property P such that, within a time-interval of zero duration, P came to be and also ceased to be instantiated. Those events, involving as they do the very same property-instance, cannot possibly be simultaneous. So the sequence consisting of those two events would necessarily occupy a time-interval that was greater than an instant. Thus, there could not possibly be a thing that existed for just one instant. Since, as we saw a moment ago, any case of a thingÂ’s enduring for more than instant is parasitic on the existence of change, it follows that changes, or events, are the most fundamental and, ultimately, the only occupants of space-time. 
That said, our views may not be as far apart as they initially seem to be. The concept of substance is incoherent if it's taken to coincide with the concept of a featureless entity (albeit one that underlies property-instances). But there is another way to understand the concept of substance, relative to which that concept is coherent. Assuming the concept of substance to be a coherent one, substances are forces of a certain kind. They are those forces that bind events together in such a way that the resulting structure has prediction/explanation-enhancing properties characteristic of rocks, statues, and other paradigm-cases of so-called "things." 
But if substances are forces that bind events together into things, then substances are causal relations holding among events. So, assuming the concept of substance to be a coherent one, things are composed wholly of events. Which, taken in conjunction with some of the points made earlier, entails that events are the most fundamental constituents of the spatiotemporal world. 
In conclusion, there is no coherent defense of the position that events are not the most fundamental constituents of the spatiotemporal world or, consequently, of the view that any of the spatiotemporal worldÂ’s occupants are not either identical with events or composed of them. 
4.9 A Puzzle 
The following not only seems reasonable but positively de rigueur: 
(TF[420]) The idea of there being free-floating property-instances makes no sense. Property-instances must belong to things. Surely there canÂ’t be free-floating instances of shape or mass or color. For there to be an instance of the property of being spherical, for example, there must be some thing that has that property. That property is either instantiated by some thing, e.g. a bowling ball, or it isnÂ’t instantiated at all. 
But weÂ’ve just seen that the following view, which is incompatible with TF, must be correct: 
(PB)[421] 
Things consist solely of property instances. Â“SubstancesÂ” are either surds or theyÂ’re causal relations holding among property-instances. If theyÂ’re surds, they donÂ’t exist. If theyÂ’re causal relations of just-described kind, then everything that exists is either a property-instances or is wholly composed of property-instances. 
I don't know how to solve this problem, and I know of no one who has worked on it. But here's what I'd say if forced to hazard a guess, the operative word being "guess." Up to a point, TF is right. There canÂ’t be free-floating shapes or masses. Where there arenÂ’t things, there arenÂ’t shapes or masses. But, I would propose, the most basic property-instances, these being the ones out of which every occupant of space-time is constructed, are not instances of roundness or redness or of any of the other properties in terms of which we naturally understand the world. I propose the most fundamental building blocks of the constituents of space-time are instances of properties that, unlike instances of shape or mass, can coherently be thought of as free-floating. 
5.0 Degrees of identity 
ItÂ’s generally held that, for any object x and any object y, x and y are either identical or theyÂ’re not; they canÂ’t be identical to a certain degree. 
Is this correct? Remember that we distinguished between diachronic and synchronic identity-claims. Â“Barack Obama is the current U.S. PresidentÂ” is a synchronic identity claim, and Â“I [JMK in 2009] am identical with that blobby infant [in the photo from 1973]Â” is a diachronic identity claim. Where synchronic identity claims are concerned, there are indeed no degrees of identity. x and y are synchronically identical or they arenÂ’tÂ—thereÂ’s nothing intermediate between total synchronic identity and total synchronic distinctness. 
But diachronic identity is a different matter altogether. Diachronic identity not only can come in degrees, but must do so. Let Â“x = yÂ” be an arbitrary diachronic identity claim. So far as itÂ’s true, itÂ’s only if the following conditions are met. First, y is a causal successor of x. In other words, there is some sequence of events, such that each event in that sequence is caused to occur by its predecessor (if it has one) and causes its successor to occur (if it has one), and such that x and y are both installments in that sequence. But for Â“x = yÂ” to be true, it isnÂ’t enough that these conditions be met. If x is the particular gamete that, in due course, became me, and y is me, Â“x = yÂ” isnÂ’t true. 
But why not? Because x and y are too different. For "x=y" to be correct, it is necessary not only that y be xÂ’s successor in some causal sequence, but also that the relationship borne by xÂ’s condition with respect to yÂ’s condition be a predictively and explanatorily robust one. I am structurally so different from the gamete that eventuated in me, and the bridges that had to be crossed in order for that gamete to eventuate in anything at all like myself were so rickety, that the relationship borne by that gamete to my present self isnÂ’t that of young JMK to old JMK, but is more like that of ancestor to descendant. To be sure, a single entity can change a great deal. The caterpillar is structurally very different from the butterfly it becomes. But the predictive and explanatory relations borne by the caterpillar with respect to the butterfly are sufficiently tight enough that itÂ’s more fruitful to see the change in question as internal to the existence of some one thing than it is to see it as a case of one thingÂ’s being replaced by some distinct thing. 
Explanatoriness and predictiveness come in degrees. Since Â“x = yÂ” is true to the degree that x bears the relevant explanatory and predictive relations to y, thinghood is a matter of degree. ItÂ’s also a matter of context. In some explanatory contexts, it would be correct to say of some gamete that it is identical, in the diachronic sense, with some philosophy professor. These points are developed in Sections 7.0Â–7.5 of the present chapter, which is concerned with the conditions that two different states of affairs must satisfy if they are to both be constitutive of some one entity. 
5.0.1 Degrees of personal identity (continued) 
We tend to think that personal identity either holds or it doesnÂ’t. Â“I remember being little Timmy,Â” it will be said. Â“I remember playing kickball with my friends; I remember learning how to read; etc. If I remember being Timmy, then I am Timmy. It makes no sense to say that I might be 83% identical with so and so.Â” 
On the contrary, it makes plenty of sense. TrueÂ—you have various memories (of playing kickball, watching cartoons, waiting for the ice-cream truck to come to your block, etc.) But all that shows is that certain currently existing mental structures and events are derivatives of the mental structures and events associated with some body (literally, some body) that is related to the body you now occupy in the way that a caterpillarÂ’s body is related to that of the butterfly into which it metamorphoses. 
WeÂ’re dealing with relations of succession and causationÂ—nothing more. There isnÂ’t some mysterious inner flame, some underlying substance, that remains untouched throughout it all and that somehow underlies the fact that you and the little kickball player are identical. (Our tendency to believe otherwise is an expression of our need to condense vast, intricately structured constellations of events into homogenous units.[422]) Even if there is such an inner flame, it is inert except in so far as it facilitates the relevant psychological and physiological events. But so far as it does facilitate them, those events do all the workÂ—they are what Â“keep you going," so to speak. The inner-flame is a free wheel and thus drops out of the picture. Thus, so far as you are identical with the little kickball player of yesteryear, it is because you and he are connected to each other by a sequence of events whose earlier members provide information about, and provide the causal basis for, its later members. 
Â“If youÂ’re right,Â” it will be asked, Â“why are we so convinced that diachronic identity is absoluteÂ—that I either am, or am not, the little kickball player?Â” We are not so convinced. What does a person even mean when he says that he is the little tyke in the photo? Does he mean that there is some underlying, unphased soul-substance that inhabits that little tyke and also inhabits him? ItÂ’s hard to see how this could even possibly be what he means: since the terms Â“substance,Â” and therefore Â“soul-substance,Â” donÂ’t mean anything, so is the sentence that we are identical with Â“soul-substancesÂ”; so, in saying it, one cannot possibly mean anything (unless of course one is speaking in an ironic or otherwise non-literal fashion). So, when a person says that he is the little tyke in the photo, he must mean that there is some sort of connection between himself (i.e., his current self) and that little fellow; and that connection, obviously, is one that consists, at least in part, in his being the outcome of a series of changes the first of which was undergone by that little tyke. (As weÂ’ll soon see, those changes must satisfy certain conditions; otherwise, instead of constituting the little tykeÂ’s developing into an adult, theyÂ’ll constitute his ceasing to exist.) 
What, more specifically, is the nature of this connection? (To sidestep unnecessary complications, weÂ’ll assume that the little tyke in the picture is the person who is alleging that he is that little tyke.) There is obviously a causal dimension to it. That personÂ’s current self is the end-result of the series of changes first undergone by the little kickball player. 
But that connection cannot be of strictly causal nature: the relevant series of changes must form a coherent narrative. OneÂ’s adult self inevitably has many beliefs, intentions, and values that his four year old self did not have. Nonetheless, setting aside the terminal links in the sequence of episodes composing oneÂ’s life, each such link must have a certain continuity with its predecessors and its successors. What one is doing on Monday is the result of an intention one formed on Sunday; and, depending on whether oneÂ’s beliefs as to how fruitful oneÂ’s Monday-efforts were, what one is doing on Wednesday is either a continuation of those efforts, a modification of them, or an abandonment of the intention driving them. 
Thus, what unifies various different psychological states into a single person is that they are agentially unified. Each state must represent the initiation, execution, modification, or disintegration of some single endeavor. Selves are the product, not the basis, of intentions---and therefore of the desires, beliefs, and values underlying those intentions. Language misleadingly suggests that it is the other way around. Â“First there are people," it suggests to us. Â“Initially these people are empty vessels. But they come to be occupied by beliefs, values, and the like. An intention must belong to some existing person. There canÂ’t be orphan intentions.Â” 
The thinking underlying this argument involves a subtle but hideous fallacy. This fallacy resembles, and is actually an instance of, the fallacy embodied in the idea that space-time is an empty vessel that exists independently of the events that occupy it. 
5.0.2 An illustration of the principle being defended 
A brief detour through metaphysics may help loosen the resistances that people have to the analysis of selfhood that I wish to defend. (This detour will end at the beginning of Section 5.0.6. I say this so as to enable readers who donÂ’t need to make this detour to skip it.) It makes no sense to suppose that, although xÂ’s causal relation to y is qualitatively identical with zÂ’s causal relation to w, xÂ’s spatiotemporal relation to z differs from zÂ’s spatiotemporal relation to w. It makes no sense to say that, although x and y are causally related to each other in exactly the way in which z and w are causally related to each other, x is 100 feet from y, whereas z is 10 feet from w. For the distance between x and y to be 10 times greater than the distance between z and y is for the one pair to be causally interrelated in a way in which the other pair is not causally interrelated; it is for a causal signal emitted by x to take 10 times longer to reach y than it does for a causal signal emitted by z to reach w; it is, other things being equal, for radiation sent from x to y to compare unfavorably in intensity with the radiation sent from z to w. To say of one event that it bears spatiotemporal relation R with respect to some other event is to say that the former bears a certain causal relation to the latter; it is to make a claim as to the conditions that x must fulfill if it is to have a given effect on y. 
One can of course imagine two pairs of objects, one of which consists of objects that seem close to each other and the other of which consists of objects that seem remote from each other. And, with that image in oneÂ’s mind, one can stipulate that the members of the one pair are causally interrelated in the same way as the members of the other pair. But this argument undermines itself. In imagining that the members of the one pair appear closer to each other than do the members of the other pair, so far as oneÂ’s thinking is coherent, one is assuming that, other things being equal, the light-signals transmitted to oneÂ’s eyes by the objects that appear to be close to each other differ from those transmitted to oneÂ’s eyes by the objects that appear to be far from each other. And, so far as oneÂ’s thinking is coherent, one is therefore assuming that, other things being equal, the light traveling by way of oneÂ’s sensory surfaces between the objects that appear to be close to each other is different from the light traveling by way of oneÂ’s sensory surfaces from the light traveling between the objects that are remote from each other, in some way or other. Thus, one is assuming that, if one of the two objects that appear to be close to each other is to have a given effect on the other (viz. that of disturbing the latter by striking it with a light signal that first bounces off of oneÂ’s eyes), what it must do to have that effect differs from what one of the other two objects must do to have a comparable effect on its mate. 
It follows that the causal structure of the world is more basic than its spatiotemporal structure. If it assumed that xÂ’s causal relations to y are identical with wÂ’s causal relations to z, it makes no sense to say that xÂ’s distance from y is different from wÂ’s distance from z. We can change the causal relations without changing the distance between them (e.g., we can give x a positive electric charge without bringing it any closer to y); but we cannot change the distances between x and y without changing the causal relations between them. 
This entails that spatial relations (and, for exactly similar reasons, temporal relations) are derivatives of causal relations. A brief discussion of the concept of supervenience may help. Two people who are microphysically identical cannot possibly be biologically different. (Two biologically identical people wonÂ’t cease to be biologically identical if there is some isolated microphysical change in the one personÂ’s body that has no counterpart in the other personÂ’s body.) But two people who are biologically different must be microphysically different. (If the one person has a heart-attack and the other does not, all manner of microphysical changes occur in the one personÂ’s body that donÂ’t occur in the other.) Thus, the biological, though different from the microphysical, is Â“fixedÂ” by it; to use the contemporary jargon, the biological Â“supervenesÂ” on the microphysical. Given that the biological cannot vary without the microphysical varying, but that the microphysical can vary without the biological varying, it follows that there is some very important sense in which the microphysical is more basic than the biological. 
Just as the biological cannot be changed without changing the microphysical, so spatiotemporal relations cannot be changed without changing causal relations. And just as the microphysical can be changed without changing the biological, so the causal relations can be changed without changing spatiotemporal relations. Thus, just as biological supervenes on the microphysical, so spatiotemporal relations supervene on causal relations. 

5.0.3 An illustration of this principle (continued) 
There is a clock resting on top of body x. Bodies y and z are far from x and also from each other. We will leave it open for now whether the distance between x and z coincides with either the distance between x and y or between y and z. Apart from containing x, y, and z, the region of space containing those three objects is a hard vacuum (i.e. itÂ’s perfectly empty). So there is nothing other than the distances involved to explain why a given light beam would take longer to travel from one of those objects to one of the other two. At time t, x simultaneously emits two light beams. The clock on top of x duly notes this fact. The one light beam heads towards y, and the other heads towards z. The clockÂ’s way of measuring time is to bounce a light-beam in between mirrors at opposite ends of its interior. (Every time one of the mirrors is struck, the structure of the mirror is altered just enough to leave a trace, so that itÂ’s possible to count the number of hits that occur during a given interval, but not enough to have a non-negligible effect on the reflective properties of the mirrors.) After striking y and z, respectively, the light beams emitted by x return to x. But those light beams donÂ’t return at the same time. During the interval between t and the time of the return of the y-bound light-beam, the light beam inside the clock has made ten billion round-trips. During the interval between t and the time of the return of the z-bound light-beam, the light beam inside the clock has made a hundred billion round-trips. 
Obviously x is closer to y than it is to z. But the fact that the clock-internal light-beam made more round-trips during the one light beamÂ’s journey than it did during the other is not a consequence of the fact that x is closer to y than it is to z. ItÂ’s what it is for x to be closer to y than it is to z. 
5.0.4 Some qualifications 
Of course, there are different ways of measuring distances. Light rays, and causal signals generally, neednÂ’t be used, and are hard to use, where small distances are concerned. One doesnÂ’t use light-waves, or even sound waves, to measure the length of a swimming pool. Instead, one uses a measuring tape, or one counts the number of times that a rod laid end-wise fits into a distance parallel to that of the side of the pool. 
But this only reaffirms our point. Supposing that D1 and D2 are the endÂ­points of the side of one pool, and that D3 and D4 are the end-points of some other, it is by performing operations that relate the causal properties of the 
one poolÂ’s end points to the otherÂ’s that one determines the relative distances between those two pairs of end-points. In connecting D1 and D2 with, say, a measuring tape, one is ipso facto transmitting a causal signal from D1 to D2, and the same is true if one uses a meter-rod instead. The distance between D1 
and D2 is greater than that between D3 and D4 if, other things being equal, the relevant meter-rod must be moved more times in the first case than in the second----or, supposing that measuring-tape is being used----if, other things being equal, the one measuring-tape exceeds the other in respect of how great the post-measurement distance is between its two end-points. 
A given magnitude (e.g., a given distance) can typically be measured by means of different causal mechanisms. (A given distance can be measured using light-rays, meter-rods, measuring-tapes, etc.) Some might take this to show that distances are not causal relations. This is precisely the conclusion not to draw. The conclusion to draw is that distances are abstract causal relations. More precisely, they are commonalities holding among causal relations. 
5.0.5 These points in relation to the measurement of time 
Everything just said about the measurement of distance holds mutatis mutandis with respect to the measurement of time. For one instant in time to precede another by a greater amount than it precedes some third interval is for there to be causal differences between those intervals; it is for there to occur more periodic processes during the one interval than during the other. It is to be noted that a periodic process (light bouncing between two mirrors, an atom rotating, a measuring tape being stretched to connect two points in space, a yard-stick being moved from one place to another) is a causal process. So the idea of a space-time that is bereft of events is absurd, since space-time relations are higher-order causal relations; i.e. they are commonalities holding among causal relations holding among states of affairs. 
5.0.6 The bearing of the points just made on the nature of diachronic personal identity 
Exact analogues of these points hold with respect to personal identity. The idea of a vacant-mind---one devoid not only of specific mental occurrences, but also of the enduring psychological structures that give rise to such occurrences---is absurd. 
Further, supposing per impossibile that such a nullity could exist, it would have no effect on oneÂ’s psychobiography. Given two minds, each initially an empty vessel, any difference in the mental lives of the owners (so to speak) of those minds is a function solely of what happens in them---of what events occur in them and of what structures come to constitute them. This shows that what we call minds are much like spaces. We tend to think of a vessel that happens to be occupied but needn't be. But that's not the right view. An event-free space is a surd. To the extent that it even makes sense to say that such a thing as space exists, it must be identified with the totality of spatial relations holding among events. Put incoherently but graphically, what happens Â“inÂ” space constitutes space. Put less incoherently, but no less graphically, space is no more independent of the events that we (misguidedly) describe as being Â“inÂ” it than a table is independent of the molecules that compose it. 
Space is distinct from events only in the sense that that the structure of space is determined by the interrelations holding among events, and not by the specific identities of those events. The same thing mutatis mutandis holds of tables. That is why, if M is one of the molecules composing a given table, replacing M with some other molecule that occupies the same relative position as M wonÂ’t destroy the table. It is only in the way in which tables are distinct from the molecules that compose them that they are distinct from the thoughts, and thought-generating structures, that stock them. 
5.1 The limits of LeibnizÂ’s Law 
ThereÂ’s no doubt that LeibnizÂ’s Law correctly models the logic of synchronic uses of expressions such as Â“identical with." Given that Barack Obama is identical with the Commander-in-Chief, LeibnizÂ’s Law correctly warrants the inference that the Commander-in-Chief has a given property iff Barack Obama has that property. 
The orthodox position is to say that LeibnizÂ’s law also governs the diachronic use of such expressions. But this is most doubtful. Right now IÂ’m a professor. The blobby infant in the picture IÂ’m now holding is not a professor. So I have a property that it does not have. Therefore, by LeibnizÂ’s Law, I am not it. 
5.1.1 Time-indexing 
Nonetheless, identity-theorists typically say that the blobby infant and I do have the same properties. To make this idea work, they bring in the highly artificial notion of a Â“time-indexedÂ” property. I have the property of being-aÂ­philosophy-professor-in-2009, and so does the blobby infant. The blobby infant has the property of being-preverbal-in-1973 and so do I.[423] 
Therefore, the fact that, unlike my six month old self, I am not now a blobby infant, being instead a non-blobby professor, does not make me different from my six month old self. Given any other property that I now have that I used to lack, or vice versa, a similar argument shows that I have always had that property. For this reason, it is said, LeibnizÂ’s Law does govern diachronic uses of expressions like Â“identity,Â” Â“isÂ” (in the non-predicative sense), and so on. 
5.1.2 Time-indexing not a source of insight into questions concerning identity 
In addition to being obviously contrived, this view has the absurd consequence that nothing changes. Whatever properties I have now, IÂ’ve always had them and always will have them. In general, nothing acquires properties and, consequently, nothing ever loses a property. (Any case of property-acquisition is a case of property-loss. When a person acquires the property of being able to tie his shoes, he loses the property of being incapable of tying his shoes.) So if nothing ever acquires properties, nothing changes. Given that there is change, the no-change must be false. 
5.1.3 Four-dimensionalism 
To move forward, we must say a word about the debate that rages between those who accept a doctrine known as Â“four-dimensionalismÂ” (henceforth, Â“4-DÂ”) and those who reject that doctrine. According to 4-D, any given object is identical with a Â“space-time worm.Â” A space-time worm is an entity that is spread out in both space and time. Thus, according to 4-D, you are identical with a space-time worm that comprises all of the events and states of affairs constituting you from the moment of your birth (or conception) till the moment of your demise. 
Bearing this in mind, let t be any instant in time during your lifetime. If 4Â­D is right, some segment of you exists at t; but you do not exist at t, since you, according to 4-D, are spread out over a period of (say) 80 years. So if 4Â­D is right, I cannot see you or shake hands with you; I can see and shake hands only some segment of you. The thing I shake hands with, says the advocate of 4-D, is some time-slice of you.[424] 

In my view, I can shake hands with people, and also see them, play tennis with them, and otherwise interact with them. I thus reject 4-D. 
5.1.3.1 Four-dimensionalism (continued) 
Things change. 4-D denies this. If 4-D is right, the thing that is reading this sentence right now isnÂ’t you; itÂ’s just some time-slice of you. And the slightly different thing that was reading the first sentence of this chapter isnÂ’t you either; itÂ’s just another time-slice of you. The same is true of the thing that decided to buy this book a few weeks ago. According to 4-D, although the thing reading this sentence is different in some ways from the thing that was reading the first sentence of this chapter, those differences arenÂ’t expressions of the fact that some one thing has changed. According to 4-D, you donÂ’t change. For a given object to change is for the way that object is at one time to be different from the way it is at some other time. According to 4Â­D, for any time t, what exists at t isnÂ’t an object, and is only some Â“time-sliceÂ” of an object. Therefore, there are no two moments of time t and t* such that how some one object is at t is different from how that same object is at t*. Therefore, if 4-D is right, things donÂ’t change. 
But this is absurd. Things change. I have changed, and so have you. And each of us will continue to change. 4-D is either dead wrong or it amounts to nothing more than a proposal that we use the words Â“thingÂ” and Â“changeÂ” in non-standard ways. And even if by some remote chance it turns out that things donÂ’t change, it would be bad methodology to make our theory of personal identity depend on that turning out to be the case. In doing so, weÂ’d be assuming facts (or non-facts, rather) that arenÂ’t yet in evidence. 
Assuming, as we probably must, that things change, the only way to go is to say that identity, in the diachronic sense, is to be understood in terms of relations of causal connectednessÂ—that statements like Â“Bill is the guy in the photo who is wearing a rugby shirtÂ” are to be analyzed in the way described earlier. Since the relevant sort of connectedness obviously comes in degrees, so does identity. 
It should be pointed out that David Hume (1711Â–1776), whose views weÂ’ll discuss in Section 6.0, takes a similar view, and so does Derek Parfit (1942-). 
[425] 

5.1.4 One possible source of the confusion underlying acceptance of four-dimensionalism 
It should also be pointed out that those who accept 4-D very much seem to be reading metaphysics off of sentential surface structure. The expressions we use to denote the relation of diachronic identity are homonyms of the expressions we use to denote the relation of synchronic identity. Given only that fact, along with some obscure and ambiguous intuitions about selfhood, 4-dimensionalists infer that synchronic identity is diachronic identity. That inference is completely spurious; and itÂ’s one that no self-respecting analytic philosopher would make, given that the essence of analytic philosophy is a stubborn refusal to take surface structure to be a foolproof guide to truth. 
5.2 An identity-related paradox and the need for a diachronic conception of identity 
A story will make it clear that that 4-D is simply too revisionist to take seriously. At time t, person X1 splits, like an amoeba, into two people, X2 and X3. X2 is just like X1Â—in any case, X2 resembles X1 as much as you, in your current condition, resemble the person you were a minute ago. And X3 resembles X1 to the same degree. Further, the causal connection that X1 bears to X2 is qualitatively identical with the causal connection that X1 bears to X3. 
ItÂ’s obvious that X2. X3. After all, theyÂ’re in different places. And it would obviously be arbitrary to say that X2, but not X3, was X1. Whatever claim X2 can make to being X1, X3 can make precisely the same claim. David LewisÂ’ solution is to say that X2 and X3 have been there all along: as soon as X1 came into existence, so did X2 and X3. There were three people rolled into one body and one mind. 
LewisÂ’ position is absurd. Before he split into two, X1 was no more a compendium of different people than you are. There is no relevant psychological or physiological difference between X1 before the split, and anyone else. If X1 had died before the split, not even a shadow of a case could be made that Â“heÂ” was really a Â“theyÂ”Â—that he was really three people. So, supposing that X1 does live and, in due course, splits into X2 and X3, his undergoing that split retroactively puts two extra people in X1Â’s body. So LewisÂ’ solution goes through only if there is retroactive causation. 
That is bad enough, but it gets worse. Even though, if LewisÂ’ solution is to go through, there must be retroactive causation, that causation must fail to make any psychological or physiological difference to X1 or, for that matter, 
to the state of the universe before X1Â’s split. But to be a cause is to create change. So LewisÂ’s position collapses into the absurdity that there are causes that arenÂ’t causes. 
5.2.1 An identity-related paradox and the need for a diachronic conception of identity (continued) 
ItÂ’s obvious that Lewis is jumping through hoops. HeÂ’s working with a broken concept and is trying to cover up the cracks in it by mutilating wholesome and intact concepts. But LewisÂ’ position is de rigueur if one holds that the sense in which adult-JMK is Â“identicalÂ” with baby-JMK is identical with the sense in which 2 is identical with 1 + 1. WeÂ’ve already seen why. X2 is no less Â“identical withÂ” X1 than is X3. And X2 is no less identical with X1 than you are identical with the person you were a minute ago. Therefore, if we say that you are Â“identicalÂ” with that person in the same sense in which 2 is identical with 1 + 1, we must say that both X2 and X3 are identical with X1 in the very same sense. Since itÂ’s a datum that X2 and X3, being in different places, are distinct from each other, it follows that, just as Lewis says, the mind and body had by X1, prior to the split, were shared by X2 and X3. It follows, in other words, that X1, X2, and X3 were there all along, all rolled into one package. 
Given how preposterous that is, itÂ’s clear what we must say. X2 is Â“identicalÂ” with X1 in the sense that it is X1Â’s successor; the same is true of X3. And the same thing mutatis mutandis is therefore true of you. You are identical with your teen self in the sense that you are that entityÂ’s successor. 
TrueÂ—the expressions we use (Â“identity,Â” Â“identical with,Â” etc.) to describe the relationship between Barack Obama and the current President, or between 2 and 1 + 1 are the same ones we use to describe your relationship to your teen self. But so what? Language is mirror of thought; thought isnÂ’t always perfect. Thought is especially prone to error when it comes to emotion-laden issues, such as personal identity. Human beings donÂ’t want to believe that they are event-sequences that can become frayed, like an old rope, and dwindle into nothingness. Human beings donÂ’t want to believe that their identities are internal to emotion-driven narratives. But what we want to believe is irrelevant. What is relevant is that, if we take the conventional view, then we must follow Lewis in embracing the absurdity that you could be 80 different people, even though you are physiologically and psychologically just like somebody who is but one person. 
6.0 Personal identity revisited: HumeÂ’s analysis 
Few have done as much to clarify the structure of the psyche and nature of personal identity as David Hume (1711Â–1776). Hume had a mentalistic conception of personal identity. In his view, there are no people where there are no minds. But, unlike us, he held that there are no minds where there are no occurrent thoughtsÂ—where, in other words, there is no mental activity. 
Why does Hume hold this? Because Hume is a mentalist who doesnÂ’t believe in the existence of structures of any kind. Hume acknowledges that there are events; but he denies that there is anything underneath those events that guide them. There are no forces, no structures, no powers. (See Chapter 17.) And this is why, being a mentalist, he must identify the self with a stream of mental events. 
There is an obvious objection to this view: Â“If Hume is right, then the person who wakes up in the morning isn't identical with the person who went to sleep at night.Â” Hume is aware of this objection, and his response to it is very profound. He says that diachronic identity is pseudo-identity. The concept expressed by the occurrence of Â“is identical withÂ” in Â“JMK is identical with the blobby infant in the photoÂ” simply isnÂ’t the same concept as the one expressed by its counterpart in Â“Barack Obama is identical with the current U.S. President.Â” Taking it for granted that synchronic identity is a genuine form of identity, he infers, very reasonably, that diachronic identity is pseudo-identity. 
6.1 A preliminary point: HumeÂ’s empiricism 
Empiricism is the doctrine that everything that is known is known through sense-perception.[426] 
So far as empiricists grant that anything can be known that isnÂ’t directly observed, they hold that it is inferred from what is directly observed provided that the inference-rules involved are themselves known from direct observation alone. 
No sooner is empiricism defined than its coherence is called into question. An inference-rule is a normative truth. It tells you what you ought to infer from a given premise. But so far as it apprises you of anything, observation apprises you of what is, not of what ought to be. 
Unlike other self-described empiricists, Hume didnÂ’t help himself to any rules of inference whose legitimacy doesnÂ’t have a strictly perceptual basis. This was because, unlike his empiricist brethren, he had the acuity to see that many inference-rules that seem to be empiricism-friendly ones are not. HumeÂ’s empiricism was doubly strict. First, he had extremely conservative views as to which rules of inference had the requisite perceptual basis. Second, he had extremely conservative views about what sense-perception directly tells us.[427] 
What Hume says about personal identity must be understood in terms of the fact that he is a very strict empiricist. 
6.1.2 HumeÂ’s first argument 
Hume gives two arguments for his contention that selves are composed of the mental contents that occupy them. Here is the first: 
For my part, when I enter most intimately into what I call myself, I always stumble on some particular perception or other, of heat or cold, light or shade, love or hatred, pain or pleasure. I can never catch myself at any time without a perception, and never can observe anything but the perception. 
[428] 

There are two ways to interpret this. On the one hand, Hume could be saying that selves donÂ’t exist. On the other, he could be saying that selves are constituted by the thoughts, feelings, etc., that we describe them as Â“having.Â” 
The right interpretation is the second one. Notice how frequently the word Â“IÂ” occurs in his argument. He obviously believes that, when he uses that word, he's referring to himself and thus to his self. And surely he's right about this. It seems a truism that, if they refer to anything, tokens of "I" refer to selves; and it also seems a truism that tokens of "I" do refer. Also, in other parts of the Treatise, Hume talks at length about the relation that two different mental contents must bear to each other to belong to the same mind or self. Thus, HumeÂ’s position is that, although selves do exist, they are no more distinct from the mental events that occupy them than a swarm of wasps exists independently of the wasps that compose it. For an event to occupy a mind is for it to constitute it. 
The just-quoted argument, it will be noticed, is empirical. Hume is arguing on observational, as opposed to strictly logical or conceptual, grounds that there isnÂ’t anything that underlies his various thoughts. When he looks inward, he finds thoughts and nothing else; in particular, he doesnÂ’t find a non-thought that Â“supportsÂ” these various thoughts. This fact is important, as weÂ’ll now see. 
6.1.3 Problems with HumeÂ’s argument 
Given only that we canÂ’t observe something, it doesnÂ’t follow that it doesnÂ’t exist. There are many unobservable entities (e.g., electrons). If Freud (1915) is right, there are unobservable (unintrospectible) mental entities (e.g., unconscious urges). Saying that selves donÂ’t exist since we canÂ’t introspect them is like saying that electrons donÂ’t exist since we canÂ’t see them. 
A related possibility that Hume is ignoring is that minds are structures of the kind described earlier. (This oversight is probably deliberate, as weÂ’ll see in a moment.) HeÂ’s also ignoring the correlative possibility that specific mental occurrences (e.g., images, tickles) are products of minds, and are not themselves constitutive of them. 
In ignoring these possibilities, Hume is stacking the deck in his favor. We are pretheoretically inclined to see minds as being to specific tickles, itches etc., what car factories are to cars. In other words, weÂ’re inclined to see minds as being the things that give rise to specific mental contents, and weÂ’re therefore inclined to see minds as not being constituted by those contents. (In this context, by Â“specific mental content, I mean occurrent mental content--Â­e.g., a mental event, as opposed to an enduring mental structure.) 
In any case, weÂ’re pretheoretically much more inclined to see minds in this way than we are to see them in HumeÂ’s way, viz., as sequences of mental occurrences, none of which has any moorings in any structure and each of which, therefore, just happens. And in simply dismissing that possibility out of hand, Hume is question-beggingly assuming the falsehood of what is probably the most plausible rival to his own view. 
In any case, supposing, as Hume does, that such structures arenÂ’t known through introspection, it isnÂ’t necessary to conclude that they donÂ’t exist; for it would be equally reasonable, if not considerably more reasonable, to conclude that introspection is a limited medium. 
6.1.4 Why does Hume deny that there are mental structures? 
Hume is a hardcore empiricist. You know it only if you (i) observe it or 
(ii) observe direct evidence for it. (x is Â“directÂ” evidence of y if, given no inference rules whose legitimacy cannot be established strictly on the basis of observation, yÂ’s existence can be inferred from xÂ’s.) Hume believes that mental structures cannot be known in either of these two ways. (HeÂ’s right.) So they donÂ’t exist as far as heÂ’s concerned. 
Hume doesnÂ’t believe in structures of any kind. A structure is something that underlies events and guides them. Hume doesnÂ’t believe that anything guides anything. He doesnÂ’t believe that anything makes anything happen or otherwise influences anything. In his view, words like Â“force,Â” Â“power,Â” Â“coercion,Â” Â“guide,Â” and Â“regulateÂ” are meaningless. He holds this because, so he believes, forces cannot be observed and neither can direct evidence of them. (HumeÂ’s views on causality are the subject of Chapters 15 and 16.) 
Thus, HumeÂ’s empiricism blocks him from granting the existence of mental structures, given that such structures canÂ’t be known (para)perceptually. Second, given HumeÂ’s very reasonable view that one canÂ’t observe forces or any direct evidence of them, his empiricism prohibits him from granting the existence of structures of any kind. Thus, HumeÂ’s empiricism makes it doubly impossible for him to grant that there is anything to oneÂ’s mind other than fleeting, conscious events. (In Chapter 15, we saw that, contrary to what Hume holds, forces can be directly observed---that, in fact, everything one observes is a force and, moreover, is observed as a force.) 
6.1.5 Problems with HumeÂ’s argument (continued) 
In an attempt to show that there isnÂ’t anything to oneÂ’s mind other than the various specific mental occurrences that it houses, Hume says that, when he looks inward, he doesnÂ’t find an inner flame; all he finds, he says, are specific images, tickles, etc. 
But unless this inner flame is itself a fleeting mental occurrenceÂ—unless itÂ’s the sort of thing that can be disclosed to one in the form of an introspectible image or sensationÂ—nothing significant follows from the fact that, when he introspects, he doesnÂ’t find this inner flame. So for HumeÂ’s argument to go through, it must be assumed that the self, if existent, is to be known to one in the same way as tickles and itches. It must be assumed, in other words, that the self is a fleeting conscious occurrence. But thatÂ’s the very thing Hume is trying to show; and, were Hume to assume it, his argument would be viciously circular. 
6.1.6 The problems with HumeÂ’s argument are reflections of his hardline empiricism 
It is through images that our perceptual modalities (sight, touch, etc.) tell us about the world. (Not all images are visual; there are acoustical images, tactile images, etc.) Your seeing a tree consists in your having an image of that tree; your feeling the tree with your hand consists in your having a tactile image of that tree; and so on. ThereÂ’s no perception where thereÂ’s no image. It follows that, if introspection is an inwardly directed perceptual modality, it tells one nothing when it isnÂ’t giving one an image. 
Hume says that, when he looks inward, he encounters various Â“perceptionsÂ” (images), but no self. On this basis, he says that there is no self. But the right conclusion is that, if there is a self, it isnÂ’t disclosed to one in the form of an image. 
Supposing that it exists, there are, ultimately, two possibilities as to what the self is: 
(i) it could be oneÂ’s center of awareness; 
or 
(ii) it could be some structure underlying the events in oneÂ’s mind and guiding them. 
(i) and (ii) are not mutually exclusive. So a self could be a person's center of awareness that is also a structure underlying and regulating that person's mental activity. 
Given that either (i) or (ii) describes what the self, supposing it to exist, must be, it follows that the self cannot be known in a way that can be modeled on sense-perception, and there is thus no merit to HumeÂ’s paraperceptual demonstration of the non-existence of the self. 
It is uncontroversial that we are directly, non-inferentially aware of many mental entities that we donÂ’t know of in some image-mediated, perception-like way. I know I believe that 1 + 1 = 2. ItÂ’s obviously not through inference that I know thisÂ—I know it directly. And it obviously isnÂ’t through sense-perception that I know it. Finally, it isnÂ’t by virtue of my experiencing, or being aware of, some mental image that I know it. But surely I know it. So I know it directly. ItÂ’s a pretheoretic datumÂ—not the result of an intellectual working over of raw data. NoÂ—it is one of the raw data. 
The same is true of many other mental contents of mine. I know that I intend to write about causation later today. It obviously isnÂ’t through inference that I know thisÂ—it isnÂ’t because I psychoanalyzed myself or engaged in any other such artifices. And it obviously isnÂ’t through sense perception (sight, hearing, etc.) that I know it. Nor is it through the inwardly directed paraperceptual modality that Hume describes. But I know it. I know it in the same way that I know that 1 + 1 = 2, that I regret not calling my mother on her birthday, that I plan on improving my skills as a pianist, etc. 
I know these things through some faculty that gives me direct, non-inferential knowledge of at least some facts about my own mind. Were Hume to deny the existence of this faculty, heÂ’d be butchering obvious facts to make his argument go through and his position would be a most unempirical one. It is thus an empirical fact that not every fact about oneÂ’s mind that one is non-inferentially aware of is disclosed to one in the form of an image; and itÂ’s thus an empirical fact that not all knowledge is arrived at through perception or through anything at all like it. It is thus an empirical fact that empiricism is wrong! 
6.2 HumeÂ’s second argument: a preliminary point 
HumeÂ’s first argument is presented as an empirical argument. He says that his observations yield no evidence that there is some central fire around which his various thoughts orbit. His wording, and the wording that it is natural to use when paraphrasing his argument, suggests that Hume is trying to establish the non-existence of the self on grounds comparable to those on which an astronomer would try to establish the non-existence of a certain planet. Â“If I had evidence, IÂ’d believe. But I donÂ’t, so I donÂ’t.Â” 
But so far as self-observation yields any relevant evidence that evidence seems to suggest that there does exist within oneself a center of awareness. When I self-observe, I do feel that there is a core-being around which everything else orbits. 
This feeling of mine is by no means probative. I donÂ’t know that itÂ’s accurate. I don't know that itÂ’s a correct observation. In fact, I donÂ’t know that itÂ’s an observation at all. It may be that, in having this feeling, IÂ’m experiencing as an empirical datum what is in fact a projection into the observational arena of my acceptance of an erroneous, theory-driven interpretation of the relevant data. In fact, this is Hume's position. Hume explicitly says that those who, like myself, claim to be aware of an inner flame are either lying or theyÂ’re in the grips of some preexisting, empirically unfounded theory of what the self must be. 
The problem is that, even if, as Hume claims, my feeling that thereÂ’s an inner flame is an illusion powered by a very wrong theory, itÂ’s a datum that this feeling exists. And it isnÂ’t a datum, though it may be a truth, that this feeling is an illusion. So, even though HumeÂ’s opponent may be wrong, itÂ’s Hume, not his opponent, whoÂ’s making the theoretical point. This suggests that he has some theory in mind, his acceptance of which, and not some body of observations, led him to accept the Â“no inner flameÂ” view. 
6.2.1 HumeÂ’s second argument (verbatim) 
And, in fact, Hume does have just such a theory (I quote): 
When my perceptions are removÂ’d for any time, as by sound sleep; so long am I insensible of myself, and may truly be said not to exist. And were all my perceptions removÂ’d by death, and couÂ’d I neither think, nor feel, nor see, nor love, nor hate after the dissolution of my body, I should be entirely annihilated, nor do I conceive what is farther requisite to make me a perfect non-entity.[429] 

This argument, unlike the first, isnÂ’t empirical at all. This time, Hume is trying to show on purely conceptual grounds that there is nothing underlying the various events occupying a personÂ’s mind. HeÂ’s arguing that the very idea of such a thing is an incoherent one, like that of a square circle. Why is this idea incoherent? Because, says Hume, it has the absurd consequence that there could be thought-free minds. 
6.2.2 Evaluating this argument: HumeÂ’s failure to distinguish between two very different meanings of the word Â“thoughtÂ” 
Hume is right that if there is some inner flame underlying oneÂ’s thoughts, and therefore distinct from them, it does follow that oneÂ’s self could exist in a thought-free condition. But Hume is wrong to say that a thought-free self is an absurdity. The reason Hume thinks it absurd is that he fails to distinguish two very different meanings of the word Â“thought.Â” 
Sometimes the word Â“thoughtÂ” refers to mental occurrencesÂ—to what are now known as occurrent mental phenomena. An occurrent mental phenomenon is anything mental that happens. Sense-perceptions are occurrent mental phenomena; and so are acts of ratiocination and emotional epiphanies. (This list is far from complete.) 
But sometimes the word Â“thoughtÂ” refers to the relatively stable structures that underlie mental occurrences. Â“For the first twenty years of my academic career,Â” a philosopher once said to me, Â“I thought that Platonism was false.Â” This person was describing a stable, structural constituent of his mind, not a mental happening.
