If, by Â“thoughtÂ” Hume means Â“mental happeningÂ” then, contrary to what he alleges, thereÂ’s nothing incoherent in the idea of a mind that, during some period, isnÂ’t populated by thoughts. 
If by Â“thoughtÂ” Hume means Â“stable mental structureÂ” then Hume is right to say that there couldnÂ’t be thought-free minds. Earlier, we saw why this is so. If selves were distinct from their thoughts, there could be thought-free minds. So, given that there cannot be thought-free minds, selves are constituted by the thoughts that belong to them. 
So, after a fashion, Hume is right. Just as he says, there is nothing to oneÂ’s self other than the thoughts one has. But this claim of his isnÂ’t right in the way he thought it was. He thought that oneÂ’s self consists of the thoughts (i.e., fleeting mental occurrences) that occupy it, and not of the thoughts (i.e., stable structures that create and regulate such occurrences). WeÂ’ve already discussed why Hume didnÂ’t even grant the existence of stable mental structures or, indeed, of structures of any kind. 
7.0 Objectual identity revisited: Which causal sequences are thing-constitutive? 
Earlier in this chapter, we saw that every objectÂ—every rock, tree, and vaseÂ—is a causal sequence. But not every causal sequence constitutes some one object. Some constitute more than one. Others constitute none. 
HereÂ’s an example of one that constitutes no objects. Suppose that billiard ball #1 strikes hitherto stationary billiard ball #2, causing it to roll. Ball #2 then strikes hitherto stationary billiard ball #3, causing it to roll. And so on. This sequence of events doesnÂ’t constitute a single entity; this sequence isnÂ’t like a rock or a tree or an ice cube. 
HereÂ’s an example of a causal sequence that constitutes more than one object. Let S1 be the series of events constituting some seed and the process by which that seed turns into a tree and the tree itself. S1 is a causal seriesÂ—a textbook case. But it constitutes two distinct objects, not one. The seed isnÂ’t a mini-tree. ItÂ’s a tree-precursor, not a tree, just as a gamete is a person-precursor, not an actual person. (Unlike people, gametes donÂ’t have thoughts or fall in love or play the harmonica.) 
Two questions arise. What is the difference between those causal sequences that are thing-constitutive and those that are not? Second, what is the difference between thing-internal change, on the one hand, and wholesale transformation, on the other? 
7.1 Some general features of thing-constitutive causal sequences 
Nothing that endures for more than an instant is not a causal process. But what is distinctive about those causal processes that we think of as objects (e.g., frozen ice cubes) is that the changes constitutive of them occur within certain narrow and fixed limits. 
ThereÂ’s nothing unchanging about any ice cubeÂ—even one that for the last fifty years has been inside in an undisturbed deep freezer. Given such an ice-cube, every particle constituting it is in constant flux; and the ice-cube itself is nothing but a flurry of activity. 
But even though those particles are all moving vigorously, theyÂ’re moving only in ways that allow the flurry they compose to retain more or less the same properties. The flurry doesnÂ’t change, even though the things composing it do. The reason the flurry doesnÂ’t change is that, although its components are changing incessantly, the way in which they change doesnÂ’t change. 
Thus, what we usually describe as Â“changesÂ” are really second-order changes: changes in the changes themselves. Each molecule composing a given ice-cube is an arena within which ceaseless change occurs. But so long as the ice-cube remains intact, there are no significant changes in the relations borne to one another by these different arenas of change. ThatÂ’s why the ice-cube is unphased by such changes. But if the ice-cube is smashed or melts into a puddle, those mutual relations are significantly changed. ThatÂ’s why the ice-cube does not survive such changes. 
7.2 Change vs. obliteration 
Not all objects are as static as ice cubes, and our analysis must be refined if it is to deal with more dynamic entities (e.g., a living human body). Like a rock or an ice cube, a living body consists of individual particles each of which bristles with activity. But where living bodies are concerned, there are changes, sometimes dramatic ones, in the relations that these arenas of change bear to one another. This happens whenever an organism develops in a positive direction, as when maturation or recovery strengthen it, or in a negative direction, as when old age or illness enfeeble it. 
Thus, not all second-order changes jeopardize a thingÂ’s existence, and sometimes theyÂ’re actually necessary for it. When do second-order changes destroy existence and when do they sustain it? Â“Such changes are existence-unfriendly,Â” it might be suggested, Â“when theyÂ’re abrupt or discontinuous and theyÂ’re existence-friendly when theyÂ’re not.Â” But this isnÂ’t the right answer, since the melting of an ice cube, though decidedly thing-unfriendly, is as smooth a process as the development of an organism, which is a decidedly thing-friendly process. 
Â“Changes are thing-preserving,Â” it will be said, Â“when theyÂ’re structure preserving. The general morphology of an adult human being is similar to that of an infant. There are differences, of course, but theyÂ’re internal to more fundamental similarities. Thus, the changes that connect the infant to the adult preserve structures. In general, thing-sustaining changes are structure-sustaining changes.Â” 
This position obviously has merit, but it wonÂ’t quite do. There are cases where, without going out of existence, some one thing changes in fundamental structural respects. The butterfly doesnÂ’t resemble the caterpillar; but there is some one organism that is first a caterpillar and then a butterfly. So why is it that caterpillars that turn into butterflies continue to exist whereas ice-cubes that turn into puddles do not? 
7.3 Dynamic integrity the essence of thinghood 
Puddles by no means defy prediction. If you see a puddle that is expanding, you may know roughly how long it will continue to expand and roughly what its shape will be when it stops expanding. But in addition to being of limited scope and low quality, such predictions presuppose ad hoc, circumstance-specific knowledge. The predictive payoff is minimal, given the size of the epistemic investment. 
By learning more about the relevant variables (e.g., the shape of the floor, the rate at which the puddle is expanding, etc.), you can increase the predictive payoff. But given a vast improvement in oneÂ’s knowledge of these variables, there would be only a slight improvement in the predictive payoff. To have any chance of predicting with any precision what the puddleÂ’s shape will be when it stops expanding, one would need extraordinarily high-resolution knowledge. Further, interference-effects would guarantee that, no matter how good your measuring instruments were or how adept you were at using them, your knowledge of initial conditions would not exceed a rather low threshold. And supposing that, within these limits, you acquired as much knowledge as possible of the relevant variables, any predictions you could make on the basis of that knowledge would be of minimal scope. Given high-resolution knowledge of the puddleÂ’s state at a given time, you could make low-probability, low-resolution predictions about the puddleÂ’s state at times soon thereafter. 
But the story is very different where butterflies, human beings, and other bona fidethings are involved. Given a knowledge of slight disturbances to a caterpillarÂ’s anatomy, one can make high-resolution, high-probability predictions about the anatomical condition of the butterfly into which, in due course, it will metamorphose. Easily acquired low-resolution knowledge of an animalÂ’s state at a given time may yield a high-resolution knowledge of its state at a much later time. 
Given a pregnant mother who consumes large enough amounts of alcohol, it can be predicted that, 50 years hence, the person to whom she gives birth (supposing that person to be alive) will be severely damaged, and it can be said with some precision how that person will be damaged. The other, brighter side of the coin is that, given easily acquired, low-resolution knowledge to the effect that a certain person, while in his formative years, is given certain kinds of stimulation, allowed certain kinds of freedom, etc., one can make high-probability, high-resolution predictions about that personÂ’s condition in late adulthood. 
Of course, butterflies and children arenÂ’t just thingsÂ—theyÂ’re organisms. And not everything that is true of organisms is true of all things. But points relevantly similar to the ones just made hold of non-organisms. A sculptor who is chipping away at a hunk of marble knows that, barring some extraordinary event, the shape had by the hunk when heÂ’s done chipping away at it is the shape it will keep for centuries to come. The people who built the Washington Monument knew that, barring some extraordinary event, it would remain standing, its shape and general physical condition more or less unchanged, for hundreds if not thousands of years to come. In general, a limited knowledge of a thingÂ’s state at a given time yields high-probability, high-resolution knowledge of that thingÂ’s state at a much later time. 
Knowledge of this principle underlies all physical labor. It underlies the manufacturing of cars, houses, fishing rods, and elevators. All of this activity would be pointless were it not for the prediction-friendliness inherent in thinghood. 
These predictions are defeasible, of course.[430] 
Well-built houses are destroyed by earthquakes. Well-educated children from loving homes turn out to be moronic ghouls. But itÂ’s despite, not by virtue of, its being a thing that a sculpture or child or anything else has a counterpredictive future. Embittered by his lack of artistic ability, some unknown kook breaks into the Louvre and destroys famous sculpture X. The world is shocked. Nobody could have predicted that the world would ever be without this masterpiece. XÂ’s future was indeed an unpredictable one. But until its thing-status was completely undermined, XÂ’s future was a predictable one. Thus, XÂ’s future was unpredictable only to the extent that XÂ’s thing-status wasnÂ’t determinative of it. So given only that XÂ’s future was not predictable, it doesnÂ’t follow that things qua things arenÂ’t prediction-enablers; and given that XÂ’s future was predictable to the extent that its thing-status had a hand in it, it follows that things qua things are prediction-enablers. 
In general, to be a thing is to be a prediction enabler. It would, of course, be viciously circular to define a Â“thingÂ” as a prediction-and explanation-enabling thing. But when we replace the second occurrence of the word Â“thingÂ” in the last sentence with Â“complex of events,Â” the circularity goes away. Thus, to be a thing is to be a prediction-enabling complex of events (or Â“event-complex,Â” as weÂ’ll say). By the same token, an event-complex that is predictively inert is, to that extent, a non-thing. 
Prediction and explanation are conjugates of each other. An explanation uses known laws to go from effect to cause. (I know that Smith is now belittling Brown. I know that insecure, touchy people become angry when belittled. I know that Brown is such a person. So I predict that Brown will become angry.) The corresponding prediction uses the same laws to go from cause to effect. Thus, a swarm of events is a thing to the extent that it is prediction-and explanation-conducive. 
7.4 Thinghood is a matter of degree 
The property of being prediction-enabling comes in degrees, as does the property of being explanation-enabling. A brick house is richer in these properties than a plywood house; a plywood house is richer in them than a cloud; a cloud is richer in them than a breeze. 
A consequence of our analysis is that thinghood comes in degrees. Some things are Â“thingierÂ” than others. I accept this consequence. A brick house is more of a thing than a cloud; itÂ’s more Â“thingy.Â” This means only that it provides a broader and more stable basis than does a cloud for prediction and explanation. Since this is what we are inclined to think anyway, it isnÂ’t to the discredit of our analysis that it has this consequence. 
We are inclined to think that things must literally be solid, like rocks and ice cubes, and unlike puddles. So far as there is a connection between actual solidity and thinghood, it is that, within the narrow horizons within which we live, solid things typically provide a firmer basis for prediction than non-solid things. But non-solids can be as thingy as rocks. Though theyÂ’re gaseous, as opposed to solid, stars are things to no less a degree than rocks. The reason is that, even though theyÂ’re not solid, they have the dynamic integrity of things that, in terrestrial contexts, are typically had by solid things. 
7.5 The contextual nature of thinghood 
Despite its internal lack of cohesiveness, a galaxy can be highly thing-like in the context of an explanation of why certain extremely large-scale astronomical events are occurringÂ—of why, for example, there is a marked tendency for objects in a certain very large region of space to head in a certain direction. And despite its high degree of internal cohesiveness, a rock can be as unthing-like as, in most contexts, gusts of air would be. To creatures whose minds moved millions of times more slowly than ours, rocks would be as unthing-like as gusts of air are to us. And to creatures whose minds moved millions of times more quickly than ours, gusts of air would be as durable, cohesive, and predictable as marble statues are to us. 
Thus, a given system of events can be a thingÂ—in certain respects, at certain juncturesÂ—in some explanatory contexts, while being unthing-likeÂ— in different respects, at those same juncturesÂ—in others. But that doesnÂ’t mean that things are created by our explanations. 
8.0 Time-travel 
It is debated whether time-travel is possible. Thanks to our analysis of what it is to persist in time, we can shed some light on this problem. 
Setting aside the trivial and irrelevant fact that we travel forward in time at a rate of one minute/minute, the statement Â“time-travel is possibleÂ” has three distinct meanings: 
(a) 
One can Â“leapÂ” from one time to some non-adjacent time; i.e., one can move in a discontinuous manner from one time to another. 

(b) 
One can travel forward in time at a rate of more than one minute/minute. 


(c) One can travel backwards in time. 
It is generally thought that (a)Â–(c) are empirical questions that fall within the jurisdiction of physics. In actuality, they are questions of logic, not of empirical fact. Moreover, each of (a)Â–(c) is logically false and therefore couldnÂ’t possibly be correct. 
LetÂ’s discuss (a) first. In this chapter, we have seen that anything that persists for any amount of time is a causal series. A causal series is a continuous series of states of affairs such that, given any two of them, one is the (in)direct cause of the other. 
An illustration may be helpful. At any given moment during its existence, your car consists of an incessant flurry of mass-energy displacements; and your car is thus a series of Â“event-flurries,Â” as weÂ’ll call them. Twenty-four hours ago, your car was constituted by one event-flurry. Right now itÂ’s constituted by a different event-flurry. (Let S1 be the first event-flurry and let S2 be the second.) And, of course, my car is currently constituted by some event-flurry. (Let S3 be that flurry.) 
Bearing all of this in mind, imagine the following. While your car was parked in your driveway, somebody crashed into it, severely damaging it. 
Your car therefore bears little resemblance to what it was twenty-four hours ago. It follows that S1 and S2 are qualitatively very different from each other. By contrast, S1 and S3 are as similar to each other as their being in different places permits. This is sheer coincidence: S1 and S3 are, we will suppose, as 
causally disconnected from each other as any two non-simultaneous events on this planet can be. It follows that my car, as it is right now, is just like your car, as it was twenty-four hours ago, before it was damaged. It also follows that S1 is much less similar to S2 than it is to S3. 
Be all of this as it may, the car in your driveway is, whereas the car in my driveway is not, numerically identical with the car you owned twenty-four hours ago. Mediating between S1 and S2 is a continuous series of events such 
that, given any two of them, one is the (in)direct cause of the other. No such 
series mediates between S1 and S3. ThatÂ’s why (i) the car in my driveway isnÂ’t the very same car as the one you parked in your driveway twenty-four hours ago, their uncanny mutual resemblance notwithstanding. And thatÂ’s also why (ii) the car sitting in your driveway is the very same car as the one you parked in your driveway yesterday, their lack of mutual resemblance notwithstanding. Obvious generalizations of these points establish our thesis that objects are identical with causal series. 
A consequence of the fact that objects are such series is that a given object ceases to exist the moment the corresponding causal series is severed. If, instead of just being damaged last night, your car was vaporized, my car, though an exact duplicate of your (pre-vaporized) car, still isnÂ’t numerically identical with it. 
Given that an object ceases to exist the moment the corresponding causal series is severed, it follows that, so far as it isnÂ’t logically false, the statement: 
(i) Smith disappears in 2009 and re-appears in the year 2023. 
collapses into the statement: 
(ii) Smith is annihilated in 2009 and a Smith-like entity that isnÂ’t actually Smith ex nihilo comes into existence in the year 2023. 
A question will help clarify the reasoning behind this last assertion: Where is Smith during that fourteen year interval? HeÂ’s either nowhere or heÂ’s somewhere. LetÂ’s suppose that heÂ’s nowhere. In that case, for the reasons illustrated in connection with your car, whatever it is that pops into existence in the year 2023 isnÂ’t numerically identical with Smith. So letÂ’s suppose that heÂ’s somewhereÂ— that, at any given instant during that time period, he is in some place or other. But in that case heÂ’s no more time-traveling than anything else that exists during that interval. If heÂ’s next to some one tree during that entire period, heÂ’s no more time-traveling than that tree. If heÂ’s going from place to place, heÂ’s no more time-traveling than any one of the satellites that will orbit the earth during that period.[431] 

So depending on whether heÂ’s somewhere or nowhere, Smith is either permanently annihilated in 2009 or heÂ’s no more time-traveling than anything else that exists during that period. Therefore, (i) is false. 
To see why (ii) is false we need do little more than repeat some of the points just made. Suppose that Smith travels from 2009 to 2023 at a rate of one million minutes/minute. WeÂ’ve just seen that Smith cannot make this journey in a discontinuous manner; he cannot disappear from one time and reappear at some other, non-adjacent time. So Smith must make this journey in a continuous manner. So at any given moment during this interval, Smith must be in some place or other. It follows, as we saw a moment ago, that he is no more time-traveling than anything else that exists during that interval. The supposition that Smith is traveling forward in time at a rate of one million minutes/minute thus turns out to collapse into the supposition that he isnÂ’t time-traveling at all. Given any positive number n, an analogous argument shows that continuous forward time-travel at a rate of n minutes/minute collapses into forward time-travel at a rate of one minute/minute. 
There is another, quite different problem with the concept of discontinuous time-travel. Let W1 be a universe where (i) is true and (ii) is 
false; and let W2 be an otherwise indistinguishable universe where (ii) is true and (i) is false. What happens in the one universe at any given time coincides with what happens in the other universe at that time. It follows that, even if (per impossibile) an occupant of the one universe knew exactly what happened in that universe at any given time, he would not, in virtue of that fact, have any legitimate reason for preferring (i) to (ii). A fortiori, no possible observation that one might have would provide one with any reason for believing oneself to be in W1 as opposed to W2. Since observation 
couldnÂ’t possibly provide one with such a reason, only logic could do so. But logic cannot do so, since (i) is logically false, as weÂ’ve already seen.[432] 

Similar points hold in connection with discontinuous backwards timeÂ­
travel. In the movie Back to the Future, young Marty McFly vanishes from the year 1985 and shows up in the year 1955. This means that, in the year 1985, the causal sequence that constitutes his existence is severed. Like everything else that persists for any length of time, Marty McFly is a causal sequence. It follows that, so far as it isnÂ’t incoherent, the statement: 
(1) In 1985, Marty McFly traveled backwards in time to the year 1955 and is otherwise unchanged. 
collapses into: 
(2) Marty McFly was annihilated in 1985, and in 1955 there appears ex nihilo somebody who is numerically distinct from him but otherwise just like him. 
Also, given obvious adaptations of what we said a moment ago, there is no conceivable event that, were it known, would provide more support for (1) than for (2). 
Since, therefore, there couldnÂ’t possibly be any observation-based reason for preferring (1) to (2), the only possible reasons for doing so would be of a logical nature. This means that there are no reasons for doing so, given that 
(1) is incoherent. The concept of discontinuous backwards time-travel is therefore a broken one. 
What about the idea of continuous backwards time-travel? For argumentÂ’s sake, letÂ’s suppose that, during his continuous journey from the year 1985 to the year 1955, Marty McFly is right next to some stop-sign that was built in 1920 and stays in the same place for several centuries. That means that, at any given moment during that thirty year period, Marty McFly is no more time-traveling than the stop-sign. Each is just sitting there. 
There are, of course, some important differences between Mary McFly and the stop-sign. First of all, whereas the stop-sign is crushed or burnt or otherwise destroyed in some pedestrian way, Marty McFly must simply vanish in the year 1985. (If he doesnÂ’t, then heÂ’s still hanging around in the year 1985, in which case he obviously hasnÂ’t gone back in time.) And, whereas the stop-signÂ’s presence in the year 1955 is to be explained in the customary way, Marty McFly just popped up ex nihilo. 
Bearing these points in mind, let W3 be a universe in which: 
(3) Marty McFly continuously traveled backwards in time from the year 1985 to the year 1955 but is otherwise unchanged. 
is true, and in which (2) is false; and let W4 be a universe that is exactly like W3 except that, in it, (2) is true and (3) is false. Echoing what we said earlier, there is no conceivable event that, were it known, would enable one to determine whether one was in W3 as opposed to W4, or vice versa. Which, taken together with the fact that being annihilated in 1985 didnÂ’t exactly tighten young MartyÂ’s grip on existence, suggests that, other things being equal, (2) is the better way to model the observational data. 
There is another, even deeper issue. For there to be backwards time-travel of any kind, there must be retroactive causation: some events must be the effects of later events. Marty McFlyÂ’s appearing in 1955 must be an effect of some event occurring in 1985. But there are empirical and also strictly logical reasons for thinking backwards time-travel an impossibility. 
If Relativity Theory (RT) is right, which weÂ’ll henceforth assume that it is, the statement Â“E2 is an effect of E1, but E1 post-dates E2Â” is tautologically false. According to RT, order in time is defined in terms of causation: anything caused by a given event ipso facto follows that event. Thus, the view that one could travel backwards in time is in the same category as the view that triangles could have five sides. 
A well-known consequence of RT is that a given event may precede one event relative to one framework, be simultaneous with it relative to some second framework, and follow it relative to some third framework. Some conclude from this that backwards time-travel is possible. 
This is not the right inference to draw. For reasons that arenÂ’t important here, the framework-relative nature of temporal order is a consequence of, among other things, the fact that any effect of an event ipso facto follows that event. In other words, itÂ’s a consequence of the fact that Â“E2 precedes E1 and 
is also an effect of itÂ” is tautologically false. 
Like any other scientific theory, RT is empirical. ItÂ’s based on observation; and acceptance of it is warranted only as long as our observations are consistent with it. Nonetheless, the principle that causes ipso facto precede their effects is an analytic, not an empirical, truth. (WeÂ’ll henceforth refer to this principle Â“CTÂ”Â—short for Â“causality and temporal order.Â”) So CT is true even if RT is false. 
Â“But how can CT be analytic,Â” it will be asked, Â“given that RT is an observation-based theory?Â” Two reasons. (1) Not every statement composing an empirical (observation-based) theory is itself observation-based. Every theory comprises statements of pure logic (e.g., Â“no true statement entails the negation of anything entailed by any of its consequencesÂ”) that arenÂ’t observation-based. (2) Not everything learned with the help of observation is learned through observation. If one learns some complex mathematical theorem by reading a proof of it, one learns that theorem through observations of ink-deposits; but it isnÂ’t by observing such deposits that one learns it. The observations of ink-deposits merely occasion or Â“triggerÂ” the purely logical ratiocinative activity that does lead to a genuine knowledge of that principle.[433] 
Somebody with 20/20 vision who has carefully studied those ink-deposits (i.e., who has studied those ink-deposits themselves, as opposed to their meanings) may completely and utterly fail to understand the corresponding proof; whereas somebody whose vision is just good enough to see some of the key lines of the proof may, on the basis only of those observations along with the thoughts they precipitated, understand it extremely well. 
Also, somebody who has heard the proof stated but hasnÂ’t read it may, on the basis only of those auditory observations along with the thoughts they precipitated, thoroughly understand the proof. Ink-deposits bear no physical resemblance to noises. Therefore, it isnÂ’t by studying ink-deposits that one learns the proof.[434] 
So given only that empirical discoveries led to our becoming aware of CT, it doesnÂ’t follow that CT was itself discovered empirically. 
And, in fact, CT couldnÂ’t have been discovered empirically. Assuming it a certainty that SmithÂ’s pushing the button caused the elevator to come, there is no conceivable event that, were it known, could warrant a revision of oneÂ’s subsequent judgment that the pushing of the button preceded the arrival of the elevator. 
Einstein himself very clearly said that CT was not an empirical hypothesis. He also said (unfortunately for me) that it was a conventionÂ—a definition of Â“order in timeÂ”Â—and, therefore, not a substantive truth. I would suggest that, although he described CT as a definition, he chose this particular definition, as opposed to others, because he saw in it a substantive truth whose roots lie 
in the very concept of what it is for one event to precede another. 
Chapter 25 The Compatibilist Conception of Freedom 
1.0 Determinism in relation to the debate between materialism and dualism 
A set of events is deterministic if it obeys laws that, given the systemÂ’s state at any given point in time, fix the systemÂ’s state at all later points in time.[435] 
The physical world is a deterministic system. (In any case, itÂ’s very nearly so. And in this context, weÂ’ll assume that it is. Later, weÂ’ll drop the assumption.) This means that the world itself is a deterministic system to the extent that itÂ’s physical. 
There are both physical and mental entities. Anything that involves thought or feeling is mental; anything that does not (but is spatiotemporal; i.e., is in space or time) is physical. So beliefs, intentions, and regrets are mental; and rocks, trees, and explosions are physical. 
It is an open and delicate question how the mental and physical are related. (See Chapter 22 for a discussion of this matter.) Some hold that mental entities are identical with certain physical entities (presumably neural events or structures). This position is known as materialism. Others deny this, saying that the mental is non-physical. This position is known as dualism. 
If materialism is right, then the mental world is just part of the physical world. So if E is some experience that you either have had, are having, or will have, then given the way the world was 10 million years ago, the state of the universe 10 million years ago made EÂ’s occurrence inevitable. Whatever you decide to do today is an inevitable consequence of the way the world was a million years ago. 
Supposing that the physical world is deterministic, and supposing also that materialism is right, itÂ’s hard to see how there could be free will. If the state of the universe a million years ago completely settled what choices I would make today, then presumably I couldnÂ’t make any choices other than those that I do make. And it would seem that, under those circumstances, I donÂ’t have anything resembling Â“freedom of choice.Â” In a moment, we will find that some case can be made that one may have a kind of freedom in a deterministic world. But letÂ’s hold off on that for a moment and talk right now about the relationship between indeterminism and freedom. 
2.0 Free will in an indeterministic world? 
Because of the apparent irreconcilability of materialism with the 
presumption that we are free, some believers in free will accept dualism, while others accept materialism but reject determinism.[436] 
LetÂ’s consider both options, starting with the first. 
First of all, supposing that there is indeterminism in the world, it doesnÂ’t necessarily mean that our mental processes arenÂ’t determined. If the atomic processes making up some rock happen to be indeterministic, that doesnÂ’t mean that your brain or mind arenÂ’t deterministic. So the indeterminism must be in the right place. 
What is that place? Where must the indeterminism be if our choices are to be made freely? The indeterminism must relate to the processes involved in making choices. For, if the mechanisms of which our choices are results are deterministic, then our decisions are as determined as anything else. Thus, a free personÂ’s choices are undetermined. 
But a choice that isnÂ’t predetermined by anything isnÂ’t predetermined by any facts about oneÂ’s personality, and a choice of the latter kind is not one that we would have any inclination to regard as Â“free.Â” A short story may illustrate my meaning. Smith is walking along. All of a sudden, he decides to become a pilot. This decision has no basis in his personality. He never liked flying. He already has a career that he enjoys and he depends on. So it would be inconvenient for him to become a pilot, and he would derive no pleasure from it. He knows all of this. Nonetheless, he makes this choice. It just comes out of the blue. 
Was this choice made freely? It doesnÂ’t seem like it. It actually seems rather compulsiveÂ—like something that just overcame Smith. Suppose that Â“choicesÂ” similar to the one just described were a frequent occurrence in SmithÂ’s psychological life. Would we say that Smith was Â“freeÂ”? No. WeÂ’d describe him as having a kind of disorder. WeÂ’d describe the fact that he was visited by these strange compulsions as indicative of a lack of psychological integrity on his part; and see his submission to these forces as showing a lack of freedom on his part. Smith is a puppet dancing at the end of strings pulled by psychopathology. 
This suggests that, in order to be made Â“freely,Â” a choice has to be rooted in facts about oneÂ’s personality, and must express oneÂ’s values, desires, beliefs, and previous intentions. A choice that lacks these roots seems to involve a disintegration of the personÂ’s psyche and, paradoxical though this may seem, a consequent diminution of the subjectÂ’s freedom. So even if there is indeterminism, it doesnÂ’t help people be free; indeterminism actually seems to hurt our chances of being free. 
But to the extent that a choice is appropriately rooted in a personÂ’s personality, that choice is not the result of indeterminism but, on the contrary, of a deterministic structure. And itÂ’s hard to see how, under those circumstances, we could be free. So weÂ’re damned if we do and damned if we donÂ’t! 
3.0 Free will in a dualistic world? 
Now letÂ’s consider the view that, although the physical world is deterministic, the mental is not physical. First of all, even if the mental is not physical, there is considerable evidence that the mental sphere is deterministic. The decisions that one makes are clearly a product of oneÂ’s pre-existing mental condition.[437] 

We must also take into account that, at least according to some viewpoints, the choices we make have extremely deep roots in our unconscious mental lives. Analysis tends to suggest that decisions that seem, at the level of consciousness, to be Â“randomÂ” are, in fact, strictly determined by unconscious forces. In any case, this is one point of view, and it is one for which there is some corroboration. 
But suppose, if only for argumentÂ’s sake, that your choices were not fixed by the state of the universe prior to their occurrence. For the reasons given earlier, that wouldnÂ’t make those choices be free. On the contrary, it would make them more like fits or seizures than like considered, freely made judgments. 
A story similar to the one just told may help make this clear. You are a student at State University. You have an A-average. All of a sudden, you choose to drop out of college and become a drug dealer. Your choice was not caused to occur by anything; the state of your personality prior to the choice had nothing to do with your making it, and neither did the state of the universe. It just happened. So, in the middle of a test, you throw down your pen, bolt out of the room, and get to work as a drug dealer. 
Does this sound like a freely made choice? No. It sounds more like a compulsion. ItÂ’s as though you were Â“taken overÂ” by another person and lost control of your body. Again, we see that indeterminism doesnÂ’t help freedom and actually undermines it. 
4.0 The Compatibilist Conception of Freedom 
The problem is that, as we saw, determinism also seems to threaten freedom. Obviously you have no control over the past. If determinism is right, then what happened in the past completely determines exactly whatÂ’s happening in the present and, in particular, completely fixes what choices youÂ’re making now. So something over which you have no control is completely responsible for the choices that youÂ’re making. ItÂ’s hard to see how, under these circumstances, you could be said to have free will. 
Nonetheless, some hold that there can be free will in a deterministic world. Such people are known as compatibilists. Those who deny it are incompatibilists. 
4.1 The crude form of compatibilism 
There are ultimately two different forms of compatibilism. One of these is very straightforward; the other is quite sophisticated. 
According to the straightforward version, which weÂ’ll discuss in this section, you are free to the extent that you can do what you want, and you are unfree to the extent that you cannot. If you want to leave your room and you can, you are free. (In any case, youÂ’re free in that respect. You may be unfree in other respects; e.g., once you leave the room, you may want to leave the house youÂ’re in but not be able to.) According to the other version of compatibilism, which weÂ’ll discuss in Section 4.2, being able to do what you want, though necessary for freedom, isnÂ’t sufficient for it. It is necessary also that your choices be adequately rooted in who you are as a person.[438] 

4.1.1 G.E. MooreÂ’s compatibilism 
According to G.E. Moore (1873Â–1958),[439] 
an act is performed freely if the agent would have done something else if he had chosen to do so. An act is free if the agent Â“could have done otherwise.Â” 
The idea is pretty straightforward. Although IÂ’m considering striking Harry, I choose not to. But, immediately upon making that choice, an extremely strong person grabs my arm and forces me to hit Harry. My act was clearly unfree. But why? Because, says Moore, even though I chose to do otherwise, I ended up striking Harry. Now suppose that I voluntarily strike Harry. I do it, not because somebody forces me to, but because I donÂ’t like Harry and want him to suffer. In this case, my act is free. But why? Because, says Moore, if I hadnÂ’t chosen to strike Harry, I wouldnÂ’t have done so. Thus, my striking Harry is voluntary, Moore says, iff I wouldnÂ’t have done so had I chosen not to do so. 
MooreÂ’s position is a form of compatibilism. Free acts arenÂ’t those that are uncaused; theyÂ’re those that are caused in a certain wayÂ—theyÂ’re those that are caused by decisions on the part of the people (or animals) who commit them. 
4.1.2 ChisholmÂ’s objection to MooreÂ’s analysis 
In Human Freedom and the Self, Roderick Chisholm (1916Â–1999) makes a compelling objection to this analysis. LetÂ’s suppose that, if I had chosen not to strike Harry, I would indeed have refrained from doing so. Unless I was at liberty to not make[440] 
that choice, itÂ’s hard to see how my doing so was free. If every choice I make is inevitable, then itÂ’s irrelevant that, had I made different choices, I would have acted differently. For I couldnÂ’t have made those choices under those circumstances, and I therefore couldnÂ’t have acted in those ways. And if I couldnÂ’t have acted in those ways, then I couldnÂ’t have done anything other than what I did, making it hard to see how, in acting as I did, I was acting freely. 
4.1.3 A Lockean counter-objection 
Though powerful, Chisholm's point involves a serious confusion, which may undermine it. We won't identify that confusion until Section 4.1.5, since we havenÂ’t yet covered some of the material that must be absorbed to understand it. 
Right now we will concentrate on a point made by John Locke (1632Â– 1704), who held a view similar to MooreÂ’s, that either refutes, or comes close to refuting, ChisholmÂ’s analysis.[441] 
In LockeÂ’s view, freedom is a property of actions. It makes no sense to speak of anything other than actions as being free. Only things that one can intend to do are done freely. I can intend to do 20 push-ups, and thatÂ’s why I can do it freely. But I canÂ’t intend to make a certain choice. What would it be to intend to make a certain choice (e.g., to intend to do 20 push-ups)? If I really intend to choose to do 20 push-ups, then, for that very reason, I have chosen to do 20 push-ups. Second-order intentions (intentions to intend) collapse into first-order intentions. Thus, so far as it isnÂ’t a pleonasm, the expression Â“intentional choiceÂ” is meaningless. 
4.1.4 A Lockean counter-objection (continued) 
Locke has surely identified one kind of freedom or---what, as weÂ’ll now see, is probably more accurate---an essential component of one kind of freedom. But the following scenario suggests: 
(i) 
that LockeÂ’s analysis, though certainly a part of the truth, is not the whole of it; 

(ii) 
that, although LockeÂ’s analysis may well partially undermine ChisholmÂ’s analysis, it doesnÂ’t do so completely; 


and, finally, 
(iii) that ChisholmÂ’s has shown that the concept associated by the lay-person with the term Â“freeÂ” is incoherent and, moreover, that the same is true, though not for the same reasons, with LockeÂ’s attempt to remove the incoherencies from that concept (while leaving it otherwise unchanged). 
A story will clarify these points. 
On Monday, you undergo hypnosis. You do so because you believe that it will help you kick your addiction to nicotine. While under hypnosis, the hypnotist, who is a prankster and loves to abuse the power he has over his subjects, tells you that, on Wednesday, you should choose to put on a tin-foil hat, go into your bossÂ’s office, and tell him that aliens are about take over the Earth. On Wednesday, you choose to do these things. So you voluntarily put on a tin-foil hat, etc. 
Your act was voluntary. You chose to do it. But was it free? My opinion: there was a sense in which it was free, but there was also an important sense in which it was not free. You are not, by virtue of choosing to engage in this odd behavior, in the same category as somebody who wants to walk to his car but is physically restrained. But, for reasons that are not immediately obvious but that we will now try to elucidate, your behavior is either unfree or free only in some attenuated sense. 
One way of interpreting what Chisholm is saying is as follows[442]: 
(CR) There is only one significant difference between, on the one hand, your voluntary decision to don a tin-foil hat, etc. and, on the other hand, a Â‘normalÂ’ decision (e.g., a decision to play tennis made by somebody whose choice isnÂ’t the result of hypnotic suggestion or any other comparable event). The difference in question is that, whereas your decision was implanted in you by some sentient being, the tennis-playerÂ’s decision was implanted in him by impersonal forces. But does that really make a difference? To be sure, your decision (to put on a tin-foil hat, etc.) is the result of malfeasance on somebodyÂ’s part, whereas the tennis-playerÂ’s decision is not. So, from a moral perspective, there are important differences between the two situations. But, when evaluating whether a personÂ’s decision to do X is free, what is relevant is whether that person had control over the forces leading to that decision; itÂ’s irrelevant what sort of morality, if any, those forces embodied. 
An adaptation of the story told a moment ago (about the hypnotist) makes this clear. One day, while you are snoozing under a coconut tree, a coconut falls on your head. The resulting brain-disturbances lead to your deciding to put on a tin-foil hat, go into your bossÂ’s office, etc. Surely your decision to do this---though voluntary, and though not the product of malfeasance on anyoneÂ’s part---is unfree or, at best, is free only in some reduced sense. So LockeÂ’s thesis (Â“an act is free iff itÂ’s voluntaryÂ”) isnÂ’t correct and must either be rejected or at least heavily qualified. 
4.1.5 An oversight on ChisholmÂ’s part 
Partly for the reasons just given, and partly for reasons to be stated later in this chapter, I believe that LockeÂ’s analysis is inadequate. To that extent, I must agree with Chisholm. But ChisholmÂ’s analysis involves a subtle but important confusion. Because it involves this confusion, ChisholmÂ’s analysis fails to show that actions cannot be free. (However, despite its involving this confusion, ChisholmÂ’s analysis---or, rather, the extension of it put forth in the previous section---does successfully undermine LockeÂ’s position.) 
Let t be some instant in the year 50,000 B.C., and let t* some instant in the 21st century. Suppose that, at t*, Smith decides to go for a jog. Bearing this in mind, consider the following two statements: 
(1) 
The state of the universe at time t compelled Smith to decide to go for a jog at time t*. 

(2) 
The state of the universe at time t made it inevitable that, approximately 52,000 years later, Smith would come into existence a few years prior to t* and, because of the combined effects of his pre-t* experiences and his native constitution, would decide at time t* to go for a jog. 


(1) entails that, given the state of the universe at t, it was nomically impossible (i.e., prohibited by natural law) for Smith not to decide to go for a jog at t*; and (2) also entails this. But there is a difference between (1) and (2). (1) says that the state of the universe at t compelled Smith to make a certain decision. (2) doesnÂ’t say this. It says that it was inevitable that he would decide at t* to for a jog. But that's compatible with his not being compelled at t* to decide to go for a jog. It's inevitable that I will choose to have a meal in the next 12 hours; but that doesn't mean that my decision to eat isn't free. Rational people freely but inevitably choose to act in certain ways. 
HereÂ’s a case of SmithÂ’s being compelled to behave in a certain way. A very strong person takes hold of SmithÂ’s arms and, despite SmithÂ’s valiant resistance, makes Smith hit himself with his own hands (or, what is probably a more accurate way of putting it, hits Smith with SmithÂ’s own hands). Why is it that, in this case, SmithÂ’s behavior is the result of compulsion? Because the immediate causes of that behavior were not Smith-internal. The forces that led to SmithÂ’s arm-movements were not constitutive of Smith; they failed to be Smith-constitutive even in the attenuated sense in which an impulse is constitutive of a person of a person who regards that impulse as having no value, having thus made every effort to dissociate himself from it, and to which he therefore gives no weight when making decisions. 
Even though (2) is to the effect that it is compulsory that Smith come into existence and, in due course, do such and such, (2) is quite consistent with SmithÂ’s never being compelled in any way. For (2) is consistent with the proposition that the thing that is being compelled is the universe, not Smith, and that what the universe is being compelled to do is to produce a being, namely Smith, who will decide at t* to go jogging, and whose decision to do so, having for its proximal cause a conglomerate of Smith-constitutive forces, is not compelled---at least not in the sense in which, in the other story, Smith was compelled to hit himself and, indeed, not in any ordinary sense of the word Â“compelled.Â” 
A continuation of our story will help us move forward. The state of the universe at t makes it necessary, as a matter of natural law, that Smith come into existence, that he have thus and such thoughts, feelings, beliefs, etc. and that, at time t*, he decide to go jogging. But the state of the universe makes it inevitable that SmithÂ’s decision to go jogging be the result of forces that make up Smith. Obviously SmithÂ’s decision will reflect his beliefs concerning the external world; and those believes are obviously, in part, the results of events (collisions of photons with SmithÂ’s eyes, etc.) over which Smith has no control. But these Smith-non-constitutive events caused Smith to choose to go jogging only by way of Smith-constitutive forces---by way of SmithÂ’s preferences acting in conjunction with SmithÂ’s beliefs. So, ultimately, nothing that wasnÂ’t Smith-constitutive made Smith do anything. The only thing that made Smith go jogging was Smith himself. So, even though natural law made it inevitable that Smith would come into existence and, at time t*, decide to go jogging, the way in which natural law made that inevitable didnÂ’t involve SmithÂ’s being compelled. It involved the worldÂ’s being compelled to produce a person (Smith) whose own self was the sole (proximal) cause of his choice and who therefore freely went jogging. So (2) is compatible with the following proposition: 
(2*) Given the state of the universe at t, it was necessary, for reasons of natural law, that the universe be compelled to produce a person (Smith) who, at time t*, freely went jogging. 
If you were the sole immediate cause of some action of yours, then you acted freely. It may be that your existence, along with everything you think and feel (etc.), is the inevitable result of how the world was before you were born. But, by virtue of producing you, the world was not compelling you to do (or be) anything. There was no you to compel. (In producing somebody, you are not compelling them to exist. In conceiving a child, you are not compelling that child to exist. The child isnÂ’t yet in existence and therefore isnÂ’t there to be compelled. What is being compelled is the coming into existence of that child. The universe is being compelled, by your carnal acts, to create junior. But junior himself isnÂ’t in any way being compelled, at least not by virtue of being conceived, since what doesnÂ’t exist canÂ’t be compelled.) 
And once you are in existence, your actions are free if their causes are forces that are constitutive of you. For so far as your deeds result from such forces, they result from you: you are the author of those actions. And even though the state of the universe prior to your birth made it inevitable that you would exist to perform those actions, it did not (setting aside cases where forces not constitutive of you; e.g., a bullyÂ’s arm-twisting, are the proximal causes of your behavior) compel you to perform those actions. Rather, the state of the universe prior to your birth compelled events to produce a person (you) who (setting aside bully-caused behaviors, etc.) would freely perform various acts. 
4.1.5 FrankfurtÂ’s refutation of Moore: why Â“x acted freelyÂ” . Â“x could have done otherwiseÂ” 
Harry Frankfurt (1929Â–) decisively demonstrated the falsity of MooreÂ’s position by identifying scenarios in which somebody performs some act freely even though that person could not have abstained from performing that act.[443] 
Here is such a scenario: 
(SM)[444] 
Mr. Smith intends to kill Mr. Jones. Like Mr. Smith, Mrs. Green also wants Mr. Jones dead. But Smith doesnÂ’t want to go to jail for murder. Without SmithÂ’s knowing it, Mrs. Green installs a microchip in his cranium. (We neednÂ’t worry about how exactly she does this or how exactly the microchip works.) By means of this microchip, she can control SmithÂ’s actionsÂ—she can make him do whatever she wants. She knows that Smith is intent on killing Jones. But if Smith should get cold feet, Mrs. Green will use the microchip to force Smith to go through with it. Smith doesnÂ’t know about the microchip; nor does he even know of GreenÂ’s existence. Smith kills JonesÂ—he doesnÂ’t chicken out at the last minute. And he does so freely (at least insofar as anyone does anything freely Â—he is not in the grips of any delusions, or compulsions, etc.). 
Thus, Smith freely kills Jones, even though Smith could not have done otherwise. For, had he decided at the last minute not to kill Jones, Green would have forced him to. 
Hence, contrary to what Moore alleges, Â“x performs act A freelyÂ” is not equivalent with Â“x does A and, had x chosen not to do A, x would not have done A.Â” 
4.1.6 The irrelevance of FrankfurtÂ’s refutation of the counterfactual analysis of freedom 
But even though, interpreted narrowly, MooreÂ’s analysis is false, itÂ’s really just a misguided way of stating the principle, which FrankfurtÂ’s argument does nothing to undermine, that a free act is one that is choice-driven. Moore was led to equate Â“x acted freelyÂ” with Â“x could have done otherwiseÂ” not by a misconception concerning the nature of freedom, but by his acceptance of a certain analysis of causalityÂ—the so-called Â“counterfactual analysis of causalityÂ” (CFA). According to CFA, x caused y to occur just in case if x hadnÂ’t happened, y wouldnÂ’t have happened. Â“SmithÂ’s pushing the button caused the elevator to comeÂ” means the same thing as Â“if Smith hadnÂ’t pushed the button, the elevator wouldnÂ’t have come.Â” 
CFA is wrong. This is because there is causal redundancy in the world. I push the elevator button, causing the elevator to come; but if I hadnÂ’t pushed it, one of the other 20 people waiting for it would have done so, and the elevator would have come.[445] 

But a close cousin of CFA is correct, namely: 
(CFA*) x caused y to occur just in case, if x hadnÂ’t happened, then ceteris paribus y wouldnÂ’t have happened. 
Similarly, even though, for the reasons just given: 
(PAP)[446] 
Â“x did A freely if and only if x did A and, further, had x chosen not to do A, x wouldnÂ’t have done A,Â” 
is false, nonetheless: 
(PAP*) Â“x did A freely if and only if x did A and, further, had x chosen not to do A, then ceteris paribus x wouldnÂ’t have done A,Â” 
is correct. ItÂ’s well known that, if they are to come out correct, counterfactuals 
typically have to be hedged with ceteris paribus clauses. Even though: 
(JFK) Â“If JFK hadnÂ’t been assassinated, he would have been re-elected,Â” 
is a plausible counterfactual, it isnÂ’t necessarily true. What if, sometime after Nov. 22, 1963, but before the Â‘64 elections, JFK died of natural causes or was disgraced by some scandal? In that case, he would not have been reÂ­elected. So the right counterfactual is: 
(JFK*) Â“If JFK hadnÂ’t been assassinated, then ceteris paribus he would have been re-elected.Â” 
In other words, if JFK hadnÂ’t been assassinated, but otherwise things were the same, so that JFK was healthy and popular, etc., then he would have been re-elected.[447] 

Notice that JFK* is really a causal claim, since itÂ’s just another way of saying: 
(JFK#) Â“JFKÂ’s being assassinated caused an otherwise re-election-bound JFK to not be re-elected.Â” 
As a rule, counterfactuals are causal claims.[448] 
Thus, Â“Smith killed Jones freelyÂ” is true just in case (i) Smith killed Jones and (ii) if Smith had chosen not to kill Jones, then ceteris paribus Smith would have not killed Jones. 
Basically, Smith killed Jones freely if his doing so expressed his decision to do so, as opposed to some other force. In general: 
(FA)[449] 
an act is free if it expresses oneÂ’s decision to act that way. 
This is clearly the right analysis of a kind of freedom or---what may be a more accurate way of putting it---a certain aspect of freedom. 
4.1.7 Freedom not a property of choices 
If FA is right, acts are free, not choices. This is what Locke held. Locke was the first advocate of FA, and he was an exceptionally effective one. One chooses to act, Locke said; one doesnÂ’t choose to choose. It makes no sense to suppose that one chooses to choose. For if one always chose what to choose, Locke points out, one would have to make infinitely many choices in order to make a single one, and one therefore couldnÂ’t make any choices at all. In order to choose to open the door, one would have to choose to choose to open the door; and in order to choose to choose to open the door, one would have to choose to choose to choose to open the door; and so on. 
So freedom is freedom to act, not freedom to choose. As Locke puts it, freedom is a relationship between choice and act, and not between subject and choice. 
It follows that, so far as oneÂ’s freedom is concerned, it is irrelevant whether oneÂ’s choices are caused or not. Since freedom is a relationship between choices and acts, not between choices and their own antecedents, it doesnÂ’t matter whether choices are caused. Nor, therefore, does it matter how theyÂ’re caused. 
In fact, if FA is right, determinism is not only compatible with freedom, but is a prerequisite for it. Wanting to make the elevator come to your floor, you intend to push the button. If a degenerative neurological condition has undermined the integrity of the mechanisms linking your brain to your hand, thereby making them indeterministic, your intention to move your hand may be more likely to fail than to succeed. And, supposing that you do manage to push the button, if the mechanisms linking the button to the elevator are indeterministic, your pushing the button may be more likely than not to fail to get the elevator to come. To the extent that the mechanisms involved in the implementation of our choices are indeterministic, we are in the grim position of somebody who has ParkinsonÂ’s. The spirit is willing, but the flesh canÂ’t be counted on to obey, and neither can the relevant mechanisms in the external world. 
5.0 FrankfurtÂ’s analysis of freedom[450] 

According to Locke, you are free to the extent that you can do what you want to do, and you are unfree to the extent that you cannot. This is obviously 
a kind of freedomÂ—a very important kind. 
But it isnÂ’t the only kind. Contrary to what Locke says, there is a sense in which choices can be free or unfree. Harry Frankfurt made this clear.[451] 
A story will help us begin to understand FrankfurtÂ’s insightful analysis of freedom. 
Jones is a great writer who is addicted to heroin. Because his addiction is only moderate, he is able to function perfectly well even when he is heroin-deprived. (When heroin-deprived, he doesnÂ’t feel good, but he is in no way incapacitated.) He knows that, if he were to shoot up right now, the subsequent lethargy would make it impossible for him to write a single word for the rest of the day. He also knows that, if he doesnÂ’t write 10 pages today, he will lose his book contract. Jones does not want to lose the contract. Plus, he wants to grow as a writer, which he wonÂ’t do, at least not today, if he shoots up. He thus has a desire to not take the heroinÂ—even though he simultaneously has a desire to take the heroin. 
JonesÂ’ desire to take heroin is a first-order desire. JonesÂ’ desire not to act on this desire is a second-order desire. This is because JonesÂ’ desire not to take heroin is a desire as to what to do with another desire; it is a desire not to cave in to a desire to take heroin. 
Suppose that Jones caves in and he takes the heroin. In that case, Jones is a slave to his desires. His will has been compromised. He is not acting freely. 
But now suppose that Jones does not cave in. He does the right thing: instead of taking the heroin, he endures the discomfort of a heroin-free day and manages to get his work done. In this context, Jones is not a slave to his desires. His will has not been bent. His conduct expresses a Â“free will.Â” 
In light of considerations such as these, Frankfurt says that somebody has a free will to the extent that his conduct aligns with his second-order desires. 
But here a question arises. Why are second-order desires so special? Why is it that freedom consists in one's doing the bidding of oneÂ’s second-order desiresÂ—as opposed to oneÂ’s third-order, or fourth-order, or first-order desires? What, in this context, is so special about the number two? 
When the heroin-addicted writer decides not to take heroin, what is driving him is a rational appraisal of his situation. But when the heroin-addicted writer gives in to his addiction, it is not his rationality (or his morality) that is driving him. 
Before we can close this argument, we must address FrankfurtÂ’s discussion of the concept of a Â“person.Â” By a Â“person,Â” Frankfurt does not mean a member of the species homo sapiens. He means anything that has the same basic psychological architecture that we have. What is so special about that structure? First of all, we are self-conscious. Second, we are rational. Third, we are rational not only about how to attain our objectives, but also about what those objectives should be. What distinguishes persons from nonÂ­persons is that the former, but not the latter, subject their own desires (and, more generally, their own mental states) to critical scrutiny. 
Non-persons are often very clever when it comes to figuring out how to attain their objectives; for example, beavers show a lot of intelligence when it comes to building dams. But they are not smart about whether they should be building dams in the first place. The question doesnÂ’t arise. They have the desire, and they act on it (or they die trying). In general, persons do, whereas non-persons do not, subject their own desires to rational scrutiny. NonÂ­persons do not ask themselves: Â“What would the consequences of acting on this desire be? And should I act on this desire?Â” 
We persons, on the other hand, do subject our objectives to rational assessment. And this is obviously made possible by the fact that we are self-conscious. If I am overtaken by a desire to build a dam, I will ask myself: Â“how would my acting on this desire help my overall interests?Â” 
We can now close the argument. Whenever someone is driven by a rational assessment of their own desires, they are driven by a desire about a desire. Thus, one is rational only to the extent that it is oneÂ’s second-order desires that drive oneÂ’s conduct. There is a sense in which rational conduct is free and in which irrational conduct is not. 
To make it clear what this sense is, we must first distinguish between intelligent conduct and rational conduct. An irrational act can involve an enormous amount of intelligence. Smith is a brilliant inventor. He tries to impress his wife by building a giant robot that sings romantic songs in a metallic voice. This alienates her and she divorces him. Moreover, the financial and personal resources he sunk into this project have left him destitute. Smith's act might have been about as intelligent as an act can be. But it was not a rational act. For intelligently carried out though the act was, the immediate object of that act (namely, the construction of a robot that would sing love songs to his wife so that heÂ’d be spared the trouble of doing so) was not intelligently arrived and failed to embody consideration of relevant facts that it was well within SmithÂ’s ability to consider. 
A rational act is one that embodies due regard for one's various interests. 
An irrational act is one that does not. An intelligent but impulsive act (e.g., Smith's speedily building this robot to allay his rapidly growing anxieties about his marital situation, all of which are projective but which become legitimate as a result of this endeavor on his part) fails to embody due regard for one's own interests. (Smith isn't taking into account the consequences of his actions; he is misdeploying his vast stores of intelligence. And, granting that there are different kinds of intelligence, he obviously has whatever kind of intelligence one needs to have to know that (supposing for argument's sake that there's no chance that this project would bring him to the attention of any potential benefactors) this project is bound to land him on Skid Row.) So far as one is driven by first order desires, one is neglecting to gratify one's second order desires. So, given that second order desires are clearly more closely hewed to one's middle-and long-term welfare---or, if it isn't one's own welfare that one cares about, one's middle-and long-term situations---it is clearly more rational to act on one's second than on one's first order desires. Also, to make a point we'll develop in Chapter 26, it's often rational to perform actions in which, were one's first-order desires allowed to discharge themselves, they'd be expressed. Too much self-restraint is dysfunctional and, in addition to being unpleasurable, seals off possible well springs of insight and creativity. But, setting aside cases of psychopathology, when a person performs one of these enjoyment-oriented actions, he isn't acting on an impulse; he's acting on his approval of an impulse. In other words, he's considered the impulse, determined that it lines up with second order desires (or, what I believe to be different, his values), and, on that basis, lifted the initial inhibition on his impulse. So, while the resulting action may be indistinguishable from what he would have done had the impulse itself been the proximal cause of his deeds, his psychological condition, given that his action was not directly prompted by that impulse, is radically different from what it would have been had that action been thus prompted.[452] 

Having distinguished between rational conduct and intelligent, we may proceed with our discussion of FrankfurtÂ’s analysis of freedom. 
5.01 FrankfurtÂ’s analysis of freedom (continued) 
ThereÂ’s more to being free than being able to do what you want to do. Your desires must reflect who you are. If they donÂ’t, those desires belong to you but arenÂ’t of you. And in that case, you are alienated from your own mental states, in much the way that a person with ParkinsonÂ’s is alienated from his body. 
But, in a way, the alienation is even worse. Involuntary behavior is unintentional behavior. Intentional behavior is voluntary behavior. Voluntary behavior is desire-driven behavior. (If you donÂ’t want to raise your arm, but it goes up anyway, you didnÂ’t intend for it to happen.) Epileptic fits are not actions. Unintended behaviors are not actions. Unlike actions, theyÂ’re undergone, not done. So estrangement from oneÂ’s own actions amounts to estrangement from all of oneÂ’s own desires; and itÂ’s hard to imagine a condition less free than that. 
5.1 FrankfurtÂ’s emendation of this analysis 
Another story will help expose a problem with the analysis of freedom just described, and it will also clarify the raison dÂ’Ãªtre for FrankfurtÂ’s soon to be discussed emendations of it. 
SmithÂ’s first-order desires are seriously out of alignment with his second. He values writing poetry; heÂ’s good at it; and he enjoys it about as much as itÂ’s humanly possible to enjoy it. But he has a voracious craving for drugs. His craving for drugs, especially cocaine, is unusually strong; and his desire to write poetry, though intense, is not as intense as his desire to do cocaine. 
SmithÂ’s desire to do cocaine is out of alignment with many of his values (second-order desires). Were he to give into this desire, he couldnÂ’t write poetry; nor could he maintain friendships or play sports or, with only a few exceptions, do any of the other things he values. For this reason, he doesnÂ’t give in. But given how intense his craving is, every day is a struggle for Smith. If, as Frankfurt suggests, one is free to the extent that one acts on oneÂ’s second-order desires, Smith is as free as a person can be. But given how hard life is for Smith, itÂ’s counterintuitive to suppose that heÂ’s maximally free. To be sure he has a kind of freedom, and he has it in abundance. But thereÂ’s some other sort of freedom that he doesnÂ’t have. 
Frankfurt is aware of this problem, and he revises his view to deal with it. According to his revised view, if an act is to be free, it is necessary that it be driven by a second-order desire, but it isnÂ’t sufficient. Another condition must be met: oneÂ’s first-order desires must be consistent with the second-order desires that are driving that act. 
HereÂ’s the idea. Person X has no self-control. He binges on drugs and food, and he hates himself for doing this; but he canÂ’t stopÂ—heÂ’s too weak and his urges are too strong. His life has no meaning and he knows it; but he will not, or cannot, do anything about it. Unlike X, Person Y has a huge amount of self-control and never caves into temptation. But everything is a struggle, since heÂ’s always fighting temptation, like a drowning man trying to stay afloat. (Y is like Smith.) Person Z cannot be categorized with X or with 
Y. Z always does what he values, which is composing music. And what he values is what he wants. He wants what he wants to want. Because heÂ’s doing what he wants, he has the freedom that X has that Y lacks. Because heÂ’s doing what he wants to want, he has the kind of freedom that Y has that X lacks. And since, of the three, heÂ’s the only one who has both kinds of freedom, heÂ’s obviously the most free of them all. 
Thus, one is free insofar as two conditions are met: (i) one acts on oneÂ’s second-order desires, as opposed to oneÂ’s first-order desires; and (ii) oneÂ’s second-order desires are in alignment with oneÂ’s first-order desires. 
To see the merits, and also the shortcomings, of FrankfurtÂ’s brilliant analysis, we must take a moment to say how that analysis relates to compatibilism. 
5.2 Â“x is freeÂ”= Â“x does what x wants to provided that what he wants to do is adequately rooted in his personality structureÂ” 
WeÂ’ve considered two analyses of freedom: (i) Â“x performed act A freelyÂ” = 
Â“it is because x chose to do A that he did it,Â” and (ii) Â“performed A freelyÂ’Â’ = Â“A 
reflects who x really is.Â” These two views can be combined into the view that 
(iii) Â“x performed act A freelyÂ” = Â“it is because x chose to A that he did it, provided that this choice of xÂ’s reflects who x really is.Â” 
This analysis, which is basically FrankfurtÂ’s, embodies a profound insight 
into the nature of human freedom. WeÂ’ll see in Chapter 26 that, although itÂ’s a 
step in the right direction, it isnÂ’t correct: for it is possible to warp oneÂ’s higher-
order desires to suit oneÂ’s first-order desires and, thus, to make oneÂ’s higher-
order desires be mere vehicles for first-order desires. 
But right now, IÂ’d like to concentrate on an apparent problem with FrankfurtÂ’s analysis that, although, I suspect, some would be inclined to think otherwise, isnÂ’t an actual problem with it: 
(FD)[453] 
Smith has given himself over to drug addiction. He spends days doing drugs. (He has unlimited supplies of money and never has trouble getting them.) Smith has many talentsÂ— heÂ’s a great water-skier, a great short-story writer, etc., but, because of his addiction, these gifts of his lie fallow. 
Green, on the other hand, hasnÂ’t given himself over to addiction. He spends his days doing things that augment who he is. Green canÂ’t indulge every craving that he has. Unlike Smith, he doesnÂ’t have the money to do so. 
You (JMK/Frankfurt) would say that Green is freer than Smith, and your reason would be that, even though he canÂ’t gratify as many desires as Smith can, the desires that Green does gratify have the right roots, whereas those that Smith gratifies do not. 
I grant that SmithÂ’s condition is worse than GreenÂ’s, and also that Smith is less free than Green. But, contrary to what you say, that is because, when it comes to desire gratification, GreenÂ’s batting average is better than SmithÂ’s. There are a lot of aspirations that Smith has that will be thwarted as long as heÂ’s imprisoned by addiction. Smith wants to do cocaine more than he wants to be a writer, but it doesnÂ’t follow that he no longer wants 
to be a writer. He could very well want both.[454] 
LetÂ’s suppose he does. In that case, a very strong desire of his is being frustrated. ItÂ’s true that heÂ’s the one whoÂ’s frustrating it, but that doesnÂ’t mean it isnÂ’t frustrated. 
Smith will inevitably have many other desires that his cocaine addiction dooms to frustration. In his pre-addiction days, we may suppose, Smith enjoyed many things that he no longer enjoys. We can assume that he desired to do each of these things, and we can also assume that he still desires them, even though he obviously doesnÂ’t desire them as strongly as he desires cocaine. Many desires are rooted in personality structures. A desire to play the piano or read Nietzsche doesnÂ’t just overtake one; itÂ’s rooted in enduring structural facts about oneÂ’s personality. And as long as the personality structure is there, oneÂ’s inability to express it in the form of action is, practically by definition, a form of frustration. SmithÂ’s personality structure may still support those desires. (And almost certainly will. Addiction doesnÂ’t turn people into complete vegetables, at least not right away, and usually not ever.) It could be that Smith thinks it would be greater. But itÂ’s not so clear that it would in fact be greater. The phenomenological expression of that frustration would be more intense. But that doesnÂ’t necessarily mean that the desire in question is itself more intense. Desires, even short-lived ones, are structures; they arenÂ’t feelings. And the feelings to which a desire gives rise donÂ’t necessarily make it clear how intense that desire really is. 
FD is close to the truth, but it falls just short. Another story shows why. Aaronson is a coward who has no self-confidence. So even though he wants to write novels and is extremely talented at it, he doesnÂ’t do so. It isnÂ’t safe enough. ItÂ’s too bohemian for his stodgy, blinkered parents and for his equally stodgy friends (who he doesnÂ’t even likeÂ—he just pretends to like them, since heÂ’s supposed to). To make a living, Aaronson sells insurance, which he hates. His life is a waking death. 
In living as others want him to, Smith is surrendering his freedom and he is also dooming many desires of his to frustration. But those two failings, though related, are not identical. Aaronson is suppressing an important side of himself. The personality structures that he is suppressing give rise to many ardent desires, but they arenÂ’t identical with such desires. His losing his freedom consists in his suppressing these structures. The desire frustration that follows is an effect of this loss of freedom and isnÂ’t identical with it. 
So AaronsonÂ’s loss of freedom isnÂ’t identical with his being unable to do what he wants; his being unable to do what he wants is a by-product of his loss of freedom. To be sure, his inability to do what he wants is itself a loss of freedom. But, important though this second kind of freedom is, itÂ’s distinct from the first kind and a derivative of it. So being free consists primarily in being oneself, and secondarily in being able to do what one wants. And this is obviously close to what Frankfurt is saying, if it doesnÂ’t coincide with it. 
5.4. Frankfurt's analysis systemically flawed 
Many analyses that philosophers put forth seem not to embody genuine attempts to find the truth. Frankfurt's analysis of freedom does embody such an attempt. And that attempt is almost successful. 
But it falls short. In the next chapter, we'll see why. Here's an outline of what we'll find. Acts that are driven by one's Higher-order desires need not be free; for people can, and often do, warp their higher-order desires, so as to make them fit their first-order desires. Higher-order desires, in other words, can become vehicles for first-order desires. A lazy, weak person can warp his higher-order desires so that they merely rubber-stamp the craven first-order desires of which his actions are compulsive expressions. 
We will find that truly free acts are those that are driven, not by higher-order desires, but by values. We will find that there is no agency of any kind where there are no selves, and we will find that, where there are no values, there are no selves, though there may be minds. I will leave it at that for now, since the entirety of the next chapter will be spent decrypting these remarks. I'll end the present chapter by making some points about psychopathology that bear out what we'll say in the next chapter and also make it clear to what a large extent what we're going to say is derivative of what Frankfurt already has said. 
6.0 Ego-dystonic vs. ego-syntonic 
To be free, we have argued, one must identify with oneÂ’s desiresÂ—gratifying them isnÂ’t enough. Psychologists refer to mental contents that one identifies with as ego-syntonic and to those that one doesnÂ’t identify with as ego-dystonic. An understanding of this distinction may clarify why determinism is necessary for freedom and why indeterminism threatens it. 
Some people who suffer from psychological disturbances identify with their symptoms. They donÂ’t see their symptoms as symptoms. For example, the acute schizophrenic who sees goblins dancing on his bed thinks that heÂ’s seeing things as they are. To his mind, itÂ’s other people who are wrong: they canÂ’t see whatÂ’s there; he can. The same holds of the paranoiac who thinks her phone conversations are being monitored by the President. 
These are ego-syntonic disorders. The viewpoint embodied in the patientÂ’s symptoms coincides with the viewpoint of the patient himself. The latter doesnÂ’t regard the former as an Â“alien intruder.Â” 
But not all psychological disturbances are like this. The classic example is 
obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).[455] 
Those afflicted with this disorder obsess over matters hardly worthy of their attention; theyÂ’re compelled to perform absurd acts (e.g., theyÂ’re compelled to snap their fingers if they have a thought about the number seven); theyÂ’re also compelled to perform normal acts an abnormal number of times or for an abnormally long period (e.g., theyÂ’re compelled to brush their teeth 20 times a day or to shower for hours on end). But sufferers of OCD know that their obsessions and compulsions are irrational. They succumb to the compulsions not because they believe there to be any objective reason to do so, but because, for reasons unknown to them, they suffer intolerable anxiety if they donÂ’t. And they know that their obsessions are not legitimate; they know that those obsessions arenÂ’t comparable to EinsteinÂ’s obsession with identifying framework-invariant physical laws or BeethovenÂ’s obsessive dedication to perfecting the Hammerklavier Sonata. They obsess despite themselves. They donÂ’t think their obsessions have any legitimate basis. They just canÂ’t stop them. 
Thus, those afflicted with OCD donÂ’t identify with their symptoms. Unlike schizophrenics, they see their symptoms as symptoms. Their symptoms belong to their minds but not to them; they are like alien-invaders that have taken root in their psyches. 
Bearing these points in mind, consider the following scenario. You hate numbers. You are not detail-oriented. You want to spend all day writing novels. (YouÂ’re a very talented novelist.) You know all of this. But one day you are overcome with an intense desire to become an accountant. This desire came out of nowhere. It has no roots in your personality. 
You obviously donÂ’t identify with this desire. This is because it has no roots in who you are. And the reason it has no such roots is that your existing values, desires, aspirations, and so on, had no hand in giving rise to it. 
Were you to act on this desire, there is a sense in which youÂ’d be acting freely, but thereÂ’s a deeper sense in which youÂ’d be acting unfreely. YouÂ’d be acting (un)freely in a sense similar to (though not quite coincident with, as weÂ’ll see) the sense in which somebody who hands his money over to a gunman is acting (un)freely. 
Suppose that, while pointing a gun at Smith, Green says Â“your money or your life.Â” In handing over his money, Smith is acting freely in the sense that heÂ’s doing what it is that, the circumstances being what they are, he wants to do; and heÂ’s acting unfreely in the sense that, the circumstances being what they are, what he wants to do is not what he wants to want to do. 
Much like Smith, youÂ’re damned if you do and damned if you donÂ’t.
