And that's how one wants to keep it. So one doesn't exercise due diligence in the way of interpreting existing evidence or generating new evidence. LetÂ’s refer to this kind of repression as Â“repression1.Â” 
So repression1 doesnÂ’t involve driving some already formed belief into the unconscious. It involves abstaining from doing the things that, so one strongly suspects, would generate the sort of evidence that make acceptance of that belief de rigueur. 
The other kind of repression, which weÂ’ll refer to as Â“repression2," does involve already formed beliefs. The essence of repression2 is dissociation. When trying to determine how to act, one tries to give due weight to each of the decision-relevant beliefs. So, in effect, each decision-relevant idea Â‘gets a vote.Â’ To repress2 an idea is to take its vote away; it is to decide to give it no weight. 
Both repression1 and repression2 involve conflict between, on the one hand, forces within oneself of which one is aware and, on the other hand, forces within oneself of which one is unaware. But the natures of the unconscious forces, and also of the conscious forces, involved in the one case of the one sort of repression are different from those involved in cases of the other sort. 
Both forms of repression involve the construction and operationalization of a narrative alternative to the one that, supposing the repressed idea to be correct (which it typically is), describes reality as it really is. In other words, both forms of repression involve rationalization. Without rationalization, it is hard, if not impossible, to repress an idea and also to keep it repressed. (That said, rationalization-construction is more heavily involved in ensuring that already repressed ideas stay repressed than it is in initially repressing them.) 
Right now weÂ’ll talk about Â“self-deception," since references to Â“repressionÂ” would resonate in a confusion-engendering way with the points just made. In due course, weÂ’ll map what we say about self-deception onto repression1 and repression2. 
2.0 How is repression possible? 
The possibility of self-deception, and therefore of both repression1 and repression2, is a consequence of the following three facts. 
(1) 
The mind is not a perfectly unified entity; it consists of various parts that communicate with each other only very imperfectly. The right hand doesnÂ’t always know what the left is doing. 

(2). There are two very different ways in which one can be aware of a given thing. One can either have Â“knowledge by acquaintanceÂ” of that thing or one can have Â“knowledge by descriptionÂ” of it. See Chapter 10, Section 9.0, for definitions of these terms and explanations of the corresponding concepts. 

(3) 
There are two very different senses in which a given mental content can be Â‘conscious.Â’ On the one hand, it can be conscious in the sense that it is a constituent of consciousness. (Sense-perceptions are such constituents; so are itches, tickles, and other sensations.) On the other hand, it can be conscious in the sense that it is a mental entity of which one is conscious. Your belief that 1 + 1 = 2 is not a constituent of consciousness. It is "conscious" in the sense that you are, or can readily become, conscious of it. Of course, we are conscious of rocks, trees, and stars, but donÂ’t describe such things as Â‘conscious.Â’ But that, I think, is because they are not mental entities and we thus have no tendency to co-categorize them with constituents of consciousness or with mental entities of any other kind. But since constituents of consciousness are the most obvious examples of mentality, and since we describe them as Â‘conscious,Â’ we have an inclination to describe mental entities that are not themselves constituents of consciousness but that we are (non-inferentially) aware of as Â‘conscious.Â’ We thus, without knowing it, use the word Â‘consciousÂ’ equivocally: sometimes it means Â‘mental entity that is a constituent of consciousnessÂ’ and sometimes it means 


Â‘mental entity that we are directly conscious of.Â’ 
2.1 How is repression possible? (continued) 
Given (3), it immediately follows that there is a sense in which all mental entities that arenÂ’t constituents of consciousness are unconscious. Your knowledge that 1 + 1 = 2 is not a constituent of consciousness. So far as it is conscious, it is only in the sense that you can readily become conscious of it. And most of the time you are not conscious of it. But it exists, and is operative, even when you are not conscious of it. If you didnÂ’t know that 1 + 1 = 2, then the way in which you dealt with the world---the way in which you transacted with others, as well as the way you dealt with problems not having an interpersonal dimension----would differ radically from the way in which, even when youÂ’re not consciously thinking that 1 + 1 = 2 or a fortiori thinking about your knowledge that 1 + 1 = 2, you in fact deal with the world. The way in which you reason is not only consistent with, but expressive of, a knowledge that 1 + 1 = 2, the same being true of the way in which you interact with people and also of the way in which you manage matters that donÂ’t involve others. But it is only during, at most, a tiny few of the occasions when oneÂ’s thoughts and overt acts are guided by a conscious awareness of the fact that 1 + 1 = 2. It is only rarely that one consciously thinks about the fact that 1 + 1 = 2 or, therefore, that one thinks about oneÂ’s belief that 1 + 1 = 2. 
Bearing this in mind, suppose, if only for argumentÂ’s sake, that your knowledge that 1 + 1 = 2 is identical with some physiological structure. It follows from what weÂ’ve said that, even when you are not conscious of the fact 1 + 1 = 2, or therefore of your knowledge of that fact, this belief of yours is psychologically operative. Of course, given that itÂ’s a physiological structure, itÂ’s inevitably operative in the same, thought-free way as an involuntary muscle-spasm. But, even when not the object of consciousness, that physiological structure is also psychologically active; itÂ’s active, in other words, as a belief, and not just as a heap of molecules. Your knowledge that 1 + 1 = 2 informs the way in which you deal with the world even when you arenÂ’t consciously thinking that 1 + 1 = 2; and, were this belief of yours inoperative whenever it was blazing a trail across your consciousness, your way of dealing with the world would bear little resemblance to your actual way of dealing with it. 
Given (2), it follows that you may not recognize a given mental content of yours for what it is. You can have thoughts about Charlemagne and you thus have a concept of him. But if you met him, you wouldn't recognize him; and so long as you didn't figure out who he was, you would, without knowing it, have two distinct concepts of him (one based on personal encounters with him, the other based on statements of historians). Given anything that isn't itself a constituent of consciousness, one can fail to recognize it for what it is and, consequently, one can unwittingly have two distinct concepts of that thing. Propositional attitudes are not constituents of consciousness. So one could, without knowing it, have two distinct concepts of one of one's own propositional attitudes. 
2.2 How is repression possible? (continued) 
A story will clarify these points. You live next to the Â“Springfield StranglerÂ”: a prolific serial killer who, in the town of Springfield, has killed many children by strangling them. His identity is unknown to everyone (except, of course, the Springfield Strangler himself). You know this person as Â“Ted Jones.Â” Since you watch the news, you know of the Springfield Killer. But you donÂ’t know that Ted Jones is the Springfield Strangler. You find TedÂ’s company agreeable and you play tennis with him. 
In this situation just described, there is some one individual x such that: 
(i) 
you are acquainted with x, 

(ii) 
you have knowledge by description of x, 


and: 
(iii) you know that, in virtue of these facts, you have two distinct conceptions of some one individual. 
But this changes. For, at time t, you find out that Ted Jones is the Springfield Strangler. You see him being arrested. You hear the subsequent news reports. You consider various facts directly known to you about Ted Jones: his sudden nightly disappearances, which typically involved TedÂ’s dragging large trunks to his pick-up truck; the stench emanating from his house, which he implausibly explained by saying that he had a clogged sink; etc. You thus realize that Ted Jones is indeed the Springfield Killer. 
Just as one can, without knowing it, be acquainted with a given individual while also having descriptive knowledge of it, so one can be acquainted with a given one of oneÂ’s own mental contents while also having descriptive knowledge of it. A corollary is that, given some mental entity E that belongs to one, one can discover that one actually has some attitude towards E that one did not previously know oneself to have. You can discover that the gnawing feeling of unpleasantness you experience whenever somebody mentions Smith is your detestation of Smith. Emotions are distinct from their manifestations in consciousness. Your love of your mother (supposing for argumentÂ’s sake that sheÂ’s alive and that you do love her) is an enduring psychological structure; it is not an ephemeral event. But it gives rise to ephemeral conscious events (to pangs of remorse when you inadvertently hurt her feelings, to surges of joy when, after not hearing from her for three months, she calls you, etc.). But your love for her is not itself a conscious event. It is "conscious" only in the Pickwickian sense that you are conscious of it. Beliefs, like emotions, are enduring structures and are to be distinguished from the constituents of consciousness to which they may give rise. All propositional attitudes are enduring structures and are thus to be distinguished from any constituents of consciousness for whose existence theyÂ’re responsible. And a given emotion, e.g., your hatred of Smith, can give rise to conscious events of very different kinds. It can give rise to gnawing feelings of unpleasantness (as when you hear that heÂ’s coming over), to intense feelings of satisfaction (as when you hear that he flunked his economics exam), etc. And given two qualitatively distinct conscious events, both of them expressions in consciousness of some one propositional attitude x and both of them, consequently, ways in which that emotion presents itself to consciousness, there isnÂ’t necessarily any reason why you should recognize x in both of those conscious events. To sum up, given only that x and y are both conscious derivatives of some propositional attitude z, it doesnÂ’t follow that any one part of oneÂ’s mind has the information needed to recognize z in both x and y. For this reason, it follows that one can have two divergent attitudes towards z. 
Given (1), therefore, it follows that one can have very different attitudes towards a given one of oneÂ’s own propositional attitudes. And it also follows that, without knowing it, one can view a given one of oneÂ’s own propositional attitudes as despicable and as laudatory, as deserving to be cultivated and expressed in action and as deserving to be annihilated. 
2.3 Intrapsychic conflict in relation to repression 
But self-deception is not mere ignorance of what one is feeling. In fact, self-deception seems to presuppose that, at some level, one has knowledge of the thing of which one lacks conscious knowledge. So given only that one can fail to recognize some one propositional attitude in two different conscious expressions of it, all that follows is that one is not completely transparent to oneself; it doesnÂ’t follow that one can self-deceive; it doesnÂ’t follow that there can be some sort of internal conflict---between what one knows and what one wants to know, between what is unconscious (because repressed) and what is conscious (because countenanced). A few additions to the three points made thus far will make it clear how self-deception is possible. 
First of all, one must distinguish having a given propositional attitude (or, more generally, mental content) from knowing that one has it. Setting aside anything that has to do with repression, one can feel a certain way towards so and so but not know it. Knowing that one feels that way involves making a judgment about oneÂ’s mental state. 
Also, propositional attitudes never make an appearance in consciousness in propria persona---or, rather, they do so, but only in the indirect sense in which rocks and trees do. What is in consciousness; i.e., what is constitutive of consciousness, is at best some representative or derivative of a propositional attitude. On Monday, Smith feels a surge of anger towards his dad. On Tuesday, he feels another surge of anger. These surges of anger, let us suppose, are expressions of hatred. But the hatred per se isnÂ’t what entered his consciousness. What Smith is directly given are various indications that he hates his father. These indications are strong. (In any case, we can imagine developing the story in such a way that, supposing Smith sane, they left no room for reasonable doubt on his part as to whether he hated his father.) But he still has to Â“synthesizeÂ” them; he still has to make a judgment to the effect that they express some enduring attitude. In most cases, this is done so automatically, that he is unaware that any judgment has been made. 
Those judgments are often quite wrong. We like the person towards whom we have constant surges of rage. We dislike the person who repeatedly makes us feel good. (He makes you feel good because he wants to disarm you. And he knows that by Â“pushing the right buttonsÂ”---buying you chocolates, taking you to the zoo, etc.---heÂ’ll generate feelings that, when not the result of this sort of chicanery, tend to express genuine affection. YouÂ’ll know in your bones that there is something very wrong about the situation. But you wonÂ’t able to say what it is. Assuming that your views about others are mainstream and are thus hewed to the glib, emotionally-driven narratives in terms of which all but the most penetrating thinkers understand others, you wonÂ’t have developed the ability to articulate your gut feelings or, therefore, to give them a form in which you or others are likely to give them the credence they deserve. Given that fact, along with the red-herrings that this manipulator is pouring into evidence-repository on the basis of which you make your conscious judgments, your verdict will be that he is a good person. 
In any case, supposing that one has a given propositional attitude, what one is given is not that attitude per se, but various evidences thereof, and those evidences may be dispersed over time and may occur in multifarious contexts. When the propositional attitude is an emotionally sterile one---when it concerns a belief about number-theory or epistemology---we have no trouble making the 
needed judgments.[467] 

2.3.1 Intrapsychic conflict in relation to repression1 
ItÂ’s one thing to suspect that something is the case; itÂ’s quite another to know it. The police suspect that Smith is the murderer. The evidence points to him (the bloody footprints leading to his front door step, the hair samples, the smudged fingerprints which are consistent with SmithÂ’s being the killer even though they donÂ’t prove it). But the police donÂ’t yet know that Smith is their man. For there are gaps in the evidence they have on him, as a result of which there are semi-reasonable ways of modeling the scenario that, if correct, would entail that Smith was not the murderer. 
Bearing these facts in mind, suppose the following. Smith is your best friend. You owe him your life many times over. The police strongly suspect that heÂ’s the murderer. You're the detective who is assigned the case. Like your colleagues, you strongly suspect that he's guilty. But you aren't sure. And you don't want to be sure. So you choose not to exercise due diligence. 
What we call Â“repressionÂ” involves failure to exercise due diligence. We suspect, but we donÂ’t know, which is how we want to it to keep it. 
So the customary conception of repression is erroneous. The customary conception is given by assertion that (Â“CCRÂ” is short for conventional conception of repressionÂ”): 
(CCR) the person in question has some propositional attitude P such that (a) he knowingly chooses to cease to be aware of it; i.e., he knowingly drives it into his unconscious; and such that (b) P is constantly struggling to break into consciousness, failing to do so only because the patient keeps it out. 
Part (b) of CCR is indeed paradoxical. For, presumably, to keep P out of his consciousness, the patient must know what P is: otherwise he wonÂ’t know what it is heÂ’s trying to keep out. But if he knows what it is heÂ’s trying to keep out, then heÂ’s conscious of it and it is ipso facto unrepressed. 
But CCR doesnÂ’t correctly describe the nature of repression. ItÂ’s one thing to know that your best friend is the Springfield Killer. ItÂ’s another thing to suspect it but choose not to follow the relevant trail of evidence. Repression---or, rather, repression1 (the subscript has again become relevant)---is a failure to do 
something; it is a failure to perform the operations by which one customarily generates oneÂ’s beliefs; it isnÂ’t an operation performed on existing beliefs (or propositional attitudes of any other kind). So repression1 involves choosing not to learn something that, if learned and therefore known, one would wish that one had never learned, but only after it was too late. 
While your parents are on vacation, let us suppose, you look through their bedroom and come across your motherÂ’s private journal. On the basis of its external appearance, along with the information that youÂ’ve gleaned from a cursory glance at its interior, you know enough to know that the journal provides detailed information about your motherÂ’s sexual exploits over the last few years. You thus know that, were you to read on, youÂ’d learn things about your mother that you know you donÂ’t want to know. So you choose not to read on. Your wish not to be traumatized overpowers your curiosity. 
Repression1 is to be understood along these lines. When we speak, 
inaccurately, of Â“repressed knowledge," weÂ’re referring (in at least some cases, viz., those that arenÂ’t cases of repression2) to suspicions that we have chosen not to verify, since we suspect that, were we to do so, weÂ’d be stuck with 
knowledge that we wish we didnÂ’t have. 
Every case of repression1 does, as CCR says, involve intrapsychic conflict. But, contrary to what CCR says, the conflict is not between unconscious knowledge of some truth T on the one hand, and conscious ignorance of T on the other. The conflict is between a wish to know the truth and a wish to not know the truth. 
2.3.2 One reason why repression1 often fails 
OneÂ’s agency only goes so far; there is much within oneÂ’s mind that falls outside its scope. Among the various mental entities that lie beyond the reach of what it is for one to choose to occur are the aforementioned judgment-producing processes. So it is not within my power to completely suspend those processes. 
And so far as it is within my power to do so, it is not in the direct, robust sense in which one can choose to move oneÂ’s arm, but in the indirect and attenuated sense in which one can choose to become obese. One doesnÂ’t really choose to become obese; one chooses to do things that will redirect automatic processes in such a way that obesity is the inevitable result. Similarly, one can no more choose to stop making judgments than one choose to stop digesting food. One can choose courses of action that will have the effect of redirecting the automatically occurring stream of mental activity that yields judgments (e.g., one can choose activities that will flood that judgment-making faculty with information concerning the judgments that one wants to avoid making); and one can also choose to do things that will deplete that faculty of the energy it needs to function (e.g., one can do intense exercise for hours on end). One can also choose to paralyze or even permanently damage the physiological underpinnings of those judgments (e.g., one can get drunk, thereby paralyzing them, or one can get a lobotomy, thereby destroying them). But, unless one goes so far as to damage oneÂ’s brain, that stream of activity will eventually start yielding the very judgments that you donÂ’t want it to. 
2.3.3 The concept of anxiety in relation to repression1 
The anxiety that the subject feels when the forces of repression1 break down isnÂ’t the result of some hitherto unconscious knowledge entering consciousness. It is the result oneÂ’s own thought-processes, despite oneÂ’s attempt to stymie them, following up on clues that it had good reason to believe would lead to a belief that one doesnÂ’t want to have. 
Â“But if you already know that you donÂ’t want to have that belief, then you must already know what that belief is and must already have it.Â” This is false. Suspicion isnÂ’t knowledge; and thereÂ’s nothing paradoxical about not wanting to pursue suspicions that one suspects would, if pursued, lead to knowledge one would rather not have. 
Also, one can know what sort of thing something is without knowing which thing it is. If I ask you to find a unique number n such that the square root of n is over 10 and such that two people whose middle names are Â“RobertÂ” each own n1/3 acres of land, and I prove to you, without identifying the number in question, that there is indeed exactly one such number, you know what sort of thing youÂ’re looking for without as of yet being able to identify any number that fits the description. 
A story will make this clear. You are acquainted with Sally. You know that exactly one person has been stealing money from your wallet---but you donÂ’t know who it is. So, by virtue of knowing the description Â“person who has been stealing money from my walletÂ” to be uniquely satisfied, you have descriptive knowledge of Sally. But you donÂ’t know that Sally satisfies that description. 
3.0 Repression2 
Whereas repression1 involves failing to form a belief, repression2 involves blinding oneself to an existing belief that one has already formed. 
How is repression2 possible? How does one repress a belief that has already been formed? And how does one keep such a belief repressed? To clarify the second question, how does one keep a belief that one doesnÂ’t want to enter consciousness from doing so? For one must be conscious of the enemy hammering at the walls of oneÂ’s fortress if one is to take measures to keep him out. But, in this context, one cannot be conscious of the enemy, since what one is conscious of ipso facto isnÂ’t repressed. 
3.1 A necessary condition for repression2 
For a propositional attitude to be a candidate for repression2, it must be a 
source of conflict within oneÂ’s own psyche. It isnÂ’t enough that it be a source of pain. One often fails to repress2 oneÂ’s most painful memories. (Holocaust survivors remember what theyÂ’ve been through.) People typically choose to 
suppress painful memories. In other words, they choose not to think about them. But suppression isnÂ’t repression2. 
One represses2 knowledge that one has about oneÂ’s husband, because oneÂ’s life is so structured that it would be severely disrupted were the truths thereby known to be admitted. One likes many aspects of oneÂ’s life; it may well be that, despite the ugly truths in question about oneÂ’s husband, one believes (perhaps rightly) that being married to him really is better than not being married to him. But, since one couldnÂ’t stomach marriage to him if one admitted to oneself that he was a child-molesting ghoul, one represses2 that knowledge. 
And one may be right to. Repression2 isnÂ’t always a bad thing. In many contexts, itÂ’s the optimal thing. It may be that Sally's quality of life would plummet if she left her child-molesting husband; it may be that, were she to 
leave him, her children would be in danger. Since she couldnÂ’t be with him if she consciously knew that he was child-molester, sheÂ’s well advised to repress2 that knowledge, at least for the time being. 
A person who never repressed2 anything would quickly go mad. Repressions2 are necessary. So how is repression2 bad? First of all, repressions2 outlive their usefulness. The circumstances that prompts one to repress2 a given belief may well be replaced by circumstances in which oneÂ’s consciously 
having that belief is vital to oneÂ’s wellbeing. (In this context, take Â“beliefÂ” to 
stand for any propositional attitude.) But, repression2 being what it is, one will have no idea what it is that one is supposed to be aware of. In fact, one is unlikely to know that one has represssed2 anything important to oneÂ’s welfare. 
Also, repression2 isnÂ’t a one-off affair; it is an on-going process. Whenever one comes across information that confirms the repressed2 belief, one must either repress2 oneÂ’s knowledge of that information or one must convince oneself of the cogency of some spurious interpretation of that information. Since 
these cover-ups must themselves be covered up, more knowledge ends up being repressed2 and more spurious rationalizations are accepted. Each instance of 
repression2 creates a hole in oneÂ’s body of knowledge that one must explain away. Since these explanations cannot be genuine, and since each one incentivizes the creation of more bogus, anomaly-creating explanations, the need to plug up these holes disposes one to devalue truth and to hyper-value the methods of reasoning whose legitimacy these faux-explanations falsely assume. The result is a loss of both ratiocinative and ethical integrity. 
So, while repressions2 are not necessarily bad things, sometimes being indispensable to oneÂ’s well-being, they tend to stick around long after theyÂ’ve served any legitimate purpose; and during that time, they tend to spread and, as a result, to eat away at oneÂ’s psychological architecture. 
3.2 A repression2-conducive factor 
One can know something without that thingÂ’s being obvious to one. I know that there is a war in Iraq. But itÂ’s not obvious to me the way that it would be if I were there witnessing it. ItÂ’s harder to repress2 knowledge of 
the obvious than of the non-obvious. If your knowledge that your husband is a serial killer is based on inferences, even air-tight ones, it will be easier to repress2 it than it would be if it were based on personal observations of him killing people. 
That said, people can repress2 knowledge of truths that are as obvious as truths can be. But one cannot repress2 such knowledge without, in effect, telling oneself that one isnÂ’t capable of knowing the truth. Since the purpose of repression2 is the elimination of conflict within oneself, and since a complete 
loss of faith in oneÂ’s ratiocinative ability usually, but not always, creates more such conflict than it eliminates, repression2 tends to target knowledge of what is not totally obvious. In most cases of repression2, there must be what lawyers refer to as Â“plausible deniability.Â” 
3.2.1 A related point 
The things that one represses2 tend to be things that, although one knows them to be true, involve oneÂ’s making judgment-calls. Until your husbandÂ’s psychopathy assumes some particularly brazen form, any knowledge that you have of it involves your putting together various bits of data (e.g., various odd comments heÂ’s made, various murders that you hear about on the news, his unexplained absences during the times that when the murders occurred, his fitting the descriptions given to the police of the murderer). But, having as it does a basis in some many pieces of data, your subsequent knowledge that your husband is the murderer is shaky and is thus vulnerable to repression2, in a way that strictly sense-based knowledge is not. 
Â“But if oneÂ’s Â‘knowledgeÂ’ of some truth is shaky," it will be said, Â“then one isnÂ’t convinced of that truth. And if one isnÂ’t convinced of it, one doesnÂ’t have knowledge of it. One only has suspicions.Â” 
There are different reasons why one may lack confidence in one of oneÂ’s beliefs. It may be that one has not, as of yet, encountered adequate evidence for that belief. Or it may be that, even though one has encountered adequate evidence and even though, consequently, that belief would ordinarily be firm, one wants that belief to be false. If a belief concerns something personal, oneÂ’s standard of proof tends to be ridiculously high. What it would take to convince you that somebody youÂ’re not married to is cheating on his wife is miniscule to what it would take to convince you that your husband is cheating on you. 
To take a different example: the amount of evidence that favors the theory of evolution is simply enormous. But because that theory says, in effect, that weÂ’re orangutans whose lives have no meaning, we wonÂ’t judge it worthy of acceptance until itÂ’s met absurdly high standards of evidence. I have no doubt that people have always known that we evolved from other life forms. Given the anatomical, behavioral, and psychological similarities between us, on the one hand, and members of other mammalian species, on the other, itÂ’s inconceivable that we arenÂ’t related to them. Denying that orangutans are our biological kin is like denying that the one person in the room with grape jelly and crumbs around his mouth is the one who ate your jelly-doughnut. 
Of course, religious people say that God created us. But, if so, why did he choose to make us look so much like apes, and why did he choose to stock our minds with ignominious urges that constantly show us that those external similarities are but representations of internal ones? 
This brings us to another illustration of the principle in question: itÂ’s often said that FreudÂ’s theories arenÂ’t warranted by the empirical data. If you actually read what he says and then, bearing what you read in mind, study a single personÂ’s behavior for a period of around 10 minutes, it becomes clear that FreudÂ’s theories are theoretically extraordinarily conservative; it also becomes clear that he was simply making explicit the principles that we ordinarily use when making intuitive judgments about other people. People donÂ’t want to be told that they lie to themselves. People donÂ’t want to part with rationalizations; they donÂ’t want to face ugly realities. TheyÂ’d rather be a king in their dreams than a janitor in reality. So itÂ’s not hard to see why it is often dismissed, despite its staggering explanatory power and despite the extraordinarily high degree to which his claims accord with the principles that underlie our judgments. We'll state Freud's principle claims right now. 
3.2.2 Freud's Principle Claims 
Here is a one-paragraph outline of Freud's primary contentions: 
Nobody is perfectly transparent to himself. Nobody is conscious of everything that goes on in his mind. There are different reasons why one may not be conscious of given constituent of one's own mind. In some cases, one can readily become conscious of a constituent of one's mind of which one was previously unconscious. For example, let's suppose that, since the time you woke up this morning, you haven't been conscious of your belief that 2+2=4. You just became conscious of it. Given how effortless this transition was, it didn't involve your resisting any forces within yourself. It was unconscious because, until just a moment ago, you lacked a positive incentive to pay attention to it----not because you had a positive incentive to turn a blind eye to it. 
But in other cases, a given person may be unaware of a given constituent of his mind for the reason that he doesn't want to be aware of it. He finds it so distressing that he chooses to turn a blind eye to it---to repress it, in other words. In repressing that entity, the subject didn't destroy it; he merely blinded himself to it. The subject wouldn't have found that entity important enough to repress if he hadn't known it to have a profound bearing on how he should live and, therefore, on what he should aspire to do. Consequently, the desires to which it gives rise are necessarily especially intense ones, and the subject will experience intolerable frustration until they are discharged. 
Such a desire cannot be discharged unless it employs a subterfuge of some kind, given that it cannot possibly be the subject's conscious intention to gratify it. Such subterfuges are always of one of two types. 
Type #1: The desire in question can disguise itself as a desire that the subject consciously does wish to act on. An example: the subject detests his ailing mother. But he refuses to believe that he has anything but love for her. His detestation for her presents itself to his consciousness as a fanatical devotion to her being safe from both microbial and human predators. So he bathes her in scalding hot water and refuses to let her leave the house. In this way, his repressed hatred of her is discharged in the form of behavior that the subject believes to be motivated entirely by unalloyed concern for her wellÂ­being. 
Type #2: It can be expressed as a symptom. An example: Having repressed her complete detestation of her husband, a young woman finds herself gripped by a compulsive desire to do housework whenever her betrothed wishes to engage her in acts of physical intimacy. 
So far as the opposition to these contentions has been given an argumentative foundation, the arguments in question are pitifully weak and involve regressions to extremely crude and, in some cases, demonstrably false positions. Â“WeÂ’re computersÂ” (Fodor). Â“There is no consciousnessÂ” (Dennett). Â“There are no mindsÂ” (Quine). Â“The mind is completely transparent to itselfÂ” (Searle). Nobody believes or doubts or hopes for anything; terms referring to propositional attitudes (e.g. "hope," "believe," "intend") belong to Â‘folk-psychologyÂ’, which is no more accurate than folk-physicsÂ” (Paul and Patricia Churchland). Â“WeÂ’re better off trying to understand Baryshnikov's skill as a dancer in terms of fluid levels in his ears than his ability to upload, process, and distribute information in ways that ensure that his movements are appropriately coordinated.Â” (Searle). 
These willful denials of the obvious are often embedded in larger philosophical projects that are nothing short of risible, e.g. the Dretske-Fodor view that, details aside, there is no difference between my concept of a given a person and a photograph of a given person. 
And yet all of these flights into inanity are touted as Â“scientificÂ” and Â“rigorous.Â” Why? Â“BecauseÂ”, we are told, Â“in denying the existence of the mental, weÂ’re simply completing the process of ceasing to understand nature in animistic terms and weÂ’re thereby completing the victory of science over non-science.Â” 
But this argument is no good, and it's clear why. While it's certainly a good idea not to impute minds to stones, it's obviously not such a good idea not to impute them to people. So while itÂ’s a good idea not to understand the world 
projectively, we must remember that the projector itself cannot be a projection. 
3.3 Intrapsychic conflict in relation to repression2: some preliminaries (continued) 
A story, based on the remarks made in Sections 3.0-3.2.1., will help us clarify and develop the points weÂ’ve made about self-deception and repression2. You discover that your husbandÂ’s a psychopath. You donÂ’t see him killing anyone. But within the limits set by that fact, you are as sure of it as a rational person could be. Since this knowledge (or near-knowledge) cannot be reconciled with your life, at least not in its current form, and thus creates intolerable conflict within your psyche, you choose to repress it. 
Here is what repressing2 this knowledge involves. First of all, when taken with other propositions whose truth we may reasonably assume you to accept, the proposition: 
(1) My husband is a psychopathic ghoul all of whose protestations of love were fraudulent, as was everything else about him; which, given what it is to be a psychopath along with the well-known (to people interested in the subject) symptoms of psychopathy (glibness, specific lack of insight, etc.) 
entails the much more generic proposition: 
(2) There is some property P such that my husband has P and such that, by virtue of having P, my husband is a worse person than he would otherwise be; and a personÂ’s having P involves his doing the sorts of things that my husband does that trouble me (e.g., it involves his smoothly lying, his vacillating between inexplicable rage and glib charm, the contrast between how he acts and who he claims to be, his inability to authentic his claim that he was an admiral in the Navy). 
By virtue of knowing (1), therefore, you also know (2). So, during the fleeting moment when you consciously know (1), you also know (2). LetÂ’s henceforth refer to that fleeting moment as Â“FM.Â” 
(2), unlike (1), is something that you can keep in consciousness without having to overhaul your entire life. For (2), unlike (1), is sufficiently vague that your knowledge of it wonÂ’t make you want to retch at the mere sight of your husband. During FM, you realize that you wish you hadnÂ’t discovered (1). But, as you know, if you simply decide not to think about (1)---if you suppress, but do not repress, that knowledge---you wonÂ’t be able to live with yourself. You know that you must bury your knowledge of (1). But you also know that youÂ’ll be confronted with the same facts---the strange behaviors, the news reports, etc.Â­--that led you to know (1) in the first place; and you know that, unless you make some drastic change, those same facts will lead you right back to the same ugly place. 
So you make a decision. You know (2). And you know that you know it. With this knowledge in mind, you resolve that, henceforth, when confronted with the sort of datum that that led you to believe (1), youÂ’ll model it in a way that is consistent with (2) but that doesnÂ’t coincide with (1) or with anything else that would be equally disruptive to your current situation. 
Before we can move forward, we must recall some facts that weÂ’ve already discussed about propositional attitudes, and we must point out a couple of new ones. First of all, propositional attitudes are not, as weÂ’ve made clear, constituents of consciousness. For a propositional attitude to be Â“consciousÂ” is either for one to be conscious of it or for it to be such that one can readily become conscious of it. Your knowledge that 7 + 3 = 10 is conscious in the sense that you can readily become conscious of it. You werenÂ’t conscious of it a few seconds ago, however. But, even then, it was Â“consciousÂ” because it was readily made into an object of consciousness. (Freud (1915, 1921) describes such propositional attitudes as Â“pre-conscious.Â”) So for your knowledge of (1) to be Â“consciousÂ” is for it to be a ready object of consciousness. 
3.4 Intrapsychic conflict in relation to repression2: some final preliminaries 
There are some other relevant facts. Beliefs are inert except to the extent that one draws consequences from them and, more generally, that they are allowed to beget or otherwise engage other beliefs. The making of inferences at least sometimes involves a deliberate, conscious effort on oneÂ’s part. But some inferences are made involuntarily. Insights often just occur to one; but those insights are based on rational consideration of the relevant evidence. But, even though (so I believe) many an inference is made involuntarily, one has at least some control over what sorts of inferences oneÂ’s mind makes. So, given some belief B that one has, one can so structure oneÂ’s life that it is very unlikely that one will (consciously) make inferences from B that one would otherwise make. 
[468] 
Thus, one can so structure oneÂ’s life that a belief, though still conscious, is (at the level of consciousness[469]) isolated---prevented from engaging the bodies of belief that it would otherwise engage and prevented from begetting the beliefs that it would otherwise beget. Such a belief is conscious in some formal sense; but, at the level of consciousness, it has become inert, like oneÂ’s knowledge of some random, uninteresting fact. 
By de-operationalizing one's acceptance of a given fact, one can cease to have anything more than an abstract, formal understanding of what that fact amounts to. I know that there are people who are being tortured. But, because I have not witnessed a torture session, I donÂ’t know what the proposition there are people who are being tortured amounts to as well as I would if ceteris paribus I had witnessed a torture session. So even though I am in some technical sense no less aware of that truth than somebody who has first-hand knowledge of what torture-sessions involve, my awareness of that fact doesn't mean very much to me, whereas his awareness of it means a great deal to him. 
There is one last preliminary fact. Your knowledge of (1) is not derived from some one sense-perception; (1) isnÂ’t the sort of truth that can be known in such a direct way. It embodies a case of inference to the best explanation. (See Chapters 10 and 11 for a definition of this term and an analysis of concept expressed by it.) That doesnÂ’t mean that it isnÂ’t knowledge. (Unless knowledge can be acquired through inferences to the best explanation, then what we actually know is only an infinitesimally small part of what we think we know.) But it does mean that it embodies an attempt on your part (a successful one, in fact) to model various pieces of information. 
There are different ways to model that body of data. (This is not a peculiarity of the data involved in this particular case. Given a body of data, it is more likely than not than there is more than one reasonable, or at least semi-reasonable, way to model it.) [470] 
In this case, so we will suppose, (1) is the best such model. But it isnÂ’t, so we will also suppose, the only one that isnÂ’t totally implausible. The following proposition constitutes an alternative way of modeling that data: 
(3) 
Given that mental activity is governed by brain-activity, it follows that there are (possible, if not actual) physiological conditions whose symptoms include behavior similar to my husbands, accompanied by bouts of forgetfulness. (Not being a physician, I donÂ’t know the specifics.) And his having such a condition would explain how it is that, without being intentionally dishonest, he often says things that are false, and otherwise behaves in substandard ways. 

(3) 
is not a spectacularly good model of the data. But itÂ’s far from being obviously false. And this, for reasons that weÂ’ll now discuss, is enough to repress your knowledge of (1). 


3.5 Intrapsychic conflict in relation to repression2: a conjecture as to what it involves 
In light of these points, I put forth the following conjecture. During FM (the fleeting moment when your knowledge of (1) was conscious), you resolve that, on the occasions that you become conscious (not pre-conscious, but actively conscious; i.e., conscious in the sense in which you are now conscious of reading these very words) of your acceptance of (1), you will take the following steps. First, youÂ’ll isolate that belief. You will, to the best of your ability, refrain from drawing inferences from it (or from conjunctive propositions of which it is one of the conjuncts). You wonÂ’t voluntarily make any inferences from it; and if you find yourself having made one involuntarily, youÂ’ll do your best to refrain from pursuing it. YouÂ’ll encapsulate this knowledge. 
This will neutralize your belief in (1). First, for reasons given a moment ago, it will blind you to corollaries of (1) of which you'd otherwise be aware, and (1) will start to seem relatively innocuous as a result. A story will help us develop this point. 
You discover that your husband has done X, Y, and Z. (Some jewelry is missing from your drawer. Your husband is wearing new clothes, even though he has no money. And so forth.) Since youÂ’ve decided not to draw inferences from (1), youÂ’ll be more likely than you would otherwise be to take these on a case-by-case basis. Inevitably, youÂ’ll sometimes connect these curious phenomena to your knowledge of (1). But, just as inevitably, bits of knowledge that you have that would otherwise congregate will remain isolated from one another. As a result, your appreciation of just what it is that (1) entails will remain superficial; youÂ’ll be slow to recognize its consequences for your own welfare, and to recognize the extent to which your husbandÂ’s condition is impoverishing your life. 
Having decided to isolate (1) youÂ’ll resolve that, whenever you encounter data that clearly confirms (1), youÂ’ll try to look at it from the viewpoint of somebody who believes that (3) is correct. Of course, since you are not such a person, this will, at first, be a kind of intellectual exercise for you: youÂ’ll still know that (1), not (3), is the right way to model the data. But by engaging in this exercise, you are ensuring that energy and thought that would otherwise deepen your understanding of the consequences of (1) donÂ’t have that effect at all: Those energies are now on a foolÂ’s errand. Also, this way of responding to such data will soon become automatic, for reasons similar to those for which, if an actor rehearses his lines often enough, it becomes automatic, even though it wasnÂ’t before, for him to say Y if he just said X. 
This response-mechanism will further isolate your knowledge of (1). That knowledge will, at least at the level of consciousness, become more and more inconsequential. One cannot in any direct way choose what to believe. (One can choose what to believe only in the sense in which one can choose to gain weight. One can choose to do things that one knows will add mass to oneÂ’s body; one cannot choose to gain weight in the way in which one can choose to move oneÂ’s arm.) But, within limits, one can choose which beliefs to make operational and which ones to make non-operational; one can choose to do things that will make a given belief impotent and irrelevant. IÂ’m an actor; IÂ’m mediocre at it. I know that fact. I cannot directly choose to cease to have that belief. But I can choose to make it irrelevant; for I can choose an occupation in which my lack of acting ability is irrelevant. Similarly, you can, though to a lesser extent, choose to adopt certain practices that make your knowledge of (1) irrelevant or, in any case, make it less relevant than it would otherwise be. 
In this way, your acceptance of (1) becomes, at the conscious level, a mere shadow of what it would otherwise have been and of what it once was. It becomes like an old officer who, having become senile, is no longer allowed to command troops but who, because the higher-ups feel sorry for him, is allowed to keep his title. 
3.6 Why repressions are never complete successes 
Most data-synthesis occurs below the threshold of consciousness. When you walk into a room, you automatically upload a mass of information and you automatically make many inferences from that data. The uploading and synthesizing of information doesnÂ’t need your conscious cooperation. If it did, youÂ’d know very little indeed. (In fact, it doesnÂ’t involve your cooperation at all, since most of it happens sub-personally. As weÂ’ve seen, minds are more basic than selves. Your self is an agency that regulates existing mental activity, most, if not all, of which consists in the uploading and synthesizing of information. So, speaking both logically and chronologically, the sub-personal gathering and processing of information is more fundamental than the personal gathering and uploading and processing of information.) 
It follows, and is clear on independent grounds, that your decisions as to what goes on in your own mind are of limited scope. Those decisions affect how well the conscious (and pre-conscious) strata of the mind communicate with other strata. They donÂ’t affect in any direct way affect what goes on in other, deeper strata. So, even if you've sincerely resolved to make no effort to interpret aberrant behaviors on your husband's part, that resolution fails to shut off a great deal of the ratiocinative activity that such a discovery automatically precipitates. 
Armed with this information, let us return to our story. You have turned your knowledge of (1) into a dead husk, at least as far as its engagements with other denizens of consciousness are concerned. You have deliberately structured your life in a way that drains your knowledge of (1) of much of its importance. So far as it was in your power to do so, you have chosen to refrain from asking questions that youÂ’d otherwise ask and, therefore, from making inferences that youÂ’d otherwise make. You have thus so eviscerated your knowledge of (1), qua denizen of consciousness, that it might as well not even be conscious. You have thus repressed it. 
But we have a problem. As we made clear in the second to last paragraph, you werenÂ’t able to shut off all of the processes that link that knowledge with other beliefs of yours. You could redirect some of those processes and contaminate others; and maybe you could altogether shut off some of them. But you failed to shut off, or even adulterate, much of that activity. And you didnÂ’t really cease to accept (1); rather, you ceased to treat that beliefÂ’s manifestations in consciousness in the way in which you treat those of other beliefs. But, just as you cannot typically uninstall a computer program by dragging the desktop icon for it into the desktop garbage can, you cannot Â“uninstallÂ” a belief by tinkering with its representations in consciousness. Beliefs are enduring structures. Your belief that 1 + 1 = 2 has been around a long time; it does a lot of work for you even when youÂ’re not consciously deploying it. If you really stopped knowing that 1 + 1 = 2, your way of dealing with the world would suddenly change in a radical way; and the changes would pervade practically every field of endeavor, not just those in which you are required to consciously think that 1 + 1 = 2. That belief isnÂ’t like a mood or any of the other will-o-the-wisps that populate consciousness. And, like any other enduring structure that is constitutive of oneÂ’s metabolism, one has, at most, partial control over its fortunes; and, so far as one does have such control, it tends to be of the indirect kind previously discussed. Given any other propositional attitude, the same thing mutatis mutandis is true of it. 
Thus, the conscious representative of your belief in (1) is an innocuous shell. It has been repressed. But it still lives on, and it Â“presses for dischargeÂ” to use FreudÂ’s term. Since, however, you no longer acknowledge its existence, it cannot be discharged through intentional behavior on your part; it must, without your knowing it, insinuate itself into your intentions (e.g., you displace your repressed rage at your father by being mean to your students) or it must be expressed as a symptom (e.g., when you come into contact with situations that remind of your rage towards him, you become crippled by anxiety). 
Whatever it is that youÂ’ve repressed, in order to keep it repressed, you must be able to identify it. But if you can identify it, then youÂ’re conscious of it, and itÂ’s not repressed. So how can it be repressed? WeÂ’ll now answer that question. 
3.7 Intrapsychic conflict in relation to repression2: conclusion 
I submit that, if completed in the following way, our story describes one way in which repression2 can occur. 
During FM, you learned that (2) is the case, and you consciously choose to retain that knowledge. This enables you to have your cake and eat it too. (1) and 
(2) hold in virtue of the same, ugly fact. But (1) is much more specific than (2), and an acceptance of (1) is commensurately less likely than an acceptance of (2) to upset an existing psychological integration. At the same time, by virtue of knowing (2), you enable yourself to continue to be aware of an ugly an undeniable fact, and you've thus spared yourself a constant, difficult struggle to not see the obvious. (2) is enough like (1) that, by consciously accepting (2), one's conscious disposition isn't completely antagonistic to the still rational side of you that urges you to accept (1). So, by accepting (2), you're not locked into a draining struggle with the forces of rationality and truthfulness within oneself. At the same time, by accepting (2), you are neutralizing the message of which those forces are trying to apprise you, and you are thus spared some painful realizations as well as the labor-intensive changes to oneself that they demand. 
3.8 Summing up 
We can't choose to destroy the beliefs we don't want to have. But we can partly de-operationalize them. We can choose not to make any conscious effort to delineate their consequences. We can choose to immerse ourselves in activities or lifestyle that don't permit us to pay attention to them. And, though belief is no more voluntary than disbelief, we can also choose to look for reasons to have beliefs that are opposed to those that we wish we didn't have. We can look for such reasons without having much faith that we'll ever find them, just as a lawyer can build a case for a client he knows to be guilty. And the mere fact that we're looking for them means that the belief we wish to destroy no longer fits smoothly into our psychological architecture, since it no longer has the support of the psychological structures implicated in the search. So even though we can't directly choose our beliefs, we can choose to do things that make it harder to pay attention to a given belief than to withdraw our attention from it. The result may be that it becomes so hard to attend to that belief that it becomes one of which we becomes altogether unconscious. 
3.9 Rationalizing rationalization 
People sometimes repress their knowledge of ugly truths about themselves, and they must rationalize in order to prevent the knowledge they've repressed from re-entering consciousness. Unfortunately, the science of psychology has itself become little more than a means by which people rationalize ludicrous attempts to repress their knowledge of these obvious facts. 
Many claim to believe that there is no unconscious mental activity and a fortiori that self-deception, repression, etc. are all artifacts of dated psychoanalytic theories; many claim that the concepts of repression, etc. are internal to a discipline (psychoanalysis) that have been superseded by Â‘rigorousÂ’ studies of the physiological underpinnings of thought. The thoroughly hypocritical and self-deceptive character of such pronouncements is evident when one looks at the judgments and conduct of these naysayers. Not a single one of those judgments concern the physiological underpinnings of a personÂ’s psychology; they concern that personÂ’s psychology. And, though this could technically be explained in terms of the fact that people canÂ’t routinely subject others to PET-scans, those PET-scans would be of no psychological interest---to anyone---unless it were shown that the findings of those PET-scans correlated with independently known facts about psychology. The giant discoloration on SmithÂ’s PET-scan would be of no interest to psychology were it not known independently of the results of that PET-scan that SmithÂ’s mentation was aberrant---that Smith thought that he was E.T., or some such, and was therefore mentally ill. Were it discovered that mental activity were mediated by the gallÂ­bladder, the results of PET-scans would immediately cease to be of any psychological interest; for they would no longer be correlated with independently known, and independently explained, psychological data. Which shows that brain-science, to the extent that itÂ’s of any relevance to psychology, is parasitic on psychological knowledge. 
Most of those guilty of this hypocrisy provide no arguments for their view, other than empty, boiler-plate repetitions of the slogan that Â“scienceÂ” studies brains and molecules, not intangibles such as emotions and thoughts. 
As for the idea that emotions, thoughts, etc. are too intangible to be worthy of scientific study---that position is decidedly implausible. Whatever we know about the external worldÂ—and, therefore, about brains, etc.---we know it through perceptions and thoughts and thus through such alleged intangibles. So while brains and neurons may be ontologically more basic than thoughts, thoughts and perceptions are epistemologically more basic than neurons and brains. Indeed, the term Â“brainÂ” is, believe it or not, a theoretical term; in characterizing something as a Â“brain," you are ascribing to it various functions that, without engaging in a great deal of theory-soaked extrapolating, you cannot know it to discharge. Â“BrainÂ” is a theoretical term that is deeply entrenched in a well-confirmed body of theory. (Hence the illusion that it is a non-theoretical term.) So, speaking epistemologically, these psychological Â“intangiblesÂ” are much more tangible, and their existence infinitely less dubitable, than Â“tangibleÂ” things such as brains. 
But even though many rail against the inevitable encroachment on their lives of psychodynamic truths that theyÂ’d very much like to stave offÂ—even though contemporary professional psychologists, having invested their lives in the bankrupt and tautologously false idea that psychology ought to be studied non-psychologically, are especially shrill in their antipathy towards any attitude towards the psychodynamic approach that isnÂ’t one of unalloyed, unquestioning antipathy---very few people have tried to produce bona fidereasons to reject the tenets of such an approach. 
IÂ’ve heard more than one professor of psychology explicitly state that the study of emotions must be replaced by the study of neurons. Why? Â“Because,Â” they say, Â“the study of emotions is itself an emotional enterprise.Â” This is like saying that thoughts about plants are themselves plants. That anyone of even minimal intelligence should commit such a crass and grievous ratiocinative gaffe is incomprehensible. But it becomes comprehensible if we adopt the hypothesis that, within the mind of a person who advocates this view, there is something with which such discussions resonate uncomfortably and to which that person wants to continue to remain blind. Thus, the denial of emotions is itself a thoroughly emotional position, and the denial of repression is itself an instance of repression. 
Those who deny the existence of emotions and repression say that, in so doing, theyÂ’re being Â“scientific.Â” But itÂ’s hard to see how such dishonesty and obtuseness could deserve to be so characterized. People donÂ’t see themselves for what they are. Is it scientific to deny this? In some cases, lack of self-knowledge has the same causes as other forms of ignorance: lack of ratiocinative ability, lack of effort, lack of raw data. But given the empirical fact that hyper-intelligent people are quite as prone to not seeing themselves for who they are as their less gifted brethren, it is de rigueur, from the viewpoint of scientific methodology, to suppose another factor to be operative. And itÂ’s pretty clear what this other fact is: People donÂ’t want to see themselves for who they are; so they donÂ’t. Given the obvious and, outside of the discipline of psychology, universally acknowledged fact that people deceive themselves, thereÂ’s no coherent way to deny that repression is not only possible, but actual, and not only actual, but integral to the human condition. 
3.4.4 Sartre on repression and the unconscious 
Jean-Paul Sartre held there is no such thing as unconscious mental activity and a fortiori no such thing as repression. His position was that the mind is completely and utterly transparent to itself, it being in the nature of mentationthat a given mind should have immediate and complete access to all of its own contents. But unlike the previously mentioned authors, Sartre argued for his position. And his argument is initially persuasive: 
(SA)[471] 
One must know, said Sartre, what it is that one is trying to keep out of consciousness if one is to succeed in doing so. But so far as one has that knowledge, he continued, one is conscious of the very thing that one is trying to keep out of consciousness; and so far as one is conscious of thing, it isnÂ’t repressed. 
Given this argument, there are two positions one might take: 
(1) Sartre is right and his reasoning is cogent. 
(2) Sartre is wrong. So his argument must be fallacious and we must pinpoint the fallacy in it. 
In my book Conceptual Atomism and the Computational Theory of Mind,I try to identify an error in SartreÂ’s reasoning. In this chapter, I have developed what I said in that book. But I must make it clear that, although I have no doubt that people do deceive themselves, repress conflicting engendering beliefs and sentiments, etc., I am not convinced that: 
(i) My attempts to show the concepts of self-deception (etc.) to be coherent were entirely successful. 
And supposing for argumentÂ’s sake that I have shown those concepts to be coherent, I am not convinced that: 
(ii) The specific forms I have shown them to be capable of 
taking are the forms that they in fact take. 
IÂ’ve identified one possible model (or, rather, two such models: one for repressions1 and one for repression2). But I don't know that IÂ’ve identified models that correctly identify the forms that those phenomena do take. Still, I am convinced that there are elements of truth in those models. And I think it is a philosophical task of the utmost urgency to make it crystal clear what is wrong with SartreÂ’s powerful argument and also to make it crystal clear what exactly self-deception and repression involve. Unfortunately, philosophers have neglected to do this; which, so far as itÂ’s had any effect on psychology, has encouraged it to go down the blind allies of scientism, methodological incoherence, and (cf. the view now widely endorsed by theoretical psychologists) the obviously false views that constitute contemporary theoretical psychology. 
Chapter 27 Psychopathy, Sociopathy, and Non-Psychopathic, Non-Sociopathic Criminality 
1.0 some preliminary points concerning the concept of mind 
A mind is a collection of structures such that 
(i) those structures create and direct mental activity; 
and such that 
(ii) if X1 and Xn are any two of those structures, one of two conditions is satisfied: (i) at least one of them can directly 
transmit the information stored in it to the other faculty; (ii) there is a set of faculties X1, X2Â…Xn such that, for each i (1= i = n), Xi, can directly transmit the information it bears to Xi+1. 
(i) is self-explanatory; but (ii) requires clarification. In order for you to acquire information as to what I believe (or hope or fear, etc.), one of three conditions must be met: 
(a) 
I must engage in overt bodily behaviors (e.g., laughing, throwing furniture around) that you can interpret as indicative of my having a certain belief (or whatnot). 

(b) 
I must engage in behaviors that that result in ink-deposits, bursts of noise, or otherwise publicly knowable entities, that you can interpret as being thus indicative. 

(c) 
I must engage behaviors of the sort described in (a) and (b) that, although you do not personally witness them, initiate a testimonial-sequence of which you are on the receiving end. 


Thus, the exchange of information between minds involves non-mental intermediaries and, for that reason, is in some important sense Â“indirect.Â” 
But information-transmissions that occur within a mind is either direct or, if it isnÂ’t direct, consists solely of direct information-transmissions (i.e. that consist of sequences of information-transmissions, each one of which is direct, even though, obviously, those direct transmissions jointly constitute an indirect transmission). I know that Jerry is a vicious and prolific murderer. All of a sudden, I see JerryÂ’s grinning face pressed against my window. The result: IÂ’m afraid. (I wouldnÂ’t have reacted with fear if my pre-existing belief had been to the effect that Jerry was a harmless prankster who, in his attempts to be funny, pressed his grinning face against peopleÂ’s windows.) Clearly, the information encoded in my knowledge about Jerry is Â“pooledÂ” with the contents of my sense-perception, that being why I am struck by fear. That pooling occurs without anyoneÂ’s engaging in any overt behaviors and, therefore, without anyoneÂ’s employing any symbolic intermediaries. The one mental entityÂ’s contents directly merge (if thatÂ’s the right word) with the others. 
The fact that these two bodies of information can merge thus directly is not a consequence of their both belonging to the same mind: it is constitutive of their belonging to the same mind. Two mental entities whose contents are thus related ipso facto both Â“belongÂ” to some one mind. 
Of course, there are distinct mental entities that belong to some one mind that are not as directly related to each other as are the two just-mentioned mental entities. For example, none of the mental entities constitutive of my mind in 1987 is related in that way to any given one of my current mental contents. And there are mental entities in my mind right at this very moment that are not thus interrelated. But, given one of those 1987-mental entities, how are its contents pooled with those of a given one of my 2010 mental contents? Through overt behaviors on my (or somebody elseÂ’s) part? No. Through symbolic intermediaries? No. The pooling is accomplished via a series of mental states S1Â…Sn such that S1Â’s contents directly merge with those of the aforementioned 1987 mental entity, such that SnÂ’s contents directly merge with those of the aforementioned 2010 mental entity, and such that, for each i, the contents of Si directly merge with those of Si+1. The same thing mutatis mutandis is true of any two mental entities that simultaneously inhabit a given mind but that, perhaps because the oneÂ’s position in that mind is remote from the otherÂ’s, cannot pool their contents with the directness with which my knowledge of Jerry and my sense-perception of JerryÂ’s pale, grinning face can pool their contents. 
Of course, a given mental entity may fail to leave a trace of itself and may thus fail to transmit its contents to other mental entities belonging to the same mind, and the contents of two mental entities that simultaneously belong to a given mind may fail to be pooled together. But were such a pooling of contents to occur, it would be through a series of mental states of the just-described kind; it would not be through non-symbolic intermediaries (e.g., overt behaviors). 
It incoherent to hold that, underlying the various wasps that compose a swarm of wasps, there is some entity, this entity being the swarm per se, to which those various wasps belong but of which they are not constitutive. It is similarly incoherent to suppose that, underlying the contents of a given mind, there is some Â“selfÂ” that has those contents but is distinct from them. Were such a thing to exist, its presence wouldn't enable wrongly interrelated mental entities to belong to the same mind, and its absence wouldn't prevent appropriately interrelated ones from belonging to the same mind. Such a thing would do nothing and would therefore be nothing. 
2.0 Desires vs. values 
Bearing in mind the points just made, let M be some mind (notice that I did not use the word Â“selfÂ”), and let S1Â…Sn be the series of aggregates of mental entities constituting M.[472] 
In every respect but one, M is just like a human mind. Being housed in a suitably equipped body, M can see things, touch them, etc., and it can thus acquire information concerning the external world. Being rational, M has the ability to draw inferences from that information that enable it to gratify its desires. And, because the body housing it is in good working order, it can act on the intentions to which those inferences lead. But M values nothing. This is the one respect in which it differs from (most) human minds. M wants things, one of those things being to survive. 
But M, we will suppose, values nothing. M sometimes seems to value things; for there are things that it wants that donÂ’t have any obvious survival-value and that donÂ’t relate in any obvious way to the gratification of its urges. But, in such cases, M believes the thing in question to conduce to the gratification of its desires; and so far as M appears to value it for its own sake, it is only because M isnÂ’t disclosing why it believes that thing to be thus conducive. 
There is a sense in which M has a concept of self-improvement. If it knows that acquiring the ability to sing well will, for some reason or other, enable it to gratify some desire that it cannot otherwise gratify, M can resolve to learn to sing well. In general, if M knows that, in order to gratify some urge that it has, it has to change itself in such and such a way, M is able to resolve to make that change. But, beyond that, M cannot possibly have any concept of self-improvement. To improve oneself is to change oneself in such a way that one comes closer to satisfying some standard that one has that, for that reason, one judges to endow one with more value than one had previously. Given that, by hypothesis, M values nothing, it thus has no conception of self-improvement apart from the strictly prudential one just described. 
It follows that all of MÂ’s actions are really reactions. It has desiresÂ—it wants to eat, sleep, and so on. Changes in circumstances sometimes bring about changes in what M has to do to gratify these desires; and M is reasonably adept at making the needed changes. But, given that M values nothing, M cannot possibly aspire to make any changes to itself that arenÂ’t intended to gratify some base urge. So any given action on MÂ’s part that isnÂ’t a direct attempt to gratify a base urge is an indirect attempt to so. Each of MÂ’s actions falls into one of two categories: either itÂ’s an attempt (possibly a successful one) to eat or sleep (or some such) or itÂ’s an attempt to do something that, in its judgment, it must to do in order to eat or sleep (or some such). MÂ’s conduct is always reactive. 
So far as M has a self, it does nothing other than mediate between, on the one hand, MÂ’s urges and, on the other hand, MÂ’s beliefs as to what, given the circumstances, must be done if those urges are to be gratified. 
By virtue of having no values, M is necessarily incapable of understanding much that creatures with values, but that are otherwise comparable to M, are capable of understanding. M wonÂ’t really have the concept of friendship. (M will have a concept of a strategic alliance, but not of friendship.) M wonÂ’t understand why Smith chose a non-lucrative and difficult career path over a lucrative and easy one. M cannot possibly have any concept of intrinsic, as opposed to purely instrumental, value. 
The essence of the human condition will elude M. He feels nothing that involves an ability to value something for its own sake. He can feel frustration (because his efforts to find food are unsuccessful); he can feel rage (towards those who stand between him and the successful execution of his machinations). But he doesnÂ’t love anybody; he doesnÂ’t even like anybody. And there is nothing towards which he aspires. 
M has no concept of legitimacy. There are desirable outcomes and there are undesirable outcomes. But nothing is any more right than anything else. 
2..1 Desires vs. values (continued) 
Some other facts about M deserve mention. M values nothing and therefore doesnÂ’t value the truth, at least not for its own sake. He values the truth only to the extent that, in his judgment, knowledge of it will help him gratify his desires. 
For purely strategic reasons, M may learn to Â‘hit the right notesÂ’---to say the right things. In fact, since there isnÂ’t anything that he wants to do or, therefore, to say that he doesnÂ’t believe to be to his strategic advantage, heÂ’ll do his best to do and say the Â‘rightÂ’ things; unlike actual people, whose deeds and utterances Â‘come from the heartÂ’ and, therefore, are often not strategic, M, though in actuality completely heartless, will strike many as having an exceptionally pure heart. M always says the correct thing, as opposed to the human thing. He says what he believes it to be to his practical advantage to say, given what he has learned about human nature from his examination of it. 
It is from an outsider's perspective that M examines people. It is thus to be expected that M's analysis of human nature will be hollow and off-the-mark. At the same time, M's analysis will strike less acute observers as unusually cogent. And, ironically, this is precisely because M is so blind to how people really are. Being incapable of saying anything substantive about the human mind, M will be forced to produce an analysis that is formally good, a corollary being that his analysis will be free of the ragged edges and inconsistencies that vitiate analyses put forth by people who, unlike M, have access to far more psychological data than can possibly be embodied in a few well-manicured truisms. 
Also, in attempting to describe the human mind, M will be his forced by his lack of psychological insight to give undue weight to what people say about themselves. What a person says about himself doesn't reflect who he is so much as it reflect who wants to be and who, depending how convinced he is by his own rationalizations, believes himself to be. Thus, M's descriptions of people will be consonant with their self-serving rationalizations and congenial to their fragile emotional integrations. As a result, they will strike people as accurate and heartening. By contrast, somebody who is psychologically insightful will see people for who they are; and, depending on how much stock people put in their own narratives, his psychological analyses strike people as false or threatening and will be rejected either way. 
2.2 Desires vs. values (continued) 
A corollary of the fact that M doesnÂ’t value truth for its own sake is that he doesnÂ’t negatively value falsehood for its own sake. He has no inhibitions, other than purely prudential ones, to accepting anything, so long as he thinks that, by doing so, he stands to come out ahead. 
Granting that most people are dishonest to some degree---a very high degree, in most cases---they value truth for its own sake. This doesnÂ’t necessarily mean that theyÂ’ll tell the truth or that theyÂ’ll (consciously) accept it when they see it. But it means that a high, non-prudential regard for truth is operative within them and, in some way or other, will affect what they say, do, and feel. If they lie, theyÂ’ll feel guilty; and what they refuse to accept but believe deep down often comes out in their actions. (They refuse to believe that Smith is an evil man and have but kind words to say about him. But they just canÂ’t find it in themselves to go visit him in the hospital when heÂ’s sick, they forget to pick him up at the airport, etc.) 
But it goes without saying that much of the time a personÂ’s high regard for truth is expressed in his telling the truth. IÂ’ve heard many a police officer say that criminals want to tell you the truth. Freud said that what a person doesnÂ’t explicitly say Â‘oozesÂ’ (FreudÂ’s own term) out of him; he fidgets; he unwittingly spins what he believes to be purely fictitious yarns that, when the names are changed, are precisely what the individual in question is trying to keep a lid on. (I donÂ’t know whether Freud or the aforementioned police officers had psychopaths in mind when they made these statements. I suspect that they were thinking of non-psychopaths who were dissembling.) 
The reason that truth-serum (sodium pentothal) works so well is that it lowers the inhibitions that one has to erect, and expend considerable energy maintaining, in order to prevent the truth from pouring out of oneÂ’s mouth. People are fundamentally truthful---even those that lie 99% of the time. I personally believe that very little of what people say is completely sincere and that the pervasiveness of mendacity cannot be overstated. But that isnÂ’t because people donÂ’t value the truth for its own sake. ItÂ’s because, in addition to valuing the truth, they value their own welfare; and their concern for their own welfare overpowers their wish to tell the truth. But, echoing what we just said, this doesnÂ’t mean that a non-psychopathic liar has successfully decommissioned his regard for the truth. His high valuation of it comes out in rearguard ways: he feels guilty; he volunteers at an orphanage (to alleviate his feelings of guilt); he is an unremittingly faithful husband; and, most importantly, the (nonÂ­psychopathic) liar will, at least at some level, keep a mental record of the truth, this being, at least in this context, the most important difference between non-psychopaths, be they liars are or truth-tellers, and psychopaths. 
3.0 These points in relation to psychopathy 
M is what is known as a Â“psychopath.Â” This is because, for M, what is true has no more (non-instrumental) value than what is untrue, and the essence of psychopathy lies is a complete failure to regard the truth as having any non-instrumental value. Whereas the non-psychopath keeps a mental log of the truth and, since he genuinely values the truth for its own sake, does so even when he doesnÂ’t judge there to be any practical reason to know the truth, M keeps a log of the truth only to the extent that, in his judgment, doing so is a practical necessity. 
This fact about M leads to no end of trouble for him. ItÂ’s very hard to know which truths will be of use and which oneÂ’s wonÂ’t. (In fact, given points made in the previous chapter concerning the limits to which, even in a deterministic universe, the future can be predicted, it is, technically speaking, impossible to be unerring in oneÂ’s judgments as to which truths will have which consequences and, therefore, as to which truths are worth knowing and which ones are not.) So itÂ’s extremely easy to make false judgments as to which truths are, and which ones are not, worth logging. 
By the same reasoning mutatis mutandis, itÂ’s hard (or, strictly speaking, impossible) to know exactly which falsehoods are worth regarding as truths--Â­or, in any case, as operational truths---and which ones are not. Since MÂ’s commitment to keeping the facts straight extends no further than his conviction that itÂ’s in his interest to keep the facts straight, and since itÂ’s hard, if not impossible, to know which facts are the ones that are relevant to oneÂ’s designs or a fortiori exactly how they are thus relevant, M often has no mental record, or only a very distorted one, of the facts. These gaps themselves change what it is to MÂ’s practical advantage to believe.
