Since, by obvious extensions of the points just made, these gaps in MÂ’s knowledge tend to spread, M is forced to have an extremely flexible relationship to the truth; MÂ’s failure to see the truth as having any intrinsic (non-strategic) value has the consequence that the purely instrumental value that the truth has for M tends to shrink with the passage of time. 











3.1 These points in relation to psychopathy (continued) 
For these reasons, MÂ’s Â“narrativeÂ”---what he tells both himself and others--Â­isnÂ’t consistent. In fact, MÂ’s narrative is as mercurial as the weather. M has no stable self-concept. M values nothing. Apart from his having certain base desires, there is nothing fixed about MÂ’s personality. Consequently, MÂ’s personality changes every time he judges there to be a reason to change the manner in which he attempts to gratify those desires. His personality thus changes every time he judges there to be a change in his circumstances that is relevant to the methods he must employ to gratify his desires. 
This means that MÂ’s personality is as fleeting as a summer breeze. And this, in its turn, means that M doesnÂ’t really have a personality. He doesnÂ’t really have a self. He has base desires; he has (mis)information as to how to gratify those desires; and he has intentions corresponding to that (mis)information. But thatÂ’s all he has. He is whatever circumstances require him to be. So he is a Potemkin village---an empty suit, a mask covering, not a face, but a void. M is a mind, clearly, but M is not a self; for it no more makes sense to speak of a self that changes with every decision-relevant change in circumstances than it does to speak of a square circle. A self is, by definition, what remains, or tends to remain, constant throughout the changes in the circumstances in which one is operating. 
In the last section of this book, I discuss some famous psychopaths. 

3.2 Who does the psychopath fool? 
Even though everyone lies, the non-psychopath tends to speak from the heart and thus to say what he believes, as opposed to what others want to hear. The psychopath has no tendency at all to say what he believes. For he has no heart and, therefore, no heart to speak from. Since, therefore, his only reasons for speaking are strategic, he says what people want to hear. Thus, even though he doesn't have a heart, the psychopath is more likely than others to strike people as having an exceptionally pure one . 
But the psychopath doesnÂ’t fool everybody. He only fools only those who fall into one of two categories: 
(i) Those who simply lack the acumen to see through his chicanery 
and 
(ii) Those who, because of special circumstances, have an emotional incentive not to see through it. 
Among those falling into the second category are 
(a) Those who are themselves children or parents of psychopaths 
and 
(b) Those who, having been brutalized in some way or other, possibly by some other psychopath, find much needed solace in his trite blandishments and thus have an emotional need to believe in the authenticity of their source. 
Those not thus blinded will see hollow performances in the psychopathÂ’s noble deeds and empty clichÃ©s in his insights. In due course, those who see through the psychopath are likely to see that there isnÂ’t a person behind the mask, only a proto-person who believes in nothing, values nothing, and is nothing, and who, so far as he isnÂ’t trying to convince himself and others otherwise, aspires only to gratify base animalistic urges and quasi-human derivatives thereof, such as a need (not a desireÂ—a need) for adulation or wealth. 
4.0 Sociopathy vs. psychopathy vs. non-sociopathic, non-psychopathic criminality 
The terms Â“sociopathÂ” and Â“psychopathÂ” are frequently used. Unfortunately, most people, without knowing that they are doing so, tend to use each of those terms to refer to three very different classes of people: 
(1) Those who donÂ’t have consciences at all; 
(2) Those who have consciences but whose consciences have been corrupted by rationalization; 
and: 
(3) Those who have consciences, and whose consciences have not been corrupted by rationalization (or, necessarily, by anything else) but who are evil. 
The result is that these three conditions, each of which is both psychologically and ethically very different from each of the others, are lumped together. 
People in Category 1 are psychopaths. Before we talk about what psychopathy is, we must talk about what it isnÂ’t. Psychopathy must be distinguished from psychosis. Psychosis is the psychological disorganization that results when there is a lowering of the inhibitions that ordinarily limit the freedom with which different parts of the psyche exchange information. A possible consequence of psychosis, but not an inevitable one, is a Â‘break from realityÂ’: the psychotic ceases to be able to distinguish between reality and fantasy. But, it must be stressed, such breaks from reality (which may, or may not, include hallucinations), are a by-product of psychosis, not the essence of it. (Incidentally, the hallucinations in question are usually auditory, not visual.) Psychotics are as likely as non-psychotics to have consciences. So psychosis is not psychopathy. Having cleared this up, we will now clear up some widespread misconceptions about psychopathy. 
When people of my nationality and approximate age hear the term Â“psychopath," they tend to think of Dr. Hannibal Lecter---the evil super-genius in the move Silence of the Lambs. The character of Hannibal Lecter is fictional in every possible sense. There is no real person on whose character his is modeled; and, human psychology being what it is, there couldnÂ’t possibly be such a person. He is about as unrealistic a character as one could imagine. He bears no resemblance to psychopaths---or, really, to anyone else. There is nothing to be learned from the character of Hannibal Lecter about psychopathy, psychopathology, or (setting aside the fact he has certain extremely generic traits in common with actual human beings; e.g., he doesnÂ’t like being in a cage) human psychology generally. 
A related point is that historyÂ’s great evil-doers are seldom, if ever, psychopaths. Stalin, for example, was not a psychopath.[473] 
For reasons that weÂ’ll now discuss, psychopaths donÂ’t have the attention-span to do what Stalin did and they cannot experience hatred, or any other emotion, with the depth with which Stalin did. 
OneÂ’s conscience has many functions. In certain cases, under certain circumstances, one such function is to prevent one from acting in anti-social ways. But that isnÂ’t the only function of conscience or even the primary one. Non-psychopathic individuals hold themselves to standards. OneÂ’s conscience is the part of oneÂ’s mind that stores oneÂ’s standards and that punishes one if one falls short of them. The standards in question may not be morally good ones. To make the same point, but in a way that doesnÂ’t prejudge any moral questions: those standards may be ones that, if complied with, hurt others more than they help them and (what is a related, but not a coincident, fact) tend to undermine the social institutions on which peopleÂ’s welfare depends. 
But speaking from a psychological, as opposed to an ethical, viewpoint, there is all the difference in the world between, on the one hand, holding oneself to Â“badÂ” standards, whatever that means, and, on the other hand, holding oneself to no standards. Were it not for the standards to which we hold ourselves, we wouldnÂ’t have selves to begin with. Creatures that donÂ’t hold themselves to standards may have minds---but they donÂ’t selves. 
To understand how selves can be different from minds, we must first state some basic truths relating to what minds are. The points about to be made (in Section 4.1) may initially seem purely digressive and irrelevant. But their relevance will soon become clear. 

4.1 Why psychopaths are dysfunctional 
M is a very pure example of psychopathy. Actual psychopaths tend to have some values. They like to tinker with cars, to build model airplanes, or whatnot. But the minds of actual psychopaths differ surprisingly little from M. 
There is one respect in which actual psychopaths resemble M that deserves special mention: like M, they have an extremely flexible relationship to the truth. (Psychopaths are unusually likely to be able to pass lie-detector tests. This isnÂ’t because they are good liars. ItÂ’s because----setting aside the rationalization-proof deliverances of their current, as opposed to their remembered, senseÂ­perceptions---a psychopathÂ’s relationship to the truth is so elastic that there isnÂ’t anything that he believes. So the psychopath doesn't have to lie. For the psychopath, some beliefs are more useful than others; so, for him, there is operational truth and falsehood. But there is no such thing as truth and falsehood simpliciter. Thus, psychopaths donÂ’t have to lie. They can pass lie detectors because, to them, the distinctions between truth and falsehood, and therefore between honesty and fraud, are purely technical ones. 
Since, consequently, a psychopathÂ’s grasp on the truth is so tenuous, he is very unlikely to succeed in life.[474] 
His fakery, braggadocio, and showmanship often make him appear in his youth and early adulthood to be success-bound; and sometimes he achieves success, at least in a narrow professional sense. But their careers tend to fall apart. The highly conditional nature of their commitment to the truth forces them to make decisions on the basis of an unduly constricted body of knowledge, the results being that they are likely to commit horrible gaffes that alienate them from institutions within which one has to operate to succeed. 
Also, because their grasp of the truth is so feeble, they are prone to act impulsively and therefore to commit acts that, to any non-psychopath, would obviously have consequences for them of the most adverse kind. According to Hervey Cleckley, whose book The Mask of Sanity is undoubtedly the best one on the subject of psychopathy, they do not do this because of an unconscious sense of guilt. There is, Cleckley says, no independent evidence that any such force is operative in these people. My own experience strongly supports CleckleyÂ’s contention. 
4.1.1 Why psychopaths are dysfunctional (continued) 
A related point is that psychopaths are extraordinarily bad at learning from their mistakes. [475] 
They make the same mistakes over and over again. They always have a story. And those stories often seem cogent when taken in isolation from one another and when considered in abstraction of the psychopathÂ’s back story. But their stories---which, in my experience, they describe using words such as Â“cogent," Â“rigorous," and Â“scientificÂ”---turn out to be models of flimsy reasoning from half-true premises; and they have nothing more than a veneer of cogency, which, on the rare occasions when you can pin them down, are easily penetrated. 
Psychopaths thus bear no resemblance to Hannibal Lecter and other Hollywood villains who are often (mis)characterized as Â“psychopathsÂ”; and they bear no resemblance to similarly mischaracterized, real life villains, such as Stalin and Mao. 
Psychopaths are dysfunctional. They can pull off cons. But that is pretty much all they can do. They can put on a good show for a while. They are charming, at least at first; they are, or seem to be, witty; and they often strike one as exceedingly intelligent and learned. 
But psychopaths are like a house of cards.[476] 
To borrow a simile used by Mary Aston in her novel The Incredible Charlie Carewe[477], which depicts a psychopath, psychopaths are to people what snake-skins are to snakes. For one thing, the proverbial charm of the psychopathÂ’s is doubly fraudulent. First of all, it hides their absolute indifference to others. Second, at the end of the day, they arenÂ’t charming. Or, rather, they arenÂ’t charming: it is the people from whom they plagiarize that are charming. More often than not, a psychopathÂ’s genuinely witty comments turn out to have been lifted. And, when a psychopathÂ’s attempts at charm donÂ’t involve plagiarism, it isnÂ’t witty at all, consisting as it does of stale clichÃ©s and curiously two-dimensional pseudoÂ­apercus. 


4.2 The psychopath's veneer of intelligence 
These points mutatis mutandis hold of the psychopath's proverbial intelligence. Psychopaths are more likely than non-psychopaths to show-case what they know, and they're more likely than non-psychopaths to choose endeavors that will lead to results they can show-case. Given a particular field, the psychopath will learn just enough to convince non-experts that he's an expert in it. If he knows that a given person is an expert in a certain field, he'll avoid that topic when talking with him or he'll avoid that person altogether. What the psychopath lacks in actual insight, he makes up for in plagiarized insights. What he lacks in both actual and plagiarized insights, he makes up for in his delivery. Psychopaths are long on delivery and short on content. A lecture given by a psychopath is likely to strike those who attend it as profound and to strike those who read transcripts of it as curiously hollow. 
I would like to quote from Robert LindnerÂ’s (1944) classic Rebel Without a Cause (no relation to the movie of the same name, which it predates): 
In the literature on [psychopathy] frequent mention is made of the Â“highÂ” intelligence of psychopathsÂ…However derived, these notions are misleading or at least insufficient to serve either as diagnostic aids or explanatory propositionsÂ….So far as intelligence per se is concernedÂ…what is outstanding about psychopathy is not its arithmetic proportions but is its peculiar variety and designÂ…The intelligence of the psychopath can be described only adjectivally and in terms of the [psychopathÂ’s] whole personality. Perfectly adapted to his needs in the same way as protective coloring is suited to the preservation of the life of an animal, all those psychological functions (thinking, understanding, imagining, remembering, etc.) which are held to be components of Â“intelligenceÂ” have in the psychopath superimposed on them an aura of shrewdness and secretive cunning, of calculating canniness. These elements not only serve psychopathic ends but effectively distort and divert all known measuring instruments, the rigid designs of which prevent their divinatory use with such individualsÂ…A further striking feature of the intelligence of the psychopath, and one which appears only after long time acquaintance with such individuals, is concerned with the amazing excess-cargo of uncoordinated and useless information they possess. Frequently one is misled by their typically encyclopaedic range into considering them persons of high intellect, even of culture. Penetration with time, however, discloses that, like the veneer of mahogany applied to inferior wood, this mass of Â“knowledgeÂ” is superficial and undigested; that it is free-floating, lacking the requisite elements of cohesiveness and relativity.[478] 


4.3 The reverence that people have for psychopaths 
The reverence that people have for these empty vessels has nothing to do with the all but non-existent content of what theyÂ’re saying; it has instead to do with their charisma and braggadocio. They exude an unabashed self-confidence and authoritativeness. When discussing U.S. history, a non-psychopathic expert on U.S. history is likely to appear self-confident, because he really is self-confident. And when heÂ’s talking about non-standard analysis (supposing that he isnÂ’t also a mathematician), heÂ’s likely to lack self-confidence and, therefore, to appear to lack it. 
A psychopath, on the other hand, always exudes self-confidence. He may be an expert on what heÂ’s talking about, or may know nothing about it at all. In each case, he will exude the same level of confidence. There will be no changes in mannerisms, no vocal modulations, no trace of anxiety that would indicate self-doubt or compensatory hubris. Regardless how confident he ought to be, he will appear utterly self-assured. He is likely to use histrionics to draw attention away from what heÂ’s actually saying. In general, psychopaths are confidence-men (con-men). They con by exuding confidence. 
There are two doctrines to which all but one or two of the many psychopathic professors IÂ’ve known were drawn: Marxism and Cultural Relativism. What these doctrines have in common is that they deny there is such a thing as truth. Marxism: Â“The truth is a lie told by the ruling class; so there is no truth.Â” Cultural Relativism: Â“Truth is whatever a given culture believes it to be; so there is no truth.Â” 
Setting aside the fact that any doctrine to the effect that there is no truth is self-defeating, any such doctrine is maximally easy to absorb, since, if that doctrine is right, there is ipso facto nothing to absorb. And to the extent that a given discipline accepts such a doctrine, its methods are ipso facto purely exhortatory; for, if there is no truth, then the traditional way of finding the truthÂ­--namely, objectively considering the relevant evidence and making inferences from that evidence that are licensed by rules of inference whose truth-conduciveness has been established---belongs in the ash-can. 

4.3 The PsychopathÂ’s psychological architecture fundamentally different from that of the non-psychopath 
In any case, psychopaths are not at all like Hannibal Lecter. Psychopaths are frauds. They canÂ’t accomplish anything without cheating. Hannibal Lecter is evil. But he isnÂ’t a fraud; he isnÂ’t a cheat; his intellectual accomplishments are legitimate. 
Also, Hannibal Lecter was a person, in FrankfurtÂ’s sense of the word. That by itself means that heÂ’s not a psychopath. Psychopaths are pseudo-people. Psychopaths have minds, but they donÂ’t have selves. They have narratives that replace the selves they lack. This is why (intellectually minded) psychopaths are drawn towards nihilism (nothing means anything) and relativism (thereÂ’s no right or wrong; no personÂ’s viewpoint is any more accurate than anyone elseÂ’s; no cultureÂ’s values are any more reasonable than any other cultureÂ’s). As far as a psychopath can tell, there is no difference between truth and propaganda. So, after a fashion, he really does believe that all opinions are equally correct. An opinion is a view as to what the truth is. So, by virtue of having an opinion, one is assuming that there is such a thing as truth. That assumption is false, according to the psychopath: all opinions 100% wrong, he believes, and are therefore equally wrong. 
The word Â“valueÂ” means nothing to the psychopath. He can acquire a rudimentary understanding of how to use value-related words. He can figure out that theft is Â“badÂ” and that saving a drowning child is Â“good.Â” But he doesnÂ’t know what these terms mean. (Wittgenstein urged acceptance of the thesis that there is nothing to a wordÂ’s meaning that isnÂ’t known by knowing how that word is used. (See Chapter 1 for an examination of this thesis.) In Section 6.4, it will become clear why this is relevant.) So he really does believe that all value-systems are equal: they are all, he believes, 100% wrong and they are therefore equally wrong. 

4.4 Psychopaths are legion 
Psychologists say that psychopaths make up around 3% of the population. There are two reasons why I put little stock in that statistic. First, itÂ’s unclear what it means. Any degradation of psychological architecture due to a loss of truthfulness with oneself is ipso facto psychopathy. OneÂ’s psychological integrity can be intact in some respects but not in others. Also, psychological integrity comes in degrees. So, unless weÂ’re told in what respect a personÂ’s psychological integrity must be damaged, and to what degree, weÂ’re not being told anything in being told psychopaths make up 3% of the population. 
Second, the diagnostic techniques employed by psychology presuppose that there are very rigid and simple connections between a personÂ’s psychological condition and his outward behavior. This, I suspect, is a by-product of psychologyÂ’s attempt over the last 50 years to scientize itself. That attempt is driven by a combination of anti-mentalism and strict empiricism. These doctrines jointly constitute a framework that recognizes no diagnostic methods that donÂ’t link psychological conditions with forms of behavior so narrowly defined that instances of them are as unmistakable as the color of litmus-strip. 
It follows that such tests are of limited probative value, given that different conditions can assume the same outward form and that a given condition can assume different outward forms. Also, such tests being what they are, it is easy for someone to figure out how must act, when being administered such a test, if the resulting diagnosis is to be exactly what he wants it to be. Being the con-artists that they are, psychopaths are inevitably quick to acquire precisely this knowledge. 
In any case, unlike the psychologists who came up with the previously-mentioned statistic, Cleckley succeeds in giving us some understanding of the extent to which psychopathy is a part of mankindÂ’s lot: 
It becomes difficult to imagine how much of the sham and hollowness which cynical commentators have immemorially pointed out in life may come from contact in serious issues with persons affected in some degree by the disorder [namely psychopathy] we are trying to describe. The fake poet who really feels little; the painter who, despite his loftiness, had his eye chiefly on the lucrative fad of his day; the fashionable clergyman who, despite his burning eloquence or his lively castigation of the devil, is primarily concerned with his advancement; the flirt who can readily awaken love but cannot feel love or recognize its absence; parents who, despite smooth convictions that they have only the childÂ’s welfare at heart, actually reject him except as it suits their own petty or selfish aims: all these types, so familiar in literature and in anybodyÂ’s experience, may be as they are because of a slight affliction with the personality disorder now under discussion. I believe probable that many persons outwardly imposing yet actually of insignificant import really are so affected.[479] 

5.0 Sociopathy vs. Psychopathy 
A psychopath: somebody with no conscience. 
A sociopath: somebody who has a very corrupt conscience or no conscience but who, during his formative years, did have a non-corrupt conscience and whose psychological architecture, developing as it did during those years, is that of a non-psychopathic person. 
The mechanisms of self-censure and self-correction that distinguish the non-psychopath from the psychopath are present in the sociopath. And, in most cases of sociopathy, those mechanisms are laid down and developed before sociopathization occurs; so theyÂ’re fairly hardy. Thus, at least in its structural respects, the sociopathÂ’s psychological integration is, at least during the early phases of sociopathy, more similar to the non-psychopathÂ’s than to the psychopathÂ’s. 
To be sure, the sociopathÂ’s mind lacks the values that give integrity to a nonÂ­psychopathÂ’s mind. (IÂ’m referring to psychological, not moral, integrity.) But since those values were once present in the sociopath, and since his psychological architecture was formed when he still had values and wasnÂ’t yet a sociopath, that architecture is basically that of a non-psychopath. 
That said, it is entirely by virtue of the force of inertia that the sociopathÂ’s psychological architecture doesnÂ’t collapse. The sociopathÂ’s psychological integrity, which is what distinguishes him from the psychopath, is, at this point, purely vestigial. Consequently, there is little keeping the sociopath from becoming a psychopath. 
A psychopath is a pseudo-person. He constructs a narrative that acts as a surrogate for the life-history that, had he actually had a self, he would have had. To be sure, the psychopath has experiences, just like everyone else, and he remembers them as well the next person. But he doesnÂ’t have a lifeÂ’s story. Much of what a normal person refers to as his Â“life-experienceÂ” or his Â“storyÂ” consists, not of his experiences, but of his reactions to his experiences: the distress they caused him; the self-criticism they prompted him; the subsequent changing of his values and his objectives; the elation he felt at having triumphed over the deficiencies in himself that led to his previous failures. These meta-experiences that unify a personÂ’s various first-order experiences into a cohesive structure. That structure is his Â“lifeÂ’s story.Â” The psychopath experiences doesnÂ’t have such meta-experiences. His life is a mere sequence of experience. The psychopath values nothing. Therefore, he doesnÂ’t analyze his experiences, unless there is some immediate practical reason to do so. He doesnÂ’t experience the internal struggles make us who we are (Â“who am I?,Â” Â“ what do I really want?,Â” Â“am I going to law school because I really want to be a lawyer, or because thatÂ’s the Â‘rightÂ’ thing to do?Â”, etc.). The psychopath is never conflicted (except in some pragmatic sense---he may not know whether or not he has to take a right turn if heÂ’s to make it to work on time). He never wonders whether heÂ’s being true to himself. For a person who values nothing, and therefore doesnÂ’t value truth, doesnÂ’t care whether heÂ’s being true himself; he doesnÂ’t even know what it is to be true to oneself. Nor does the psychopath come into conflict with other people. Of course, other people inevitably stand in his way. But the psychopath merely sees people as threats or nuisances; he is no more in conflict with them than you are in conflict with a bobcat that youÂ’re defending yourself against. The bobcat is a threat to your survival. But it isnÂ’t by representing an indictment of your psychological integration, or the values constitutive thereof, that itÂ’s a threat to you. So your altercation with the bobcat, though a serious and potentially life-altering or life-terminating matter, isnÂ’t a drama. ThereÂ’s nothing distinctively human about it. ThereÂ’s drama only where there is a clash of values, and thereÂ’s a life story only where thereÂ’s drama---Â­only, that is to say, where one has value-driven experiences in response to oneÂ’s experiences and where, consequently, oneÂ’s current experiences, thoughts, and decisions are informed, not merely by what has happened to one, but the value-driven changes that one made to oneself in response to those experiences. Since the psychopath has no values, his current experiences, etc. are not thus informed; he lives in the moment, in a pseudo-Zen manner. He has no lifeÂ’s story. There is no Â“himÂ”, really. There is a mind; but the meta-mental superstructure that is a personÂ’s self is quite absent. 
The psychopath has to seem like an actual person. Otherwise, heÂ’ll be seen for the freak that he is and wonÂ’t be able to gain peopleÂ’s trust or therefore to predate upon them. So, because he has to fit in and therefore seem human, he has to create a lifeÂ’s story; he has to manufacture a narrative. He is likely to have different narratives, since a narrative that works with one person may not work with another. Those narratives are not based on a first-hand understanding of what personhood really is. They are based on what, in the psychopathÂ’s judgment, is most likely to work. What sort of narrative he concocts depends on who heÂ’s dealing with and what he wants. Inevitably, his narratives are not completely false; in fact, they may be largely accurate. But that isnÂ’t because he values the truth; itÂ’s because a pure lie is much less effective than one that has a component of truth; and itÂ’s also because, if his narratives were pure lies, he would have a hard time keeping them straight and would seen be seen for what he is. 
The psychopathÂ’s self is just a script, albeit one that, like many scripts, isnÂ’t pure fiction. The psychopath isnÂ’t speaking from the heart; heÂ’s reading from a teleprompter. Since he doesnÂ’t exist, except in the same sense as Elmer Fudd, there is nothing in himself to which he wishes to be true and thus no off-message point that he wants to make. So the psychopath is unusually likely to say just what will make the boss promote him, just what will make Sally fall in love with him, just what will make Bill hand over his lifeÂ’s savings to him. HeÂ’s unusually likely to be seen as Â“a great guy.Â” 
One corollary of the fact that the psychopath has no self deserves special mention. When you refer to a non-psychopath by his name---when you refer to him as "Smith", or whatnot----the way in which you are using that expression is different from the way in which you are using that expression when referring to a pet parakeet of the same name. The parakeet is an organism that has a mind but not a self. Since personal names (e.g. "Smith"), as opposed to impersonal names (e.g. "Paris"), are, by virtue of their semantics, to be given only to beings that have selves, parakeets cannot have personal names, and attempts to give them such names, when not ironic, embody some seriously misguided views about parakeet-psychology (or about semantics). When we refer to a psychopath by his legal name, we are using that expression in the same, improper way in which we would use it to refer to a parakeet. 
5.0.1 Cleckley on the nature of psychopathy 
Two quotations from Cleckley will reinforce and clarify what weÂ’ve been saying: 
The [psychopathÂ’s] out functional aspect masks or disguises something quite different within, concealing behind a perfect mimicry of normal emotional, fine intelligence, and social responsibility a grossly disabled and irresponsible personality. 
Cleckley (1964), p. 420. 
Attempts to interpret the [psychopathÂ’s] disorder do not, of course, furnish evidence that he has a disorder or that it is serious. For reliable evidence of this we must examine his behavior. Only here, not in psychopathologic formulations, can we apply our judgment to what is objective and demonstrable. Functionally and structurally all is intact on the outside. Good function (healthy reactivity) will be demonstrated in all theoretical truths. Judgment as well as sound reasoning will appear at verbal levels. Ethical as well as practical considerations will be recognized in the abstract. A brilliant mimicry or sound, social reactions will occur in every test except the test of life itself. In the psychopath, we confront a personality neither broken nor outwardly distorted but of a substance that lacks ingredients without which normal function in major life issues is impossible. Cleckley (1964), p. 422. 


5.1 Rationalization: The gateway to sociopathy 
Smith is a talented novelist, and he considers novel writing to be an extremely valuable activity and he also rightly considers it to be the most valuable activity of which he personally is capable. For a while, Smith tries to write novels and to indulge his craving for pot and junk food. But he soon finds that his pot-induced lethargy put him in an either/or situation. Either smoke pot or write novels. But donÂ’t do both. It isnÂ’t possible. 
Being lazy and self-indulgent, Smith chooses to smoke pot and eat junk foot. At first, he feels terrible guilt as a result. But his guilt, though intense, isnÂ’t intense enough to overpower the forces, or lack thereof, within him that are responsible for his ditching his career as a novelist in favor of a non-career as a binge-eating junky. Still, the ever present, gnawing feeling of guilt is souring his otherwise unalloyedly blissful existence. 
He thus has a choice. Either: 
(1) Start writing novels and stop smoking pot/eating junk food; 
or: 
(2) Eliminate the part of conscience that makes him feel guilty for taking the easy path (smoking pot, etc.), as opposed to the difficult, but right, path (writing novels). 
Taking path (2) involves SmithÂ’s telling himself that, in fact, heÂ’s doing the right thing, as opposed to the easy thing. It involves SmithÂ’s reconstituting his values so as to validate the weakness-driven choice that he has made. Taking path (2) involves SmithÂ’s rationalizing. It involves his constructing a spurious narrative relative to which the wrong choice is the right one. Such a narrative might be along the following lines[480]: 
(SR) I like writing novels, and IÂ’m good at it. But it's morally wrong to write novels, since people's use novels to escape from ugly truths instead of dealing with them. The apparent counterexamples to this are actually the best illustrations of it. X, let us suppose, is a latter day Steinbeck. He writes about the insidious machinations of the wealthy and their devastating effects on the poor. His novels are masterpieces. But they do anything in the way of helping bring about the needed social changes? No. They do the opposite, in fact. XÂ’s novels turn the sufferings of societyÂ’s victims into a source of amusement. Token concern for their plight becomes all the rage; it becomes chic to wear T-shirts emblazoned with anti-establishment slogans. The corporation that manufactures those T-shirts uses over-seas sweatshop-labor. It dumps toxic waste into reservoirs. Its board members vivisect poor people for fund. So it is itself a pillar of the iniquitous social order that it was XÂ’s novels describe. 
So, even though XÂ’s heart was in the right place, he his hands are covered in blood. But his hands would be clean if he'd smoked pot, instead of writing his novels. Thus, it is my ethical duty not to write novels and to smoke pot all the time. 
Even if SR is correct, Smith is still living a lie and, as a result, he is, or will in due course become, a hollow shell. For, even if SR is correct, it isnÂ’t SmithÂ’s acceptance of SR that leads him to take Path (2): it is his laziness that does so. In deferring to his laziness, Smith is alienating himself from his core values. And, in doing this, Smith is alienating himself from himself and from the sources of energy on which, when attempting to perform any sort of action, he must draw. For, as weÂ’ve established, the self is a set of values---or, more precisely, an agency that oversees and manages an otherwise desultory stream of mental activity, giving it cohesiveness and thereby endowing that mind-constituting, but self-less stream with an enduring identity; and, as weÂ’ve also established, it is through its imposition of values on this empty, identity-less stream of mentation that this supervisory agency accomplishes these feats. So, in so far as his conduct is rationalization-driven, it isnÂ’t self-driven, a consequence being that, so far as SmithÂ’s rationalizations play an increasing role in SmithÂ’s life-path, Smith is regressing into a condition of not having a self---of being an empty shell, who, lacking in any real identity, has to fall back on the pseudo-identities of which his rationalizations and false narratives avail him. 
5.1.1 Rationalization: The gateway to sociopathy (continued) 
Rationalizations tend to involve putting sincerely held beliefs to insincere use. Individual facts are not denied; but they are taken out of context, and the patterns they form are conveniently overlooked. Part of what makes it relatively easy to overlook such patterns is that, whereas one literally sees (or otherwise sense-perceives) raw data, patterns arenÂ’t in any literally sense seen. To "see" a pattern is to become aware of a commonality holding among many different events, between any two of which there is a gap in time and which, taken collectively, may occupy a long period of time. Thus, seeing a pattern involves making correct judgments on the basis of information stored in memories. 
It follows that patterns are easily overlooked. Memories are easily corrupted, especially when they relate to emotionally touchy subject-matter. Also, the making of any judgment of any sophistication involves acceptance of an intricate network of inference rules and general principles. Given a person who is incapable of rigorous thought and is just slightly biased, or who is capable of rigorous thought but is deeply biased, it doesnÂ’t take much to make that person doubt the accuracy of the aforementioned constellation of beliefs. A rigorous thinker is ipso facto likely to have the wherewithal to produce arguments that, although hollow and sophistical, initially appear to meet his own high standards of proof and that consequently suffice to give him reason to doubt the accuracy of a once cherished belief. An unrigorous thinker ipso facto needs little argumentative inducement to part with a once cherished belief and therefore probably does have the modicum of argumentative sophistication needed to give himself that inducement. 
Actually, I doubt that any real acumen is needed to rationalize; and I suspect that, although intelligent people are probably better rationalizers ceteris paribus than unintelligent people, the degree to which the former surpass the latter as rationalizers isnÂ’t even close to being commensurate to the degree to which the former surpass the latter as thinkers. These points are discussed and defended in the next section; so IÂ’ll hold off on them for now. 
The rationalizer does not do what he thinks is right. Moreover, itÂ’s not through simple ignorance that he does the wrong thing. HeÂ’s not in the same category as somebody who mistakenly thinks that smoking is healthy and therefore smokes. HeÂ’s in the same category as a smoker who knows that smoking is unhealthy and tries to stave off the subsequent wrath of his conscience by concocting some narrative relative to which his hands are clean (e.g., Â“ItÂ’s not as though IÂ’m an axe-murderer---in the big scheme of things, smoking is a harmless vice,Â” Â“we all die anyway---why not do what I enjoy while IÂ’m still alive?,Â” etc.). 

5.1.2 Why do people rationalize?[481] 

Rationalizers see the world as they want it to be, not as it is. Thinkers see the world as it is not as they want to be. So people have an incentive both to rationalize and to not think. 
Also, rationalizing is the path of least resistance. Working for what you want is hard; pretending that you have it is easy. This obviously gives people another incentive both to rationalize and to not think. 
Also, thinking does, whereas rationalization does not, involve recognizing that one is fallible and, therefore, that the world was not designed to validate one's opinions. Thinking involves subordinating one's mental activities to objective norms. This involves evaluating one's own thoughts and, oftentimes, admitting that they're wrong. Rationalization involves not subordinating one's thoughts to objective norms and not admitting that one is wrong. So the rationalizer's ego is spared the hard knocks that the thinker's ego has to endure. 
Rationalization is a manifestation of our instinct to flee from danger. Through physical flight, we flee from an external threat; through 
rationalization, we flee from an internal threat.[482] 
Thus, a person's tendency to rationalize has deep instinctual roots. For this reason, rationalizing doesn't involve exercising one's agency. In fact, it involves letting sub-agential, instinctual forces triumph over one's agency. So far as one's agency is involved in the construction of a rationalization, it is nothing more than the puppet of sub-agential instincts, its sole function being to make instinct-driven, lapses in self-discipline and rationality appear to oneself to be expressions of rationality and self-control. Of course, everyone rationalizes, even the greatest of thinkers. But to the extent that oneÂ’s mental activity mediates rationalization, that activity is sub-agential; and to the extent that oneÂ’s mental activity mediates genuine thought, it is agential. These points are conjectural, it must be emphasized. Nonetheless, I wish to end this section with a point that is even more conjectural than those just made. We all know people who are extraordinarily Â“street smartÂ”, even though their discursive abilities are those of somebody whose level of intelligence is extremely low. Speaking personally, I used to believe that a street smart person was an intelligentwho didn't have the good fortune to receive a decent education; I used to believe that, if a given street smart person had been properly educated, he would be as discursively intelligent as, in actuality, he was street smart. 
Having had a number of illuminating exchanges with a talented student of mine, Jared Murphy, I no longer hold this view. Mr. Murphy isn't a criminal in any sense of the word. But he grew up on the streets. Most of his childhood friends became career gang-members. Many of them are either dead or in jail and those who arenÂ’t soon will be. I apprised Mr. Murphy of my view that street intelligence was merely a different manifestation of the cognitive faculties that, in an educated person, are manifested as discursive intelligence. Mr. Murphy disagreed. Here is what he said verbatim: 
First of all, most criminals are extraordinarily Â“street smartÂ”, and very few non-criminals are particularly street smart. I have had many friends who chose a life of crime and who, quite early in life, become phenomenally street smart. Most of those people were not only not intellectually gifted, but were of below average intelligence. 
My experiences have made it clear to me that so-called street smart people arenÂ’t smart at all. They are not natively intelligent people who werenÂ’t educated; and had they been educated, they would have been intellectually mediocre, at best. 
Of course, some criminals are smart; the ones at the top of the heap---the Pablo Escobars, the Al Capones---are obviously highly intelligent. (IÂ’ve dealt only with lower-echelon criminals; IÂ’ve never met a crime-lord. But given what such people accomplish, one doesnÂ’t have to met them to know that theyÂ’re smart.) 
But, apart from a few kingpins, criminals are, pretty much invariably, not intelligent. In fact, a prerequisite for street smarts is an absence of intelligence. The intelligent personÂ’s cognitive search space is too large. When he has to make a speedy decision, he has to rummage through so many possible scenarios, that, before heÂ’s made up his mind, heÂ’s dead. 
Surviving on the streets isnÂ’t about being smart; itÂ’s about 
having very highly developed instincts. The only way to 
have such highly developed instincts is to be an instinct-
driven person. And the only way to be an instinct-driven 
person is to lack intelligence. 
There are a couple of reasons for this. First, intelligent 
people reflect on their decisions and therefore tend to 
devalue their instincts. Second, for the intelligent person, 
thought becomes an end unto itself and the structures that 
mediate thought end up crowding out those that mediate 
instinctive responses.Thus, the instincts of a thinker cannot 
possibly be as finely honed as those of a non-thinker. 
To be sure, IÂ’ve known people who are reasonably smart 
and have reasonably good instincts. But, on the streets, 
Â“reasonably goodÂ” isnÂ’t good enough. The margins are too 
thin. Things happen to quickly. And the things that happen 
are irreversible. On the streets, you arenÂ’t given two weeks' 
notice; youÂ’re given two in the back of the head. No matter 
how little formal education a person has had, that person is a 
dead mean on the streets if his natural bent to is to be a 
thinker. That person will start to question his lifestyle. As a 
result, he'll be less "in the zone" than his unintelligent 
counterpart and therefore less attentive to the nuances to 
which, as a criminal, he must be attentive and less quick on 
the draw in situations where the first person to pull the 
trigger is the one who lives. So, long story short, street smart 
people arenÂ’t smart. They can't be. They have to be people 
whose only option is to hone their animal instincts. If they 
have any intelligence, that won't be their only option. 
Since, unlike Mr. Murphy, I didn't grow up on the streets, I don't whether 
he's right or wrong. But my suspicion is that, while there is almost certainly 
an element of hyperbole in his words, there is more truth than falsehood in 
them. 
5.2. Why rationalization is inevitable and often healthy 
Everybody rationalizes. Setting aside people who are exceedingly damaged (e.g., people who have sustained serious brain-damage) it is psychologically impossible for a person not to rationalize. 
Moreover, it isnÂ’t always bad to rationalize. In fact, it would be bad to never rationalize. There would be decision-paralysis if the brain-centers tasked with making decisions were flooded with too much truth. Also, oneÂ’s conscious mind can only withstand a modicum of truth, lest oneÂ’s self-concept sustain irreparable damage. Speaking from an evolutionary-biological perspective, knowledge is a means to an end, the end being health. A complete absence of conscious knowledge isnÂ’t health-conducive, but neither is an excess of such knowledge. One has to make decisions in real-time. OneÂ’s Â“search-spaceÂ” canÂ’t be too large. Moreover, so many truths of which one is aware, at some level or other, are so ugly that one cannot confront them all at once and must do so in a piecemeal fashion. 
People canÂ’t deal with everything at once. So they compartmentalize. Sometimes bodies of information that are conscious (i.e., are readily accessible to consciousness, not being held down by the forces of repression) are compartmentalized. But this form of compartmentalization is unstable. Two pieces of information both of which one is consciously aware, tend to coalesce. ThereÂ’s only so long one can consciously know both (a) that oneÂ’s good buddy Smith is the only person who could have put arsenic in oneÂ’s tea and (b) that one has been hospitalized repeatedly for arsenic poisoning without also knowing (c) that Smith isnÂ’t really oneÂ’s good buddy. 
Also, there isnÂ’t a sharp line between rationalization, on the one hand, and the legitimate employment of rationality on the other. There are three reasons for this: 
(1) 
The construction of rationalizations tends to involve the legitimate employment of rationality. 

(2) 
As previously stated, some rationalizations are true. And, in at least some cases, the difference between a belief that results from rationalization-based belief and a Â‘legitimateÂ’ belief isnÂ’t that the former is, whereas the latter is not, true; nor, necessarily, is it even that the former is, whereas the latter is not, arrived at in 

a spurious manner. In at least some cases, the difference lies in the use to which the belief---which may be true and legitimately arrived atÂ—is put. And a given (legitimate and legitimately arrived at) belief can be put to different uses. It can be used to figure out how to help struggling nations become more prosperous and it can also be used to figure out how to impoverish those same nations. 

(3) 
A given belief can be a rationalization in one respect and a non-rationalization in others. One may have different reasons for arriving at a given belief, some of them embodying wishful thinking and others embodying sober consideration of the facts; and one may use a given belief as the basis for a rationalization and for a legitimate pursuit of the truth. You believe that you mom is a good person partly because you want to believe that and partly because itÂ’s true to a large extent, though not as large an extent as youÂ’d like to think, and the evidence supports it, though not as much youÂ’d like. And you can put your belief that your mother is a good person to different uses: you can use it as an excuse to look the other way when she does something that a good person would not do (rationalization) or you can use it to subject a claim made about her to sober examination (nonÂ­rationalization); e.g. on the basis of your belief that your mother is a good person, you may accept the rationalization that her not allowing you to do athletics wasnÂ’t intended to emasculate you or to vent her rage at your father (who was a professional athlete and incessantly carried on with other women before dumping your mother); and on the basis of that same belief, you can determine that so and so is demented or deliberately untruthful, since he routinely makes claims about your mother (e.g. Â“she eats little childrenÂ”) that plainly arenÂ’t true. 




5.3 When rationalization is not healthy 
Given that everybody is, to some degree or other, a rationalizer, what is the difference between those rationalizers who sociopathize and those who don't? There are two differences: 
(1) 
For non-sociopaths, rationalizations are misfortunes, not deeds. For sociopaths, they're deeds, not misfortunes. Non-sociopaths don't seek out rationalizations; rationalizations are sought out in them but not by them. In the non-sociopath, rationalization happens sub-agentially. In the sociopath, rationalizations are deeds; he seeks them out, perfects them, and accepts them. In the sociopath, rationalizations also occur subÂ­agentially. So the difference between the sociopath and the non-sociopath isn't that the faculties responsible for the construction of rationalizations have been transferred; it's that, without losing any of their original (sub-agential) jurisdiction, they spread: they appropriate the subject's agency, leading in some cases to a complete reconstitution of the self.[483] 


(2) 
Non-sociopaths care about the truth. Sociopaths do not. The non-sociopath's concern for the truth keeps his personality intact; it insulates it from his rationalizations. The sociopath's self has no such insulation. As a result, it is eventually taken over by its own rationalizations. 


The sociopath, unlike the psychopath, was once a person. The sociopath's personality-architecture, at least during the initial stages of sociopathization, is far more like that of nonÂ­sociopathic non-psychopathic than is the personality architecture, what rudiments of it there happen to be, of the psychopath. When the soon-to-be sociopath stops caring about the truth, the rationalizations that swoop in occupy the same positions in that personality as the beliefs and values that they displaced. Thus, for a while at least, a sociopath's rationalizations operate within the same sort of structure as a non-sociopath's genuinely held beliefs. But that structure embodies values that the person in question no longer has, and it eventually collapses. 
(2) is a corollary of (1). If a given person has no concern for the truth, there is nothing preventing him from actively seeking out rationalizations. 

5.3 Sociopaths incessantly moralize 
Sociopaths are very moralizing. When speaking with them, one cannot be oneself; one must behave in a hyper-correct fashion, lest one incur their virulently ill-willed, pseudo-moral vituperations Being with a sociopath is like being in Oceania, the hyper-totalitarian society described in OrwellÂ’s novel 1984. Just as, in Oceania, one is vaporized if one has any resistance to accepting the governmentÂ’s lies, so, when speaking with a sociopath, one is censured, and thus vaporized, as it were, if one doesnÂ’t operate within the sociopathÂ’s candy-coated, morality-drenched narrative. 
But the morality is fake; it has nothing to do with the sociopathÂ’s beliefs as to how the world ought to be. This fake morality has four sources. 
First, sociopaths donÂ’t want people to see them for the vampires that they are. They want people to think that theyÂ’re good. It isn't only for strategic reasons that they want this. The sociopath has nothing but his image. Whatever substance he one once had has been drained away and replaced with a narrative. He's reading from a teleprompter, not speaking from the heart. There is no heart left. There is no self, in other words. So sociopaths need the approval of others to feel that they have selves. And that's why they insist on saying "correct" things, instead of human things. It's also why they're drawn to "glamour." Show business is replete with sociopaths. Second, because sociopaths are so alienated from what is (or, when it existed, was) human in themselves, they are forced to Â“phone it inÂ”: they have to read scripts; there is no longer a person, a self, within them for whom they can speak; if their statements expressed their true inner lives, it would consist of nothing but the tirades of an infant who hasnÂ’t yet acquired a self and whose emotional life is driven by infantile narcissism and, for that reason, sheer detestation of those who interfere with their infantile aspirations. 
Third, sociopaths resent their condition; they resent selling their souls; they resent being made to give up their selves; and, for that reason, theyÂ’re envious of those who have hung on to their selves. So they lash out at those people--Â­but, not wanting to be seen for the empty, tyrannical frauds that they are, they do so under the banner of morality. Which, if the recipient of their morality-coated rage is naÃ¯ve, will hurt him and which, at the same time, will help nobody, since its only real effect is to send the message that itÂ’s better to be a non-entity who wears a diamond-studded mask (underneath which there is no self, only a disorganized mixture of self-hatred, compensatory rage, and infantile (and also shame-driven) feelings of entitlement) than it is to be the real person who is who he is. 
Fourth, for the sociopath, morality is a weapon. By being moralizing, sociopaths have what theyÂ’ve always wanted but never had: power. Powerlessness makes one sociopathize; and once one has sociopathized, and has thus overthrown oneÂ’s conscience, one has no compunctions about using morality to belittle others. 
Earlier we mentioned OrwellÂ’s book 1984. Speaking from a psychodynamic viewpoint, 1984 is not fiction. It is an accurate description of mass sociopathization. If the forces at work within the real world were embodied in our political institutions, the result would be the world that Orwell describes. 1984 is not primarily about politics; itÂ’s about people being driven by fear into believing what they know to be lies and, as a result, ceasing to be human. Fortunately, a system of government in which there are checks and balances is capable of inhibiting, and sometimes altogether preventing, the sociopathization of the political institutions on which people depend for their welfare. 

5.4 Vampirism a metaphor for sociopathy

(iv)

Third, they need others to adulate them. The reason for this is different from the reason for which they need others to tell them that theyÂ’re not frauds. People who value the truth can validate themselves. An author who values the truth can take pride in a book he's written that nobody ever reads but that he knows to be good. But, to somebody who doesnÂ’t value the truth, true statements are no more valuable than false one. Since sociopaths have to believe their own spurious narratives, they identify the appearance of truth with truth itself. A writer whose works aren't read appears to be a failure. So, from the sociopath's viewpoint, he is a failure. A writer whose works are best-sellers appears to be a success. So, from the sociopath's viewpoint, he is a success. Since the image is the reality, a book is only as good as it is praised, and a person is as good as he is adored. 
Though he doesnÂ’t want be adulated, the non-sociopathic literary genius wants to be recognized. Adulation is different from recognition. Recognition=being praise because of what one has done. Adulation=being praised, not because of what one has done, but because of who one is. For Smith to be adulated is for Smith to be praised for being Smith. For Smith to be recognized is for Smith to be praised for composing a great symphony. 
People of conscience want see justice done, and they thus want credit to be given where credit is due. To be sure, there is an element of sheer egoism in a writerÂ’s desire for recognition. But the way in which egoism is expressed in a person of conscience is very different from the way it is a expressed in a sociopath. The writerÂ’s egoism is expressed in his wanting to be praised and in his not caring very much whether other, equally deserving writers are praised; his sense of justice is expressed in his wanting to be praised because he deserves it. Many writers, thinkers, and artists of genius are praised for works of theirs that they rightly regard as among their worst. The reason that Rachmaninov found it so dispiriting that he was praised for this work of his is that he wanted to be praised for the right reasons: he wanted the commendations that he received to be ones that he earned; if only within the confines of his attitude towards peopleÂ’s feelings towards his work, he wanted justice. 
RachmaninovÂ’s attitude towards the misguided adulation that he was received was quintessentially non-sociopathic. The sociopathic wants praise for its own sake. Â“According to you,Â”, it is likely to be said, Â“authors who know that theyÂ’re work is good donÂ’t want praise. But that isnÂ’t true. And surely that discredits much, if not all, of what youÂ’ve just said.Â”

(i)

Some are likely to reject (i). Â“If an author knows that what heÂ’s written is good,Â” it will be said, Â“he ipso facto cannot possibly be at all insecure about its merits.Â” This criticism falsely assumes that people cannot have mutually opposed beliefs. 5.6 Fame as sociopathogen 
Fame is a great sociopathizer. People who, within narrow limits, had merit are, for some random reason, propelled to the heights of stardom, at which point they are grossly overvalued by the public and start to feel like frauds. They then have a choice: 
(i) They can believe the lie that everyone is telling them (you're great, you're a real thinker, not just some comedian whose sense of humor was so anodyne that some board of directors knew it risked nothing by making you a talk-show host); 
or: 
(ii) They can admit that they're not great and then either renounce the benefits of fame or consciously live a lie. 
One can understand why, confronted with this choice, many people go with (i). 
6.0 The non-sociopathic/non-psychopathic predator 
A person who doesnÂ’t rationalize---who doesnÂ’t replace his true self with a fake narrative---is not a sociopath. Non-sociopaths are sometimes evil. Some of them, in fact, are supremely evil. This is because sociopaths want to believe that theyÂ’re not as empty as they really are. Â“SociopathÂ” doesnÂ’t mean Â“evil person.Â” Â“SociopathÂ” means Â“fake person with a corrupt conscience.Â” (Â“PsychopathÂ” means Â“non-person who never had a conscience and who, for that reason never had a self, has always lived through narratives fabricated ad hoc.Â”) Sociopaths are always evil. Sociopaths aren't human. They've stopped being human. Evil non-psychopathic, non-sociopaths are thoroughly human. But, whereas my objective is to write treatises and yours, let us suppose, is to become a pediatrician, their objectives are to do harm. 

6.1 The non-sociopathic/non-psychopathic predator (continued) 
Â“How is it possible," it will be asked, "for that to be the objective of somebody who isnÂ’t deranged in some way?Â”
