6.2 Donald DavisonÂ’s analysis of what intentions are 
According to Donald Davidson (1963), an intention is simply oneÂ’s strongest desire. More precisely, it is oneÂ’s strongest contextually relevant desire. So, if I am in an ice-cream store and, for some reason, itÂ’s incumbent on me to eat ice-cream, my subsequent intention to eat chocolate ice-cream is the strongest intention that I have that is an intention to eat ice-cream at that time, in that place; it is stronger than my desire to eat any of the other kinds of ice-cream that are available. At the same time, of course, my desire to eat chocolate ice-cream is not my strongest desire tout court. (In what follows, any references to oneÂ’s Â“strongestÂ” desire are always abbreviated references to oneÂ’s strongest contextually relevant desire.) So, according to Davidson, an intention is the desire that, because of its strength, beats out the other desires with which it is in competition and thus, unlike them, expresses itself in action.[487] 

This reasonable-seeming analysis embodies several confusions. (I should point out that, in his excellent book The Faces of Intention, Michael Bratman makes points similar to, but not coincident with, those that I am about to make.[488]) A desire that is directly converted into overt behavior is a reaction, not an action proper. For a desire to lead to action, it must be inhibited and scrutinized, so as to ensure that it embodies the right values. By virtue of surviving such scrutiny, a desire becomes an intention and, to the extent that circumstances allow, automatically discharges itself in action. 
Even those desires that are expressed in action despite not surviving such scrutiny are not cases of desires being directly converted into action. They are cases of desires being scrutinized, then found to fall short, but being allowed to discharge themselves anyway. The reason the tobacco-addict feels ashamed is that, despite what his conscience tells him as heÂ’s considering his wish to smoke, he nonetheless lifts the initial inhibition that he has on smoking. And even though, in respect of his overt behavior, he may pounce on the cigarette the way a tiger pounces on red meat, the addictÂ’s behavior is that of somebody in whom the impulse to smoke is the result of a decision: his impulse is initially quarantined, then scrutinized, and only then, despite its falling short of the relevant valuative benchmarks, allowed to be discharged in action. The tigerÂ’s desire, on the other hand, is directly translated into action. Where selves are concerned, few so-called impulsive behaviors, if any, involve a desireÂ’s being directly translated into action; they typically involve cases where there is an initial inhibition which, despite his better judgment, the person in question chooses to lift. 
That said, the decision to lift the inhibition sometimes is a wise one. The person in question wishes to appear like a violent, unpredictable animal, since he knows that, given the circumstances, this is to his strategic advantage; and he knows that, if he punches the person who just insulted him, that is precisely how he will appear. Many apparently impetuous actions are carefully considered. We must remember that Â“carefully consideredÂ” . Â“slowly considered.Â” A carefully considered decision can be made virtually instantaneously. This is partly because we think fast. But itÂ’s primarily because, given previous decisions that we spent a great deal of time making and that weÂ’ve decided to comply with, itÂ’s immediately obvious how to behave, when contingencies arise, in a manner that is consistent with those decisions. 
Our desires are fleeting. They constantly change. If Davidson were right, weÂ’d be buoyed hither and thither by our desires. Every time a sufficiently strong desire came along, weÂ’d Â“act out.Â” But, in so doing, we wouldnÂ’t really be acting at all. For our overt behavior wouldnÂ’t be the outcome of a decision. 
In fact, if DavidsonÂ’s theory were correct, we wouldnÂ’t be involved at all. Our impulses would use us to express themselves.[489] 
The overt behavior in which that desire was issued wouldnÂ’t be an action at all, at least not in the relevant sense. (It would be an action only in the sense in which a tigerÂ’s instinctual reactions are actions; it wouldnÂ’t be an action in the sense in which your rational and carefully considered decision to become a physician is an action.) 
To be sure, if a desire is overwhelmingly strong, we will tend to act on it. But, setting aside bona fidepsychopaths, what tends going in such cases isnÂ’t that the desire directly results in action, and is instead that the screening process leading to the lifting of the relevant inhibition is fast-tracked and, possibly (but not necessarily[490]), done shoddily. 
Contrary to what Davison holds, an action isnÂ’t the direct expression of any desire, be it oneÂ’s strongest desire or oneÂ’s weakest. An action is the direct expression of a value-driven decision to lift an inhibition on a desire. When deciding whether to lift that inhibition, one considers how doing so would affect oneÂ’s self-concept and oneÂ’s overall life-course. 
Thus, an intention, contrary to what Davidson holds, isnÂ’t a desire at all. It is a judgment. That judgment is intended to gratify some desire; but the desire is not the intention. To sum up: if Davidson were right, weÂ’d never act; weÂ’d only react. WeÂ’d be like pinballs, bouncing from bumper to bumper, each bumper being our strongest desire at the time. 
But that isnÂ’t how we are. As Bratman says, we make plans. Once we make these plans, we tend to stick with them. Desires come along that, if acted upon, would thwart those desires. We tend to inhibit those desires. Sometimes the desire in question is too strong; so we gratify it and thus either suspend or altogether junk the plan. But such a situation, though all too common, represents a breakdown in the structure that mediates between desires, on the one hand, and bona fideactions, on the other. 
Also, although these plans are to a large extent intended to gratify desires, and although that is what to a large extent they should be intended to do, the desires in which they have roots are not typically raw, instinctual ones. They are desires that incorporate oneÂ’s values and also typically reflect previous decisions that one has made. I donÂ’t much want to read so and soÂ’s latest book on semantics. But my intention to become a semanticist requires that I do so. In reading so and soÂ’s book, I am acting on a desire that I have. But that desire is a consequence of a previous intention that I formed, and that previous intention reflects my values and my self-concept. Those values, in their turn, reflect---though they are not mere puppets of---raw instinctual desires.[491] 
But those values are not desires. Those values are judgments as to how to extend the hegemony of the agency within myself that polices subÂ­agential mental activity on my part. (Why Â“sub-agentialÂ” mental activity? Because that regulatory agency is my self. Of course, after my self comes into existence, that regulatory agency polices its own activities and thus polices agential activity.) 

6.2 Donald DavisonÂ’s analysis of what intentions are (continued) 
Davidson identifies oneÂ’s intentions with oneÂ’s Â“strongestÂ” desires. But the term Â“oneÂ’s strongest desiresÂ” is ambiguous. There are two kinds of strength that a desire can have, which IÂ’ll refer to as Â“intrinsic strengthÂ” and Â“organization-dependent strength.Â” An analogy will help us move forward. 
Smith is, without any doubt, the best hand-to-hand fighter in the world. He is the best boxer, the best wrestler, and so on. So there is obviously some sense in which he is an extremely powerful human being. But none of the organizations that officially manage these sports will let him join them. So he wins no official competitions; he is given no awards; he has no titles. He has fought with the best and won without so much as breaking a sweat. And this fact is well known. But heÂ’s still not part of Â“the club,Â” so to speak. So as much of a threat as he might be on the street, his fighting-prowess doesnÂ’t mean anything: it doesnÂ’t translate into money or acclaim or influence. 
Jones is a reasonably good professional pugilist. He isnÂ’t remotely in the same league as Smith. (The two have fought. Jones didnÂ’t even land a punch.) But he is part of the club. So he does win awards for his fighting-talents, relatively modest though they are; he does make money; he does receive acclaim. 
Even though Smith is a much better boxer and all around pugilist than Jones, Jones is a more powerful figure within the boxing world than Smith. In fact, Smith is powerless within that world, even though he is the best boxer alive. 
The mind is much like the sort of organization of which Jones is a member. ItÂ’s a club; and if a desire isnÂ’t a member of it, it doesnÂ’t lead to action. (It may become a member and then lead to action. And, as a nonÂ­member, it can have effects. But those effects will be symptoms, not actions, since the desire, not being a member of the club, cannot avail itself of the reigns of agency.) A desire can be extremely strong; but if it isnÂ’t part of the club, its likelihood of being converted into action is small. (I say Â“small," as opposed to Â“zero," because, if a desire is a strong enough, it is likely to become a part of oneÂ’s psychological integration and, on that basis, to be converted into action---just as, given his level of talent, Smith would be likely, other things being equal, to be given a break and given membership in the boxing-federation.) And if a desire is weak, but itÂ’s deeply embedded in Â“the club," itÂ’s likely to be converted into action. 
So in saying that an intention is oneÂ’s strongest desire, Davidson hasnÂ’t said anything. If heÂ’s saying that it is the strongest desire that is in oneÂ’s mind, regardless of whether it is part of oneÂ’s psychological organization, then Davidson is wrong; for such organization-external desires donÂ’t have access to the Â“reigns of agencyÂ” and are less likely than organization-internal ones, even quite weak ones, to be expressed as actions. If Davidson is talking about organization-internal desires, he runs into the same problem. For, given two desires, the stronger one may be more out of line with the plans, self-concept, and general psychological organization, and may therefore be less likely than its weaker counterpart to lead to action. If by oneÂ’s Â“strongest desire," Davidson is referring to that desire of oneÂ’s that, given its position in oneÂ’s personality-architecture, is most likely to lead to action, no matter how intrinsically weak it is, then his position is false or empty. For Davidson is then saying either: 
(a) That an intention is that desire that, despite very possibly having less strength than other desires, is so positioned that it will beat out those other desires; 
or: 
(b) The true measure of a desireÂ’s strength is its likelihood of being expressed in action. 
If (a) is the right interpretation, Davidson is simply wrong to say that oneÂ’s intention is oneÂ’s strongest desire. If (b) is the right interpretation, Davidson is stating the empty truism that the desire that is most likely to lead to action is the one that is most likely to lead to action. 
The most fundamental problem with DavidsonÂ’s analysis, however, is the one that, following Bratman[492], we identified earlier. Behaviors that directly result from desires are reactions, not actions. The immediate cause of any bona fideaction is, not that desire itself, but the judgment-driven lifting of an inhibition on a desire. 

6.3 NietzscheÂ’s ethical egoism: An exhortation to avoid sociopathy[493] 

Nietzsche infamously argued for a doctrine known as ethical egoism (EE). According to this doctrine, it is oneÂ’s sole ethical obligation to promote oneÂ’s own welfare. 
One important desideratum that an ethical theory must satisfy is to say how people should treat others. Obviously EE fails to satisfy this desideratum. Since no viable ethical theory can fail to satisfy this desideratum, EE fails as an ethical theory. 
But there are desiderata that an ethical theory ought to satisfy and that, unlike every other ethical theory, EE does satisfy. First of all, an ethical theory shouldnÂ’t require people to diminish themselves. The most pure way of being evil towards someone is to diminish them. An ethical theory that diminishes those who follow it is therefore evil. And an ethical theory that is itself evil is ipso facto not a coherent one. Aside from EE, all ethical theories do require people to diminish themselves: they require people to do what others want and need them to do, not what they want and need to do. EE doesnÂ’t require people to diminish themselves. For EEÂ’s sole injunction is: DonÂ’t diminish yourself! EE isnÂ’t evil towards those who follow it. Thus, there is a respect in which EE is coherent and in which all other ethical theories are incoherent. (That said, there are respects in which EE is incoherent and in which most, if not all, other ethical theories are coherent.) 
There is another important desideratum that EE satisfies and that all other ethical theories fail to satisfy. People are self-centered. People who donÂ’t allow themselves to do what they want to do are frustrated, unhealthy people. (When I talk about Â“what people want to do," I mean what people want to do in so far as what they want to do isnÂ’t the result of cowardice or complacency or otherwise self-diminishing factors. In other words, I am talking about the wishes that peopleÂ’s selves have, and I am therefore not talking about the craven impulses that, although in people, are not of them---i.e., that, although in peopleÂ’s minds, are not constitutive of their selves.) One can obey EE faultlessly without jeopardizing oneÂ’s psychological health. The same cannot be said of any other ethical theory. All other ethical theories require one to put other peopleÂ’s interests ahead of oneÂ’s own. And, setting aside people who are already severely damaged, nobody can do this unremittingly. A system of morality with which it is not psychologically possible to be unremittingly compliant is ipso facto incoherent; for one has no obligation to do what one cannot do (Â“ought implies canÂ”). 
Â“But some people may genuinely want to be kind to others,Â” it will be said. Â“EE forces people to be evil and thus to go against their own natures. So, contrary to what you say, EE is evil towards its own followers.Â” Not true. EE says: Â“Do what you want to do, so long as what you want to do is authentic and doesnÂ’t involve a diminution of who you are.Â” Not everybody always wants to be a predator. In fact, few people are completely predatory, and many people are nurturers by nature. Kindness and altruism, though often given exogenous reinforcement, usually have endogenous roots. So EE does not demand that one hurt people whom one doesnÂ’t want to hurt. 
Bearing all of this in mind, let AET be an arbitrary ethical theory other than ethical egoism, and let Smith be an arbitrary person who advocates AET. Given what weÂ’ve said, Smith is damaged if he follows AET to the letter; and supposing that Smith isnÂ’t damaged, heÂ’s a hypocrite, since he tells people to follow AET, even though he himself does not do so. ItÂ’s psychologically impossible for anyone who, like Smith, is not damaged, to be unremitting in his adherence to any ethical doctrine other than EE. Smith is therefore a hypocrite. Given that heÂ’s a hypocrite, he has a choice: 
(i) he can admit to himself that heÂ’s a hypocrite, 
or: 
(ii) he can deny that heÂ’s a hypocrite. 
No one wants to believe that heÂ’s a fraud. So Smith will probably choose (ii). (Speaking empirically, Smith may choose (i)Â—but itÂ’s unlikely.[494]) 
So, given the reasonable supposition that Smith doesnÂ’t see himself as a fraud, heÂ’ll take path (ii). This means that heÂ’ll rationalize and that, to that extent at least, heÂ’ll ipso facto sociopathize. I suspect that, in advocating EE, Nietzsche was trying steer people away from the path of sociopathyÂ­conducive rationalizations. Nietzsche was obviously smart enough to know that EE is not viable as a theory as to how people should treat one another. But he also said explicitly that ethical theories other than EE either damage their adherents or turn them into frauds or both. 
Nietzsche said many things that, when taken out of context, suggest that he wanted people to be evil towards others. Presumably, we should take authors at their word. But supposing, if only for argumentÂ’s sake, that Nietzsche did want people to be evil towards one another, his wanting that was subordinate to his wanting people to be authentic. 
Â“Supposing that youÂ’re right,Â” I have been asked, Â“why didnÂ’t Nietzsche say what you just said? Why did he not duly disclaim his exhortations that people look out for themselves? Why did not he say Â‘I donÂ’t really want you to be evil towards others; what I really want is for you not to be hypocrites.Â’?Â” 
NietzscheÂ’s basic message was: Â“people are weak and cowardly, but they tell themselves that their weakness and cowardice are virtues; and as long as they keep believing this, they cannot live authentically.Â” Obviously one of NietzscheÂ’s objectives in making this point was to point out an interesting fact about the human condition. But that wasnÂ’t his only or, indeed, his primary objective. His primary objective was to cut through the rationalizations by which people convinced themselves that their cowardice and weakness were virtues and by which, consequently, they kept themselves in a diminished state. Nietzsche was trying to crack the whip. Had he duly disclaimed his words, he would have failed to do that; his points would have registered with people as purely theoretical ones. Moreover, his equivocations and qualifications would have undermined his own message. For they would (rightly) have been seen as embodying the slimy evasiveness of the scholar who, not wanting to be pinned down, rationalizes his pedantry as Â“rigorÂ”; and he would thus have been seen as exemplifying the very cowardice and hypocrisy that it was his intention to extirpate. 
In this connection it is to be noted that Nietzsche invented the concept of Â“intellectualization.Â” To intellectualize is to make a painful truth seem innocuous by treating it as being purely theoretical. Intellectualization is a form of repression. But, in intellectualizing, what one represses (or keeps repressed) is not oneÂ’s knowledge of the painful truth per se and instead oneÂ’s knowledge of how that truth bears on oneÂ’s life-situation. 
By keeping oneÂ’s knowledge of that truth per se unrepressed, one is at liberty to use it in discursive contexts, and one is also spared having to rationalize away any evidence for it that one encounters. Intellectualization is thus a Â“thinking manÂ’sÂ” form of repression. Like everyone else, intellectuals engage in repression. Sometimes, what they wish to repress is knowledge of a truth that, so long as they consciously know it, enhances their intellectual powers. Not wanting to forfeit the intellectual benefits of having that knowledge, they compromise: they donÂ’t repress that knowledge per se but they do repress their knowledge of its bearing on their lives. So, qua piece of theoretical weaponry, that knowledge remains conscious. But, qua knowledge that warrants their changing themselves in fundamental ways, it is repressed. 
Let us end this section by dealing with a problem that came up earlier but that we did not then have the chance to address. We saw some reason to believe that ethical theories are categorically incoherent. Supposing this to be correct, if only for argumentÂ’s sake, a question arises: If we find an ethical theory to be incoherent, should we cease to endorse it? No. Any viable ethical theory is necessarily incoherent. We have a word for that incoherence: injustice. 
Unless restrained, people will destroy the institutions that give our lives much of their meaning and value. Thus, any viable ethical theory restrains people. At the same time, any instance case of restraining someone is ipso facto unjust, since injustice is the thwarting of aspirations, even though such an injustice may be necessary to off-set some far greater injustice. 
When choosing between ethical theories, we are choosing between bad and worse, not between good and better. An extensive defense of this contention is given in my (2010) book Morality, Politics, and Law. So I will say no more about it here. 

6.4 Some famous psychopaths 
I would like to end by revisiting the topic of psychopathy. 
Psychopaths are always charlatans. For this reason, among others, they tend to be cult leaders. Many an Â“enlightenedÂ” sage is a psychopath. If someone is described as having a Â“spacious consciousnessÂ”, odds are: heÂ’s a psychopath. 
Ira Einhorn, an icon of the 1960Â’s, was a very pure example of a psychopath. After being put on trial for murdering his girlfriend, Einhorn fled, was convicted, and sentenced to death in absentia. During that time, he lived in France. (At the time, FranceÂ’s policy was not to extradite fugitives who faced the death penalty. Hence IraÂ’s decision to reside there.) Despite being well known in France as somebody who had been convicted of murdering his girlfriend, he was extraordinarily successful at attracting women. He managed to convince them, as he did many males, that he was the victim of a government conspiracy----notwithstanding that, by his own admission, the mummified corpse of his girlfriend had been in a trunk in his closet for two years. 
EinhornÂ’s murder of his girlfriend was a mere by-product of his psychopathy. Most psychopaths are not murderers. The essence of psychopathy isnÂ’t murderousness; itÂ’s emptiness. What made Einhorn a psychopath was the fact that he was an empty shell who hid his emptiness with a veneer of learnedness and of compassion for others. Because Einhorn was so empty, nothing meant anything to him. Therefore, killing his girlfriend meant nothing to him. In a non-psychopath, a desire to kill a loved one have to power through heavy-duty bulwarks erected by oneÂ’s conscience. So there would have to be intense rage. In a non-psychopath, there is no conscience; so an act that, if committed by a non-psychopath, would indicate white-hot passion might, if committed by a psychopath, indicate nothing more than a passing whim. 
While a student at the University of Pennsylvania, EinhornÂ’s mentor was a distinguished historian by the name of Morse Peckham. Peckham was very much not a psychopath. Peckham was initially deeply impressed by Einhorn; he thought he had had found a protÃ©gÃ© in Einhorn. After a couple of years, Peckham realized that EinhornÂ’s theatrical way of speaking had blinded him to the fact that Einhorn never said anything that wasnÂ’t simply a repetition of a point that he (Peckham) had made to him. 
Famous for his speeches on behalf of both environmentalism and pacifism, his advocacy of each doctrine was insincere. He used environmentalism not to enhance people, but to diminish them. In telling people that virtually everything they did was bad for the environment, he was, in effect, telling them that they were bad for the environment and therefore they did not deserve to exist. His environmentalism was quite as pure an expression of homicidal rage as his murder of his girlfriend. 
His advocacy of pacifism was similarly underhanded. Like many psychopaths, he advocated moral relativism (Â“there is no right or wrongÂ”) as well as alethic[495] 
relativism (Â“there is no truth; itÂ’s all subjectiveÂ”). His advocacy of world-peace was based, not on the principle that certain things are objectively wrong, but on the principle that, since nothing is objectively right or wrong, no culture has the right to act aggressively towards another. What Einhorn didnÂ’t say is that if nothing is right or wrong thereÂ’s no moral reason not to hurt others. (According to Marxism, the concept of right and wrong are bourgeois hogwash. This made it possible for Stalin, Mao, and Pol Pot to kill on an unprecedented scale.) Also, by advocating alethic relativism, Einhorn was wiping away thousands of yearsÂ’worth of hard work, since the message he was sending was that the accomplishments of thinkers over the ages were worth nothing. This message obviously appeals to people who want to be great thinkers but either lack the requisite talent or arenÂ’t willing to do the requisite work. 
The themes underlying his speeches, and often explicitly affirmed in them, were: 
(i) OneÂ’s emotions are as good a guide to truth as a scientistÂ’s experiments. 
(ii) Astrology is no less worthy of study than physics. 
(iii) Commerce is inherently evil. 
(iv) Institutionalized authority is inherently evil. 
These views seem liberal and progressive. They are not. For they are misleading ways of saying that 
(a) 
Hard work, personal integrity, and genuine ability mean nothing. 

(b) 
OneÂ’s emotions, and thus oneÂ’s prejudices, are the royal road to truth (that being why astrology, which one can practice without having ever so much as cracked a book, is no less worthy 

a discipline than physics, which requires years of patient study). 

(c) 
The appropriate attitude for a human being is the unbridled narcissism of an infant, an expression of which is a virulent hatred of anyone who frustrates his desires. 

(d) 
There is nothing of value in the institutions that prevent us from killing one another and that require us to rise above the narcissistic pettiness to which, in the absence of external inducements, we default. 


In urging acceptance of (i)-(iv), Einhorn was really urging acceptance of (a)Â­(d), and he was thus imploring people to understand the world in the same emotion-driven, projective manner as our cave-dwelling ancestors. Thus, EinhornÂ’s supposed progressiveness was the purest form of regressivism. Because Einhorn was representative in this respect of an entire generation of so-called liberals, people who donÂ’t want to return to a tribal mode of existence are given an incentive to not be liberal, even if they havenÂ’t a conservative bone in their body. 
I feel that a few remarks about my personal experiences may not be out of order, so long as itÂ’s kept in mind that those remarks may well be nothing more than prejudice-driven interpretations of facts about my life that, even if interpreted dispassionately, would reveal little about the world. I personally have known many leading members of the 1960Â’s counterculture; a very close relative of mine is one of the two or three best known astrologers in the nation. These particular individuals are among the most ill-willed and intellectually rigid people that I know. And, having attended many functions over which they presided, I have found the same to be true of their followers. For this reason, I suspect that acceptance of 1960Â’s-style liberalism often has roots in one, or both, of the following factors: 
(1) A wish to disguise, both from oneself and from others, a virulent, all-consuming ill-will, 
and: 
(2) A combination of a rabid desire for power, coupled with a narcissistic unwillingness to put in the work required to achieve success within institutions where they donÂ’t make the rules and where theyÂ’ll be subjected to meaningful scrutiny. 
6.4.1 Wittgenstein 
Einhorn was a big Wittgenstein fan. This was no accident. Wittgenstein was a psychopath. A below average student in both high-school and college, he received a PhD from Cambridge without taking any of the standard entrance-exams, without taking a single class, and without writing so much as a single paper, apart from the TLP. He submitted the TLP as his dissertation and, on that basis, was Â“awardedÂ” a doctorate in Philosophy. 
Wittgenstein supposedly labored over the TLP. If this is true, his efforts were to no avail. The end result was an absolute failure. ItÂ’s maximally obscure, except when what it is saying isnÂ’t trivial or obviously false. No effort is made to clarify the obscure statements or to substantiate them. Each sentence is labored and artificial and fails to flow into the next one. 
Also, Wittgenstein doesnÂ’t say how one sentence, or one section, relates to the next. Instead, he uses an elaborate numbering system that is meant to identify the logical interrelations holding among the various statements composing the TLP. But the numbering system, though giving the TLP a much needed appearance of rigor and coherence, only adds to the obscurity. To this day, scholars have failed to produce a single interpretation of WittgensteinÂ’s numbering system that doesnÂ’t add more incoherencies to the TLP than are already known to be there. 
In Chapter 1, we consider the TLPÂ’s main contentions and saw how wrong and shallow they were. But Bertrand Russell, the worldÂ’s most distinguished philosopher at the time, and still considered by many (including the present author) to be the greatest philosopher of the last 150 years or so, gave the TLP his seal of approval. (He later deeply regretted doing so.) And voila! Wittgenstein had a PhD in philosophy, despite WittgensteinÂ’s previously mentioned lack of credentials and the despite the TLPÂ’s lack of merit. The TLP is discussed at length and in depth, in Chapter 1. In any case, here are a few of the many problems with the TLP that we discussed. 
The Tractatus contains no argumentation. It consists of assertions that, on the rare occasions when theyÂ’re intelligible, are very obviously false. Consider his thesis that all meaningful statements are verifiable. No sooner did philosophers read that sentence than they saw it to be subject to obvious counter-examples 
(e.g. Â“all copper conducts electricityÂ”). To take another example: Consider this thesis that all complex statements (statements consisting of other statements) are truth-functions of the component statements.[496] 
In other words, given a 
complex sentence, e.g. Â“Smith is tall and Jones is shortÂ”, whether that sentence is true is determined by whether its components (Â“Smith is tallÂ” and Â“Jones is tallÂ”) are true.) Again, no sooner does one read this sentence than one sees it to be subject to obvious counterexamples. (Consider the sentence: Â“Jones got fired because he has poor people skills.Â” Given only that each of Â“Jones got firedÂ” and Â“he has poor people-skillsÂ” is true, itÂ’s an open question whether JonesÂ’ getting fired had anything to do with his having poor people-skills.) Given the profound differences between iconic and non-iconic forms of representation (which are discussed in Chapter 5), WittgensteinÂ’s Â“picture-theory of meaningÂ” can only be seen as making the empty point that sentences are picture-like in that, like pictures, they are (sometimes) representational. With a few trivial exceptions, none of the other intelligible sentences in the Tractatus fares any better. 
The Tractatus is a tiny work. If printed in the same font as the sentence you are reading, and on pages the size of the one before you, it would be around 10 pages long. But it appears much longer than it is. The reason for this is that it isnÂ’t written in paragraphs, like other books. It consists of numbered remarks, each of which is separated from its neighbors by large spaces, as if to emphasize its importance. 
The remarks are numbered by decimals, not whole numbers. The decimals are supposed to indicate relations of subordination. (So, remark #5.211 is subordinate to remark #5.21, as is remark # 5.212. I use a similar system in this book.) Thus, the numbers are supposed to indicate the logical relations holding among the corresponding statements. 
But in the Tractatus, there is no discernible relationship between a given statementÂ’s number and its relation to the statement, or statements, to which it is supposedly subordinate. A philosopher named Kevin Gibson wrote a paper with the title Â“Is the numbering system in the Tractatus a joke?Â”[497] 
Presumably the author thought so. I agree with him.) The numbers give the Tractatus an appearance of hard-hitting rigor that a reading of it fails to bear out. 
At the time, Russell was the most influential and respected figure in the philosophical world. Having convinced Russell of his philosophical greatness, Wittgenstein enlisted RussellÂ’s help in finding a publisher for the Tractatus. Russell was obviously as capable as anyone in the philosophical community of convincing publishers to accept a work they would otherwise reject. Evidently, the publishers judged that they had more to lose in the way of would-be publishers. (And that determination would have been correct had they been operating in any context where book sales are driven by market-forces, as opposed to hegemony-internal politics.) Nonetheless, the first 20 publishers whom Russell urged to publish WittgensteinÂ’s credibility by publishing WittgensteinÂ’s work than by being black-listed by Russell. In any case, the 21st publishing house agreed to publish it, but only on the condition that Russell write a substantial preface to it, so that the book would basically be a paper by Russell, which would inevitably be good, followed by WittgensteinÂ’s curious little effort, which, it was presumably hoped, it would overshadow. 
RussellÂ’s preface is both illuminating and enjoyable to read. Wittgenstein rewarded Russell for his efforts by saying that his preface thoroughly misrepresented the Tractatus, but without saying how it did so and without entertaining the possibility that it might be his fault that nobody, including Russell, could understand what he was saying. (Russell did in fact misrepresent some of WittgensteinÂ’s claims. But, in so doing, he attributed views to Wittgenstein that were more cogent than those advocated by Wittgenstein himself.) Wittgenstein fumed for the entirety of his career about how nobody understood what he wrote. He never blamed himself for this. It was always the readerÂ’s fault. Soon after the Tractatus was published, every clear statement in it, with a few unimportant exceptions, was shown to be false, thoroughly confused and, unlike other false, confused statements, not even obliquely suggestive of anything that was true or fruitful. (See Chapter 1.) Since it was written by Wittgenstein, who everybody knew to have been given RussellÂ’s seal of approval, the Tractatus was treated with reverence (and still is). But not a single philosopher could find anything in the Tractatus that, no matter how liberally interpreted, was even remotely close to the truth or that provided clear evidence that its author had any philosophical ability. 
In the immediate aftermath of its publication, when the grievous problems with the Tractatus became public knowledge, Wittgenstein vanished for ten years, resigning his professorship and severing all contact with anyone in the philosophical community. During that time, he had no jobs of substance. He was a middle school teacher for a while, but was fired for physically abusing his students. 
When he returned to Cambridge, he argued that there is no truth (or, what is the same, that truth is culture-dependent, being nothing more than a myth we create to validate our linguistic practices); that, so far as they donÂ’t consist of sensations, minds are identical with overt bodily movements; that all philosophical puzzles are immediately solved by looking at how words are ordinarily used; and that mathematical statements never represented discoveries and were in all cases conventions or stipulations. 
After returning to philosophy, Wittgenstein published nothing. He disseminated his thought through lectures. He did not permit people to attend his lectures unless he had a personal relationship with them. Distinguished philosophers from other universities were not allowed to attend his lectures. He thus ensured that the Tractatus would be the last work of his that, during his lifetime, was made available to anyone over whom he didnÂ’t have personal power. 
Most of his lectures were transcribed. The ones that his followers judged to be the more presentable ones have been published. Once somebody who desperately wanted to see merit in WittgensteinÂ’s work, I have read them carefully. They consist of scattered remarks. The remarks are in most cases devoid of any discernible meaning. They are seldom clarified or substantiated. 
That said, certain themes clearly run through them. There is no truth; what scientists refer to as Â“discoveriesÂ” are just changes in the conventions governing certain terms; if one knows how a word is used, one knows everything there is no know about its meaning. Psychopaths donÂ’t really understand terms like Â“rightÂ” and Â“wrong,Â” Â“goodÂ” and Â“bad.Â” But they know how to use such terms. In saying that, once one knows how a word is used, one ipso facto knows everything there is to know about its meaning, Wittgenstein was, I suspect, trying to convince himself that, falsely, that he did grasp the meanings of moral terms, given that he knew how they were used (at least relative to a conception of word-usage, such as the one that Wittgenstein advocated, that takes into account public behaviors, but not their psychological underpinnings). 
What all of these themes have in common is that, if theyÂ’re right, everybody who has ever sought truth was on a foolÂ’s errand. The nihilistic currents that run through the various remarks composing his lectures give them a superficial unity. But ultimately those lectures are heaps of disjoint comments, which, unlike the two-liners produced by other thinkers, are uninformative and painful to read. 
But those who listened to those very lectures were mesmerized by WittgensteinÂ’s charisma. (Among those was Norman Malcolm, who, following Wittgenstein, claimed that people donÂ’t actually have dreams, our misguided belief to the contrary being a product of our mistakenly thinking that the words that people utter when discussing their (non-existent) dreams are anything more than empty noises.) It is suggestive that, setting aside self-described Wittgensteinians, those who read his lectures have a negative reaction to them, if they have any reaction at all, whereas those who saw him talk reacted very favorably. ItÂ’s also suggestive how carefully Wittgenstein vetted those who wished to attend his talks. 
One point that Wittgenstein did make clearly is that there is no psychological component to linguistic behavior. He said that thought Â“consists in manipulations of symbols.Â” He also said that linguistic symbols are inherently public. In his view, it isnÂ’t by virtue of any mental state of yours that when you say Â“snow is white," you mean what you are saying, whereas, when a parrot says it, it doesnÂ’t mean anything. Although he wrote in a sufficiently loose and obscure manner that always allowed him the option to back away from what he seemed to have said, he made remarks that either mean nothing or mean that beliefs, values, and other enduring psychological structures, are identical with the overt behaviors of which, so it is generally presumed, they are but the effects; and he made remarks that strongly suggest that he didnÂ’t believe there to be such a thing as consciousness. His ridiculous view that thought is an inherently social, as opposed to individual, phenomenon is an artifact of these clearly erroneous assumptions. 
WittgensteinÂ’s false identification of the mind with bodily behavior (plus consciousness) makes it pointless to examine oneself. It is thus an attractive view for somebody who doesnÂ’t want to examine himself. Wittgenstein said that Â“there are no mysteries.Â” It was unclear whether he was referring to the mind or to philosophy. He seems to have been referring to both. If he were right about this, then one would have carte blanche to believe oneÂ’s own rationalizations. 
When he first met him, Russell described Wittgenstein as Â“the purest example of genius that I know.Â” In so describing Wittgenstein, Russell was describing the latterÂ’s mannerisms, not his thought. When substantiating this characterization of Wittgenstein, he cites the fact that Wittgenstein would alternate between long silences, during which he appeared engrossed in thought, and sudden bursts of speech, which, though obscure, were accompanied by energetic, almost aggressive, gestures that made it clear that, think what one may of them, those outbursts contained true insights. Russell mentions only one comment that Wittgenstein made during his conversations with him. Russell had put forth an argument, in which it was assumed for argumentÂ’s sake there wasnÂ’t a rhinoceros in the room they were in. WittgensteinÂ’s only response to this argument: Â“how do you know that there isnÂ’t a rhinoceros in the room?Â” As any philosophy professor knows, this is a perfect instance of the knee-jerk skepticism on which people with no talent for this discipline fall back when they donÂ’t know how else to engage what theyÂ’re being told. [498] 
After knowing Wittgenstein for a month or so, Russell wrote that Wittgenstein had nothing of substance to say and that conversations with him were a "waste of time." 
When Wittgenstein met Russell, WittgensteinÂ’s father was the wealthiest man in Europe. After inheriting much of his fatherÂ’s wealth, Wittgenstein himself was the wealthiest man in Europe. Why mention this? Because if a billionaire shows up and asks you for a professorship, youÂ’ll have a strong incentive to give it to him (if, like Russell, you have the power to do so); and youÂ’ll look very hard for legitimate reasons to do so. And if you can find anything resembling such a reason---anything that, by any stretch, could pass for such a reason----youÂ’ll pounce on it. In any case, it seems unlikely that, if Wittgenstein had been a coal minerÂ’s son, his sudden appearance at RussellÂ’s door would have elicited such hospitality. 
In his later years, Russell (1958) withdrew his support for WittgensteinÂ’s work. Though Russell doesnÂ’t say so explicitly, he seems to have thought that Wittgenstein had played for him for a fool and that his support of him was misguided. What Russell does say explicitly is that WittgensteinÂ’s post-Tractarian work Â“did not influence me at all.Â” And what he says he says about the Tractatus consists mostly of arguments, all of them cogent, to the effect that specific points made in it are false. His remaining comments about the Tractatus express irritation (and, I suspect, a certain moral outrage) at the fact that his points are delivered without any justification, Â“like a CzarÂ’s ukaseÂ”, and at the related fact that, because he felt his statement not to require substantiation, he didnÂ’t clarify them. WittgensteinÂ’s writing is obscure in the extreme. When people put forth interpretations of his work, Wittgenstein always said that they were wrong, but never said exactly how they were wrong. There was one exception to this. Wittgenstein claimed that Frank Ramsey, a distinguished philosopher and logician who died at age 26, had correctly interpreted the Tractatus. I strongly believe that WittgensteinÂ’s saying this was a strategic move. At the time, Ramsey was regarded as a luminary by both philosophers and economists. (He is still so regarded.) By saying that Frank Ramsey understood the Tractatus, he was saying that his work wasnÂ’t meaningless: it only appeared that way to people who, unlike Ramsey and himself, were too stupid to understand it. Also, given how respected Ramsey was, had Wittgenstein claimed that Ramsey didnÂ’t understand what he was saying, he would have aroused immediate suspicion, and the ensuing reappraisal of his work would have put a swift end to his career. 
Also, by claiming that Ramsey was the only person who understood his work, Wittgenstein was affiliating himself with actual geniuses, like Einstein, whose work is initially understood by only a few select people. Wittgenstein was also thereby affiliating himself with Ramsey, which, speaking tactically, was a very shrewd move on WittgensteinÂ’s part. When WittgensteinÂ’s cult of personality was still in its formative stages, it depended largely on the spurious presumption that he was a gifted mathematical logician; and by associating himself with Ramsey, Wittgenstein was able to give temporary credibility to that presumption. WittgensteinÂ’s cult of personality was already airborne by the time it was common knowledge that the Tractatus contained pseudo-mathematical fatuities where it was initially believed to contain mathematical profundities. 
People in WittgensteinÂ’s inner circle didnÂ’t question the Master or ask him to clarify what he was saying. Contemporary Wittgensteinians become very uneasy around people who ask for clarification. IÂ’ve noticed that every competent student that IÂ’ve had was left cold by WittgensteinÂ’s work. I've also noticed that when asked to discuss anything that was written clearly, these students of mine reacted with blank incomprehension, followed by acute embarrassment. 
Wittgenstein never completed anything. The Tractatus is not in any significant sense a complete work. ItÂ’s not really a work at all. It consists of loosely connected remarks, on which WittgensteinÂ’s bogus numbering-system imposes an appearance of unity. Taken individual, those remarks, when intelligible, are false or trite. The only authors whose work he engages are those whom he personally knew; and he engages their work only in a cursory fashion. In his writings, Wittgenstein repeatedly exhorts his readers not to do philosophy. He explicitly says that his works should be the last philosophical works ever written. He discouraged would-be philosophers from going into philosophy. 
Wittgenstein admitted that he rarely read the work of other philosophers. In his own writing, he never develops ideas, at least not in a clear or systematic fashion. It is left to the reader to do WittgensteinÂ’s work for him---to interpret WittgensteinÂ’s unintelligible remarks in such a way that they express defensible contentions and, at that point, to provide arguments for those contentions. 
Wittgenstein projected an air of Â“unremitting integrityÂ”, as one author (not a personal acquaintance of his) put it. But it isnÂ’t clear wherein his integrity lay. His work consists of unsubstantiated statements to the effect that nothing means anything; he was physically abusive to his students and, on one occasion, to Karl Popper, a very capable contemporary philosopher with whom he was having a conversation in which Popper identified fallacies in what Wittgenstein was saying; although he technically did hold a professorship at Cambridge, he had no clearly defined responsibilities. The philosophers who matriculated under him continued to toe his line after his death, leading in some cases to positively ludicrous assertions becoming orthodoxies (e.g., Gilbert RyleÂ’s insistence that other people are better than oneself at knowing what one is consciously thinking). 
It is often said that Wittgenstein was a Â“genius,Â” but those who say this never cite any actual instances of his genius; and, although some people of great intelligence (e.g., Michael Dummett) have said it, their saying it is almost always followed by an argument, usually a cogent one, as to why WittgensteinÂ’s views are false.[499] 

WittgensteinÂ’s professional success was based entirely on the air of mystique that he cultivated. His post-Tractarian work consisted entirely in his blocking off fruitful avenues of inquiry. He insisted, in fact, that any attempt to solve any philosophical problem was ipso facto misguided. In the work in which he made that claim, he said, without ever saying what he meant, that Â“everything is as it appearsÂ” and Â“there are no mysteries.Â” He also says, without clarifying what he means, that Â“the purpose of philosophy is to show the fly the way out of the bottle.Â” 
One can see how one could see great depth in such statements. But one could also see how one could project depths into those statements that they donÂ’t have. In fact, there is little, if anything, in WittgensteinÂ’s work that, when interpreted literally as opposed to projectively, has any meaning at all. 
WittgensteinÂ’s native language was German, not English. He never became fluent and always spoke with a heavy accent. This, I suspect, was much of the reason he wasnÂ’t seen for what he was. It immediately disposed people not to take what he was saying at face value, to assume that his obscure utterances bore hidden meanings, and, consequently, to project meanings into words that werenÂ’t there. 
Wittgenstein spoke little English when he first met Russell. But, even though Russell spoke fluent German, Wittgenstein insisted on speaking English. This is because Wittgenstein knew that, had he spoken in German, Russell would have seen that his failure to say anything meaningful was a result, not of his being unable to articulate his thoughts, but of his not having any. Also, because at that time Wittgenstein's English was so poor and because, as a result, he wasn't saying anything meaningful, Wittgenstein's words were, I more than suspect, a blank a canvass onto which Russell liberally projected his own insights, this being why, despite initially believing Wittgenstein to be an imbecile and a phony, Russell came to see great depths in Wittgenstein's broken sentences. 
During his lectures, Wittgenstein would pause for unusually long periods of time. During these pauses, his face and bodily movements projected deep pensiveness along with an almost maniacally intense level of concentration. To a large extent, I suspect, these silences were WittgensteinÂ’s way of avoiding having to say anything and, therewith, of allowing his audience-members to project into his fragmentary speech the very insights that he was unable to come up with himself. But, so far as they werenÂ’t just bogus theatrics, his long pauses and looks of consternation were, I would conjecture, expressions of the fact that he had to struggle to put his thoughts into English. 
WittgensteinÂ’s work was hollow. He refused to clarify anything that he said. He refused to concede that anyone understood anything that he said. Given its thoroughly nihilistic character and its curt dismissal of any attempt to seek philosophical truth, WittgensteinÂ’s work would have put an end to philosophical thought, had it not been for the fact that many philosophers didnÂ’t give any credence to what he said. He failed to complete anything of substance. He earned degrees and titles without going through anything resembling the process that others had to go through to earn similar accolades. His speedy journey from below-average high-school student to holder of a Chair in Philosophy at Cambridge was based entirely on the impressions that people had of his character. (More likely, it was based on one personÂ’s impressions of his character. The academic world being what it is, once Bertrand Russell threw his weight behind Wittgenstein, everyone fell in line.) These are all textbook signs of psychopathy. 
Wittgenstein unremittingly attempted to discourage anyone, apart from a select few, from entering into the discipline of philosophy. The few intelligible remarks that he made were glib and platitudinous. When criticisms of the Tractatus began to roll in, he petulantly quit his job and ceased to have any communication with anyone in the discipline of philosophy. (It is worth noting that before publishing the Tractatus, he described it as being the last philosophical work that need ever written. His reasons: first, there was no legitimate philosophical question to which it didnÂ’t provide a definitive answer; second, it exposed defects in the discipline of philosophy that, once seen, would warrant a universal abandonment of it.) In his post-Tractarian work, he repeatedly said that no work in philosophy should be done after his death. He used personal relationships as a surrogate for work. Given all of this, I conclude that Wittgenstein was a psychopath. 
Wittgenstein gave away his large fortune. This may seem inconsistent with the contention that Wittgenstein was a psychopath. It is not. He did this to consolidate his false veneer of legitimacy. Â“How could a bad person do such a good thing?Â” Answer: To give credibility to his false veneer of legitimacy. What drives the psychopath isnÂ’t a desire for money. ItÂ’s a desire to construct an identity to take the place of the one he doesnÂ’t have. WittgensteinÂ’s famous final words were: Â“Tell them I had a good life.Â” He did not have a good life. His life was a lie. Like his acts of charity, those words were meant to make a corrupt and bogus life seem real and, thus, worthy of emulation. (Why would somebody who had actually had a good life say that on his death bed?) 
What I personally find striking about Wittgenstein is that, although he wrote in what were clearly meant to be punchy two liners, nothing he wrote goes over well if quoted. Abraham Lincoln had several brilliant two-lines; so did Yogi Berra. La Rouchefoucauld had dozens. Wittgenstein had not a single one. And not for lack of trying. 

6.4.2 Foucault 
Michel Foucault is philosopher who was an even more pure example of psychopathy than Wittgenstein. Wittgenstein, I believe, wasnÂ’t always a psychopath. WittgensteinÂ’s early days, he tried to do good work. When he failed, rather than admit defeat and rather than deal with the shame he must have felt, he psychopathized. (He needed time to construct a new, bogus narrative relative to which his painful Tractatus-related realizations about himself meant nothing---he needed time to psychopathize---this being why he retreated into virtual solitude for ten years.) 
But Foucault was a psychopath from day one. At no point in his career did he show the slightest interest in the truth. His writing is even more obscure than WittgensteinÂ’s. And when he contracted H.I.V., he had unprotected sexual intercourse with hundreds of women, without telling them about his condition. Despite this well known fact, he is revered by professors of womenÂ’s studies and other disciplines (e.g. anthropology) that are staffed primarily by women and one of whose objectives is to identify the forces responsible for the oppression of women. How can this be? Even though FoucaultÂ’s work, like WittgensteinÂ’s, makes little or no sense, certain themes clearly run through it, 
e.g. Truth is a lie told by the patriarchy (and therefore doesnÂ’t exist). So-called Â“principles of reasoningÂ” and Â“rules of logicÂ” are machinations, devised by the running dogs of capitalism, to ensure that women and other traditionally disempowered groups continue to be dominated by moneyed Westerners. This is a Marxist, as well as a feminist (or, at least, apparently feminist), version of what Wittgenstein said. (Why the parenthetical hedge? Because this message says, in effect, that women are such victims of propaganda that their powers of judgment cannot possibly be true. So FoucaultÂ’s message was pseudo-feminist and anti-feminist---even though it is the very message of many self-described contemporary feminists. See Chapter 1, Section 18.0 of Morality, Politics, and Law for an extensive discussion of genuine vs. fraudulent forms of feminism.) This at least partly explains why many feminists are willing to overlook the fact that, in effect, Foucault tried to murder scores of women. 
Another important similarity between Foucault and Wittgenstein was that each cultivated an enormous cult of personality. Had they written clearly, like Carl Hempel or Arthur Pap, they wouldnÂ’t have been seen as gurus and their work would have been evaluated in the same dispassionate way in which people evaluate the work of Hempel and Pap. 
Even Russell, who to this day is still considered the greatest philosopher of the last 100 years, isnÂ’t seen as a guru; there is no cult of personality surrounding him; and those who find fault with his work never try to save it by ascribing hidden meanings to it. The reason is that respect for RussellÂ’s person is contingent on respect for his work. But with Wittgenstein and Foucault it is the opposite. It is only as far as one has respect for Wittgenstein and Foucault that one has respect for their work. Their work, taken on its own, is meaningless. After reading one page of either author, practically anyone would stop reading unless he were given some ex parte assurance that, if only heÂ’d press on, heÂ’d discover treasure-troves of genius. Having read most of what Wittgenstein wrote (that was published), along with the leading explanations of it, and having read a fair amount of Foucault, I can only say: ThereÂ’s nothing there; those epiphanous discoveries never happen. What does sometimes happen is that one invests so much time and energy in these authors that, rather than admit that one has been on a foolÂ’s errand for however many years and rather than admit that oneÂ’s dissertation was a farce, one becomes part of the lie that perpetuates the thought-crippling myth that itÂ’s worth oneÂ’s time to study what these two wrote. 
Willful obscurity is not merely evidence of psychopathy; it is psychopathy. There are great thinkers (e.g. Kant) who write obscurely. But the obscurity is not deliberate; and, ultimately, much of what theyÂ’re saying is clear, even though it has to be read a few times for its meaning to emerge. Had Kant written more clearly, it would be more enjoyable to read his prose, and one wouldnÂ’t have to work so hard to figure out what he was saying. But if one is willing to trudge through KantÂ’s prose, one usually finds that itÂ’s unambiguously making a point; and that point is very often an illuminating one. 
I cannot understand most of SpinozaÂ’s Ethics. He tried to model that work of his on EuclidÂ’s Elements. The result, for some reason, was a text that few people understand. But there are long passages in the Ethics that are as clear as a bell and that contain sparkling insights. And SpinozaÂ’s other works are clear and insightful. 
Kant and Spinoza were not psychopaths. So obscurity isnÂ’t necessarily a sign of psychopathy. But willful obscurity is a sign of psychopathy, especially when itÂ’s accompanied, as it was in WittgensteinÂ’s case and in FoucaultÂ’s, by a refusal to provide clarification. 
I will end this book right here. There will be no concluding remarks. Any attempt to distill the material put forth in the preceding pages into a single, tidy conclusion would involve my imposing a false veneer of unity on that material. Which, in its turn, would involve either my lying to myself, and thus sociopathizing, or lying to you, and thus criminalizing. 
Appendix: Definitions of key terms 
Algorithm: A fixed procedure for carrying out a task The rules that we learn in grade school to multiply, add, etc., multi-digit numbers are algorithms. By formalizing inferences, logicians create algorithms for determining whether, given two statements, one of them follows from the other. 
A problem with algorithms is that what one has to know in order to know whether a given algorithm is applicable to a given task is often much heftier than what one would have to know to carry out that task in an ad hoc manner. In this fact lies the doom of attempts to algorithmizeÂ—or, to use the more popular termÂ—Â“mechanizeÂ” thought. 
Ambiguity vs. indexicality: An ambiguous expression is one that is assigned meaning by two or more different rules. So Â“dumbÂ” is ambiguous, since there are two rules that assign meaning to utterances of it. One of those rules is: given an utterance of Â“x is dumb,Â” that utterance is true just in case x cannot speak. The other is: given an utterance of Â“x is dumb,Â” that utterance is true just in case x is not intelligent. 
An Â“indexicalÂ” is a context-sensitive expression. For an expression to be context-sensitive is for there to be some one semantic rule that assigns different meanings (or referents) to it, depending on the context. An example of such expression would be the pronoun Â“I.Â” That expression isnÂ’t ambiguous. Some one semantic rule assigns meaning to any two tokens of it. (That rule is: given any token t of Â“I,Â” t refers to the person who produced t.) But, that rule being what it is, different tokens of Â“IÂ” refer to different people. 
Ambiguity vs. vagueness: Whereas an expression is ambiguous if itÂ’s assigned meaning by more than one semantic rule, an expression is Â“vagueÂ” if, supposing it unambiguous, it is assigned meaning by no well-defined semantic rule, and if, supposing it ambiguous, one of its disambiguations is assigned meaning by no well-defined semantic rule. Someone with zero hairs is definitely Â“bald,Â” and someone with a million hairs (provided that theyÂ’re suitably located and have the requisite thickness) definitely is Â“not bald.Â” But there are many people with an intermediate number of hairs with respect to whom neither Â“baldÂ” nor Â“not baldÂ” is clearly applicable. Since, therefore, the semantics of Â“baldÂ” is given by a rule that is undefined for these intermediate cases, Â“baldÂ” is vague. 
Like many other expressions, the word Â“dumbÂ” is both vague and ambiguous, since it is assigned meaning by two distinct semantic rules, neither one of which is entirely determinate. 
Commentary: There is a raging debate as to what vagueness is. Some hold that it is a property only of words, thoughts, and the like. Those who hold this are said to have an epistemic view of vagueness, and are sometimes known as Â“epistemicists.Â” (Â“EpistemicÂ” means Â“having to do with knowledge.Â”) This is because they see vagueness as a property, not of the thing known, but of our knowledge of it. 
Others hold that vagueness is a property of the thing known, and not, at least not merely, of our knowledge of it. Those who hold this are said to believe in Â“objectiveÂ” vagueness, the reason being that they believe vagueness to be a property of objects, as opposed to our methods of 
representing them.[500] 
According to this view, there may be no fact as to whether Pat is a male or not or as to whether Pat is kind or not, etc. If this is right, then the law of excluded middle (any given proposition P is either 100% true or 100% false) is false. 
Here is my view. There is no objective vagueness. Â“WhatÂ’s out there is out there,Â” as my former colleague Chris Buford once put it. Talk of vagueness in the world is projective. WeÂ’re projecting deficiencies in our representations of the world onto the world itself. Vagueness is a property of beliefs, symbols, and other representations. 
HereÂ’s why I say to this. To say of a predicate P that itÂ’s vague is to say that there is, or at least could be, some object x such that Â‹PxÂ› isnÂ’t true and Â‹not-PxÂ› isnÂ’t true. ThereÂ’s nothing mystifying about this sort of vagueness. Symbols have the meanings we give them. If we decide that Px is true if x is 1, 2, or 3, and false if x is 4, 5, or 6 then Â‹P7Â› isnÂ’t true and neither is Â‹notÂ­P7.Â› But this isnÂ’t because there is some proposition that is neither true nor false. ItÂ’s because, given how P has been defined, Â‹P7Â› doesnÂ’t encode a proposition and neither does Â‹not-P7.Â› For a representation or symbol to be Â“vagueÂ” is simply for it to be under-defined. 
But what would it be for a symbol-meaning to be vague? But what would it be, for example, for a sentence-meaning (a proposition) to be vague? 
Propositions are individuated by their entailment-relations. In other words, a propositionÂ’s identity is a function of what it entails and also of what entails it. If proposition P1 entails P2, but P3 does not, or P2 entails P1 but not P3, 
then P1 and P3 are ipso facto different propositions. Thus, the very idea of a proposition whose entailment-relations are indeterminate is a non-starter. This means that propositions always have determinate truth-conditions. After all, for proposition to have such and such truth-conditions is for such and such propositions to entail it. Thus, a propositionÂ’s truth-conditions are either fulfilled or they arenÂ’t. There is no other possibility. Thus, there are no indeterminate propositions, and the law of excluded middle (every proposition is either 100% true or 100% false) is correct. See Â“entailment,Â” Â“propositions.Â” 
Antecedent and consequent: In if P, then Q, P is the antecedent and Q is the consequent. So in if snow is cold, then snow is not hot, the statement snow is cold is the antecedent, and snow is not hot is the consequent. See Â“conditional.Â” 
Analytic truth: Â“Squares have four sidesÂ” is analytic, since it makes no sense to suppose that squares might fail to have four sides. Â“Anything that is literate is animateÂ” is analytic since it makes no sense to suppose that anything inanimate should be literate. In general, a statement is analytically true if its negation is incoherent. 
See Â“coherent,Â” Â“empirical truth,Â” Â“entailment,Â” and Â“meaning vs. entailment-relations.Â” 
Atomic proposition: A proposition that isnÂ’t molecular (e.g., John snores). An atomic sentence is a sentence that expresses such a proposition (e.g., Â“John snoresÂ”). See Â“molecular proposition.Â” 
A priori: Knowledge is a priori if one has it, not in virtue of any observations that one has made, but in virtue of oneÂ’s innate cognitive structure of oneÂ’s mind. See Â“empirical knowledge.Â” 
A posteriori: Knowledge is a posteriori if it isnÂ’t a priori. See Â“A priori.Â” 
Axiom: A statement that, in some context, is assumed to be true and therefore isnÂ’t argued for. 
Axiom (second definition): A statement-form that, in some context, is assumed to have a true interpretation. See Â“interpretation.Â” 
The axiom of comprehension: This is the principle that, given any property, there is a set containing all and only those objects that have that property. There is a set containing all and only those things that are people (i.e., that have the property of being a person). ThereÂ’s a set containing all and only those things that are acorns (i.e., that have the property of being an acorn). And so on. 
The axiom of comprehension seems self-evident. But Bertrand Russell discovered that it has self-contradictory consequences and is therefore false. The set of people is not a member of itself, since no person is a set. But some sets do seem to be members of themselves. The set of sets would seem to be such a set. 
In light of these points, consider the property of being a set that contains all and only those sets that are not members of themselves. Let S be the set that contains all and only those things that have property. Does S itself have that property? In other words, is S itself a self-member? If it is, then it isnÂ’t, since it contains only sets that arenÂ’t self-members. But it if isnÂ’t, then it is, since it contains every set that is a self-member. Thus: 
(i) S has the property of being a self-member entails its own negation, and so does 
(ii) S doesnÂ’t have that property. 
Given the axiom of comprehension, one of those two statements must be true. Since the axiom of comprehension therefore entails a contradiction, it is false. How exactly it must be modified is a matter of debate. See Â“axiom,Â” Â“property,Â” and Â“set.Â” 
Axiom of extensionality: Sets are identical if and only if they have exactly the same members. 
Axiomatic system: The set of statements consisting of certain axioms along with the statements that follow from them. See Â“axiom.Â” 
Axiomatization: To axiomatize a discipline is to identify a small number of propositions and a small number of inference-rules such that all of the results of that discipline follow from those propositions by means of those inference rules. An axiomatization of a discipline is what results when it is successfully axiomatized. See Â“inference rule.Â”

Causal law: A law to the effect that, if one thing occurs (e.g., fire), some other thing must occur (e.g., smoke).

Causal series: A series of events such that, given any two of them, one is the (in)direct cause of the other; in other words, a single series of events any one of which is (in)directly caused by some one state of affairs. 
Like all series, causal series donÂ’t branch. This is a tautology. A Â‘seriesÂ’ is defined to be a non-branching structure. 
Of course, just a river can fork, so a causal series can branch out. In fact, the forking of a river is a special cause of the branching out of a causal series. But for a river to fork is for it to become two rivers (supposing that the two tributaries donÂ’t later merge). It isnÂ’t for a river to become two independent streams of water. Similarly, for a causal series to branch is for it to become multiple series. It is not for a series to comprise independent tributaries.

Coherence and incoherence: An Â“incoherentÂ” statement is one that undermines itself. Consider the statement:

Conceptual role semantics (CRS): the view that meaning is use, i.e., for two expressions to mean the same thing is for them to be used in the same way and, therefore, that for a given expression to have this, as opposed to that, meaning is for it to be used in this, as opposed to that, way. 
In his (1963) paper Â“Some reflections on language games,Â” Wilfrid Sellars clearly puts forth a version of CRS. But itÂ’s quite definitely present in WittgensteinÂ’s book The Philosophical Investigations, which was completed in the late 40Â’s. In his (1994) book Making it explicit, Robert Brandom advocates CRS. Nowhere in that 900 page book, or in any writings of advocates of CRS, is the existence of any of the following reasonable positions so much as acknowledged, let alone addressed: 
(i) A knowledge of a wordÂ’s meaning is at least part of what guides a person to use it in the way she does. When the waiter asks you what you would like to eat, you say Â“IÂ’d like a bowl of clam chowder,Â” and not Â“IÂ’d like a bowl of rotten entrails.Â” Why do you say Â“clam chowderÂ” instead of Â“rotten entrailsÂ”? Because you know that, given what it is that you want, Â“rotten entrailsÂ” has the wrong meaning and Â“clam chowderÂ” has the right meaning. Of course, how an expression is used is likely to change its meaning. If enough people use the word Â“restiveÂ” to mean tired, it may well come to have that meaning. But until that time comes, those people are misusing that expression; and their usage of it, being discrepant from its actual meaning, canÂ’t possibly be constitutive of it. 
(ii) Mere noises arenÂ’t linguistic expressions. It is only noises coupled with meanings that are such expressions. In a world where there are no semantic conventions, a noise just like the noise you make when you say Â“snow is whiteÂ” would mean nothing. If, in such a world, the gases leaving a volcano happened to make that noise, they would mean nothing. (In fact, theyÂ’d mean nothing in our world, except at most in some derivative sense.) Since, therefore, noises must be coupled with meanings in order to qualify as linguistic expressions, it makes no sense to say that what an expression means is a function of how it is used. After all, there is no expression to be used until the noises (and ink-marks and so forth) have been coupled with meanings. Therefore, CRS is false. 
Of course, there are different views as to what meanings are, and there are different views as to what it is for noises to be coupled with them. But relative to any such view, CRS is false. 
The contention that is closest to CRS that isnÂ’t obviously false is the trivial contention that what noises (and ink-marks and the like) mean is a (partial) causal consequence of what people do with them. (This suggests that CRS is based on a failure to distinguish the concept of a logical consequence from that of a causal consequence.) 
(iii) Expressions that havenÂ’t ever been used have determinate meanings. There are infinitely many sentences of English that havenÂ’t been used but that have determinate meanings. If this werenÂ’t the case, then nobody could ever utter a new sentence of English, at least not without making some ad hoc extension to the English language. But previously unuttered sentences are uttered all the time; and no sooner are they uttered than they have determinate meanings. 
According to CRS, what an expression means is determined by how it is used. So if CRS is right, an expression that hasnÂ’t been used ipso facto has no meaning. 
To parry this, advocates of CRS would have to say the following. Â“Where some expressions are concerned, meaning is fixed by use. But where other expressions are concerned, use doesnÂ’t fix meaning, at least not singleÂ­handedly. Some other factor is at work.Â” 
In making this concession, the advocate of CRS is admitting that CRS is false. Setting this aside, let us ask: what is this other factor? 
The answer: syntax. The meaning of Â“Bob kicked the canÂ” is a function of 
(i) 
what each of its components means (in other words, itÂ’s a function of what is meant by each of Â“Bob,Â” Â“kick,Â” and so on); and itÂ’s also a function of (ii) the syntactic rules of English (in other words, itÂ’s a function of the rules that assign meanings to complex expressions on the basis of the meanings of their constituents). 

Thus, the meaning of a complex expression is not determined by its use, and is determined by existing semantic and syntactic conventions. So CRS is false, if taken as an analysis of complex expressions. Earlier, we saw why itÂ’s false if taken as an analysis of simple expressions. 

(iv) 
If the meaning of a sentence S were determined by its Â“conceptual roleÂ”Â—that is, by what people inferred from S, when they thought it correct Â—any inference that people made from S would ipso facto be constitutive of SÂ’s meaning. If enough people thought that Â“Stalin the dictator of the Soviet Union from 1923Â–1953Â” entailed Â“somebody who was over 6 ft tall was the dictator of the Soviet Union from 1923Â–1953,Â” the former would entail the latter. But even if the latter were correct (which it isnÂ’t since Stalin was barely over 5 ft tall), it wouldnÂ’t follow from the first sentence. 


In their (2001) book The Compositionality Papers, Jerry Fodor and Ernie Lepore put forth several blistering criticisms of CRS. In that work, any gaps in the criticisms of CRS just put forth are very much filled in. 
Conditional: A conditional statement is one that has the form if P, then Q. Confirm: For P to confirm Q is for P to provide support for Q. (P: Â‘SmithÂ’s fingerprints are found in the murder-weapon used to kill Jones.Â’ Q: Â“Smith killed Jones.Â” P supports Q.) Confirmation: P confirms Q if, supposing that P is true, itÂ’s possible that Q is false but itÂ’s more likely than not that Q is true. Â“Smith is a Harvard professorÂ” confirms Â“Smith is not a complete moron,Â” but it doesnÂ’t entail it. See Â“confirmÂ” and Â“entailment.Â”

Commentary: A connective can be thought of as a sentence-level adjective. That is, it can be thought of as an expression C such that, given a sentence S, C yields a new sentence C(S) (read: Â“C of SÂ”) such that C(S) attributes some characteristic to the proposition (or open proposition) expressed by S. For example, Â“Fred knows thatÂ” is a connective. And if you say Â“Fred knows that snow is white,Â” you are attributing a property to the proposition that snow is white; you are saying of that proposition that it has the property that Fred knows it to be true. Â“BecauseÂ” is a connective, and if you say Â“snow is white because grass is green,Â” you are seeing of the propositions that snow is white and grass is green that the former is a causal consequence of the latter. One last example: Â“for all xÂ” is a connective, and if you say Â“for all x, x is a mammal if x is a whale,Â” you are attributing a characteristic (that of being correct) to each of infinitely many propositions. (That is why, even though Â“for all xÂ” and other quantifiers donÂ’t operate on sentences, they nonetheless qualify as connectives. 
Connectives attribute properties to propositions. This is what quantifiers do. In fact, quantifiers do it on an even larger scale than other connectives. Consider the quantifier Â“for all x.Â” When coupled with the open sentence Â“x is tall,Â” this yields a sentence (Â“for all x, x is tallÂ”) that says of an infinitely large class of propositions (viz. those having the form x is tall) that each of its members is true. (By contrast, Â“Fred believes that,Â” when coupled with Â“Jim is tall,Â” yields a sentence (Â“Fred believes that Jim is tallÂ”) that attributes a property (that of being believed by Fred) to only one proposition.) That is why, even though quantifiers operate on open sentences, whereas other connectives operate on actual sentences, quantifiers are generally treated as connectives. 
A sentence can have more than one connective. An example of such a sentence would be: 
(*) Â“either Jim is in Idaho and Larry is in Idaho with Jim, or Larry is in Delaware and Fred is with Larry in Delaware.Â” 
The main connective of (*) is Â“or.Â” Why is it the main connective? (*) attributes a property to the set containing the propositions either Jim is in Idaho and Larry is in Idaho with Jim and Larry is in Delaware and Fred is with Larry in Delaware. The property that it attributes to that set is the property of containing at least one true member. The other connectives occurring in (*) donÂ’t attribute properties to that pair of propositions; they attribute properties to propositions composing the propositions composing (*). That is why none of those connectives is the main connective. I leave it to the reader as an exercise to produce an explicit definition of the term Â“main connectiveÂ” on the basis of these remarks.
