Duhem-Quine thesis: The thesis, which was advocated by W.V.O. Quine 
(1908Â–2001)[501], that no theory does either a better job or a worse job than any other theory of modeling any given body of data. In other words, given any body of observations B and given any two theories T and T*, T does no better and no worse a job than T* of modeling B. 
QuineÂ’s argument was that, given any datum D that appears to confirm T and to disconfirm T*, one can make D disconfirm T and disconfirm T* by tinkering with oneÂ’s background assumptions. 
QuineÂ’s thesis is either empty or itÂ’s false. Scientific theories arenÂ’t analytically entailed by the observations that support them. Induction isnÂ’t deduction. This is an obvious triviality. So, assuming that what Quine is saying isnÂ’t trivial, it must be to the effect that no theory does a better job or a worse job than any other theory of accounting for any given body of data. To account for a body of data is to show that the occurrence of each datum composing it is non-anomalous. Thus, QuineÂ’s thesis, supposing it nonÂ­trivial, is to the effect that no theory does a better job than any other theory of removing causal anomalies from any given body of data. 
Thus interpreted, QuineÂ’s thesis is clearly false. The acne of each of the millions of acne-sufferers who takes medication X gets ten times worse within ten minutes of the time at which said acne-sufferer takes X. Theory T entails that anyone who has acne who takes X will immediately be cured of his acne forever. Rival theory T* entails that theory T is false. According to Quine, by tinkering around with background assumptions, T models the observational data as well as T*. But thatÂ’s clearly false. 
Quine says that, in situations like this, we should Â“plead hallucination.Â” In other words, we should assume that the observations in question, most of which are had by people who do not otherwise have any history of hallucinations, are hallucinations. If we make this assumption, weÂ’re stuck with a huge number of otherwise non-existent anomalies. WeÂ’re stuck having to explain, or to regard it as incapable of explanation, why it is that people who never had hallucinations before all of a sudden started hallucinating; and we are also stuck having to explain/regard as inexplicable why it is that people who did have hallucinations before all of a sudden started having acne-related hallucinations that, in terms of their content and in terms of their etiology, are completely unlike the hallucinations they had previously. 
Empirical knowledge, analytic knowledge, synthetic, a priori, a posteriori: Empirical knowledge is knowledge that is based at least partly on the testimony of the senses. Not all knowledge is empirical; some is analytic.

Synthetic knowledge is non-analytic knowledge. 
A priori knowledge is knowledge that is constitutive of our cognitive machinery; itÂ’s knowledge that is hardwired into us and that we therefore donÂ’t acquire. 
A posteriori knowledge is knowledge that is not a priori.

An example is the obsessive-compulsive personâ€™s compulsion to ritualize, even though he knows there to be no objective reason for doing so. The obsessive-compulsive does not judge his obsessions and subsequent compulsions to be irrational. He experiences them as being irrational. 
The schizophrenicâ€™s ability to distinguish between fantasy and reality has been damaged. The obsessive-compulsiveâ€™s ability to make this distinction has been damaged, but his ability to do the things that he knows to be demanded by reality has been damaged. It is his will, not his judgment, that his been damaged. 
What the schizophrenic and the obsessive-compulsive have in common is a fundamentally infantile outlook. Each has retained the narcissism of the infant, even though each has the intellect of an adult. The schizophrenicâ€™s ego is also the ego of this still very much alive inner infant. As a result, his ego has two distinct and incompatible outlooks, and it therefore has no coherent way of processing information. The obsessive-compulsiveâ€™s ego is not identical with that of the infant within him, and this is way his ego, unlike that of the schizophrenic, has no trouble distinguishing between fantasy and reality. But because there are two egos within the obsessive-compulsive, both competing for the reigns of agency, the obesssive-compulsive cannot act rationally, even though he can think rationally. 
In general, an ego-syntonic illness is an inability to think rationally, and ego-dystonic illness is an inability to act rationally.

Dr. K: Exactly.

Neurosis vs. Psychosis 
Psychosis is a mental impairment that is precipitated and sustained by a break with external reality. Neurosis is a mental impairment that is precipitated and sustained by a break with oneâ€™s emotional condition. 
The neurotic flees from his emotions; the psychotic flees from reality. Neurosis may lead to a blunting of oneâ€™s awareness of certain aspects of external reality, but any such loss of awareness is subordinate to loss of awareness of oneâ€™s emotional condition. 
Similarly, psychosis may lead to a disruption of oneâ€™s understanding of oneâ€™s emotional condition, but any such disturbance is subordinate to the psychoticâ€™s loss of awareness of external reality. 
Though symmetrical in the just-described respects, neurosis and psychosis are ultimately not mirror images of each other. This is a consequence of the fact that psychosis involves a partial regression to a condition of psychological infancy, the operative term being â€œpartial.â€ An infant is not psychotic. The reason is that the infantâ€™s psychological integration is not simultaneously that of an adult and an infant; it is simply that of an infant. For this reason, the infantâ€™s psychological condition is integrated and healthy, even though the infantâ€™s understanding of reality is even more subjective, and therefore more projective, than that of the adult psychotic. 
The adult psychotic, on the other hand, has the psychological architecture of an adult as well as that of an infant. Therefore, the psychotic has two entirely distinct and incompatible ways of processing information. He does not have a unified value system; he does not have a unified understanding of how to implement such values as he has; and his psychological condition is therefore therefore one of utter disarray. And therein lies the peculiarly damaging nature of psychosis. 
Nothing comparable holds of the neurotic. Neurosis is about containing threats to oneâ€™s integration by repressing them. To repress a conceit is not to bury oneâ€™s knowledge of it in the unconscious; it is rather to bury oneâ€™s knowledge of its emotional valence in the unconscious. As a result, the neuroticâ€™s condition is one of relatively unimpaired intellectual awareness. 
In fact, in some circumscribed ways, it may be even be a condition heightened intellectual awareness, owing to the fact that the neurotic is likely to compensate for his impoverished emotional state by hypercathecting his intellect. Moreover, by stripping the contents of consciousness of their emotional valences, the neurotic guarantees that he has a hyper-stable, though also an ossified psyche. 
The essence of psychosis is an inability to organize consciously experienced emotion; the essence of neurosis is an inability to have consciously experienced emotion. The former is paralyzed by a superabundance of emotion, the latter by lack of it. 

Compulsive Work 
Compulsive Work is about avoidance. Here one must distinguish between two kinds of workaholics. There is the workaholic who loves what he is doing: this person works because he wants to work. Then there is the workaholic who hates what he is doing: this person works because he doesnâ€™t want to work. The workaholic who loves his work is not working compulsively, and this form of workaholism is not about avoidance. But the workaholic who hates his work isworking compulsively, and this form of workaholism is about avoidance. This type of workaholic is avoiding doing what he wants to do, and because he hates what he is doing, he has to do it compulsively. 

Obsessions and Compulsions 
When one is obsessively afraid of something, that is because one really wants that thing to happen. The son who is morbidly preoccupied with the idea that his father will cut off his trust fund, even though there is no reason to believe this to happen, really wants his father to cut him. He is ashamed of being dependent on his father, and deep down wants to be free and strike out on his own. 
To give a personal example, I was morbidly afraid that my dissertation adviser would die of a heart attack. I remember that, at the time, I used to joke with my girlfriend about how I wanted this to happen, but those jokes were only jokes---or so I told myself. My adviser turned out to be incredibly malicious, and I had to switch dissertation advisers. 
In any case, I knew all along that he was ill willed, but initially, before I switched advisers, I was dependent on him, so I did not want to admit this to myself. So my desire that he die of a heart attack had to remain unconscious. Once I ceased to have any dependence on him, my actual feelings became conscious. 
After I switched advisers, everything worked out. It was enormously difficult at first, since I had to start my dissertation from scratch, and I also had to write it in a completely new area. But I wrote it in three weeks, and in the process new intellectual and professional vistas opened up for me. 
The point is that when I was obsessively afraid that my first adviser would die, my unconscious was trying to tell me something. But it could not tell me directly, since I didnâ€™t want to hear what it was trying to tell me. So it had to express itself circuitously, through what Freud calls a negation. 
A negation is a case of letting oneâ€™s real feelings into consciousness only on the condition that they negated. Here is an example. You and a lawyer friend of yours are discussing your careers, and she says, without any prompting from you, â€œI know what youâ€™re thinking: you think I hate being a lawyer. You think I want to quit and do something else. Well, youâ€™re wrong. This is definitely what I want to do. Yes it is.â€ 
What this person is saying is: â€œI really hate being a lawyer. I hate it so very, very much. God, I hate being a lawyer.â€ But she canâ€™t admit it to herself. After all, sheâ€™s locked in, or at least believes herself to be. She spent three years in law school; she may have spent several years practing law; and she may not know what else to do. 
She wonâ€™t admit her real feelings to herself, so when those feelings rise to the surface of her psyche, she hastily slaps a big â€œnotâ€ on them, to make sure she doesnâ€™t see them for what they are. 
A lot of religious fanaticism consists of negation. When people are hysterical about their religious beliefs, that is because they arenâ€™t their real beliefs. Fanaticism is a way of containing doubt. 
Extreme views are often cases of negation. People who have extremely puritanical views about sex are, without exception, people with extremely intense strong libidos; and people who have extreme views about alcohol--Â­who think that it is the root of all evil and should not be tolerated---are people alcoholics who yearn for a drink but know they mustnâ€™t succumb to this temptation. 
Compulsions are negations that are expressed in action. I will give an example from my own life. For a while, I tried to make money working with machines. I had no aptitude for what I was doing and no real desire to do it. But I would work for days on end with these machines, sometimes going without sleep. I would not let myself stop working. 
And the reason is that if I had let myself stop working, my real feelings would have flooded to the surface. Which is eventually what happened, and it was incredibly liberating. 
The reason my machine business failed so utterly is that I never really wanted to do it in the first place, and that is also why, when I was doing it, I had to do in such a compulsive manner. Itâ€™s also why all of that work yielded nothing. It yielded nothing, because my unconscious motivation---my real motivation---was to not to what I was doing. The reason I was compulsive in efforts to get this business off the ground was that my real motivation was to put it in the ground. 
People ask how they can free themselves from OCD. 
A first step is to know the following truths. 
Obsessions are negations. If you are obsessively afraid of such and such, that is because what you want is such and such. 
Compulsions are negations that are being acted out. If you compulsively to such and such, that is because what you really desire, and what you are really trying to accomplish through your compulsive actions, is the opposite of such and such. 
The reason people obsess is that they donâ€™t admit their real feelings to themselves. And the reason they donâ€™t admit their feelings to themselves is that, if they did, they would have to do a lot of hard work. They would have to change their lives, and themselves, which is the hardest kind of work. And their compulsive workâ€”their endless hours at the law firm or their endless hours doting on the ailing parent whom they secretely hate----are pseudo-work: they are laziness expressed as work. These people are too weak and lazy to do the hard thing, which is to change, so they do the easy thing, which is to keep doing the same thing, even though it doesnâ€™t work, but to do so much of that thing that it appears as though they are working. 
The good news is that, if you actually make those changes, instead of remaining on your treadmill of compulsion, it turns out to be far easier than you thought. You are no longer fighting yourself, and everything falls into place. 
You would not admit your true feelings into consciousness, so you had to negate them. Because your real feelings were so intense, you had to redouble those negations; so those negations became obsessions. But your obsessions were not enough to contain your real feelings, so those obsessions became compulsions. The reason those compulsions are so unpleasant is that you really want to do the opposite. 
So do it. Donâ€™t fight yourself. Be yourself. 
You obsess when you believe the opposite of what you consciously believe. You act compulsively when you do the opposite of what you are really trying to do. 
The compulsion is a compulsive cover-up. You are trying to bury your real feelings. And you are trying to bury them because you are weak and lazy. But your life would be easier, and you would have less to be afraid of, if you copped to your feelings. A life of obsessions and compulsions quickly leads to oblivion and is itself oblivion. 
So the way to get over OCD is simple: Do what you want to do. 
When you do what you are compelled to do, you are doing the opposite of what you want to do. 
Read Totem and Taboo, by Sigmund Freud, where the role of negations and compulsions in the construction of morality and other social institutions is expertly explained.

OCD and Philosophy
Obsessive-compulsives and philosophers have a lot in common. First if all, they are both compulsive doubters. They doubt the obvious. They rationalize their doing so by saying that they are trying to be rigorous and that they are trying not to believe things that are false. But that is, indeed, a mere rationalization. Both the obsessive-compulsive and the philosopher are impotent, being too fearful to engage the world. And to the extent that they have potency, it lies in their ability to manipulate linguistic or otherwise symbolic proxies of reality. So instead of dealing with the world on its own terms---instead of dealing with the world in the worldâ€”they try to internalize as much of the world as possible into the sphere of their own thought, where they are dominant. And they are dominant there both because they are more inclined towards thought than towards action and also, more importantly, because it is their own mind where, of course, they ipso facto have total power.
Or at least the illusion thereofâ€”more on this in a moment.
Then there is the fact that both the philosopher and the obsessive-compulsive are unduly preoccupied with logical niceties and fine points of argumentation. This is at least partly a derivative of their sense of impotence: when one has no material of oneâ€™s own to work onâ€” which is the case whenever one is too afraid of the world to venture out into it and get material--- one preoccupies oneself with secondary materialâ€”with matters of grammar, logic, argumentation and the like.
Plus, by conditionalizing the acceptance of hypotheses on subtleties of proof and argumentation, they are able to rationalize continuing to remain in their own heads; they are able to rationalize commandeering debates, and holing them up within their own thought-scape, pending the resolution of niceties of logic and dialectical protocol which, of their very nature, are incapable of being definitely resolved.
There is another, somewhat less invidious dimension to the just-discussed similarity between the philosopher and the obsessive-compulsive. Neither the philosopher nor the obsessive-compulsive has any real doubts, even of a purely intellectual variety, as to the contents of the external world. In any case, neither has any more such doubts than the next person. But both are indeed more doubtful than the next person. They are more doubtful, and with good reason, as to the contents of the internal world. With the both the philosopher and the obsessive- compulsive, their supposed doubts about the external world are displaced, projected doubts about the internal world. They are both people whose minds are veritable caldrons of primal desires but who, being moral, do their best to suppress and repress their basal urges. The result is that, while their understanding of the external world is in fact perfectly good, notwithstanding their asseverations to their contrary, they are quite in the dark as to the internal world, believing or half-believing themselves to be logic-driven, Cartesian ratiocinators, when, in fact, their Cartesianism is only a veneer, which holds only of the thinnest and most uppermost mental stratum of theirs, the rest of their respective psyches being Nietzschean cesspools.
And both of these types of people fancy themselves â€˜rational actorsâ€™â€”people who have gotten the better of the base side of themselves---when in reality they are anything but rational actors, the truth being that they are driven by rage, narcissism and fear. Indeed, their intellectualism is a reaction to, and attempt to cloak their own darkly retrograde psychological condition.
And their insistence on the rationality of man is merely an idealizationâ€”a projection of a self-image that they half-have and are 100% trying to have. And the Lockean/Cartesian
 
insistence on the non-existence of the unconsciousâ€”on the brazenly spurious idea that mind extends only as far consciousness---is merely another tendentious rationalization, and a decidedly more sterile and superficial one than their false, but not entirely misconceived insistence on the primacy within people of rationality.
There is a second similarity between the obsessive-compulsive and the philosopher. They are both pathologically concerned with ethicsâ€”with questions of right and wrong and good vs. evil. In both cases, this is because they are crypto-criminalsâ€”people whose fundamental orientation with respect to others is anti-socialâ€”this being reflected in their solipsism and skepticism---but who also have strong, nay draconian, superegos and thus do everything in their power to suppress their criminal side. And to this end they enlist their pre-existing penchant for dwelling on technicalities of logic; which, when transferred from the sphere of knowledge-theory into the domain of ethics, results in their dwelling on technicalities of a legalistic nature. And this is why many an obsessive-compulsive, and also many a philosopher, goes into law.
Philosophers tend to be extremely sensitive to, and intelligent about, niceties of language.
This is obviously true of some obsessive-compulsives, but it is unknown whether it is categorically true of them. But supposing that it is, this, I think, is a derivative of their fear-based retreat from the external world, which is the realm of action, into the internal world, which is the realm of thought. After all, sensitivity to linguistic niceties being cut from much the same cloth as sensitivity to logical niceties, and the latter being, as we have already seen, a by-product of the philosopherâ€™s and the obsessive-compulsives replacing of reality with cognitive proxies thereof.
One last point: I have noticed that a hugely disproportionate number of philosophers, including myself, are professional level musicians. Around 40% of philosophy professors fall into this category. I donâ€™t know whether the same is true of the class of obsessive compulsivesâ€” it presumably isnâ€™t. But even though there is not, in all likelihood, a categorical connection between OCD and musicality, there may be a sub-categorical connection, as in, there may be a relatively comprehensive sub-set of the class of obsessive-compulsives whose members are also musical and whose being musical is connected to their OCD. In any case, it seems that musicianship and philosophical ability are related in that both involve decrypting and then re- encrypting information; they are both about organizing informationâ€”and doing so with obsessional concern for the logical interrelations holding among bits of information organized, and a proportionate disregard for the correspondence of that information to external reality.
 
What are Some Characteristics of OCD in Children?

A listener of mine, Emma, asked me: What are some early signs of OCD in children?
Here is my answer: First of all, all children are OCD. In fact, OCD is actually a prolongation into adulthood of the child's 'binary' emotional relation to the world. When you send a child to camp, he kicks and screams and cries. Then he has to come home, he cries again. Also, children, much like obsessive-compulsives, are soothed by repetition and like familiarity. They like to be told the same story at bedtime, night after night, and sleep with the same stuffed animal. That said, children who are actually OCD--i.e. who will be OCD as adults--do have some distinctinve characteristics. The main difference between them and non-OCD children is that they tend to have rituals and peculiarities that are specific to them. All children like to sleep with same stuffed animal night after and be told the same story night after night. But only OCD children have to sleep with a glass of water next to the bed or have to put their left shoe on before their first. Also, OCD children tend to be more cholicy and more emotionally intense and extreme than others children---more prone to bouts of depressive withdrawal. But I stress that OCD is never itself the issue, and OCD is not eliminated by being confronted head-on. OCD is about withdrawal from a frightening world into a safe space of thought and ritual, and the only way to conquer OCD is to conquer fear. Which one does by developing strengths of character and intellect. OCD is given rise to by emotional vulnerability, which in turn is given rise to by actual vulnerability--by defenselessness. And the way to defeat OCD is to give proper, non- neurotic defenses to the person in question.
 
The Failure of Political Philosophy to Engage Reality
I wrote an audio-article in which I said that both philosophyâ€”specifically, philosophical skepticism---and OCD were about retreating from the exigencies of external actual reality into the safety of internal pseudo-reality. And in keeping with this, I said that both OCD and philosophy are intellectualized impotence.
In any case, a listener of mine who goes by the name of L and H Productions, made the following point in response to my article. He said: â€œWhat about political philosophers? Donâ€™t they engage the world? Arenâ€™t they a counter-example to your point, that philosophy is about autistic non-engagement?â€
Yes and no. Mostly no. Consider Plato, as he is a paradigm case of political philosophers. Platoâ€™s system was completely a priori. Yesâ€”he was talking about how to reform the world. But really, that isnâ€™t what he was doing. He really talking about how to replace the world with a world of his ownâ€”a world that had little reality, and little justification, outside of his own thought-space. So Plato was really talking about replacing the actual world his thought-world.
He wasnâ€™t in any real way engaging the actual world.
And the absurdity of what Plato was doing comes out in a lot of ways. In, for example, the rigidity of the society that he was proposing; in the stereotypedâ€”and in that respect decidedly OCD---protocols governing both education and, more generally, interactions between different people; and, moreover, in the absurd idea, put forth in this dialogue The Laws, that even the most minor violations of law should be punished by death; and, finally, in the incoherent idea that society should be ruled by a philosopher kingâ€”incoherent, because societies are to be run by sapient doers, not sapient thinkers; societies are to be run by people who do not flee from the world into intellectual constructions and, therefore, are not to be run by philosophers, granting, of course, that they are to be run by people who are philosopher-like to the extent, but only to the extent, that they are intelligent.
Or consider Marx, another textbook case of a philosophical philosopher. Yesâ€”he was talking about how to change the world. But really, he was talking, quite explicitly, about destroying the existing social structure and replacing it with one that had no real basis---other than a totally fabricated one	in reality, and which, when it was implemented, led to loss of life
and opportunity on an unprecedented scale.
Now, not all political philosophers are as guilty as Marx and Plato of failing to engage actual political realities. Some political philosophers do not simply propose that existing political realities be replaced with their childish a priori fantasies.
For example, John Locke made a number of extremely reasonable points about law and economics that, when implemented, were enormously successful. And much the same is true, though in some respects to an even greater degree, of Adam Smith and David Hume, who, along with Locke, created the discipline of modern free-market economics.
But Adam Smith was really an ex-philosopher who left the discipline of philosopher in order to start a new discipline. And Locke and Hume were hard-core empiricists: their whole agenda, as philosophers, was to empiricize philosophy. Their criticism of existing philosophy was that it failed to engage the world, and their objective was to reinvent the discipline in such a way that it did engage the world.
So, yes, their political philosophiesâ€”which were very good	did engage the world; but
to the extent that they did, they were almost anti-philosophical political philosophies.
That said, political theory can engage the world, and that does represent a limitation on
 
the scope of my point about philosophy categorically being in the nature of an autistic withdrawal from reality.
But there is one last point to make, which does to some extent buttress my conception of philosophy as autistic retreat. Hume and Locke were arch-empiricists, meaning that, in their view, you donâ€™t know it if you donâ€™t see it (or otherwise have direct sensory evidence of it).
Now, empiricism collapses into the view that we can of nothing except our own conscious states; for the empiricist rejects all rules of inference would enable us to posit the existence of anything-
--the empiricist says that we can know it only if it is a datum of consciousness and, therefore, that if we have to posit it, meaning infer its existence, then it doesnâ€™t exist.
So in their attempt to make philosophy engage the world, Locke and Hume empiricized philosophy. But in empiricizing philosophy, Locke and Hume made philosophy collapse into pure skepticism, pure skepticism being the most compete conceivable autistic withdrawal from reality into oneâ€™s own mind. And what this shows is that, even when philosophers try to make philosophy not be an autistic retreat, it ends up being precisely that. Which does rather confirm my conception of philosophy as autistic retreat.
 
How to Get Rid of OCD


A listener of mine asked me the following question: Is there an effective treatment that can eliminate OCD for good?

Here is my answer:
There is only one way to 'get rid' of OCD, and that is to find a calling in life in which one's obsessive compulsive tendencies are an asset, as opposed to a liability. OCD is not so much an illness as it is a distinctive way of processing emotional information. In the wrong environment, that psychological architecture can hold one back; in right one, it can push one forward. Many writers, composers, mathematicians, lawyers, philosophers and creative and analytical people of many stripes (e.g. Beethoven, Einstein, Dr. Johnson) have OCD; such people have found callings in which their OCD works for them. So it's not about eliminating it; it's about putting it to one's advantage. I myself have done that in a very big way. I am being OCD right now, in writing such a thorough answer, but in being so thorough in this context, I am putting to my obsessive-compulsive tendencies to non-pathological use, instead of letting them express themselves as OCD. And that is point: one doesn't get rid of mental illnesses by getting rid of them; one chooses to work in areas in which those mental illnesses are functional and, therefore, not mental illnesses

Is OCD a Disease?


When a condition is described as a â€˜diseaseâ€™, it is usually implied that the person who has it cannot simply â€˜will itâ€™ away. Social Anxiety is about Rage


People who have social anxiety donâ€™t want to be around people. And they donâ€™t want to be around people because they hate people, or at least are angry at them.

Structural Therapy
The preferred way of treating OCD these days is known as â€œcognitive behavioral therapy.â€ CBT be called â€œbehavioral therapyâ€ since there is nothing cognitive about it, as it consists entirely in changing the obsessive-compulsiveâ€™s behavior directly, and not way of changing the emotional conflicts responsible for his behavior.

But taken by itself, behavior modification is not enough. The only real way to treat OCD is through structural therapy. Structural therapy is the process of changing the obsessive-compulsiveâ€™s mentality from that of someone who is reality- avoidant, and therefore fantasy-oriented, to being someone who is reality-oriented, and therefore fantasy-avoidant. The obsessive-compulsiveâ€™s obsessionality is about his preferring symbolic representations of reality to reality and, consequently, his preferring thought to action. And his compulsions are merely externalized obsessions and therefore represent overt expressions of his reality-avoidance.
In order to effect this change of orientation within the obsessive-compulsive, it is necessary to modify his behavior; and cognitive behavioral therapy is therefore a component of structural therapy. The Limitations of CBT in the Treatment of OCD
There is a method of treating OCD known as â€˜cognitive-behavioral therapyâ€™ (CBT). CBT involves getting obsessive-compulsives to do the things that they are phobic about doing. Cognitive-behavioral therapy really just be called â€˜Behavioral therapyâ€™, since there is nothing cognitive about it. In fact, it is anti-cognitive: all cognitive issues are ignored or addressed only by way of their behavioral derivatives.
In any case, it is patently obvious that getting over OCD involves changing oneâ€™s behavior. If a given obsessive-compulsive showers 20 times a day, then the first thing he must do is to stop showering twenty times a day. This does not mean that all is lost for the obsessive-compulsive. All is most definitely not lost. It just means that the underlying cause of the obsessive-compulsives various obsessions and compulsions must be addressed.
And ultimately there is always one such cause. That cause is that the obsessive- compulsive has fled from reality into a world of symbolic proxies of reality. His obsessions have ideas for their objects, not the external realties for which ideas stand. And his compulsions are merely obsessions that are externalized in behavior.
The cause of this flight from reality into symbolic proxies thereof varies from case to case. So the cause of the cause of OCD varies from person to person. But the cause of OCD does not so vary. It is, in each case, a fear-driven flight from reality into a safe internal world in which ideas have taken the place of realities and in which thinking has taken the place of doing.
And ultimately the only way to improve the obsessive-compulsiveâ€™s condition is to get him out of this bubble of pseudo-reality. Getting him out of this bubble involves getting him to behave normally. There is no way to get him to rejoin the living without breaking the back of his various compulsions. For these compulsions---for example, the endless showering and hand- washing, the cleaning, the various repetitive and stereotyped behaviors to which OCD gives rise-

The obsessive-compulsiveâ€™s various compulsives actions serve as a kind of veil between himself and reality, that prevents him from directly engaging it. And he has to engage it.

But the essence of the restoration of the obsessive-compulsiveâ€™s sanity is getting him to engage reality. Turn OCD Against Itself


If you put a two-year old in ocean-water, it will start crying. But then it gets used to the water. And when you try to take it out two hours later, it starts crying again!
Children are OCD like in many respects. They need comforting routines. They need to be told certain bedtime stories over and over again. They need to sleep with specific stuffed animals. And so on.
But this clinginess of theirs can be turned against itself. Right now, they need to sleep with the snoopy stuffed animal, and they will howl and scream if you try to get them switch to their Dumbo stuffed animal But then, after an initial period of protest, the clinginess they had towards Snoopy will transfer over to Dumbo.
With OCD itâ€™s the same way. Itâ€™s the same way, because itâ€™s the very same thing. OCD isnâ€™t just like the just-described obsessive clinginess of children: it is that clinginess. Like all mental illnesses, OCD is regressive: it is the mindâ€™s returning to a modus operandi from its earlier days.
Put another way, OCD is the persistence into adulthood of a childhood defense- mechanism. And that childhood defense-mechanism is one of clinging to certain habits, so as to insulate oneself from a frightening world within a safe little autistic bubble.
And that is what OCD is. OCD is about clinging to certain rituals and habits that make one feel safe. It is the presence, in an adult, of a defense-mechanism that, in other people, ceases to be operative during early childhood.
The other side of the coin is that, underlying the obsessive-compulsiveâ€™s rigidity is the same neural plasticityâ€”the same transferability of clinginenssâ€”that is present in the childâ€”that is, indeed, the hallmark of a childâ€™s mind.
The obsessive-compulsive is binary: he is all about all or nothing. Either he loves or hates.
Either he does no exercise or he compulsively exercises. Either he has to have bananas in his morning cereal or he has to not have them in his cereal.
So the obsessive-compulsiveness obsessive-compulsivenessâ€”his clingnessâ€”is about binariness; it is about all or nothing-ism. And inherent in his all or nothing-ism is a child-like ability to change---to do 180 degree shifts. So, paradoxically, underlying the obsessive- compulsiveâ€™s rigidity is non-rigidityâ€”is neural plasticity.
And the obsessive-compulsiveâ€™s greatest asset, therefore, is his OCD itself! He must use the binariness, and concomitant ability to change, to combat the rigidity and fixity of habits to which his OCD disposes him.
Let me be more concrete. There is always something that the obsessive-compulsive has to do that he is afraid of doing---in the same way that the child is afraid of getting into the bathtub. And the obsessive-compulsive must confront this fear, and do it quickly and unblinkingly. And then what will happen is that he will be as obsessive-compulsive about doing this new thingâ€”the thing he had to do but was afraid to doâ€”as he was about not doing it before. Just as the child, once he settles into his bath, will kick and scream when he has to get out of the bath tub.
So turn OCD against itself, by using the all-or-nothingism inherent in, and the neural plasticity inherent in and hidden in that all-or-nothingins, to effectuate growth-critical changes in oneself.
 
How do I get over my OCD?
Somebody on Quora.com asked: How do I get over my OCD? Here is my response:

Intrusive Thoughts

Why People with OCD Have Them


If you have a goal, it is easy not to be lazy. But if you donâ€™t have goal. It is hard not to be lazy, since there is no point in not being lazy. Similarly, if you have a goal, it is easy not to succumb to neurotic compulsions. But if you donâ€™t have a goal, it is hard not to do so since there is no point in tolerating the anxiety brought on by not doing so.
As for obsessions, these are always displacements: one obsesses about such and such as a way of not confronting thus and such. And when one has a goal, oneâ€™s obsessional energies are naturally channeled in the right direction, since, under that circumstance, oneâ€™s mind stands to gain more in the way of relief from anxiety by not obsessing than by obsessing. And when doesnâ€™t have a goal, oneâ€™s mind stands to gain more in the way of anxiety-relief by obsessing than by not obsessing, and one is therefore inclined to keep on obsessing.
As for intrusive thoughts, these are oneâ€™s mindâ€™s way of telling oneâ€”in a compressed, crude, and distorted way---what one has to do. In any case, the way to get over obtrusive thoughts is to have a goal in life. And one can be free from psychopathology only so long as a one has a goal that oneâ€™s mental energies can organize themselves around and that oneâ€™s drives can discharge themselves through.

All people are dominated by compulsions. In the case of the non-obsessive-compulsive, those compulsions are unconscious. In the case of the obsessive-compulsive, they are conscious. And that is what it is to have OCD: it is to consciously experience the compulsions that others only experience unconsciously. Thus, where the non-obsessive-compulsive has the illusion of freedom, the obsessive-compulsive has the illusion of its absence. In actuality, the obsessive- compulsive, by virtue of being aware of the compulsions to which he is subjected, has the ability to liberate himself from those compulsions, whereas the non-obsessive-compulsive, by virtue of not being thus aware, does not.
 
Physical vs. Mental Illness
Almost all physical illnesses are simply deficitsâ€”as in, they donâ€™t do those who have them any good. And most mental illnesses are simply deficits. But OCDâ€”though functionally a deficitâ€”is an asset in two important ways. First, those who have it are highly intelligent, meaning that they are good at processing intellectual or cognitive information, and highly sensitive, meaning that they are good at processing affective or emotional information.
Philosophical aside: What we refer to as â€˜sensitivityâ€™ is a form of internal awarenessâ€”of inwardly directed intelligence: it is about different parts of the mind being in good communication with each other. And what we refer to as â€œintelligenceâ€ is outwardly directed intelligence; it is about being aware of dependence-relations holding among mind-external entities. In any case, the obsessive-compulsive has both kinds of intelligence; indeed, his condition is about those two forms of intelligence being hyper-operative---being over-deployed. So, yes, so long as they are over-deployed, he is seriously impaired; but his impairment has to do with the mutually cancelling effects of powerful cognitive forces, not, as is the case with most psychological impairments, with an absence of such forces.
And this relates to the second respect in which obsessive-compulsives are at an advantage.
Obsessive-compulsives are psycho-dynamic. They are internally conflicted. Which, though not an asset in and of itself, shows that they have ideals and, moreover, that they are taking themselves to task for falling short of those ideals. Where there is no conception of right and wrongâ€”no conception of how, morally and otherwise, things should beâ€”there is no internal conflict. And where there is a conception of right and wrong, there is ipso facto a willingness to try to make things right. And where such willingness exists, it can always be used by the person who has it to make himself better. In the case of the obsessive-compulsive, this willingness is not being optimally deployed; but it is there, which is what matters, since, so long as it exists, it can always be redeployed.
So the obsessive-compulsive, though in a very unpleasant and in some ways objectively bad situation, is best thought as being in a situation not of sheer minuses, but of inverted pluses--
-of assets that are being turned against themselves, not of mere deficits. And this means that in the right hands, the obsessive-compulsive stands not only to make a good recovery but to have a positively good life.
 
How to Treat Compulsions that are not Accompanied by Obsessions?



One of my listeners, Earth Pet, asked the following question. I quote:
â€œHow would you advise attenuating or controlling compulsions for those without the obsessive component?â€
Here is my answer.
Obsessions are thwarted compulsions. In other words, when one has a compulsion that one is prevented from acting on, one is left with an obsession. Equivalently, compulsions are obsessions that are expressed in behavior.
So the relationship between the obsession and the compulsion parallels the relationship between intention and subsequent action.
And just as there is always an intention whenever there is an action, so there is always an obsession whenever there is a compulsions. Of course, the obsession does not become an object of consideration in its own right so long as it is discharged sufficiently quickly in action, just as an intention does not become an object of attention in its own right if sufficiently quickly discharged in action. But just as there is an intention whenever there is action, so there is an obsession whenever there is a compulsive action.
So the situation presupposed by the question does not in fact exist.

Why Psychopaths Overachieve


I was going for my nightly walk and, as is my wont, thinking about the various ventures that I am trying to get off the ground. And, as is also my want, I was plagued with doubtsâ€”with self-doubts. And it then occurred to me why psychopaths are so successful: they are not neurotic. Self-doubt is inherently neurotic. It is one thing to know oneâ€™s own limitations: that is not self- doubt; that is just plain self-knowledge. But self-doubt is not about self-knowledge or even
quasi-self-knowledge; it is moralistic self-undermining; it is neurotic self-punishment. And because psychopaths donâ€™t have consciences, they donâ€™t doubt themselves and, more generally, they are not neurotic. Neurosis is about a conflict between oneâ€™s primal desires and oneâ€™s conscience. So psychopaths, having as they do no conscience, are not neurotic; and they are therefore not held by neurosis or, consequently, by neurotic self-doubt or, consequently, by any self-doubt. Non-psychopaths, on the other hand, even exceptionally gifted onesâ€”nay, especially exceptionally gifted onesâ€”are riddled with neurosis and therefore with self-doubt and are therefore prone to self-sabotage. The ideal condition is to be a non-neurotic, non-psychopath; and that condition is achievable, and it is my objective as an analyst to get people attain that condition.
 
The Therapeutic Significance of a Healthy Sex Life



The purpose of psychoanalysis and indeed of all forms of psychotherapy is to get the patient to live in the real world. Freud himself knew this: he explicitly said that the sole functions of psychoanalysis were to get the patient to be able to work and to love.
At the same time, Freud said, or certainly seemed at certain junctures to say, that mental health is all about sexâ€”that mental illness is all about not having a good sex life and that mental well-being is all about having a good one.
Which, if indeed he did say this, is seriously overstated, not positively erroneous.
But there is a way of interpreting this supposed conceit of Freudâ€™s that gives it legitimacy.
Letâ€™s start with the premise that sanity is about living in the real world and insanity is about living in oneâ€™s imagination.
To the extent that people are not actually having sex with other human beings, their sex lives are masturbatory and fantasy-based, and are therefore dissociated from reality and, quite literally, insane. And to the extent that people are having sex---provided that it is emotionally engaged sex, as opposed to just masturbation that happens to another personâ€™s body---oneâ€™s sex life is reality-based, non- dissociated and, therefore, quite literally sane.
Is there more to having a non-dissociated and sane existence than having a non- dissociated sex life? Yes. Is there more to having a dissociated and insane existence than having a dissociated sex life? Yes. But oneâ€™s life is non-dissociated to the extent that oneâ€™s sex life is non-dissociated and dissociated others. Moreover, as Freud said, however overstatedly, oneâ€™s sex life is to some extent a prototype for the rest of oneâ€™s life, as in, there is at least some tendency for the non-sexual component of oneâ€™s existence to be non-dissociated if the sexual component of oneâ€™s existence is non-dissociated and dissociated otherwise.
To sum up: Sanity is about living in the real world. Masturbation is about not living in the real world. So if oneâ€™s sex life is masturbation-based, one is to that extent not sane, even if one is otherwise sane. And if oneâ€™s sex-life is masturbation-based, it is unlikely that one is otherwise completely sane.
 
Autism as Pseudo-self-containment

Autistic people seem to live in their own world, and the obvious thing to say about them, therefore, is that they are self-contained. But they are not self-contained. They are pseudo-self- contained. Autism is about needing people early in life and being given trauma instead. And the traumatized child reacts by withdrawing into himself. But his withdrawal is not about being emotionally self-sufficient. It is about quite the opposite. It is about being so dependent on others that unless one is given just the right cocktail of emotional support from others, one hysterically flees into psychotic seclusion. Consider the jilted bride who, instead of going back on the dating scene, continues to wear her wedding dress while pretending that the marriage actually happened. This person is psychotically secluded and therefore isolated from realityâ€”but not
self-contained. Quite the opposite. And the same is true of the autistic.
Being genuinely self-contained is about balance. It is about being givenâ€”or having been givenâ€”the right level, and the right kind of emotional sustenance from others and, on that basis, being able, like a dolphin that has taken in enough air or a camel that has taken in enough water, to go out on oneâ€™s own. This is not what the autistic person is doing. Autism is a way of being damaged. True independence is about the opposite of being damaged. And a sign of true independence is flexibility, and rigidity is a sign of damage-based pseudo-independence.
One last point: Bureaucrats are people who are damaged and have no free will.
Bureaucrats need others to tell them what to do. And when they come across someone who is genuinely independently, they invidiously describe him as having â€˜autismâ€™ or â€˜Aspergerâ€™sâ€™, sometimes going so far as to get psychiatrists to formally diagnose them in this way. But such characterizations are, as we have just seen, the opposite of the truth---and, like many invidious characterizations, not just false but also projective.
 
The Two Ways in which Intellectual Activity Promotes Intelligence


There are two distinct ways in which reading increases intelligence. On the one hand, reading makes one aware of truths of which one was previously unaware, and each such truth is a new weapon in the arsenal of oneâ€™s intellect. On the other hand, reading stimulates thought, and its effect on oneâ€™s intellect is similar in this respect to the effect that physical exercise has on oneâ€™s body. When one exercises, a message is sent to oneâ€™s metabolism that it must build
muscle-tissue and make all of the other changes to itself that are required for an exercise- intensive existence. And when one reads or otherwise engages oneâ€™s intellect, a message is sent to oneâ€™s central nervous system that it must forge new neural pathways and make all of the other changes to itself that are require for a thought-intensive existence. So, reading is not simply about uploading new information. It is also about keeping oneâ€™s central nervous system constantly stimulated, so that it continues to keep itself combat-ready, so to speak, and able to take on new tasks and develop new capabilities. And just as one loses stamina, muscle-power and coordination if one does not engage in athletic training, so one loses neural plasticity and intellect if one does not engage in cognitive training. By reading and otherwise engaging oneâ€™s intellect, one keeps oneâ€™s mind nimble and elastic. Indeed, it is more by keeping oneâ€™s mind supple and active than it is by making one aware of new facts that reading promotes intelligence, and the same is true of other forms of intellectual activity. The primary intellectual benefit of vigorous intellectual activity is not that it stocks oneâ€™s mind with new ideas, so much as it is that it keeps oneâ€™s mind in a state of constant readiness and consequent responsiveness. And this heightened responsiveness, in its turn, makes oneâ€™s mind more able to acquire new information.
 
How Mental Illness Differs from Physical Illness

Somebody on Quora dot com asked the following question. I quote:
Do you believe mental illness is â€œan illness like any otherâ€ or is it a distinct and unique phenomenon? Why?
Here is my answer:
Mental illness is not an â€˜illness like any other.â€™ Mental illnesses are contextual in nature.
In some contexts, being obsessive-compulsive is a liability and thus an illness, and in other contexts, being obsessive-compulsive is an asset and thus not a mental illness. And the same is true, to varying degrees, of all other mental illnesses. By contrast, physical illnesses are not contextual in nature: if somebody has asthma or lupus or cancer, that is not asset in some contexts and a liability in others: it is simply a liability. Also, mental illnesses serve a defensive function. Even though, in at least some contexts, OCD is a liability, it serves a protective function: it insulates the subject in a psychological â€˜safe-spaceâ€™: his obsessions and compulsions encircle that safe-space and, although dysfunctional in some respects, provide him some measure of safety from a toxic and threatening environment. And the same is true of psychosis: the psychotic did not become psychotic for no reason. He was in a situation in which he was being threatened and pumped full of negative validations and detriments to his sense of self-worth.
And he therefore decided to distance himself from that destructive negativity by withdrawing into a world of psychotic delusion. So even though psychosis is an illness and is some respects gravely dysfunctional, it does serve at least some protective function. Also, to develop a point hinted at earlier, some mental illnesses involve misdeployed strengths of intellect and character. OCD involves misdeployed intelligence and focus; schizophrenia involves misdeployed creativity and emotional sensitivity. So mental illnesses, though in many respects gravely debilitating, sometimes seem to involve heightened, albeit misdeployed, abilities.
 
Psychiatric Munchausenâ€™s by Proxy

Parents are getting psychiatrists to falsely diagnose their children as having autism, Aspergerâ€™s, ADHD, and the like. Such diagnosesâ€”especially false diagnoses of Aspersers and Autismâ€”are nothing more than cloaked child murder. The parent---usually the mother---wants her husbandâ€™s attention; canâ€™t get it; and then, in an effort to get itâ€”or to get some surrogate thereofâ€”figuratively murders the child with a false psychiatric diagnosis, which dooms the child in question to the over-attentions of idiot educationalists, psychologists, psychiatrists, and bureaucrats---the effect of which is to damage the child in some way or other, sometimes going so far as damage him in a way that retroactively validates the initial diagnosis. Of course, with rare exceptions, psychiatrists and educational psychologists are none too bright and are all too willing to foist bunk diagnoses on hapless youths, both because they need money and also because they need to feel that their line of goods has some legitimate application, which it doesnâ€™t. But rule of thumb: when a child is sent to a psychiatrist, the first place to look for psychological maladies is in the Munchausen-by-proxy motherâ€™s head, not the childâ€™s. The childâ€™s mind is the place to look for fall out from the blast, not for the blastâ€™s mom-centric epicenter.
 
What is the Prognosis for People with OCD?

Somebody on Quora.com asked the following question:
What is the prognosis for patients with Obsessiveâ€“compulsive disorder (OCD)? Here is my answer:
People who have OCD have it because it provides them with relief from anxietyâ€”from anxiety so intense as to be almost inconceivable to people who have not had OCD. But OCD is just a defense-mechanism. And as is the case with most defense-mechanisms, there comes a time in the subjectâ€™s life when it starts to do more harm than good. At that point, the obsessive- compulsive has to make a decision: What do I want? Do I want mere freedom from anxiety? Or do I want to live and grow? It is 100% up to him what he chooses. If he chooses to grow, he will, and his OCD, without exactly vanishing, will assume productive forms. If he chooses not to grow, he wonâ€™t.
OCD, though an affliction, is ultimately a voluntary one. If the obsessive-compulsive chooses to remain in his defensive bubble of isolation from the world, then his OCD will defeat him. If he chooses to re-engage the world, then his OCD will assume non-pathological and in fact productive forms, as it did with Beethoven and Einstein.
OCD, though an affliction, is an affliction of the willâ€”and is thus unlike cancer or asthma, which have nothing to do with the integrity of oneâ€™s will. And OCD is eliminated, or at least made to assume adaptive forms by duly exercising oneâ€™s will in growth-oriented ways.
The symptoms of OCD are involuntary only in a relative sense. Relative to a determination to remain within his defensive bubble of non-engagement, there is nothing much that the obsessive-compulsive can do about those symptoms. He can engage in a bit of â€˜cognitive-behavioral therapyâ€™, but the effects of such therapy will be shallow and short-lived, absent a determination on the obsessive-compulsiveâ€™s part to grow and change himself in a way that makes his OCD irrelevant. On the other, if he does choose to leave his defensive bubble and
re-engage the world, then, indeed, his OCD will become irrelevant. So relative to a determination on his part to re-engage the world, the symptoms of OCD are voluntary.
So ultimately OCD is indeed voluntary, and if one sees it for the voluntary condition that it ultimate is, then the prognosis is 100% positive. But if one sees it as a garden-variety pathology, then the prognosis is negative. A garden-variety condition is one that does not afflict oneâ€™s will and that falls outside the scope of the oneâ€™s will. OCD is an affliction of oneâ€™s will; it is a weakening of oneâ€™s will, in consequence of a withdrawal from the world. And by choosing to go back out into the world, the obsessive-compulsive strengthens his will and causes oneâ€™s OCD to assume benign if not productive forms.
 
How is Rationalization Different from Auto-hypnosis?
Auto-hypnosis can be an enormously powerful tool. First of all, to auto-hypnotize is not to put oneself in a trance or daze. It is simply to give oneself a command to think or feel or act in a certain way, the efficacy of which command does not depend on the outcome of an act of conscious judgment on oneâ€™s part. Usually, such commands are issued as well as received unconsciously.
An element of auto-hypnosis is involved in any case where one has a feeling about such and such that extends beyond what the use of oneâ€™s critical faculties would warrant. Thus, there is an element of auto-hypnosis in any case where one has the requisite degree of excitement about the plan in question to succeed in carrying it out. Somebody who only followed through on plans that he been validated by his critical faculty would be somebody who never did anything: he would be the ultimate bureaucrat. So an element of auto-hypnosis is involved in doing anything that requires sustained enthusiasm. And auto-hypnosis is therefore not only not a bad thing but a positively essential thing, as in, it is essential for oneâ€™s not being the psychological equivalent of a quadriplegic.
Be it noted that auto-hypnosis can also be a bad thing: whenever one stews or obsesses or ruminates or wallows, one is negatively hypnotizing oneself. When autohypnosis has an affirmative character, it encourages action and when it has a negative character it prevents action. So given how much of oneâ€™s time one wastes and how much action one oneâ€™s part one prevents by negatively auto-hypnotizing, it is clear that auto-hypnosis can indeed be a very bad thing.
But auto-hypnosis is not inherently bad: it is rather that it can be put to bad use. And even when it is bad, its negative effects are surprisingly easily reversed. Once one knows that in obsessing or wallowing, one is really just negatively hypnotizing oneself, it is surprisingly easy to flip a mental switch and replace that negative auto-hypnosis with affirmative auto-hypnosis.
But rationalization is inherently bad.
But how exactly does auto-hypnosis different from rationalization? Isnâ€™t auto-hypnosis the act of making oneself believe something that one knows not to be true or that one at least regards as doubtful, and isnâ€™t auto-hypnosis the same thing?
No. Auto-hypnosis is about generating an attitude of some kind without making oneâ€™s acceptance of the legitimacy of that attitude depend on some edict issued by oneâ€™s faculty of judgment. The whole point of hypnosis, and of auto-hypnosis, is to create conviction without deploying or therefore misdeploying oneâ€™s critical faculties. Auto-hypnosis is about drawing enthusiasm from within oneself, as opposed to from a warped understanding of reality.
Rationalization on the other hand is about generating emotional conviction from a warped understanding of reality, rather than from within the depths of oneâ€™s soul.
So auto-hypnosis doesnâ€™t involve a misdeployment of oneâ€™s faculty of judgment and it therefore doesnâ€™t result in a perversion of those faculties. By contrast, rationalization does involve such a misdeployment and therefore does result in such a perversion.

%%EOFDoes possible world semantics turn all propositions into necessary ones?

Journal of Pragmatics 39 (2007) 872â€“916

John-Michael Kuczynski
Department of Philosophy, University of California, 5631 South Hall, Santa-Barbara, CA 931060-3090, USA

Abstract

A number of philosophical and semantic analyses make essential use of the concept of a possible world. Following tradition, we will refer to this family of analyses as "possible world semantics" (PWS). The present work argues that there is no interpretation of the term "world" that validates even a single one of the doctrines composing PWS. It is argued that, depending on what the word "world" is taken to mean, PWS entails either that all modal terms (words like "necessarily" and "possibly") are infinitely ambiguous or that all true propositions are necessarily true. It is also argued that David Lewis' PWS-based analysis of counterfactuals can succeed only relative to decidedly retrograde conceptions of space and time. Most importantly, it is shown that PWS is false even if it finds a way to neutralize the arguments just described. Given certain truisms about spatiotemporal existence, it is a substantive modal question whether the worlds needed to validate PWS are even possible. (As we will see, there is reason to believe that many of those worlds are in the same category as worlds that comprise light but not electromagnetic radiation.) The modal status of these worlds cannot be non-circularly resolved within a PWS-framework, and must be therefore resolved within some other modal framework, showing that PWS is parasitic on some more fundamental understanding of modality.

Keywords: Possible-world semantics; David Lewis; Necessity; Modality; Modal knowledge; Modal realism; Counterfactuals; Causality

1. Introduction

A view known as "possible world semantics" (PWS) provides the basis for clear and rigorous analyses of many important concepts. PWS is given by three contentions:

(1) A proposition is possibly true exactly if it is true in some world.
(2) A proposition is necessarily true exactly if it is true in every world.
(3) A proposition is the set of worlds where it is true (or, equivalently, it is a function that assigns truth to all and only the worlds in that set).

The most obvious applications of PWS relate to the concepts of possibility, necessity, and meaning. But PWS has proven capable of shedding great light on the nature of counterfactuals, mental content, and even moral obligation.

Despite its virtues, PWS is bedeviled by a number of problems. The main purpose of this paper is to show that PWS is even more problematic than has hitherto been realized. In particular, it will be argued that PWS has the unwelcome consequence that all true propositions become necessarily true, and all false propositions become necessarily false. So George W. Bush is U.S. president in 2006 is in the same modal category as 2 + 2 = 4, the same being true of John Kerry is U.S. president in 2006 and 2 + 2 = 5.

Let us say a word on the basic structure of this paper. In Part I, we will discuss the motivations for PWS, and will delineate some of the applications of that doctrine. In Part II, we will argue that PWS is eviscerated unless the term "world" is taken literally. (Our arguments here will include, but will also go beyond, Lewis' (1986) arguments for the same point.) In Part III, we will find that, given the realistic conception of other worlds demanded by PWS, that doctrine has a number of unpalatable consequences, among them the one previously noted. In Part IV, we will examine some of Hintikka's applications of PWS to the analysis of substitution failures and of propositional attitudes. Finally, in Part V, we will examine Lewis' analysis of counterfactuals. Our discussion of PWS will take into account, and find many applications for, some striking insights due to Bealer (1998).

2. Part I. Some of the virtues of PWS

Let us begin with a brief discussion of the merits of PWS. (1) and (2) reduce the problematic notions of possible and necessary truth to that of truth simpliciter. (3) reduces the problematic notion of a proposition to the less problematic notion of a set. (1)â€“(3) thus reduce the intensional to the extensional.

PWS analyzes other concepts along similar lines. Let P be the proposition Smith is a tall person, and let C be the set of worlds where that proposition is true. P is true in world W exactly if W is a member of C. We may thus identify P's being true in W with W's being a member of a certain set. The obscure but pivotal notion of a proposition's being true is elegantly articulated in terms of the transparent notion of membership in a set.

PWS extensionalizes other important notions. According to that doctrine, for a proposition P1 to entail a proposition P2 is for the set of worlds identical with the first to be included in the set of worlds identical with the second. The concept of compatibility is also thereby explained, since P1 is compatible with P2 exactly if P1 does not entail the negation of P2.

Let us turn to another of PWS's great (apparent) triumphs. The concept of a property is as problematic as it is fundamental. Instances of properties are spatio-temporal objects, but properties themselves are outside of space and time. The very notion of a non-spatiotemporal object is one that, almost by definition, lacks empirical respectability and that has consequently been resisted by thinkers of an empiricist turn of mind. At the same time, the notion of a property is not easily dispensed with: statements like "Smith and Jones have many properties in common" are often true, and they seem to presuppose the existence not just of property-instances, but of properties themselves.

PWS gives us a way of ameliorating this uncomfortable situation. Let F be a function that assigns truth to an object exactly if that object is tall. Smith is tall exactly if Smith is assigned truth by F. Given this, we might as well identify the property of tallness with F, and the fact of Smith's being tall with his being assigned truth by F. In this way a clear and precise meaning is given to obscure and metaphysically loaded statements like "Bob and Fred both instantiate the property of tallness."

The great virtue of PWS is that, if successful, it reduces the intensional to the extensional. Sets take the place of mysterious entities like propositions and properties. Dark relations like necessitation are replaced by perspicuous facts about set-overlap. An important corollary â€“ one that will play a large role in the present paper â€“ is that PWS is threatened to the extent that intensions cannot be eliminated in favor of extensions.

[Paper continues with detailed philosophical analysis of possible world semantics, modal logic, necessity, and counterfactuals...]
Pragmatism: Epistemology Posing as Metaphysics
