In general, for any property phi, â€¹the phiâ€º is defined, not denotatively, but contextuallyâ€”that is, by saying what whole sentences containing it mean. And what whole sentences containing it mean is (in general, though not, as weâ€™ll see, in all cases) given by the rule: â€¹the phi has psiâ€º is true if there exists something uniquely having phi, and any such thing has psi.

1.3 Contextual definition and the semantics of definite descriptions

Where definite descriptions are concerned, grammatical and logical form pull apart. â€œJane is tallâ€ (JT) has the same grammar as â€œthe captain of the volleyball team is tallâ€ (CT). But the propositions they express are structurally very different. JT is, whereas CT is not, such that, for some person x, it is true just in case x is tall.

Like the semantic rule for â€œsomeone,â€ the meaning of â€œthe inventor of Velcroâ€ is given by saying what whole sentences containing it mean; and in at least some cases â€¹the inventor of Velcro has psiâ€º is true if the property of being a Velcro-inventor is uniquely instantiated and, moreover, that property has one instance in common with the property of being a psi.

1.4 The Theory of Descriptions defined

This theory of Russellâ€™s is known as the â€œTheory of Descriptionsâ€ (TD). The essence of TD is given by two assertions: (i) definite descriptions donâ€™t refer to anything; and (ii) in virtue of containing a definite description, a sentence attributes properties to other properties, not to individuals.

â€œThe inventor of Velcroâ€ doesnâ€™t refer to anyone or anything. â€œThe inventor of Velcro is seven-feet tallâ€ doesnâ€™t attribute the property of being 7-feet tall to anyone. That sentence says that the property of being a unique inventor of Velcro is instantiated and, in addition, that the property of being a 7-feet tall Velcro-inventor is also instantiated. So â€œthe inventor of Velcro is seven-feet tallâ€ is about properties, not individuals. It attributes the property of being instantiated to each of the two properties just mentioned.

2.0 Some arguments for the theory of descriptions: belief reports

Given only what weâ€™ve said about TD, it might not seem like a very important theory. But it opens up new vistas, not just in semantics, but in metaphysics, epistemology, and the philosophy of mind.

Consider the sentence:



(PFY) â€œPonce de Leon believes that the fountain of youth exists.â€



PFY is true. (To avoid irrelevant subleties relating to the use of past-tense markers, weâ€™ll assume, falsely but innocuously, that Ponce de Leon is still with us.) Itâ€™s a simple historical fact. But does â€œthe fountain of youthâ€ refer to anything? No. There is no fountain of youth. For argumentâ€™s sake, suppose that â€œthe fountain of youthâ€ refers to something. It follows trivially that there exists some object such that â€œthe fountain of youthâ€ refers to that object. Given what is meant by â€œfountain,â€ â€œyouth,â€ etc., that object must be a fountain of youthâ€”that is, it must be something whose waters, when inbibed, give one eternal youth. But there is no such thing. So â€œthe fountain of youthâ€ isnâ€™t a referring term.

But now we have a problem. PFY is true. And itâ€™s therefore meaningful. (Nothing can be true or false without being meaningful.) Before Russell, most philosophers didnâ€™t want to give up on the idea that â€œthe fountain of youthâ€ does refer to something. They saw that it was meaningful, and they assumed, given its grammatical role, that it had to refer to something. This left them with the question: What does â€œthe fountain of youthâ€ refer to? As you might expect, a lot of them said that it exists â€œas an idea.â€

This doesnâ€™t work. Fountains are not ideas. When people disagree about whether there is a fountain of youth, they arenâ€™t disagreeing about whether some idea exists. I believe that Ponce de Leon was wrong. I believe it because I think that there is no actual fountain having the needed characteristics. For all I know, Ponce de Leon and I might see eye to eye when it comes to what ideas exist.

Maybe when people say that the fountain of youth exists as an idea, they only mean that we have an idea of such a thing. To have an idea of such a thing is to know what such a thing would be like, were it to exist. Thus interpreted, â€œthe fountain of youth exists as an ideaâ€ is just another way of saying: â€œthere is no fountain of youth (but people know what something would have to be like in order to be one)â€ which leaves us no further along than before.

Alexius Meinong (1853â€“1920) proposed a different solution. He said that, although it doesnâ€™t exist, the fountain of youth â€œsubsists.â€ For a thing to subsist is for it to have some status intermediate between existence and non-existence.

This doesnâ€™t work. First of all, something either exists or it doesnâ€™t; there is no intermediate condition. Second, even if there is, it doesnâ€™t help, since subsistence is, by Meinongâ€™s own hypothesis, a way of failing to exist, which leaves us no further along than before.

Russell straightened this whole mess out. Hereâ€™s what he said. (What follows will involve a repetion of some points made in Section 1.0.) â€œThe fountain of youthâ€ is a definite description. Definite descriptions donâ€™t refer to anything and neither, therefore, does â€œfountain of youth.â€ Definite descriptions are to be defined contextually, and sentences containing them must be reparsed if their meaning is to be made clear.

If itâ€™s grammatical form were to be trusted,



(E1) â€œthe fountain of youth existsâ€



would attribute existence to some fountain. But, since it must be reparsed if its meaning is to be made clear, its grammatical form is not to be trusted. Appropriately reparsed, that sentence becomes:



(E2) â€œthe property of being a fountain of youth is uniquely instantiated.â€



The meaning of PFY is therefore:



(E3) â€œPonce de Leon believes that the property of being a fountain of youth is uniquely instantiated.â€

2.1 Some arguments for the theory of descriptions: negative existentials

Consider the statement:



(N1) â€œthe monster under little Timmyâ€™s bed doesnâ€™t exist.â€



N1 is true. But if â€œthe monster under little Timmyâ€™s bedâ€ referred to something, it wouldnâ€™t be true, since there would then exist some monster under little Timmyâ€™s bed to which that definite description referred, in which case, of course, there would exist a monster under Timmyâ€™s bed.

Whatâ€™s going on? For now familiar reasons, N1 must be reparsed if its meaning is to be exposed. The needed reparsing yields:



(N2) â€œthe property of being a monster under little Timmyâ€™s bed isnâ€™t instantiated.â€



That property exists. (All this means is that there is a way something would have to be in order to be such a monster.) But nothing has that property. N2 doesnâ€™t refer to anything that doesnâ€™t exist. Problem solved.

This makes it clear how to deal with statements like â€œthe monster under Timmyâ€™s bed doesnâ€™t exist.â€ The going line before Russell was to say that it says of some object that it doesnâ€™t exist. But that makes no sense at all, since itâ€™s the same as saying â€œthere exists an object (viz. a certain monster) that doesnâ€™t exist.â€ What it really says, Russell showed, is that a certain existent property (viz. that of being a certain sort of monster, etc.) has a very existent property (viz. that of being un-instantiated).

2.2 Some arguments for the theory of descriptions (continued): identity-statements

Letâ€™s start with a few platitudes about reference. To say that expression R refers to object O is to say that, for any property phi, â€¹R has phiâ€º attributes phi to O. If you want to say of Benjamin Franklin (BF) that heâ€™s bald, you can do so by saying â€œBenjamin Franklin is bald.â€ (Of course, BF is no longer with us. But to set aside some extremely intricate and, in this context, irrelevant issues relating to tense, let us pretend that Franklin is alive and that we can speak of him in the present tense.) And if you couldnâ€™t attribute baldness to BF by uttering that sentence, then â€œBenjamin Franklinâ€ wouldnâ€™t refer to BF. If, in saying â€œBenjamin Franklin is bald,â€ one was attributing baldness to Aristotle, then, in that context at least, â€œBenjamin Franklinâ€ would refer to Aristotle.

Letâ€™s generalize these points. For any property phi, â€œBenjamin Franklinâ€ refers to BF (and not to Aristotle, for example) because â€¹Benjamin Franklin has phiâ€º attributes phi to Benjamin Franklin; and if one couldnâ€™t attribute phi to Benjamin Franklin by saying â€¹Benjamin Franklin has phiâ€º then â€œBenjamin Franklinâ€ would not refer to BF. Further, if, in uttering that sentence, one was attributing baldness to Aristotle (but not BF), then â€œBenjamin Franklinâ€ would refer to Aristotle (but not Benjamin Franklin).Thus, for â€œBenjamin Franklinâ€ to refer to BF it is both necessary and sufficient that â€¹Benjamin Franklin has phiâ€º attribute phi to BF. The fact that â€œBenjamin Franklinâ€ refers to BF is identical with the fact that â€¹Benjamin Franklin has phiâ€º attributes phi to Benjamin Franklin, for any property phi.

In general, expression E refers to O if and only if for any property phi â€¹E has phiâ€º attributes phi to O. Eâ€™s referring to O may be identified with Eâ€™s being such that, in virtue of containing it, a sentence ipso facto attributes a property to O.

In light of these points, let us look at an age-old puzzle that Russell neatly solved. Benjamin Franklin (BF)



invented bifocals and he was also the first postmaster general. Therefore:



(CB) the inventor of bifocals is identical with the first postmaster general.



Itâ€™s also true, of course, that:



(TB) the inventor of bifocals is identical with the inventor of bifocals.



But, whereas TB is trivial, CB is non-trivial.

The non-triviality of CB is hard to explain if definite descriptions are supposed to be referring terms. As we just saw, â€œthe inventors of bifocalsâ€ refers to BF exactly if â€œBenjamin Franklin has phiâ€ attributes phi to BF. Given that â€œthe inventors of bifocalsâ€ does in fact refer to BF, it follows that CB attributes the property of being identical with the first postmaster general to BF. And given that â€œthe first postmaster generalâ€ refers to BF, it follows that CB attributes the property of being identical with the inventor of bifocals to BF. And given both of these facts (viz. the facts stated in the last two sentences), it follows that CB says of BF that it has the property of being identical with BF. Which is trivial.

Frege proposed a famous solution to this. But weâ€™re going to consider Russellâ€™s solution first, since itâ€™s easier to understand Fregeâ€™s solution in terms of Russellâ€™s than vice versa.

According to the theory of descriptions (TD) â€¹the inventor of bifocals has phiâ€º says that something uniquely invented bifocals, and any such thing has phi. And, according to TD, â€¹the first postmaster general has phiâ€º says that something was a unique first postmaster general, and any such thing has phi. It follows that, if TD is right, CB says the same thing as:



(CB3) â€œsomething uniquely invented bifocals, and any such thing is a unique first postmaster general; and something was a unique first postmaster general, and any such thing is a unique inventor of bifocals.â€



It is readily seen that CB3 is more succinctly expressed as follows:



(CBR) â€œthere is some one thing that uniquely invented bifocals and was also a unique first postmaster general.â€



To sum up, if TD is right, then CB means the same thing as CBR. It is easily verified that, indeed, CB is true exactly if CBR is true. TD gets the right result. Given that CBR is non-trivialâ€”given that historical knowledge is needed to know itâ€”TD readily explains why CB is non-trivial.

2.3 Some arguments for the theory of descriptions: positive existentials

For argumentâ€™s sake, suppose there to be some non-existent object O such that



(E1) â€œthe fountain of youth existsâ€



says that O exists. In that case, there ipso facto exists nothing to which E1 attributes existence. Thus, if it is to say anything at all, E1 must attribute existence to some existing object. Thus, supposing that E1 says of some object that it exists, a precondition for E1â€™s saying anything is that the object in question exist. But in that case, we could conclude from the mere fact that utterances of E1 are meaningful that E1 is true. Thus, a consequence of supposing that E1 says of some object that exists is that E1 is not only true, but trivially so.

But, in actuality, E1 is both false and non-trivial. Itâ€™s false since thereâ€™s no fountain of youth. Itâ€™s nontrivial since, to know whether itâ€™s true, is isnâ€™t enough to know what it meansâ€”let alone to know that it has a meaning.

The right analysis is the one proposed by Russell. It says that the property of being a fountain of youth is instantiated. Though nothing has it, the property of being a fountain of youth exists. In general, â€¹the phi existsâ€º doesnâ€™t make the absurd claim that some non-entity exists; nor does it make the trivial claim that some entity exists: it makes the non-absurd, non-trivial claim that the property of being a phi is instantiated.

3.0 The incoherencies in Fregeâ€™s semantic system

Let us now consider how Frege deals with just-described puzzle concerning identity. This will expose some profound problems with Fregeâ€™s semantics, which we will discuss.

Benjamin Franklin (BF) invented bifocals and he was also the first postmaster general. Therefore:



(CB) the inventors of bifocals is identical with the first postmaster general.



Itâ€™s also true, of course, that:



(TB) the inventor of bifocals is identical with the inventor of bifocals.



But, whereas TB is trivial, CB is non-trivial.

A moment ago, we considered Russellâ€™s solution to this problem. Now weâ€™re going to consider Fregeâ€™s solution. Fregeâ€™s solution is much more congenial to commonsense. But, when scrutinized, it turns out either to coincide with Russellâ€™s solution or to be totally incoherent.

3.1 Sense vs. reference

Here is Fregeâ€™s solution:

(FR) â€œThe inventor of bifocalsâ€ is a referring term; it picks something out. That expression refers to a given thing if and only if that thing has the property of being a unique bifocal-inventor. If a given thing didnâ€™t invent bifocals then â€œthe inventors of bifocalsâ€ doesnâ€™t refer to it. If lots of different individuals invented bifocals, then â€œthe inventors of bifocalsâ€ doesnâ€™t refer to anything. (If ten people collectively wrote War and Peace, it would be wrong to speak of the author of that book.) And if a given thing did uniquely invent bifocals, then â€œthe inventors of bifocalsâ€ does refer to it.

So there are two dimensions to the semantics of â€œthe inventors of bifocals.â€ There is what it refers to: this is the referent of â€œthe inventors of bifocals.â€ (Sometimes â€œreferenceâ€ is used instead of â€œreferent.â€) And thereâ€™s the property that a thing must have to be its referent; this property is the sense of that expression. The referent is BF, and the sense is the property of being a unique bifocal inventor.

Analogues of these points hold with respect to â€œthe first postmaster general.â€ There is its referent (which is BF); and there is its sense (which is the property of being a unique first postmaster general).

The reason that TB is non-trivial is that, although the definite descriptions in it have the same referent, they have different senses. A comparison may help. Imagine that youâ€™re looking at a certain person in the distance. That person is in fact Ralph, but you donâ€™t know it, because heâ€™s so far away and also, let us suppose, because he is (for reasons that arenâ€™t important) wearing a suit of armor. You see that he is doing jumping jacks. Later Ralph is standing right in front of you and, of course, you see him. Heâ€™s wearing a plaid shirt. Once again, heâ€™s doing jumping jacks.

The first visual perception has the same object as the second. And each of those perceptions says of that object he or she is doing jumping jacks. But those two perceptions pick out that object in different ways. In the first case, that object is presented to you as something that has one set of properties (itâ€™s far away, wearing a suit of armor, etc.); in the other case itâ€™s presented as having a different set of properties (itâ€™s nearby, is wearing a plaid shirt, etc.). And thatâ€™s why, even though those perceptions have the same object, and even though both attribute the property of doing jumping jacks to that object, those perceptions tell you different things.

The relationship between â€œthe inventors of bifocalsâ€ and â€œthe first postmaster generalâ€ is to be understood along similar lines. They have the same object (referent); but they pick that thing out through different bodies of information. Thatâ€™s why â€¹the inventors of bifocals has phiâ€º and â€¹the first postmaster general has phiâ€º tell you different things, even though they attribute the same property (phi) to the same object (BF).

3.2 The partial collapse of Fregeanism into Russellianism

This all seems not only plausible, but practically self-evident.

But itâ€™s false and, indeed, incoherent. Letâ€™s consider the two sense-perceptions discussed in FR. The one perception tells you that there is something in the distance, wearing a suit of armor, etc., and that thing is doing jumping jacks. So the sense in which Ralph is the object of that perception is that your perception describes Ralph. Your perception says: â€œsomething or other is over there, in the distance, wearing a suit of armor, [etc.].â€ Who (or what) fits that description? In other words, who has the relevant properties? Ralph. So Ralph is the object of that perception in the sense it describes him.

The information borne by that perception has the form â€œsomething has such and such properties [itâ€™s wearing a suit of armor, etc.], and any such thing is doing jumping jacks.â€ Thus, the content of that perception is given by an existence-claim (a claim of the form â€œsomething has phiâ€). Ralph uniquely satisfies that existence-claim. (In other words, he and he alone has the relevant property.) And it is in virtue of his doing so that he is the object of the perception in question.

The same thing mutatis mutandis is true of your second perception. The information borne by that perception is along the lines of â€œsomething has thus and such properties [itâ€™s standing nearby, is wearing a plaid shirt ,etc.], and any such thing is doing jumping jacks.â€ Ralph is the object of that perception by virtue of the fact that he and he alone has the relevant propertiesâ€”that he and he alone is a thing standing in the relevant place while wearing a plaid shirt, etc.

In general, when a given thing x is picked out by way of descriptive information, whatâ€™s really going on is that some statement of the form â€œsomething has such and such propertiesâ€ is being affirmed (not necessarily verbally), and x is what fits the description.

If we bear this point in mind, we find that, so far as it isnâ€™t totally incoherent, Fregeâ€™s analysis collapses into Russellâ€™s. Consider the sentence:



(IB) â€œthe inventor of bifocals is tall.â€



By Fregeâ€™s own admission, â€œthe inventors of bifocalsâ€ picks something out if and only if something fits the relevant description (i.e., if and only if something is a unique inventor of bifocals). And if there is a unique inventor of bifocals, that thing, whatever it is, is the thing to which â€œthe inventors of bifocalsâ€ refers. Supposing

that there is such a thing and that x is it, IB describes x as being tall. It goes without saying that, if there is no unique inventor of bifocals, then there is no way that IB can be true. (Frege himself emphasizes this last point. And heâ€™s right. Thereâ€™s no way that â€œthe elephant in the corner is eating peanutsâ€ can be true if thereâ€™s no elephant in the corner.)

The upshot is that IB is true if and only if:



(IB*) something uniquely invented befocals, and any such thing is tall.



But what does the Theory of Discriptions (TD) say about IB? According to TD, the meaning of IB is: IB*. So Fregeâ€™s theory collapses into Russellâ€™s.

By obvious extensions of this, it follows that, if Fregeâ€™s theory is right, then CBâ€™s meaning is identical with that of CBR. So Fregeâ€™s theory accounts for the non-triviality of CB in the same way as Russellâ€™s theory (as TD).

3.3 Why Fregeanism doesnâ€™t completely collapse into Russellianism

As we know, Russellâ€™s theory is pretty good. The same is therefore true of Fregeâ€™s, at least to the extent that it coincides with Russellâ€™s. The problem is that Fregeâ€™s theory doesnâ€™t entirely coincide with Russellâ€™s. Unlike Russell, Frege took it for granted that definite descriptions are just what, given their grammar, they appear to be: referring terms. Weâ€™ve just seen that, if Fregeâ€™s own theory of why CB is non-trivial is to be correct, then TD must be the right account of how definite descriptions work. But the essence of TD is that definite descriptions are not referring terms. It would obviously be incoherent to accept TD while also believing that definite descriptions are referring terms. Weâ€™ve just seen that it is precisely this incoherence that Frege is accepting, however unwittingly, in holding that definite descriptions are sense-bearing referring terms.

3.4 The incoherencies in Fregeâ€™s semantics

Fregeâ€™s view that definite descriptions are referring terms that have both sense and reference is one that has a lot of intuitive appeal, and people will hold onto it unless given very strong arguments to the contrary. Since the arguments just given may not be enough for some, here is another.

Consider the following four sentences:



(1) â€œSmith believes that the inventor of bifocals is 6-feet tall.â€

(2) â€œSmith believes that the inventor of bifocals is not 6-feet tall.â€

(3) â€œSmith believes that the first postmaster general is 6-feet tall.â€

(4) â€œSmith believes that the first postmaster general is not 6-feet tall.â€



Were Smith to believe both 1 and 4, he would not, at least not for that reason alone, be irrational. Of course, given the empirical fact that some one person uniquely invented bifocals and was a unique first postmaster general, one of those beliefs must be wrong. But taken by themselves, the italized parts of 1 and 4 are consistent with each other. At the same time, neither entails the other. In other words, each is compatible with the negation of the other. So supposing that Smith is rational and that 1 is true, it doesnâ€™t follow that 3 is true or that 3 is false.

For the time being, letâ€™s suppose with Frege that definite descriptions are referring terms. In that case, the definite description in 1 co-refers with the definite description in 4. They both refer to BF. 1 says of BF that he has the property of being believed by Smith to be 6-feet tall; and 4 says of BF that he has the property of being believed by Smith to not be 6-feet tall. So Fregeâ€™s view that definite descriptions are referring terms has the false consequence that 1 and 4 cannot both be true if Smith is rational.

Hereâ€™s another way of stating the problem. According to Leibnizâ€™s Law, if x is identical with y, then x has a given property if and only if y too has that property. Leibnizâ€™s Law isnâ€™t directly concerned with language.

But it has a semantic corollary, namely, that if two expressions co-refer, they can be inter-substituted salva veritate. This means that, if E and E* co-refer, and S is a sentence containing E, then replacing E with E* will result in a sentence that is true if S is true and false if S is false. (Itâ€™s assumed that the expressions being inter-substituted belong to the same language, are inflected in the same way, etc.) â€œCicero was a Roman oratorâ€ is true; and so, therefore, is â€œTully was a Roman orator,â€ given that â€œTullyâ€ co-refers with â€œCicero.â€ â€œCicero was a 19th-century logicianâ€ is false; and so, therefore, is â€œTully was a 19th-century logician.â€ Another way of stating this principle is that â€œinter-substituting co-referring terms preserves truth-value.â€ The original sentence (â€œthere is water in my glassâ€) is true (false) iff the new sentence (â€œthere is H2O in my glassâ€) is true (false).

Supposing, as Frege does, that â€œthe inventor of bifocalsâ€ and â€œthe first postmaster generalâ€ are referring terms, then, given that those expressions co-refer, replacing the one with the other should preserve truth-value. But it doesnâ€™t. 1 may be false if 3 is true and vice versa.

TD solves this problem. According to TD, the meanings of 1â€“4 are, respectively:



(1R) â€œSmith believes that something uniquely invented bifocals, and any such thing is 6 ft tall.â€

(2R) â€œSmith believes that something uniquely invented bifocals, and any such thing is not 6 ft tall.â€

(3R) â€œSmith believes that something was a unique first postmaster general and any such thing is 6 ft tall.â€

(4R) â€œSmith believes that something was a unique first postmaster general and any such thing is not 6 ft tall.â€



1 doesnâ€™t entail 3, and 1 is compatible with 4. 2 doesnâ€™t entail 4 and 2 is compatible with 3. (This is the hard data.) 1R doesnâ€™t entail 3R, and 1R is compatible with 4R. 2R doesnâ€™t entail 4R and 2R is compatible with 3R. So TD is compatible with the hard-data, whereas Fregeâ€™s theory is not. Frege was aware of the problem just described, and he added an epicycle to his theory that he hoped would save it. It did not, as weâ€™ll now see.

3.4.1 Fregeâ€™s cover-up: the creation of intensional contexts

Frege made profound contributions to logic and the philosophy of language. None of these disciplines even existed in anything like their modern form before he invented them, and most of the principles that he laid down in doing so hold up.

But Frege, like everyone else, had his less than stellar moments. Unfortunately, his blunders are treated with the same reverence as his discoveries. For this reason some very wrong and incoherent ideas of his are alive and well and continue to retard intellectual progress.

One of the worst of these is Fregeâ€™s distinction between â€œextensionalâ€ and â€œintensionalâ€ contexts. An extensional context is an expression that is â€œsubstitution tolerant.â€ An expression E is substitution-tolerant if replacing any one of the referring terms occurring in it with a co-referring term yields a true sentence iff the sentence that hosted E was true and a false sentence iff the sentence hosted E was false. So â€œSmith is tallâ€ is such a context, since replacing â€œSmithâ€ a co-referring term will result in a sentence that has the same truth-value as the first. An intensional context is one which is substitution-intolerant.

A story will help us move forward. The prettiest woman on the planet is also the most evil person on the planet. Smith wants to marry the prettiest woman on the planet, whoever that might be, but wants nothing to do with anyone who is evil. In that case:

(1) â€œSmith wants to marry the prettiest woman on the planetâ€

is true, but

(2) â€œSmith wants to marry the most evil person on the planetâ€

is false. And, of course,

(3) â€œit is necessarily the case that the prettiest woman on the planet is identical with the prettiest person on the planetâ€

is true, whereas

(4) â€œit is necessarily the case that the prettiest woman on the planet is identical with the most evil person on the planetâ€

is false.

According to Frege, 2 is what results when a referring term in 1 is replaced with a co-referring term, and 4 is what results when a referring term in 3 is replaced with a co-referring term.

But this isnâ€™t what is going on. What (1) really says is that:

(1*) Smith wants it to be the case that Smith is married to a woman who is prettier than any other.

And what (2) really says is that

(2*) Smith wants it to be the case that Smith is married to somebody who is more evil than anyone else.

(1*) and (2*) thus make it clear what (1) and (2), respectively, are actually saying. In other words, (1*) and (2*) expose the logical forms of (1) and (2). Notice that, in (1), the grammatical object is an expression referring to a person (â€œthe prettiest woman on Earthâ€), whereas in (1*) the grammatical object (the italicized part) is an expression referring to a proposition. And in (2), the grammatical object is an expression referring to a person (â€œthe most evil person on the planetâ€), whereas in (2*) the grammatical object (the italicized part) is an expression referring to a proposition.

Thus, (1*) makes it clear that, if (1) is true, the object of Smithâ€™s desire is not a person, but rather a proposition. In other words, Smith wants a certain proposition to hold, namely, that Smith is married to a woman who is prettier than anyone else. Similarly, (2*) makes it clear that, if (2) is true, the object of Smithâ€™s desire is not a person, but a proposition, namely, that Smith is married to somebody who is more evil than anyone else. Since those two propositions are different, the fact that one of them has the property of being desired to be true by Smith, whereas the other does not lack that property, does not constitute a violation of Leibnizâ€™s Law.

Similar points hold in connection with 3 and 4. The real meanings of those sentences are, respectively:

(3*) it is necessarily the case that any woman who is prettier than every other woman is prettier than every other woman.

and

(4*) it is necessarily the case that any woman who is prettier than every other woman is also more evil than every other person.

(3*) attributes the property of being necessarily true to one proposition (the one meant by the italicized part), and (4*) expresses that same property to some other proposition. Since those propositions are distinct, the fact that the one proposition is necessarily true doesnâ€™t entail that the same is true of the other; and there is thus violation of Leibnizâ€™s Law.

Thus, there are no intensional contexts. (In other words, all contexts are substitution-tolerant.) Whenever two expressions that appear to refer to the same individual cannot be inter-substituted, they actually refer to different propositions. Nonetheless, the term â€œintensionalâ€ is useful as a way of abbreviating otherwise hard-to- state truths. Thus used, an â€œintensional contextâ€ in which expressions that otherwise refer to individuals (e.g., â€œBenjamin Franklinâ€) refer to propositions. An expression occurring in an intensional context does so intensionally. A context that isnâ€™t intensional is extensional, and expressions occurring in it do so extensionally.

A brief review will help us identify one last problem with Fregeâ€™s system. Fregeâ€™s distinction between sense and reference embodies a failure to distinguish between reference and quantification.  What Frege believes to

be sense-bearing referring terms (e.g., â€œthe person who invented Velcroâ€) are quantifiers. (That is why â€œthe man who invented Velcro is wealthyâ€ is, by Fregeâ€™s own admission, equivalent with â€œsomebody or other uniquely invented Velcro, and any such person is wealthyâ€). Fregeâ€™s distinction between intensional and extensional contexts embodies a failure to see that expressions that, given their grammatical properties, appear to refer to some one individual in fact refer to distinct propositions. Even though the inventor of bifocals is identical with the first post-master general,

(A) â€œFred believes that the inventor of bifocals is smartâ€

may be true, even if

(B) â€œFred believes that the first post-master general is smart,â€

is false.

The italicized expression in A refers to one proposition; its counterpart in B refers to a different proposition. (Weâ€™ll refer to the italicized expressions in A and B, respectively, as A* and B*). But B* is what results when a referring term is replaced with a co-referring term. According to the principle of special compositionality (PSC), A* and B* should co-refer.

PSC says that what an expression refers to depends on what its parts refer to. â€œMaryâ€™s favorite personâ€ refers to Smith, whereas â€œBillyâ€™s favorite personâ€ refers to Jones. Why the difference in reference? Because â€œMaryâ€ and â€œBillyâ€ donâ€™t co-refer, and what a given expression refers to affects what expressions containing it refer to. For the same reason mutatis mutandis, if â€œCrusherâ€ is Maryâ€™s nickname, and thus co-refers with â€œMary,â€ â€œCrusherâ€™s favorite personâ€ co-refers with â€œMaryâ€™s favorite person.â€ PSC is the obviously correct semantic corollary of the obviously correct principle that replacing equals with equals results in equals.

But Fregeâ€™s semantics violates PSC. According to it, B* is what results when a referring term in A* is replaced with a co-referring term, and yet A* and B* donâ€™t co-refer. Russellâ€™s system doesnâ€™t have this problem. Russell said, correctly, that A* and B* are contractions of, respectively:

(A#) â€œsome smart person single-handedly invented bifocalsâ€

and

(B#) â€œsome smart person post-master general before anyone else.â€

It didnâ€™t even occur to Frege to take anything at all like Russellâ€™s position. To compatibilize his system with PSC, Frege said that, when expressions occur in intensional contexts, they undergo reference-shifts. According to Frege, â€œthe inventor of bifocalsâ€ ordinarily refers to Benjamin Franklin (BF); in other words, its so refers when it occurs in extensional contexts. But when it falls within the scope of one intensionality-inducing operator, it refers to the sense of â€œthe inventor of bifocals.â€ (An intensionality-inducing is what most other authos refer to as a â€œnon-extensional connective.â€ It is an operator having the property that any sentences or open-sentences falling within its scope are substitution-intolerant.) â€œFred believesâ€ is such an operator. Given that he insists on seeing definite descriptions as sense-bearing referring terms, Frege has no choice but to take this desperate measure: if he doesnâ€™t, his system violates PSC, in which case itâ€™s false, since PSC is true.

Thus, if Fregeâ€™s system is right, then the occurrence of â€œthe inventor of bifocalsâ€ in

(C) â€œFred believes that Larry believes that the inventor of bifocals is smartâ€

refers, not to BF, nor yet to the sense of â€œthe inventor of bifocals,â€ but to the sense of an expression that denotes the sense of that expression.

For the same reason mutatis mutandis, a consequence of Fregeâ€™s system is that no two of the occurrences of â€œsnowâ€ in

(D) â€œsnow is white, but Brad thinks that snow is green, even though Brad is convinced that Mary thinks that snow is purpleâ€

co-refer, and only one of those occurrences (the first one) refers to snow. In addition to being radically counterintuitive, Fregeâ€™s position is logically and methodologically indefensible (or so I argue in Kuczynski (2007) and other places).

4.0 The theory of descriptions revisited: the wide-scope/narrow-scope distinction10

Let us refer to sentences containing definite descriptions as â€œD-sentences.â€ So a D-sentence is any sentence of the form â€¹...the phi...â€º There is a certain sub-class of D-sentences that are systematically ambiguous. One of the virtues of the theory of descriptions is that it, unlike its Fregean competitor, accounts for the fact that these sentences are ambiguous and it also accounts for the exact way in which they are ambiguous.

In this context, it will be helpful to remember that an open sentence is an expression that contains a free variable, and is therefore neither true nor false, but is otherwise just like a sentence. So â€¹x is a human beingâ€º is an open-sentence; so is â€¹x is even. â€º These open sentences are â€œtrue forâ€ some values of their free variables. (The first is true for â€œSocrates,â€ â€œPlato,â€ etc. The second is true for â€œ2,â€ â€œ4,â€ etc.) But it must be emphasized that an open sentence is not itself true or false. (In this context, the word â€œsentenceâ€ will be short for â€œsentences or open sentences.â€)

An expression (or class of expressions11) is said to satisfy an open sentence if a true sentence results when that expression replaces the free variables in that sentence. Thus, â€œtwoâ€ satisfies the open sentence â€œx is an even number,â€ whereas â€œMr. Tâ€ does not satisfy it, and neither does â€œthree.â€

4.1 Scope, operators, and syntactic ambiguity

The semantics of these sentences is to be understood in terms of the concept of scope.

Scope is a property of operatorsâ€”that is, of expressions that, given sentences or open-sentences, form new sentences. So â€œJohn believes thatâ€ is an operator, since, when joined with â€œgrass is green,â€ it yields the sentence â€œJohn believes that grass is green.â€

All quantifiers are operators. Examples of quantifiers are â€œall humans,â€ â€œsome triangles,â€ â€œmost dolphins.â€ So are their counterparts in formalized extensions of English (e.g., â€œgiven any human being x,â€ â€œfor some triangle y,â€ etc.). Why is â€œall humansâ€ a quantifier? First of all, given a predicate (e.g., â€œare tallâ€), â€œall humansâ€ yields a sentence (â€œall humans are tallâ€). And predicates are all open sentences (e.g., â€œare tallâ€ can be thought of as synonymous with â€œx is tallâ€). Given that â€œall humansâ€ can be thought of as synonymous with â€œgiven any human x,â€ itâ€™s clear why â€œall humansâ€ is an operator. When coupled with the predicate (= open sentence) â€œare tallâ€ (= â€œx is tallâ€), â€œall humansâ€ (= â€œgiven any human xâ€), yields the sentence â€œall humans are tallâ€ (= â€œgiven any human x, x is tallâ€).

All conjunctions (e.g., â€œand,â€ â€œbecause,â€ â€œor,â€ â€œnotâ€) are operators. And, â€œbecause,â€ and â€œorâ€ are two-place operators, meaning that, given a pair of sentences as input, each yields a new sentence as output. Thus, given the pair of sentences (â€œgrass is green,â€ â€œsnow is whiteâ€), â€œandâ€ yields the sentence â€œgrass is green and snow is white.â€ Where â€œbecauseâ€ is concerned the pair must be ordered, since â€œgrass is green because snow is whiteâ€ doesnâ€™t have the same meaning as â€œsnow is white because grass is green.â€ Itâ€™s a matter of debate whether â€œareâ€ and â€œorâ€ operate on ordered, or unordered, sentence-pairs. â€œNotâ€ is a one-place operator. Given the sentence â€œsnow is white,â€ â€œnotâ€ yields a new sentence (â€œsnow is not whiteâ€).

In light of these points, consider the sentence:

(1) â€œIn New York, someone gets mugged every five minutes.â€

This is ambiguous.12 It could mean either:

(2) In New York, given any given five-minute interval x, there is some individual y, such that y gets mugged during x.

or

(3) In New York, there is some individual y such that, given any given five-minute interval x, y gets mugged during x.

(2) says that, in New York, no five-minute interval is free of muggings. It doesnâ€™t say that there is some one unfortunate individual who gets mugged every five minutes. But that is what (3) says.

The difference results from the fact that the relevant operatorsâ€”the boldfaced and underlined expressionsâ€”are ordered differently. In (2), the operator â€œgiven any five-minute interval xâ€ has wide-scope with respect to the operator â€œthere is some individual yâ€ (or, equivalently, the latter operator has narrow scope with respect to the former), whereas in (3) itâ€™s the other way around.

(1) isnâ€™t ambiguous for the same reason as â€œJim is dumbâ€ or â€œSally is going to bank.â€ Those sentences are ambiguous because the words â€œdumbâ€ and â€œbankâ€ are ambiguous. By contrast, none of the expressions occurring in (1) is ambiguous. (1) is syntactically ambiguous. It has multiple meanings because it stands for two distinct syntactic arrangements of expressions that are themselves unambiguous.

The stock example of syntactic ambiguity is:

(4) â€œeveryone loves someone,â€

which could mean either

(5) given any person x, there is some person y, such that x loves y,

or

(6) there is some person y, such that given any person x, x loves y.

(5) says that no person is without love for some person or other. It doesnâ€™t say that some one person is the object of every personâ€™s love. But that is what (6) says.

Grammatical surface structure makes it unclear how much scope operators actually have. For example, the scope of â€œbecauseâ€ in â€œsnow is white because grass is greenâ€ includes both â€œsnow is whiteâ€ and â€œgrass is green,â€ even though grammatical surface structure would suggest otherwise. And the scope of â€œnotâ€ in â€œsnow is not whiteâ€ includes â€œsnow is white.â€ (â€œNotâ€ = â€œit is not the case that.â€ â€œSnow is not whiteâ€ = â€œit is not the case that snow is white.â€) There would be no syntactically ambiguous sentences if grammatical surface-structure didnâ€™t fall short in this respect.

The fact that D-sentences are syntactically ambiguous can be understood in terms of these facts. The sentence:

(i) â€œSmith believes that the guy who is trying to kill him, after torturing him for several days, is well-disposed towards him.â€

This sentence is ambiguous. It could mean either:

(ii) Somebody x wants to kill Smith, after torturing him for several hours, and Smith believes that x is well disposed towards him

or

(iii) Smith believes that somebody x wants to kill him, after torturing him for several hours, and also that x is well disposed towards him.

(iii) has little chance of being true. People donâ€™t believe that people who are trying to torture and kill them are well disposed towards them. But itâ€™s easy to think of a situation where (ii) is true. Jerry is Smithâ€™s best friend. Jerry is actually very evil. But, like many evil people, he has mastered the art of appearing well-intentioned; and unbeknownst to Smith, Jerry wants to torture and kill him.

Whenever a definite description falls within the scope of a modal or epistemic operator, the result is a syntactically ambiguous sentence. Before Russell came along, such syntactic ambiguities, not being seen for what they were, led people to accept the most rank absurdities. Consider the sentence:

(iv) Jerry is looking for the fountain of youth.

Obviously there doesnâ€™t have to exist a fountain of youth for (iv) to be true. People look for things that donâ€™t exist. Russell saw this, and saw that, for this reason, (iv)â€™s meaning is:

(v) Jerry wants it to be the case that there exist a (unique) fountain of youth x, and, moreover, that he (uniquely) discover any such fountain.13

Pre-Russellian philosophers and contemporary non-Russellianism philosophers take (iv) to say that there exists a fountain of youth that Jerry is looking for. This is Nathan Salmonâ€™s (2005) position. Salmon qualifies his position by saying that the fountain of youth, though existent, is a â€œmythicalâ€ object. But, since mythical objects donâ€™t gush water, let alone immortality-giving water, Jerry wonâ€™t consider his search to have to an end when he discoveries the non-entity that Salmon describes. Given Russellâ€™s insight, thereâ€™s no need to accept Salmonâ€™s rather doubtful position.

Because of his failure to grasp the implications of the wide-scope/narrow-scope distinction, another well known 20th century philosopher, W.V.O Quine (1908â€“2000), advocated the highly implausible view that â€œnecessary,â€ â€œpossible,â€ and modal terms in general, have no coherent meanings and that statements such as â€œitâ€™s possible that there will be rainâ€ and â€œitâ€™s a necessary truth that triangles have three sidesâ€ are either false or meaningless.14

Here is his argument.15 For argumentâ€™s sake, suppose that the concepts expressed by â€œnecessaryâ€ and â€œpossibleâ€ are meaningful. In that case:

(FB) â€œitâ€™s a necessary truth that the inventor of bifocals was the inventor of bifocalsâ€

expresses a truth, even though

(BF) â€œitâ€™s a necessary truth that the inventor of bifocals was the first postmaster generalâ€

expresses a falsehood. Given the truth of FB, says Quine, it follows that the inventor of bifocals necessarily has the property of being identical with the inventor of bifocals. It follows by Leibnizâ€™s Law16 that the first postmaster general also has the property. But if he did, then BF would be true, which it is not.

With one exception, all of our assumptions were clearly correct. Leibnizâ€™s Law holds, and FB is a necessary truth if ever there was one. Since the only remaining assumption is that â€œnecessaryâ€ and â€œpossibleâ€ express coherent concepts, that assumption is wrong. It follows that all statements to the effect that something is possible or necessary or impossible (etc.) are either meaningless or false.

Arthur Smullyan (1948) saw that, given Russellâ€™s points about definite descriptions, there is no problem. BF is ambiguous between wide-scope and narrow-scope readings, these being:

(BFWS) itâ€™s a necessary truth that some one individual uniquely invented bifocals and, in addition, was the first postmaster general

and

(BFNW) some one individual x uniquely invented bifocals; and some individual y was uniquely a first postmaster general

and itâ€™s a necessary truth that x = y.

BFWS is straightforwardly false. BFNW is true. As a whole, it is not necessarily true. (It didnâ€™t have to be the case that some one person was a bifocal inventor and postmaster general.) But the underlined part is necessarily true: given any individual x, and given any individual y such that x is identical with y, it is a fact that x must be identical with y.17
